chunks.title: 4-HO-DiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-DiPT was first described in the scientific literature in 1977, with its synthesis published by chemist David B. Repke. Two decades later, Alexander Shulgin investigated the substance's effects in humans and characterized it in his 1997 book TiHKAL ("Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved"). Shulgin noted that 4-HO-DiPT possessed an unusual combination of properties among psychedelics, including rapid onset (becoming apparent approximately 15 minutes after ingestion), considerable intensity at relatively low doses (with 20 milligrams capable of producing a transcendent peak experience), brief overall duration (typically 2-3 hours), and pronounced dose sensitivity.

chunks.title: 4-HO-DiPT
chunks.text: The compound was subsequently encountered as a novel designer drug by 2005 and has since circulated on the online research chemical market, though it remains relatively uncommon. Today, 4-HO-DiPT is used for both recreational and entheogenic purposes, though it has a limited history of human use. In the 2020s, pharmaceutical interest emerged with the development of luvesilocin (also known as RE-104, FT-104, or 4-GO-DiPT), a prodrug of 4-HO-DiPT that has entered phase 2 clinical trials for the treatment of psychiatric conditions including postpartum depression and treatment-resistant depression.

chunks.title: 4-HO-DPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-DPT is a psychedelic substance of the tryptamine class and the 4-hydroxyl analog of DPT. It was first described in the scientific literature by David Repke and colleagues in 1977 and later documented by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. Due to its difficult synthesis, the compound remains relatively uncommon and has very little history of human use. Its toxicity and long-term health effects have not been scientifically studied.

chunks.text: 4-HO-EPT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, structurally related to psilocin. It first emerged as a research chemical sold online around 2016 and was not included in Shulgin's TiHKAL. Compared to other 4-substituted tryptamines, it is noted for relatively subdued visual effects alongside a pronounced euphoric body high. Very little data exists regarding its toxicity, metabolism, or long-term health effects in humans.

As a research chemical with very limited documented human use, there is scarce information available regarding its effects, safety profile, and pharmacological properties. Extreme caution is advised due to the lack of established data on its toxicity and appropriate dosing parameters.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: 4-HO-MET is a synthetic psychedelic tryptamine first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin and documented in his 1997 book TiHKAL. Structurally related to psilocin, it produces effects through serotonin receptor agonism. Users typically describe it as more recreational than psilocybin mushrooms, characterized by vivid colorful visuals with a less mentally intense headspace. Reports of human use emerged in the late 2000s following its appearance on the research chemical market. Very little data exists regarding its toxicity profile.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Physical dependence is extremely unlikely.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: 4-HO-MET is not habit-forming and the desire to use it can actually decrease with use. It is most often self-regulating and is not known to be associated with compulsive use.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: There are reports of very high doses leading to drug-induced psychosis. A formal case report described a teenager who used approximately 100 mg, resulting in severe psychotic symptoms including visual hallucinations, paranoid delusions, sensation of insects under the skin, and dangerous behavior requiring week-long hospitalization. Psychotic symptoms typically resolve with supportive care, though paranoid ideation may persist for several days. At common doses, psychotic reactions are uncommon.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Like other psychedelics, 4-HO-MET is believed to lower the seizure threshold and may increase the likelihood of seizures in those with personal susceptibility or family history of epilepsy. This is not considered a risk in healthy people at typical doses. Seizures at overdose levels are conceivable but remain hypothetical.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Tachycardia and elevated blood pressure may occur during acute intoxication; serious cardiovascular complications are hypothetical and would be expected primarily at overdose levels.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Tachycardia was among the main symptoms observed in clinical cases. Hypertension is considered a potential risk based on pharmacological profile.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Kidney damage is a hypothetical risk at overdose levels based on pharmacological considerations; no documented cases of renal toxicity from typical use.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk is considered only hypothetical based on pharmacology, not established through case reports.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: 4-HO-MET is a serotonergic psychedelic that produces its effects primarily through partial agonism of the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor. It also binds to other serotonin receptors including 5-HT1A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C, functioning as an agonist at these sites. Beyond the serotonin system, 4-HO-MET shows affinity for histamine H1 receptors, trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), dopamine D2 and D3 receptors, and α1A and α2A adrenergic receptors. The compound also demonstrates high affinity for the serotonin transporter with modest reuptake inhibition effects, though direct receptor agonism is considered the primary contributor to its psychedelic activity. Notably, 4-HO-MET does not possess monoamine releasing properties.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: 4-HO-MET undergoes hepatic metabolism. In vivo studies using human forensic cases identified four metabolites, with metabolic transformations including hydroxylation, glucuronidation of the parent compound, and glucuronidation of an N-oxide metabolite. In vitro studies using pooled human liver microsomes identified twelve metabolites through pathways including monohydroxylation, dihydroxylation, N-oxide formation, demethylation, carboxylic acid formation, and desethylation. Three of the monohydroxylated metabolites were modified at the benzene ring of the indole structure.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of 4-HO-MET develops almost immediately after ingestion. Notably, 4-HO-MET appears to be more amenable to redosing than many other psychedelics, with reports suggesting that taking an additional dose 1.5-2.5 hours after initial administration can restore or intensify effects without showing strong evidence of acute tolerance buildup.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: 4-HO-MET was first synthesized by American chemist Alexander Shulgin during the 1970s. The compound was subsequently described in the scientific literature by David Repke and colleagues in 1981. Shulgin later documented 4-HO-MET in his 1997 book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved), where he characterized its qualitative effects as "very much like psilocin" to the extent that it would likely be indistinguishable from psilocin in a blinded study. The substance has been characterized as wave-like, with an oral dose of 10-20 mg and a duration of 4 to 6 hours.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text:
Internet-based vendors began selling 4-HO-MET around the 2000s, generating a substantial number of online reports describing the drug's effects. The substance was first encountered as a novel recreational and designer drug in Europe by 2008. It has been sold alongside other psilocybin analogues such as 4-AcO-DMT and 4-HO-MiPT.

Analysis of 436 tryptamine drug samples sent to the Spanish drug checking service Energy Control between 2006 and 2015 revealed that 19 samples were believed by users to be 4-HO-MET, with 17 confirmed as such upon testing. Surveys of Spanish research chemical users conducted between August 2010 and June 2011 indicated that 4-HO-MET remained relatively uncommon compared to other substances, with only 3% of 230 respondents reporting use.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Emergence on the Research Chemical Market

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Sweden's STRIDA project, which analyzes biological samples from hospital cases suspected to involve novel psychoactive substance use, provided clinical data on 4-HO-MET. During its first year of operation beginning in 2010, 4-HO-MET was the only tryptamine detected among 103 emergency department cases, appearing in eight instances. The median age of users was 22, with most administering the drug orally or intranasally. Primary symptoms associated with use included mydriasis, agitation, tachycardia, nausea, and hallucinations. Notably, half of these cases originated from a single small town in southeastern Sweden. After eighteen months of operation, STRIDA had analyzed samples from 189 patients, 14 of which involved 4-HO-MET. In 11 cases where the drug was used alone, symptoms were classified as minor or moderate and typically resolved with supportive care, though sedatives were occasionally administered. Analysis of body fluids and drug products from 173 cases between 2010 and 2015 found 4-HO-MET in powder form on four occasions.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MET
chunks.text: Sweden historically represented a major market for 4-HO-MET, though interest declined significantly after the substance became controlled in May 2012. The drug has continued to be sold through research chemical markets and remains one of the more popular novel psychedelics globally.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MiPT is a synthetic psychedelic tryptamine structurally related to psilocin, the primary active compound in psilocybin mushrooms. First described in scientific literature in 1981 and later evaluated by Alexander Shulgin, it produces psilocin-like effects with a somewhat shorter duration. The substance remains relatively uncommon with limited human use history. No fatalities have been reported despite documented high-dose experiences, suggesting reasonable physiological tolerability, though formal toxicity data remains scarce.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MiPT is not known to produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: As a classical psychedelic, 4-HO-MiPT is not considered to have significant abuse potential or habit-forming properties. There are no reports suggesting psychological dependence develops with use.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: As with other psychedelics, 4-HO-MiPT may produce confusion, delusions, paranoia, and feelings of impending doom, particularly at higher doses. The risk of psychotic reactions increases when combined with cannabis or stimulants, and in those predisposed to such conditions.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: Seizures are considered a rare potential effect that may occur in those predisposed to them, particularly under physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, fatigue, or overheating. No documented cases of seizures have been reported with this compound alone.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MiPT acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist with its psychedelic effects primarily attributed to activity at the 5-HT2A receptor. It shows the highest potency and efficacy as an agonist of the 5-HT2A receptor, moderate potency as a partial agonist of the 5-HT2B receptor, and low potency with high efficacy as a partial agonist of the 5-HT2C receptor. The compound exhibits approximately 7-fold selectivity for activation of the 5-HT2A receptor over the 5-HT2C receptor. Additionally, 4-HO-MiPT acts as a moderate-potency serotonin reuptake inhibitor, with approximately 4-fold preference for 5-HT2A activation relative to serotonin transporter inhibition. Its low affinity at the 5-HT1A receptor suggests minimal contribution from this target to the drug's overall effects.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MiPT is taken orally and is structurally analogous to psilocin. The acetate ester prodrug 4-AcO-MiPT may be metabolized to 4-HO-MiPT in the body, similar to how psilocybin is converted to psilocin. The 4-hydroxyl group on the indole ring is believed to contribute to oral activity. Detailed pharmacokinetic parameters in humans have not been established.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of 4-HO-MiPT develops almost immediately after ingestion. When used on consecutive days, users typically need to double their dosage each time to achieve comparable effects.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text:
4-HO-MiPT was first synthesized and described in the scientific literature by David Repke and colleagues in 1981. The compound's effects in humans were subsequently evaluated and documented by Repke in collaboration with Alexander Shulgin in 1985. During this period, the pharmacology of 4-HO-MiPT at serotonin receptors was characterized by Dennis McKenna, Repke, and colleagues in 1990.

Repke and Shulgin later collaborated on research evaluating the effects of different oxygen substituents on the MiPT structure, with 4-HO-MiPT being described as the most interesting compound in the series and the only one to possess classical hallucinogen effects.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text:
A comprehensive description of 4-HO-MiPT appeared in Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved), where it is listed as entry #22. The book includes detailed qualitative comments from multiple trials at various dosages, documenting experiences ranging from 12 to 30 milligrams. Shulgin's personal trial at 12 milligrams, conducted in 1979, was described as a richly insightful and highly erotic experience with vivid closed-eye imagery and exceptional musical appreciation.

The trials documented in TiHKAL and other anecdotal reports suggest that 4-HO-MiPT is similar in activity to psilocin, the active component in psilocybin mushrooms, though some reports indicate it may be considerably more potent at comparable doses.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MiPT remains a relatively uncommon substance with only a short history of human use. Today, it is used either recreationally or as an entheogenic substance and is typically distributed as a grey-area research chemical through online vendors.

chunks.text: 4-HO-MPMI is a psychedelic substance belonging to the pyrrolidinylmethylindole and cyclized tryptamine chemical families. Developed by the team of David E. Nichols at Purdue University in the late 1990s, it is notable for its high potency, comparable to that of DOI and active in the microgram range. The compound has rarely been documented outside of laboratory settings, and very little is known about its effects or safety profile in humans.

chunks.title: 4-HO-MPT
chunks.text: 4-HO-MPT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class and a higher homologue of psilocin. First described in the scientific literature by David Repke and colleagues in 1981, it was later included in Alexander Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL, where its dosage and duration were listed as unknown. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, or toxicity, and it has primarily circulated as a research chemical since emerging on the designer drug market around 2021.

chunks.title: 4-MEC
chunks.text: 4-MEC is a substituted cathinone with stimulant and entactogen properties, structurally related to mephedrone. It has been marketed alone or blended with other cathinones under names such as "NRG-2" and has been identified as an active ingredient in counterfeit ecstasy tablets in some countries. Compared to mephedrone, it is considered less potent with a more pronounced stimulant character. Little is known about its safety profile.

chunks.title: 4-MEC
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a substituted cathinone stimulant believed to have similar effects to mephedrone, it likely carries comparable psychological addiction potential, though little is known about its safety profile.

chunks.title: 4-MEC

chunks.title: 4-MeO-Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: 4-MeO-Butyrfentanyl is a rare synthetic opioid and analogue of fentanyl, distinct from the related compound butyrfentanyl. It is classified as a research chemical with habit-forming properties. Extremely limited information exists regarding its pharmacology, safety profile, and appropriate dosing parameters. As with other fentanyl analogues, overdose carries a significant risk of respiratory depression. Extreme caution is strongly advised, and it should not be combined with other stimulants or depressants.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. Very limited information is available due to the rarity of this substance.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: 4-MeO-Butyrfentanyl is a rare synthetic opioid belonging to the fentanyl analogue class of compounds. The substance has received minimal documentation in both scientific literature and online harm reduction communities, and its precise history of synthesis and development remains poorly documented. It should be distinguished from the related compound butyrfentanyl, which has been more extensively characterized.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 4-MeO-MiPT is a lesser-known synthetic psychedelic of the substituted tryptamine class, first described by David Repke and Alexander Shulgin in 1985 and later detailed in Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL. Sometimes referred to as the "little brother" of 5-MeO-MiPT, it is distinguished by notably mild visual effects compared to most tryptamines, alongside pronounced erotic-enhancing properties. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, and toxicity.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: 4-MeO-PCP is an arylcyclohexylamine synthetic dissociative that can produce hallucinogenic and anesthetic effects. First synthesized in 1965 by Parke-Davis chemist Victor Maddox, it became the first arylcyclohexylamine research chemical sold online when it appeared in late 2008. It is reported to have reduced potency relative to PCP. Dosage information remains tentative, potentially due to variations in the potency of available supplies.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: Withdrawal effects have been reported upon cessation of chronic use, though specific physical withdrawal symptoms are not well characterized due to limited research history.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: Chronic use can be moderately addictive with high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence among certain users. Cravings may occur if usage is suddenly stopped.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: Psychotic episodes, disturbing hallucinations, delusions, anxiety, and paranoia are reported as potential negative effects. Risk of adverse psychological reactions increases with higher doses and redosing.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: No antimicrobial properties have been studied.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated excessive use over extended periods may cause bladder and urinary tract problems similar to those seen with ketamine, including urinary frequency and urgency, pelvic and bladder pain, hematuria, and incontinence; these effects can be avoided by limiting use to less than weekly.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Effects appear to be less severe than ketamine due to higher potency requiring smaller doses. Symptoms can become extremely serious with chronic heavy use but are easily avoidable with moderate use patterns.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: 4-MeO-PCP acts primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist. Its NMDA affinity is lower than that of PCP but higher than that of ketamine. The compound also binds with notable affinity to σ1 and σ2 receptors, and shows moderate affinity for the norepinephrine and serotonin transporters. It is considered a relatively selective NMDA receptor ligand, lacking appreciable affinity for the dopamine transporter.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: 4-MeO-PCP is orally active, indicating sufficient oral bioavailability for pharmacological effects. No detailed data on its metabolic pathways, metabolizing enzymes, or elimination half-life have been reported.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text: With sustained repeated use, many effects may weaken, requiring higher doses for comparable results.

chunks.title: 4-MeO-PCP
chunks.text:
4-MeO-PCP was originally synthesized in 1965 by Victor Maddox, a medicinal chemist working at the pharmaceutical company Parke-Davis. The compound remained largely obscure for decades following its initial creation.

Interest in 4-MeO-PCP resurfaced in the late 1990s when a chemist writing under the pseudonym John Q. Beagle published a 1999 review suggesting that the substance possessed reduced potency compared to its parent compound PCP. In 2001, Beagle followed this with a more comprehensive publication detailing the synthesis procedure and describing the qualitative effects, estimating its potency at approximately 70% that of PCP.

The compound holds a notable place in the history of online research chemical markets as the first arylcyclohexylamine to be sold through internet vendors. It was introduced to the market in late 2008 by a supplier operating under the name CBAY. This marked the beginning of a wave of related dissociative compounds entering the research chemical scene, with 3-MeO-PCP and methoxetamine (MXE) following shortly thereafter.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.text: 4-Methylaminorex is a potent stimulant of the 2-amino-5-aryloxazoline class, first synthesized in 1960 by McNeil Laboratories. It produces effects comparable to methamphetamine but with a notably longer duration, often lasting up to 16 hours when taken orally. As one of the most potent dopamine releasing agents known, it carries significant abuse potential. Pulmonary hypertension has been associated with its use, and at least one fatality has been reported.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.text: Animal studies indicate abuse potential comparable to cocaine and amphetamine, suggesting a significant risk of psychological dependence and compulsive patterns of use.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.text: High doses have caused clonic seizures in rat studies, with some fatalities occurring at the highest doses tested (20 mg/kg).

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: One reported fatality involved blood concentrations of 21.3 mg/L with concurrent diazepam use. Doses above 15-20mg are considered dangerous.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Pulmonary hypertension has been associated with 4-methylaminorex use, similar to the related appetite suppressant aminorex which caused an epidemic of pulmonary hypertension.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Three individuals with pulmonary hypertension diagnoses were found to have 4-methylaminorex on their property.

chunks.title: 4-Methylaminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High doses in animal studies caused reduction in tryptophan hydroxylase activity, a possible marker for serotonin neurotoxicity; the highest doses tested caused clonic seizures and some deaths in rats.

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text: 4-Methylmethylphenidate is a stimulant research chemical structurally related to methylphenidate. It appeared briefly on the market in mid-2015 following bans on ethylphenidate and other phenidates. The substance is reported to be slightly less potent than methylphenidate, with relatively low efficacy at blocking dopamine reuptake despite high binding affinity. It has been described as producing functional stimulation with limited recreational effects and was investigated as a potential substitute treatment for stimulant abuse.

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. Its relatively low efficacy at blocking dopamine reuptake despite high binding affinity led to its investigation as a possible substitute drug for treatment of stimulant abuse, suggesting potentially lower reinforcing effects compared to other stimulants.

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text: 4-Methylmethylphenidate (4-MeTMP) is a stimulant structurally related to methylphenidate that acts on the dopamine transporter. It exhibits high binding affinity at the dopamine transporter but relatively low efficacy at blocking dopamine reuptake, making it slightly less potent than methylphenidate as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor.

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text:
4-Methylmethylphenidate emerged on the designer stimulant market in mid-2015, appearing shortly after regulatory actions in the United Kingdom restricted ethylphenidate and other phenidate compounds. Its commercial availability as an unscheduled research chemical proved exceptionally brief, lasting only several months before facing its own regulatory restrictions.

Beyond its brief presence on the grey market, the compound has attracted interest in formal research settings. Its distinctive pharmacological profile prompted investigation as a potential substitute medication for the treatment of stimulant use disorders.

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine reuptake inhibitor

chunks.title: 4-Methylmethylphenidate
chunks.text:

chunks.title: 4-MPD
chunks.text: 4-MPD is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone class, first developed in 1960. Structurally, it is a higher homologue of mephedrone and the para-methyl derivative of pentedrone. Like other cathinones, it is considered habit-forming. Notably, a related compound known as 4-MEAP has been found incorrectly sold as 4-MPD, raising concerns about mislabeled products in unregulated markets.

chunks.title: 4-MPD
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, consistent with the general profile of cathinone stimulants.

chunks.title: 4-MPD
chunks.text: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI)

chunks.title: 4-MPD
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI); SERT substrate (partial releaser)

chunks.title: 4-MPM
chunks.text: 4-MPM is a substituted phenylmorpholine with stimulant and entactogenic properties, closely related to phenmetrazine and 3-fluorophenmetrazine. First identified in Slovenia in 2015 as a designer drug, it functions as a monoamine releaser with a notable preference for serotonin. It is considered habit-forming, with reports indicating that tolerance develops rapidly. As a research chemical, it has limited documented history of human use.

chunks.title: 4-MPM
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming with reports indicating tolerance builds quickly, suggesting potential for compulsive use patterns typical of stimulant-entactogen compounds.

chunks.title: 4-MPM
chunks.text: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA)

chunks.title: 4-MPM
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA)

chunks.title: 4-PrO-DMT
chunks.text: 4-PrO-DMT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class believed to act as a prodrug of psilocin, analogous to the relationship between 4-AcO-DMT and psilocin. It first appeared as a designer drug in 2019 and was initially identified as a new psychoactive substance in Sweden. Very little formal research exists regarding its pharmacology or toxicity in humans, and its effects have not been studied in controlled human trials.

chunks.title: 4-PrO-DMT
chunks.text: 4-PrO-DMT resembles psilacetin in both structure and pharmacological profile, and psilacetin is not linked with physical dependence.

chunks.title: 4-PrO-DMT
chunks.text: 4-PrO-DMT has structural and pharmacological similarities to psilacetin, a compound not associated with compulsive patterns of use.

chunks.title: 4-PrO-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Toxicity data for 4-PrO-DMT remain very limited. No deaths involving 4-PrO-DMT have been reported to date.

chunks.title: 4-PrO-DMT
chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (full); 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT1B receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT1D receptor agonist (partial)

chunks.title: 4,4'-DMAR
chunks.text: 4,4'-DMAR is a synthetic stimulant and entactogen of the aminorex class, closely related to aminorex, 4-methylaminorex, and pemoline. First detected in the Netherlands in December 2012, it emerged as a designer drug across Europe by mid-2013. It functions as a potent and balanced serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent. Notably, 4,4'-DMAR has been linked to at least 31 deaths across multiple European countries, predominantly when consumed alongside other substances.

chunks.title: 4,4'-DMAR
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: At least 31 deaths have been linked to 4,4'-DMAR in Hungary, Poland, and the UK by February 2014, with an additional 19 deaths reported in Northern Ireland during the same period. Most fatalities occurred when the substance was consumed in combination with other drugs.

chunks.title: 4,4'-DMAR
chunks.text: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent

chunks.title: 4,4'-DMAR
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent

chunks.title: 4,4'-DMAR
chunks.text:
Legal status of 4,4'-DMAR by country:
- Germany: 4'-DMAR is an Anlage II controlled substance
- United States: 4'-DMAR is a Schedule I controlled substance

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.text: 4F-EPH is a synthetic stimulant of the phenidate class that emerged as a research chemical in 2015–2016. It was developed as a successor to ethylphenidate following its prohibition in the United Kingdom. Structurally related to both ethylphenidate and the commonly prescribed ADHD medication methylphenidate, it is believed to act primarily as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Like other phenidates, it is notably caustic to the nasal cavities when insufflated, and its long-term toxicity profile remains unstudied.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.text: Chronic 4F-EPH use is viewed as moderately addictive, with substantial abuse potential and a risk of psychological dependence for some users. Once addiction develops, stopping abruptly may bring on cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Insufflation can cause mild to moderate damage to the nasal mucous membranes; while less caustic than ethylphenidate, repeated intranasal use without adequate recovery time will likely result in nasal cavity damage.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Direct caustic irritation of nasal epithelium

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Sterile saline rinse recommended 15 minutes after insufflation. Unknown whether damage is permanent or acute. Insufflation is probably best avoided.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Vasoconstriction occurs and can become uncomfortable or hazardous as very high doses wear off, or for people who already have circulatory problems; blue or purple discoloration of extremities indicates a medical emergency.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Effect is milder than most dopaminergic stimulants at peak but can intensify during offset at high doses.

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine reuptake inhibitor; Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.text:

chunks.title: 4F-EPH
chunks.text:
Legal status of 4F-EPH by country:
- Germany: 4-Fluoroethylphenidate is controlled under the NpSG ( New Psychoactive Substances Act ) as of November 26, 2016. — Under German law, production or importation intended to put 4F-EPH into commerce, administering it to another person, and trading are punishable. Possession is unlawful, but is not penalized.
- Switzerland: 4F-EPH is a controlled substance specifically named under Verzeichnis E.
- United Kingdom: 4-Fluoroethylphenidate is a class B drug in the UK as of May 31st 2017, making it illegal to possess, produce or supply.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.text: 4-Fluoromethylphenidate is a synthetic stimulant of the phenidate class and a fluorinated analog of the widely prescribed ADHD medication methylphenidate. It emerged on the research chemical market around 2015 as a replacement for ethylphenidate following its ban in the United Kingdom. 4F-MPH is reported to be considerably more potent than its parent compound. Its toxicity profile remains unstudied, and its potency at low doses warrants particular caution with dosing.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.text: 4F-MPH has abuse potential on par with amphetamine or MDMA due to its euphoric effects and action upon dopamine transporters. Some users have become addicted to this substance, and compulsive redosing is reported, particularly at high doses or with non-oral routes of administration.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.text: Risk of delusions, mania, and psychosis has been noted, particularly when combined with dissociatives. The substance may carry inherent psychosis risk at higher doses.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.text: Seizures have been mentioned as a potential risk in extreme cases, particularly in combination with certain other substances.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including abnormal heartbeat and vasoconstriction occur during use; excessive stimulation may result in dangerous increases in blood pressure and heart strain, particularly at higher doses or in combination with other stimulants.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Heart failure has been mentioned as a risk in extreme cases when combined with certain other substances.

chunks.title: 4f-MPH
chunks.text:
Legal status of 4f-MPH by country:
- Germany: Legal — 4F-MPH had been controlled under the NpSG from November 26, 2016, but a September 2022 change left it described as legal.
- Italy: Schedule I — 4F-MPH is Schedule I and is unlawful to possess, produce, sell, or buy.
- Switzerland: Controlled — 4F-MPH is specifically named under Verzeichnis E.
- Turkey: Illegal — 4F-MPH is unlawful to possess, produce, supply, or import.
- United Kingdom: Class B — 4-fluoromethylphenidate became a Class B drug on May 31, 2017, making possession, production, and supply unlawful.
- United States: Schedule I in Alabama — 4F-MPH is Schedule I in Alabama, with no nationwide U.S. schedule specified.

chunks.title: 4f-NEB
chunks.text: 4F-NEB is a synthetic substance of the cathinone class, specifically the 4-fluorinated analogue of N-ethylbuphedrone (NEB). As a substituted cathinone, it is structurally related to other compounds in this widely varied family. Very little is known about its pharmacology, toxicity, or subjective effect profile, and it has minimal documented history of human use. Due to this significant lack of research, users should exercise extreme caution regarding dosing and frequency of administration.

chunks.title: 4F-PHP
chunks.text: 4F-PHP is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone and pyrrolidine classes, representing the 4-fluoro analogue of α-PHP. It first emerged on the designer drug market around 2017 and is sought for its energizing and euphoric properties. Anecdotal reports suggest it may produce somewhat less manic effects compared to its parent compound α-PHP, though dosage ranges appear similar. Like other substituted cathinones, it is considered habit-forming.

chunks.title: 4F-PHP
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting potential for psychological dependence consistent with other pyrrolidine stimulants.

chunks.title: 4F-PHP
chunks.text: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI)

chunks.title: 4F-PHP
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (DNRI)

chunks.title: 4f-PVP
chunks.text: 4F-PVP is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone class, specifically a fluorinated analogue of α-pyrrolidinopentiophenone (α-PVP). It has emerged as a novel designer drug and is reported to be slightly more potent than its parent compound. As a relatively obscure research chemical, there is very limited data available regarding its pharmacology, toxicity, and long-term health effects, making it a particularly risky substance to use.

chunks.title: 4f-PVP
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting potential for psychological dependence consistent with other pyrovalerone-class stimulants.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: 5-APB is a synthetic entactogen of the benzofuran and substituted amphetamine classes that produces MDA-like empathogenic and stimulating effects. First synthesized by David Nichols in 1993 as a potential non-neurotoxic alternative to MDMA, it emerged as a designer drug around 2010, marketed alongside related benzofurans under the name "Benzofury." Compared to relatives like 6-APB and 5-MAPB, 5-APB is noted for being particularly stimulating and euphoric. It is commonly found as succinate or hydrochloride salts, which differ in potency by mass.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Moderate abuse potential with high potential for compulsive use and capacity for psychological dependence. When addiction develops, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur upon cessation. Compulsive redosing has been reported as a notable effect.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Abuse of amphetamine-class compounds at high doses for prolonged periods can result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Approximately 5-15% of users who develop stimulant psychosis may fail to recover completely. Acute symptoms typically respond to antipsychotic treatment.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use may carry risk of cardiotoxicity based on the substance's potent 5-HT2B receptor agonism; this risk is inferred from similar compounds like fenfluramine and MDMA rather than direct studies on 5-APB itself.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: 5-HT2B receptor agonism, which in related compounds causes fibroblast proliferation in cardiac valve tissue leading to valvular heart disease

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: No direct human studies on 5-APB cardiotoxicity exist. Risk extrapolated from pharmacological profile similarity to established serotonergic cardiotoxins.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: 5-APB acts primarily as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor with roughly balanced potency across all three monoamine transporters. It is also a potent agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor and a partial agonist at the 5-HT2A receptor, with additional agonist activity at 5-HT2C receptors and affinity for 5-HT1A receptors. 5-APB also shows high affinity for the trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) in rodent models.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Very little data exists regarding the metabolism and pharmacokinetics of 5-APB in humans.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: EC50 19 nM (release)

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: EC50 21 nM (release)

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: EC50 31 nM (release)

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: High affinity (mouse and rat)

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Many 5-APB effects become less responsive with prolonged, repeated use, often requiring larger doses to obtain similar effects.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text:
The development of 5-APB emerged from research into benzofuran-based entactogens during the 1990s. Medicinal chemist David E. Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University conducted foundational work on benzofuran analogues, examining the role of the MDA dioxole ring structure in interacting with serotonergic neurons. This research was motivated in part by efforts to identify a potentially non-neurotoxic alternative to MDMA, which was being investigated as a possible adjunct to psychotherapy but was also raising concerns about neurotoxic effects.

5-APB and its positional isomer 6-APB were formally described in a patent by Karin Briner and colleagues at Eli Lilly and Company in 2000. These compounds were studied as serotonin 5-HT2C receptor agonists for potential therapeutic applications, though they were not developed further for medical use.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text:
Recreational use of 5-APB was not documented until 2010, when it emerged for sale on the global research chemical market. The compound became particularly prominent in the United Kingdom's "legal highs" market, where 5-APB and related benzofuran entactogens were sold under the brand name "Benzofury" and gained a following in the rave scene.

This period of legal availability was relatively short-lived. Following recommendations from the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, 5-APB and related analogues were classified as controlled substances in the UK in 2014, effectively ending the legal sale of benzofuran entactogens in that country. Similar regulatory actions followed in other jurisdictions.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Emergence on the Research Chemical Market

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dopaminergic stimulants

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin releasing agent; Norepinephrine releasing agent; Dopamine releasing agent; 5-HT2B receptor agonist; 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2C receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT1A; TAAR1

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text:

- DXM

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text:
Legal status of 5-APB by country:
- Brazil: Illegal — Listed on Portaria SVS/MS nº 344. Possession, production, and sale are prohibited under Brazilian drug control legislation.
- France: Narcotic — Classified as a narcotic substance since May 9, 2018, alongside other benzofuran-derived compounds.
- Germany: Anlage II BtMG — Controlled under Anlage II of the Betäubungsmittelgesetz (Narcotics Act, Schedule II) since July 17, 2013. Manufacturing, possession, import, export, purchase, sale, procurement, or dispensing…
- Japan: Controlled substance — Designated as a controlled substance effective September 16, 2015.
- Netherlands: Legal (under review) — Currently unscheduled, though it belongs to a substance group that may be prohibited under recently passed New Psychoactive Substances (NPS) legislation.
- Switzerland: Controlled (Verzeichnis E) — Specifically named as a controlled substance under Verzeichnis E of Swiss drug control legislation.
- United Kingdom: Class B — Initially classified as a Temporary Class Drug on June 10, 2013.

chunks.title: 5-APB
chunks.text:
Made a permanent Class B, Schedule 1 substance on June 10, 2014 alongside all other benzofuran entactogens and structurally related…
- United States: Unscheduled (Analogue Act applies) — Not specifically scheduled at the federal level. However, due to structural similarity to MDA, it may be prosecuted under the Federal Analogue Act if sold or possessed with intent for human…

chunks.title: 5-APDB
chunks.text: 5-APDB is an entactogenic compound of the phenethylamine, amphetamine, and dihydrobenzofuran classes. Developed by David E. Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University in 1993 as part of research into non-neurotoxic analogues of MDMA, it is structurally related to MDA. 5-APDB functions as a highly selective serotonin releasing agent, producing empathogenic effects. It is frequently confused with its non-dihydrogenated analogue 5-APB, which later emerged as a novel designer drug.

chunks.title: 5-APDB
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As an entactogenic stimulant with serotonin-releasing properties similar to MDMA, some potential for psychological habituation exists.

chunks.title: 5-APDB
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as negative effects.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.text: 5-APDI is an entactogen and psychedelic drug of the aminoindane class. Originally described in a 1968 patent for its cardiovascular properties, it emerged as a designer drug in 2003, though its popularity has since diminished. It acts primarily as a potent serotonin releasing agent, producing empathogenic and mild psychedelic effects. Users have frequently reported problems with overheating and gastrointestinal discomfort during use.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as negative effects, along with aggressiveness and moodiness.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Users have reported issues with overheating during use, suggesting potential for hyperthermia-related complications.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Sweating is also commonly reported, which may be related to thermoregulatory disruption.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Unwelcome bowel movements have been reported as a notable adverse effect during use.

chunks.title: 5-APDI
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin releasing agent (selective); Dopamine reuptake inhibitor; Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor

chunks.title: 5-BPDi
chunks.text: 5-BPDi is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone and pyrrolidinophenone classes. It is a structural analogue of α-PHP and has been described as producing a similar effect profile, though some users report comparatively lighter stimulation and a reduced urge to compulsively redose. As a research chemical with very limited documented human use, its safety profile and long-term risks remain poorly understood. It is considered habit-forming.

chunks.title: 5-BPDi
chunks.text: Categorized as habit-forming, though some users report less compulsive redosing compared to related pyrrolidinophenones like α-PHP.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.text: 5-Bromo-DMT is a brominated indole alkaloid of the tryptamine class and the 5-bromo derivative of DMT. It occurs naturally in several marine sponges, including Smenospongia aurea and Verongula rigida. Briefly mentioned but not tested by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL, its psychoactive properties in humans were first reported in 2013. It is described as producing mild psychedelic effects comparable to low-dose DMT, alongside sedative qualities. It is minimally active orally.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: A 50 mg amount was described as near the physical limit of inhalation, but it is not identified as a toxic or lethal dose.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rodent studies reported hypolocomotion or sedative-like effects.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: These findings are from rodents, not reported human toxicity.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: These findings are from rodents, not reported human toxicity.

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial; EC50 3,090 nM); 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial)

chunks.title: 5-Bromo-DMT
chunks.text:
Legal status of 5-Bromo-DMT by country:
- Singapore: 5-Bromo-DMT is specifically listed as a controlled drug

chunks.title: 5-DBFPV
chunks.text: 5-DBFPV is a synthetic stimulant belonging to the substituted cathinone and pyrrolidine classes. It is a structural analogue of MDPV in which the methylenedioxyphenyl group has been replaced with a dihydrobenzofuran moiety. It has been marketed online as a designer drug and is considered habit-forming. As a research chemical, there is very limited documentation regarding its pharmacological profile and safety in humans.

chunks.title: 5-DBFPV
chunks.text: As a pyrrolidine cathinone analogue of MDPV, this substance is classified as habit-forming with significant potential for compulsive redosing patterns characteristic of this drug class.

chunks.title: 5-DBFPV
chunks.text: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI)

chunks.title: 5-DBFPV
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI)

chunks.title: 5-DBFPV
chunks.text:
Legal status of 5-DBFPV by country:
- Sweden: 5-DBFPV is illegal

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text: 5-EAPB is a substituted amphetamine and benzofuran compound with entactogenic and stimulant properties. Structurally related to 5-APB and 5-MAPB, it initially emerged as a replacement for the latter. Despite its availability as a research chemical, the pharmacology of 5-EAPB remains largely unstudied. At least one fatality has been associated with its use, occurring in 2013 after an individual consumed an exceptionally high dose at a music festival in the UK.

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a stimulant-entactogen, it likely carries moderate psychological addiction potential similar to related compounds.

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as negative effects.

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: One fatality occurred after ingestion of approximately 500 mg at a music festival in 2013, though this was in a context where three individuals were hospitalized after taking similar doses.

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA)

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA); 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2B receptor agonist

chunks.title: 5-EAPB
chunks.text:
Legal status of 5-EAPB by country:
- Singapore: 5-EAPB is listed in the Fifth Schedule of the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) and therefore illegal in Singapore as of May 2015.
- United Kingdom: In the UK, all benzofurans are considered Class B drugs and are therefore illegal.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.text: 5-Hydroxytryptophan is a naturally occurring amino acid that serves as a metabolic intermediate in the biosynthesis of serotonin. It is widely available over the counter as a dietary supplement marketed for its antidepressant, appetite-suppressant, and sleep-promoting properties, and is prescribed in some European countries for the treatment of major depression. It is commonly used for recovery following MDMA and other serotonin-depleting substances. Combining it with serotonergic drugs carries a risk of potentially life-threatening serotonin syndrome.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Prolonged use may carry a significant risk of heart valve disease due to serotonin's effects on cardiac tissue; this risk is associated with chronic supplementation rather than occasional use.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Agonism of 5-HT2B receptors present on heart valve tissue

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk is thought to arise from conversion of 5-HTP to serotonin by the liver with subsequent cardiac exposure.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS), a serious condition causing extreme muscle tenderness, myalgia, and blood abnormalities, has been associated with 5-HTP supplementation, though evidence suggests this may have been caused by contaminants rather than the substance itself.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Historical cases of EMS were likely linked to contaminated supplement batches rather than pure 5-HTP.

chunks.title: 5-Hydroxytryptophan
chunks.text:
Legal status of 5-Hydroxytryptophan by country:
- Canada: Over-the-counter dietary supplement — 5-HTP is sold OTC in Canada and is not covered by illicit-drug controls.
- United Kingdom: Over-the-counter dietary supplement — 5-HTP is sold OTC in the United Kingdom and is not covered by illicit-drug controls.
- United States: Over-the-counter dietary supplement — 5-HTP is sold OTC in the United States and is not covered by illicit-drug controls.

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.text: 5-IAI is an entactogenic substance of the aminoindane class. First described by David Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University in 1991, it functions as a triple monoamine releasing agent with properties comparable to MDMA. However, it is reported to produce notably less euphoria and stimulation, which likely contributed to its lack of widespread recreational popularity after emerging as a designer drug around 2010. Some degree of serotonergic neurotoxicity has been observed in animal studies.

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting some potential for psychological dependence, though specific patterns of compulsive use are not well documented.

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Regular high-dose use has been associated with serotonergic neurotoxicity and cognitive deficits in animal studies; the neurotoxic effects observed were relatively modest compared to related compounds and occurred at extremely high doses.

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxicity causing reduction of serotonergic markers

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Rat studies showed 15% or less reduction of serotonergic markers. Less neurotoxic than the corresponding amphetamine homologue para-iodoamphetamine. Cognitive and memory deficits observed in rodents with regular high-dose administration.

chunks.title: 5-IAI
chunks.text: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA)

chunks.title: 5-IAI

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.text: 5-IT is an indole and amphetamine derivative with primarily stimulant and empathogenic effects. Its preparation was first reported by Albert Hofmann in 1962, and it appeared as a recreational designer drug sold online from 2011. Although a positional isomer of αMT, it is not itself a tryptamine and produces notably more stimulating than psychedelic effects. 5-IT poses serious safety risks including hyperthermia and MAOI activity that can cause fatal interactions with contraindicated substances.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. The stimulant and empathogenic properties may contribute to psychological reinforcement and compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations, disorientation, agitation, restlessness, and anxiety have been reported. Aggressiveness and moodiness are also noted as negative effects.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: 5-IT has been attributed to 14 deaths in Sweden between April and July 2012, all in young men aged 20-30. While 5-IT was the sole intoxicant in two cases, other drugs were present in the remaining twelve. Eleven non-fatal poisonings also occurred during the same period.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including tachycardia and increased blood pressure occur during intoxication; these effects were noted even at relatively low doses of 20mg.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular symptoms are consistent features of 5-IT intoxication and were documented in both Shulgin's notes and clinical poisoning cases.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: The drug is prone to cause overheating and hyperthermia, which has been identified as a significant toxicity concern and may have contributed to reported fatalities.

chunks.title: 5-IT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Hyperthermia is listed among the primary symptoms of 5-IT intoxication. Excessive sweating is also commonly reported.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: 5-MAPB is a synthetic entactogen of the substituted benzofuran and amphetamine classes. It is the N-methylated form of 5-APB, structurally analogous to how MDMA relates to MDA. First encountered as a designer drug around 2010, it produces euphoric, entactogenic, stimulating, and mildly hallucinogenic effects. It has been described as one of the closest known analogues to MDMA in terms of subjective quality and has been patented for potential therapeutic use.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: Withdrawal effects may occur if a person suddenly stops usage after addiction has developed, though specific physical dependence symptoms are not well characterized due to limited research history.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: Chronic use may be moderately habit-forming, with high abuse potential and a risk of psychological dependence. Cravings and repeated redosing can occur, although 5-MAPB's less stimulating profile compared with MDMA appears to make compulsive redosing somewhat less pronounced than with related drugs.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: As with other amphetamine-class compounds, abuse at high dosages for prolonged periods can potentially result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Approximately 5-15% of those experiencing amphetamine-induced psychosis may not fully recover, though psychosis very rarely arises from typical use patterns.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: Not studied for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use may be cardiotoxic due to 5-HT2B receptor agonism, which has been associated with valvular heart disease; this risk is theoretical based on the mechanism shared with other 5-HT2B agonists rather than documented cases specific to 5-MAPB.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: 5-HT2B receptor agonism promoting cardiac fibroblast proliferation and valvulopathy

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Similar mechanism to fenfluramine and MDMA, both associated with cardiac valve damage with chronic use.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rodent studies indicate dose-dependent serotonergic neurotoxicity similar to MDMA, and the compound may also be a dopaminergic neurotoxin; relevance to occasional human use at typical doses remains unclear.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxicity demonstrated in animal models, though notably does not form the α-methyldopamine metabolite that contributes to MDMA neurotoxicity

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: May also exhibit dopaminergic neurotoxicity. Long-term effects in humans have not been studied.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: 5-MAPB acts primarily as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent, with EC50 values of 24 nM for norepinephrine, 41 nM for dopamine, and 64 nM for serotonin in rat brain synaptosomes. It has also been characterized as a triple monoamine reuptake inhibitor. Beyond its transporter-mediated activity, 5-MAPB is a partial agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors, and a potent agonist at the 5-HT1B receptor.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: Limited formal pharmacokinetic data is available for 5-MAPB. In rats, the major metabolites have been identified as 5-APB and 3-carboxymethyl-4-hydroxymethamphetamine. Unlike MDMA, 5-MAPB does not form the α-methyldopamine metabolite.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text: Repeated 5-MAPB use over time can produce tolerance to many effects, so users may need larger doses to obtain similar effects.

chunks.title: 5-MAPB
chunks.text:
5-MAPB emerged on the designer drug market around 2010 as part of the wave of novel benzofuran entactogens developed as alternatives to controlled substances like MDMA. The compound was first formally identified and documented by researchers in 2013, with the initial scientific literature describing its properties published in 2014.

Following its appearance on the recreational market and subsequent scheduling in multiple countries, 5-MAPB has attracted interest for potential therapeutic applications. The compound has been patented by Tactogen, a pharmaceutical company exploring entactogens as candidates for development into regulated medicines.

chunks.title: 5-MAPDB
chunks.text: 5-MAPDB is an entactogen of the dihydrobenzofuran class, structurally related to 5-MAPB and 5-APDB. It functions as a relatively selective serotonin releaser with weaker activity at other monoamine transporters and 5-HT2 receptors, producing effects comparable to MDMA. Despite never having been widely sold as a recreational substance, it was preemptively scheduled in some jurisdictions due to its similarity to related compounds. Neurotoxicity concerns similar to those associated with MDMA have been raised.

chunks.title: 5-MAPDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Suspected neurotoxicity concerns similar to MDMA, though specific data for 5-MAPDB is not established.

chunks.text: Neurotoxicity is suspected based on structural similarity to MDMA and presumed serotonin release, but direct studies on 5-MAPDB neurotoxicity are not documented.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DiPT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class first described by Alexander Shulgin in 1980. It is considered an atypical psychedelic, characterized by prominent stimulating and mildly entactogenic effects rather than typical visual distortions. The compound is particularly noted for producing strong tactile and sexual enhancement alongside auditory distortions similar to those of the related compound DiPT. Higher doses are frequently reported to produce an unpleasant body load.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: Like other serotonergic psychedelics, 5-MeO-DiPT is not habit-forming. Evidence remains limited, but related tryptamines are not typically described as addictive or prone to compulsive use.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: One report describes a prolonged delusional state associated with 5-MeO-DiPT. Those whose family history includes schizophrenia or early-onset mental illness should be cautious, because psychedelics may trigger latent psychological or mental problems.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted. However, the drug has been associated with marked genotoxicity and oxidative DNA damage in research, similar to findings with MDMA and methamphetamine. It is described as the first known tryptamine to be associated with such toxicity.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxicity has been demonstrated in rodent models, with cognitive deficits in spatial navigation, cognitive flexibility, and attention observed following adolescent exposure; effects are described as less severe than those of MDMA, and human relevance remains unclear.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Produces substantial 26-49% reductions in cortical and hippocampal serotonin levels; may also cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity with long-lasting decreases in dopamine levels; associated with cytotoxicity affecting serotonergic neurons ex vivo

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Uniquely described as the first known tryptamine to produce such serotonergic neurotoxicity. Also associated with marked genotoxicity and oxidative DNA damage similar to MDMA and methamphetamine.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure have been reported in the context of overdose; this appears to be an acute toxicity concern rather than a chronic use issue.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DiPT acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist with activity at 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT1D, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors, among others. Its psychedelic effects are thought to result primarily from 5-HT2A receptor agonism, though the full mechanism of action remains unclear. Binding affinity studies show variably strong preference for the 5-HT1A receptor over 5-HT2A, ranging from 2-fold to 161-fold selectivity across different studies; however, receptor activation potency appears similar at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A, with several-fold preference for these over 5-HT2C. 5-MeO-DiPT also acts as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with potency ranging from comparable to its 5-HT2A agonism to very low across studies, while showing no significant dopamine or norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and no activity as a monoamine releasing agent. The substance can elevate brain serotonin levels in rodents, presumably via serotonin reuptake inhibition, and may also elevate dopamine levels in certain brain regions, although findings on the latter are mixed.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: Highest binding affinity; 2- to 161-fold over 5-HT2A across studies

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: Approximately 7 days of abstinence, though some reports suggest that spacing doses 5-7 or more days apart effectively eliminates tolerance-related diminishment.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DiPT can produce tolerance very soon after it is taken. Consecutive-day use typically makes the second-day experience noticeably weaker.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DiPT
chunks.text:
5-MeO-DiPT was first synthesized and tested by American chemist Alexander Shulgin, who conducted the initial human trials of the compound in 1975. Shulgin subsequently co-authored a paper with M. F. Carter detailing the synthesis and human psychopharmacology of both 5-MeO-DiPT and its parent compound diisopropyltryptamine (DiPT), which was published in 1980. A more comprehensive summary of the synthesis procedure and extensive reports of human use later appeared in Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved).

The compound first appeared as a novel designer drug in 1999, emerging in recreational drug markets where it gained the street name "Foxy" or "Foxy Methoxy." It has been used recreationally as a party drug and is noted for its reported aphrodisiac and tactile-enhancing properties. The substance has seen particular use in chemsex contexts, with notable prevalence among gay men and transgender women seeking its reputed sexual enhancement effects.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT is a naturally occurring psychedelic of the tryptamine class, found in numerous plant species and in the venom of the Colorado River toad (Incilius alvarius). It has been used in South American shamanic snuff preparations for centuries and was first identified in the plant Dictyoloma incanescens. Reputed to produce among the most powerful and intense psychedelic states within its class, it is considerably more potent by weight than its close relative DMT — a confusion between the two can lead to dangerous overdoses.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT is not physically addicting and does not produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT is considered non-addictive with low abuse potential. Animal self-administration studies, which predict abuse liability, have been unsuccessful, indicating it lacks the pharmacology to initiate or maintain dependence.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT can trigger latent psychoses in predisposed individuals and may cause lasting psychological effects including PTSD-type reactions, chronic anxiety, and difficulty integrating experiences. Documented cases include multi-day psychotic episodes requiring antipsychotic medication, typically associated with high doses. Permanent disturbances in self- and reality recognition are possible, and extreme caution is warranted for people with schizophrenia in their family history or early-onset mental illness.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: Convulsions have been documented in at least one case involving combination with MAOIs, but seizure risk from 5-MeO-DMT alone is not established in the available literature. Muscle contractions, spasms, and tremors are reported physical effects.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted on 5-MeO-DMT.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Smoking 5-MeO-DMT can cause throat and lung irritation due to the harsh nature of the vapor; severe lung pain has been reported in rare cases, though risk is generally low given the small doses typically used.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Users may perceive difficulty breathing during intense experiences, but this is not considered genuine respiratory depression and is generally safe, though formal studies are lacking.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including increased heart rate and elevated blood pressure occur during intoxication; possible cardiotoxic properties have been suggested but remain unconfirmed.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: People with high blood pressure are advised not to consume 5-MeO-DMT. Cardiotoxicity claims lack formal citation in available literature.

chunks.text: Bufotenin (active)

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist with activity at the 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors. It displays approximately 1,000-fold greater affinity for the 5-HT1A receptor compared to the 5-HT2A receptor and potently suppresses the firing of dorsal raphe serotonin neurons. Beyond the serotonin system, 5-MeO-DMT is an agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors. It also functions as a weak serotonin reuptake inhibitor (IC50 of 2,184 nM) but does not appear to act as a monoamine releasing agent.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-DMT is lipophilic and is thought to readily cross the blood-brain barrier. It undergoes O-demethylation by CYP2D6 to produce the active metabolite bufotenin. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors substantially reduce its metabolism, prolonging its activity and allowing it to become orally active. The elimination half-life following sublingual administration is approximately 28 minutes.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: Not orally active on its own; monoamine oxidase inhibitors prevent rapid breakdown and allow oral activity

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Sublingual
chunks.text: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors can substantially slow metabolism and prolong activity

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: Returns to baseline within 2 hours in the absence of further consumption. Some sources suggest full tolerance reset occurs within 24 hours.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: Develops almost immediately after a single dose, greatly diminishing effects if one attempts to redose.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text:
5-MeO-DMT has a lengthy history of human use spanning over a millennium. Archaeological evidence from a burial site in Northern Chile, dated to approximately the 8th century A.D., revealed snuffing paraphernalia alongside traces of N,N-DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, and bufotenine. Additional archaeological sites from the same period have uncovered seeds from Anadenanthera species known to contain the compound.

The substance appears as a common constituent in numerous plant species and has been employed traditionally in various psychoactive preparations across South America and the Caribbean. Indigenous groups have utilized it in intranasal snuffs including Yopo, prepared from Anadenanthera colubrina seeds, and Epena, derived from Virola sap. It has also been incorporated as an admixture in certain ayahuasca-type brews. In the early 1950s, researchers identified 5-MeO-DMT as one of the primary psychoactive components in cohoba snuffs used by peoples of the northern Amazon basin.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: The compound was first synthesized in 1936 by Japanese chemists Toshio Hoshino and Kenya Shimodaira. Over two decades later, in 1959, it was isolated and identified as one of the psychoactive constituents of Anadenanthera peregrina seeds used in the preparation of Yopo snuff. While 5-MeO-DMT was initially believed to be a major contributor to the psychoactive properties of such snuffs, subsequent research has suggested this is unlikely due to its limited or sometimes negligible presence in the seeds, which instead appear to derive their effects primarily from bufotenine.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: The first published report identifying toad venom as a natural source of 5-MeO-DMT appeared in 1968. The Colorado River toad (Incilius alvarius, also known as Bufo alvarius) was found to produce venom containing concentrations of up to 15% 5-MeO-DMT. This discovery established the species as the only known psychoactive toad and has since led to its venom becoming a sought-after source of the compound.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-DMT
chunks.text: Recreational and non-traditional use of 5-MeO-DMT expanded throughout the 1980s and 1990s. Alexander Shulgin documented the synthesis and psychoactive effects of the compound in his 1997 book TiHKAL ("Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved"), which also described the use of Colorado River toad venom. In contemporary times, the substance is primarily obtained in its pure synthetic form through online research chemical vendors. Recent studies have investigated its capacity to induce mystical experiences, and there is growing scientific interest in exploring potential therapeutic applications.

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2B receptor agonist; 5-HT2C receptor agonist; Melatonin MT1 receptor agonist; Melatonin MT2 receptor agonist; SERT

First described in the scientific literature by Richard Glennon and colleagues around 1979, it was later explored by Alexander Shulgin in his 1997 book TiHKAL. Shulgin characterized its effects as ambiguous and not entirely positive, ultimately deeming the compound unpromising. Very little is known about this substance, and available dosage information remains tentative.

First described by Alexander Shulgin around 2002, it was notably never synthesized or explored by him and was not included in TiHKAL. The substance has since appeared as a designer drug with very few experience reports or formal studies available. Animal research suggests it may produce weaker hallucinogenic effects compared to related tryptamines. Due to the significant lack of safety data, extreme caution is warranted.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT is a synthetic psychedelic and entactogenic substance of the tryptamine class. Its synthesis and human psychopharmacology were first published by Shulgin, Repke, and colleagues in 1985, with further documentation in Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL. The substance is characterized by its notably stimulating and body-oriented effects, including pronounced tactile and sexual enhancement, while generally producing fewer visual distortions than typical psychedelics. It is almost exclusively obtained as a research chemical through online vendors.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT is not physically addictive. There is no evidence of physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms associated with its use.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT is not typically associated with habit formation, and interest in taking it may lessen after repeated experiences. Its use is usually self-limiting, though some people may still use it more often than feels comfortable.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: Temporary psychosis, confusion, disorientation, and agitation have been documented in several clinical case reports, typically associated with high doses or combination with other substances. One case involved a 32-year-old male found disoriented and aggressive after confirmed use. People with schizophrenia in their family history or a history of early-onset mental illness should be extremely cautious, because psychedelics may bring underlying psychological vulnerabilities to the surface.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: People with seizure or convulsive disorders could face increased health risks from psychedelic use, although the literature does not provide specific seizure risk data for 5-MeO-MiPT.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT itself does not appear to have been studied for carcinogenicity. The closely related compound 5-MeO-DiPT has shown genotoxicity in rodent studies, but this has not been confirmed for 5-MeO-MiPT.
