chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects appear to be transient and dose-dependent. Body load contributing to cardiovascular discomfort underlies much of the drug's anxiogenic potential.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT acts primarily as a serotonin receptor agonist, with its psychedelic effects attributed mainly to partial agonism at the 5-HT2A receptor (83% maximum efficacy). It binds most potently to the 5-HT1A receptor and also engages 5-HT2B and 5-HT2C receptors at higher concentrations, though with lower potency and minimal functional activation of 5-HT2B (12% efficacy). Whether the compound has meaningful activity at monoamine transporters remains uncertain: one study reported moderate affinity at the serotonin transporter, while subsequent research found no significant transporter binding or inhibition. The compound is inactive as a monoamine releasing agent, and while inhibition of monoamine oxidase has been speculated as an additional mechanism, this has not been scientifically demonstrated.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT undergoes extensive phase I hepatic metabolism mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes. The major metabolic pathways include O-demethylation, N-demethylation, hydroxylation, and N-oxide formation. Multiple metabolites have been detected in human urine within two hours of exposure, and measurable blood concentrations appear within one hour, suggesting relatively rapid metabolism and elimination. Renal excretion is likely a major route of elimination. Notably, the compound is reported to be several times more potent when taken orally than when smoked, suggesting favorable oral bioavailability.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: EC50 = 0.023 μM (Emax 83%); ED50 = 7.82 nM (calcium signaling); ED50 = 566 nM (β-arrestin recruitment)

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: IC50 = 22 μM; one study found no significant inhibition at up to 10 μM

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 7 days of abstinence typically restores baseline sensitivity, though some sources suggest 5-7 days may be sufficient for most users.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: Tolerance develops almost immediately after ingestion, though 5-MeO-MiPT appears to produce less tolerance than many other psychedelics. Some users report successful experiences on consecutive days, suggesting tolerance buildup is more moderate than typical for the class.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-MiPT, commonly known as "Moxy," was first synthesized and characterized in 1985 when David Repke, Donald Grotjahn, and Alexander Shulgin published its synthesis and pharmacological profile in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry. This publication represented the first known documentation of the compound, establishing that it had no prior history of human usage before this academic work. Shulgin later documented the substance more extensively in his influential book TiHKAL ("Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved"), which described its effects in humans and contributed to broader awareness within the psychedelic research community.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text: Following its initial characterization, 5-MeO-MiPT remained relatively obscure until it began appearing as a novel designer drug around 2005. Since then, it has circulated primarily through the research chemical market rather than traditional street drug channels. The compound is used both recreationally and as an entheogen, typically obtained through online vendors operating in regulatory grey areas rather than through in-person distribution networks. Its presence in the research chemical market has continued for approximately two decades since its emergence into wider use.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MiPT
chunks.text:
5-MeO-MiPT — caution combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds (Both classes of compounds can be unpredictable alone)
- 2C-x compounds (The 5-MeO psychedelics can interact unpredictably to potentiate other psychedelics)
- Cannabis (Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.)
- DOx compounds (The 5-MeO class of tryptamines can be unpredictable in their interactions, particularly increasing the risk of unpleasant physical side effects.)
- MDMA (Some of the 5-MeO tryptamines are a bit unpredictable and should be mixed with MDMA with care)
- Mescaline (The 5-MeO class of tryptamines can be unpredictable in their interactions)
- NBOMe compounds (The 5-MeO class of tryptamines can be unpredictable in their interactions and the NBOMes are known to be unpredictable even alone. This combination is best avoided)
- Pregabalin (Caution should be given due to 5-MeO-xxT drugs stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of 5-MeO-xxT drugs. Additionally, Pregabalin may increase 5-MeO-xxT drugs inhibition and risk of injury.)

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-AMT is a psychedelic and entactogenic tryptamine first synthesized in 1958, with its psychoactive properties in humans documented by 1976. It is regarded as one of the most potent psychedelics among simple tryptamines, active at single-digit milligram doses. The substance has occasionally been misrepresented as LSD, a particularly dangerous scenario given that, unlike LSD, 5-MeO-AMT carries significant overdose risk including cardiac complications and seizures, with at least one reported fatality.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MT
chunks.text: Seizures have been noted in overdose cases. The seizure risk appears to be associated with the compound's sympathomimetic effects and may occur at doses that some users consider within normal range.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: At least one death has been documented from overdose. Particularly sensitive individuals can experience overdose symptoms at doses as low as 20 mg, which falls within the normal range for most users. Hospitalizations have occurred at doses as low as 8 mg. The compound appears to have a narrow margin of safety, and oral consumption seems safer than insufflation.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-MT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiac arrhythmia has been noted in overdose cases, likely due to the compound's sympathomimetic effects.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-NiPT
chunks.text: 5-MeO-NiPT is a psychedelic tryptamine structurally related to 5-MeO-DMT, 5-MeO-DiPT, and 5-MeO-MiPT. It first emerged as a novel designer drug around 2014 and was notably absent from Alexander Shulgin's TiHKAL. It is an active metabolite of both 5-MeO-MiPT and 5-MeO-DiPT. Very limited information is available regarding its effects and safety profile in humans, and it should be approached with considerable caution.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.text: 5-MeO-Pyr-T is a synthetic tryptamine first described by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. Despite its structural relationship to classical psychedelic tryptamines, its effects are notably atypical — producing rapid-onset anesthesia-like unconsciousness and complete amnesia rather than traditional psychedelic experiences, even at very low smoked doses. Reports describe prolonged blackouts lasting hours, severe nausea, and significant individual variability. This substance carries serious safety concerns and should never be used without sober observers present.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.text: Produces anesthesia-like unconsciousness with complete amnesia at doses as low as 3 mg smoked. Users have exhibited alarming behaviors including flailing, rolling, quivering, shaking, and wandering in public with no memory formation. One observer noted the user's actions were 'scary' to witness.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Skin abnormalities lasting several days have been reported following use at doses as low as 3 mg smoked.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: One case report described skin appearing 'funny' for several days after exposure.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Nausea and vomiting appear to be common during the recovery period, occurring even at low doses of 3-4 mg smoked.

chunks.title: 5-MeO-Pyr-T
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Vomiting reported in multiple trial reports; described as occurring during emergence from unconscious state.

chunks.title: 5-Methylethylone
chunks.text: 5-Methylethylone is a synthetic cathinone of the amphetamine and phenethylamine chemical classes, structurally related to ethylone. It has been sold as a designer drug and is reported to produce empathogenic, stimulant, and psychedelic effects, with a potency suspected to be slightly higher than ethylone. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacological properties, metabolism, or toxicity, making it a particularly poorly understood research chemical.

chunks.title: 5-Methylethylone
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations are listed among possible effects, though specific psychosis risk data is not available.

chunks.title: 5-Methylethylone
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available for 5-methylethylone.

chunks.title: 5-Methylethylone
chunks.text: Relatively little data exists about the pharmacological properties of 5-methylethylone. Based on its structural relationship to ethylone and other synthetic cathinones, it has been suggested to act as a monoamine releasing agent, though this has not been conclusively established.

chunks.title: 5-Methylethylone
chunks.text: 5-Methylethylone emerged as a novel designer drug within the synthetic cathinone class. As a structural analogue of ethylone, it belongs to the broader category of substituted cathinones that have appeared in recreational drug markets. The compound remains poorly characterized in the scientific literature, with relatively little data available regarding its pharmacological properties or toxicity profile.

chunks.title: 5-PPDI
chunks.text: 5-PPDI is an obscure research chemical believed to be a structural analogue of α-PBP, which is itself related to the pyrovalerone stimulant α-PVP. This compound has virtually no documented history of human use, and some anecdotal reports suggest it may be inactive. In the event that it does produce effects, its profile would likely resemble that of other pyrovalerone-type stimulants. Due to its extreme obscurity, reliable safety or pharmacological data is essentially nonexistent.

chunks.title: 5-PPDI
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a pyrovalerone-class stimulant, it likely shares the compulsive redosing potential characteristic of this chemical class, though specific data on psychological addiction for this compound is not available.

chunks.title: 5-PPDI
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as potential negative effects, along with aggressiveness and moodiness, suggesting possible psychotomimetic properties at some doses.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: 6-APB is a synthetic entactogen of the benzofuran class, structurally related to MDA. First synthesized in 1993 by David E. Nichols as a potential non-neurotoxic alternative to MDMA, it did not see recreational use until over a decade later, when it was briefly sold on the research chemical market under the name "Benzofury." Compared to MDMA, 6-APB is reported to produce stronger psychedelic and visual effects while retaining comparable entactogenic qualities. Wide variability in dose response has been noted.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Cravings and withdrawal effects may occur when chronic use is suddenly stopped. After-effects including depression, irritability, and cognitive fatigue for several days following use are commonly reported, attributed to neurotransmitter depletion rather than true physical dependence.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Moderately addictive with high potential for abuse, capable of causing psychological dependence in some users. Compulsive redosing can occur due to euphoric effects, though this urge is often reported as less pressing than with MDMA due to the longer duration.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Acute psychosis has been reported in combination with synthetic cannabinoids. Delusions are listed among possible cognitive effects, typically at higher doses or during the offset phase of the experience.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Rare effect primarily occurring in predisposed individuals, particularly when taking high doses or redosing while dehydrated, fatigued, undernourished, or overheated.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term or chronic use involving regular daily or weekly dosing is likely cardiotoxic and may lead to valvulopathy; occasional recreational use at typical doses carries significantly lower risk.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Potent full agonism of the 5-HT2B receptor promotes fibroblast proliferation in cardiac valve tissue, similar to the mechanism identified with the withdrawn anorectic fenfluramine.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: 6-APB shows 100-fold selectivity for 5-HT2B over 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors. Acute cardiovascular strain including increased heart rate and blood pressure occurs during intoxication.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated or high-dose administration may result in neurotoxicity presenting as deficits in cognitive, affective, and psychomotor function, though 6-APB was specifically designed to be less neurotoxic than MDA or MDMA and single responsible uses are likely physically safe.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Designed to circumvent production of alpha-methyl-dopamine, a metabolic byproduct thought to underlie amphetamine-related serotonergic neurotoxicity.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Neurotoxicity remains subject to ongoing debate due to limited human research. Environmental temperature may significantly influence serotonergic neurotoxicity as observed with MDMA.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: 6-APB acts as a serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor, with EC50 values for monoamine release of 10 nM (dopamine), 14 nM (norepinephrine), and 36 nM (serotonin) in rat brain synaptosomes. Its highest-affinity binding target is the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor (Ki = 3.7 nM), for which it shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors; it has been characterized as either a high-efficacy partial agonist or full agonist at this site (Emax = 70%). 6-APB also displays partial agonism at the 5-HT2A receptor and agonist activity at the 5-HT2C receptor at considerably lower potencies, and binds with high affinity to the α2C-adrenergic receptor (Ki = 45 nM), though the functional significance of this binding in humans is unknown.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Available metabolic data, derived from rat studies, indicates that 6-APB undergoes Phase I metabolism involving hydroxylation and cleavage of the furan ring, followed by reduction of the resulting unsaturated aldehyde. This intermediate is then either oxidized to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an alcohol and subsequently hydroxylated. Phase II metabolism proceeds via glucuronidation.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: EC50 = 36 nM (release); IC50 = 930 nM (reuptake inhibition)

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: EC50 = 14 nM (release); IC50 = 190 nM (reuptake inhibition)

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: EC50 = 10 nM (release); IC50 = 3,300 nM (reuptake inhibition)

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text: Repeated or sustained use can cause tolerance to rise quickly. As a potent serotonin releaser, continued administration reduces positive effects over time and can eventually leave users with anxious, dysphoric stimulation rather than the desired entactogenic experience.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text:
The benzofuran entactogens emerged from academic research into the structure-activity relationships of MDMA and related compounds. In 1993, medicinal chemist David E. Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University investigated 5-APDB and 6-APDB as serotonin releasing agents and entactogens, examining the role of the MDA dioxole ring structure in serotonergic neuron interactions. This research was partly motivated by efforts to identify potential non-neurotoxic alternatives to MDMA, which was gaining recognition as a potentially useful adjunct in psychotherapy while simultaneously being linked to neurotoxic effects.

Following this foundational work, 6-APB and its structural relative 5-APB were first described in the scientific literature in 2000 by Karin Briner and colleagues at Eli Lilly and Company in a patent application. At this time, the compounds were specifically studied as serotonin 5-HT2C receptor agonists for potential medical applications rather than as recreational substances.

chunks.title: 6-APB
chunks.text:
Despite being characterized in the scientific literature a decade earlier, human recreational use of 6-APB was not documented until 2010, when the compound emerged for sale on the global research chemical market. It became particularly prominent in the United Kingdom's "legal highs" market, where it was sold under the brand name "Benzofury" in distinctive bright orange packaging that became instantly recognizable.

The compound's conspicuous branding attracted significant media attention during this period. 6-APB became one of the most frequently cited research chemicals in media coverage critical of legal highs, contributing to calls for regulatory action. This ultimately led to classification as a Temporary Class Drug in June 2013, followed by permanent scheduling as a Class B substance alongside all other benzofuran entactogens in June 2014, effectively ending its presence in the legal market.

chunks.title: 6-APB

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.text: 6-APDB is an entactogenic and stimulant research chemical of the phenethylamine, amphetamine, and benzofuran classes. It is a structural analogue of MDA, first described in 1993 by David E. Nichols at Purdue University as part of research into potentially non-neurotoxic alternatives to MDMA. Compared to MDMA, 6-APDB is reported to be notably more sedating and less energetic, with a stimulation style more reminiscent of mescaline. It has a limited history of human use, and its toxicity profile remains poorly understood.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.text: Chronic 6-APDB use is regarded as moderately addictive, with substantial abuse potential and a possible risk of psychological dependence in some users. If addiction has developed, abruptly stopping use may produce cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: The exact toxic dosage is unknown due to the substance's short history of human use.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term heavy use may damage the heart and is suspected of contributing to valvulopathy, similar to concerns documented with MDMA.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Agonist activity at the 5-HT2B receptor, which is associated with cardiac valve fibrosis.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk is associated with repeated or high-dose administration over extended periods.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated or high-dose administration could potentially cause neurotoxic effects, which may appear as problems with cognition, mood-related function, or psychomotor performance.

chunks.title: 6-APDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: 6-EAPB
chunks.text: 6-EAPB is a rare entactogenic research chemical of the benzofuran class, structurally related to both MDMA and 6-APB. It functions primarily as a monoamine reuptake inhibitor while showing very low potency at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Pharmacological understanding of this compound remains limited, and it is generally reported to produce weaker effects compared to its structural relatives. As with many research chemicals, its safety profile is poorly established.

chunks.title: 6-EAPB
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a suspected monoamine releaser and/or reuptake inhibitor with entactogenic properties, psychological addiction potential may be present, though specific data is limited.

chunks.title: 6-EAPB
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as negative effects. Aggressiveness and moodiness are also documented, though the frequency and severity of these effects remain poorly characterized due to limited pharmacological knowledge.

chunks.title: 6-MAPB
chunks.text: 6-MAPB is an entactogenic compound of the substituted benzofuran class, structurally related to both 6-APB and MDMA. First identified as a novel designer drug in 2013, it functions as a serotonin releasing agent and, unlike MDMA, a potent serotonin 5-HT1B receptor agonist. 6-MAPB has not been widely distributed on its own but has been detected in analytical samples from individuals hospitalized after consuming combinations of benzofuran derivatives.

chunks.title: 6-MAPB
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As an empathogen-stimulant, it may carry moderate psychological addiction potential similar to related compounds.

chunks.title: 6-MAPB
chunks.text: Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported as negative effects, along with aggressiveness and moodiness.

chunks.title: 6-Mddm
chunks.text: 6-MDDM is a semisynthetic opioid and derivative of hydromorphone that is structurally related to desomorphine. It is estimated to possess approximately 80 times the analgesic potency of morphine. This substance has very little documented history of human use, and current dosage information is largely extrapolated from potency comparisons rather than direct clinical data. As with all potent opioids, it carries significant risks including respiratory depression and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: 6-Mddm
chunks.text: As an opioid, physical dependence is expected with regular use, with withdrawal symptoms typical of the opioid class.

chunks.title: 6-Mddm
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As an opioid, it carries significant psychological addiction potential with risk of compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: 6-Mddm
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: No human lethal dose data available. Extreme potency (approximately 80 times that of morphine) means the margin between active and potentially lethal doses is very narrow, significantly increasing overdose risk.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.text: α-PHP is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone and pyrrolidine classes, first developed in the 1960s. It emerged as a popular replacement for α-PVP following that substance's prohibition and may be even more potent. α-PHP produces powerful but short-lived euphoric effects and is notorious for its high potential for compulsive redosing, psychological dependence, and the ability to induce paranoia and psychosis, particularly during extended binges.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.text: Chronic use is regarded as highly addictive, with substantial abuse potential and a capacity to cause psychological dependence. A-PHP is especially associated with compulsive redosing, where users may find it extremely difficult to stop taking more even after psychotic symptoms appear. Abruptly stopping after sustained use may be followed by cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.text: Can result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions, particularly when dosed too highly or frequently. A review of treatment for similar stimulant-induced psychosis reports that approximately 5-15% of users do not fully recover. Psychotic and schizophrenic symptoms may occur even before users stop redosing, and delusional states are commonly reported when the substance is abused.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.text: Misuse may make seizures more likely in some individuals by reducing the seizure threshold.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Because its rush can be very powerful, α-PHP may produce uncomfortable or painful cardiac sensations, particularly with abuse or prolonged use; sudden spikes of blood pressure may manifest as an extremely uncomfortable sensation, particularly when vaporized or injected.

chunks.title: A-PHP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: People with a personal or family history of heart problems should avoid the most potent routes of administration for this drug.

chunks.title: A-PIHP
chunks.text: A-PIHP is a pyrrolidine-based stimulant of the cathinone class. It is a relatively new research chemical about which limited information is currently available. The substance is also reported to produce empathogenic qualities and is considered habit-forming. A-PIHP is notable for its reportedly rapid tolerance development, with users finding that effects diminish significantly with repeated use. It should not be combined with other stimulants or substances that elevate blood pressure.

chunks.title: A-PIHP
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. Rapid tolerance development with diminishing effects over time suggests a pattern conducive to compulsive redosing and escalating use.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and pyrrolidinophenone classes, chemically related to prolintane and pyrovalerone. Originally patented by Boehringer Ingelheim in the 1960s but never marketed, it emerged as a recreational substance in the early 2010s. Known colloquially as flakka, α-PVP acts as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, producing powerful but short-lived effects comparable to methamphetamine and cocaine. It has been linked to numerous hospitalizations and deaths, with very limited toxicity data available.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: Chronic use is considered highly addictive with a high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence. Compulsive use patterns are commonly associated with this substance, and when addiction has developed, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur if usage is suddenly stopped.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: This compound is known to readily induce psychosis if abused for prolonged periods. Symptoms can easily escalate into frightening delusions, paranoid psychosis, extreme agitation, and other altered mental states. In emergency settings, psychosis-like states, agitation, aggression, and hallucinations are commonly observed. Approximately 5-15% of users who develop stimulant psychosis fail to recover completely.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP may lower the seizure threshold in some individuals, especially when abused.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Due to the potency of its rush, α-PVP can cause various uncomfortable or painful sensations in the heart, especially when abused or used for extended periods; sudden spikes in blood pressure may occur particularly when vaporized or injected.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Potent catecholamine release and reuptake inhibition causing acute cardiovascular strain

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Those with genetic or family history of heart issues are discouraged from using this drug, particularly via potent routes of administration. At least one death involved heart failure when combined with pentedrone, and another involved a heart attack following a state of delirium.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP acts as a potent and selective norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI), with similar potency to MDPV. It does not act as a transporter substrate, meaning it does not cause neurotransmitter release. The drug is substantially more potent than classical stimulants in vitro, showing 46-fold greater potency than amphetamine for dopamine reuptake inhibition and 7-fold greater potency for norepinephrine reuptake inhibition in HEK293 cells. It is one of the most potent dopamine reuptake inhibitors known in vitro. In contrast to its effects on catecholamine reuptake, α-PVP has negligible effects on serotonin reuptake.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP is absorbed very rapidly following administration. The drug is highly lipophilic due to its pyrrolidine ring, which markedly enhances its ability to permeate the blood-brain barrier relative to other cathinones. The distribution, metabolism, and elimination of α-PVP have been studied, though detailed metabolic pathways are not well characterized in the available literature.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: Tolerance to many of the effects of α-PVP develops with prolonged and repeated use, resulting in users needing to administer increasingly large doses to achieve the same effects.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP (alpha-pyrrolidinovalerophenone) was first described in scientific literature in 1963 and subsequently patented by the pharmaceutical company Boehringer Ingelheim during the 1960s, though it was never developed for medical use or brought to market. The compound remained largely obscure until reports of recreational use began emerging in the early 2010s, with significant recreational consumption documented from around 2013 onwards. During this period, α-PVP was mass-produced in China and distributed globally through online vendors as a research chemical.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: α-PVP gained notoriety as one of the active ingredients found in products marketed as "bath salts" or "legal highs." In the United States, it became known by various street names including "flakka" (particularly in Florida) and "gravel" in other regions. The substance became notable for its low cost, reportedly available for as little as five dollars per dose. Laboratory analysis from one Florida county documented a dramatic increase in α-PVP detections in seized drug samples, rising from zero cases in early 2014 to 84 detections by September of that year. The compound has been associated with numerous hospitalizations and overdose fatalities.

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dopaminergic stimulants

chunks.title: A-PVP
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine reuptake inhibitor; Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SERT

chunks.title: AB-CHMINACA
chunks.text: AB-CHMINACA is an indazole-based synthetic cannabinoid and a potent agonist of both CB1 and CB2 receptors, reported to be significantly more potent than THC. It is structurally related to AB-FUBINACA and AB-PINACA, sharing a valine amino acid amide residue characteristic of its generation of synthetic cannabinoids. AB-CHMINACA is active in the microgram range and has been associated with seizures, deaths, and psychotic episodes, warranting extreme caution.

chunks.title: AB-CHMINACA
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a synthetic cannabinoid, psychological dependence may develop with regular use.

chunks.title: AB-CHMINACA
chunks.text: Multiple psychotic episodes have been reported in connection with this synthetic cannabinoid.

chunks.title: AB-CHMINACA
chunks.text: Multiple seizure cases have been reported in connection with this synthetic cannabinoid.

chunks.title: AB-CHMINACA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Deaths have been reported in overdose. The substance has a low threshold dose, meaning the margin between active and dangerous doses may be narrow.

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: AB-FUBINACA is a synthetic cannabinoid of the indazolecarboxamide class. Originally developed by Pfizer in 2009 as an analgesic, it was never pursued for human use and first surfaced in synthetic cannabinoid blends in Japan in 2012. It is a highly potent cannabinoid receptor agonist, and its extreme potency—combined with its widespread inclusion in unregulated herbal blends—poses significant overdose risk, with fatalities reported.

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. Psychological dependence may develop with regular use, similar to other synthetic cannabinoids.

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: Cannabinoids (both synthetic and plant-derived)

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: AB-FUBINACA was initially synthesized by Pfizer in 2009 during research into novel analgesic compounds. The pharmaceutical company never advanced the substance to human clinical trials, and it was subsequently abandoned as a potential medication. The compound first appeared on the recreational drug market in 2012, when Japanese researchers identified it as an active ingredient in synthetic cannabinoid products being sold in that country. It was discovered alongside AB-PINACA, a structurally related compound that had not been previously documented in the scientific literature. AB-FUBINACA subsequently became one of the more prevalent synthetic cannabinoids circulating in recreational drug markets.

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: In August 2018, AB-FUBINACA gained significant public attention following a mass overdose event in New Haven, Connecticut. Beginning on August 15, approximately 70 individuals overdosed in the vicinity of Yale University's campus after consuming adulterated synthetic cannabis products. By the end of that week, over 100 people had required emergency medical transport to local hospitals. Law enforcement subsequently arrested three individuals on charges related to dealing synthetic cannabis products containing AB-FUBINACA.

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Cannabinoids (both synthetic and plant-derived)

chunks.title: AB-FUBINACA
chunks.text: Binding profile: CB1 receptor agonist (full, Ki 0.9 nM, EC50 1.8 nM); CB2 receptor agonist (full, Ki 23.2 nM, EC50 3.2 nM) with some selectivity for CB2

chunks.title: Acetildenafil
chunks.text: Acetildenafil is a synthetic phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor and structural analog of sildenafil (Viagra). It has not undergone formal testing in humans or animals and possesses an unknown safety profile. Acetildenafil has been widely detected as an undisclosed ingredient in over-the-counter "herbal aphrodisiac" products marketed for erectile dysfunction and libido enhancement, representing a significant health risk to consumers unaware of its presence in otherwise unregulated supplements.

chunks.title: Acetildenafil
chunks.text: No formal testing in humans or animals has been conducted, leaving carcinogenic potential completely unknown.

chunks.title: Acetildenafil
chunks.text: Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor

chunks.text: prevents degradation of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)

chunks.title: Acetildenafil
chunks.text: Binding profile: Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor; prevents degradation of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acetylfentanyl is a synthetic opioid of the anilidopiperidine class and a structural analog of fentanyl. Originally described in the 1960s alongside fentanyl itself, it has never been approved for medical use and has only appeared on the illicit market as a designer drug. It is estimated to be several times more potent than heroin yet roughly fifteen times less potent than fentanyl, still presenting significant overdose risk.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Chronic use leads to extreme physical dependence. Cravings and withdrawal symptoms occur upon sudden cessation. Animal studies have demonstrated that acetylfentanyl can completely suppress morphine withdrawal symptoms, confirming significant cross-dependence liability with other opioids.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acetylfentanyl presents an extremely high risk of addiction and abuse, and its use can lead to psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, especially because its effects are short-lived.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Animal toxicity studies observed significant bleeding in the small intestines of mice administered acetylfentanyl; the relevance of this finding to human use at typical doses remains unclear.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Observed in acute toxicity studies in mice at doses approaching LD50. This finding is notable as the comparison compound fentanyl had a higher LD50 (62 mg/kg) in the same studies, suggesting acetylfentanyl may have additional toxic mechanisms.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression occurs at doses proportionally closer to the psychoactive range than with many other opioids; this effect can rapidly progress to fatal anoxia, with pulmonary edema documented in overdose fatalities.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: μ-opioid receptor agonism suppresses the breathing reflex proportional to dosage consumed

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The comparatively low safety ratio (LD50:ED50) in animal tests indicates easier progression to dangerous respiratory depression compared to other opioids. Case reports document lung edema as cause of death.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acetylfentanyl acts as a μ-opioid receptor agonist, producing its effects through binding at the same receptor sites engaged by endogenous endorphins. Its high lipophilicity allows it to penetrate the central nervous system more readily than many other opioids, contributing to its potency. In animal studies using selective antagonists, its activity was confirmed to be mediated primarily through the μ-opioid receptor; a δ-opioid antagonist did not alter its effects, while a μ-opioid antagonist reduced them and naltrexone fully reversed them. Acetylfentanyl has been estimated to be approximately 15 times more potent than morphine as an analgesic (with an ED50 of 0.021 mg/kg in the mouse acetic acid writhing test) and roughly 15 times less potent than fentanyl.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Full inhibition in mouse vas deferens stimulated twitch test

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Repeated acetylfentanyl use over time can lead to tolerance for many effects. The pace differs by effect, with constipation-related tolerance developing especially slowly relative to other opioid effects. Because of this uneven tolerance pattern, users may need progressively larger doses to obtain the same subjective effects.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text:
Acetylfentanyl was first described in patents from Research Laboratorium Dr. C. Janssen (Janssen Pharmaceutica), a Belgian pharmaceutical company. Its analgesic activity was characterized in a 1968 patent by Paul Janssen, the company's founder. The compound was discovered contemporaneously with fentanyl itself during Janssen's extensive research into piperidine-based analgesics.

Despite its discovery alongside fentanyl, acetylfentanyl was never developed for therapeutic applications or licensed for medical use. During the late 1980s, the compound appeared occasionally on illicit drug markets but remained uncommon compared to other opioids available at the time.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acetylfentanyl's modern history began in 2012 when online discussion about the substance increased and reports of seizures appeared. Initial reports of recreational use emerged from Russia, where the compound was detected in smoking "spices" (synthetic cannabinoid products). At least twelve deaths associated with acetylfentanyl, some involving morphine as a co-intoxicant, were reported in this region. By 2013, the substance had spread more widely. In late April 2013, police in Montreal, Canada conducted raids on seven locations and recovered approximately 300,000 drug tablets, of which 11,000 were found to contain acetylfentanyl. A separate three kilograms of acetylfentanyl powder was also confiscated during these operations. In the United States, the first laboratory submission involving acetylfentanyl occurred in Maine in April 2013. The drug was frequently mixed with heroin or sold in its place, contributing to unexpected overdoses among users unaware of its presence.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: The compound continued to proliferate through 2014 and 2015. According to the EU Early Warning System Network, the first European Union seizure was reported in Poland in 2014, followed by three seizures in Finland—two originating from China and one from Belgium. Japan first identified acetylfentanyl in drug products in 2014. In November 2015, the substance was seized for the first time in Western Australia, where it was found pressed into tablets designed to resemble PEZ candies. Most large shipment seizures during this period involved packages originating in China.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: The proliferation of acetylfentanyl precipitated a significant public health crisis, particularly in the United States and Europe. Between March and May 2013, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued a health alert following fourteen overdose deaths among intravenous drug users in Rhode Island, with victims ranging in age from 19 to 57 years. Pennsylvania experienced a pronounced outbreak, prompting state authorities to request that coroners and medical examiners screen for acetylfentanyl. This investigation attributed at least fifty fatalities to either fentanyl or acetylfentanyl during the first half of 2013. Florida similarly reported a rise in fentanyl and acetylfentanyl-related deaths beginning in late 2013. By July 2015, the DEA had confirmed fifty-two fatalities involving acetylfentanyl in the United States between 2013 and 2015.

chunks.title: Acetylfentanyl
chunks.text: In Europe, acetylfentanyl was analytically confirmed in thirty-two fatalities across four member states between 2013 and August 2015, with Sweden recording twenty-seven deaths, the United Kingdom two, Germany two, and Poland one. The European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction issued an alert about the drug in September 2015 following twenty-two confirmed deaths. More broadly, fentanyl analogs have been responsible for hundreds of deaths throughout Europe and the former Soviet republics since a resurgence in their use began in Estonia in the early 2000s.

chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Opioids (all classes)

chunks.text: Binding profile: μ-opioid receptor agonist (full)

- Alcohol (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess. Memory blackouts are likely)
- Benzodiazepines (Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)
- Cocaine (Stimulants increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of opiates than normal. If the stimulant wears off first then the opiate may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest.)

- MXE (This combination can potentiate the effects of the opioid)

- Tramadol (Concomitant use of tramadol increases the seizure risk in individuals taking other opioids. These agents are often individually epileptogenic and may have additive effects on seizure threshold during coadministration. The interaction will cause greater inhibition and risk of injury. DPH reduces histamine release by opioids, which reduces the itching side effect from opioids. DPH may reduce the nausea caused by opioids. DPH inhibits CYP2D6 activity which can lead to a reduction of effects in some opioids and potentiation of effects in others.)

There appear to be two types of interaction, an excitatory and a depressive one. Symptoms of the excitatory reaction may include agitation, headache, diaphoresis, hyperpyrexia, flushing, shivering, myoclonus, rigidity, tremor, diarrhea, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, and coma. Death has occurred in some cases.)

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acrylfentanyl is a synthetic opioid of the anilinopiperidine class and a structural analog of fentanyl that has been sold online as a designer drug. It is reported to be slightly more potent than fentanyl itself, with a longer duration of action. Very little reliable information exists regarding its safe use or dosage parameters. It is considered potentially neurotoxic and carcinogenic, and overdose carries significant risk of fatal respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a potent fentanyl analog, it carries the high addiction potential characteristic of opioids.

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text: Has been described as potentially carcinogenic.

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Has been described as potentially neurotoxic.

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text: Acrylfentanyl is a highly potent opioid analgesic that acts at the μ-opioid receptor. In animal studies, it displaces naloxone with an IC50 of 1.4 nM, making it slightly more potent than fentanyl itself (1.6 nM). Because acrylamide derivatives are often used in drug discovery to produce covalent inhibitors that bind irreversibly to their targets, acrylfentanyl has been claimed to be naloxone-resistant. However, acute intoxication studies in mice have demonstrated that naloxone can displace acrylfentanyl from the opioid receptor.

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text: Opioids (full cross-tolerance expected with all μ-opioid receptor agonists)

chunks.title: Acrylfentanyl
chunks.text:
Acrylfentanyl emerged as a novel psychoactive substance in the designer drug market during the mid-2010s as part of a broader wave of illicit fentanyl analogs. The compound is a structural analog of fentanyl, featuring an acryloyl group modification, and was primarily distributed through online vendors catering to the research chemical market.

The substance came to significant public health attention in summer 2016 when it was linked to a cluster of fatal overdoses across Scandinavia, including twenty deaths in Sweden and two deaths in Denmark. These fatalities prompted rapid regulatory responses, with Sweden classifying acrylfentanyl as an illegal medicine in August 2016. The compound represents one of numerous fentanyl analogs that proliferated during this period as manufacturers sought to circumvent existing controlled substance legislation while meeting demand for potent synthetic opioids.

chunks.title: Adinazolam
chunks.text: Adinazolam is a triazolobenzodiazepine developed by Jackson B. Hester in the 1980s as an attempt to enhance the antidepressant properties of alprazolam. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and notable antidepressant effects, distinguishing it from most benzodiazepines. Adinazolam was never approved by the FDA and never reached the public pharmaceutical market. It reemerged around 2015 as a designer drug, raising concerns about unregulated use and misuse potential.

chunks.title: Adinazolam
chunks.text: Prolonged use can result in physical dependence. Reducing the dose too quickly may cause withdrawal, from rebound anxiety and insomnia through severe outcomes such as seizures.

chunks.title: Adinazolam
chunks.text: Extended use carries the possibility of psychological dependence, where individuals may become reliant on the medication to manage anxiety symptoms. As a benzodiazepine, it is classified as habit-forming.

chunks.title: Adinazolam
chunks.text: Seizures can occur as a withdrawal symptom following rapid dose reduction or cessation after prolonged use. This risk is associated with benzodiazepine dependence rather than acute intoxication.

chunks.title: Adinazolam

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil is a eugeroic stimulant of the benzhydryl class that acts as a prodrug for modafinil. Discovered in 1974 by chemists at the French pharmaceutical company Laboratoires Lafon during screening for analgesic compounds, it was formerly marketed under the brand name Olmifon. It promotes wakefulness and alertness without amphetamine-like effects. Long-term use is not advised due to potential liver stress from elevated hepatic enzymes associated with its metabolism.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil is considered not addictive with a low potential for abuse. It does not appear to be capable of causing psychological dependence among most users.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Mania has been reported as a side effect, particularly in individuals with a predisposition to mood disorders such as bipolar disorder. Confusion, aggression, and overstimulation may also occur but are described as transitory effects that resolve upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil is contraindicated in individuals with epilepsy.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Prolonged use may cause elevated liver enzymes and slight hepatotoxicity due to the requirement for hepatic metabolism to convert adrafinil to its active metabolite modafinil; occasional use at typical doses appears to carry minimal hepatic risk.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Long-term supplementation is not advised. Contraindicated in individuals with pre-existing liver disease or dysfunction. Adrafinil was voluntarily withdrawn from the French market in 2011 due to an unfavorable risk-benefit ratio.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil is a prodrug that is primarily converted to modafinil in vivo, producing nearly identical pharmacological effects once the active metabolite has accumulated to sufficient concentrations. In animal studies, its locomotor-stimulating effects are blocked by α1-adrenergic and α2-adrenergic receptor antagonists, suggesting involvement of postsynaptic adrenergic signaling in its wakefulness-promoting activity. However, neither adrafinil nor modafinil has been found to bind the α1-adrenergic receptor directly, and the evidence for adrenergic agonism is considered weak. Modafinil has been identified as a weak, atypical inhibitor of the dopamine transporter, and this action may account for some or all of its pharmacological effects.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil is metabolized hepatically and may follow one of two pathways: the primary route converts it to the active metabolite modafinil, while a secondary route produces inactive modafinilic acid directly without prior conversion to modafinil. This dual pathway may account for adrafinil's lower potency relative to modafinil. Modafinil is itself further metabolized to inactive modafinilic acid and modafinil sulfone. As a prodrug, adrafinil requires time for its active metabolite to accumulate to effective concentrations in the bloodstream.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: Adrafinil was discovered in 1974 by two chemists working at the French pharmaceutical company Laboratoires Lafon. The compound emerged unexpectedly during a screening program aimed at identifying novel analgesic agents. Rather than demonstrating pain-relieving properties, pharmacological studies revealed that adrafinil produced psychostimulant-like effects in animals, including hyperactivity and sustained wakefulness. Two years after the initial discovery, in 1976, researchers identified modafinil as the primary active metabolite responsible for adrafinil's wakefulness-promoting effects. Modafinil demonstrated greater potency than its parent compound in animal studies and was subsequently selected for parallel clinical development alongside adrafinil.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text: The first human trials of adrafinil were conducted between 1977 and 1978, specifically investigating its potential for treating narcolepsy. Alexander Shulgin published the first detailed account of the compound's synthesis and pharmacology in 1980 in the journal Communications in Psychopharmacology. Despite this publication, adrafinil remained an extremely obscure chemical for nearly two decades. The drug reached the French market in 1984 under the trade name Olmifon, with approval for narcolepsy treatment following in 1985.

chunks.title: Adrafinil
chunks.text:
While adrafinil was establishing its presence in European markets, its more potent metabolite modafinil continued through clinical development, receiving approval in France in 1994 and subsequently in the United States in 1998. Both compounds were marketed simultaneously, though modafinil gained significantly more international traction.

In 2001, the American pharmaceutical company Cephalon acquired Laboratoires Lafon, gaining control of both adrafinil and modafinil products. A decade later, in September 2011, Cephalon voluntarily discontinued Olmifon following a reassessment by French regulatory authorities that determined the drug had an unfavorable risk-benefit ratio. While adrafinil was withdrawn from the legitimate pharmaceutical market, modafinil continued to be marketed globally.

Following its pharmaceutical discontinuation, adrafinil gained renewed attention in the late 1990s and early 2000s as a commercially produced research chemical and purported nootropic supplement, particularly in markets where it remained unscheduled.

chunks.title: Afloqualone
chunks.text: Afloqualone is a GABAergic depressant of the quinazolinone class and an analogue of methaqualone. Developed in the 1970s by the Japanese pharmaceutical company Tanabe Seiyaku, it produces sedative and muscle-relaxant effects. Though it has seen some clinical use and recreational popularity in Japan, it never achieved widespread adoption due to notable photosensitization side effects that can cause skin problems such as dermatitis.

chunks.title: AH-7921
chunks.text: AH-7921 is a synthetic opioid analgesic with an atypical structure, selective for the μ-opioid receptor with a potency approaching that of morphine. It was developed in the 1970s by Allen and Hanburys in the United Kingdom but never progressed to clinical trials. It appeared on the research chemical market around 2012 and has been linked to over a dozen fatalities, most involving co-administration of other CNS depressants. Respiratory depression is a primary safety concern.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: AL-LAD is a semi-synthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class and a close structural analog of LSD. First described in scientific literature during the 1970s, it was further investigated by Andrew J. Hoffman and David Nichols in 1984 and subsequently documented by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. It entered the research chemical market around 2013 as a grey-market alternative to LSD. Users often report enhanced visual activity with comparatively reduced cognitive intensity relative to LSD.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: No physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms have been documented. As with LSD, AL-LAD does not appear to produce physical dependence, though formal studies have not been conducted.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: AL-LAD is non-habit forming and the desire to use it can actually decrease with use. It is considered self-regulating in the same manner as LSD and other classic psychedelics.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: AL-LAD may act as a potential trigger for psychotic episodes in those with underlying psychiatric conditions. Those with a personal or family history of mental illness are advised not to use this substance. Delusions and adverse psychological reactions become more likely at higher doses, though overt psychosis appears uncommon in otherwise healthy individuals using the substance alone.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Seizures are rare but have been reported, primarily in those who are genetically predisposed to them, particularly when accompanied by physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, fatigue, or undernourishment. Those with preexisting seizure disorders should avoid AL-LAD.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: No studies have examined AL-LAD for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data is available for AL-LAD.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Full baseline tolerance is typically restored after approximately 14 days of abstinence from AL-LAD and other serotonergic psychedelics. Some sources suggest noticeable effects may return after 4-7 days, though full sensitivity requires the longer abstinence period.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Serotonergic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, DMT)

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of AL-LAD develops almost immediately after ingestion. As with other serotonergic psychedelics, repeated dosing within a short timeframe will result in significantly diminished effects unless the dose is substantially increased.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Approximately 5-7 days after ingestion, tolerance is estimated to reduce to roughly half of its peak level.

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: AL-LAD was first synthesized and described in the scientific literature in 1976. The compound received further attention in 1984 when researchers Andrew J. Hoffman and David Nichols investigated it as part of a broader series of LSD analogues, which also included ETH-LAD and PRO-LAD. This academic interest culminated in 1997 when Alexander Shulgin documented the substance in his landmark book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known And Loved), providing a dose range of 80-160 µg and a duration of 6-8 hours. Shulgin characterized AL-LAD as "one of the several very potent compounds in a large series of nor-LSD analogues."

chunks.title: AL-LAD
chunks.text: Despite this early academic documentation, AL-LAD saw little to no recreational use until 2013, when it emerged on the online research chemical market. The compound quickly gained traction as a grey-market alternative to LSD, commonly marketed alongside other novel lysergamides such as 1P-LSD, ALD-52, and ETH-LAD. By 2015, the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (EMCDDA) reported its presence in the European drug market for the first time, marking its transition from an obscure research compound to a recognized designer drug. The substance is sometimes referred to by the street name "Aladdin."

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol (ethanol) is a central nervous system depressant and one of the most widely used psychoactive substances in human history, with evidence of consumption dating back thousands of years. It acts primarily through GABAergic mechanisms to produce anxiolytic, euphoriant, and sedative effects. At common doses, alcohol reduces inhibition and increases sociability, while higher doses can cause blackouts and potentially fatal respiratory depression. Despite its legal status in most countries, alcohol carries significant addiction potential and causes serious physical and psychological harm with chronic heavy use.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol causes significant physical dependence with chronic use. Withdrawal symptoms range from mild effects such as insomnia, tremors, and irritability to severe and potentially fatal symptoms including delirium tremens, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol is highly addictive and habit-forming, with psychological dependence developing commonly with regular use. Cultural normalization and global marketing contribute to widespread patterns of problematic use.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Seizures are a recognized severe symptom of alcohol withdrawal and can be potentially fatal. Chronic alcohol abuse is also associated with epilepsy.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: All alcoholic drinks including red and white wine, beer, and liquor are linked with cancer. Cancer risk increases with the amount consumed.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic alcohol use causes progressive liver damage ranging from fatty liver to hepatitis and cirrhosis; the liver is the organ most dramatically impacted by alcohol, with damage severity correlating with cumulative exposure.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Liver damage is a well-documented consequence of chronic alcohol use and can be irreversible in advanced stages.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term alcohol abuse can cause irreversible brain damage, alcoholic dementia, polyneuropathy, and epilepsy; chronic heavy use is associated with cognitive impairment and neurological deterioration.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: CNS depression is an acute effect; chronic use leads to structural and functional brain changes.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic alcohol use is associated with heart disease and can contribute to cardiovascular failure; acute overdose may cause cardiovascular collapse.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk increases with cumulative lifetime exposure and heavy drinking patterns.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Alcohol causes gastrointestinal irritation and is associated with peptic ulcers and pancreatitis with chronic use.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Alcohol consumption during pregnancy can cause brain damage to the fetus and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs), a range of developmental problems resulting from prenatal alcohol exposure.

chunks.title: Alcohol

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol primarily acts as a central nervous system depressant through positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors, enhancing the inhibitory effects of gamma-aminobutyric acid in the brain. It simultaneously functions as an antagonist at NMDA glutamate receptors, reducing excitatory neurotransmission. Alcohol also acts as an agonist at glycine receptors and inhibits voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels. The substance directly affects multiple additional neurotransmitter systems including those of acetylcholine and serotonin. The pleasurable effects of alcohol ingestion result from increased levels of dopamine and endogenous opioids in reward pathways.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol is rapidly absorbed after oral ingestion via the stomach and intestines into the bloodstream. It is highly water-soluble and diffuses passively throughout the body, including the brain. Approximately 90% or more is metabolized hepatically, primarily by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase and cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2E1. One standard drink is sufficient to nearly saturate the liver's metabolic capacity. The remaining 5 to 10% is excreted unchanged in breath, urine, and sweat.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text:
Alcohol stands as one of humanity's oldest recreational substances, with evidence of its production and consumption spanning at least 13,000 years. The earliest known beer was likely brewed from barley by the Natufian culture in the Middle East around this time. In northern China, alcoholic beverages were being produced as early as 7000 to 6650 BCE, while the earliest evidence of winemaking dates to approximately 6000 to 5800 BCE in Georgia in the South Caucasus.

The ancient Romans developed sophisticated viticulture, with Pliny the Elder documenting what he considered the golden age of Roman winemaking during the 2nd century BCE, a period marked by extensive vineyard cultivation throughout the empire.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: The Gin Craze represents a notable period in alcohol history, occurring during the first half of the 18th century when gin consumption increased dramatically in Great Britain, particularly in London. By 1743, per capita consumption in England had reached 2.2 gallons (10 litres) of gin annually. This widespread consumption was viewed as a primary driver of crime in London, prompting legislative action. The Sale of Spirits Act 1750, commonly known as the Gin Act 1751, was enacted by the Parliament of Great Britain specifically to curb the consumption of gin and other distilled spirits.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text:
The modern era saw various governmental attempts to regulate alcohol consumption. The Royal Navy maintained a rum ration, providing sailors with a daily allotment of rum from 1866 until its abolition in 1970, when concerns arose that strong alcohol consumption could impair the steady hands required for operating machinery.

Several countries implemented rationing systems to control consumption. Sweden employed the Bratt System from 1919 to 1955, while Finland used a similar approach from 1944 to 1970. Under these systems, citizens permitted to consume alcohol received a booklet in which purchases were recorded, limiting the amount that could be bought within a given period. Estonia briefly operated a comparable system from 1920 to 1925.

The United States enacted the most sweeping alcohol regulation with Prohibition, banning the production, importation, transportation, and sale of alcoholic beverages from 1920 until the Twenty-first Amendment repealed the ban on December 5, 1933. The Medicinal Liquor Prescriptions Act of 1933 addressed abuses of medicinal alcohol prescriptions that had occurred during the Prohibition era.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol consumption is deeply embedded in social practices and rituals across cultures, often serving as a cornerstone of community gatherings and personal milestones. Drinking culture encompasses the traditions and social behaviours surrounding alcohol as both a recreational substance and social lubricant. Drinking establishments such as bars and nightclubs center primarily on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages, while parties, festivals, and social gatherings commonly incorporate alcohol. Research from the United Kingdom found correlations between regular moderate drinking at community pubs and measures of social wellbeing, including higher trust in others and stronger connections with local communities. These establishments showed longer, more focused conversations and different social dynamics compared to city centre bars, though analysis suggested that life satisfaction led to pub attendance rather than the reverse.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: The relationship between religion and alcohol reflects diverse cultural and spiritual traditions. While some religions strictly prohibit alcohol consumption, viewing it as harmful to spiritual and physical wellbeing, others incorporate it into sacred rituals. Christianity uses sacramental wine in its ceremonies, while Shinto purification rituals include the offering and moderate consumption of omiki, a sacramental sake. This spectrum of religious attitudes toward alcohol illustrates its complex role in human spiritual practice throughout history.

chunks.title: Alcohol
chunks.text: Alcohol has maintained a long association with military operations, earning the colloquial designation "liquid courage" for its historical role in preparing troops for battle. Beyond its use before combat, alcohol served to anesthetize injured soldiers and mark military victories. It has also functioned as a coping mechanism for combat stress reactions and as a means of transitioning from combat conditions back to everyday life.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: ALD-52 is a psychedelic lysergamide structurally related to LSD, first synthesized by Albert Hofmann at Sandoz in 1957. It functions as a prodrug that readily converts to LSD in the body, producing virtually indistinguishable effects at comparable potency. The compound gained notoriety through false claims that it was distributed as 'Orange Sunshine' during the 1960s counterculture era. Like LSD, it is not considered addictive or toxic, though unpredictable adverse psychological reactions remain possible.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: As a classical psychedelic lysergamide, ALD-52 is not considered to have significant abuse potential or habit-forming properties, though adverse effects become increasingly likely with higher doses.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: Unpredictable adverse reactions including anxiety, paranoia, delusions, and psychosis are possible, particularly among those predisposed to psychiatric disorders. These reactions can occur spontaneously even among experienced users. ALD-52 may act as a potential trigger for those with underlying psychiatric conditions, and use is discouraged for individuals with a personal or family history of bipolar disorder or schizoaffective disorder.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: Although no cases of ALD-52-induced seizures have been documented, it is believed to have a similar seizure risk as LSD. LSD is thought to lower the seizure threshold, though seizures are very rarely reported and believed to only be a risk to those predisposed to them, particularly when combined with physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, undernourishment, overheating, or general fatigue.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: ALD-52 functions as a prodrug for LSD, with a large percentage of the administered dose metabolizing into LSD in the body. The conversion to LSD has been confirmed with human liver enzymes in vitro and in rodents in vivo. Through its metabolite LSD, ALD-52 acts as a partial agonist at multiple serotonin receptor subtypes, including 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT6 receptors, with the psychedelic effects believed to primarily stem from activity at the 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT1A receptors. The parent compound ALD-52 itself shows dramatically reduced affinities for the serotonin 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors compared to LSD, with markedly reduced activational potency and efficacy at the 5-HT2A receptor, while agonistic activity at the 5-HT2B and 5-HT2C receptors was lost entirely. ALD-52 is also expected to act as an agonist at dopamine receptors such as D2 through its conversion to LSD.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: ALD-52 acts as a prodrug that is readily converted to LSD following administration. The formation of LSD from ALD-52 is primarily mediated by CYP3A4, which catalyzes the deacetylation of ALD-52 into LSD. This conversion can be largely blocked by the strong cytochrome P450 inhibitor ketoconazole. CYP2D6 is also involved in hydroxylation processes. In addition to LSD as the primary metabolite, ALD-52 is metabolized into N-deethyl ALD-52 and N6-demethyl ALD-52 (nor-ALD-52). Circulating levels of LSD following administration are virtually identical between ALD-52 and the related prodrug 1P-LSD.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: ALD-52 was first synthesized and described in the scientific literature by Albert Hofmann and Franz Troxler at Sandoz in 1957 as part of Hofmann's broader study of LSD analogs. The properties and effects of ALD-52 were studied and reported in the late 1950s and early 1960s, though it remains unclear whether the compound ever circulated as a recreational drug during this period in a manner similar to LSD.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: In 1968 and 1969, a famous batch of LSD known as "Orange Sunshine" was synthesized by Nick Sand and Tim Scully and made widely available in California during the Summer of Love era. For decades, this "Orange Sunshine" was believed by many in the counterculture to be ALD-52 rather than LSD. When Sand and Scully were apprehended by law enforcement in 1973, they argued in court that they had distributed ALD-52 rather than LSD, as ALD-52 was not a controlled substance at the time. However, the prosecution countered that ALD-52 readily converts into LSD and that its synthesis requires going through LSD as an intermediate. Additionally, a sample of supposed ALD-52 that Sand and Scully provided via a friend was tested and found to be LSD. The pair were found guilty, including of lying in court, with Scully receiving a 20-year sentence and Sand receiving 15 years.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text: In 2005, Nick Sand publicly revealed that "Orange Sunshine" was simply a particularly well-made batch of LSD dosed at 300 micrograms per unit. Tim Scully confirmed this in a 2017 Reddit AMA, explaining that the claim about ALD-52 arose from an "ill-advised desperate defense strategy that failed miserably" during his trial. Both later expressed regret over their unsuccessful attempt to exploit a legal loophole. The subject of the "Orange Sunshine" LSD was covered in the 2015 documentary "The Sunshine Makers" by Cosmo Feilding Mellen.

chunks.title: ALD-52
chunks.text:
ALD-52 is a key parent compound of the 1-acyllysergamide LSD prodrugs and served as inspiration for the development of subsequent compounds in this series such as 1P-LSD, 1V-LSD, and 1cP-LSD. These LSD prodrugs were developed by Lizard Labs and emerged as novel designer drugs starting in the mid-2010s.

The detection of 1P-LSD slightly preceded that of ALD-52, having been first encountered in 2015. ALD-52 itself was first definitively encountered as a novel designer drug in Europe in 2016, and soon thereafter was detected in Japan and Brazil. While ALD-52 had been thought to act as a prodrug of LSD since at least the 1960s, this was not definitively confirmed until formal studies were conducted in the 2010s and 2020s.

chunks.text: Swiss chemist at Sandoz who first synthesized ALD-52 alongside Franz Troxler in 1957 as part of his broader research into LSD analogs. Hofmann is best known for his earlier discovery of LSD's psychoactive properties in 1943.

chunks.title: ALEPH
chunks.text: ALEPH is a psychedelic amphetamine of the substituted phenethylamine class, notable for being the first sulfur-containing phenethylamine evaluated for central nervous system activity as a stimulant or psychedelic. Its full chemical name is 2,5-dimethoxy-4-methylthioamphetamine. The substance remains relatively unexplored compared to its higher homologues in the ALEPH series, a group named after the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet due to their potentially extraordinary shared properties.

chunks.title: ALEPH
chunks.text:
ALEPH holds a notable place in psychedelic chemistry as the first sulfur-containing phenethylamine to be evaluated for central nervous system activity, specifically for its potential stimulant or psychedelic properties. This pioneering incorporation of a methylthio group at the 4-position of the amphetamine structure opened a new avenue of exploration in psychoactive compound development.

The substance derives its name from the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a designation chosen to reflect the potentially extraordinary properties shared by this structural class. Despite its historical significance as a founding member of this series, ALEPH itself remains relatively unexplored compared to its derivatives. The compound has two positional isomers, known as ortho-DOT and meta-DOT, though these have received even less investigation.

The structural insights gained from ALEPH proved more valuable than the compound itself. Three higher homologues in the ALEPH series received more thorough examination, but the most significant developments came from exploring the two-carbon homologues, which led to the creation of the 2C-T family of compounds.

chunks.title: ALEPH-2
chunks.text: ALEPH-2 is a rare psychedelic of the substituted amphetamine and phenethylamine classes, belonging to both the Aleph series and DOx family. First described by Alexander Shulgin in 1978 and later documented in his 1991 book PiHKAL, it functions as the DOx analogue of 2C-T-2. It is reported to be potent and to produce long-lasting, highly visual experiences. Very little human use data is available.

A more comprehensive account of ALEPH-2's synthesis, dosage, duration, and qualitative effects appeared in Shulgin's 1991 book PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved), where it was catalogued as entry #4. Despite this documentation, ALEPH-2 has remained an exceptionally rare compound with very limited human use reported in the decades since its initial characterization.

chunks.title: Allobarbital
chunks.text: Allobarbital is a barbiturate derivative invented in 1912 by Ernst Preiswerk and Ernst Grether while working for CIBA. It was used primarily as an anticonvulsant, though it also saw application in treating insomnia and anxiety, and as an adjuvant to boost the activity of analgesic medications. Never widely adopted compared to better-known barbiturates, it has largely been replaced by newer drugs with improved safety profiles. As with all barbiturates, combination with other CNS depressants should be avoided.

chunks.title: Allylescaline
chunks.text: Allylescaline is a psychedelic substance in the phenethylamine and scaline classes, and is structurally related to mescaline and escaline. Otakar Leminger reported the compound in 1972, and Alexander Shulgin later discussed it in his 1991 book PiHKAL. It appeared as a novel designer drug in 2013. Allylescaline remains relatively uncommon, with little documented history of human use.
