chunks.title: Allylescaline
chunks.text:
Allylescaline was first documented in the scientific literature by Czech chemist Otakar Leminger in 1972. The compound received broader attention when American chemist Alexander Shulgin synthesized and characterized its psychoactive effects, publishing his findings in the 1991 book PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story. In PiHKAL, Shulgin described allylescaline's subjective effects and established dosage parameters based on his bioassay methodology.

The compound remained relatively obscure for over two decades following PiHKAL's publication. It emerged on the research chemical market in 2013, when it was identified as a novel designer drug being sold online. This appearance prompted regulatory responses in several countries during the mid-2010s.

chunks.title: Alpha-GPC
chunks.text: Alpha-GPC is a naturally occurring choline compound found in the brain, classified as a nootropic. It functions as a highly bioavailable acetylcholine precursor that efficiently crosses the blood-brain barrier, making it the most effective orally supplemented choline prodrug. It has been investigated for its potential in treating Alzheimer's disease and other dementias. Athletes also use it for its purported performance-enhancing properties. It is widely available as a dietary supplement.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Alprazolam is a fast-acting depressant of the triazolobenzodiazepine class. Developed by Jackson Hester Jr. at the Upjohn Company, it was patented in 1971 and approved for medical use in the United States in 1981. It is widely prescribed for the management of anxiety and panic disorders and remains one of the most commonly prescribed medications in the U.S. Regular or excessive use can lead to physical dependence and addiction.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops reliably with regular use, particularly at doses above 4 mg daily or with use exceeding six months. Withdrawal is potentially life-threatening and can include tremors, seizures, marked delirium, and in rare cases coma or death. Medical supervision and gradual tapering over weeks or months is essential; abrupt discontinuation is extremely dangerous.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Alprazolam is considered highly psychologically addictive with significant abuse potential. Its high binding affinity, high potency, and rapid onset increase abuse liability. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported among users seeking a 'high', which frequently leads to blackout states and impaired judgment.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Hallucinations are rare during alprazolam use. Paradoxical reactions including mania, agitation, and rage occur with an incidence below 1% in the general population but are more frequent in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, children, and patients on high-dose regimens. Delirium and hallucinations may also occur during withdrawal.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Alprazolam itself has anticonvulsant properties during use. However, abrupt discontinuation after regular use carries significant seizure risk that can be life-threatening. Paradoxical increased seizure activity has been reported in epileptics. Gradual dose tapering over weeks is essential to minimize withdrawal seizure risk.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Misuse of alprazolam has been shown to cause cognitive impairment including memory deficits; occasional use at therapeutic doses does not appear to cause lasting neurological damage.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Anterograde amnesia is a common acute effect. Retrograde amnesia has been demonstrated in animal models. Long-term heavy use may cause emotional dissociation or derealization. Severe overdose may result in respiratory depression and coma.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Injection of oral alprazolam preparations has caused dangerous damage to blood vessels, embolization, and rhabdomyolysis; this risk is specific to injection misuse and does not apply to oral administration.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Physical occlusion of blood vessels by tablet binders and particulate matter

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Anecdotally reported in recreational misuse contexts involving injection of dissolved tablets.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression can occur at high doses or in overdose, particularly when combined with other depressants; patients with pre-existing respiratory impairment are at increased risk.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: CNS depression affecting brainstem respiratory centers

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiopulmonary collapse has been observed following massive intravenous doses in animal experiments.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: 4-hydroxyalprazolam (weakly active, 20% binding affinity of parent)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: α-hydroxyalprazolam (weakly active, 66% binding affinity of parent)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Alprazolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, binding nonselectively to the benzodiazepine site on the receptor complex. This enhances the effects of GABA, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, by increasing chloride ion conductance through the receptor channel, hyperpolarizing neurons and reducing their excitability. The drug affects receptor complexes containing α1 subunits (associated with sedation and amnesia) and α2 subunits (associated with anxiolysis). Alprazolam also acts as an agonist at the translocator protein and suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity. Compared to some other benzodiazepines, alprazolam administration increases extracellular dopamine concentrations in the striatum.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Alprazolam is rapidly absorbed orally with high bioavailability and readily crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is primarily metabolized in the liver via CYP3A4, with minor contributions from CYP3A5, CYP3A7, and CYP2C9. Hydroxylation produces at least 29 metabolites, primarily 4-hydroxyalprazolam and α-hydroxyalprazolam, though these are present at low concentrations with reduced receptor affinity and contribute minimally to the drug's effects. The majority of the dose is eliminated in the urine, largely as unmetabolized alprazolam.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Rapidly absorbed with peak blood levels reached in 1-2 hours
Evening dosing may increase peak concentrations by approximately 30% compared to morning dosing
Readily crosses the blood-brain barrier
About 80% binds to blood proteins, primarily albumin

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Wide individual variation with reported range of 6-27 hours in healthy adults
Half-life is significantly longer in elderly individuals (average 16 hours), obese patients (average 22 hours), and those with liver disease (up to 65 hours)
Asian individuals may have approximately 25% longer half-life compared to Caucasians
Drugs that block CYP3A4 enzyme slow elimination and extend duration

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Following cessation, tolerance typically returns to baseline within 7-14 days. However, individuals with prolonged or intensive use patterns may require significantly longer periods for complete tolerance reset, proportional to the duration and intensity of their prior use.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Benzodiazepines (all members of the class)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Tolerance to sedative-hypnotic effects can emerge quickly, often after only several days of uninterrupted use. Tolerance to cognitive impairment and sedation appears to develop over 1-3 weeks of daily administration, with some research indicating that impairment on most tests resolves by this timeframe. Receptor studies have demonstrated reduced GABA-A benzodiazepine receptor density after approximately 24 days of regular use at therapeutic doses.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Alprazolam was first synthesized in 1971 by J.B. Hester at the Upjohn Company, a pharmaceutical manufacturer that would later become part of Pfizer. The compound was developed as a triazolobenzodiazepine, featuring a triazole ring fused to the core benzodiazepine structure. Following its synthesis, alprazolam was patented in the United States in 1976.

The drug received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on October 16, 1981, for the treatment of panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. It was subsequently marketed under the brand name Xanax in the United States, with various other brand names used internationally including Tafil, Kalma, Ksalol, and Niravam.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Alprazolam has become the most commonly prescribed and misused benzodiazepine in the United States. It has consistently ranked as the most prescribed psychiatric medication in the country, with prescriptions exceeding 40 million annually. This widespread medical use has contributed to its significant presence in both clinical and recreational contexts.

The drug's high binding affinity, potency, and rapid onset of effects have contributed to its abuse potential. It has accumulated numerous street names reflecting its cultural prominence, including "Xannies," "Bars," "Z-bars," "Handlebars," and "Footballs," with the latter terms often referencing the shape of different tablet formulations.

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzodiazepines (all members of the class)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (benzodiazepine site); Translocator protein

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Alprazolam — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol (Ethanol ingestion may potentiate the CNS effects of many benzodiazepines. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.)
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Opioids (Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)
- Tramadol (Central nervous system- and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. Vomit aspiration is a risk when passed out, lay down in recovery position if ingested.)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Alprazolam — unsafe combinations:
- Diphenhydramine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely. Low medical doses are unlikely to be of concern.)
- PCP (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely)

chunks.title: Alprazolam
chunks.text:
Alprazolam — caution combinations:
- DXM (Small doses of benzos can end a bad trip, but both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and this can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Ketamine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- MXE (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess.)

chunks.title: AM-2201
chunks.text: AM-2201 is a synthetic cannabinoid of the AM series, discovered by Alexandros Makriyannis at Northeastern University. It acts as a potent full agonist at cannabinoid receptors, with active doses in the microgram range. Widely distributed in branded smoking blends such as Black Mamba, it was central to a wave of synthetic cannabinoid addiction in British cities around 2017. AM-2201 carries significant risks including convulsions and episodes of extreme anxiety and paranoia.

chunks.title: AM-2201
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. AM-2201 was central to a surge of addiction amongst homeless populations in British cities circa 2017, suggesting significant psychological dependence potential with regular use.

chunks.title: AM-2201
chunks.text: Produces extreme anxiety, acute fear, and intense paranoia that can be almost overwhelming. Users report terror that is difficult to articulate, with effects described as cannabis-type anxiety multiplied by a factor of 100. These severe psychological reactions can occur even at modest doses.

chunks.title: AM-2201
chunks.text: Convulsions have been reported at doses as low as 10 mg. Caution is strongly recommended due to this seizure risk.

chunks.title: AM-2201
chunks.text: Binding profile: CB1 and CB2 receptor full agonist

chunks.title: AM-694
chunks.text: AM-694 is a synthetic cannabinoid of the benzoylindole class that acts as a potent and selective CB1 receptor agonist. Originally developed for scientific research into cannabinoid receptor mapping, it emerged on the recreational market around 2010 as a component of herbal smoking mixtures following bans on earlier synthetic cannabinoids. Notably, oral consumption should be strictly avoided, as AM-694 may metabolize into highly toxic fluoroacetic acid.

chunks.title: AM-694
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Oral administration may produce the highly toxic metabolite fluoroacetic acid, posing significant systemic toxicity risk; this route of administration should be strictly avoided.

chunks.title: AM-694
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Metabolic defluorination of the fluorine-containing structure may generate fluoroacetic acid, a potent inhibitor of the citric acid cycle

chunks.title: AM-694
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Based on recent reports; oral route specifically implicated. Other routes of administration may carry different risk profiles.

chunks.title: AM-694
chunks.text: Binding profile: CB1 receptor agonist (full); CB2 receptor agonist (full)

chunks.title: Amfecloral
chunks.text: Amfecloral is a discontinued combination drug of the substituted amphetamine class that acts as a prodrug to both dextroamphetamine and chloral hydrate, combining stimulant and sedative-hypnotic properties. It was FDA-approved as an anti-obesity anorectic and marketed under the brand name Acutran. Notably, it was reported to display little to no stimulant activity, likely due to the sedating effects of its chloral hydrate component. Production ceased in 1973 following increased regulatory scrutiny.

chunks.title: Amfecloral
chunks.text: Physical dependence may develop with regular use due to its dual action as a prodrug to both amphetamine and chloral hydrate, with potential for withdrawal symptoms from both stimulant and sedative components.

chunks.title: Amfecloral
chunks.text: As a prodrug to amphetamine, amfecloral carries significant psychological addiction potential consistent with the amphetamine class, including risk of compulsive use and difficulty discontinuing.

chunks.title: Amfecloral
chunks.text: Dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (from amphetamine metabolite)

chunks.title: Amfecloral
chunks.text: Binding profile: Dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (from amphetamine metabolite); GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (from chloral hydrate/trichloroethanol metabolite)

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.text: Amfonelic acid is a dopaminergic stimulant and research chemical with antibiotic properties. It was discovered incidentally at Sterling-Winthrop during research on the antibiotic nalidixic acid. Clinical trials conducted in the 1970s were discontinued after the drug was found to exacerbate psychotic symptoms and produce undesirable stimulant effects. A potent and highly selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor, it has been available on the grey market since 2013 and is considered habit-forming.

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming with demonstrated abuse potential. Rats self-administer amfonelic acid in a dose-dependent manner, and the compound displays 150% the stimulant potency of dextroamphetamine in discriminatory substitution studies.

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.text: Clinical evaluation was discontinued after amfonelic acid was found to exacerbate psychotic symptoms in schizophrenic patients. Visual and auditory hallucinations have been reported among adverse effects.

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.text: Amfonelic acid is a 4-quinolone derivative with antibacterial properties, though it is less active as an antibacterial agent compared to other 4-quinolones.

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Studies in mammalian cells have shown amfonelic acid to be markedly more toxic than related 4-quinolone compounds; sublethal doses induced changes in cellular protein production patterns, suggesting effects on gene transcription.

chunks.title: Amfonelic-Acid
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Possible interference with gene transcription in mammalian cells, evidenced by altered protein production patterns at sublethal doses

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.text: Aminorex is a stimulant of the 2-amino-5-aryloxazoline class, developed by McNeil Laboratories in 1962. It was introduced as a prescription appetite suppressant in Europe in 1965 but withdrawn in 1972 after being found to cause pulmonary hypertension in roughly 0.2% of patients, linked to a number of deaths. Its stimulant potency falls between dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine. Aminorex can also be produced as a metabolite of levamisole, a common adulterant in illicit cocaine.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.text: Aminorex is classified as habit-forming and is approximately 2.5 times more potent than dextroamphetamine, suggesting significant psychological addiction potential consistent with potent stimulants.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aminorex causes pulmonary arterial hypertension in approximately 0.2% of patients, which led to its withdrawal from the market after being linked to a number of deaths.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors, either directly via agonism or indirectly via serotonin release, has been implicated in the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: This adverse effect was significant enough to result in market withdrawal in 1972 after introduction in 1965.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiac valvulopathy has been associated with aminorex use.

chunks.title: Aminorex
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors, either directly via agonism or indirectly via serotonin release, has been implicated in the development of cardiac valvulopathy.

chunks.text: Serotonin-dopamine-norepinephrine releasing agent (SNDRA)

chunks.title: Aminotadalafil
chunks.text: Aminotadalafil is a synthetic analogue of tadalafil, the active ingredient in the prescription erectile dysfunction medication Cialis. It gained notoriety for being found as an undisclosed ingredient in the 'Alpha Male' sexual enhancement supplement, raising significant safety concerns. As an unapproved pharmaceutical analogue marketed without proper labeling, it poses risks due to the absence of regulatory oversight and unknown drug interaction profiles.

chunks.title: Aminotadalafil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aminotadalafil is described as a Cialis/tadalafil analogue that was sold as an undeclared ingredient in a sexual-enhancement supplement.

chunks.title: Aminotadalafil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Unknowingly consuming an active tadalafil-like pharmaceutical can be dangerous for people using contraindicated medications such as nitrates.

chunks.title: Aminotadalafil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The extracted text frames the risk through undeclared exposure and contraindicated co-medications rather than direct toxicity data.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Amobarbital is a barbiturate derivative with sedative-hypnotic properties, first synthesized in Germany in 1923. Classified as a short to intermediate acting barbiturate, it has been used clinically for sedation, short-term insomnia management, and acute seizure control. Once widely misused, its popularity declined as benzodiazepines offered safer alternatives in overdose. Amobarbital carries a high risk of dependence with continued use, and dose-related central nervous system depression remains a primary safety concern.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with extended use. Withdrawal mimics delirium tremens and may be life-threatening, requiring medical supervision for discontinuation.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: High abuse potential with significant risk of psychological dependence. Amobarbital was widely misused recreationally, known on the street as 'Blue Heavens,' 'blue angels,' and 'blue devils,' and is classified as habit-forming.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Amobarbital acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABAA receptor, binding at the barbiturate site on alpha or beta subunits, which is distinct from both the GABA and benzodiazepine binding sites. This potentiates GABAergic inhibition by increasing chloride channel conductance and prolonging inhibitory postsynaptic currents. It also antagonizes AMPA and kainate-type glutamate receptors, reducing excitatory neurotransmission, and acts as an antagonist at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (alpha-4 and alpha-7 subtypes).

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Amobarbital is metabolized via hydroxylation to form 3'-hydroxyamobarbital and via N-glucosidation to form 1-(beta-D-glucopyranosyl)-amobarbital.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Potentiator; acts across alpha-1 through alpha-6 subunits

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text:
Amobarbital was first synthesized in Germany in 1923, emerging as a short to intermediate acting barbiturate derivative. The compound gained commercial prominence through Eli Lilly and Company, which manufactured it in the United States under the brand name Amytal. The medication was distinctively presented in bright blue bullet-shaped capsules called Pulvules, as well as pink tablets known as Diskets.

Eli Lilly also produced Tuinal, a combination product containing equal quantities of amobarbital and secobarbital, which remained in production until the late 1990s. The standalone Amytal product was discontinued in the 1980s as benzodiazepines emerged as the preferred class of sedative-hypnotic medications.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text:
When administered slowly by intravenous route, sodium amobarbital developed a reputation as a so-called "truth serum." This application was first employed clinically by William Bleckwenn at the University of Wisconsin, who used the drug to circumvent inhibitions in psychiatric patients during therapeutic sessions.

The United States armed forces utilized amobarbital during World War II in attempts to treat shell shock, with the goal of returning affected soldiers to front-line duties. This military application was subsequently discontinued.

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text:
Amobarbital became associated with several notable deaths in the entertainment industry. On the night of August 28, 1951, American actor Robert Walker died at 32 years old after his psychiatrist administered amobarbital for sedation while Walker was allegedly drinking. In 1968, British actor and comedian Tony Hancock died by suicide in Australia using amobarbital in combination with alcohol.

The drug was widely abused during its period of commercial availability. Its distinctive blue capsules gave rise to numerous street names including "blues," "blue angels," "blue birds," "blue devils," and "blue heavens."

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Barbiturates, Other GABAergic depressants

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (barbiturate site); AMPA receptor antagonist; Kainate receptor antagonist; Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist

chunks.title: Amobarbital
chunks.text:
Amobarbital — caution combinations:
- 1,2-Benzodiazepine
- Abaloparatide
- Abemaciclib
- Acalabrutinib
- Acebutolol

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine is a central nervous system stimulant of the substituted phenethylamine class, first discovered in 1887 by Lazăr Edeleanu. It exists as two enantiomers—levoamphetamine and dextroamphetamine—and serves as the parent compound of its own structural class, which includes substances such as methamphetamine and MDMA. Prescribed clinically for ADHD and narcolepsy, it is also used recreationally for its euphoriant and wakefulness-promoting properties.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Tolerance develops rapidly with recreational use, requiring increasingly larger doses. Withdrawal symptoms occur in roughly 88% of chronic high-dose users, persisting for 3-4 weeks with a marked crash phase during the first week. Symptoms include fatigue, depression, anxiety, irritability, intense hunger, disturbed sleep, and drug craving.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine has high abuse potential and can cause psychological dependence with chronic use. Addiction is a serious risk with heavy recreational use but is unlikely to arise from typical medical use at therapeutic doses. Cravings and withdrawal effects occur if use is suddenly discontinued.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Stimulant psychosis can occur with severe overdose or chronic heavy use, presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, delusions, and bizarre or violent behavior. Symptoms usually disappear within weeks after cessation, but approximately 5-15% of users fail to recover completely. Psychosis rarely arises from therapeutic use. Risk increases with multi-day use, sleep deprivation, and high doses.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine reduces seizure threshold and convulsions can occur at high doses. Fatal poisoning is usually preceded by convulsions and coma. Seizures are rare at typical doses but represent a serious risk in overdose situations.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects including hypertension, tachycardia, and arrhythmias occur during intoxication; severe hypertensive crises, heart attacks, and circulatory collapse are primarily associated with high doses or pre-existing cardiovascular conditions.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Sympathomimetic effects increase catecholamine release, causing vasoconstriction, elevated heart rate, and increased blood pressure

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Raynaud's phenomenon (reduced blood flow to extremities) and vasovagal responses also reported. Stroke risk increases with dose.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: No evidence of direct neurotoxicity in humans at typical doses; however, high-dose exposure may cause indirect neurotoxicity, particularly when hyperpyrexia occurs. Prolonged heavy use can lead to speech and thought disturbances.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Indirect neurotoxicity results from increased oxidative stress via reactive oxygen species and autoxidation of dopamine, causing dopamine terminal degeneration and reduced transporter and receptor function

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Animal models indicate hyperpyrexia (core body temperature ≥40°C) is necessary for development of amphetamine-induced neurotoxicity. Chronic consumption may favor brain hemorrhages and strokes.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Kidney damage is primarily associated with rhabdomyolysis from high-dose use, particularly when hyperthermia occurs; acute renal failure has been reported in overdose and fatality cases.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Myoglobin released from rhabdomyolysis-damaged muscle fibers causes acute tubular necrosis; ischemic renal failure from cardiovascular strain also contributes

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Urine becomes dark as rhabdomyolysis progresses. Renal damage ranges from mild to severe.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hepatic injury has been reported in overdose contexts; liver damage and failure are possible with chronic high-dose use.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Limited documentation of hepatotoxicity mechanism in sources.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use is associated with dental caries, tooth loss, and gingivitis; jaw tension causes bruxism leading to permanent tooth wear and cracking.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Prolonged dry mouth (xerostomia) reduces saliva's protective effects on teeth and gums, increasing caries risk; bruxism causes direct mechanical damage

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: More common with chronic heavy use patterns.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine exerts its primary pharmacological effects by promoting the release of dopamine and norepinephrine from presynaptic nerve terminals. It enters neurons via monoamine transporters (DAT, NET, and to a lesser extent SERT), where it acts as a competitive substrate that inhibits monoamine reuptake. Once inside the terminal, amphetamine displaces monoamines from vesicular storage by interacting with VMAT2, collapsing the vesicular pH gradient and expanding the cytosolic monoamine pool available for reverse transport. Amphetamine is also a potent full agonist at trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), activation of which triggers intracellular kinase cascades (PKA, PKC, CaMKIIα) that phosphorylate monoamine transporters, further promoting neurotransmitter efflux into the synapse. At very high doses, amphetamine weakly inhibits monoamine oxidase. It also inhibits the neuronal glutamate transporter EAAT3 (SLC1A1), reducing glutamate clearance and potentiating excitatory neurotransmission. The only known post-synaptic receptor at which amphetamine binds in humans is the 5-HT1A receptor, where it acts as an agonist with low micromolar affinity.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with oral bioavailability typically around 90%. Absorption is favored in more basic intestinal environments, where the drug exists in a more lipid-soluble form. Peak plasma concentrations are reached approximately 1 to 3 hours after oral administration. Roughly 20% of circulating amphetamine is bound to plasma proteins, and the drug distributes readily into most tissues including brain and cerebrospinal fluid. Amphetamine is metabolized hepatically, primarily by CYP2D6, along with dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH), flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3), butyrate-CoA ligase (XM-ligase), and glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT). The major metabolic pathways include aromatic hydroxylation, aliphatic hydroxylation, and N-dealkylation, though a significant portion of the drug is excreted unchanged. Elimination half-life varies by enantiomer and is strongly influenced by urinary pH: at normal urine pH, the d-enantiomer has a half-life of approximately 9 to 11 hours and the l-enantiomer 11 to 14 hours, with highly acidic urine reducing these to around 7 hours and highly alkaline urine extending them up to 34 hours.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Prolonged repeated amphetamine use can reduce responsiveness to many effects, often rapidly when chronic high doses are involved. As tolerance rises, larger doses may be needed for comparable effects. Outside medical settings, tolerance usually develops quickly and can reduce many beneficial effects. Different effects may also show tolerance on different timelines.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Amphetamine was first synthesized in 1887 by Romanian chemist Lazăr Edeleanu while working in Germany. Edeleanu originally named the compound phenylisopropylamine, though its central nervous system effects remained entirely unknown for the next four decades. The substance's stimulant properties were not discovered until 1927, when American chemist Gordon Alles independently resynthesized the compound while searching for a replacement for ephedrine. Alles subsequently reported that the drug possessed significant sympathomimetic properties, marking the beginning of scientific interest in amphetamine's potential applications.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text:
Following the discovery of its stimulant effects, amphetamine quickly moved toward commercial development. In 1932, the pharmaceutical company Smith, Kline & French introduced the Benzedrine inhaler, initially marketed as a nasal decongestant. By 1934, the company had expanded sales of the volatile salt form for this purpose.

Medical applications broadened rapidly during this period. The first report describing amphetamine's therapeutic use for narcolepsy appeared in 1935, the same year Smith, Kline and French registered the racemic mixture. In 1937, researcher Charles Bradley published findings demonstrating that amphetamine could effectively treat behavioral problems in children, representing one of the earliest documented uses of stimulant medication for what would later be recognized as attention deficit disorders.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Commercial Development and Medical Applications

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text:
During World War II, amphetamine and methamphetamine saw widespread deployment among military forces on both sides of the conflict. Allied and Axis powers alike distributed these stimulants to soldiers to promote wakefulness, combat fatigue, and enhance performance during extended operations.

The wartime demand led to massive overproduction of amphetamine. When hostilities concluded, the substantial surplus that had accumulated found its way into black markets, catalyzing the beginning of widespread illicit amphetamine abuse. As the addictive properties of the drug became increasingly apparent through this post-war period, governments around the world began implementing strict controls on its manufacture and sale.

chunks.title: Amphetamine
chunks.text: Contemporary medical use of amphetamine centers largely on combination formulations developed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy. Adderall, a preparation containing dextroamphetamine and levoamphetamine in a 75% to 25% ratio, was introduced in 1996. A generic version of this formulation received approval in 2002, expanding accessibility to amphetamine-based treatment for these conditions.

chunks.title: AMT
chunks.text: AMT is a synthetic psychedelic, stimulant, and entactogen of the tryptamine class. Originally developed by Upjohn in the 1960s, it was briefly prescribed as an antidepressant in the Soviet Union before being discontinued. Its effects are often described as a cross between classical psychedelics and MDMA, combining perceptual alterations with empathogenic and stimulant qualities. It also possesses weak, reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) activity.

chunks.title: AMT
chunks.text: Extreme confusion and depersonalization have been reported at high doses. Neurologic side effects include agitation, restlessness, and confusion. True psychotic episodes are not commonly documented, but high doses can produce significantly disorienting mental states.

chunks.text: AMT acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist, with its psychedelic effects primarily attributed to partial agonism at the 5-HT2A receptor. It also functions as a relatively balanced releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Additionally, AMT is a weak, non-selective, and reversible inhibitor of the enzyme monoamine oxidase (MAO).

chunks.title: AMT
chunks.text: The alpha-methyl substituent on AMT's tryptamine backbone renders it a relatively poor substrate for monoamine oxidase A, protecting the amine group from metabolic deamination and prolonging its half-life sufficiently to reach the central nervous system. Hydroxylation and oxidation appear to be the primary metabolic pathways, as indicated by metabolites identified in rat studies.

chunks.title: AMT
chunks.text:
Alpha-methyltryptamine appears to have first been described in the scientific literature around 1929, though it remained relatively unstudied until the late 1950s. More intensive research on AMT began in the late 1950s and early 1960s, conducted alongside its close structural relative alpha-ethyltryptamine (aET). The compound was investigated by multiple pharmaceutical companies during this period, with Upjohn in the United States assigning it the code name U-14,164E, while Sandoz researched it under the designation IT-290.

During the 1960s, AMT was briefly marketed in the Soviet Union as an antidepressant under the trade name Indopan (sometimes spelled Indopane). The medication was prescribed in tablet form at doses of 5 to 10 milligrams. However, its clinical use was short-lived, and the drug was withdrawn from the market after only a brief period of therapeutic application. The related compound aET saw somewhat broader pharmaceutical use, being sold commercially in the United States as an antidepressant under the brand name Monase before being placed in Schedule I in 1971.

chunks.title: AMT
chunks.text:
AMT began to see recreational use during the 1960s, concurrent with its pharmaceutical development. The compound was also employed in certain psychotherapeutic studies during this decade. Despite this early use, AMT remained a relatively obscure substance for several decades following its withdrawal from clinical application.

The compound experienced renewed interest in the late 1990s when it became one of the first psychoactive tryptamines to be widely sold as a "research chemical" through online vendors. This period marked the beginning of the modern research chemical market, with AMT becoming available to a significantly broader user base through internet commerce. The increased availability and use of AMT during this era eventually led to regulatory action, with the substance being emergency scheduled in the United States in April 2003 and permanently placed in Schedule I in September 2004.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: Armodafinil is a eugeroic substance of the benzhydryl class, consisting of the enantiopure (R)-enantiomer of the racemic mixture modafinil. Approved by the FDA in 2007, it is prescribed to treat excessive sleepiness associated with narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and shift work disorder. Compared to racemic modafinil, armodafinil is considered more potent and longer-acting. Its effects are primarily functional and wakefulness-promoting rather than overtly recreational.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: Armodafinil is considered mildly addictive with low abuse potential. Animal self-administration studies suggest some reinforcing properties, and it produces psychoactive and euphoric effects comparable to methylphenidate, though psychological dependence appears uncommon among users.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: Hallucinations and mania are listed as possible side effects, particularly at overdose levels. These effects appear uncommon at typical therapeutic or recreational doses.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: The precise mechanism of action of armodafinil is not fully understood. Its best-characterized activity is binding to the dopamine transporter (DAT) and inhibiting dopamine reuptake, functioning as an atypical dopamine reuptake inhibitor. This activity is associated with increased extracellular dopamine levels. Evidence also suggests it may block the norepinephrine transporter (NET), and the resulting elevations in dopamine and norepinephrine are thought to contribute to its wake-promoting properties. Additional hypothesized contributions include indirect promotion of orexinergic and histaminergic activity alongside reduction of GABAergic tone.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: Armodafinil is readily absorbed after oral administration, reaching peak plasma concentrations in approximately 2 hours in the fasted state. Food has minimal effect on overall bioavailability but may delay peak levels by 2 to 4 hours. The absolute oral bioavailability has not been determined due to the aqueous insolubility of armodafinil precluding intravenous administration. The terminal elimination half-life is approximately 15 hours. The primary metabolic pathway is hydrolytic deamidation, followed by sulfone formation catalyzed by CYP3A4/5. Additional routes include aromatic ring hydroxylation with subsequent glucuronide conjugation. Two metabolites reach appreciable plasma concentrations: R-modafinil acid and modafinil sulfone. Armodafinil moderately induces CYP3A4 and moderately inhibits CYP2C19.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text:
Armodafinil is the isolated R-enantiomer of the racemic wakefulness-promoting agent modafinil. It was developed by Cephalon Inc., a pharmaceutical company that later became a wholly owned subsidiary of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. The compound received approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration in June 2007 for the treatment of excessive sleepiness associated with obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy, and shift work disorder. It was marketed under the brand name Nuvigil.

In 2016, the FDA granted Mylan the rights to produce and market the first generic version of armodafinil in the United States, expanding access to the medication beyond the original branded formulation.

chunks.title: Armodafinil
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzhydryl nootropics (modafinil, adrafinil)

chunks.title: Ashwagandha
chunks.text: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an evergreen shrub of the Solanaceae family, native to the Middle East, North Africa, and the Indian subcontinent. Classified as an adaptogen, its root powder has been used for centuries in traditional Indian medicine, primarily for its purported anxiolytic and sleep-promoting properties. Its principal phytochemicals are withanolides, structurally similar to the ginsenosides of Panax ginseng. While generally well tolerated short-term, it has been linked to rare cases of liver injury and should be avoided during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Ashwagandha
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, particularly in individuals with preexisting liver conditions; hepatotoxicity appears uncommon in those without underlying hepatic disease.

chunks.title: Ashwagandha
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Linked to herb-induced liver injury. Caution advised for those with preexisting liver conditions.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.text: Aspirin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) produced through acetylation of salicylic acid, a compound with medicinal roots in willow bark stretching back over 2,400 years. First synthesized in 1853 and produced in pure, stable form by Bayer in 1897, it is among the most widely used medications globally. Aspirin reduces pain, fever, and inflammation, and at lower doses serves as an antithrombotic agent. Notable risks include gastrointestinal bleeding and stomach ulcers.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.text: Aspirin does not produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.text: Aspirin has no known psychological addiction potential and is not associated with compulsive use patterns or abuse.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Aspirin can be dangerous at doses of 4 g and higher. Acute overdose has an estimated mortality rate of 2%, while repeated or ongoing overdose is associated with about 25% mortality and may be particularly serious in children.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aspirin commonly causes stomach upset and raises the chance of stomach ulcers and upper gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in older people, alcohol users, people taking other NSAIDs, and people taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis reduces protective mucus production in the gastric lining

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Enteric-coated aspirin has not been shown to lower the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. People with peptic ulcers or gastritis should seek medical advice before use.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Short-term aspirin use at therapeutic doses may precipitate reversible acute kidney injury in patients with glomerulonephritis or cirrhosis; aspirin is contraindicated in some patients with chronic kidney disease.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Also contraindicated in some children with congestive heart failure.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Giving aspirin to children or adolescents for fever or viral illness can be associated with Reye syndrome, an uncommon but serious condition involving acute brain dysfunction and fatty changes in the liver.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: US FDA recommends aspirin not be given to anyone under 12 with fever. UK NHS recommends children under 16 should not take aspirin except on medical advice.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aspirin increases bleeding risk and is known to cause hemolytic anemia in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; it should not be used by people with hemophilia or other bleeding tendencies.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Use before surgical procedures is associated with increased bleeding events. Not recommended during dengue fever due to increased bleeding tendency.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aspirin causes an increased risk of cerebral microbleeds and intracerebral hemorrhage, with an estimated absolute risk increase of 12 events per 10,000 persons at average doses of 270 mg per day.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: When intracerebral hemorrhage has already occurred, aspirin use is linked with higher mortality; doses near 250 mg/day have been associated with an approximately 2.5-fold relative risk of death within three months.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High doses may result in tinnitus (ringing in the ears).

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: For some individuals, aspirin can cause hives, swelling, headache, and angioedema appearing one to six hours after ingestion; aspirin may also delay healing of skin wounds.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Can exacerbate symptoms in those with chronic hives.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Aspirin may worsen asthma and cause NSAID-precipitated bronchospasm in susceptible individuals.

chunks.title: Aspirin
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: People with asthma or a history of NSAID-triggered bronchospasm should use aspirin only with appropriate caution.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.text: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (sNRI) marketed under the brand name Strattera. Originally developed as an antidepressant by Eli Lilly, it was found ineffective for depression but proved beneficial for ADHD, receiving FDA approval in 2002. Unlike stimulant ADHD medications, atomoxetine carries little known abuse potential. Notable safety concerns include cardiovascular effects, rare severe liver injury, and an FDA black box warning for suicidal ideation in pediatric patients.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.text: Treatment-emergent psychotic or manic symptoms including hallucinations, delusional thinking, or mania can occur in children and adolescents without prior history of psychotic illness at usual doses. Mental changes including disorientation and hallucinations have been reported less commonly in overdose situations.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.text: Seizures have been reported in some cases of overdose involving atomoxetine.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare cases of severe liver injury, including liver failure requiring transplant, have been reported in postmarketing experience; clinical trials of approximately 6000 patients did not detect evidence of liver injury.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Atomoxetine should be stopped if jaundice or laboratory signs of liver injury occur, and treatment should not be resumed afterward.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Patients receiving usual atomoxetine doses have had reports of sudden death, stroke, and myocardial infarction. The drug may increase blood pressure and heart rate and should be avoided in people with severe cardiac or vascular disease.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Direct inhibition of hERG potassium currents with an IC50 of 6.3 μM, which has the potential to cause arrhythmia.

chunks.title: Atomoxetine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: QT prolongation has been reported both at therapeutic doses and after overdose. Atomoxetine is contraindicated in severe cardiovascular disorders, including moderate or severe hypertension, atrial fibrillation or flutter, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation or flutter, and advanced arteriosclerosis.

chunks.text:

- Canada: Prescription product — Brand-name and generic oral capsule products are listed in Canada.
- United States: Previously marketed product — Strattera atomoxetine kit entries list United States marketing starts in 2009 and marketing end dates in 2009 or 2011.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca is a psychoactive decoction traditionally prepared from the Banisteriopsis caapi vine and a DMT-containing plant, used by indigenous peoples of the Amazon basin in ceremonial and shamanic contexts since before recorded history. The β-carboline alkaloids in B. caapi act as monoamine oxidase inhibitors, rendering DMT orally active. Its name derives from Quechuan languages, meaning 'spirit rope' or 'liana of the soul.' Ayahuasca is known for producing intense spiritual and psychological experiences.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca is not physically addictive and does not produce physical dependence. The substance builds no significant tolerance and can theoretically be used frequently without developing dependence.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca shows no psychological addiction potential and many users report a self-regulating quality to the substance. Research has shown it may actually be effective in treating addictions, with lower Addiction Severity Index scores observed in ayahuasca users compared to controls.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca is suspected of triggering psychosis and schizophrenia in individuals with a predisposition to these conditions. Acute delusions, paranoia, and confusional states may occur during the experience, particularly when accompanied by severe nausea. Family history of psychotic disorders is considered a contraindication.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Seizures are listed among the rarer side effects of ayahuasca.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Harmaline has been reported to exhibit antimicrobial, antileishmanial, and antiplasmodial properties. Harmala alkaloids have demonstrated ability to expel parasitic worms by stunning or killing them.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted. Harmaline has shown antitumoral activity in some contexts, but this does not constitute evidence regarding carcinogenic potential.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea ('la purga') are common acute effects during the experience; these are transient symptoms related to the mechanism of action and are not indicative of organ damage.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Increased serotonergic signaling in the gut directly stimulates the vagus nerve, promoting emesis.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The purging process is considered a traditional part of the experience by many shamans and users. Harmala alkaloids may also expel intestinal parasites. Effects resolve after the session.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute increases in blood pressure and heart rate (tachycardia) occur during intoxication; these effects are transient and resolve after the experience ends.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Contraindicated in individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Limited safety information is available for this population.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Transient increases in prolactin, cortisone, and growth hormone secretion have been correlated with ayahuasca consumption; these hormonal changes occur during the acute experience.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Endocrine problems are listed among contraindications for ayahuasca use.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca's psychoactive effects arise from the combined actions of DMT and harmala alkaloids. DMT stimulates serotonin receptors in the brain, with activity at the 5-HT2A receptor subtype most directly associated with its psychoactive properties. The harmala alkaloids harmine and harmaline function as selective, reversible inhibitors of monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A, classified as RIMAs). The β-carbolines in B. caapi also exhibit independent activity at serotonin and benzodiazepine receptors. Tetrahydroharmine, another constituent alkaloid, displays weak serotonin reuptake inhibition.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: DMT is ordinarily degraded by monoamine oxidase enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract, rendering it orally inactive when consumed alone. The reversible inhibition of MAO-A by harmine and harmaline prevents this oxidation, allowing DMT to pass unmetabolized through the stomach and small intestine and subsequently cross the blood-brain barrier. Individual polymorphisms of the CYP2D6 enzyme affect the rate at which harmine is metabolized.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Selective and reversible (RIMA; harmine, harmaline)

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Serotonergic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline)

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Ayahuasca does not produce significant tolerance with repeated use. The substance can theoretically be used on consecutive days without notable diminishment of effects.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text:
Ayahuasca has been used by the indigenous peoples of South America since before recorded history. The word itself derives from Quechuan languages spoken in the Andes, with its name translating to "spirit rope" or "liana of the soul," referring both to the Banisteriopsis caapi vine and the psychoactive brew prepared from it.

Archaeological evidence suggests the use of psychoactive plants in the northeastern Amazon dates back to 1500–2000 BCE. Artifacts from this period include anthropomorphic figurines, snuffing trays, and pottery vessels adorned with mythological figures and sacred animals, offering glimpses into pre-Columbian ritual culture. More direct evidence of B. caapi use emerged from a pouch discovered in a cave in southwestern Bolivia in 2008, while chemical traces of harmine were identified in the hair of two mummies found in northern Chile. Both findings have been linked to the Tiwanaku civilization, dating to approximately 900 CE.

By the 19th century, the specific ritual use of ayahuasca was widespread among Indigenous groups throughout the Amazon and Orinoco basins, though its precise origins remain uncertain.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Indigenous Origins and Archaeological Evidence

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text:
The first Western references to the ayahuasca beverage appeared during the 17th century, coinciding with the European colonization of the Americas. The earliest known report is a letter from Vicente de Valverde to the Holy Office of the Inquisition. Jose Chantre y Herrera, also writing in the 17th century, provided the first detailed description of what he termed a "devilish potion" prepared from bitter herbs and lianas (referred to as ayaguasca), along with accounts of its associated rituals.

Christian missionaries from Spain and Portugal who encountered ayahuasca during this period predictably characterized it as the work of the devil, establishing a pattern of colonial suspicion toward indigenous plant medicines that would persist for centuries.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text:
Throughout its history, ayahuasca has been employed across diverse South American cultures for spiritual, social, and medicinal purposes. Traditional preparation involves a ritualistic, multi-day process of macerating and boiling B. caapi with other plants such as Psychotria viridis. These ceremonies are typically guided by shamans and involve specific dietary restrictions and ritual practices that have evolved over generations to support the psychological and spiritual dimensions of the experience.

The Shipibo-Konibo people of the Peruvian Amazon have played a particularly significant historical and cultural role in the development and preservation of ayahuasca traditions. Among those who undergo the ayahuasca experience, reports of profound spiritual revelations regarding one's purpose, the nature of existence, and personal insight are common, with many describing lasting positive changes following their encounters with the brew.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text:
Ayahuasca spread beyond its traditional Amazonian context by the mid-20th century, primarily through syncretic religious movements originating in Brazil. These organizations blended indigenous ayahuasca practices with Christian and other spiritual traditions, establishing formal churches that would eventually carry the brew to Europe, North America, and beyond.

The contemporary ayahuasca landscape includes both traditional indigenous ceremonial use and participation in organized religious contexts, as well as a growing phenomenon of ayahuasca tourism, with retreat centers operating throughout South America offering ceremonial experiences to international visitors.

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Serotonergic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline), Other 5-HT2A agonists

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text: Binding profile: Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAO-A); 5-HT2A; Serotonin reuptake inhibitor (selective, SSRI); GABA-A (benzodiazepine site)

- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines

Ayahuasca — unsafe combinations:
- Alcohol (Tyramine found in many alcoholic beverages can have dangerous reactions with MAOIs, causing an increase in blood pressure.)
- Diphenhydramine (There is a significant risk of serotonin syndrome with this combination. Monoamine oxidase A inhibitors may extend and increase the anticholinergic effects of DPH. The combination increases each other’s side effects, such as drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, and headaches. Medical dosages are not reported to be of concern.)

chunks.title: Ayahuasca
chunks.text:
Ayahuasca — caution combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably, which could be dangerous given the unpredictability of the 2C-T-x series)
- 2C-x compounds (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably)
- DOx compounds (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably)
- Ketamine (MAO-B inhibitors appear to increase the potency of Ketamine. MAO-A inhbitors have some negative reports associated with the combination but there isn't much information available)
- Mescaline
- NBOMe compounds (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably)
- Opioids (Coadministration of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) with certain opioids has been associated with rare reports of severe and fatal adverse reactions. There appear to be two types of interaction, an excitatory and a depressive one. Symptoms of the excitatory reaction may include agitation, headache, diaphoresis, hyperpyrexia, flushing, shivering, myoclonus, rigidity, tremor, diarrhea, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, and coma.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Baclofen is a depressant and muscle relaxant of the butyric acid class that acts as a GABA-B receptor agonist. Originally synthesized in 1962 to treat epilepsy, it proved ineffective for that purpose but was later approved in 1977 for managing muscle spasticity. Chemically related to phenibut, pregabalin, and gabapentin, it produces sedation, anxiety suppression, and moderate euphoria. It has also been researched as a potential treatment for alcohol dependence.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with chronic use, potentially occurring within weeks of regular dosing at low or high doses. Withdrawal syndrome resembles benzodiazepine and alcohol withdrawal, with symptoms ranging from anxiety, tremors, and insomnia to severe manifestations including hallucinations, delirium, psychosis, seizures, and extreme muscle rigidity resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Abrupt discontinuation is not advised; gradual tapering is necessary.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Moderate abuse potential with risk of psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing has been reported as an after effect of use.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Psychosis, hallucinations (auditory, visual, and tactile), delusions, delirium, confusion, disorientation, and mania may occur during withdrawal from chronic use, particularly with abrupt discontinuation. These psychiatric symptoms are associated with the withdrawal syndrome rather than acute intoxication.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Seizures may occur in overdose or with abrupt discontinuation after chronic use. Withdrawal-related seizures are a serious concern requiring gradual tapering when discontinuing therapy. High-dose combinations with sedatives may also precipitate de novo seizures.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: CNS depression including sedation, somnolence, and ataxia occurs at therapeutic and recreational doses; overdose may cause altered mental status, hypothermia, and coma that can mimic brain death.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: GABA-B receptor agonism causing central nervous system depression

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Most overdose symptoms are neurological. Symptoms may persist even after serum baclofen levels become undetectable.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression and insufficiency may occur, particularly at higher doses or in overdose; risk increases significantly when combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: CNS depression affecting respiratory drive

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Overdose may require intubation and mechanical ventilation.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular depression is possible at high doses; overdose may cause bradycardia, tachycardia, hypertension, and cardiac conduction abnormalities, though these effects are uncommon.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects are typically observed only in overdose settings.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis may occur if baclofen use is stopped abruptly after chronic administration; this is a withdrawal complication rather than a direct toxic effect during use.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Rebound spasticity and extreme muscle rigidity resulting from abrupt cessation

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Gradual tapering prevents this complication.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Baclofen should be avoided in chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease as even small doses can cause excessive toxicity due to impaired drug clearance; this represents accumulation toxicity rather than direct nephrotoxicity.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Dose adjustment or avoidance necessary in renal impairment.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: β-(p-chlorophenyl)-4-hydroxybutyric acid (inactive)

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Baclofen acts as an agonist at the GABA-B receptor, binding to both the B1 and B2 subunits on pre- and post-synaptic neurons. Receptor activation causes neuronal hyperpolarization through potassium influx, reducing presynaptic calcium entry and decreasing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters, which inhibits both mono- and polysynaptic reflex transmission at the spinal cord. Baclofen also blocks α2δ subunit-containing voltage-gated calcium channels, though with weak affinity (Ki = 156 μM) that is considered likely not clinically relevant. GABA-B receptor activation is additionally thought to reduce dopaminergic activity in the mesolimbic pathway.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Baclofen is rapidly absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract following oral administration, with a bioavailability of approximately 70-85%. Only about 15% of the oral dose is metabolized in the liver, primarily through deamination. The elimination half-life following oral administration ranges from approximately 2 to 6 hours, with longer estimates of approximately 5.6 to 6.8 hours also described.

chunks.text:

Only about 15% of the oral dose is metabolized in the liver

chunks.text: Following cessation, tolerance returns to baseline within 7-14 days.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text: Tolerance to sedative-hypnotic effects can appear after only several days of uninterrupted baclofen use.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text:
Baclofen was first synthesized in 1962 by Swiss chemist Heinrich Keberle at Ciba-Geigy in Basel, Switzerland. The compound was designed with the intention of enhancing the lipophilicity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) to enable penetration of the blood-brain barrier, with epilepsy treatment as the primary therapeutic goal.

Although the drug proved ineffective for epilepsy, researchers discovered that it reduced spasticity in certain patients. This finding led to its reintroduction in 1971 as a treatment for spasticity conditions. The following year, it was marketed under the brand name Lioresal. The United States Food and Drug Administration subsequently granted approval in 1977.

Development continued with the introduction of intrathecal administration in 1984, enabling direct delivery into the spinal canal for the treatment of severe spinal spasticity.

chunks.title: Baclofen
chunks.text:
Interest in baclofen as a treatment for alcohol dependence emerged in the early 2000s, driven largely by French-American cardiologist Olivier Ameisen. Beginning in 2004, Ameisen advocated for clinical trials investigating high-dose baclofen for alcoholism. In 2008, he published "Le Dernier Verre" (translated as "The Last Glass" or "The End of My Addiction"), documenting his self-treatment of alcohol dependence using the medication.

The book generated significant interest within the medical community and among potential benefactors. An anonymous donor contributed $750,000 to the University of Amsterdam to initiate clinical trials examining high-dose baclofen for alcohol use disorder. Regulatory acceptance followed in France, where the drug received temporary authorization in 2014 and formal approval for alcoholism treatment in 2018 for cases where other therapies have proven ineffective.

chunks.title: Barbital
chunks.text: Barbital is a barbiturate depressant and the first commercially available substance of its class. Synthesized in 1902 by Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering, it was marketed by Bayer as "Veronal" beginning in 1904 and widely prescribed as a hypnotic until the mid-1950s. Prolonged use was associated with significant tolerance development, and fatal overdoses were common due to its slow-acting nature and relatively narrow margin between therapeutic and lethal doses.

chunks.title: Barbital
chunks.text: As a barbiturate, barbital produces physical dependence with chronic use. Tolerance development is well-documented, indicating physiological adaptation that would result in withdrawal symptoms upon cessation.

chunks.title: Barbital
chunks.text: Barbital is classified as habit-forming with significant potential for psychological dependence. Prolonged usage leads to tolerance, requiring higher doses to achieve desired effects, which can drive compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: Barbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: The lethal dose is approximately 3.5 to 4.4 grams orally. Fatal overdoses were historically common due to the drug's slow onset of action, which led users to take additional doses before feeling effects. Numerous documented deaths occurred both accidentally and intentionally.

chunks.title: Bentazepam
chunks.text: Bentazepam is a thienodiazepine, a benzodiazepine analog that possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties. It is considered an effective anxiolytic with a relatively short duration of action. Notably, bentazepam has been associated with severe liver damage and hepatitis, and liver function monitoring is recommended for all individuals taking it. As with other benzodiazepines, severe overdose may result in coma and respiratory failure.

chunks.title: Bentazepam
chunks.text: As a benzodiazepine, physical dependence is expected to develop with regular use, with potential for withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Bentazepam

chunks.text: bk-2C-B is a psychedelic substance of the phenethylamine class and a β-keto derivative of 2C-B. Richard Glennon and colleagues first reported it in the scientific literature in 2004, and it later appeared as a novel designer drug on European markets in 2013. While it did not generate significant excitement upon its appearance, it remained consistently available and was sampled by a relatively large number of users. The drug is administered orally.

chunks.title: bk-2c-B
chunks.text:
bk-2C-B was first characterized in the scientific literature in 2004 by pharmacologist Richard Glennon and his research team, who synthesized and studied the compound as part of investigations into phenethylamine structure-activity relationships. The substance remained largely obscure until 2013, when it emerged on European designer drug markets as a novel psychoactive substance.

Following its market appearance, bk-2C-B maintained a consistent presence without generating significant enthusiasm or notoriety within the research chemical community. Despite this relatively muted reception, the compound was sampled by a substantial number of users over subsequent years. It was typically distributed in both pressed pill and powder forms. Its availability persisted in the gray market until regulatory measures were implemented across several countries beginning in 2016.

chunks.title: BOD
chunks.text: BOD is a synthetic psychedelic of the substituted phenethylamine class, documented by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL. It is the β-methoxy analogue of 2C-D, designed by incorporating an oxygen atom at the benzylic position — a modification inspired by the natural enzymatic conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine. BOD is generally reported to produce milder psychedelic effects compared to related 2C-x and DOx compounds, though experiences of body load vary considerably between individuals.

chunks.title: Bromantane
chunks.text: Bromantane is an atypical stimulant and anxiolytic of the adamantane class, developed in the 1980s at the Zakusov State Institute of Pharmacology in the USSR. Unlike conventional stimulants, it primarily enhances dopamine synthesis through upregulation of biosynthetic enzymes rather than reuptake inhibition. It is approved in Russia for treating neurasthenia and does not appear to produce tolerance or dependence. It can produce unexpectedly strong reactions when combined with other stimulants.

chunks.title: Bromantane
chunks.text: Bromantane appears to have low abuse potential. Clinical trials showed very low discontinuation rates, and its unique mechanism of action involving gene expression changes rather than direct dopamine release suggests reduced reinforcing properties compared to typical stimulants.
