chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Bromazepam is a benzodiazepine patented in 1961 by Roche and approved for medical use in 1974. It is primarily prescribed as an anxiolytic for treating anxiety and panic disorders, and is occasionally used as a premedicant prior to minor surgery. Compared to other classical benzodiazepines, bromazepam is noted for being less sedating at typical doses while producing greater muscle relaxation. Some experts suggest it carries elevated abuse potential due to its rapid onset of action.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop within one to six months of continuous use, with up to 30% of long-term users developing dependence. Abrupt withdrawal after chronic use, even at therapeutic doses, can lead to severe withdrawal syndrome including status epilepticus and symptoms resembling delirium tremens. Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, nausea, seizures, hallucinations, and hyperthermia.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Bromazepam presents significant abuse potential, reportedly greater than other benzodiazepines due to its fast absorption and rapid onset of action. Compulsive redosing is documented, and rebound anxiety following use can perpetuate cycles of dependence.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Paradoxical reactions including violent behavior, loss of impulse control, and suicidal behavior occur rarely, with an incidence rate below 1% in the general population. These reactions occur more frequently in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, children, and patients on high-dosage regimens. Withdrawal may produce hallucinations and delirium in severe cases.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Paradoxical increased seizures in epileptics are rare during use. However, abrupt withdrawal after chronic use poses significant seizure risk, including potential for status epilepticus. Gradual dose reduction eliminates withdrawal-related seizure risk.

chunks.text: Studies in healthy subjects showed significant impairment in learning capacity after two weeks of use at 6mg three times daily. Tolerance to sedative effects usually develops during therapy, but cognitive effects may persist.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Bromazepam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. It binds to this site and produces a conformational change that potentiates the inhibitory effects of GABA, enhancing the receptor's response when GABA is present. Other neurotransmitter systems are not directly influenced.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text: Bromazepam is well absorbed orally with a bioavailability of approximately 84%. It is metabolized hepatically via oxidative pathways involving a cytochrome P450 enzyme, producing hydroxybromazepam as its major metabolite, which is pharmacologically active and has a half-life similar to the parent compound. The elimination half-life of bromazepam is 10 to 20 hours.

chunks.title: Bromazepam
chunks.text:
Bromazepam was developed by the Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche, receiving its patent in 1961. The compound was subsequently approved for medical use in 1974, entering the pharmaceutical market as an intermediate-acting anxiolytic medication.

Like other benzodiazepines, bromazepam carries recognized concerns regarding misuse and diversion. Research conducted in France examining motor vehicle accidents involving psychotropic substances found that benzodiazepines—particularly diazepam, nordiazepam, and bromazepam—were among the most frequently detected drugs in drivers' blood when combined with alcohol. The substance has also been documented in connection with serious criminal activities, including cases of robbery, homicide, and sexual assault.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: Bromazolam is a synthetic triazolobenzodiazepine first synthesized in 1976 but never marketed for medical use. It emerged as a designer drug, first definitively identified in Sweden by the EMCDDA in 2016. Structurally, it is the bromo analogue of alprazolam and produces comparable sedative and anxiolytic effects at a similar potency. As with other benzodiazepines, bromazolam carries significant habit-forming potential and poses risks of dependence with repeated use.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, similar to prescription benzodiazepines. Chronic use leads to neuroadaptation requiring continued dosing to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: Bromazolam demonstrates abuse potential comparable to other benzodiazepines. Drug discrimination studies in rats showed full dose-dependent substitution for midazolam, with an ED50 of 0.54 mg/kg, indicating significant reinforcing properties mediated through α1 subunit binding.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: At high doses, bromazolam may induce delirium and auditory or visual hallucinations. These effects are dose-dependent and not typically observed at standard doses.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: While bromazolam possesses anticonvulsant properties at typical doses, high doses may paradoxically induce seizures. Benzodiazepine withdrawal is also associated with seizure risk, though specific data for bromazolam is limited.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted on bromazolam.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: Bromazolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABAA receptor, binding non-selectively at the benzodiazepine site across multiple receptor subtypes. It displays highest affinity for the α5 and α2 subunits (Ki of 0.62 nM and 0.69 nM, respectively) with somewhat lower but still high affinity at the α1 subunit (Ki of 2.81 nM).

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text: Bromazolam undergoes hepatic phase I metabolism through hydroxylation, catalyzed primarily by CYP3A4, CYP2B6, and CYP2C19, with additional contributions from CYP3A5 and CYP2C9. Phase II metabolism involves glucuronidation of both the parent compound and its hydroxylated metabolites, mediated by several UGT enzymes including UGT1A4, UGT2B10, UGT2B4, UGT1A3, UGT1A6, UGT1A9, UGT2B7, and UGT2B15.

chunks.title: Bromazolam
chunks.text:
Bromazolam was first synthesized in 1976 as part of benzodiazepine research, representing a structural modification of alprazolam where the chlorine atom is replaced with bromine. Despite its early synthesis, the compound was never developed as a pharmaceutical product or brought to market for medical use.

The substance remained largely obscure until it emerged in the designer drug market decades later. In 2016, bromazolam was definitively identified by the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (EMCDDA) after appearing in Sweden, marking its entry into the novel psychoactive substances landscape. Since then, it has become one of the more prevalent novel benzodiazepines in circulation.

In parts of North America, particularly Canada, bromazolam has become intertwined with the illicit opioid supply. Street-level products combining bromazolam with opioids such as heroin or fentanyl analogues have emerged, sometimes referred to colloquially as "benzo-dope." This adulteration pattern has raised significant public health concerns due to the compounded risks of combining central nervous system depressants.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Bromo-DragonFLY is a synthetic psychedelic of the substituted phenethylamine and benzodifuran classes. First described in the scientific literature in 1998, its name derives from the insect-like appearance of two furan rings fused to a central benzene ring. The substance is extremely potent, estimated at roughly one-third the potency of LSD by weight, and produces unusually prolonged effects. It is considered highly dose-sensitive and has been associated with numerous hospitalizations and fatalities.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Bromo-DragonFLY is generally not associated with compulsive reuse. Motivation to take it again may decline with repeated use, and use is usually self-limiting.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Overdose effects include bizarre, delusional, and sometimes violent behavior, along with terrifying hallucinations, severe confusion, and amnesia. The extremely long duration of effects and the substance's abnormally prolonged presence in the body may increase psychological distress. Users may become severely agitated and unable to communicate.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Seizures and convulsions have been reported as side effects, particularly in overdose situations. Multiple fatalities involved seizures as part of the clinical presentation, including cases where individuals experienced seizures, vomited blood, and suffered terrifying hallucinations before death.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Severe overdose causes extreme, prolonged vasoconstriction that can lead to dangerous hypertension, tissue necrosis of extremities, gangrene, and potentially limb amputation; elevated heart rate and blood pressure occur during typical intoxication but serious vascular damage is associated with massive overdoses.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Potent, long-acting vasoconstrictor action causing prolonged hypoxia and ischemia in peripheral tissues.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: At least one documented case required amputation of the front part of the feet and several fingers after a massive overdose. Vasoconstriction typically develops to peak several hours into intoxication and can persist for an extremely long time. Necrosis and gangrene may become apparent weeks after the overdose. Tolazoline is reportedly an effective treatment where available. Continuous administration of a vasodilator may be needed to prevent hypertensive emergency, necrosis, organ failure, and death from hypoxia.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Bromo-DragonFLY is a potent full agonist at serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT2B receptors, with sub-nanomolar binding affinities across all three subtypes. Rather than being selective for 5-HT2A, it is best characterized as a non-subtype-selective 5-HT2 agonist, displaying roughly twice the potency at 5-HT2C compared to 5-HT2A. Bromo-DragonFLY is also a potent inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A). The (R)-enantiomer possesses greater binding affinity at the 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors than the (S)-enantiomer.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Bromo-DragonFLY's potent inhibition of MAO-A has been suggested to impair its own metabolic degradation, which may contribute to its unusually prolonged duration of action.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Approximately 14 days without further consumption

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of Bromo-DragonFLY develops almost immediately following ingestion.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Bromo-DragonFLY emerged from academic research conducted at Purdue University during the mid-1990s, where it was initially developed as a novel chemical tool for studying serotonin receptor binding in rat brain tissue. The compound was formally synthesized and characterized in 1998 by Matthew Parker, who derived it from the structurally related DOB-FLY. That same year, the substance was first described in the scientific literature by David E. Nichols and colleagues, establishing its pharmacological profile and extreme potency relative to other phenethylamine psychedelics.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: Following nearly a decade of existence solely within academic contexts, Bromo-DragonFLY transitioned into human experimental psychoactive markets in May 2005 when quantities of the compound became commercially available. By 2006, it had been encountered as a novel designer drug, marking its first documented appearance in recreational contexts. The substance briefly gained popularity within research chemical communities around 2010, though this period of availability would prove short-lived due to the serious incidents that followed.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: The extreme potency and prolonged duration of Bromo-DragonFLY contributed to several severe adverse events that significantly impacted its availability and legal status. In September 2007, a 35-year-old Swedish man suffered catastrophic tissue necrosis following a massive overdose of unknown quantity, ultimately requiring amputation of the front portion of his feet and several fingers due to the compound's severe vasoconstrictive effects. A particularly consequential incident occurred in October 2009 when laboratory testing confirmed that a batch of Bromo-DragonFLY had been distributed mislabeled as 2C-B-FLY, a structurally related compound approximately twenty times less potent by weight. This labeling error is believed to have contributed to multiple lethal overdoses and additional hospitalizations as users inadvertently consumed doses far exceeding safe thresholds.

chunks.title: Bromo-DragonFLY
chunks.text: On May 7, 2011, two young adults in the United States died and several others required hospitalization after overdosing on Bromo-DragonFLY that they believed was 2C-E. These fatal incidents, stemming largely from misidentification and mislabeling rather than informed use, led to the substance's prohibition in multiple jurisdictions and its rapid disappearance from research chemical markets.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Brotizolam is a sedative-hypnotic of the thienotriazolodiazepine class, a benzodiazepine analog patented in 1974 and introduced into medical use in 1984. It is prescribed for short-term treatment of severe insomnia in parts of Europe, Israel, and Japan. Brotizolam is notable for its exceptional potency and rapid elimination, producing effects comparable to triazolam and midazolam. As with other benzodiazepines, it carries risks of respiratory depression when combined with other depressants, as well as amnesia and habit formation.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop with regular use. Treatment is recommended for only 2-4 weeks for severe insomnia. Mild rebound insomnia may occur when treatment is stopped, indicating physiological adaptation to the drug.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Brotizolam has recognized potential for abuse and is classified as habit-forming. Abuse was significant enough in Hong Kong during the late 1980s and 1990s to warrant government reclassification as a Dangerous Drug, with regulatory controls subsequently extended to all benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Hallucinations and paradoxical reactions including aggression, anxiety, and violent behavior are listed as less common side effects. These psychiatric disturbances appear to be uncommon at recommended doses.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Brotizolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine binding site. Through this mechanism, it produces anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, hypnotic, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant effects. It is considered pharmacologically similar to other short-acting hypnotic benzodiazepines such as triazolam and midazolam.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Brotizolam is rapidly absorbed following administration and is rapidly eliminated, with an average half-life of 4.4 hours (range 3.6–7.9 hours). It is metabolized into two primary metabolites: a 4-hydroxy derivative with far less potency than the parent compound, and a 1-methylhydroxy derivative thought to have comparable activity. However, the 1-methylhydroxy metabolite is not present in measurable plasma concentrations following a single dose in healthy subjects, so neither metabolite contributes significantly to the overall pharmacological effect in humans.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text: Brotizolam was first patented in 1974. The compound's synthesis was subsequently documented by Weber, Bauer, Danneberg, and Kuhn through a 1978 United States patent. The substance entered clinical practice a decade after its initial patent in 1984, finding adoption primarily in European markets and Japan as a prescription hypnotic medication.

chunks.title: Brotizolam
chunks.text:
Brotizolam became subject to regulatory scrutiny in Hong Kong during the late 1980s and early 1990s following emerging patterns of misuse. In October 1990, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board responded by reclassifying brotizolam alongside triazolam and flunitrazepam as Dangerous Drugs, instituting requirements for formal prescriptions and detailed record-keeping for the supply and dispensing of these substances.

Analysis of sales patterns between 1990 and 1993 revealed mixed outcomes from this initial intervention. While flunitrazepam and triazolam sales declined in 1991, five unrestricted benzodiazepines saw increased sales during the same period. New problems emerged with nimetazepam trafficking and temazepam misuse that year. These developments prompted the extension of the regulatory framework to encompass all benzodiazepines by January 1992. The comprehensive prescription and record-keeping requirements appear to have partially curbed benzodiazepine misuse in Hong Kong, though some ongoing concerns with temazepam, nimetazepam, triazolam, and brotizolam remained.

chunks.title: Buphedrone
chunks.text: Buphedrone is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and phenethylamine chemical classes, first synthesized in 1928. A synthetic analogue of cathinone — a compound naturally found in the khat plant — it has gained modest popularity as a mephedrone replacement and is reported to be roughly 2-3 times more potent than methcathinone. Its specific effects and toxicity remain poorly studied, and it may dangerously reduce the subjective sensation of thirst.

chunks.title: Buphedrone
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a synthetic cathinone stimulant, it is expected to have abuse potential similar to other compounds in this class.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Buprenorphine is a semisynthetic opioid of the morphinan class, first discovered in 1966 at Reckitt & Colman's research laboratories in England. It functions as a partial mu-opioid receptor agonist with high binding affinity but lower intrinsic activity than full agonists such as heroin or methadone. Used clinically for both pain management and opioid addiction treatment, its slow receptor dissociation produces an unusually long duration of action. Respiratory depression from overdose is considered less likely than with other opioids.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: With continued use, buprenorphine can cause opioid-type physical dependence, so stopping suddenly or tapering too quickly may produce withdrawal signs and symptoms. The withdrawal syndrome is typically milder than seen with full agonists and may be delayed in onset. Symptoms include body aches, diarrhea, nausea, anxiety, tremors, tachycardia, insomnia, sweating, and weakness.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Long-term buprenorphine use is moderately addictive, carries a high risk of abuse, and can cause psychological dependence in some users. Once addiction has developed, stopping suddenly may lead to cravings.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Among those with a history of seizures, a risk exists of further seizures. No notable seizure risk is documented in individuals without pre-existing seizure disorders.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hepatotoxicity ranging from transient asymptomatic elevations in liver enzymes to rare cases of hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic encephalopathy has been observed; many cases involved pre-existing liver disease, viral hepatitis co-infection, concurrent hepatotoxic drugs, or ongoing injection drug use.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Reports include cytolytic hepatitis and hepatitis with jaundice. In some cases, liver inflammation improved after buprenorphine was stopped. Liver function testing before treatment and periodic monitoring during treatment are recommended.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Ongoing opioid use can affect hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signaling and result in androgen deficiency, which may appear as reduced libido, impotence, erectile dysfunction, amenorrhea, or infertility; adrenal insufficiency has also been reported, more often after use lasting longer than one month.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Opioids inhibit the secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), cortisol, and luteinizing hormone (LH), while stimulating prolactin and growth hormone secretion.

chunks.text: Central sleep apnea has been reported as a side effect of long-term buprenorphine use, though it may resolve with dose reduction.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Buprenorphine acts as a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor with high binding affinity but lower intrinsic activity relative to full agonists, producing a ceiling effect at higher doses where its effects plateau rather than continuing to increase. It functions as an antagonist at both the kappa-opioid and delta-opioid receptors. Buprenorphine also acts at the nociceptin (ORL-1) receptor, where it has been characterized as both a full agonist and a partial agonist. Its slow dissociation from the mu-opioid receptor (approximately 166 minutes) contributes to its prolonged duration of action.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Buprenorphine is primarily metabolized in the liver via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5-mediated N-dealkylation to norbuprenorphine. Both buprenorphine and norbuprenorphine undergo further glucuronidation to inactive metabolites (buprenorphine-3-glucuronide and norbuprenorphine-3-glucuronide). Bioavailability is very high following intravenous administration, lower by the sublingual or buccal route, and very low when taken orally. The elimination half-life of sublingual buprenorphine has been measured at approximately 31 hours.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Tolerance to many effects develops with prolonged and repeated use, though the rate varies for different effects. Notably, tolerance to constipation-inducing effects develops particularly slowly. Some evidence suggests that buprenorphine tolerance may not develop as readily with chronic use compared to full opioid agonists, possibly due to its lack of delta-opioid agonism.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text:
Buprenorphine emerged from a decade-long research program at Reckitt & Colman (now Reckitt Benckiser) in Hull, England, where scientists sought to synthesize opioid compounds that retained therapeutic analgesic properties while minimizing the problematic effects of physical dependence and abuse liability. The compound was discovered in 1966 and designated RX6029 after demonstrating success in reducing dependence in animal models. It was patented in 1965 and entered human clinical trials in 1971.

The medication was first launched commercially in the United Kingdom in 1978 as an injectable formulation for the treatment of severe pain, followed by a sublingual tablet preparation in 1982. In the United States, Reckitt licensed Norwich-Eaton to distribute the injectable formulation under the brand name Buprenex, which received FDA approval and was launched in 1985. By that year, injectable buprenorphine had been marketed for analgesic purposes in 29 countries and the sublingual tablet in 16 countries.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: The investigation of buprenorphine as a potential treatment for opioid addiction began in 1975, when researcher Donald Jasinski at the Lexington Addiction Research Center identified the compound as having especially unique pharmacology in humans. His research demonstrated that buprenorphine produced very little physical dependence even with chronic administration, leading him to speculate that it could serve both as an analgesic with low abuse potential and as a novel treatment for opioid addiction.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Jasinski characterized buprenorphine as producing long-lasting changes in subjective experience that were acceptable to individuals with opioid addiction while being less toxic than methadone. He concluded that the compound appeared to combine the advantages of both methadone and the opioid antagonist naltrexone without the major disadvantages of either. In 1979, the Addiction Research Center's clinical research program relocated from Lexington to the Johns Hopkins University medical campus in Baltimore, with the preclinical program following in 1981. The Baltimore location was selected in part because it provided access to a population of inner-city heroin users who could serve as research subjects.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Research into Addiction Treatment Potential

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: Prior to buprenorphine's approval for addiction treatment in the United States, the Drug Addiction Treatment Act of 2000 was enacted following lobbying efforts by Reckitt Benckiser. This legislation granted the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to issue waivers allowing physicians with appropriate training to prescribe Schedule III through V controlled substances for the treatment of addiction outside of specialized clinic settings, which had previously been the only permitted location for such treatment.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text: The FDA approved buprenorphine and the buprenorphine-naloxone combination product for opioid use disorder in October 2002. Immediately prior to this approval, the DEA rescheduled buprenorphine from Schedule V to Schedule III. The waiver system initially limited each approved physician to treating only 10 patients. This cap was raised to 30, then to 100 in May 2008, and subsequently to 275 patients in 2016 under the Obama administration. In January 2021, responding to record levels of opioid overdose deaths, the Department of Health and Human Services eliminated the waiver requirement entirely for physicians prescribing buprenorphine to up to 30 patients concurrently.

chunks.title: Buprenorphine
chunks.text:
France adopted a notably different regulatory approach, permitting general practitioners to prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder beginning in the mid-1990s without requiring special training or restrictions. This policy was implemented as a harm reduction response to HIV transmission and overdose mortality among people who inject drugs. The result was treatment of approximately ten times more patients per year with buprenorphine than with methadone in the following decade. Between 1994 and 2002, deaths from heroin overdose in France decreased by approximately 80 percent, and the incidence of AIDS among people who inject drugs fell from 25 percent in the mid-1990s to 6 percent by 2010.

In the European Union more broadly, the high-dose sublingual tablet preparations Subutex and Suboxone received approval for opioid use disorder treatment in September 2006. Extended-release injectable formulations have since been approved in multiple jurisdictions, including Buvidal in the United Kingdom, Europe, and Australia in 2018, and Sublocade in the United States the same year.

The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion is an atypical antidepressant belonging to the substituted cathinone and phenethylamine classes. First marketed under the brand name Wellbutrin, it functions as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) and is prescribed for major depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder, and smoking cessation. Unlike typical antidepressants, bupropion is less associated with sexual dysfunction and weight gain. It carries an elevated seizure risk, particularly in predisposed individuals, and should not be combined with other drugs without caution.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: A handful of case reports suggest that abrupt discontinuation may cause antidepressant discontinuation syndrome, but significant physical dependence is not a prominent feature of bupropion use.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion has been identified as having mild abuse potential with amphetamine-like activity, particularly when insufflated or injected. At oral doses around 400 mg, patients with substance abuse history may experience mild amphetamine-like effects. Some recreational use has been reported, though the substance is usually not very pleasant.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion-induced psychosis may develop in rare cases, typically associated with higher than recommended doses. Symptoms include visual hallucinations such as figures walking around, auditory hallucinations including voices, severe agitation, and disorientation to time. Hallucinations are fairly often seen with significant overdoses. At least one report described hallucinated voices suggesting self-harm.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Seizures are the primary severe medical concern with bupropion and are strongly dose-dependent. At therapeutic doses of 300-450 mg daily, seizure incidence is approximately 0.4%, but this climbs almost ten-fold at 600 mg. The median seizure dose in overdose is 1-2 grams, with one analysis finding seizures in 11% of intentional overdoses overall, increasing to 41% in cases with other clinical effects. An Australian review found 37% of overdoses resulted in seizure. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold even at doses of 150-450 mg, which poses risk for susceptible individuals. The drug has a narrow safety range given this seizure risk, and the FDA initially withdrew it from the market due to seizure concerns before reintroducing it with adjusted dosing.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cases of liver toxicity leading to death or liver transplantation have been reported; bupropion is considered one of several antidepressants with greater hepatotoxicity risk, with documented cases developing within the first 6 months of treatment.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) that weakly inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine by binding to the norepinephrine transporter (NET) and dopamine transporter (DAT), prolonging their action in the synaptic cleft. It also acts as a negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, with activity at α3β2, α4β2, and α7 subtypes, being most potent at α3β2 and least potent at α7. This nicotinic antagonism is thought to contribute to its efficacy as a smoking cessation aid by blunting the effects of nicotine and affecting receptor subtypes associated with dopamine and norepinephrine release. Bupropion is essentially inactive at the serotonin transporter and has no meaningful direct activity at adrenergic, dopamine, serotonin, histamine, or muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. PET studies show that bupropion at therapeutic doses occupies only approximately 20% of dopamine transporters in the human brain, considerably lower than other NDRIs like methylphenidate, raising questions about the relative contribution of dopamine reuptake inhibition to its clinical effects.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Due to the higher plasma concentrations of its metabolite hydroxybupropion, which has greater affinity for NET than DAT, the overall pharmacological profile in humans may be more consistent with noradrenergic than dopaminergic activity. Bupropion and its primary metabolite hydroxybupropion have also been found to block serotonin 5-HT3A receptors.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion is rapidly and completely absorbed after oral administration, but absolute bioavailability is presumed to be low (5-20%) due to extensive first-pass metabolism. It is extensively metabolized via multiple pathways, with CYP2B6 being the principal enzyme responsible for formation of the major active metabolite hydroxybupropion, while CYP2C19 contributes to a lesser degree. Additional reductive pathways involving 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 in the liver and AKR7A2/AKR7A3 in the intestine produce threohydrobupropion and erythrohydrobupropion. Metabolism is highly variable between individuals, with effective doses differing by as much as 5.5-fold for bupropion and 7.5-fold for hydroxybupropion. The half-life is approximately 21-24 hours with chronic use, while metabolites have half-lives of 20-30 hours or greater and accumulate with repeated dosing. Hydroxybupropion reaches steady-state concentrations 7-10 times higher than the parent compound. Bupropion is 84% bound to plasma proteins. Following oral administration, 87% of the dose is recovered in urine and 10% in feces, with only 0.5% excreted unchanged.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion also inhibits CYP2D6, which can lead to clinically significant drug interactions.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Bupropion was synthesized in 1969 by Nariman Mehta, a chemist working at Burroughs Wellcome (now GlaxoSmithKline), during efforts to develop a new antidepressant compound. The US patent was granted in 1974. Testing proceeded through the 1970s, with researchers reporting in 1977 that the drug's in vivo effects differed notably from those of amphetamine. The US Food and Drug Administration granted approval for bupropion as an antidepressant on December 30, 1985, and it was marketed under the brand name Wellbutrin.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Shortly after its initial approval, bupropion was withdrawn from the market in 1986 due to a significant incidence of seizures at the originally recommended dosage of 400-600 mg per day. A notable seizure risk emerged particularly in studies involving bulimic patients. Subsequent research determined that seizure risk was highly dose-dependent, and with more careful dosing protocols, the drug could be used safely. Bupropion was reintroduced to the US market in 1989 with a reduced maximum recommended daily dose of 450 mg.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: During the 1980s and 1990s, Dr. Linda Ferry and other researchers observed that depressed patients receiving bupropion would sometimes spontaneously reduce or quit tobacco use. Controlled trials in non-depressed individuals subsequently supported its efficacy as a smoking cessation aid. In 1997, the FDA approved bupropion for smoking cessation under the brand name Zyban, a sustained-release formulation. This made bupropion the first pharmacotherapy for tobacco addiction other than nicotine replacement to receive approval in the United States. By 2007, it was reported to be the leading smoking cessation aid in the US, with an estimated 8.7 million prescriptions dispensed annually.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: The FDA approved a sustained-release formulation called Wellbutrin SR in 1996, designed as a twice-daily tablet compared to the three-times-daily dosing required for immediate-release Wellbutrin. In 2003, another sustained-release formulation called Wellbutrin XL received approval, entering the market in 2004 as a once-daily hard-shelled tablet. Wellbutrin XL was additionally approved in 2006 for treatment of seasonal affective disorder. In April 2008, the FDA approved a hydrobromide salt formulation marketed as Aplenzin, an extended-release tablet for once-daily use.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: In 2004, the FDA issued a warning about possible severe neuropsychiatric problems associated with antidepressants including bupropion, extending this warning to cover smoking cessation use in 2009. The advisory noted reports of unusual behavior changes, agitation, hostility, depression worsening, and suicidal ideation. This was based on a review identifying 75 reports of suicidal adverse events for bupropion over a ten-year period from 1997 to 2007, though a clear causal connection between bupropion and suicidal activity remained uncertain. Following results from additional trials, this warning was removed in 2016.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: In October 2007, ConsumerLab.com and The People's Pharmacy released comparative test results of different bupropion brands after receiving multiple reports of increased side effects and decreased efficacy with generic formulations. Testing indicated that one generic version of Wellbutrin XL 300 mg, sold as Budeprion XL 300 mg, did not perform equivalently to the brand-name product in laboratory tests. The FDA initially concluded that Budeprion XL was equivalent to Wellbutrin XL, attributing reported problems to natural mood variation. However, in October 2012, the FDA reversed this position, announcing that Budeprion XL 300 mg failed to demonstrate therapeutic equivalence to Wellbutrin XL 300 mg.

chunks.title: Bupropion
chunks.text: Reports of recreational bupropion use emerged during the 2000s, often involving intranasal administration. Some cases involved individuals who had been prescribed the drug, including adolescents receiving it for ADHD. Prison populations represented one setting where recreational use occurred to a notable degree. From the mid-2000s through the 2010s, reports of intravenous administration appeared, with some cases resulting in tissue damage. Most chronic recreational use has been documented among individuals with prior substance use disorders. While case reports describe effects similar to cocaine or amphetamine but with less intensity, recreational use remains uncommon overall, as bupropion's pharmacological profile limits its abuse potential compared to other stimulants.

chunks.title: Buspirone
chunks.text: Buspirone is an anxiolytic of the azapirone class that acts as a serotonin 5-HT1A receptor partial agonist. First synthesized in 1968 and approved by the FDA in 1986, it is primarily prescribed for generalized anxiety disorder. Unlike benzodiazepines, buspirone does not interact with GABA receptors and carries no significant risk of sedation, physical dependence, or withdrawal. Its therapeutic effects typically require 2 to 4 weeks to fully manifest.

chunks.title: Buspirone
chunks.text: Adverse effects including addiction become increasingly likely with higher doses, though buspirone is generally considered to have low abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Butylone is a synthetic entactogen and stimulant of the substituted cathinone class. It is the β-keto analogue of MBDB and bears a structural relationship to methylone analogous to that between MBDB and MDMA. First synthesized in 1967, it remained academically obscure until 2005 when it emerged as a designer drug. Butylone is frequently sold as a substitute or counterfeit for MDMA and methylone under the collective street label "Molly," though its subjective effects are not identical to either substance.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Withdrawal effects may occur when regular users suddenly stop, though these appear to primarily involve neurotransmitter depletion symptoms such as anxiety, depression, cognitive fatigue, and irritability rather than severe physical withdrawal.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Chronic use is considered moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and may cause psychological dependence. Cravings may develop with regular use, and users may experience difficulty stopping once a pattern of use has been established.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Abuse at high dosages for prolonged periods can potentially result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Based on data from related amphetamine-class stimulants, approximately 5-15% of users who develop stimulant psychosis may not fully recover. Psychosis is unlikely with occasional use at moderate doses.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Butylone acts as a mixed reuptake inhibitor and releasing agent at the serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine transporters, increasing extracellular monoamine levels. Its activity profile is weighted toward reuptake inhibition, though it retains relatively robust monoamine releasing capabilities. Relative to methylone, butylone has approximately 4-fold lower affinity for the norepinephrine transporter, while its serotonin and dopamine transporter affinities are comparable.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Butylone is metabolized through three primary pathways. The most prominent are demethylenation followed by O-methylation and β-ketone reduction, with N-dealkylation occurring less frequently. The most commonly observed metabolite in human urine is the 4-OH-3-MeO form. Hydroxyl-containing metabolites are excreted as conjugates in urine.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: Butylone was first synthesized in 1967 by Koeppe, Ludwig, and Zeile, who documented their work in a paper from that year. Following its initial synthesis, the compound remained an obscure product of academic chemistry for nearly four decades, receiving little attention outside of laboratory settings. The substance emerged on the designer drug market in 2005, when it began to be sold as a recreational product. Structurally, butylone bears the same relationship to methylone that MBDB bears to MDMA—both are beta-keto analogues of their respective parent compounds. Formal pharmacological research on butylone did not commence until 2009, when studies demonstrated that it undergoes metabolic processes similar to those of related cathinones such as methylone.

chunks.title: Butylone
chunks.text: As methylone's availability on the research chemical market declined, butylone became commonly sold alongside ethylone as a substitute or counterfeit for MDMA and methylone. These substances, along with other cathinones, have collectively come to be referred to as "Molly" in street terminology. Despite behavioral and pharmacological similarities to MDMA, butylone has a very short history of documented human use, and limited data exists regarding its full range of effects in humans.

chunks.title: Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: Butyrfentanyl is a potent short-acting synthetic opioid and analog of fentanyl, possessing approximately one quarter of its parent compound's potency. It has no established clinical applications and is sold exclusively as a designer drug. One of the earliest references to this compound appears in documentation by The College on Problems of Drug Dependence. As with other fentanyl analogs, butyrfentanyl carries significant risk of respiratory depression and fatal overdose, demanding extreme caution.

chunks.title: Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a potent synthetic opioid and fentanyl analog, it carries significant abuse potential.

chunks.title: Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: Butyrfentanyl acts as an agonist at μ-opioid receptors. In radioligand displacement assays using [3H]fentanyl, it exhibits a Ki of 32 ± 4.1 nM, indicating substantially lower binding affinity than fentanyl itself (Ki 1.06 ± 0.15 nM) and roughly one quarter of its potency as an opioid agonist.

chunks.title: Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text: Butyrfentanyl is rapidly cleared from the body. In studies of urinary excretion following injection, nearly all of the administered dose was excreted or metabolized within the first 3 hours, with only very low concentrations detectable thereafter.

chunks.title: Butyrfentanyl
chunks.text:
Butyrfentanyl first appears in scientific literature through documentation by the College on Problems of Drug Dependence, where it was referenced as an N-butyramide fentanyl analog. Pharmacological characterization of the compound—including analgesic efficacy studies, opioid receptor binding profiles, and related measures of narcotic properties—was published in 1987.

Despite this early scientific description, the substance was never developed for clinical use. It later emerged as a designer drug, appearing as part of a broader resurgence of illicit fentanyl analogs that began in Estonia in the early 2000s and subsequently spread throughout Europe and former Soviet republics. This wave of novel fentanyl derivatives has been linked to hundreds of fatalities across these regions as new compounds continue to appear on unregulated markets.

International scheduling efforts culminated in March 2017 when the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs voted to add butyrfentanyl to Schedule I of the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs.

chunks.title: BZP
chunks.text: BZP is a synthetic stimulant of the piperazine class, first synthesized in 1944 by Burroughs Wellcome & Company. Initially investigated as an antiparasitic agent and later as an antidepressant, it was abandoned after studies revealed amphetamine-like abuse potential. BZP gained widespread recreational use in the 2000s, often marketed as "legal ecstasy" or sold as an MDMA substitute. Adverse effects include seizures, acute psychosis, and renal toxicity, with at least one death attributed to BZP alone.

chunks.title: BZP
chunks.text: BZP has amphetamine-like effects and was identified as liable to abuse during early research. Studies indicate it can substitute for methamphetamine in addicted animals, though it is approximately one-tenth as potent and produces correspondingly weaker addictive effects.

chunks.title: BZP
chunks.text: Acute psychosis and adverse psychiatric events have been reported following BZP use. Hallucinations, confusion, agitation, and anxiety are among the documented side effects.

chunks.title: BZP
chunks.text: Seizures are a documented serious adverse effect of BZP. Life-threatening toxicity with status epilepticus has been recorded, with fourteen toxic seizures observed in two patients who also developed severe respiratory and metabolic acidosis. BZP can cause unpredictable and serious toxicity in some individuals.

chunks.title: BZP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Deaths from BZP alone are extremely rare, but at least one fatality has been attributed to BZP ingestion alone with a measured blood concentration of 8 mg/L. Multiple deaths have been reported when BZP was combined with alcohol, TFMPP, or MDMA.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant of the methylxanthine class and the most widely consumed psychoactive substance in the world. Found in coffee beans, tea leaves, cacao, and numerous other plants, it is primarily used for its wakefulness-promoting, cognitive-enhancing, and physical performance-boosting properties. While it has a generally favorable safety profile, regular heavy use can produce physical dependence. Pure powder forms carry a greater risk of accidental overdose.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: A mild form of physical dependence develops with regular daily use above 100 mg. Withdrawal symptoms include headache, fatigue, irritability, depressed mood, difficulty concentrating, and flu-like symptoms, typically beginning within 24 hours of cessation and generally resolving within one day.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine is habit-forming and commonly used daily by millions, though compulsive consumption under any circumstances has not been scientifically observed. Some diagnostic manuals classify caffeine addiction, and some users report difficulty reducing intake despite awareness of negative effects.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Psychotic symptoms including delusions, hallucinations, mania, disorientation, and disinhibition may occur only at very high doses exceeding 5 grams, approaching lethal levels. At typical consumption, caffeine may induce or worsen anxiety rather than psychosis; caffeine-induced anxiety disorder is recognized in the DSM-5.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Seizures may occur in cases of caffeine overdose due to central nervous system overstimulation. Individuals with epilepsy or other seizure disorders should use caffeine with extreme caution.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High caffeine intake, particularly from energy drinks exceeding 320 mg, is associated with short-term cardiovascular effects including elevated blood pressure, prolonged QT interval, tachycardia, and heart palpitations; these effects are typically acute and dose-dependent, with tolerance developing to autonomic cardiovascular effects with chronic use.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Individuals with certain CYP1A2 genotypes (C allele carriers) may have increased risk of non-fatal myocardial infarction with caffeine consumption. Generally well-tolerated at typical doses in healthy individuals.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Caffeine stimulates gastric acid secretion and increases gastrointestinal motility; long-term high-dose consumption of coffee may contribute to stomach ulcer formation.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Overdose symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal upset. The acidity of coffee itself may contribute to ulcer formation beyond caffeine's effects alone.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: In postmenopausal women, high caffeine consumption has been associated with accelerated bone loss.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk appears specific to postmenopausal women; general population effects are less documented.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis has been reported in cases of very high caffeine intake exceeding 5 grams, a dose approaching lethal levels.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Only documented at extreme overdose levels; not a concern at typical consumption.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine primarily acts as an antagonist at all four adenosine receptor subtypes (A1, A2A, A2B, and A3) in the central nervous system, blocking adenosine binding and inhibiting its depressant effects. The wakefulness-promoting properties are specifically attributed to A2A receptor antagonism, which reduces inhibitory GABA neurotransmission to histaminergic arousal centers in the tuberomammillary nucleus. Caffeine also indirectly modulates dopamine signaling through adenosine-dopamine receptor heteromers in the striatum (A1-D1 and A2A-D2) and promotes neurotransmitter release including monoamines and acetylcholine. At higher concentrations, caffeine nonselectively inhibits phosphodiesterase enzymes, enhances intracellular calcium release via ryanodine receptor activation, and antagonizes GABA receptors, though these secondary mechanisms typically engage at concentrations beyond those achieved through normal consumption.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine is rapidly and nearly completely absorbed after oral administration, with bioavailability approaching 100% in adults and peak plasma concentrations reached within 30 minutes to 2 hours. Metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via the CYP1A2 enzyme through sequential demethylation, producing paraxanthine as the major metabolite (84%) along with theobromine (12%) and theophylline (4%). Xanthine oxidase and N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) also contribute to its metabolism, and the resulting products are further processed and excreted in urine as urates. The elimination half-life is approximately 5 hours in healthy adults, though this varies considerably with smoking status, pregnancy, and age.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Antagonist (at supratherapeutic concentrations)

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Peak plasma concentration is reached within 30 minutes to 2 hours
Food may delay absorption
Smoking can reduce the half-life by up to 50%
Pregnancy increases the half-life to 15 hours or more, particularly in the third trimester
Newborns eliminate caffeine much more slowly, with a half-life of about 8 hours at full term and up to 100 hours in premature infants

chunks.text: Other methylxanthines (theophylline, theobromine)

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Tolerance to certain effects, particularly cardiovascular responses such as elevated blood pressure, develops with regular daily consumption. Habitual users demonstrate significantly reduced blood pressure elevation compared to non-regular consumers.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine-containing plants have been utilized by human cultures across multiple continents for millennia, with various civilizations independently discovering the stimulating properties of different botanical sources. According to Chinese legend, the emperor Shennong inadvertently discovered tea around 3000 BCE when leaves fell into boiling water, producing a fragrant and restorative drink. This account is referenced in Lu Yu's Cha Jing, an influential early treatise on tea. Meanwhile, in the Americas, residue analysis from an ancient Mayan vessel dated to 600 BCE provides the earliest evidence of cocoa bean consumption. Pre-Columbian Mesoamerican cultures prepared a bitter, spiced beverage called xocolatl, flavored with vanilla, chile pepper, and achiote, which was believed to combat fatigue—an effect likely attributable to its theobromine and caffeine content. Cocoa beans held such value that they were frequently used as currency.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: In West Africa, kola nut chewing appears to have ancient origins, practiced in both private and social contexts to restore vitality and suppress hunger. Native Americans of eastern North America brewed a tea called asi or "black drink" from the leaves and stems of yaupon holly, with archaeological evidence suggesting this tradition may date to Late Archaic times. The earliest credible evidence of coffee drinking emerges from fifteenth-century Sufi monasteries in Yemen. From the port of Mokha, coffee culture spread northward to Egypt and across North Africa, reaching the broader Middle East, Persia, and Turkey by the sixteenth century. European exposure followed, with Dutch traders eventually transporting coffee cultivation to the East Indies and the Americas. Chocolate reached Europe through Spanish colonizers and had become a popular beverage across the continent by 1700.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: The isolation of caffeine as a distinct chemical compound occurred through parallel efforts by several European chemists in the early nineteenth century. In 1819, the German chemist Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge successfully isolated relatively pure caffeine, which he termed "Kaffebase" in reference to its presence in coffee. Two years later, French chemist Pierre Jean Robiquet independently achieved isolation, as did the French team of Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou. The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius documented that these researchers had made their discoveries without knowledge of each other's work. Robiquet distinguished himself as among the first to describe pure caffeine's properties, while Pelletier conducted the initial elemental analysis. In 1827, M. Oudry isolated what he called "théine" from tea, though subsequent work by Mulder and Carl Jobst in 1838 demonstrated that théine was chemically identical to caffeine.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: The complete chemical characterization of caffeine culminated in the work of German chemist Hermann Emil Fischer, who achieved the first total synthesis of caffeine from its constituent elements in 1895. Two years later, Fischer determined the compound's structural formula. This research contributed to his Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text:
The recognition that coffee contained stimulating compounds prompted various regulatory efforts across different jurisdictions and eras. During the sixteenth century, Islamic authorities in Mecca and the Ottoman Empire enacted prohibitions against coffee for certain populations. In Europe, Charles II of England attempted to ban coffee in 1676, Frederick II of Prussia instituted a prohibition in 1777, and Sweden implemented coffee bans intermittently between 1756 and 1823.

Caffeine became the subject of one of the earliest documented American health scares in 1911, when the United States government seized forty barrels and twenty kegs of Coca-Cola syrup in Chattanooga, Tennessee, alleging that the caffeine content was injurious to health. Although the Supreme Court ultimately ruled in favor of Coca-Cola, the incident prompted legislative action: two bills were introduced to the House of Representatives in 1912 seeking to amend the Pure Food and Drug Act by adding caffeine to the list of habit-forming and deleterious substances requiring mandatory label disclosure.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text:
Various religious traditions have developed distinct positions regarding caffeine consumption. The Seventh-day Adventist Church historically requested that members abstain from caffeinated beverages, though this requirement has been removed from baptismal vows while abstention remains a recommended practice. Gaudiya Vaishnavas generally avoid caffeine based on beliefs that it clouds the mind and overstimulates the senses; initiation under a guru traditionally requires abstinence from caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, and other drugs for at least one year.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints maintains that its foundational health revelation does not specifically mention caffeine, though it prohibits "hot drinks," which church leaders have interpreted as referring to tea and coffee specifically. Among Muslims, caffeinated beverages are widely consumed, despite some sixteenth-century attempts by religious authorities to classify them as forbidden intoxicants under Islamic dietary law—efforts that ultimately proved unsuccessful.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: Caffeine occupies a unique position as the world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance, distinguished from nearly all other such compounds by its near-universal legal status and social acceptability. Unlike most psychoactive drugs, caffeine remains largely unregulated globally and is not merely tolerated but actively encouraged in many cultural contexts. The integration of caffeine into daily life has been profound, particularly following the Industrial Revolution. The relatively benign stimulation provided by caffeinated beverages has given rise to elaborate rituals, social bonding practices, and communication traditions, with sophisticated connoisseur cultures developing around coffee, tea, and other preparations. This state of sustained alertness has proven conducive to productive labor, aligning caffeine consumption with the demands of industrial and post-industrial capitalism.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text: For substantial portions of the global population, caffeine use has become habitual to a degree that some characterize as addiction, though this framing often provokes resistance similar to that encountered when applying such terminology to alcohol. The familiarity of caffeine has contributed to limited public awareness regarding its long-term effects on health and quality of life, compounded by the stigmatization of other stimulants that precludes meaningful comparison.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text:
Caffeine — unsafe combinations:
- Pregabalin (There is a risk of seizures from this combination, especially at higher dosages. Caffeine additionally reduces pregabalin’s anticonvulsant effects found in lower dosages. Caffeine increases respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal. If amphetamines wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages cause strain of the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications. Medical dosages are unlikely to be of concern.)

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text:
Caffeine — caution combinations:
- Amphetamines (This combination of stimulants is not generally necessary and may increase strain on the heart, as well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort.)
- AMT (High doses of caffeine may cause anxiety which is less manageable when tripping, and since both are stimulating the combination may cause some physical discomfort.)
- Cocaine (Both stimulants, risk of tachycardia, hypertension, and in extreme cases heart failure.)
- Diphenhydramine (Caffeine as a stimulant may mask some negative side effects of DPH, leading to delusions of sobriety, which has additional concerns in states of delirium. The combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart and may cause some physical discomfort, and has the chance to cause cardiovascular issues such as complex tachycardia. The combination may increase anxiety levels and risks of thought loops at higher dosages, in addition to increasing each other's negative side effects.

chunks.title: Caffeine
chunks.text:
Medical dosages are reported to not be a concern.)

- DXM (High doses of caffeine can potentially exacerbate anxiety, especially during a dissociative experience, due to its stimulating effects. This combination might also lead to physical discomfort. However, individual responses to caffeine can vary significantly, often influenced by factors like habitual versus occasional usage.)
- MDMA (Caffeine is not really necessary with MDMA and increases any neurotoxic effects from MDMA)
- Mephedrone (This combination of stimulants is not generally necessary and may increase strain on the heart, as well as potentially causing anxiety and great physical discomfort. However, individual responses to caffeine can vary significantly, often influenced by factors like habitual versus occasional usage.)
- NBOMe compounds (Caffeine can bring out the natural stimulation from psychedelic drugs to make it uncomfortable.

High doses can cause anxiety which is hard to handle while tripping)

chunks.title: Cake
chunks.text: Cake is a widely consumed confectionery substance primarily composed of flour, sugar, eggs, and fat. Its principal psychoactive constituent is reported to be cakecadine, a novel synthetic depressant of the substituted wheat class. The substance is orally active and has a long cultural history, with origins tracing back to ancient civilizations. Cake is considered highly addictive, and chronic use has been associated with hyperglycemia-related brain damage and pancreatic harm.

chunks.title: Cake
chunks.text: Studies indicate cake is highly addictive due to the presence of cakecadine, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

chunks.title: Cake
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Regular cake use may produce hyperglycemia, which can result in permanent brain damage.

chunks.title: Camazepam
chunks.text: Camazepam is a benzodiazepine depressant and the dimethyl carbamate ester of temazepam, itself a metabolite of diazepam. It is distinguished from other benzodiazepines by its particularly prominent anxiolytic properties alongside comparatively limited sedative, hypnotic, anticonvulsant, and skeletal muscle relaxant effects. It also produces fewer cognitive and motor impairments than many related compounds. Camazepam is indicated for the short-term treatment of insomnia and anxiety, and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Camazepam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, consistent with the psychological dependence potential of the benzodiazepine class.

chunks.title: Camazepam

chunks.title: Camazepam

chunks.title: Canket
chunks.text: Canket is a dissociative substance of the arylcyclohexylamine class. It was first correctly identified by a laboratory in Canberra, Australia, through NMR analysis, which revealed that the majority of material sold online as FXE (3F-2'-Oxo-PCE) for approximately two years was actually 2F-2'-Oxo-PCE. The two positional isomers appear identical under standard GCMS testing, meaning widespread mislabeling went undetected until NMR verification was applied. Significant identity confusion between these compounds persists.

chunks.title: Canket
chunks.text: Canket became notable through a naming and identification dispute around material commonly sold or discussed as FXE. CanTEST in Canberra identified the compound as 2F-2'-Oxo-PCE using NMR, challenging an earlier assumption that the circulating material was the 3-fluoro compound.

chunks.title: Canket
chunks.text: Canket has been described as the compound many users had been calling FXE. The clearer identification was attributed to CanTEST in Canberra, where NMR testing was available through the university setting.

chunks.title: Canket
chunks.text: The source frames the FXE name as already embedded in community usage and notes that correcting the name may remain difficult unless batches of the genuine 3-fluoro material become available.

chunks.title: Canket
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (noncompetitive)

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Cannabis is a genus of flowering plant that has been used for thousands of years for medicinal, spiritual, and recreational purposes. Its primary psychoactive constituent is delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), though dozens of additional cannabinoids and terpenes contribute to its overall effects. It ranks among the most widely consumed recreational substances globally, behind only alcohol, caffeine, and tobacco. Its two principal species, sativa and indica, are recognized for producing distinct effect profiles.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Mild physical dependence can develop with regular daily use. Withdrawal symptoms include irritability, insomnia, sweating, loss of appetite, and restlessness, typically lasting 1-2 weeks but occasionally up to 6 weeks in heavy users. Symptoms are never life-threatening.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Low to moderate abuse potential with risk of psychological dependence in some individuals with chronic use. Studies estimate 5-10% of users may become daily users at some point, though most discontinue by age 30. Dependence rates are lower than both alcohol and nicotine.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Acute psychotic symptoms including paranoia, delusions, and anxiety can occur, particularly at high doses. Prolonged use may increase psychosis risk in predisposed individuals with family history of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders. A 2011 FDA report found no clear causal linkage between cannabis use and psychotic disorders in otherwise healthy people, though associations have been documented between adolescent use and later psychotic diagnoses.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Well-designed epidemiological studies involving tens of thousands of patients have not found increased risk of lung or upper airway cancer from light to moderate cannabis use. Any carcinogenic concerns appear related to combustion products when smoked rather than cannabis constituents themselves.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic smoking may cause respiratory issues including coughing, bronchitis, increased throat and lung infections, and reduced lung capacity; however, well-designed epidemiological studies have not found increased risk of lung cancer or COPD from cannabis alone, with pulmonary risks far lower than tobacco smoking.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risks primarily associated with smoked route rather than cannabis itself. Vaporization reported to reduce lung impact. A comprehensive 2013 review by Tashkin found no significant lung function abnormalities from habitual marijuana use alone and no increased cancer risk from light to moderate use.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including increased heart rate and blood pressure changes occur during intoxication; a large study of 65,000 individuals found no increased mortality in users under 50, though those with pre-existing heart conditions may face elevated risk.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: One study suggested increased heart attack risk in men over 40 but findings were weak and based on very small numbers. At high doses, circulatory problems up to circulatory collapse are possible. Use should be avoided with existing heart conditions.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Regular use may cause cognitive effects including short-term memory impairment, reduced motivation, and difficulty learning; these effects are typically reversible with abstinence, and well-controlled studies have not found evidence of permanent IQ loss or brain structure changes from cannabis use.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Inhibition of glutamate neurotransmission in the hippocampus affects short-term memory formation.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: 2015 research by Weiland et al. found no brain area volume differences in controlled study. 2016 research by Jackson et al. using matched twins found no support for causal link between cannabis and IQ reduction. Heavy adolescent use may reduce academic performance through decreased motivation rather than direct cognitive damage.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Typically returns to baseline after 2-3 weeks of abstinence, though THC has been detected in heavy users up to 77 days after last use. Withdrawal symptoms in heavy users generally persist for 1-2 weeks.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: All cannabinoids (THC, CBD, synthetic cannabinoids)

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Prolonged repeated cannabis use can produce tolerance to many effects, especially with daily consumption. Regular ingestion leads to increased tolerance to stimulating effects more rapidly than to relaxing effects due to the longer half-life of CBD (9 hours) compared to THC's stimulating effects (2-3 hours). Heavy users may require doses several times higher than cannabis-naive individuals to achieve comparable effects.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Approximately 1-2 weeks after cessation of use.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Cannabis represents one of humanity's oldest cultivated plants, first domesticated approximately 12,000 years ago in East Asia during the early Neolithic period. Genetic and archaeological evidence suggests human use may extend even further back, possibly to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B period between 8800 and 6500 BCE. Indigenous to central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, the plant has been valued throughout recorded history for multiple purposes: as a source of fiber and rope, as food and medicine, and for its psychoactive properties in both religious and recreational contexts. Written records documenting cannabis use date from the third millennium BC. The Greek historian Herodotus provided one of the earliest detailed accounts around 440 BCE, describing the central Eurasian Scythians' practice of cannabis steam baths in his *Histories*. He recorded that the Scythians would throw what he called "hemp-seed" (likely referring to the flowering tops) upon red-hot stones beneath felt coverings, producing a vapor that reportedly filled them with such pleasure that they would "shout for joy."

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Archaeological discoveries have corroborated these ancient accounts. The Yanghai Tombs, a vast cemetery in the Xinjiang region of northwestern China, contained the 2,700-year-old grave of a shaman. Near the body lay a leather basket and wooden bowl containing 789 grams of remarkably well-preserved cannabis, which laboratory analysis confirmed contained tetrahydrocannabinol. In China, the plant's psychoactive properties are documented in the Shennong Bencaojing, a pharmacological text from the third century AD, with records indicating that Daoists burned cannabis in incense burners to inhale the smoke. The word "cannabis" derives from the Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis), which itself originated from Scythian or Thracian languages. The term shares etymological roots with the Persian "kanab" and is related to the English words "canvas" and possibly "hemp."

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Cannabis holds sacred significance across numerous religious traditions spanning diverse cultures and time periods. In Hindu practice, the plant is first mentioned in the Vedas between 2000 and 1400 BCE, specifically within the Atharvaveda. By the tenth century CE, it was reportedly referred to by some practitioners in India as "food of the gods," and its ceremonial use became integrated into the Hindu festival of Holi. The traditional preparation known as bhang—cannabis consumed in food or drink—represents an intrinsic element of Hindu culture dating back at least three millennia. The city of Varanasi, situated along the banks of the Ganges, is considered the spiritual center of this tradition, where bhang lassi, a creamy cannabis-infused milk beverage, continues to be sold openly through dedicated shops. Among Sufis—practitioners of the mystical traditions within Islam—cannabis use has been documented since the thirteenth century CE, with significant influence on local religious practices in Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Turkey, and Pakistan. The Shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar in Pakistan's Sindh province is particularly noted for widespread cannabis use during its celebrations.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Other religious traditions have maintained varied relationships with the plant. In Buddhist teachings, cannabis is generally regarded as an intoxicant that may impede the development of meditation and clear awareness. Ancient Germanic cultures associated the plant with Freya, the Norse goddess of love. In contemporary practice, the Rastafari movement has embraced cannabis as a sacrament central to its spiritual observance.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text:
The scientific classification of cannabis began in 1753 when Carl Linnaeus, devising the taxonomic system still used for species naming, first categorized the genus. He regarded it as monotypic—comprising a single species—which he designated Cannabis sativa L. In 1785, the evolutionary biologist Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck published a description of a second species based on specimens collected in India. He named this Cannabis indica, distinguishing it from C. sativa based on morphological characteristics including trichome structure and leaf shape, noting that while C. indica demonstrated inferior fiber quality, it possessed greater potential as an inebriant.

Chemical investigation of the plant began in earnest during the late nineteenth century when cannabinol became the first compound successfully isolated from cannabis extract. By 1940, researchers had determined its molecular structure and achieved chemical synthesis, establishing the foundation for systematic preclinical research into the specific effects of individual cannabis-derived compounds.

chunks.text: Botanical Classification and Chemical Investigation

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: The earliest documented restrictions on cannabis appeared in the Islamic world during the fourteenth century. Regulatory measures expanded during the nineteenth century, particularly within colonial territories, where prohibition often reflected underlying racial and class tensions. During this same era, recreational and medicinal use spread from traditional strongholds in China and the Middle East to European populations, reaching America by mid-century. The plant arrived in the western hemisphere in 1545 when Spanish colonists brought it to Chile for fiber cultivation. In North America, hemp became an important agricultural product, grown extensively for rope, cloth, and paper production. Various forms of the plant developed regional significance: hashish, a concentrated resin preparation, became associated with Morocco, Lebanon, and Afghanistan, while traditional preparations maintained their importance in their regions of origin.

chunks.title: Cannabis
chunks.text: Cannabis occupied a central position in the 1960s youth counterculture movement, becoming closely identified with the art, music, and social upheaval of that period. This cultural association has persisted into contemporary times, with cities like Amsterdam developing distinctive cannabis cultures through their coffeeshop systems, where the plant is sold in licensed establishments under policies of tolerance, attracting enthusiasts from across the globe. Jamaica has similarly developed its own cannabis culture, with the plant becoming intertwined with the island's musical heritage and spiritual traditions.
