chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Carisoprodol is a carbamate sedative-hypnotic and centrally acting muscle relaxant first approved for medical use in 1959. Developed as an improvement upon meprobamate, it functions as a prodrug that is metabolized into meprobamate in the body. Prescribed for the short-term treatment of musculoskeletal pain, it also possesses anxiolytic and hypnotic properties. Its effects are often compared to barbiturates, and it has been largely supplanted by benzodiazepines due to safety concerns. Its European Union approval was withdrawn in 2008.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Physical dependence of the barbiturate type develops following prolonged use. Withdrawal can be life-threatening, particularly in high-dose users or those who stop abruptly, and may require hospitalization. Severe withdrawal can mimic alcohol withdrawal including potentially lethal status epilepticus. The accumulation of meprobamate, which has a longer half-life, contributes to withdrawal severity.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Carisoprodol has significant psychological addiction potential with documented abuse cases even when used without other drugs possessing abuse potential. Compulsive redosing is a recognized effect, and users frequently escalate to very high daily doses. Its potent anxiolytic effects and euphoria are implicated in drug-seeking behavior. Psychological dependence is more common in those who use it non-medically or have a history of substance use.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Psychotic symptoms occur primarily during withdrawal rather than acute intoxication. Approximately 20% of withdrawal cases feature hallucinations (mainly visual and auditory) or other psychotic symptoms. Case reports document patients experiencing vivid hallucinations of insects, animals, people, and voices indistinguishable from reality, along with paranoid ideation. Symptoms typically peak 3-5 days after cessation and may last up to 8-9 days.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Unlike benzodiazepines, carisoprodol increases rather than decreases seizure risk. Seizures can occur both in overdose and during withdrawal. Withdrawal seizures can progress to potentially lethal status epilepticus, similar to alcohol withdrawal. Drugs that lower seizure threshold should be avoided during withdrawal. Deaths have been reported in association with carisoprodol-related seizures.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose causes CNS depression ranging from lethargy to deep coma; chronic use and withdrawal can result in prolonged cognitive changes including memory impairment, reduced IQ, increased anxiety and depression, and in some cases these effects persist for months or years after discontinuation.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Direct GABA-A agonism at higher doses causes profound CNS depression; chronic GABA-ergic modulation leads to neuroadaptive changes

chunks.title: Carisoprodol

chunks.text: Neuromuscular symptoms including myoclonus and muscular rigidity occurred in 16% of overdose cases in one study. Cognitive effects during discontinuation may be dose-dependent but are primarily influenced by pattern of use.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression occurs primarily in overdose situations and is significantly more dangerous when carisoprodol is combined with other CNS depressants; mechanical ventilation may be required in severe cases.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol

chunks.title: Carisoprodol

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Carisoprodol is a centrally acting muscle relaxant that functions through both positive allosteric modulation and direct agonism at GABA-A receptors, with evidence suggesting separate binding sites for each mechanism, both of which appear distinct from those used by benzodiazepines and barbiturates. Its muscle relaxant effects are associated with altered interneuronal activity in the spinal cord and descending reticular formation. The drug shows subunit-dependent selectivity, with direct agonist activity more pronounced at α2-containing receptors and positive allosteric modulation showing greater efficacy at α1 and β2-containing complexes. In animal studies, flumazenil has been shown to partially inhibit the drug's activity.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Carisoprodol is metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP2C19, with a considerable proportion converted to meprobamate, an active metabolite that functions as a GABA-A receptor modulator and adenosine reuptake inhibitor. Meprobamate reaches higher peak plasma concentrations than carisoprodol itself and has a substantially longer half-life of approximately 11.3 hours. Additional metabolites include hydroxycarisoprodol and hydroxymeprobamate. The reported elimination half-life of carisoprodol is approximately 2 hours according to some sources and approximately 8 hours according to others. Excretion occurs via the kidneys.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Greater modulation at α1 and β2-containing complexes; efficacy unaffected by γ subunit presence

chunks.title: Carisoprodol

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Frank M. Berger at Wallace Laboratories (later Carter-Wallace) synthesized carisoprodol in 1956. Berger had also been part of the team responsible for creating meprobamate, which had become a widely used pharmaceutical during the 1950s. The development of carisoprodol arose from ongoing efforts to create and test various meprobamate derivatives. The critical structural modification involved substituting one hydrogen atom with an isopropyl group on one of the carbamyl nitrogens, intended to produce a compound with distinct pharmacological properties.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: In June 1959, several American pharmacologists convened at Wayne State University in Detroit, Michigan to discuss the newly discovered structural analogue. Building upon meprobamate's established pharmacological effects, carisoprodol was designed to provide improved muscle relaxing properties while offering reduced addiction potential and a lower risk of overdose. The FDA approved the drug later that year. Early publications described it as exhibiting properties similar to both mephenesin and meprobamate, though its effect profile differed significantly from its parent compound, demonstrating stronger muscle relaxant and analgesic effects.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text:
During the 1960s, animal research indicated that carisoprodol produced clear EEG changes without causing significant sedation at low doses. In this respect, researchers likened its profile to atropine. The prevailing discussion about the substance during this period suggested it possessed low abuse potential and minimal risk of physical dependence.

This perception began to shift in 1978 when a report appeared demonstrating the drug's abuse potential, ultimately contributing to growing concern about its effects and marking the beginning of a reevaluation of its safety profile.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Following additional reports documenting physical dependence and recreational use during the 1990s, concerns about carisoprodol increased considerably. Research from this period revealed that only a small percentage of physicians understood carisoprodol's status as a prodrug of meprobamate, with most believing it carried a lower abuse risk than its metabolite. The DEA recommended federal scheduling in 1996, though the FDA opposed this action at the time due to insufficient evidence. Carisoprodol was designated as a "drug of concern" instead. By 1998, it ranked eighteenth out of 123 drugs involved in emergency department visits in the United States.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Reports increasingly documented the drug being used to potentiate the effects of opioids, and sometimes benzodiazepines, cocaine, and alcohol. The practice of combining carisoprodol with opioids and benzodiazepines became colloquially known as "The Holy Trinity" due to the reported intensification of euphoric effects. The dangers of such combinations were illustrated by actress Dana Plato's death in 1999, which occurred after taking carisoprodol along with a hydrocodone and acetaminophen painkiller. In 2014, actress Skye McCole Bartusiak died from an overdose involving the combined effects of carisoprodol, hydrocodone, and difluoroethane. Even without federal scheduling, individual states began implementing their own controls. SAMHSA reported a doubling of nonmedical use between 2004 and 2008. The National Forensic Laboratory Information System listed carisoprodol among the top 25 most abused drugs in the United States in 2008, during which year approximately 10.5 million prescriptions were dispensed. The availability of carisoprodol through online sellers significantly contributed to this rise in nonmedical use.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Multiple countries began removing carisoprodol from the market or implementing stricter controls during this period. Sweden withdrew the drug from the market in November 2007 due to problems with dependence and adverse effects. Evidence from Norway demonstrating its addictive potential both as a prodrug of meprobamate and as a potentiator of opioids led to its removal from the Norwegian market in May 2008. The European Medicines Agency recommended member states suspend marketing authorization the same year. In January 2012, carisoprodol became a Schedule IV controlled substance in the United States following documented increases in misuse and adverse events. The scheduling decision noted that the drug possesses barbiturate-like effects in vitro, exhibits discriminative stimulus effects similar to other Schedule IV drugs such as barbital, meprobamate, and chlordiazepoxide, and that excessive use produces toxicity and withdrawal symptoms comparable to other controlled depressants.

chunks.title: Carisoprodol
chunks.text: Indonesia removed carisoprodol from the market in September 2013 due to concerns about diversion, dependence, and adverse effects. Despite its removal, a tragic incident occurred in Kendari, Indonesia in September 2017 when pills containing a combination of paracetamol, caffeine, and carisoprodol were mixed into children's drinks at elementary and junior high schools, resulting in one death and 50 children suffering seizures.

chunks.title: Cathinone
chunks.text: Cathinone is a naturally occurring monoamine alkaloid and the primary psychoactive constituent of khat (Catha edulis), a plant chewed for its stimulant properties across the Horn of Africa and Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years. Structurally related to amphetamine, differing only by a ketone group on the beta carbon, it produces similar effects including stimulation, euphoria, and increased cardiovascular activity. Cathinone serves as the parent structure for the large class of substituted cathinones.

chunks.title: Changa
chunks.text: Changa is a DMT-infused smoking blend combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), typically derived from plants such as Banisteriopsis caapi or Peganum harmala. Developed and named by Australian Julian Palmer around 2003-2004, the blend extends and intensifies the DMT experience compared to smoking freebase DMT alone. Compositions vary widely with no standardized recipe, making potency unpredictable between batches. The MAOI component carries significant interaction risks with many common medications and substances.

chunks.title: Chloral Hydrate
chunks.text: Chloral hydrate is a sedative-hypnotic first synthesized by Justus von Liebig in 1832, with its sleep-inducing properties formally described by Oscar Liebreich in 1869. It holds historical significance as the first widely used synthetic sedative, preceding the barbiturates. Its effects are reported to resemble those of alcohol or benzodiazepines. Long-term use is associated with rapid tolerance development, addiction, and serious adverse effects including kidney, heart, and liver damage. It is rarely prescribed today.

Accidental overdoses have occurred in young children undergoing dental or surgical procedures. The substance has been used as a date rape drug due to its sedative properties.

It is a betaine complex of trimethylglycine with chloral hydrate, functioning as an extended-acting formulation of the latter. Once administered, it is metabolized into trichloroethanol, the active metabolite responsible for most of its effects. Chloral betaine is considered habit-forming.

chunks.title: Chloroform
chunks.text: Chloroform is an organochloride compound classified as a trihalomethane. First synthesized around 1831, it saw widespread use as an inhalational general anesthetic throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries before being abandoned due to fatal cardiac arrhythmias and liver toxicity. It is a suspected carcinogen and can degrade into phosgene, an extremely poisonous gas. Chloroform has been withdrawn from the pharmaceutical market for safety reasons.

chunks.text: Choline bitartrate is a salt form of the essential nutrient choline, combining a quaternary ammonium cation with a bitartrate anion for improved stability. As a precursor to the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, it is widely marketed as a nootropic dietary supplement. It has also been investigated for use in liver disorders, Alzheimer's disease, and bipolar disorder. Generally well-tolerated with low toxicity, high doses may produce a characteristic fishy body odor due to trimethylamine excretion.

chunks.title: Choline Bitartrate

chunks.title: Choline Bitartrate

chunks.title: Cinolazepam
chunks.text: Cinolazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative with anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties. Patented in 1978 and introduced into medical use in 1992, it is primarily employed as a hypnotic due to its pronounced sedative effects. It is reported to produce milder euphoria relative to other benzodiazepines. Cinolazepam is mainly available in Romania and Slovakia and is not approved for sale in the United States or Canada.

chunks.title: Cinolazepam
chunks.text: Benzodiazepines as a class produce significant physical dependence with regular use, and withdrawal can be severe and potentially life-threatening.

chunks.title: Cinolazepam
chunks.text: As a benzodiazepine, cinolazepam carries moderate potential for psychological dependence with regular use.

chunks.title: Citalopram
chunks.text: Citalopram is an antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class, first synthesized in 1972 by Klaus Bøgesø at Lundbeck and approved for medical use in the United States in 1998. Among SSRIs, it is considered the most selective for serotonin reuptake inhibition. Citalopram is primarily prescribed for major depressive disorder and carries notable safety concerns, including dose-dependent QT prolongation, increased suicidality risk in those under 25, and discontinuation syndrome upon abrupt cessation.

chunks.title: Citalopram
chunks.text: SSRI discontinuation syndrome is well-documented and includes sensory disturbances, electric shock-like sensations, gastrointestinal symptoms, dizziness, lethargy, sleep disturbances, anxiety, agitation, irritability, and poor concentration. Treatment should be reduced gradually when discontinued.

chunks.title: Citalopram
chunks.text: Citalopram does not produce euphoria or a high and is not typically associated with abuse potential or compulsive use patterns. However, discontinuation syndrome upon stopping treatment indicates some degree of neuroadaptation.

chunks.title: Citalopram
chunks.text: Hallucinations are a rare side effect. Citalopram, like other SSRIs, may provoke manic or mixed symptoms, with particular concern for people whose bipolar disorder has not been diagnosed.

chunks.title: Citalopram

chunks.title: Citicoline
chunks.text: Citicoline is a naturally occurring nucleotide compound classified as a nootropic. It serves as an endogenous intermediate in the biosynthesis of phosphatidylcholine, a major cell membrane phospholipid, and acts as a precursor to both choline and cytidine in the brain. Widely available as a dietary supplement in over 70 countries, it is primarily used to support memory and cognitive function, particularly in aging populations. It exhibits very low toxicity and high oral bioavailability.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Clobazam is a long-acting benzodiazepine derivative belonging to the unique 1,5-benzodiazepine subclass, distinguishing it from the more common 1,4-benzodiazepines. First synthesized in 1966 and patented in 1968, it was initially marketed as an anxiolytic before gaining approval for epilepsy treatment in 1984. Clobazam demonstrates a more favorable side-effect profile than older benzodiazepines, with notably less sedation and memory impairment, and shows a distinct addictive potential compared to its 1,4-benzodiazepine counterparts.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops from continued therapy. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction may precipitate acute withdrawal reactions including life-threatening seizures. Acute withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, tremor, insomnia, tachycardia, and in severe cases catatonia, convulsions, delirium tremens, hallucinations, and psychosis. Protracted withdrawal syndrome may persist for weeks to over 12 months, characterized by anxiety, cognitive impairment, depression, paresthesia, and motor symptoms.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Clobazam is a benzodiazepine with significant potential for abuse and addiction. Animal studies have shown increased reward-seeking behaviors, and abuse has been reported internationally. Even therapeutic use may put patients at risk for abuse and misuse, which often involves doses greater than recommended and concomitant use of other substances.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Psychosis may occur as a severe withdrawal symptom during abrupt discontinuation. Paradoxical or disinhibitory reactions including agitation, confusion, and excitement may rarely occur during use or overdose. Hallucinations and delirium tremens have been reported with severe withdrawal.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: While clobazam is used as an anticonvulsant, abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures which may be life-threatening. Tolerance to anticonvulsant effects may develop with continued use, and withdrawal seizures may occur during abrupt or overly rapid withdrawal.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: In rats, oral administration for 2 years resulted in increases in thyroid gland tumors (follicular cell adenoma and carcinoma) and liver tumors (hepatocellular adenoma) at mid and high doses.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Clobazam is a 1,5-benzodiazepine that acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABA-A receptor, binding at the benzodiazepine site to potentiate GABAergic neurotransmission. This binding increases chloride conductance in neurons, causing hyperpolarization that raises the action potential threshold and reduces neuronal firing frequency, thereby depressing central nervous system activity. Clobazam demonstrates higher affinity for the α2 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, which mediates anxiolytic effects, compared to the α1 subunit responsible for sedation. This subunit selectivity, along with its proposed partial agonist activity rather than full agonism, may account for its reduced sedative and amnesic effects compared to classical 1,4-benzodiazepines. Some additional activity at sodium channels and voltage-sensitive calcium channels has been speculated.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Clobazam is rapidly and extensively absorbed following oral administration, with time to peak concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 4 hours. Oral bioavailability is approximately 100% and is unaffected by food. The drug is lipophilic and distributes rapidly throughout the body with an apparent volume of distribution of approximately 100 L at steady state. Clobazam is extensively metabolized in the liver, primarily via N-demethylation catalyzed by CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent by CYP2C19 and CYP2B6, producing the active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam (norclobazam). Hydroxylation produces 4-hydroxyclobazam, facilitated by CYP2C18 and CYP2C19. N-desmethylclobazam is the major circulating metabolite, reaching plasma concentrations 3 to 5 times higher than the parent compound at therapeutic doses. The polymorphic CYP2C19 is the major contributor to N-desmethylclobazam metabolism, with poor metabolizers showing 5-fold higher plasma levels. Approximately 82% of the dose is excreted in urine and 11% in feces, with only about 2% recovered as unchanged drug.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text: Tolerance to the therapeutic and anticonvulsant effects of clobazam develops with continued therapy. The rate of tolerance development varies by effect—while tolerance to seizure control may become clinically significant during long-term prophylactic use, little tolerance develops to the amnestic reactions and other cognitive impairments caused by the drug. This differential tolerance pattern is characteristic of benzodiazepines and may render long-term therapy less effective for epilepsy management.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text:
Clobazam was discovered at the Maestretti Research Laboratories in Milan, Italy, with the compound first synthesized in 1966 and first published in 1969. This development followed the incidental synthesis and discovery of the first benzodiazepine, chlordiazepoxide, in the 1950s. Maestretti was subsequently acquired by Roussel Uclaf, which later became part of Sanofi.

Unlike the older 1,4-benzodiazepines, clobazam belongs to the 1,5-benzodiazepine class of drugs. The primary drug-development goal was to provide greater anxiolytic and anti-obsessive efficacy with fewer benzodiazepine-related side effects, particularly reduced sedative and amnesic effects. This improved side-effect profile is attributed to clobazam's higher affinity for the α2 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, which mediates anxiolytic effects, compared to the α1 subunit responsible for sedation.

chunks.title: Clobazam
chunks.text:
Clobazam was originally developed and marketed as an anxiolytic agent. It received approval in Australia in 1970 and France in 1974 for the treatment of anxiety, with broader marketing as an anxiolytic beginning in 1975.

The drug's use expanded to epilepsy treatment, with marketing for anticonvulsant applications beginning in 1984. In October 2011, the United States Food and Drug Administration approved clobazam as an adjunctive treatment for seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in adults and children aged two years and older. Prior to this, in 2005, Health Canada had approved clobazam as an add-on therapy for generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, and focal impaired awareness seizures.

Clobazam remains the only commercially available 1,5-benzodiazepine with unique pharmacological characteristics. It is marketed under numerous brand names internationally, including Onfi, Frisium, Urbanyl, Urbanol, Castilium, and Sympazan, among others.

chunks.title: Clomethiazole
chunks.text: Clomethiazole is a sedative-hypnotic structurally related to thiamine (vitamin B1), originally developed by Hoffmann-La Roche in the 1930s. It acts through a mechanism similar to barbiturates, enhancing GABA activity to produce sedative, anxiolytic, and anticonvulsant effects. It is primarily used for managing acute alcohol withdrawal. Clomethiazole carries significant toxicity risks compared to benzodiazepines, is potentially fatal in overdose — particularly when combined with alcohol — and the benzodiazepine antidote flumazenil cannot reverse its effects.

chunks.title: Clomethiazole
chunks.text: Frequent long-term use may lead to tolerance and physical dependence. Stopping abruptly can produce withdrawal effects resembling those seen after sudden cessation of alcohol, short-acting barbiturates, or short-acting benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Clomethiazole
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming with significant abuse potential. Not recommended for patients with personal or familial history of addiction due to elevated risk for drug abuse.

chunks.title: Clomethiazole
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Particularly toxic and dangerous in overdose, potentially fatal. Alcohol multiplies the effect. The benzodiazepine antidote flumazenil cannot reverse overdose effects due to clomethiazole's unique chemical structure; treatment is restricted to mechanical ventilation until the drug is metabolized or excreted. Keith Moon of The Who died of a clomethiazole overdose.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Clonazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine that produces primarily anxiolytic effects alongside anticonvulsant, sedative, muscle relaxant, and hypnotic properties. Patented in 1960 and first marketed in the United States by Roche in 1975, it is widely prescribed for the treatment of panic disorder, anxiety disorders, and seizures. Now available as a generic medication, it remains one of the most commonly prescribed benzodiazepines, with millions of prescriptions written internationally each year.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops readily with regular use, and discontinuation can be life-threatening. Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, irritability, insomnia, tremors, sweating, confusion, and hallucinations. Severe withdrawal may cause seizures comparable to delirium tremens. Gradual tapering over weeks to months is essential for safe discontinuation.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Extremely high psychological addiction potential. Dependence develops in approximately one-third of individuals who take benzodiazepines for longer than four weeks. The U.S. FDA mandates boxed warnings describing risks of abuse, misuse, and addiction for all benzodiazepine medications.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Psychosis is a rare adverse effect during use, with paradoxical reactions including hallucinations occurring in less than 1% of the general population. Risk is elevated in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, children, and those on high-dosage regimens. Psychosis can also occur during severe withdrawal, characterized by dysphoric manifestations, aggressiveness, anxiety, and hallucinations.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Although clonazepam is an anticonvulsant, paradoxical increases in seizure frequency can occur at supratherapeutic plasma concentrations. Critically, abrupt discontinuation after regular use can induce potentially life-threatening seizures including status epilepticus. Gradual dose tapering is essential to prevent withdrawal-related seizures.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Clonazepam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors, enhancing GABAergic inhibition by increasing the opening frequency of chloride ion channels. This produces hyperpolarization of neuronal cell membranes and reduces excitability. Clonazepam has also been shown to decrease serotonin utilization by neurons and to inhibit depolarization-sensitive calcium uptake via micromolar benzodiazepine binding sites.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Clonazepam is absorbed rapidly after oral administration with an absolute bioavailability of approximately 90%. It is metabolized extensively in the liver, primarily through nitroreduction catalyzed by CYP3A4. The major metabolic pathways include reduction of the nitro group to an amine, N-acetylation, and hydroxylation at the C-3 position. The resulting metabolites are pharmacologically inactive. The elimination half-life ranges from 19 to 60 hours.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: Clonazepam was patented in 1960 and first marketed in 1964 before being released for sale in the United States by Roche in 1975. The medication was subsequently approved as a generic drug in the United States in 1997 and is now manufactured and marketed by multiple pharmaceutical companies. Since its introduction, clonazepam has become one of the most widely prescribed benzodiazepines internationally. By 2023, it had become the 62nd most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over 10 million prescriptions issued annually. Beyond its legitimate medical applications, clonazepam is commonly used recreationally in many regions of the world. A 2006 U.S. government study of hospital emergency department visits found that sedative-hypnotics were the most frequently implicated pharmaceutical drug category, with benzodiazepines accounting for the majority of these incidents; clonazepam ranked as the second most frequently implicated benzodiazepine in these visits. In some countries, the substance has been used by criminals to incapacitate victims.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text: In September 2020, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration required the boxed warning for all benzodiazepine medications to be updated to consistently describe the risks of abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal reactions across the entire drug class.

- New Zealand: Schedule 3 (Class C) — Controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Requires prescription for lawful possession and is subject to restrictions on manufacturing and distribution.
- Norway: Class B / P IV — Designated as a narcotic substance in prescription category IV. Possession without a valid prescription constitutes an offense under Norwegian drug legislation.
- Russia: Schedule III — Listed as a controlled substance in Schedule III since April 2013. Subject to strict prescription requirements and regulatory oversight.
- Switzerland: Verzeichnis B — Listed in Schedule B of controlled substances under Swiss narcotics legislation.

chunks.title: Clonazepam
chunks.text:
Medicinal use is permitted with appropriate prescription.
- Turkey: Green Prescription — Requires the special green prescription form reserved for controlled medications. Possession or sale without valid prescription documentation is prohibited.
- United Kingdom: Class C — Controlled under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971. Unauthorized possession and supply are criminal offenses, though Class C substances carry less severe penalties than Class A or B drugs.
- United States: Schedule IV — Controlled under the Controlled Substances Act as a Schedule IV depressant. Possession without a valid prescription or sale without proper licensing is prohibited. Available as a generic medication…

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam is a highly potent depressant of the triazolobenzodiazepine class, structurally related to both clonazepam and alprazolam. First synthesized in 1971, it was never marketed pharmaceutically and has been available as a research chemical since the mid-2000s. It is considered to pose higher risks than many other designer benzodiazepines due to its exceptional potency, with strong sedation and amnesia reported at very low doses. Blackouts and dependence are frequently reported concerns.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop within days of regular use, and in some cases even after a single large dose. Withdrawal is potentially life-threatening and may include anxiety, insomnia, cognitive impairment, elevated blood pressure, increased heart rate, tremor, restlessness, and in severe cases psychosis and seizures. Abrupt discontinuation is strongly discouraged; gradual tapering under medical supervision is recommended.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam is considered extremely psychologically addictive with high abuse potential. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, and the substance is noted for producing euphoria more frequently than many other benzodiazepines, which may increase its reinforcing properties. Rebound anxiety following use can facilitate cycles of dependence.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Psychosis is rare during intoxication but may occur during severe benzodiazepine withdrawal. Paradoxical reactions including aggression, violent behavior, and increased anxiety occur with an incidence below 1% in the general population but are more frequent in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, and those on high-dose regimens.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam possesses anticonvulsant properties during active use. However, abrupt discontinuation after regular use poses a significant seizure risk that can be life-threatening. Gradual tapering is essential for anyone who has developed physical dependence.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors at the benzodiazepine binding site, enhancing the activity of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA. It is notably potent, proving the most active compound in a series of triazolobenzodiazepines and sometimes effective at doses below 10 μg/kg in mice. The anticonvulsant properties of benzodiazepines may also involve binding to voltage-dependent sodium channels.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam undergoes extensive metabolism in humans. The primary metabolic routes include reduction of the nitro group to form 7-aminoclonazolam (the most abundant urinary metabolite), which is subsequently acetylated to 7-acetaminoclonazolam. Monohydroxylation also occurs, most likely at the α- and 4-positions, yielding hydroxyclonazolam. These metabolites are further conjugated with glucuronic acid.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: May contribute to anticonvulsant properties

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Following cessation, tolerance generally returns to baseline within 7-14 days. However, this timeframe may be significantly longer in cases of prolonged or intensive use, with the duration proportional to the intensity and length of prior consumption.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Tolerance to sedative-hypnotic effects can emerge quickly, often after only several days of uninterrupted use. Higher doses accelerate tolerance development, and tolerance may build at different rates for different effects--mood elevation tends to decline faster than sedation.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam was first synthesized in 1971 by The Upjohn Company, the pharmaceutical corporation that would later bring alprazolam (Xanax) to market. In the original research, the compound was described as the most active substance in the series of triazolobenzodiazepines tested. Despite this notable potency and coverage by patents, the drug was never developed for clinical use or marketed. The compound remained largely obscure until reports of its use as a research chemical began appearing online around 2013, making it one of the more recently emerged designer benzodiazepines. The European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction was first notified of clonazolam's presence in the European Union in January 2015, following a report from Sweden. By 2016, detection of novel benzodiazepines had risen markedly across Europe, with over 300,000 tablets containing designer benzodiazepines—including clonazolam, diclazepam, etizolam, and flubromazolam—seized in 2015, nearly double the figure from the previous year.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Clonazolam's extreme potency has made it a subject of particular concern within online drug communities. Early forum discussions frequently noted incidents of blackouts and the rapid development of dependence, establishing a reputation that distinguished it from other designer benzodiazepines in circulation. Its microgram-range activity led to distribution methods uncommon for benzodiazepines, with the substance appearing on blotter paper and in volumetrically prepared solutions rather than as raw powder.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzodiazepines

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (benzodiazepine site); Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text:
Legal status of Clonazolam by country:
- Australia: Schedule 9 — Classified as a Schedule 9 prohibited substance under federal law. Substances in this category are considered to have no recognized therapeutic value and high potential for misuse.
- Canada: Schedule 4 — Listed under Schedule 4 of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, restricting possession and distribution without authorization.
- Czech Republic: Schedule I (List 4) — Controlled under § 1, d), 2. of Nařízení vlády č. 463/2013 Sb. Use is restricted exclusively to limited research purposes or very limited therapeutic applications.
- Germany: Anlage II BtMG — Controlled under the Betäubungsmittelgesetz (Narcotics Act) since November 11, 2021. Production and import with intent to distribute, administration to another person, possession, and trading are…
- Japan: Controlled — Regulated under the Pharmaceutical Affairs Law. Possession and sale are illegal without authorization.
- Netherlands: List 2 (Opiumwet) — Controlled as a List 2 substance under the Opium Law. Possession, production, and distribution are illegal.
- Poland: NPS Class — Classified as a New Psychoactive Substance under Polish drug legislation.

chunks.title: Clonazolam
chunks.text:
Possession and distribution are prohibited.
- Russia: Schedule III — Listed as a Schedule III controlled substance since 2017. Subject to restrictions on production, distribution, and possession.
- Sweden: Hazardous Substance — Classified as an addictive substance following a recommendation by Sweden's public health agency on June 1, 2015. Production, import, trading, and possession require special authorization.
- Switzerland: Verzeichnis E — Specifically named as a controlled substance under Verzeichnis E (List E) of Swiss narcotics legislation.
- United Kingdom: Class C — Classified as a Class C drug under the May 2017 amendment to the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, alongside several other designer benzodiazepines. Possession, production, and supply are criminal offenses.
- United States: Schedule I — Temporarily placed under Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act effective July 26, 2023, following DEA consideration announced in December 2022. The temporary scheduling has been extended until…

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text: Clonidine is a centrally acting depressant of the arylaminoimidazoline class that functions as an α2-adrenergic receptor agonist. Originally developed as a nasal decongestant by Boehringer Ingelheim, its potent antihypertensive properties were discovered during early human trials, leading to its clinical introduction in 1966. It is also used for ADHD, anxiety disorders, and substance withdrawal management. Abrupt discontinuation can produce dangerous rebound hypertension, and caution is warranted when combining it with other depressants.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text: With chronic clonidine use, physical dependence may develop, and abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms. These effects may include a dangerous increase in blood pressure, so discontinuation is generally managed by tapering to reduce rebound hypertension risk.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text: Clonidine is not generally regarded as addictive and has low abuse potential. Misuse has nevertheless been reported in some populations with existing substance-use disorders, including use alongside opiates to prolong or strengthen their effects.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text: Severe side effects may include hallucinations and confusion, typically associated with overdose or toxic doses rather than therapeutic use.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text: Severe overdoses can cause seizures. This risk is associated with toxic doses rather than therapeutic or typical use.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: In overdose, clonidine may produce serious cardiopulmonary instability, including hypertension followed by hypotension, bradycardia, and reversible cardiac conduction defects or dysrhythmias. These effects are associated with toxic exposure rather than therapeutic use.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Bradycardia can be treated with atropine sulfate, hypotension with intravenous fluids or vasopressors, and hypertension with vasodilators.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Toxic doses can cause CNS depression including drowsiness, decreased reflexes, weakness, hypothermia, and in severe cases apnea, coma, and seizures; morbidity tends to be more severe in children than adults.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Respiratory depression may be treated with naloxone. Severe side effects may include hallucinations and confusion.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Animal studies have shown some detrimental effects on fetal development, though relevance to humans is unknown; clonidine appears in high concentration in breast milk with nursing infant serum concentrations approximately two-thirds of the mother's.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Clonidine is generally not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. The Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration classifies it as pregnancy category B3.

chunks.title: Clonidine
chunks.text:
Legal status of Clonidine by country:
- Germany: Prescription medicine — Clonidine is identified as prescription medicine under Anlage 1 AMVV.
- Switzerland: Prescription medicine — Clonidine is in a Swiss dispensing category that requires a prescription.
- United States: Prescription only; unscheduled — US federal summary describes clonidine as regulated for sale and distribution but not scheduled; possession alone is described as lawful without a prescription.

chunks.title: Cloniprazepam
chunks.text: Cloniprazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative that functions as a prodrug for clonazepam and several related metabolites, including 7-aminoclonazepam. It emerged as a designer drug classified among new psychoactive substances (NPS). As a prodrug, its effects are primarily mediated through metabolic conversion to clonazepam in the body, producing typical depressant and anxiolytic effects associated with benzodiazepines. Like all benzodiazepines, it carries a risk of habit formation and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Cloniprazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use. Abrupt discontinuation can cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including seizures.

chunks.title: Cloniprazepam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a prodrug for clonazepam, it carries significant psychological addiction potential typical of benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Clonitazene
chunks.text: Clonitazene is a synthetic opioid analgesic belonging to the nitazene family of benzimidazole compounds. It possesses approximately three times the analgesic potency of morphine and is structurally related to etonitazene, a far more potent opioid within the same chemical series. Clonitazene is not currently marketed for medical use and circulates primarily as a research chemical. As with other potent synthetic opioids, it carries significant risks of dependence and respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Clonitazene
chunks.text: Physical dependence is expected to develop with regular use, consistent with other potent opioids. Withdrawal syndrome would be anticipated upon cessation.

chunks.title: Clonitazene
chunks.text: As a potent opioid, clonitazene carries significant psychological addiction potential with high abuse liability and reinforcing effects typical of the opioid class.

chunks.title: Clonitazene
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Clonitazene is approximately three times as potent as morphine. As a member of the nitazene family, which includes etonitazene at 1000-1500 times morphine potency, the lethal dose would be correspondingly lower than morphine in opioid-naive individuals.

chunks.title: Clorazepate
chunks.text: Clorazepate is a long-acting benzodiazepine that functions as a prodrug for desmethyldiazepam, which is responsible for most of its therapeutic effects. Patented in 1965 and approved for medical use in 1967, it is prescribed primarily for anxiety disorders, alcohol withdrawal, and epilepsy. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and muscle relaxant properties. As with all benzodiazepines, clorazepate carries significant risks of dependence, tolerance, and potentially severe withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Clorazepate
chunks.text: About one in three people taking benzodiazepines beyond 4 weeks develop physical dependence. Withdrawal can range from mild anxiety and insomnia to severe effects such as seizures, toxic psychosis, and a delirium-tremens-like syndrome. Stopping high doses abruptly may produce confusion and convulsions, while sudden discontinuation from lower doses may cause depression, nervousness, rebound insomnia, sweating, and diarrhea.

chunks.title: Clorazepate
chunks.text: Clorazepate is classified as habit-forming with significant psychological dependence potential. Regular use leads to tolerance to therapeutic effects, and withdrawal can cause anxiety, apprehension, insomnia, and irritability.

chunks.title: Clorazepate
chunks.text: Withdrawal from clorazepate can cause toxic psychosis, and delirium has been noted from discontinuation. Paradoxical effects including excitement can sometimes occur during use, with higher risk in children, the elderly, and individuals with a history of alcohol use disorder or aggressive behavior.

chunks.title: Clorazepate
chunks.text: Withdrawal seizures are a documented risk, particularly with abrupt or over-rapid discontinuation. When used for seizure control, tolerance may manifest with an increased rate of seizures as well as increased risk of withdrawal seizures. Convulsions may occur with abrupt withdrawal from high doses.

chunks.title: Clotiazepam
chunks.text: Clotiazepam is a thienodiazepine drug, a benzodiazepine analog in which the benzene ring is replaced by a thiophene ring. It possesses anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties through its action at GABA(A) receptors. Prescribed primarily for the short-term management of anxiety, it is commercially available in countries such as France and Japan but is not approved in the United States or Canada. It is a recognized drug of abuse.

chunks.title: Clotiazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with chronic use, consistent with other benzodiazepine-class substances. Withdrawal syndrome may occur upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Clotiazepam
chunks.text: Clotiazepam is a recognised drug of abuse and is classified as habit-forming. As a thienodiazepine with benzodiazepine-like activity, it carries significant psychological dependence potential with regular use.

chunks.title: Clotiazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Reversible hepatitis has been described in association with clotiazepam.

chunks.title: Clotiazepam
chunks.text:
Legal status of Clotiazepam by country:
- Canada: Schedule IV; not approved for sale — Clotiazepam is identified as a Schedule IV drug in Canada and is not approved for sale there.
- United Kingdom: Approved — Clotiazepam has been approved in the UK.
- United States: Not approved for sale — Clotiazepam is not approved for sale in the United States.

chunks.title: Cloxazolam
chunks.text: Cloxazolam is a benzodiazepine derivative with anxiolytic, sedative, and anticonvulsant properties. It is primarily metabolized into delorazepam, which is responsible for most of its pharmacological effects. Cloxazolam is not widely available globally and has seen limited marketing in a small number of countries including Portugal, Brazil, and Japan. Like other benzodiazepines, it carries a risk of habit formation and dependence.

chunks.title: Cloxazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with chronic use. Withdrawal syndrome can occur upon discontinuation, potentially including seizures.

chunks.title: Cloxazolam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a benzodiazepine derivative, carries significant risk of psychological dependence with regular use.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaine is a tropane alkaloid stimulant derived from the leaves of coca plants native to South America. It has a long history of medical use as a topical anesthetic owing to its intrinsic vasoconstrictor properties, though its high abuse potential has largely supplanted this role. Cocaine functions as a serotonin–norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor, producing euphoria and heightened alertness. It is notably cardiotoxic and carries a significant potential for compulsive redosing and addiction.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops after even brief periods of regular use. Withdrawal symptoms include disrupted sleep, irritability, depression, fatigue, increased appetite, and reduced ability to experience pleasure. While uncomfortable, cocaine withdrawal is not life-threatening. Depressive withdrawal symptoms are associated with worse treatment outcomes and increased risk of relapse.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaine has a high potential for psychological addiction and compulsive redosing. Its effect on dopamine levels is primarily responsible for its addictive properties. Craving can be triggered rapidly by environmental cues, situations, or memories associated with use. Tolerance can develop after a single dose, and repeated use frequently leads to addiction and prolonged craving.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: More than half of people who abuse cocaine report experiencing psychotic symptoms at some point. Typical symptoms include paranoid delusions of being followed or watched, accompanied by supporting hallucinations. Delusional parasitosis with formication, commonly called 'cocaine bugs,' is a fairly common symptom. Cocaine-induced psychosis shows sensitization, meaning psychosis becomes more severe with repeated intermittent use.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaine can cause convulsions and reduces seizure threshold. Seizures are more commonly associated with overdose situations and high doses but can occur with acute exposure. Overdose may cause seizures alongside abnormally high body temperature and marked blood pressure elevation.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cocaine is cardiotoxic and can cause serious heart problems including arrhythmias, heart inflammation, and myocardial infarction at both acute high doses and with chronic use. Long-term use accelerates atherosclerosis and increases blood clot formation risk.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Cardiac sodium channel blockade causes QTc prolongation and arrhythmias. Norepinephrine reuptake blockade produces severe vasoconstriction and coronary artery spasms. Increased plasminogen activator inhibitor activity and platelet aggregation promote thrombosis.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Severity of heart disease correlates with duration and frequency of use. Concurrent alcohol use produces cocaethylene, which is substantially more cardiotoxic. Cocaethylene is associated with 18- to 25-fold increased risk of sudden death.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Both acute and chronic cocaine use can lead to significant reductions in cerebral blood flow, cognitive deficits, and increased risk of hemorrhagic and ischemic strokes. Gray matter damage occurs in regions critical for memory, attention, and emotion.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Disruption of neurovascular interactions and cerebral blood flow regulation. Dopamine system dysregulation accelerates brain aging. Cocaine use increases DNA damage in brain tissue, potentially causing lasting epigenetic alterations through chromatin structure modifications.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A 2014 study found that cognitive impairment, particularly in working memory, may show partial or full recovery with reduced or ceased use, especially if use began later in life.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic intranasal use causes progressive damage to nasal mucosa, septum, and surrounding structures; approximately 30% of regular users and 47% of daily users experience nasal irritation, crusting, and frequent nosebleeds. Severe cases progress to cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions with erosion of the palate and sinuses.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: As cocaine hydrochloride is absorbed through nasal mucosa, the remaining hydrochloride component forms dilute hydrochloric acid. The short half-life promotes binge use patterns that repeatedly expose tissues to this acidic environment.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Damage can progress to complete disappearance of the nasal septum, palate perforation, and saddle nose deformity. Visible nasal damage frequently leads to social isolation. Smoking crack cocaine can cause lung and respiratory tract damage from combustion residue deposition.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute hepatotoxicity can occur with overdose, typically due to toxic metabolites; most cases resolve quickly but fatal outcomes from multiple organ dysfunction are possible.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Hepatic metabolism produces toxic metabolites. Co-administration with alcohol produces cocaethylene, which is more toxic than either substance alone.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Chronic liver damage may occur with prolonged heavy use. Adulterants in illicit cocaine may contribute additional hepatotoxic burden.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Renal impairment can occur as part of cocaine toxicity syndrome, particularly in overdose situations involving rhabdomyolysis and hyperthermia.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis leads to myoglobin release and subsequent renal tubular damage.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Adulterants in illicit cocaine may pose additional risk of kidney damage.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis can occur with acute cocaine toxicity, particularly at high doses or during prolonged physical activity while intoxicated.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Vasoconstriction reduces muscle perfusion while stimulant effects increase muscular activity and heat production.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Hyperthermia exacerbates muscle breakdown risk.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic use is associated with general weakening of immune function. Levamisole-adulterated cocaine causes severe agranulocytosis in a subset of users, with skin necrosis affecting the ears, face, and extremities.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Levamisole, present in 50-87% of illicit cocaine samples, has immunomodulatory effects causing agranulocytosis and autoimmune vasculitis through effects on blood vessels and the immune system.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Levamisole-induced necrosis syndrome and cocaine/levamisole-associated autoimmune syndrome are recognized complications of street cocaine use.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaethylene (active, formed in the presence of alcohol)

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaine acts primarily as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (SNDRI), blocking the dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine transporters to prevent monoamine reuptake into presynaptic neurons. In rat models, uptake inhibition potency is greatest for norepinephrine, followed by dopamine and then serotonin. Its action at the dopamine transporter, where it stabilizes the transporter in an outward-facing conformation, is considered most responsible for its reinforcing properties. Cocaine also reversibly binds to and inactivates voltage-gated sodium channels, producing local anesthetic effects, while its norepinephrine reuptake blockade results in vasoconstriction. Additional targets include the 5-HT3 receptor (as an antagonist), sigma-1 receptor (as an agonist), κ-opioid receptor, and muscarinic M1 and M2 acetylcholine receptors (as antagonists), while the 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors have also been implicated in its locomotor-activating effects.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Cocaine is absorbed from all sites of application, including mucous membranes and gastrointestinal mucosa, with oral and intranasal bioavailability of approximately 60 to 80%. It has a short elimination half-life of 0.7 to 1.5 hours and is extensively metabolized by plasma esterases and liver cholinesterases, with only about 1% excreted unchanged in urine. The primary metabolite is benzoylecgonine. In the presence of alcohol, the additional active metabolite cocaethylene is formed.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Stabilizes transporter in outward-facing conformation

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Absorbed through mucous membranes in the nose

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Absorbed through the lining of the gastrointestinal tract

chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Insufflated
chunks.text:
Only about 1% leaves the body unchanged in urine
Rapidly broken down by enzymes in the blood (plasma esterases) and liver

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Only about 1% leaves the body unchanged in urine
Rapidly broken down by enzymes in the blood (plasma esterases) and liver

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Other stimulants (amphetamines, though cocaine may partially block amphetamine's dopaminergic effects)

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Tolerance to the euphoric effects of cocaine develops rapidly, potentially after even a single dose. The short duration of action encourages repeated dosing within a session, which accelerates tolerance development. Users often report diminishing returns with consecutive uses, requiring higher doses to achieve initial effects.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Coca chewing dates back at least 8,000 years in South America, making it one of the oldest known psychoactive plant practices. The leaves were integral to Andean civilizations including the ancient Wari and Inca cultures, where they served both stimulant and medicinal purposes. Traditional consumption methods included chewing the dried leaves, drinking them as tea (known as "Mate de Coca"), or preparing them in a sachet wrapped around alkaline burnt ashes held against the inner cheek. The combination with alkaline substances such as lime or plant ash is essential for psychoactive effect, as this activates hydrolysis and produces the alkaloid ecgonine, which can then be absorbed by the body. Without these alkaline additives, coca leaves produce only a numbing effect on the tongue. Traditional applications centered on suppressing appetite, combating cold, and alleviating altitude sickness.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: When the Spanish arrived in South America, they initially banned coca but soon reversed course after recognizing its importance to indigenous labor, instead choosing to legalize and tax the substance. The word "cocaine" traces its etymology from the Quechua word "kúka," which passed through Spanish as "coca" and subsequently into French as "Cocaïne" before entering English.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text:
The active alkaloid was first isolated from coca leaves in 1855 by German chemist Friedrich Gaedcke. The compound was later refined by Albert Niemann, who gave it the name "cocaine." During the late 1800s, cocaine gained significant popularity in Western medicine, primarily as a local anesthetic. Karl Koller's groundbreaking discovery of cocaine's anesthetic properties is regarded as the second most significant advance in the history of anesthesia. James Leonard Corning subsequently demonstrated its application in peridural anesthesia.

Beyond medical applications, cocaine became a common ingredient in various commercial products during this period, including beverages and patent remedies. However, the compound's toxic effects and potential for abuse eventually drove the search for safer alternatives, and cocaine was gradually replaced in most medical contexts by synthetic local anesthetics with more favorable safety profiles.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text:
Before the early 1900s, American newspapers primarily portrayed addiction as the main consequence of cocaine use, depicting typical users as upper or middle class White individuals. This characterization underwent a dramatic shift in the following years. In 1914, The New York Times published an article titled "Negro Cocaine 'Fiends' Are a New Southern Menace," which portrayed Black cocaine users as dangerous and possessing superhuman abilities to withstand normally fatal wounds. This racist narrative contributed to the social climate surrounding early drug legislation.

The federal government instituted national drug labeling requirements for cocaine and cocaine-containing products through the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906. The subsequent Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914 established a regulatory and licensing regime rather than outright prohibition. Notably, the Harrison Act did not recognize addiction as a treatable medical condition, thereby outlawing the therapeutic use of cocaine, heroin, or morphine for individuals suffering from dependence.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: Prior to World War II, large-scale coca cultivation and cocaine production had expanded beyond South America to Taiwan (then known as Formosa) and Java in the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia). The modern cocaine boom—characterized by a sharp rise in illegal production and trafficking—began in the late 1970s and peaked during the 1980s. From the 1980s onward, the cocaine trade became dominated by centralized, hierarchical drug cartels, most notably the Medellín and Cali organizations in Colombia, along with various successors and early factions of the FARC guerrilla group. By the early 2000s, this consolidated model fragmented into a diverse network of global trafficking links, enabling South American cocaine production to supply markets across Europe, Africa, Asia, and Oceania through multiple routes.

chunks.title: Cocaine
chunks.text: In countries where cocaine is produced illegally, an intermediate product known as cocaine paste—referred to as "poor man's cocaine"—is frequently smoked in impoverished communities. This substance is favored in these areas primarily due to its low cost and greater accessibility compared to refined cocaine, though its use poses severe health risks. Cocaine production has also contributed substantially to environmental degradation; the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime estimated that approximately 97,622 hectares of primary forest were cleared for coca cultivation between 2001 and 2004 in the Andean region alone, causing significant habitat destruction in areas recognized as biodiversity hotspots.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Codeine is a naturally occurring opiate alkaloid found in the opium poppy (*Papaver somniferum*), first discovered by Pierre Jean Robiquet in 1832. It functions primarily as a prodrug of morphine, making it a relatively weak opioid in its own right. Codeine is used medically as an analgesic, antitussive, and antidiarrheal. It is frequently available over-the-counter in combination with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and cold water extraction is commonly employed to separate codeine from these potentially harmful additives.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Chronic use causes physical dependence with potentially severe withdrawal symptoms including drug craving, runny nose, yawning, sweating, insomnia, weakness, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle spasms, chills, irritability, and pain. Withdrawal can be as painful and long-lasting as heroin withdrawal, with symptom onset typically within 4-48 hours and duration of 4-5 days.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Codeine exhibits abuse potential similar to other opioid medications, though it is considered less reinforcing than stronger opioids like morphine or heroin. There is a tendency to underestimate its harm potential, particularly with codeine-promethazine cough syrup formulations where at least two deaths in the hip-hop community have been attributed to chronic use.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Seizures are listed as a rare adverse effect. Seizures have also been observed in neonates experiencing narcotic withdrawal from maternal codeine use during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Codeine functions primarily as a prodrug, possessing relatively weak affinity for the μ-opioid receptor (MOR) on its own (Ki of approximately 1,500 nM in rat brain tissue). Its analgesic effects are largely mediated by its active metabolites morphine and codeine-6-glucuronide, both of which are substantially more potent MOR agonists. Codeine also acts as an agonist at κ-opioid and δ-opioid receptors, and suppresses the cough reflex through a direct action on the cough center in the medulla. Additionally, codeine has been reported to activate TLR4 signaling, which may contribute to increased pain sensitivity independently of its conversion to morphine.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Codeine is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, reaching peak plasma concentration approximately 60 minutes after oral administration. It is extensively metabolized in the liver, with approximately 70 to 80% of the ingested dose undergoing glucuronidation to codeine-6-glucuronide via UGT2B7 and UGT2B4. Approximately 5 to 10% is O-demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6, and about 10% is N-demethylated to norcodeine by CYP3A4. UGT2B7 further conjugates norcodeine and morphine to their corresponding 3- and 6-glucuronides. The plasma half-life of codeine and its metabolites is approximately 3 hours. CYP2D6 is highly polymorphic across populations, resulting in significant individual variation in the rate of morphine production.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text:
Codeine derives its name from the Greek word "kodeia," meaning "poppy head," reflecting its natural occurrence as an alkaloid in the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum). The compound comprises approximately 2% of raw opium, which has been used by humans for millennia. The poppy may have been cultivated as early as 3000 BC by the Sumerians of Mesopotamia, who called opium "gil" (joy) and the plant "hul gil" (plant of joy). Ancient Egyptian records, including the Ebers Papyrus from around 1500 BC, document opium-based remedies, though these preparations were recognized as potentially dangerous due to variable potencies.

Codeine was first isolated in 1832 by Pierre Jean Robiquet, a French chemist already renowned for discovering alizarin, the most widespread red dye of the era. Robiquet achieved this isolation while refining morphine extraction processes from opium. The correct molecular composition was determined by Thomas Anderson in 1853, though a complete chemical structure was not proposed until 1925 by J. M. Gulland and Robert Robinson.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text:
Prior to the isolation of individual opium alkaloids, raw opium was widely used in preparations such as laudanum and paregoric elixirs, which were particularly popular in England from the early 18th century. Following codeine's isolation, it found application in various medical contexts including attempts to treat diabetes from the 1880s through the 1950s.

For much of the early 20th century, codeine was generally considered non-addictive—a perception that began to shift in the 1930s when researchers like Himmelsbach (1934) examined its physical dependence potential. By 2013, codeine had become the most commonly used opiate worldwide, with approximately 361,000 kg produced and 249,000 kg consumed globally that year. The substance remains on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines for adults, though concerns about efficacy and safety in pediatric populations led WHO to remove it from the list of essential medications for children in March 2011.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: Recreational misuse of codeine-containing cough syrups first attracted significant attention in the United States during the 1960s and 1970s. Easily accessible over-the-counter preparations were being used recreationally, primarily by teenagers, with the cough syrup colloquially referred to as "Robe." This trend was documented in both popular media—including a 1968 Wall Street Journal article titled "Cough Syrup Kicks"—and academic research examining use among high school and university students. A distinct cultural phenomenon emerged in the early 1990s from the Houston, Texas region: the combination of codeine-promethazine cough syrup with soft drinks and candy, known variously as "lean," "purple drank," or "syrup." This practice originated primarily among young African-Americans in the southern United States and became inextricably linked with the hip-hop music scene. The culture surrounding lean has been both reflected and amplified by artists such as Lil Wayne, whose references brought attention to its effects while often glamorizing its use.

chunks.title: Codeine
chunks.text: The dangers of this practice have been tragically illustrated by deaths within the hip-hop community. Robert Davis Jr, known as DJ Screw, died in 2000, and Chad Butler, known as Pimp C of the group UGK, died in 2007—both deaths attributed in part to codeine-promethazine combinations.

chunks.title: Coluracetam
chunks.text: Coluracetam is a synthetic nootropic of the racetam family, originally developed by Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation for Alzheimer's disease. After failing to meet clinical trial endpoints, it was subsequently investigated as a potential treatment for major depressive disorder comorbid with generalized anxiety disorder. It functions by enhancing high-affinity choline uptake, the rate-limiting step of acetylcholine synthesis. Notably more potent than most racetams, it is distinguished by its sensory enhancement properties. Its long-term health effects have not been scientifically studied.

chunks.title: Coluracetam
chunks.text: Chronic coluracetam use is generally described as non-addictive and low in abuse potential, with no clear indication that it produces psychological dependence in users.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.text: Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid derivative with nootropic and mild stimulant properties. First identified in 1832 by Michel Eugène Chevreul from skeletal muscle extract, it is endogenously synthesized in the kidneys, liver, and pancreas. As a supplement, creatine provides cognitive enhancing, neuroprotective, cardioprotective, and physical performance enhancing effects, primarily through its role in cellular energy storage as phosphocreatine. It is not habit-forming and is widely used by athletes and bodybuilders.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.text: Creatine does not appear to cause physiological dependence. Its effects are not known to produce the kind of post-use tolerance pattern seen with many psychoactive substances.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.text: Creatine is not considered habit-forming and has low abuse potential. It does not appear to cause psychological dependence among users.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.text: Cooking conditions above 148 degrees C can cause creatine to react with protein and sugar, as in grilled or pan-fried meat, producing carcinogenic heterocyclic amines.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Standard creatine supplementation protocols of 4-20 g/day result in slightly elevated creatinine levels that remain within normal limits and do not induce renal damage in healthy populations; long-term use up to 5 years has been considered safe.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A 2019 National Kidney Foundation systematic review found no adverse effect on renal function. Major sports-nutrition and dietetics organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, and Dietitians of Canada, do not identify renal function as a use concern. Three case studies have reported renal effects, but these appear to be isolated incidents.

chunks.title: Creatine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Gastrointestinal distress including stomach cramps, upset stomach, and diarrhea may occur, typically from consuming too much creatine at once rather than from standard dosing protocols.

chunks.title: Creatine

chunks.title: CRL-40-940
chunks.text: CRL-40-940 is a wakefulness-promoting agent and selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor structurally related to modafinil. Originally patented in the 1980s and repatented in 2013, it has been in preclinical development for conditions including chronic fatigue syndrome and narcolepsy. It is reported to be slightly more potent than armodafinil and, unlike modafinil, does not induce cytochrome P450 enzymes. It is sold online and used non-medically as a nootropic research chemical.

chunks.title: CRL-40-941
chunks.text: CRL-40-941 is a wakefulness-promoting agent closely related to adrafinil and modafinil, being the bis(4-fluoro) phenyl ring-substituted derivative of adrafinil. First patented in the 1980s, it was never marketed and is now sold online as a nootropic. Like modafinil and its analogues, it is thought to act as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Animal studies suggest it produces antiaggressive effects not seen with adrafinil and may be several times more potent.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.text: Cyclazodone is a centrally acting stimulant of the 4-oxazolidinone class, developed by the American Cyanamid Company in the 1960s. Structurally related to pemoline and 4-methylaminorex, it functions primarily as a dopamine and norepinephrine releasing agent. The substance appeared on the research chemical market in 2017 with no prior history of recreational use. The structurally related compound pemoline was withdrawn due to hepatotoxicity, raising concerns about cyclazodone's long-term safety given its extremely limited human pharmacological data.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.text: Heavy recreational stimulant use carries a serious addiction risk, but typical long-term therapeutic dosing is unlikely to produce addiction. The related compound pemoline appears to have lower dependence risk than more typical dopaminergic stimulants, although caution remains appropriate for monoamine releasing agents.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.text: Based on pharmacological similarity to other stimulants, misuse of this compound can likely result in a state of psychosis marked by paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Approximately 5-15% of stimulant users who develop psychosis fail to recover completely. Sustained high-dose use combined with sleep deprivation makes stimulant psychosis more likely. Psychosis very rarely arises from therapeutic use.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: The exact toxic dosage is unknown due to cyclazodone's very limited history of human usage.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy or sustained use may cause liver damage. Because pemoline, a structurally related drug, was withdrawn after liver injury was identified in children, cyclazodone may also have hepatotoxic properties.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Before 2017, there was no documented record of recreational cyclazodone use in humans. Mouse studies suggest it produced less hepatotoxicity than D-amphetamine.

chunks.title: Cyclazodone

chunks.text: The structurally related compound 4-methylaminorex is associated with pulmonary hypertension, though it induces far stronger stimulation than cyclazodone; mouse studies suggest cyclazodone exhibited less cardiotoxic effects than D-amphetamine.
