chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives, NMDA receptor antagonists

chunks.title: Diphenidine
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (uncompetitive); σ1; σ2; Dopamine reuptake inhibitor

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.text: Dipipanone is a strong opioid analgesic structurally related to methadone, belonging to the 4,4-diphenylheptane-3-one class. It possesses analgesic potency comparable to morphine and is primarily prescribed for acute pain when morphine cannot be tolerated. Almost exclusively available in combination with the antihistamine cyclizine, it is rarely prescribed outside the United Kingdom and South Africa. Injection of the tablet formulation is particularly dangerous, as insoluble binders can cause serious injury or death.

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.text: As an opioid with addiction potential comparable to morphine, physical dependence is expected to develop with regular use, following typical opioid dependence patterns.

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.text: When taken orally as indicated for pain, the abuse potential and euphoric potential is similar to that of morphine. The substance is classified as habit-forming and prescription is discouraged due to perceived risk of abuse.

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: In the UK from the late 1970s through the early 1980s, misuse of this preparation was linked to many deaths, especially when it was injected. Insoluble tablet binders can cause severe injury or death if injected.

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Injection of tablet preparations can cause serious vascular injury or death due to insoluble binders present in the tablets; this risk is specific to intravenous misuse and does not apply to oral administration as prescribed.

chunks.title: Dipipanone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The combination formulation with cyclizine produces a strong 'rush' when injected, which historically encouraged this dangerous route of administration.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: DiPT is a psychedelic substance of the tryptamine class and a structural analog of DMT. First described in the scientific literature in 1959, its psychoactive properties in humans were characterized by Alexander Shulgin in the mid-1970s and detailed in his 1997 book TiHKAL. DiPT is distinctive among psychedelics for producing primarily auditory rather than visual effects, including perceived shifts in pitch and harmonic distortion. Individual sensitivity varies considerably, and it has been sold as a research chemical.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: No information exists regarding physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms. Unusually among psychedelics, DiPT did not show evidence of behavioral tolerance in rodent studies.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: DiPT is not habit-forming and the desire to use it can actually decrease with use. It is described as most often self-regulating.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: At typical doses, DiPT is described as producing lucid and clear-headed cognitive effects compared to other tryptamines. At very high doses (250mg), one report described delusional spiritual experiences including feeling spoken to by spirits and perceiving an 'anti-universe.' Confusion has been noted at higher doses.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: DiPT produces convulsions at high doses in rodent studies. No human seizure cases are documented in the available literature.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: DiPT has not been studied for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: DiPT is known to chronically alter the perception of sound and speech in some users, which may persist beyond the acute effects; ear pressure ranging from mild to painful has been reported, particularly when combined with MDMA.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The nature and permanence of chronic auditory alterations has not been scientifically evaluated. Tinnitus has been anecdotally reported as a side effect.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: Approximately 7 days without further consumption

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of DiPT develops almost immediately following ingestion.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text:
DiPT was first characterized in the scientific literature by R.B. Barlow and colleagues in 1959. Alexander Shulgin began investigating the compound's effects in humans during the mid-1970s, with his initial findings dating to 1974 and basic properties disclosed in 1976. Shulgin published more detailed characterizations of DiPT alongside 5-MeO-DiPT in a 1980 journal article, followed by additional publications throughout the 1980s.

A comprehensive synthesis and collection of human use reports appeared in Shulgin's 1997 book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known And Loved), which brought the compound to wider attention within the psychedelic research community. DiPT was subsequently encountered as a novel designer drug in Europe by 2005 and has since circulated online as a research chemical.

chunks.title: DiPT
chunks.text:
DiPT's unusual property of producing primarily auditory rather than visual effects has generated interest for potential neurological research applications. Shulgin speculated that the compound might serve as a valuable tool for studying the auditory system, potentially helping to locate the pitch-processing center of the brain if combined with imaging techniques such as positron emission tomography.

A small study was conducted administering DiPT to two individuals with perfect pitch to investigate whether any systematic relationship existed between a note's actual pitch and the perceived pitch under the drug's influence. The results revealed no meaningful correlation, though they reinforced observations that the pitch decrease produced by DiPT is not linear and involves genuine harmonic distortion rather than a simple uniform pitch shift.

chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Serotonergic psychedelics

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (full); 5-HT2B receptor agonist (full); 5-HT2C receptor agonist (full); Serotonin reuptake inhibitor (weak)

chunks.title: DMAA
chunks.text: DMAA (methylhexanamine) is a sympathomimetic stimulant originally developed by Eli Lilly in the 1940s as a nasal decongestant. It has since been marketed as a weight loss aid and has appeared as an ingredient in dietary supplements and energy drinks, often under misleading labeling. DMAA carries significant cardiovascular risks, including heart attack, stroke, and other potentially life-threatening complications. It should not be combined with other stimulants.

chunks.title: DMAA
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a stimulant, it carries potential for psychological dependence with regular use.

chunks.title: DMAA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: DMAA use has been associated with serious cardiovascular harms, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and other potentially fatal events.

chunks.title: DMAA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Sympathomimetic activity causing vasoconstriction, elevated blood pressure, and increased cardiac workload

chunks.title: DMAA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Originally developed as a nasal decongestant. It has also been improperly marketed in dietary supplements and energy drink products.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT is a naturally occurring psychedelic of the tryptamine class, found widely throughout the plant and animal kingdoms, including in trace amounts in humans. Richard Manske first synthesized it in 1931, and South American entheogenic traditions have used it for millennia. When vaporized, DMT produces an exceptionally intense but brief psychedelic experience. It can also be taken orally alongside a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, as in traditional ayahuasca preparations.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: No physical dependence or withdrawal syndrome has been documented with DMT use. The physiological dependence potential appears minimal when used infrequently.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT is considered non-addictive with low abuse potential. Many users report a self-regulating quality to the substance, and studies examining substance use disorder found almost no hallucinogens produced dependence.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT can trigger psychological reactions including intense fear, paranoia, anxiety, panic attacks, and substance-induced psychosis, particularly in predisposed individuals. Latent psychoses may be triggered, and permanent disturbances in self- and reality-recognition are possible in vulnerable populations. Case reports describe temporary psychotic episodes that typically resolved within weeks, though individuals with personal or family history of psychotic illness appear at elevated risk.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: Seizure risk from DMT alone appears minimal; documented seizure concerns primarily involve drug combinations, particularly with lithium or tramadol.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute administration causes elevated blood pressure and heart rate; chronic or frequent use may pose cardiovascular risks due to 5-HT2B receptor agonism, which has been linked to valvular heart disease with other serotonergic compounds.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: 5-HT2B receptor agonism may cause fibroblast proliferation in cardiac valve tissue, potentially leading to valvular changes with chronic exposure.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Rat studies showed altered aortic structure including wall thickening after 14 days of ayahuasca exposure. Individuals with compromised cardiovascular systems or hypertension should exercise particular caution. Changes were noted but not statistically significant for systolic blood pressure at high doses in human studies.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: N,N-Dimethylkynuramine (observed in vitro)

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT acts primarily through agonism at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, which is considered the principal mediator of its psychedelic effects. It has been characterized as a partial and biased agonist at this site, activating the Gq signaling pathway without significantly recruiting β-arrestin2. DMT also acts as an agonist at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C receptors and shows broad, non-selective binding across numerous additional serotonin subtypes. It is additionally a potent serotonin releasing agent and functions as an agonist at sigma-1 and trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), with further affinity demonstrated at dopamine D1, adrenergic, and imidazoline-1 receptors.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT is rapidly metabolized by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A), rendering it orally inactive unless combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. The primary metabolic product is indole-3-acetic acid, with DMT-N-oxide as a notable secondary metabolite. Additional pathways include N-dealkylation and cyclization to β-carbolines. To a lesser extent, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 contribute to hepatic metabolism; when smoked, a more substantial fraction (possibly 10–20%) is processed through these enzymes. Following intravenous administration, DMT has a plasma half-life of approximately 9–12 minutes and can become undetectable in blood within about one hour. DMT readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and has been observed to accumulate in brain tissue following peripheral administration in animal models.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: Biased agonist; activates Gq signaling without significant β-arrestin2 recruitment

chunks.text: Rapidly broken down by MAO-A in the gut and liver before reaching the bloodstream, making it inactive by this route unless combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor

chunks.title: DMT

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: When using smoked DMT, waiting at least one hour between sessions is recommended to allow any minor tolerance effects to subside, though the substance can generally be used multiple times in a single day without significant tolerance buildup.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: Serotonergic psychedelics (limited; research from the 1970s found LSD-tolerant individuals showed minimal cross-tolerance to DMT)

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: Tolerance to DMT develops minimally or not at all with repeated use. Studies involving multiple administrations at half-hour intervals, as well as twice-daily dosing over five days, found no significant tolerance development to autonomic or cardiovascular effects. Some subjects reported diminished subjective 'high' with repeated use, though others maintained full responses.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: DMT has been used as an entheogen in South America for thousands of years, primarily in the form of ayahuasca brews and snuffs. Archaeological evidence suggests snuff use dating back several millennia, though DMT typically served as a minor constituent in these preparations rather than the primary compound. Amazonian tribes have traditionally employed ayahuasca to receive guidance from protective spirits, gain insight into the causes and treatments of illness, perceive future events, communicate with distant groups, prepare for warfare and hunting, and identify enemies and their intentions.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text:
DMT was first synthesized in 1931 by Richard Helmuth Fredrick Manske, a Canadian chemist. The compound's hallucinogenic properties remained unknown for another quarter century until Hungarian chemist and psychiatrist Stephen Szára investigated them in 1956. Szára had initially attempted to acquire LSD from Sandoz Laboratories in Switzerland, but his request was denied on the grounds that such a potent psychotropic substance could prove dangerous in the hands of a communist country. This rejection led him to synthesize DMT in his own laboratory and test it on himself through injection. He subsequently administered it to several medical colleagues before expanding his study to thirty additional participants, predominantly physicians.

In 1955, DMT was definitively isolated from a plant source for the first time, extracted from Anadenanthera peregrina seeds used in traditional snuff preparations. Two years later, American chemists identified DMT in leaves of a plant they erroneously named "Prestonia amazonicum." This taxonomic error later influenced writer William Burroughs, who experimented with DMT in Tangier in 1961 under the belief he was using "Prestonia."

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text:
Following the Amazon rubber boom, several syncretic religious movements incorporating ayahuasca emerged in Brazil. These traditions blended indigenous South American practices with Catholic and European influences alongside Brazilian cosmological beliefs.

Santo Daime, the first of these movements, was founded in the 1930s by Raimundo Irineu Serra, a Brazilian rubber tapper. Barquinha formed in 1945 through a schism with Santo Daime. The União do Vegetal was established in 1961 by Jose Gabriel da Costa, also a rubber tapper. These religious movements would later become central to legal challenges regarding DMT's controlled status, with the UDV's 2006 U.S. Supreme Court victory establishing important precedent for religious use exemptions.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: During the 1960s in the United States, DMT earned the colloquial name "businessman's trip" due to its rapid onset, intense effects, and relatively brief duration—allowing users to experience the full depth of a psychedelic journey in considerably less time than substances like LSD or psilocybin mushrooms. Ethnobotanist Terence McKenna became instrumental in popularizing DMT during the 1980s and 1990s, particularly advocating for inhalation as the preferred route of administration. He spoke enthusiastically and frequently about his experiences, introducing many to the substance's unique phenomenology.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: In the 1990s, Rick Strassman, a medical doctor at the University of New Mexico Hospital Clinical Research Center, began the first government-approved research on DMT in decades. He selected the compound for study because of its short duration, natural occurrence in humans, potentially unexplored physiological roles, and relative obscurity. His research led to the publication of "DMT: The Spirit Molecule" in 2000 and an accompanying documentary in 2010. Strassman hypothesized that DMT might be produced in the pineal gland and released during dreams, birth, and death—ideas subsequently popularized by McKenna and others, though they remain scientifically unconfirmed.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text:
A distinctive cultural phenomenon surrounding DMT is the remarkably consistent reports of encounters with apparently autonomous entities during the experience. Terence McKenna coined the term "machine elves" for the beings he first encountered after smoking DMT in Berkeley in 1965, also describing them as "fractal elves" or "self-transforming machine elves."

In analyzing self-reports from his clinical study participants, Strassman observed striking similarities between descriptions of these entities and figures from ancient religious traditions, including the Ḥayyot haq-Qodesh from Hebrew mysticism, as well as various depictions of angels and demons. He and others have speculated that such hallucinatory experiences may underlie reports of alien abduction and extraterrestrial encounters, suggesting DMT's effects might illuminate the neurological basis of certain mystical and paranormal experiences.

chunks.title: DMT
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Serotonergic psychedelics (limited; research from the 1970s found LSD-tolerant individuals showed minimal cross-tolerance to DMT)

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2C receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2B; 5-HT1B; 5-HT1D; 5-HT5A; 5-HT6; 5-HT7; Serotonin releasing agent; Sigma-1 receptor agonist; TAAR1 agonist (trace amine-associated receptor); D1; α1-adrenergic; α2-adrenergic; Imidazoline-1; VMAT2

DMT — unsafe combinations:

DMT — caution combinations:

- Cannabis (Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.)

DMT is likely to increase the deliriant and negative effects of DPH, in addition to increasing the risk of severe injury and mental trauma.)

chunks.title: DMXE
chunks.text: DMXE is a designer dissociative of the arylcyclohexylamine class, structurally related to methoxetamine (MXE) in which the 3-methoxy group is replaced by a methyl substituent. It emerged on the recreational drug market around October 2020 and was first formally identified by a forensic laboratory in Denmark in February 2021. As a relatively novel research chemical, limited data exists regarding its safety profile, pharmacology, and long-term health effects.

chunks.title: DMXE
chunks.text: DMXE (deoxymethoxetamine) is an arylcyclohexylamine and a structural analogue of methoxetamine in which the 3-methoxy group is replaced by a methyl group. Its detailed receptor-level pharmacology has not been characterized in the available literature.

chunks.title: DMXE
chunks.text:
DMXE emerged as a novel research chemical around October 2020, when it first appeared on online designer drug markets. The compound is structurally derived from methoxetamine (MXE), with the 3-methoxy substituent replaced by a methyl group—hence its alternative designation as "3D-MXE" (3-desmethoxy-MXE). It was first definitively identified by a forensic laboratory in Denmark in February 2021, marking its formal entry into scientific documentation of novel psychoactive substances.

The compound appeared during a period of continued innovation in the arylcyclohexylamine research chemical space, following patterns established by earlier designer dissociatives. Its emergence reflects ongoing efforts within clandestine chemistry to develop structural analogues of controlled or unavailable substances like MXE.

chunks.title: DMXE
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives, NMDA receptor antagonists

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: DOB is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family, first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1967 and later documented in depth in his 1991 book PiHKAL. It was for many years considered the most potent known phenethylamine psychedelic. DOB is characterized by its unusually long duration of action and notably slow onset, which can take up to three hours — a property that increases the risk of accidental redosing.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: DOB is not physically addictive and does not produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: DOB is not habit-forming and the desire to use it typically decreases with use. It is most often self-regulating, with many users experiencing a naturally limiting quality to the substance.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: The long duration and stimulating nature of DOB increase the risk of psychological disturbance. Use can trigger latent psychoses, and frequent use carries risk of loss of reality that may manifest as anxiety states or schizophrenic traits. As sleep deprivation accumulates during extended experiences, stimulant psychosis may emerge with external hallucinations blending into psychedelic visuals around the 16-24 hour mark. Overdose can produce bizarre, delusional, and sometimes violent behavior.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: Seizures are primarily a concern at overdose levels rather than at typical recreational doses. Convulsive activity has been documented in multiple overdose case reports, sometimes contributing to fatal outcomes. The seizure threshold may be lowered when combined with other substances such as tramadol.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available; DOB has not been studied in this context.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Severe vasoconstriction is the primary toxicity concern, developing progressively and peaking several hours into intoxication; at overdose levels this has resulted in diffuse arterial spasm, peripheral vasospasm, and in extreme cases gangrene requiring amputation of extremities.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: 5-HT2 receptor agonism appears to directly impact peripheral vascular tone, causing arterial constriction; DOB demonstrates higher efficacy at triggering 5-HT2-mediated downstream effects compared to related compounds like DOI

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Vasoconstriction can be uncomfortable even at typical doses but becomes medically dangerous primarily in overdose situations. Vasospasm has responded readily to intra-arterial and intravenous vasodilators such as tolazoline and sodium nitroprusside. Pre-existing circulatory problems, heart ailments, hypertension, or stroke history increase risk.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose can produce convulsions and seizure activity, typically occurring alongside other severe symptoms such as coma, metabolic acidosis, and cerebral edema; at typical recreational doses, the primary concerns are confusion, attention lapses, and sleep disturbances.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Convulsions have been documented in multiple overdose case reports, including fatal cases. Animal studies showed convulsions at doses approaching the LD50. Sleep difficulties and bizarre dreams are common even at typical doses due to the extremely long duration.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: 2-Methoxy-5-hydroxy-4-bromoamphetamine (O-demethylation product)

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: DOB acts as a partial agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors, with its psychedelic effects primarily mediated through 5-HT2A activation. It displays notable selectivity for the 5-HT2 receptor subfamily and demonstrates high efficacy in triggering downstream 5-HT2 receptor-mediated signaling. DOB is also a very weak agonist at the human trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1). The compound is typically encountered as a racemate, with R-(−)-DOB serving as the more pharmacologically active enantiomer.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: DOB is extensively metabolized, with only a small amount of unchanged drug excreted. Metabolism proceeds through O-demethylation (at least partly catalyzed by CYP2D6), oxidative deamination, and reduction to corresponding alcohols. DOB has been reported to weakly inhibit CYP2D6, though likely not to a degree sufficient to cause significant drug interactions. Following intravenous administration, the drug initially accumulates in the lungs before distributing to the liver and brain; after oral administration, a similar distribution pattern is observed without the initial pulmonary concentration. It has been suggested that DOB may function as a prodrug that undergoes metabolism in the lungs.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: Partial agonist; high downstream signaling efficacy

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of DOB develops almost immediately after ingestion. The substance appears to have a self-regulating quality, with many users naturally spacing out their experiences.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text:
DOB was first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1967 as part of research examining how 4-position substitutions affect metabolic stability in phenethylamine compounds. The first published scientific report appeared in 1971, documenting toxicology findings and initial pharmacological observations.

A clinical trial conducted at the University of Chile found that DOB enhanced intellectual and emotional thinking while increasing fluency and attention, with subjects maintaining full communication capabilities throughout the experience. The researchers concluded that the compound appeared potentially as useful an adjunct to psychotherapy as MDA, the empathogenic amphetamine that was receiving attention in therapeutic contexts at the time.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text:
Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, DOB use was reported across multiple countries including Australia, Germany, Greece, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The substance became particularly prevalent in Australia, where it was first detected in 1976. Between 1976 and 1981, police seized DOB in Auckland, Sydney, Adelaide, and Brisbane, with the compound being confiscated more frequently than any other hallucinogen in Australia during this period. In contrast, it represented only approximately two percent of seized hallucinogens in the United Kingdom.

Analysis of seized samples revealed significant inconsistency in dosing, with one batch showing concentrations ranging from 1.4 to 4.6 mg per unit. This variability, combined with the fact that DOB was typically sold as LSD or presented in similar formats, contributed to numerous overdose incidents. Multiple nonfatal and fatal cases were recorded, including one death of a young woman who snorted a large quantity after mistaking the substance for MDA and taking what would have been an appropriate dose for that compound.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text:
DOB was placed into Schedule I of the United States Controlled Substances Act in 1973, just two years after the first scientific publication describing its effects. In 1986, the World Health Organization proposed and recommended the international nonproprietary name brolamfetamine for the compound, registering it officially as an anorexiant despite its primary recognition as a hallucinogen.

Comprehensive documentation of DOB did not appear until the 1991 publication of PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known And Loved) by Alexander Shulgin. This work provided detailed information about the compound's synthesis, dosage ranges, duration, and qualitative effects. Shulgin's research also revealed an unusual pharmacological characteristic: DOB accumulates first in lung tissue, remaining there for several hours before brain levels increase, suggesting metabolic conversion may occur in pulmonary tissue before the active compound reaches the central nervous system—a finding consistent with the substance's characteristically slow onset and prolonged duration.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: In contemporary contexts, DOB continues to see limited use as a recreational drug and entheogen. In 2005, authorities in São Paulo, Brazil received samples of gelatin capsules containing approximately 1.5 mg of DOB, with similar capsules reported from multiple sources connected to rave party scenes. The substance is now rarely encountered through specialized online vendors and is more commonly found in street distribution as misrepresented LSD, as its microgram-range potency allows it to be applied to similar-sized blotter paper.

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2B receptor agonist; 5-HT2C receptor agonist (partial); TAAR1 agonist (trace amine-associated receptor)

DOB — dangerous combinations:
- AMT
- Lithium (There are a large number of reports indicating a high seizure and psychosis risk from this combination.)

chunks.title: DOB
chunks.text:
DOB — unsafe combinations:
- Amphetamines (The combined stimulating effects of the two can lead to an uncomfortable body-load, while the focusing effects of amphetamine can easily lead to thought loops. Coming down from amphetamines while the DOx is still active can be quite anxiogenic. )
- Cocaine (The combined stimulating effects of the two can lead to an uncomfortable body-load, while the focusing effects of cocaine can easily lead to thought loops. Coming down from cocaine while the DOx is still active can be quite anxiogenic)
- DXM (The DOx class as psychedelic stimulants have the potential to mask the effects of DXM and could lead to redosing to an unsafe level. DXM can also potentiate DOx resulting in an unpleasantly intense experience.)
- PCP (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)
- Tramadol (Tramadol is well known to lower seizure threshold and psychedelics also cause occasional seizures.)

chunks.text:
DOB — caution combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds
- 2C-x compounds
- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines (The 5-MeO class of tryptamines can be unpredictable in their interactions, particularly increasing the risk of unpleasant physical side effects.)
- Caffeine (High doses of caffeine may cause anxiety which is less manageable when tripping, and since both are stimulating it may cause some physical discomfort.)
- Cannabis (Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.)
- Diphenhydramine (At 25-50mg, DPH may assist with side effects of DOx drugs such as nausea and anxiety. At higher dosages, the combination of a deliriant (DPH) and DOx drugs is cautioned against. DOx drugs are likely to increase the deliriant and negative effects of DPH, in addition to increasing the risk of severe injury and mental trauma. DOx drugs and DPH at recreational dosages have additional cardiac concerns such as vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, which in combination may be exacerbated.)
- MAOIs (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably)
- MDMA (The combined stimulating effects of the two can be uncomfortable.

Coming down on the MDMA while the DOx is still active can be quite anxiogenic. )
- Mephedrone (The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops, in addition to the possible negative side effects of coming down from said stimulant while on a psychedelic. In extreme cases, stimulants, especially in combination can result in severe vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, and heart failure.)
- Mescaline
- MXE (As an NMDA antagonist MXE potentiates DOx which can be unpleasantly intense)
- NBOMe compounds

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: DOC is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family, first synthesized in 1972 at the University of Alberta and later documented by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL (1991). It is characterized by its long duration, strong visual effects, and prominent stimulant properties. DOC is highly dose-sensitive and often sold on blotter paper. Its intense body load and potency make it particularly challenging for those inexperienced with psychedelics.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: DOC is not physically addictive and does not appear to produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: DOC is not habit-forming and the desire to use it typically decreases with use, exhibiting a self-regulating quality. However, rodent studies have demonstrated reinforcing effects including conditioned place preference and self-administration similarly to methamphetamine.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: Psychosis, delusions, and bizarre or violent behavior may occur at high doses or in overdose scenarios. The substance's high dose sensitivity and unusually long duration increase the risk of adverse psychological reactions, particularly in those without extensive hallucinogen experience.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: Seizures have been associated with DOC use in medical literature and may occur at high doses or in overdose situations.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted on DOC.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: At overdose-level doses, DOC can cause significantly elevated heart rate, blood pressure, and severe vasoconstriction; individuals with pre-existing hypertension may be particularly at risk as the amphetamine-like pharmacology causes sharp increases in systolic blood pressure.

chunks.title: DOC

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Severe vasoconstriction typically develops to peak several hours into intoxication. In serious cases, prolonged vasoconstriction may lead to hypoxia, necrosis, and organ failure. Medical intervention with vasodilators may be required to prevent hypertensive emergency.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: DOC was originally synthesized by Ronald Coutts and Jerry Malicky at the University of Alberta in Canada. Their work describing the compound was published in the scientific literature in 1973 as part of research into analogues of DOM and related substituted amphetamines. The substance remained largely obscure for nearly two decades following its initial synthesis.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: Prior to becoming widely known, DOC appeared in forensic analysis of designer amphetamine samples, with the compound being identified in Canadian drug seizures as early as 1989. Human usage was subsequently popularized following the 1991 publication of PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known And Loved) by Alexander Shulgin, which provided detailed information on the compound's synthesis and pharmacological effects. Shulgin characterized DOC as an "archetypical psychedelic" with pronounced effects, noting that everything is present "in spades" compared to the more subtle qualities of related two-carbon phenethylamines.

chunks.title: DOC
chunks.text: DOC has remained uncommon on traditional illicit drug markets, instead circulating primarily through online research chemical vendors operating in legal grey areas. Sales of DOC distributed on blotting paper and in capsule form were reported in late 2005 and again in late 2007. The compound's availability in blotter format has led to instances of misrepresentation, with DOC sometimes being sold as LSD by unscrupulous dealers. A notable example occurred in December 2007 when police in Contra Costa County, California seized blotter paper suspected to be LSD that laboratory analysis revealed to contain DOC instead.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: DOET is a potent, long-acting psychedelic stimulant of the substituted amphetamine and phenethylamine classes, belonging to the DOx family. First discovered by Alexander Shulgin in the 1960s, it is closely related to DOM and is a synthetic analogue of mescaline. DOET was briefly studied by Dow Chemical as a potential 'psychic energizer' before its development was halted following the 1967 DOM street drug crisis. Individual responses to this substance vary considerably.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: Euphoria and stimulant-like subjective effects are reported, while low-dose literature did not mention disturbing hints of abusability.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: Psychedelic effects, closed- and open-eye visuals, confusion, rapid mood changes, and difficulty finding a stable point of reference are reported. Persistent psychosis is not established.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Higher-dose effects include increased heart rate and blood pressure; low-dose clinical reports observed pupil dilation but no marked heart-rate or blood-pressure changes.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: DOET is described as a serotonin 5-HT2 receptor agonist.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular findings appear dose-dependent across the quoted human reports.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rodent pharmacology findings report serotonin receptor-dependent hyperthermic effects.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: DOET acts as a selective serotonin 5-HT2 receptor agonist with high affinity for the 5-HT2A receptor (Ki = 12 nM) and moderate affinity for the 5-HT2C receptor (Ki = 108 nM). It functions as a full agonist at the 5-HT2A receptor (Emax 99%) and as a high-efficacy partial agonist at the 5-HT2B and 5-HT2C receptors. Affinity for the 5-HT1A receptor is substantially lower (Ki = 9,727 nM). DOET shows very weak or no activity at human trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) and does not bind to the monoamine transporters.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: DOET crosses the blood-brain barrier in rodents and is metabolized by oxidation of the ethyl group at the 4 position. It appears to be metabolized more quickly than DOM. In humans, approximately 10 to 40% of the drug is excreted unchanged in urine within 24 hours, with the greatest excretion rate occurring between 3 and 6 hours after administration.

chunks.text: EC50 68 nM; Emax 73% (high-efficacy partial agonist)

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: DOET was discovered by Alexander Shulgin during the 1960s while he was employed at Dow Chemical Company. Following his synthesis of the structurally related compound DOM in 1963 and the subsequent recognition of its psychoactive properties in 1964, Shulgin began systematically assessing similar analogues. During this investigation, he found that DOET possessed distinctive characteristics as what he termed a "psychic energizer" when administered at low doses—producing cognitive enhancement without the pronounced sensory distortions associated with higher doses or other psychedelics.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text: Recognizing its potential as a pharmaceutical agent, Shulgin proposed DOET to Dow Chemical Company for development. The company found the compound sufficiently promising to advance it toward clinical investigation, commissioning neuroscientist Solomon H. Snyder at Johns Hopkins University to conduct formal human studies. However, this development pathway was abruptly terminated in 1967 when DOM emerged as a street drug in San Francisco under the name "STP." The public health crisis that ensued—precipitated by psychedelic chemist Owsley Stanley distributing very-high-dose DOM tablets after learning of the compound from Shulgin—prompted Dow Chemical Company to withdraw entirely from research on DOET and related compounds.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text:
Despite the termination of Dow's research program, Solomon Snyder continued investigating DOET through academic channels. In 1968, he and his colleagues published the first formal description of the compound in the scientific literature. Snyder remained interested in DOET's potential therapeutic applications, particularly its ability to produce cognitive enhancement at sub-psychedelic doses.

Between 1968 and 1974, Snyder conducted and published three clinical trials examining low-dose DOET in human subjects. These studies explored the compound's effects at dosage levels that enhanced cognition without producing overt psychedelic manifestations. Despite this sustained research effort demonstrating its properties, DOET was never further developed as a pharmaceutical medication.

chunks.title: DOET
chunks.text:
DOET has carried several designations throughout its history. Alexander Shulgin originally named the compound DOE, following the standard naming convention of the DOx series. However, he subsequently recognized that "DOE" was also an established acronym for desoxyephedrine (methamphetamine), creating potential confusion in the literature. To address this ambiguity, he revised the name to DOET (sometimes written DOEt), incorporating the complete "ethyl" designation to clearly distinguish it from other substances.

Beyond its systematic nomenclature, Shulgin also designated the compound Hecate after the Greek goddess, placing it among the substances he classified as the "Classic Ladies" in his writings. The abbreviation DMEA, derived from dimethoxyethylamphetamine, represents another alternative name that has appeared in reference to this compound.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: DOI is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family. First described in the scientific literature in 1973, it was later documented in detail by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL (1991). DOI is among the most potent phenethylamine psychedelics and is notable for its exceptionally long duration, which can prevent sleep for 24 hours or more. It is widely used in scientific research as a radioligand for mapping serotonin 5-HT2A receptors in the brain.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: No documented physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms have been reported.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: DOI is not habit-forming, and the desire to use it can actually decrease with use. It is most often self-regulating.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: At high doses, psychosis, bizarre delusional behavior, and paranoia may occur. Frequent use carries risk of reality distortion which may manifest as anxiety states or schizophrenic traits. DOI can trigger latent psychoses. The extended duration contributes to sleep deprivation, and stimulant psychosis symptoms may surface during the comedown, particularly around the 16-24 hour mark.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: Seizures are rarely observed but may occur in those predisposed to them, especially in physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, undernourishment, overheating, or fatigue. At appropriately high doses, seizure risk increases.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects including elevated blood pressure, increased heart rate, and vasoconstriction have been reported, particularly at higher doses; severe vasoconstriction may develop several hours into intoxication and in extreme overdose cases may require medical intervention to prevent hypertensive emergency.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: In serious overdose situations, a powerful vasodilator may need to be administered. Severe cases carry risk of necrosis, organ failure, and death from resulting hypoxia if blood flow is significantly reduced for extended periods.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: DOI acts as a potent agonist at serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors, with approximately 5- to 12-fold selectivity for 5-HT2A over 5-HT2C and biased agonism at 5-HT2C. Despite its amphetamine backbone, DOI does not function as a monoamine releasing agent of serotonin or dopamine. It is also an agonist at the rat trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), and the R-(−) enantiomer is the more pharmacologically active stereoisomer. DOI has additionally been found to potently inhibit tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)-induced inflammation at picomolar concentrations and to promote neuroplasticity through rapid dendritic spine growth and reorganization, classifying it as a psychoplastogen.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: 10-14 days in the absence of further consumption

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: Psychedelics (all serotonergic psychedelics will have reduced effect following DOI consumption)

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of DOI develops almost immediately after ingestion.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: DOI was first synthesized and described in the scientific literature by Ronald Coutts and Jerry Malicky in 1973. The compound later received more detailed documentation, including its psychoactive effects in humans, when Alexander Shulgin included it in his 1991 book PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved). Among the psychedelic amphetamines, DOI shares with DOB the distinction of being one of the most potent compounds in its class.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: DOI has become an important tool in neuroscience research, particularly for studying serotonergic systems. The compound can be synthesized with various radioactive iodine isotopes, making it valuable for mapping the distribution of serotonin 5-HT2A receptors in the brain. The radioactive iodine-125 form used in PET imaging was developed in the laboratory of David E. Nichols. The fact that DOI remained unscheduled at the federal level in the United States significantly facilitated its widespread adoption in research settings. At least one neurochemical research company on the East Coast began offering DOI commercially for experimental purposes, though the company appeared aware of the compound's psychedelic properties—at one point nearly doubling its price and adding restrictions against telephone orders.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text: Beyond its utility as a research ligand, DOI has demonstrated unexpected pharmacological properties in laboratory studies. Cell research has shown the compound to be an extremely potent inhibitor of tumour necrosis factor-alpha inflammation at picomolar concentrations. TNF-alpha is a significant target in research on degenerative conditions including rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.

chunks.title: DOI
chunks.text:
In January 2007, British police reported that three young men had fallen ill after reportedly consuming DOI at a rave in Biggleswade, near Milton Keynes. Authorities issued warnings for others who may have taken the substance to seek medical attention. This incident represented an early indication that DOI had begun circulating as a recreational drug in the United Kingdom.

A notable criminal case in South Australia involved a man named Cody Edwards, who was convicted in the killing of Synamin Bell. Edwards pleaded guilty to manslaughter rather than murder after claiming that DOI had induced paranoia, leading him to act in what he characterized as self-defence when he fatally beat the mother of three with a dumbbell. The case drew attention due to the controversial reduced charge.

chunks.title: Doip
chunks.text: DOIP (2,5-dimethoxy-4-isopropylamphetamine) is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family, first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin and documented in his book PiHKAL. It is a rare and poorly studied compound, with very little data available regarding its pharmacological properties, metabolism, or toxicity. In animal studies, it substitutes for DOM but is several-fold less potent than most other DOx compounds. Extreme caution is warranted due to the scarcity of human data.

chunks.title: Doip

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: DOM is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family, first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1963 and later documented in his 1991 book PiHKAL. It gained notoriety during the 1967 Summer of Love in San Francisco, where high-dosed tablets caused hospitalizations due to its characteristically slow onset and extremely long duration. Shulgin considered it one of his "magical half-dozen" — his personal favorite compounds. It produces stimulant effects at lower doses and hallucinogenic effects at higher doses.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: DOM is not physically addictive and does not produce physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: DOM is not habit-forming and the desire to use it typically decreases with use. It exhibits a self-regulating quality that discourages compulsive redosing or frequent administration.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: DOM can induce psychotic states particularly at high doses, manifesting as an amphetamine psychosis-like condition with bizarre, delusional, and sometimes violent behavior. Frequent use carries risk of persistent reality distortion and may trigger latent psychoses in predisposed individuals. The exceptionally long duration increases psychological burden and likelihood of adverse psychological reactions.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: Seizures are a potential risk primarily at high or overdose-level doses. Those predisposed to seizures may be at elevated risk, particularly when DOM is combined with other substances that lower seizure threshold.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: No studies on antimicrobial properties have been conducted.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted on DOM.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: DOM produces pronounced cardiovascular stimulation including large increases in heart rate and blood pressure during intoxication; these effects are described as more worrisome than those seen with classic psychedelics like LSD, and severe vasoconstriction may develop at high doses.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Amphetamine-like stimulant activity combined with serotonergic agonism; the (S)-enantiomer appears primarily responsible for cardiovascular effects independent of psychoactive activity.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Vasoconstriction typically peaks several hours into intoxication. In severe overdose, vasodilators may be required to prevent tissue hypoxia. Enantiopure (R)-DOM might theoretically be better tolerated cardiovascularly.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: DOM selectively targets the serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors as an agonist, with its psychedelic effects primarily attributed to 5-HT2A activation. Sources differ on whether DOM functions as a full or partial agonist at these receptors. R-(−)-DOM is the more active enantiomer. Outside of the 5-HT2 family, DOM is inactive as a monoamine reuptake inhibitor and releasing agent and shows only very weak inhibition of MAO-A with no activity at MAO-B. Its high selectivity for the 5-HT2 receptor subfamily has made it a widely used pharmacological research tool, and it has also been reported to possess potent anti-inflammatory properties.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: The pharmacokinetics of DOM have been only limitedly studied in humans. The drug undergoes demethylation, producing the pharmacologically active metabolites 2-O-desmethyl-DOM and 5-O-desmethyl-DOM, which may contribute to its delayed onset and long duration of action. There is also evidence suggesting that metabolic conversion may occur in the lungs prior to central nervous system activity. Approximately 5 to 20% of a dose is excreted unchanged.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of DOM develops almost immediately after ingestion. Clinical studies have demonstrated that with daily administration over three consecutive days, subjective effects diminish dramatically—ranging from 'moderately strong' responses to complete absence of effects by the third day, with one subject actually sleeping through the experience.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text:
DOM was first synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1963. The initial step of the synthesis was performed by his then fifteen-year-old son Theodore "Ted" Shulgin at Dow Chemical Company on June 22, 1963, during a brief period when the younger Shulgin had developed an interest in chemistry. Alexander Shulgin completed the synthesis on November 30, 1963. The compound was initially assigned the code name K-61,082, with "DOM" itself being an acronym derived from the code name "des-oxy-methyl" that Shulgin coined for the substance.

Shulgin first discovered the effects of DOM on January 4, 1964, when he ingested a 1 mg dose orally. The hallucinogenic properties of the compound were subsequently confirmed on February 3, 1964, when Shulgin's colleague Thornton W. Sargent ingested 2.3 mg and experienced its full psychedelic effects.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: In mid-1967, DOM appeared on the black market in the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco during the height of the counterculture movement. Tablets containing 20 mg, and later 10 mg, of DOM were distributed widely under the name "STP," which was said to stand for "Serenity, Tranquility, and Peace," though alternative interpretations such as "Super Terrific Psychedelic" and "Stop The Police" also circulated. The name was actually borrowed from a motor oil additive that bore no chemical relation to the drug. These tablets were manufactured by underground chemists Owsley Stanley and Tim Scully.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text: This distribution proved disastrous for several reasons. The tablets contained excessively high doses of the compound, and DOM's slow onset of action created particular problems for users accustomed to LSD. While LSD typically produces noticeable effects within fifteen to twenty minutes, DOM may only show initial effects at the half-hour mark, with full intensity not reached until approximately two hours after ingestion. Many users, expecting the rapid onset they knew from LSD and observing little activity after thirty minutes, assumed the dose was weak and consumed one or two additional tablets. This resulted in numerous hospitalizations, with treatment further complicated by the fact that medical personnel were initially unaware that the tablets called "STP" contained DOM. The negative publicity and health emergencies caused the supply of DOM to fade thereafter.

chunks.title: DOM
chunks.text:
Despite the troubled circumstances of its initial distribution, DOM holds a significant place in psychedelic history. Shulgin later documented the compound in his book PiHKAL and included it among his "magical half-dozen," a personal selection of the phenethylamine compounds he considered most important. This group comprises mescaline, DOM, 2C-B, 2C-E, 2C-T-2, and 2C-T-7, with DOM being one of the five that Shulgin himself developed and synthesized.

There are reports that low doses of DOM were used as a stimulant by members of the Grateful Dead, which may represent one of the earliest documented instances of psychedelic microdosing.

chunks.title: DON
chunks.text: DON is a rare psychedelic amphetamine of the substituted phenethylamine and DOx families. First described in the scientific literature by 1973, it was later reviewed by Alexander Shulgin in his 1991 book PiHKAL. DON is distinguished from related DOx compounds by its notably pronounced amphetamine-like stimulant component alongside its hallucinogenic effects. Anecdotal reports suggest it produces rougher physical effects than other members of the DOx series, including bodily discomfort and pain.

chunks.title: DON
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Stomach cramps have been reported during acute intoxication at typical doses.

chunks.title: DON
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Slight hypothermia has been reported as a physical effect during intoxication.

chunks.title: Dopr
chunks.text: DOPR is a psychedelic amphetamine of the DOx family and the amphetamine analogue of 2C-P. First described by Alexander Shulgin in 1970 and later detailed in his 1991 book PiHKAL, it is considered among the most potent members of the DO-series. Shulgin characterized it as a "heavy duty psychedelic" producing strong, unignorable visual effects. It is notable for its very slow onset and exceptionally long duration of action.

chunks.title: Dopr
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: At higher doses, nervous system disturbances have been reported, described as 'nervous system scrungies' that interfere with relaxation and sleep; these effects appear to be dose-dependent and associated with doses at the upper end of the active range.

chunks.title: Dopr
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Reported at 5.0 mg dose. Effects may persist beyond the acute phase of intoxication.

chunks.title: Dopr
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Higher doses produce hypothermia in rodent models, suggesting potential for body temperature dysregulation.

chunks.title: Dopr
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Observed in animal studies at elevated doses.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Doxylamine is a first-generation antihistamine of the ethanolamine class, first described in 1948. It is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid and is also employed to treat allergies and, in combination with pyridoxine, morning sickness. Doxylamine possesses potent anticholinergic properties, which produce deliriant effects at high doses. Its pronounced sedative and anticholinergic action profile has led to occasional recreational use. Continuous anticholinergic use is associated with increased risk of cognitive decline.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Rebound insomnia occurs upon discontinuation following repeated use, indicating mild physical dependence potential.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Tolerance develops with repeated use, which may lead to dose escalation. Rebound insomnia upon discontinuation can create a cycle of continued use.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Delirium occurs at high doses due to potent anticholinergic activity. Overdose symptoms include hallucinations, mental confusion, and delirium. Night terrors and euphoria have also been reported in overdose.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Seizures are listed among overdose symptoms. Fatal cases have been characterized by tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.text: Animal studies have found liver and thyroid cancer signals in mice and rats, with the findings most pronounced in mice. Human carcinogenicity remains poorly studied, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies doxylamine as not classifiable regarding carcinogenicity in humans.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose may rarely result in rhabdomyolysis and subsequent acute kidney injury; this is not a risk at typical therapeutic doses.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin which can cause renal tubular obstruction and direct nephrotoxicity.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Occasional case reports documented in overdose scenarios.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Continuous and cumulative use of anticholinergic medications including doxylamine is associated with higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older people; occasional use at typical doses carries minimal documented risk.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Chronic anticholinergic blockade may impair cholinergic neurotransmission involved in memory and cognition.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk is associated with long-term cumulative exposure, particularly in elderly populations.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiopulmonary arrest has been reported in fatal overdose cases, with children appearing to be at particularly high risk.

chunks.title: Doxylamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Documented primarily in overdose fatalities rather than therapeutic use.

Legal status of Doxylamine by country:

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: DPT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, closely related to DMT. First described in the scientific literature by the late 1950s, it was subsequently investigated during the 1970s as an adjunct in therapeutic settings for alcoholism and to facilitate peak experiences in terminal cancer patients. DPT is noted for producing hallucinogenic effects comparable in intensity to DMT, though with greater unpredictability and wider individual variation in response at any given dose.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: No physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms have been documented. The substance is reported to be self-limiting like other psychedelic tryptamines.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: DPT is not habit-forming and the desire to use it can actually decrease with use. As with most psychedelics, it is reported to be self-limiting.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: There is some potential for temporary psychosis during the experience. Transient anxiety and paranoia are more commonly reported adverse psychological effects. The substance is considered more psychologically challenging than many other psychedelics, with experiences often described as 'bizarre' and 'unsettling.' Those with existing psychiatric disorders should avoid this substance.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: One death has been associated with DPT and seizures, though the dose is unknown. Animal research indicates complex dose-dependent effects: at lower doses DPT demonstrated anticonvulsant properties in mouse models, while at higher doses it switched to proconvulsant action. Psychedelics may act as triggers for seizures in predisposed individuals.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted on DPT.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: DPT acts primarily as a serotonin 5-HT2A receptor agonist. Selective 5-HT2A antagonists block its behavioral actions in rodents, including the head-twitch response, and DPT fully substitutes for DOM in discriminative stimulus assays. A 5-HT1A-mediated component is also implicated, with evidence suggesting partial agonism at this receptor. DPT is an agonist at several serotonin receptors in vitro, and certain effects in animal models appear to involve non-serotonergic pathways as well.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: DMT (reported slight cross-tolerance, though less pronounced than with other psychedelics)

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: Unlike most psychedelics, DPT does not appear to produce significant tolerance with repeated use. Animal studies have demonstrated that tolerance to DPT's effects does not develop, and human reports suggest only minimal tolerance building compared to other tryptamines.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: DPT was first synthesized in 1950, with initial pharmacological testing conducted in dogs by 1954. The compound was formally described in scientific literature by 1959, and human trials during the 1960s confirmed its hallucinogenic properties. By 1968, DPT had been identified as a novel designer drug.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text:
Formal therapeutic research with DPT was first reported in 1973, when investigators began exploring low intramuscular doses ranging from 15 to 30 milligrams as an adjunct to psychotherapy for patients with alcohol dependence. The compound's capacity to enhance memory recall, promote emotional expressiveness, and facilitate self-exploration—combined with its reliably short duration of action—made it an attractive candidate for therapeutic settings.

Concurrent research examined higher intramuscular doses of 75 to 125 milligrams to facilitate peak experiences in terminally ill cancer patients. Stanislav Grof was among the researchers involved in these clinical trials. While preliminary findings showed some promise, the research program was never sufficiently developed to establish definitive conclusions regarding therapeutic efficacy. This work received mainstream media attention through a CBS 60 Minutes segment broadcast in the late 1970s.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text:
Beginning in the 1980s, reports of DPT use emerged that were largely connected to the Temple of the True Inner Light, a New York City-based religious organization that developed as an offshoot of the Native American Church. The Temple adopted DPT as its primary sacrament, referring to the compound as "a powerful Angel of the Host" and "the true flesh of God." The organization's theology holds that DPT and other entheogens represent physical manifestations of the divine.

Congregants receive their communion through either smoking or oral consumption of the sacrament. Despite maintaining a public profile, the organization has reportedly operated without interference from federal drug enforcement agencies. The Temple represents a notable instance of sustained ceremonial use of a synthetic psychedelic compound within an organized religious framework in the United States.

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: DMT (reported slight cross-tolerance, though less pronounced than with other psychedelics)

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist; 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial)

chunks.title: DPT
chunks.text:
DPT — dangerous combinations:
- Lithium
- Stimulants
- Tramadol

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Ephedrine is a naturally occurring stimulant alkaloid found in plants of the Ephedra genus, with a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine. First isolated in 1885, it is a substituted amphetamine that acts as a sympathomimetic agent. Ephedrine is used clinically as a decongestant, bronchodilator, and to treat hypotension during anesthesia, and is listed on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines. Though structurally related to methamphetamine, its central nervous system effects are considerably less potent.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Physical dependence is not well-characterized for ephedrine; dependence that develops with regular use appears to be predominantly psychological in nature.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: With chronic use, ephedrine may be moderately addictive and can produce psychological dependence in some users. Regular use can lead to tolerance and dependence, with psychological symptoms being particularly prominent.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, and mania are possible but rare, occurring primarily in individuals with pre-existing psychiatric conditions or in cases of overdose. Confusion and paranoia may occur at high doses.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Ephedrine has particularly strong effects on the cardiovascular system compared to other stimulants; chronic or high-dose use has been associated with heart attacks, strokes, and cardiac arrhythmias, with serious events more likely in those with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Stimulation of alpha and beta adrenergic receptors causes vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and elevated blood pressure through increased cardiac output and peripheral resistance.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Heart palpitations and tachycardia are more frequently reported with ephedrine than with other amphetamines. As of 2004, the FDA had received over 18,000 reports of adverse effects. Chronic use may result in persistent hypertension.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Liver damage has been reported as a potential consequence of continuous ephedrine use, though detailed characterization is limited.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Individuals with pre-existing liver damage are advised against ephedrine use.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Kidney damage has been reported with continuous use; acute effects include decreased urination due to vasoconstriction of renal arteries.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Alpha-adrenergic stimulation causes vasoconstriction of renal vasculature, reducing renal blood flow.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Individuals with pre-existing kidney damage are advised against ephedrine use.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Continuous use may result in impaired memory and concentration, irritability, and nervousness; these cognitive effects appear associated with chronic heavy use patterns.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic amine that acts through both direct and indirect mechanisms. Its principal action involves the release of norepinephrine from sympathetic neurons and inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake, thereby increasing norepinephrine signaling at postsynaptic alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. Ephedrine also directly activates beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, though the degree of direct alpha-adrenergic agonism remains controversial. It crosses the blood-brain barrier and releases both norepinephrine and dopamine centrally, functioning as a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Ephedrine has an oral bioavailability of approximately 88% and low plasma protein binding of roughly 24 to 29%. It is largely unmetabolized, with approximately 60% of an oral dose excreted unchanged in urine. The metabolized fraction primarily undergoes N-demethylation to form norephedrine (phenylpropanolamine), with smaller amounts oxidatively deaminated to benzoic acid or converted to 1,2-dihydroxy-1-phenylpropane. The oral elimination half-life is approximately 6 hours, with considerable inter-individual variability, and elimination is dependent on urinary pH.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Direct agonism reported but remains controversial

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: High bioavailability reflects that most of the drug passes through the liver without being significantly broken down

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of ephedrine develops quickly with repeated and frequent usage. Tachyphylaxis (rapid tolerance development) is a recognized clinical concern with sympathomimetic amines like ephedrine.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: Ephedrine's botanical source, the plant Ephedra sinica known as má huáng in Chinese, has been employed in traditional Chinese medicine for over two millennia. Documentation of its use as an anti-asthmatic and stimulant dates back to the Han dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD). Multiple species within the genus Ephedra have been utilized medicinally by indigenous peoples across various regions, and some researchers have proposed these plants as possible candidates for Soma, the ritual substance referenced in ancient Indo-Iranian religious texts.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text: The compound was first isolated in 1885 by Nagai Nagayoshi, a Japanese organic chemist whose research centered on traditional Japanese and Chinese herbal medicines. His work marked the transition of ephedrine from folk remedy to a chemically characterized substance suitable for pharmaceutical development.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text:
Industrial manufacture of ephedrine commenced in China during the 1920s, with the pharmaceutical company Merck marketing the drug under the trade name ephetonin. The compound achieved rapid commercial success—exports from China to Western markets increased dramatically from 4 tonnes in 1926 to 216 tonnes by 1928. Ephedrine entered medical practice in the United States in 1926, and by 1948 it appeared as the active ingredient in Vicks Vatronol nose drops for nasal decongestion.

The compound proved particularly valuable for treating asthma because, unlike adrenaline which had been the standard therapy, it could be administered orally. This practical advantage drove widespread adoption among physicians and patients. Ephedrine's use as an asthma medication reached its zenith during the late 1950s, after which newer bronchodilators gradually replaced it in clinical practice.

chunks.title: Ephedrine
chunks.text:
As ephedrine's prominence in mainstream medicine waned, the compound found renewed interest in nutritional supplements and weight loss products. Research demonstrated that ephedrine promotes modest short-term fat loss, with methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline producing synergistic effects when combined. This pharmacological synergy led to the development of the ECA stack—a formulation combining ephedrine, caffeine, and aspirin—which gained popularity among bodybuilders and athletes seeking to reduce body fat before competitions.

The compound's structural resemblance to methamphetamine has positioned it as a significant precursor chemical. Through relatively straightforward chemical reduction, the hydroxyl group can be removed to yield methamphetamine, while simple oxidation can produce methcathinone. These conversion pathways led to ephedrine's classification as a table-I precursor under the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances.

chunks.title: Ephenidine
chunks.text: Ephenidine is a dissociative anesthetic of the diarylethylamine class that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist. It emerged on research chemical markets in early 2015 and has been sold online as a designer drug. Structurally related to diphenidine and MXP, ephenidine is widely reported to produce a smoother dissociative experience compared to those compounds. Very little is known about this substance, and considerable caution is warranted given the limited safety data available.

chunks.title: Ephenidine
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming with compulsive redosing commonly reported as an effect. The overall addictive potential has not been formally studied and remains unknown.

chunks.title: Ephenidine
chunks.text: A very strong tolerance buildup occurs with repeated ephenidine use, resulting in the need to consume increasingly large doses to achieve the same level of effects.

chunks.title: Ephenidine
chunks.text:
Ephenidine emerged on the research chemical market in early 2015 as a dissociative anesthetic sold through online vendors as a designer drug. It was marketed as a potentially smoother alternative to other diarylethylamine dissociatives that were legally available at the time, particularly diphenidine and methoxphenidine, which had gained a reputation for producing comparatively harsh experiences.

As a relatively unknown research chemical, ephenidine has very little documented history of human usage. The lack of formal research into the substance means that most pharmacological understanding has been derived from its structural similarities to related dissociatives rather than from direct scientific investigation of the compound itself. Its status as a structural isomer of the banned opioid lefetamine complicated its legal standing in some jurisdictions from the outset, leading several countries to move relatively quickly toward scheduling the substance despite its brief presence on the market.

chunks.title: Ephylone
chunks.text: Ephylone is a synthetic stimulant-entactogen of the substituted cathinone class, originally developed by Boehringer Ingelheim in the 1960s but never marketed. It appeared on the recreational drug market around 2015 and has since become one of the most prevalent synthetic cathinones, frequently mis-sold as MDMA. Ephylone has been linked to numerous hospitalizations and overdose deaths and is reported to strongly promote compulsive redosing. Very little is known about its long-term health effects.

chunks.title: Ephylone
chunks.text: With repeated use, ephylone may carry moderate addictive liability and substantial abuse potential. Some users can develop psychological dependence, with cravings and withdrawal effects if use stops abruptly.

chunks.title: Ephylone
chunks.text: Hallucinations have been reported as an adverse effect.

chunks.title: Ephylone

chunks.title: Ephylone

chunks.title: EPT
chunks.text: EPT is an obscure synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, structurally related to DMT, DET, and DPT. Its original synthesis date is unknown, with the compound first appearing on the research chemical market in 2016. Notably, EPT has no documentation in the scientific literature and appears to be entirely a product of clandestine drug design. Early reports characterize its effects as mild and indistinct compared to related base tryptamines, most closely resembling a less potent DPT.

chunks.title: EPT
chunks.text: Anecdotal reports suggest EPT does not produce physical dependence.

chunks.title: EPT

chunks.title: EPT
chunks.text:
EPT's original synthesis date remains unknown. The compound first appeared for sale on the online research chemical market in 2016, emerging as what appears to be an entirely novel product of clandestine drug design rather than a compound derived from academic or pharmaceutical research. Unlike many psychedelic tryptamines, EPT was not included in Alexander Shulgin's influential book "TiHKAL" (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved), and the substance has no documentation in the scientific literature.

EPT remains a rarely encountered psychedelic with a very limited history of human use. The compound has been identified in illicit products in Japan, though it has otherwise received minimal attention within either research contexts or broader psychedelic culture.
