chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.text: Hexobarbital is a barbiturate derivative with hypnotic and sedative properties. Introduced in the 1940s and 1950s, it was primarily employed as an agent for inducing surgical anesthesia owing to its notably rapid onset and short duration of action. It has since been largely supplanted by modern barbiturates such as thiopental, which allow for better control over anesthetic depth. Hexobarbital retains limited use in scientific research. As with all barbiturates, overdose carries a risk of coma and death.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.text: As a barbiturate, hexobarbital is expected to produce physical dependence with chronic use. Barbiturate withdrawal can be severe and potentially life-threatening.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. Barbiturates as a class carry significant psychological addiction potential with regular use.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: In severe overdose cases, coma and death can result. Specific lethal dose values are not documented in available sources.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose produces progressive CNS depression including sluggishness, incoordination, difficulty thinking, slowed speech, impaired judgment, drowsiness progressing to coma, and shallow breathing.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Staggering gait is also reported in intoxication.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: May cause congenital abnormalities when used during pregnancy; classified as FDA Pregnancy Category D or C indicating potential teratogenic and fetotoxic effects.

chunks.title: Hexobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Some research indicates ingestion might cause congenital abnormalities, though evidence has been debated historically.

chunks.title: Homosildenafil
chunks.text: Homosildenafil is a synthetic phosphodiesterase inhibitor and structural analog of sildenafil (Viagra). First identified in 2003 as an adulterant in sexual enhancement products, it has since been detected in various dietary supplements and herbal blends marketed for sexual potency. It exhibits roughly one-third the potency of sildenafil at inhibiting PDE5. Very little is known about its safety profile in humans, and its undisclosed presence in unregulated products poses a notable health concern.

chunks.title: HOT-2
chunks.text: HOT-2 is a psychedelic of the substituted phenethylamine class and a member of the HOT-x series. It is the N-hydroxy derivative of 2C-T-2 and may function as a prodrug for that substance. First described by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL (1991), it has seen virtually no use since and remains poorly characterized. Shulgin described it as generally well-tolerated with both sensory and insightful qualities. Impure batches may contain traces of 2C-T-2, which notably possesses MAOI activity.

chunks.title: HOT-2
chunks.text: Mental confusion and difficulty concentrating have been reported during intoxication. Psychological discomfort and difficulty communicating were noted in some experiences.

chunks.title: HOT-2
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including elevated blood pressure and increased heart rate occur during intoxication; blood pressure elevations were noted to return to normal relatively quickly in documented experiences.

chunks.title: HOT-2
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Described as 'considerable' increases in some reports. Long-term cardiovascular effects are unknown due to limited research.

chunks.title: HOT-2
chunks.text:
Legal status of HOT-2 by country:
- United States: Not specifically controlled; possible analogue — HOT-2 lacks a specific U.S. control entry, though sales for human consumption may be treated as illegal analogue activity.

chunks.title: HOT-7
chunks.text: HOT-7 is a psychedelic substance of the phenethylamine and 2C families, and the N-hydroxy derivative of 2C-T-7. First described by Alexander Shulgin in his 1991 book PiHKAL, it is believed to function as a prodrug for 2C-T-7, producing closely comparable effects. It is characterized by rich closed-eye imagery and enhanced conceptual thinking. Its dose-response curve has been reported as abnormal, and possible MAOI-like properties have been suggested, warranting additional caution when dosing.

chunks.title: Huperzine-A
chunks.text: Huperzine-A is a naturally occurring sesquiterpene alkaloid first isolated in 1983 from Huperzia serrata, a firmoss used in Chinese folk medicine for centuries. It acts primarily as a potent and reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, increasing acetylcholine levels in the brain. Widely available as an over-the-counter supplement marketed for memory and concentration enhancement, it is also under investigation as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease, though current clinical evidence remains limited.

chunks.title: Huperzine-A
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: May contribute to bradycardia (decreased heart rate), particularly when combined with other agents that slow heart rate such as beta-blockers.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Cholinergic activity may enhance parasympathetic effects on cardiac pacemaker cells

chunks.title: Huperzine-A

chunks.title: Huperzine-A

chunks.text: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition increases acetylcholine activity in the gastrointestinal tract

chunks.title: Huperzine-A

chunks.text: Slight muscle twitching and slurred speech may occur as cholinergic side effects.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: HXE (3-HO-2'-Oxo-PCE) is a novel dissociative substance of the arylcyclohexylamine class that produces ketamine-like effects. Structurally related to methoxetamine, ketamine, and PCE, it is distinguished by a hydroxy group on the phenyl ring in place of the methoxy group found in MXE. HXE first became available on the research chemical market in late 2020 after years of synthesis difficulties. Very limited data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, and toxicity in humans.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: With chronic use, HXE is regarded as moderately addictive, has a high abuse potential, and may lead to psychological dependence in some users. Compulsive redosing has been reported. In cases where addiction occurs, stopping use may be accompanied by cravings and withdrawal effects.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Mania can potentially occur in users who are compulsively and regularly consuming large amounts. This effect occurs less often with HXE than with more stimulating dissociatives such as 3-MeO-PCP or 2'-Oxo-PCE.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: No studies on carcinogenicity have been conducted due to the substance's limited history of human use.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Very little is formally known about the pharmacology of HXE. As an arylcyclohexylamine, it is presumed to act as an NMDA receptor antagonist, consistent with the dissociative effects observed with this structural class. HXE is also known to be an active metabolite of the dissociative designer drug methoxetamine (as its O-desmethyl metabolite), which lends further support to its pharmacological activity at this target.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: No formal pharmacokinetic data for HXE appears to have been published. HXE (O-desmethylmethoxetamine) is a known active metabolite of methoxetamine, produced via demethylation of the methoxy group on the phenyl ring.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Presumed based on arylcyclohexylamine structure

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Sustained or repeated HXE use can reduce responsiveness to many effects, leading users to need higher doses for comparable results.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text:
HXE was first identified as an active metabolite of methoxetamine (MXE), the dissociative arylcyclohexylamine that preceded it on research chemical markets. Interest in HXE as a standalone substance developed within research chemical communities, with initial announcements about its potential commercial availability appearing approximately three years before it actually became obtainable. Synthesis difficulties reportedly delayed the substance's market debut.

The compound eventually appeared for sale on online research chemical markets in the late 2019 to 2020 period, transitioning from a known metabolite to a commercially available product sold in its own right.

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (uncompetitive)

chunks.title: HXE
chunks.text:
Legal status of HXE by country:
- Switzerland: Illegal — Controlled as a specially defined derivative of PCE or O-PCE under Swiss narcotics legislation. Production, possession, and distribution are prohibited.
- United Kingdom: Illegal — Controlled substance. As an arylcyclohexylamine with psychoactive properties, it likely falls under the Psychoactive Substances Act 2016, which prohibits the production, distribution, and possession…
- United States: Unscheduled — Not explicitly scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act. However, possession or distribution may be prosecuted under the Federal Analogue Act when intended for human consumption, as HXE is…

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Hydrocodone is a semi-synthetic opioid of the morphinan class, derived from codeine. First synthesized in Germany in 1920 by Carl Mannich and Helene Löwenheim, it is used primarily as an analgesic and cough suppressant. Hydrocodone is almost exclusively prescribed within the United States, where it is most commonly formulated in combination with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. The presence of acetaminophen in most preparations poses a significant risk of liver toxicity at high doses.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with chronic use, and withdrawal symptoms occur upon sudden cessation. Newborns of mothers taking opioid medications regularly will be physically dependent at birth. Tolerance develops to many effects with prolonged use, requiring increasingly large doses.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Hydrocodone has significant abuse potential with abuse liability similar to morphine. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, and chronic use is considered moderately to highly addictive with capability of causing psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Seizures are listed as a serious side effect and symptom of overdose; they are not commonly reported at typical doses but may occur in overdose situations.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Dose-related respiratory depression is the primary life-threatening toxicity; at high doses or overdose this can progress to shallow or stopped breathing, anoxia, and death, particularly when combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mu-opioid receptor agonism in the brainstem respiratory center directly suppresses the breathing reflex and affects the center controlling respiratory rhythm, potentially producing irregular and periodic breathing.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk is markedly exaggerated in presence of head injury, intracranial lesions, or pre-existing increased intracranial pressure. Naloxone can reverse respiratory depression but emergency monitoring is still required.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hydrocodone alone does not cause significant hepatotoxicity, but pharmaceutical preparations commonly contain acetaminophen which can cause serious liver damage or acute liver failure at high doses or with repeated use, particularly when combined with alcohol.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Acetaminophen doses should not exceed 4g per day. Heavy alcohol drinkers or those with liver problems face elevated risk. Cold water extraction can reduce acetaminophen intake from combination products.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Hydrocodone is a highly selective full agonist of the μ-opioid receptor (MOR), which constitutes its primary pharmacological target. It also acts as an agonist at the δ-opioid receptor (DOR) and the κ-opioid receptor (KOR), though with substantially lower affinity; its affinity at DOR is approximately six-fold less than at MOR. Through these receptor interactions, hydrocodone inhibits pain signaling in both the spinal cord and brain. It is reported to be approximately one-tenth as potent as morphine at binding to opioid receptors.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Hydrocodone is available only as an oral medication, with an estimated oral bioavailability of approximately 25%. It is metabolized in the liver through multiple pathways: CYP2D6 catalyzes O-demethylation to hydromorphone (a more potent active metabolite with approximately 5-fold higher MOR binding affinity), while CYP3A4 catalyzes N-demethylation to norhydrocodone, the major metabolite. Despite its higher receptor affinity, hydromorphone is not generally present in sufficient quantities to contribute significantly to the effects of hydrocodone. Norhydrocodone is a MOR agonist with similar receptor potency to hydrocodone but appears to produce minimal analgesia due to poor penetration of the blood-brain barrier. Approximately 40% of hydrocodone metabolism is attributed to non-cytochrome P450-catalyzed reactions. Hydrocodone and its metabolites also undergo 6-ketoreduction and glucuronide conjugation, with urinary excretion (primarily as conjugates) representing the main elimination route. The average plasma elimination half-life is reported as 3.8 hours (range 3.3–4.4 hours), though values of 7–9 hours have also been reported. Plasma protein binding ranges from 20 to 50%.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: With prolonged and repeated use, tolerance can develop to many hydrocodone effects, including therapeutic ones. As tolerance increases, larger doses may be required to obtain comparable effects. The timeline varies by effect, with constipation-related tolerance emerging especially slowly compared with analgesic and euphoric effects.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text:
Hydrocodone was first synthesized in Germany in 1920 by chemists Carl Mannich and Helene Löwenheim as a semi-synthetic derivative of codeine. The compound was patented in 1923 and first marketed by the pharmaceutical company Knoll under the trade name Dicodid beginning in February 1924. This naming convention followed Knoll's established pattern for their opioid product line, which included Dilaudid (hydromorphone, 1926), Dinarkon (oxycodone, 1917), Dihydrin (dihydrocodeine, 1911), and Dimorphan (dihydromorphine).

The United States Food and Drug Administration approved hydrocodone on March 23, 1943, initially for use as the cough suppressant syrup Hycodan. Health Canada subsequently approved the drug under the same brand name for the Canadian market.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text:
Hydrocodone prescribing became concentrated in the United States. The International Narcotics Control Board reported that the United States consumed 99% of the global supply in 2007, and that share remained consistent through 2010. In 2010, the drug reached peak prevalence as the country's most prescribed medication; that year, hydrocodone-paracetamol combination products accounted for 131.2 million prescriptions.

Vicodin, manufactured by Knoll Laboratories, has been the best-known hydrocodone formulation. Its name reportedly comes from the Roman numeral VI, alluding to hydrocodone being about six times as potent as codeine, with 5 mg of hydrocodone producing effects comparable to 30 mg of codeine.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: Beginning in late 2006, the FDA initiated recalls of numerous hydrocodone-containing cough formulations following reports of deaths in infants and children under six years of age. By August 2010, enforcement actions had resulted in the removal of 88% of these hydrocodone-containing medications from the market. Concurrently, the FDA began considering restrictions on hydrocodone and oxycodone fixed-combination products due to paracetamol-related liver toxicity concerns. In late 2012, Vicodin's manufacturer reformulated their hydrocodone tablets to reduce the acetaminophen content to 300 mg per tablet, addressing the risk of liver damage associated with higher paracetamol doses. A long-acting formulation was approved for medical use in the United States in 2013, with Zohydro ER becoming the only hydrocodone brand available without acetaminophen, offered in doses up to 50 mg.

chunks.title: Hydrocodone
chunks.text: The US government imposed more restrictive prescribing requirements in 2014, reclassifying all hydrocodone products from Schedule III to Schedule II effective October 6, 2014. This change followed a 2013 FDA advisory panel recommendation responding to DEA concerns about abuse potential. Prior to rescheduling, products containing 15 mg or less of hydrocodone per dosage unit had been classified as Schedule III, encompassing nearly all prescribed hydrocodone formulations including Vicodin. By 2011, hydrocodone products were involved in approximately 100,000 abuse-related emergency department visits in the United States, more than double the number recorded in 2004.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hydromorphone is a semisynthetic opioid of the morphinan class, derived as a hydrogenated ketone of morphine. First introduced to the mass market in 1926 under the brand name Dilaudid, it is prescribed for the management of moderate to severe pain. Hydromorphone is notably more potent than morphine and carries a high potential for addiction and dependence. It has low oral bioavailability and is most commonly administered intravenously in clinical settings.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with chronic use, and withdrawal symptoms may occur if the drug is suddenly stopped. Withdrawal effects include abdominal pain, anxiety, panic attacks, depression, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, sweating, and piloerection. Some users cannot tolerate the withdrawal symptoms, resulting in continued drug use.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hydromorphone is considered extremely addictive with high abuse potential, classified under Schedule II. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, and the intense physical and cognitive euphoria contribute to its reinforcing properties.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hallucinations may occur as a side effect, listed among more common adverse effects particularly in ambulatory patients and those not experiencing severe pain.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Seizures are listed among serious potential side effects, though they are not commonly reported with hydromorphone alone and appear to be a relatively rare occurrence.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hydromorphone was not shown to be mutagenic or clastogenic in available testing; however, long-term carcinogenicity studies have not been performed.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hydromorphone is a semi-synthetic opioid that acts primarily as a μ-opioid receptor agonist, with approximately five to seven times the potency of morphine on a per milligram basis. It also binds to kappa-opioid receptors as an agonist and to delta-opioid receptors as a partial agonist, though with minor affinity at both. As a hydrogenated ketone of morphine, it possesses higher lipid solubility, enabling more rapid and complete penetration of the blood-brain barrier.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: When taken orally, hydromorphone is absorbed primarily in the upper small intestine and undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, resulting in an oral bioavailability of approximately 60%. The primary metabolic pathway is glucuronidation by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase-2B7 (UGT2B7), producing hydromorphone-3-glucuronide as the principal urinary metabolite. Unlike many other opioids in its class, hydromorphone is not primarily metabolized through CYP450 enzymes, though minor CYP3A4- and CYP2C9-mediated pathways produce norhydromorphone. Protein binding is low (8 to 19%) and the elimination half-life of the immediate-release formulation is approximately 2 to 3 hours. Parenteral administration yields a higher bioavailability of approximately 78%, with near-immediate peak plasma levels. In patients with renal impairment, the half-life may increase to as much as 40 hours.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: After a period without opioid use, fatal overdose risk rises sharply because physical tolerance to respiratory and other depressant effects is reduced. For someone resuming use after extended abstinence, a much smaller fraction of the previous usual dose is safer. Environmental context may also influence tolerance, as studies suggest familiar drug-associated settings can provide some conditioned tolerance.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Prolonged repeated hydromorphone use can produce tolerance to many effects, including therapeutic benefits. Once tolerance develops, comparable effects may require larger doses. The pace is effect-specific, and constipation-related tolerance tends to appear more slowly than tolerance to other opioid effects.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text:
Hydromorphone is a semi-synthetic opioid derived from morphine through hydrogenation, producing a more potent hydrogenated ketone derivative. The compound has been available for clinical use since approximately 1920 and was patented in 1923.

The German pharmaceutical company Knoll introduced hydromorphone to the mass market in 1926 under the brand name Dilaudid. This trade name was chosen to indicate the compound's derivation from and similarity to morphine, referencing laudanum (a historical tincture of opium). The Dilaudid brand became so widely recognized that it is frequently used generically to refer to any formulation containing hydromorphone, regardless of manufacturer.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text:
An extended-release formulation of hydromorphone marketed as Palladone was introduced to the United States market but was voluntarily withdrawn following a July 2005 advisory from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The warning highlighted a significant overdose risk when the medication was consumed with alcohol, which could compromise the extended-release mechanism and result in rapid release of the full dose.

Despite its withdrawal from the American market, extended-release hydromorphone has remained available in other regions. As of 2010, it was marketed in Nepal under the brand name Opidol, in the United Kingdom as Palladone SR, and throughout most other European countries under various trade names.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: In 2009, the state of Ohio approved the use of hydromorphone as a component of its lethal injection protocol. The method involves an intramuscular injection of 500 milligrams of hydromorphone combined with a supratherapeutic dose of the benzodiazepine midazolam. This protocol serves as a backup procedure for capital punishment cases in which a suitable vein cannot be located for conventional intravenous injection.

chunks.title: Hydromorphone
chunks.text: Hydromorphone remains widely prescribed in clinical settings for the management of moderate to severe pain. In 2022, it ranked as the 233rd most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than one million prescriptions dispensed that year.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine of the diphenylmethane and piperazine classes, first developed in 1956. Primarily prescribed for allergic conditions such as itchiness and urticaria, it also exhibits anxiolytic and sedative properties, making it useful for treating generalized anxiety disorder and insomnia. Hydroxyzine is additionally employed to reduce nausea and has been used to potentiate opioid analgesia while diminishing opioid-related side effects like itchiness.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Physical dependence is not commonly reported with hydroxyzine use. It does not produce significant withdrawal syndromes characteristic of other sedative classes.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Hydroxyzine has low abuse potential due to its lack of euphoric effects. It is not a controlled substance and is not typically associated with compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Hallucinations and confusion have been observed in rare cases, attributed mostly to overdosage or in patients being treated for neuropsychological disorders.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Hydroxyzine is a potent and selective histamine H1 receptor inverse agonist, meaning it actively dampens receptor activity rather than simply blocking it. This inverse agonism underlies its antihistamine effects and sedative properties. Unlike many other first-generation antihistamines, hydroxyzine has lower affinity for muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, resulting in a reduced risk of anticholinergic side effects. Hydroxyzine also acts more weakly as an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, dopamine D2 receptors, and α1-adrenergic receptors. The comparably weak antiserotonergic activity likely contributes to its usefulness as an anxiolytic, as other antihistamines lacking such properties have not demonstrated efficacy for anxiety. Hydroxyzine readily crosses the blood-brain barrier; a positron emission tomography study found that a single 30 mg dose achieved 67.6% occupancy of brain H1 receptors, with subjective sleepiness correlating well with receptor occupancy. Hydroxyzine also functions as an inhibitor of acid sphingomyelinase.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Hydroxyzine is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract following oral administration, reaching peak plasma concentrations approximately 2 hours after dosing. The absolute bioavailability has not been determined due to the unavailability of intravenous formulations. Hydroxyzine is metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5. The main metabolite, comprising approximately 45-60% of an oral dose, is the second-generation antihistamine cetirizine, formed through oxidation of the alcohol moiety to a carboxylic acid. Additional metabolites include an N-dealkylated metabolite (norchlorcyclizine) and an O-dealkylated metabolite with a plasma half-life of 59 hours. The elimination half-life averages approximately 20 hours in adults, 7.1 hours in children, and 29 hours in elderly patients. Higher concentrations are found in the skin than in plasma. Approximately 70% of cetirizine is excreted unchanged in the urine.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text: Tolerance to the central nervous system effects, particularly sedation, can develop rapidly with continuous use. Studies indicate that subjective sedation levels decrease markedly over 5-7 days of use, likely due to CNS receptor desensitization. This rapid tolerance development is why hydroxyzine is typically prescribed only for short-term or as-needed use when employed as a sleep aid.

chunks.title: Hydroxyzine
chunks.text:
Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine of the diphenylmethane and piperazine classes. It was first developed in 1955 and subsequently manufactured by Union Chimique Belge in 1956. That same year, it was approved for sale in the United States by Pfizer.

Since its introduction, hydroxyzine has remained a relatively common treatment for allergic conditions such as pruritus, urticaria, and dermatoses, as well as for generalized anxiety disorder and tension associated with psychoneurosis. Its active metabolite, cetirizine, was later developed as a standalone antihistamine medication and is responsible for much of hydroxyzine's antihistaminic effect.

The drug is marketed under numerous brand names worldwide. Preparations of the pamoate salt include Vistaril, Equipose, Masmoran, and Paxistil, while hydrochloride salt formulations are sold as Atarax, Alamon, Aterax, Durrax, Tran-Q, Orgatrax, Quiess, and Tranquizine. By 2023, hydroxyzine had become the 39th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 15 million prescriptions written annually.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Ibogaine is a naturally occurring indole alkaloid primarily derived from the root bark of Tabernanthe iboga, a plant native to Central and West Africa. It has been used for centuries within the Bwiti religion of Gabon for initiation rites and spiritual communion. Ibogaine produces psychedelic and dissociative effects often described as dream-like and frequently unpleasant. Since the late 20th century, it has gained significant attention as an experimental treatment for opioid dependence, with clinics established worldwide.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Ibogaine has minimal abuse potential due to the typically unpleasant and challenging nature of the experience. The substance is actively being studied as a treatment for opioid and other substance use disorders rather than as a drug of abuse. Compulsive redosing is essentially unreported given the extreme duration and physically taxing effects.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Manic episodes may occur and can last several days, potentially including insomnia, irritability, emotional instability, delusions, aggressive behavior, and thoughts of suicide. Depression is commonly reported following use and can persist well beyond 36 hours; in some cases, a persistently low mood may progress into major depressive disorder.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Ibogaine causes long QT syndrome at higher doses, presenting serious cardiac risks that can be fatal; individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions are at substantially elevated risk.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High-dose laboratory studies in rats showed degeneration of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum; however, subsequent primate studies and limited human research found no evidence of this neurotoxicity.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Neuropathological examination of a patient who received four separate doses ranging 10-30 mg/kg over 15 months revealed no neuronal degenerative changes. A published series of fatalities also found no evidence for consistent neurotoxicity.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Ibogaine acts on multiple neurotransmitter systems simultaneously, producing a complex pharmacological profile whose specific mediating targets are not fully established. It shows significant in-vivo occupancy of the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor and appreciable affinity for the NMDA receptor, yet neither ibogaine nor its major active metabolite noribogaine appear to function as direct 5-HT2A agonists, and ibogaine does not produce the head-twitch response (a behavioral proxy of 5-HT2A activation) in rodents. Animal drug discrimination studies implicate 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptor activation, σ2 receptor signaling, and opioid receptor interactions in ibogaine's pharmacological activity, while the NMDA, 5-HT1A, 5-HT3, and σ1 receptors do not appear to contribute significantly. Noribogaine, the primary active metabolite, acts most potently as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and additionally functions as a moderate κ-opioid receptor agonist and weak μ-opioid receptor agonist or partial agonist. Noribogaine, but not ibogaine, has also been found to produce psychoplastogenic effects in vitro, an action that can be blocked by the 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Ibogaine is metabolized by CYP2D6 into its major active metabolite noribogaine (O-desmethylibogaine). In humans, ibogaine has an elimination half-life of approximately 7 hours, while noribogaine persists considerably longer with a half-life of 24 to 50 hours. Following ingestion, noribogaine reaches higher plasma concentrations than the parent compound and remains detectable for a longer period. Ibogaine may also be deposited in adipose tissue and gradually released for subsequent conversion to noribogaine.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: The use of Tabernanthe iboga has been practiced for centuries among Central African foragers in Gabon, Cameroon, and surrounding countries, with this ethnobotanical knowledge eventually passed to the Bwiti tribe of Gabon. Within the Bwiti religion, iboga serves as a sacrament central to numerous spiritual practices, including rites of passage, spiritual communion, resolution of pathological problems, and communication with ancestors. The plant remains fundamental to indigenous society in these regions, holding such cultural significance that in 2000, the Council of Ministers of the Republic of Gabon declared iboga a national treasure.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text:
The use of iboga in African spiritual ceremonies was first documented by French and Belgian explorers in the 19th century, with early reports attributed to French naval physician and Gabon explorer Marie-Théophile Griffon du Bellay. The first formal botanical description of Tabernanthe iboga was published in 1889.

Twelve years later, in 1901, ibogaine was independently isolated from the plant by two research groups: Dybowski and Landrin, and separately by Haller and Heckel, both working with samples obtained from Gabon.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text:
Total synthesis of ibogaine was achieved in 1956, with its molecular structure subsequently confirmed through X-ray crystallography in 1960. Additional synthetic methodologies continued to be developed, with G. Büchi accomplishing a complete synthesis in 1966.

During this period, ibogaine also maintained a commercial presence in France. From the 1930s through 1966, it was marketed as Lambarène, an extract of Tabernanthe manii promoted as a mental and physical stimulant. Each tablet contained approximately 200 mg of extract with relatively low doses of 4 to 8 mg ibogaine. The product gained popularity among post-World War II athletes before being withdrawn from the French market in 1966 when ibogaine-containing products were prohibited. Another formulation marketed during this era was Iperton, which contained Tabernanthe iboga extract at 40 mg per dose unit.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Anecdotal observations regarding ibogaine's potential therapeutic effects began emerging in the early 1960s. The compound's anti-addictive properties were discovered serendipitously in 1962 by Howard Lotsof, then 19 years old, when he and five friends—all heroin users—noticed subjective reductions in craving and withdrawal symptoms while taking the substance. Subsequent observations convinced Lotsof of its potential utility in treating substance dependence, leading him to contract with a Belgian company to produce ibogaine tablets for clinical trials in the Netherlands. He was awarded a United States patent for the product in 1985. Beyond addiction treatment, ibogaine was also explored in psychotherapeutic contexts during this period. Researchers documented physician-patient interactions emphasizing early memory recall and the reliving of past experiences, with notable work conducted by Claudio Naranjo.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: In 1992, Eric Taub established the first ibogaine treatment center at an offshore location near the United States, initiating treatments and advocating for broader recognition of the compound. He was subsequently joined in Costa Rica by Lex Kogan, another prominent figure in the field. Together, they systematized ibogaine administration protocols and established medically monitored treatment clinics across several countries. Since then, clinics have been founded worldwide to serve individuals seeking to reduce or eliminate dependence on other substances, particularly opioids.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text: Interest in ibogaine as a potential treatment for addiction has continued to grow. In 2025, the state of Texas allocated $50 million to fund clinical research on ibogaine, with the stated goal of developing FDA-approved treatments for opioid use disorder, co-occurring substance use disorders, and other ibogaine-responsive conditions. The initiative, supported by former Governor Rick Perry, established a consortium of universities, hospitals, and drug developers, positioning Texas as a potential center for psychedelic medicine research.

chunks.title: Ibogaine
chunks.text:
Ibogaine has appeared in various cultural and media contexts over the decades. In 1972, gonzo journalist Hunter S. Thompson published a satirical article in Rolling Stone while covering the Democratic primary campaign, falsely asserting that candidate Edmund Muskie was addicted to ibogaine. The piece was not recognized as satire by many readers and other journalists, and the unfounded accusation reportedly damaged Muskie's reputation—Thompson later expressed surprise that anyone had believed it.

The substance has also been the subject of several books. Author and Yippie activist Dana Beal co-authored "The Ibogaine Story" in 1997. Daniel Pinchbeck described his personal ibogaine experience in "Breaking Open the Head" (2002) and a subsequent Guardian article titled "Ten years of therapy in one night" (2003). More recently, musician and author Geoff Rickly based his debut novel "Someone Who Isn't Me" on his experiences with heroin addiction and treatment at an ibogaine clinic in Mexico.

chunks.title: Ibuprofen
chunks.text: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) derived from propionic acid. It was discovered by Stewart Adams and John Nicholson at the Boots Group in 1961 and first marketed in the United Kingdom in 1969, later becoming the first non-aspirin NSAID available over the counter. It is widely used as an analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory agent. Long-term use has been associated with gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and renal complications.

chunks.text: Indapex is a lesser-known synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, documented by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. It is reported to produce relaxation and sexual stimulation at lower doses, while higher doses appear to introduce a notably toxic component involving significant gastrointestinal distress, temperature dysregulation, and emotional lability. Very limited human data exists for this substance, and it is characterized by an atypical dosing curve, warranting particular caution with dose selection.

chunks.title: Indapyrophenidone
chunks.text: Indapyrophenidone is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone class that has been sold online as a designer drug. Structurally, it is the indanyl-α-phenyl analogue of the stimulant α-PVP, though it also bears resemblance to diarylethylamines such as fluorolintane and UWA-001. Its mechanism of action remains unknown. As a research chemical with very limited available data, its pharmacological properties and safety profile are poorly understood and it should be approached with considerable caution.

chunks.title: Isomethadone
chunks.text: Isomethadone is a synthetic opioid analgesic structurally related to methadone. It was formerly available as a pharmaceutical product but has since been withdrawn from the market and is seldom encountered today. It is reported to possess approximately twice the analgesic potency of methadone and is said to produce euphoric effects. As with other opioids, it carries a risk of habit formation and respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Isomethadone
chunks.text: Isomethadone acts as an agonist at both the μ-opioid and δ-opioid receptors. The (S)-enantiomer is reported to be more potent than the (R)-enantiomer.

chunks.title: Isomethadone
chunks.text: Isomethadone, also known by the alternative name isoamidone, is a synthetic opioid analgesic structurally related to methadone. It was previously marketed as a pharmaceutical product under the trade name Liden, where it saw clinical use for both pain management and cough suppression. The compound has since been withdrawn from the pharmaceutical market and is no longer commercially available as a medication.

chunks.title: Isophenmetrazine
chunks.text: Isophenmetrazine is a rare and poorly documented analogue of phenmetrazine, a morpholine-class stimulant. It is reported to be slightly more potent than related analogues and is suspected to act as a dopamine and/or norepinephrine releasing agent. The substance is thought to produce stimulant and appetite-suppressing effects. Due to its scarcity and lack of formal research, very little reliable information exists regarding its safety profile or pharmacological properties.

chunks.title: Isopropylphenidate
chunks.text: Isopropylphenidate is a piperidine-based stimulant of the phenidate class, structurally related to methylphenidate. It emerged on the research chemical market in the mid-2010s and is primarily characterized by its functional, non-recreational stimulation profile, offering improved focus with relatively mild physical side effects compared to similar stimulants. It has been investigated as a potential alternative to methylphenidate for ADHD treatment. Its long-term safety remains unknown due to its research chemical status.

chunks.title: Isoproscaline
chunks.text: Isoproscaline is a psychedelic phenethylamine and an analogue of mescaline, closely related to proscaline. It was first synthesized by David E. Nichols and colleagues and later documented by Alexander Shulgin in his book PiHKAL. The compound differs from proscaline by featuring a branched isopropyl group rather than a straight-chain propyl group at the 4-position oxygen of the aromatic ring. Its psychopharmacological profile remains poorly characterized, with very limited human data available.

chunks.title: JWH-018
chunks.text: JWH-018 is a synthetic cannabinoid of the naphthoylindole class. It gained widespread recognition from 2006 onward as the primary active ingredient in "Spice" brand herbal smoking blends, which were marketed as potpourri and labeled "not for human consumption." The Spice brand became so dominant that the name was eventually adopted as a generic term for all synthetic cannabinoids. JWH-018 produces cannabis-like effects when smoked but carries the heightened risks characteristic of synthetic cannabinoid compounds.

chunks.text: Withdrawal symptoms have been reported following prolonged daily use and were described as more severe than those experienced from cannabis dependence.

chunks.title: JWH-018
chunks.text: At least one case of JWH-018 dependence has been reported following daily use over eight months. As a full CB1 agonist with indirect dopaminergic activity, JWH-018 may have greater reinforcing potential than cannabis, though individual susceptibility varies.

chunks.text: May cause intense anxiety and agitation. Psychotic relapses and anxiety symptoms have been reported in patients with pre-existing mental illness following inhalation. Due to concerns about psychosis induction in vulnerable individuals, it is recommended that people with risk factors for psychotic disorders, such as a past or family history of psychosis, not use synthetic cannabinoids.

chunks.text: JWH-018 acts as a full agonist at both the CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors, with some selectivity for CB2. It displays binding affinities of 9.00 ± 5.00 nM at CB1 and 2.94 ± 2.65 nM at CB2, with its CB1 affinity reported as approximately five times greater than that of THC. Unlike THC, which acts as a partial agonist at CB1, JWH-018's full agonist activity produces more complete receptor activation.

chunks.text: JWH-018 undergoes extensive metabolism primarily through hydroxylation and N-dealkylation. In humans, metabolism occurs mainly on the indole ring and pentyl side chain, with the resulting hydroxylated metabolites undergoing extensive glucuronide conjugation. The parent compound and its N-dealkylated metabolite are detected only in small quantities in urine, while hydroxylated N-dealkylated metabolites constitute the primary urinary signal. When inhaled, the median elimination half-life is approximately 1.69 hours.

chunks.title: JWH-018
chunks.text: JWH-018 was synthesized by John W. Huffman, an organic chemist at Clemson University, as part of his research into compounds affecting the endocannabinoid system. The compound's designation derives from Huffman's initials.

chunks.title: JWH-018
chunks.text:
Beginning in 2006, products containing JWH-018 entered the grey market under the brand name Spice, sold as potpourri or incense and labeled "not for human consumption" to circumvent drug regulations. The brand expanded into a product family including Spice Gold, Spice Arctic Synergy, Spice Diamond, and Spice Tropical Synergy. On 15 December 2008, German pharmaceutical analysis identified JWH-018 as one of the active components in at least three versions of Spice products.

The Spice brand became so influential that the term eventually came to be used generically to describe all synthetic cannabinoids, regardless of their specific chemical composition. Following regulatory bans, manufacturers demonstrated a pattern of circumventing controls through minor chemical modifications—analysis of products obtained four weeks after German prohibition found manufacturers had shortened the alkyl chain by one carbon atom to create technically distinct compounds.

chunks.title: JWH-073
chunks.text: JWH-073 is a synthetic cannabinoid of the naphthoylindole class. It was among the first variations of JWH-018 to appear in commercially available smoking mixtures sold under the Spice brand. Its effects are frequently described as cannabis-like but only to a limited degree, with certain aspects of the natural cannabis experience notably absent or distorted. It is typically administered by smoking.

chunks.title: JWH-073
chunks.text: Repeated engagement with a cannabis-like synthetic cannabinoid product is described, and Schedule 9 definitions cover substances that may be abused or misused.

chunks.title: JWH-073
chunks.text: JWH-073 acts as a full agonist at both the CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors. It displays moderate selectivity for CB1, with approximately five-fold greater affinity at this subtype compared to CB2. Its CB1 binding affinity exceeds that of THC, while its affinity at CB2 is comparable to THC.

chunks.title: JWH-073
chunks.text: JWH-073 derives its name from John W. Huffman, the American organic chemist whose laboratory developed this and numerous other synthetic cannabinoid compounds as part of cannabinoid receptor research. The "JWH" prefix identifies compounds originating from Huffman's work. The compound entered the recreational drug market as a component of herbal smoking blends sold under the "Spice" brand name during the late 2000s. It was reportedly among the first variations from JWH-018 to appear in the original Spice product line. In April 2009, researchers at the University of Freiburg identified JWH-073 in a product deceptively marketed as "Forest Humus" fertilizer, alongside another synthetic cannabinoid. Following Germany's prohibition of JWH-018, testing of seized Spice products in July 2009 revealed that manufacturers had reformulated their blends to contain the then-unscheduled JWH-073 as a substitute compound.

chunks.title: JWH-073
chunks.text: The authentic Spice brand eventually disappeared from the market before the proliferation of more potent synthetic cannabinoids under numerous other product names and labels. However, its cultural impact endured, with the term "Spice" becoming widely adopted as a generic descriptor for synthetic cannabinoid products regardless of their actual composition—a misappropriation of the original brand name that persists in colloquial usage.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: βk-2C-B is a research chemical with psychedelic and empathogenic properties. As a beta-keto derivative of 2C-B, it produces notably longer-lasting effects, with roughly double the duration of its parent compound. The substance is known for its unpredictable effectiveness, which can make reliable dosing difficult. It is also inactivated by high pH environments, a property that may be relevant to route of administration considerations.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Insufflation is reported to be not well-tolerated, suggesting potential for local irritation or discomfort via this route.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: K-2c-B has been reported as a low-potency partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Published assay values include EC50 estimates around 905 nM with 41% maximal efficacy, and another reported 5-HT2A EC50 of 6,732 nM, both far weaker than comparator compounds such as 2C-B, 2C-I, or 2C-E. It also shows weak MAO-B inhibition at about 14,000 nM IC50, while MAO-A inhibition was not detected.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: The available pharmacology quote material does not provide human pharmacokinetic parameters for K-2c-B.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: EC50 reported as 905 nM and 6,732 nM in separate assays

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: Partial agonist; Emax reported as 41% in one assay

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: Inhibition not detected in available evidence

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: K-2c-B is the beta-keto analogue of 2C-B. Available in vitro data indicate weak serotonergic activity compared with related 2C compounds, with its clearest characterized action at the 5-HT2A receptor.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text:
βk-2C-B was first described in the scientific literature by Richard Glennon and colleagues in 2004. Despite being the β-keto derivative of the well-known psychedelic 2C-B, the compound was not included or mentioned in Alexander Shulgin's seminal work PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved).

The substance first appeared as a novel designer drug in Europe in 2013, nearly a decade after its initial scientific characterization. Following its emergence on the recreational drug market, several analytical papers were published documenting the substance's chemical properties. Its effects and characteristics became known primarily through user reports after it entered circulation as a designer drug rather than through systematic research.

chunks.title: K-2c-B
chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor partial agonist; MAO-B inhibitor; MAO-A interaction not detected

chunks.title: K-2c-I
chunks.text: βk-2C-I is a novel psychoactive substance whose nomenclature indicates it is the beta-keto analogue of 2C-I, a substituted phenethylamine psychedelic. Virtually no formal research or documentation exists regarding its pharmacology, subjective effects, toxicity, or safety profile. Due to the extreme scarcity of available data, this substance should be approached with significant caution, and thorough harm reduction practices are strongly encouraged for anyone who encounters it.

chunks.title: K-2c-I
chunks.text: The provided effects list includes psychedelic visuals, changes in perception, confusion, restlessness, and insomnia. Persistent psychosis is not established by the available reports.

chunks.title: K-IVP
chunks.text: K-IVP is a rare research chemical stimulant and the beta-ketone analogue of IVP. It belongs to the same chemical family as MDPV. Very little is known about this substance, though its effects are suspected to resemble those of MDPV, amphetamine, or high-dose caffeine. Due to its obscurity and limited available documentation, users should exercise extreme caution as its safety profile and pharmacological properties remain largely uncharacterized.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Kanna (Sceletium tortuosum) is a succulent plant native to South Africa that has been used by indigenous Khoisan peoples for thousands of years, traditionally fermented and chewed for its psychoactive effects. The first written account dates to 1662. Containing alkaloids such as mesembrine, kanna produces anxiolytic, mood-enhancing, and mildly euphoric effects primarily through serotonin reuptake inhibition and PDE4 inhibition. It is also reported to suppress appetite and enhance cannabis effects.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, though specific patterns of psychological dependence are not well characterized in the available literature.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Insufflation causes significant irritation and damage to the nasal cavity; this route of administration is not recommended.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Raw plant material appears more irritating than extracts. Effects are acute and related to route of administration rather than systemic toxicity.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Kanna acts primarily as a monoamine releaser through upregulation of vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT-2), with serotonin reuptake inhibition serving as a secondary mechanism. The plant also exhibits phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibition, which may contribute to its mood-enhancing and cognitive effects. Additional pharmacological activities include mild inhibition of acetylcholinesterase and monoamine oxidase-A, CB1 receptor antagonism, and CYP17A1 inhibition. Fermented preparations show synergistic effects among alkaloids in CB1 receptor and acetylcholinesterase inhibition that exceed those of mesembrine alone.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Kanna contains approximately 1 to 1.5% total alkaloids, with mesembrine being the most prominent. Traditional fermentation transforms mesembrine into delta-7 mesembrenone while reducing oxalate content. Fermented extracts demonstrate greater bioavailability and efficacy, particularly through mucosal absorption routes. Mesembrine transforms into mesembrenone when exposed to sunlight and aqueous conditions but remains stable in methanol or darkness.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Fermented preparations show enhanced bioavailability through mucosal absorption

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Plants of the genus Sceletium have likely been used for millennia by the San and Khoi peoples of South Africa as masticatories and traditional medicines. The indigenous Khoisan peoples traditionally fermented and chewed the plant as kougoed—an Afrikaans term meaning "chewable thing"—for its psychoactive effects. It served multiple purposes in traditional contexts, functioning as a narcotic, sedative, and analgesic while also suppressing hunger and thirst during hunting expeditions. In traditional medicine, kanna was employed to treat a variety of ailments including toothache, abdominal pain, and digestive issues. It held particular significance for pregnant women, being used to address constipation, nausea, uterine contractions, and post-birth recovery. An oil preparation made from the plant mixed with sheep's tail fat was traditionally used to relieve colic in infants.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Along with dagga (cannabis), kanna constituted an important element in southern Africa's precolonial exchange economy. The plant was highly valued and traded, sometimes combined with cannabis to enhance its effects. Much of the oral tradition surrounding its traditional preparation and use has declined over the past three centuries due to colonization, conflict, and cultural disruption.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text:
The first known written account of kanna's use was recorded in 1662 by Jan van Riebeeck, the Dutch colonial administrator who founded Cape Town. However, English East India Company official Richard Cocks had described kanna's properties as early as 1616, likening them to those of ginseng while stationed in Hirado, Japan.

During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, European writers including Peter Kolb and Guy Tachard incorrectly hypothesized that kanna might be the same plant as East Asian ginseng, based on its stimulant properties. This confusion reflected the limited botanical understanding of the era and the tendency to categorize unfamiliar plants by comparing them to known substances.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text:
The psychoactive compounds found in kanna, including mesembrone, mesembrenol, and turtuosamine, were patented in 1997. This marked a significant step in the commercialization and scientific study of the plant's active constituents. Today, kanna is sold commercially in various forms including gel caps, teas, tinctures, tablets, and snuff, with particular marketing emphasis on its potential to boost sexual performance and enhance mood.

Modern research has focused on the potential of kanna's bioactive alkaloids to support mental health. Preliminary studies using the standardized kanna extract Zembrin suggest it may have benefits for mood, anxiety, stress, sleep, and cognitive function. However, a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials found no significant effect on reducing anxiety symptoms compared to placebo, and clinical data remain insufficient to support the use of kanna for any specific medical indication.

chunks.title: Kanna
chunks.text: Binding profile: Serotonin reuptake inhibitor (selective, SSRI); VMAT-2; PDE4; CB1 receptor antagonist; Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAO-A); CYP17A1

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Kava is a psychoactive beverage and herbal product derived from the rootstock of Piper methysticum, a tropical shrub native to the western Pacific. It has been consumed in Pacific Island communities for over 3,000 years in social, ceremonial, and religious contexts. Its active constituents, known as kavalactones, produce anxiolytic, sedative, and mildly euphoric effects often compared to alcohol without significant cognitive impairment. The beverage characteristically causes a temporary numbing sensation in the mouth.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Traditionally regarded as non-addictive, especially compared to benzodiazepines. Some cases of psychological dependence have been documented in Pacific Island communities where heavy habitual use patterns similar to alcohol consumption have been observed.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Those with endogenous psychoses are advised to avoid kava.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Seizures have been listed among possible adverse reactions from chronic heavy use; however, available evidence remains limited.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: The FDA cited 'possible carcinogenicity' among concerns in its 2020 determination that kava is not generally recognized as safe for conventional foods, though specific carcinogenicity data was not detailed.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare but serious liver disease cases have been documented, primarily associated with concentrated extracts using organic solvents, non-noble kava varieties, contamination with stems or leaves, or heavy chronic use; traditional water-based preparations of noble kava roots at moderate doses appear considerably safer.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Low-level hepatic apoptosis and inhibition of hepatic enzymes in the CYP450 family. Non-water extracts may contain higher concentrations of hepatotoxic flavokavains and lack protective glutathione present in traditional preparations. Stems and leaves contain the hepatotoxic alkaloid pipermethystine.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: 18 cases of liver poisoning reported in Germany (1 death, 3 liver transplants required). Health authorities in the US, Australia, and Canada have issued warnings. Risk factors include solvent-extracted products, non-noble 'tudei' varieties, contamination, alcohol consumption, and pre-existing liver conditions. Elevated GGT enzyme levels may appear at intake levels of 240-440g kava powder per week (3,500-6,440mg kavalactones daily).

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy chronic use (31-440g powder per week) may cause 'kava dermopathy' characterized by dry, scaly skin on the palms, soles of feet, and back; this condition is reversible upon cessation of use.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Also known as 'kanikani' in Fiji. Some Pacific Islanders deliberately consume large amounts to achieve skin peeling, resulting in a layer of new skin.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Regular heavy use over extended periods has been associated with malnutrition, weight loss, mood disturbances, apathy, and increased susceptibility to infections; evidence for these effects remains limited and is confined to very heavy consumption patterns.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Limited high-quality research available on these effects.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Kava's pharmacological activity is primarily attributable to six major kavalactones (kavain, dihydrokavain, methysticin, dihydromethysticin, yangonin, and desmethoxyyangonin), which account for approximately 96% of the plant's pharmacological effects. The principal mechanism is potentiation of GABAA receptor activity, which has been attributed to alteration of lipid membrane structure and sodium channel function. Several kavalactones also inhibit norepinephrine reuptake and possibly dopamine reuptake, while all six act as reversible monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors. Additional mechanisms include CB1 cannabinoid receptor agonism by yangonin and blockade of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels by kavain and methysticin.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Kavalactones are rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract with variable bioavailability across individual compounds. In animal studies, kavain (the primary kavalactone in traditional preparations) showed an estimated oral bioavailability of approximately 50%. In humans, kavain undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism via cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme-mediated pathways, followed by phase II biotransformation processes including sulfonation, glucuronidation, and glutathione conjugation. In rats, over 90% of an administered kavain dose was eliminated within 72 hours through urine and feces, and no evidence of bioaccumulation has been observed in rats, mice, or humans.

chunks.text: Kava is reported to produce reverse tolerance in many users, where repeated use may be needed before full effects are felt; some users do not experience this pattern.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Kava originated in northern Vanuatu, where it was domesticated by farmers approximately 3,000 years ago through selective cultivation. The plant was subsequently spread eastward by the Austronesian Lapita culture into the rest of Polynesia, becoming endemic to Oceania while remaining absent from other Austronesian groups. The beverage reached Hawaii but could not establish itself in New Zealand due to the colder climate. In memory of the kava plants they brought with them and unsuccessfully attempted to cultivate, the Māori gave the name kawa-kawa to another Piperaceae species (M. excelsum). The Māori word "kawa" also came to mean "ceremonial protocol," reflecting the stylized consumption practices typical of Polynesian societies. Kava consumption is believed to be the reason betel nut chewing, otherwise ubiquitous among Austronesian peoples, was abandoned in Oceania.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: Kava has been consumed in Pacific Island communities for over three millennia in religious, political, cultural, and social contexts, typically prepared as a beverage. Throughout the Pacific, the plant is treated with great respect and holds an important place in local cultures, though each society has developed its own distinct traditions alongside shared practices. In Fiji, formal yaqona ceremonies accompany significant social, political, and religious functions, usually involving a ritual presentation of bundled roots as a sevusevu (gift) followed by communal drinking. In precolonial Hawaii, the Aliʻi (kings) coveted the Moʻi variety for its strong cerebral effects, attributed to a predominant concentration of the kavalactone kavain. This sacred cultivar was restricted exclusively to royalty, with commoners forbidden from experiencing it on pain of death. In Vanuatu, the nakamal serves as the traditional central meeting place and cultural hub where kava consumption facilitates communal gathering, dialogue, and the exchange of knowledge across generations.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text: In many Pacific communities, kava functions as a replacement for alcohol and is consumed throughout the day, particularly before spiritual rituals and social gatherings. Historically, it has been recognized as an entheogen of Pacific Island and Polynesian communities, playing an important role in various spiritual and ritualistic rites.

chunks.title: Kava
chunks.text:
Western interest in kava began with Captain Cook's voyages to the Pacific islands in 1778, though the beverage was initially regarded as inferior to alcohol. During the 18th and 19th centuries, Christian missionaries made efforts to prohibit kava drinking, which inadvertently led to changes in preparation methods. Historically, the beverage had been made exclusively from fresh kava root; in response to missionary restrictions, preparation from dried kava emerged as an alternative practice.

In recent decades, facilitated largely by the internet, kava has become available to users worldwide and has been adopted by increasing numbers of people outside the Pacific region. Nakamals and kava bars now exist in many countries, where the beverage can be consumed in a social setting similar to traditional practices. As a major traditional producer, Vanuatu has introduced legislation focused on regulating the quality of its kava exports rather than restricting domestic availability.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic of the arylcyclohexylamine class, developed in the early 1960s by Parke-Davis Laboratories as a replacement for phencyclidine (PCP). Widely employed in both human and veterinary medicine, it is considered the archetypal dissociative substance. Recreational use became widespread through the 1990s rave and nightclub scenes. More recently, it has attracted significant clinical interest for its ability to rapidly alleviate treatment-resistant depression and suicidal ideation.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop with daily use. Withdrawal symptoms reported include anxiety, tremor, sweating, and palpitations following attempts to stop.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Moderate to high abuse potential with risk of psychological dependence developing with chronic use. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, particularly with insufflation. The short duration of effects promotes bingeing patterns.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: At anesthetic doses, 10-20% of adults experience adverse psychiatric reactions during emergence, ranging from dysphoria to hallucinations and emergence delirium. Regular use is associated with paranoia, egocentrism, and increased delusional symptoms. Chronic heavy use may lead to persistent psychotic symptoms.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Seizures are rare but have been reported at very high or overdose-level doses. Tonic-clonic movements occur commonly at anesthetic doses but are distinct from true epileptic seizures.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Some evidence suggests ketamine may have antibiotic properties at higher doses, though how this affects normal human use is unclear.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Carcinogenesis studies have not been performed. Ketamine has shown clastogenic activity in mutagenesis studies.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Frequent heavy use can cause ketamine-induced cystitis, reduced bladder capacity, urge incontinence, and painful haematuria; these effects are strongly associated with chronic abuse patterns, with 20-30% of frequent users reporting bladder complaints.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Ketamine and its metabolites directly interact with urothelium, causing damage to epithelial cells of the bladder lining and increased permeability of the urothelial barrier.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Over 110 documented cases exist. All reported cases consuming greater than 5g per day showed symptoms. Functional bladder capacity can be reduced to as low as 10-150mL in severe cases. Surgical bladder removal has been required in some severe cases. Symptoms may be reversible with cessation in less severe cases.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Liver toxicity has been reported with higher doses and repeated administration; in chronic high-dose users, the frequency of liver injury is approximately 10%.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Case reports of elevated liver enzymes exist in ketamine treatment of chronic pain. Also associated with biliary colic and hepatobiliary disorder in chronic abuse.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic heavy use has been associated with kidney damage ranging from hydronephrosis to acute kidney injury; rhabdomyolysis causing kidney failure has been reported in overdose cases.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Often occurs alongside urinary tract damage in chronic users.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic heavy use is associated with cognitive deficits in memory and learning, with imaging studies showing reductions in white and grey matter and brain atrophy in frequent users; infrequent users do not appear to differ from controls on cognitive measures.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: NMDA receptor blockade leads to increased neuronal apoptosis, particularly with prolonged exposure. Non-lethal concentrations may initiate long-term alterations of the dendritic arbor in differentiated neurons.

chunks.text: Primate studies showed indicators of increased cell death in prefrontal cortex after daily 1mg/kg IV injections for six months, but not after one month. Deficits may be partially reversible with cessation. All user groups scored higher than controls on delusional symptom measures.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Ketamine principally acts as a noncompetitive, open-channel, voltage-dependent antagonist of the NMDA receptor, an ionotropic glutamate receptor that facilitates the entry of cations into neurons. It binds to the dizocilpine (PCP) site within the ion channel pore, blocking the influx of sodium, potassium, and calcium when the channel is occupied. Ketamine is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers, esketamine (S-ketamine) and arketamine (R-ketamine), with S-ketamine displaying approximately 3- to 4-fold greater NMDA receptor affinity than R-ketamine (Ki values of 0.30 μM and 1.4 μM, respectively). In the presence of physiological magnesium concentrations, ketamine shows a degree of NMDA receptor subunit selectivity, with its affinity for GluN2C- and GluN2D-containing receptors being less reduced by magnesium than its affinity for GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing receptors. Ketamine is not selective for NMDA receptors, though a broad screening study found that at 10 μM, ketamine and norketamine primarily affected NMDA receptors and did not appreciably interact with muscarinic receptors, opioid receptors, sigma receptors, serotonin receptors, or monoamine transporters.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Additional reported targets include the D2 dopamine receptor (partial agonist), kappa-opioid receptor (agonist), norepinephrine transporter (inhibitor), 5-HT3A receptor (potentiator), substance-P receptor (antagonist), and cholinesterase (inhibitor), though whether ketamine is a D2 receptor agonist remains controversial, with later studies reporting affinity greater than 10 μM. Acute NMDA receptor blockade results in increased glutamate release, which activates AMPA receptors and modulates downstream signaling pathways including upregulation of BDNF, activation of mTOR, and inhibition of eEF2 kinase phosphorylation, promoting rapid synaptic protein synthesis and neuroplasticity. Ketamine is classified as a psychoplastogen, meaning it can rapidly and durably promote neuroplasticity. The metabolite (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine has been found to indirectly activate AMPA receptors without altering NMDA receptor function and may contribute to antidepressant-relevant effects, though its necessity for ketamine's efficacy remains uncertain.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Ketamine is rapidly absorbed and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, primarily via CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, yielding norketamine through N-demethylation. Norketamine is subsequently converted by CYP2A6 and CYP2B6 into hydroxynorketamines (HNKs) and dehydronorketamine (DHNK). Additional metabolic pathways include hydroxylation of the cyclohexanone ring, conjugation with glucuronic acid, and dehydration of hydroxylated metabolites to form cyclohexene derivatives. Conjugated hydroxylated derivatives account for approximately 80% of urinary metabolites, followed by dehydronorketamine at about 16%. Overall, 85–95% of the administered dose is recovered in urine, primarily as metabolites, with minor elimination via bile and feces. Following intravenous administration, approximately 91% is recovered in urine and 3% in feces. Oral bioavailability is low (16–24%) due to substantial first-pass metabolism, while intramuscular bioavailability is approximately 93%. The distribution half-life is approximately 1.95 minutes, and the elimination half-life is approximately 120 minutes following intravenous administration. Clearance is high, approximately 95 L/h/70 kg.
