chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Tolerance may decline after abstinence, but the time needed for a full reset depends on individual physiology, amount and frequency of use, and total exposure duration. Some users report needing a month or longer for tolerance to return to baseline. Dissociatives such as ketamine are also reported to produce long-lasting or permanent tolerance ('permatolerance') that builds gradually apart from ordinary tolerance, with many chronic users saying they need much higher doses to reach dissociation even after long breaks.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text: Tolerance to dissociative, euphoric, hallucinogenic, and psychotomimetic effects can develop after sustained repeated use. The pace varies widely between individuals: some people report tolerance after one night of heavy use, while others need weeks of regular consumption before noticing it. High-dose nonmedical ketamine use can readily produce tolerance to its main effects.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Ketamine was first synthesized in 1962 by American scientist Calvin Stevens at Parke Davis Laboratories, initially designated "CI581." Stevens sought a safer anesthetic to replace phencyclidine, which produced severe and prolonged hallucinogenic effects upon recovery from anesthesia. By 1965, ketamine had demonstrated clinical utility as an anesthetic, and researcher Edward Domino coined the term "dissociative anesthetic" to describe its unique pharmacological profile. The United States Food and Drug Administration approved ketamine for human use in 1970.

Ketamine's favorable safety margin proved particularly valuable in combat medicine. Its minimal respiratory depression compared to other available anesthetics, combined with its sympathomimetic properties, led to its extensive deployment as a field anesthetic during the Vietnam War. The substance remains on the World Health Organization's Essential Drugs List as one of the minimum medical requirements for a basic healthcare system.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Recreational use of ketamine was first documented among medicinal chemists in the United States as early as 1965, spreading more widely by 1967. During the 1970s, patients recovering from ketamine anesthesia began reporting unwanted visions, drawing broader attention to the substance's psychoactive properties beyond clinical settings.

In 1978, neuroscientist John Lilly published "The Scientist," an autobiographical account describing his extensive personal explorations with ketamine that helped popularize awareness of its dissociative effects among countercultural audiences. Recreational use expanded through the 1980s, and by the early 1990s ketamine had become more widespread in Europe, where it gained notoriety as an adulterant in MDMA tablets and became closely associated with the nightclub and rave scenes. By 1995, the United States Drug Enforcement Administration had placed ketamine on its emerging drugs list due to its growing presence in electronic music culture.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Ketamine has accumulated numerous street names reflecting its diverse cultural contexts, including "Special K," "K," "Kit Kat," "kitty," "cat tranquilizer" (referencing its veterinary applications), "Cat Valium," and "Jet." The term "K-hole" describes a profound dissociative state involving visual and auditory hallucinations achieved at high doses, which has become a significant concept within psychedelic culture.

Several prominent figures documented their entheogenic experiences with ketamine extensively, including John Lilly, Marcia Moore, and D.M. Turner. Turner's death by drowning during unsupervised ketamine use became a cautionary example of the serious physical risks posed by the drug's dissociative and anesthetic properties. More recently, actor Matthew Perry's death in October 2023, attributed primarily to the acute effects of ketamine, brought renewed public attention to the substance's dangers. Statistical data revealed more than 90 ketamine-related deaths in England and Wales between 2005 and 2013.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
The identification of ketamine's rapid antidepressant effects in 2000 represented a major breakthrough in psychiatric treatment. Research demonstrated that sub-anesthetic doses could produce immediate or near-immediate relief of depressive and suicidal symptoms, with therapeutic effects persisting up to three days following a single administration. This discovery has been characterized as the single most important advance in depression treatment in more than fifty years.

The finding fundamentally shifted the direction of antidepressant research and development, generating widespread interest in NMDA receptor antagonists as a novel class of rapidly-acting treatments for mood disorders.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Ketamine — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol (Both substances cause ataxia and bring a very high risk of vomiting and unconsciousness. If the user falls unconscious while under the influence there is a severe risk of vomit aspiration if they are not placed in the recovery position.)
- Diphenhydramine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Ketamine has a high likelihood of increasing DPH's deliriant effects at higher dosages and can greatly increase the risk of injury, mania, and psychosis. Medical dosages of both substances are unlikely to cause concern.)
- GHB/GBL (Both substances cause ataxia and bring a risk of vomiting and unconsciousness. If the user falls unconscious while under the influence there is a severe risk of vomit aspiration if they are not placed in the recovery position.)
- Opioids (Both substances bring a risk of vomiting and unconsciousness.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Ketamine — caution combinations:
- Amphetamines (No unexpected interactions, though likely to increase blood pressure but not an issue with sensible doses. Moving around on high doses of this combination may be ill advised due to risk of physical injury.)
- Benzodiazepines (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Cocaine (No unexpected interactions, though likely to increase blood pressure but not an issue with sensible doses. Moving around on high doses of this combination may be ill advised due to risk of physical injury.)
- MAOIs (MAO-B inhibitors appear to increase the potency of Ketamine. MAO-A inhbitors have some negative reports associated with the combination but there isn't much information available)
- Pregabalin (Pregabalin and ketamine may synergize and increase each other's negative side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and loss of consciousness.

chunks.text: Caution is advised for beyond medical dosages due to seizure concerns, and medical dosages for individuals with higher risk seizure profiles and or behavior.)

Legal status of Ketamine by country:
- Australia: Schedule 8 — Possession, manufacture, or supply without authority is illegal. Classified as a controlled drug requiring strict regulation.
- Austria: Prescription only (NR medication) — Legal for medical and veterinary use. Repeated dispense prohibited. Illegal when sold, possessed, or produced without a prescription under the Neue-Psychoaktive-Substanzen-Gesetz (NPSG).
- Belgium: Prescription only — Legal for medical and veterinary use. Possession without prescription can result in arrest.
- Brazil: Controlled (veterinary) — Legal for veterinary use only. Illegal when sold or possessed for human use.
- Cambodia: Controlled — Not legal to possess without a prescription. Some pharmacies may sell ketamine, though most consider it forbidden.
- Canada: Schedule I (CDSA) — Controlled under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act as an analogue of phencyclidine (PCP). Sale, possession, and production are illegal unless authorized for medical, scientific, or industrial…
- China: Schedule II — China places ketamine under Class II psychiatric-drug control.

chunks.title: Ketamine
chunks.text:
Commercial trade is restricted to licensed wholesalers, and retail sale is forbidden.
- Croatia: Controlled — Possession and distribution regulated under national drug legislation.
- Czech Republic: Schedule IV (List 7) — Available exclusively with a prescription under Nařízení vlády č. 463/2013 Sb. Sales and distribution controlled under the Medicines Act.
- Denmark: Controlled — Illegal except for scientific and medicinal uses as of February 8, 2008.
- France: Schedule IV (Narcotic) — In France, ketamine is treated as a narcotic in the Liste des substances classées comme stupéfiants, Annexe IV. Injectable preparations fall under Médicine - List I and strict controls.
- Germany: Prescription only (Anlage 1 AMVV) — Available by prescription for medical and veterinary use.

chunks.title: Ketazolam
chunks.text: Ketazolam is a long-acting benzodiazepine derivative possessing anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties. It is metabolized in the body into diazepam and subsequent active metabolites, contributing to its prolonged duration of action. Ketazolam is reported to have comparable efficacy to diazepam with generally milder side effects. It is marketed in a limited number of countries and is not approved in the United States, United Kingdom, or Australia. As with all benzodiazepines, chronic use can lead to physical dependence.

chunks.title: Ketazolam
chunks.text: Chronic use can lead to physical dependence and the appearance of benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome upon cessation or dose reduction. Special precaution is required in alcohol or drug-dependent individuals.

chunks.title: Ketazolam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a benzodiazepine, ketazolam carries risk of psychological dependence with regular use.

chunks.title: Ketobemidone
chunks.text: Ketobemidone is a potent synthetic opioid analgesic first synthesized in 1942 by Eisleb and colleagues at I.G. Farbenindustrie. It possesses analgesic potency comparable to morphine and additionally exhibits NMDA-antagonist properties through its metabolite norketobemidone, which may render it effective for certain pain types resistant to other opioids. Used primarily in Scandinavian countries, it carries significant risks of respiratory depression and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Ketobemidone
chunks.text: As an opioid, ketobemidone carries a high risk of physical dependence with chronic use, consistent with its classification as habit-forming.

chunks.title: Ketobemidone
chunks.text: Experiments on former addicts indicated ketobemidone was quite addictive with potentially increased abuse potential in high doses compared to other opioids. However, conflicting evidence suggests that at analgesic doses it may produce less euphoria than morphine, potentially reducing addiction risk under clinical supervision.

chunks.title: Ketobemidone

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Khat (Catha edulis) is a flowering shrub native to eastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, whose fresh leaves are chewed for their stimulant properties. The plant contains cathinone, a phenethylamine alkaloid that produces sociability, excitement, mild appetite suppression, and euphoria. Khat chewing holds thousands of years of cultural significance in East African and Yemeni communities, comparable to coca leaf use in South America. The WHO classifies it as a drug of abuse capable of producing psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Classified by the WHO as a drug of abuse that can produce mild to moderate psychological dependence, considered less addictive than tobacco or alcohol. The WHO does not consider khat addiction to be a serious global problem.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Occasionally a psychotic episode can result, resembling a hypomanic state in presentation. Psychosis in extreme cases may occur in genetically predisposed individuals. The relationship between khat consumption and psychiatric disorders requires further research.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Khat's stimulant effects are primarily mediated by cathinone and cathine, two phenylpropanolamine alkaloids structurally related to amphetamine. Cathinone, the more potent constituent found in fresh leaves, demonstrates high affinity for serotonin receptors and inhibits the reuptake of epinephrine and norepinephrine, producing wakefulness and euphoria. Cathine acts upon adrenergic receptors to cause release of epinephrine and norepinephrine. Both compounds produce sympathomimetic effects including increased heart rate and blood pressure.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: When khat leaves are chewed, cathine and cathinone are absorbed through the oral mucosa and gastric lining. Cathinone is rapidly metabolized, with effects peaking after 15 to 30 minutes and nearly 98% of the substance converted to norephedrine by the liver. Cathine has a half-life of approximately three hours in humans. Cathinone is unstable and degrades to cathine and norephedrine within 48 hours when leaves dry.

chunks.text: Causes release of epinephrine and norepinephrine (cathine)

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text:
Khat (Catha edulis) is a flowering plant native to eastern and southeastern Africa, with a history of cultivation originating in the Harar area of present-day eastern Ethiopia. The plant likely originated in the Horn of Africa, specifically the Ethiopia-Somali region, from where it spread to Kenya and the Arabian Peninsula. According to nineteenth-century British explorer Richard Burton, khat originated in the Emirate of Harar.

The earliest known documented description of khat appears in the Kitab al-Saidala fi al-Tibb, an 11th-century work on pharmacy and materia medica written by the Persian scientist Abū Rayhān al-Bīrūnī. Unaware of its true origins, al-Bīrūnī described khat as a commodity from Turkestan, noting it was sour to taste with a reddish color and slight blackish tinge. The plant was mentioned again in a 13th-century publication by the physician Naguib Ad-Din. The inhabitants of the Ifat Sultanate were the first to be recorded using khat in the 14th century by Arab historian Ibn Fadlallah al-Umari.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text:
Among communities from the areas where the plant is native, khat-chewing has historical relevance as a social custom dating back thousands of years, analogous to the use of coca leaves in South America's Andes Mountains or betel nut preparations in South Asia. Khat has been grown for use as a stimulant for centuries in the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, where chewing khat predates the use of coffee and is employed in a similar social context.

Muslim Sufis in the surrounding areas used khat to intensify their mystical experience and to facilitate a sense of union with God. Traditionally, khat serves as a socializing substance, particularly in Yemen, where khat-chewing is predominantly a male habit combined with conversation, hookah smoking, and tea drinking.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Traditional Use and Cultural Significance

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: In 1854, Malay author Abdullah bin Abdul Kadir documented the prevalence of khat chewing in Al Hudaydah, Yemen, observing that everyone chewed leaves as goats chew cud. He described the leaves as rather wide and about two fingers in length, noting that unlike betel leaves which require condiments, khat was simply stuffed into the mouth and munched. When he inquired about the benefits, locals replied there were none whatsoever, explaining it was simply an expense they had grown accustomed to. He also noted that those who consume the leaves must eat substantial amounts of ghee and honey or risk falling ill.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: In 1856, English writer Charles Dickens described the custom of khat chewing in the Horn region and adjacent Gulf territories, likening its effects to drinking strong green tea. He noted that botanists had named the plant Catha edulis, meaning "eatable kat," and that it was sent to Arabs in camel loads consisting of small parcels containing about forty slender twigs with leaves attached, carefully wrapped to avoid air exposure. Dickens observed that Europeans accustomed to stronger stimulants were little affected by khat, but among the more temperate Arabs it was such a welcome provocative to good humor that approximately two hundred and eighty camel-loads were consumed annually in Aden alone.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text:
An estimated 5 to 10 million people globally use khat on a daily basis. Contemporary khat consumption is concentrated in East Africa and southwestern Arabia, including Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, Uganda, and Yemen. In Yemen, researchers estimate about 70-80% of Yemenis between 16 and 50 years old chew khat at least occasionally, with approximately 60-90% of males and 35% of females chewing daily. Yemenis spend an estimated 14.6 million man-hours per day chewing khat, with families spending about 17% of their income on the substance. In Ethiopia, khat is chewed by 19.5% of the population, more commonly by men than women.

In recent years, improved roads, off-road motor vehicles, and air transportation have increased the global distribution of this perishable commodity. As a result, the plant has been found in places such as Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, the United Kingdom, the Levant, Rome, New Zealand, and the United States. In the US, freshly-packed khat leaves are sold in African and Middle Eastern markets of Boston, Dallas, Los Angeles, and New York City, where demand is highest.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text:
One reason for the widespread cultivation of khat in Yemen is the high income it provides for farmers. Studies from 2001 estimated that income from cultivating khat was about 2.5 million Yemeni rials per hectare, while fruits brought only 0.57 million rials per hectare. Between 1970 and 2000, the area on which khat was cultivated grew from 8,000 to 103,000 hectares. According to a World Bank estimate from 2000, khat accounted for 30% of Yemen's economy.

Khat is so popular in Yemen that its cultivation consumes much of the country's agricultural resources. An estimated 40% of Yemen's water supply goes towards irrigating it, with production increasing by about 10-15% every year. One daily bag of khat requires an estimated 500 litres of water to produce. Water consumption is high and groundwater levels in the Sana'a basin are diminishing, prompting government officials to propose relocating large portions of the city's population to Red Sea coastal areas.

In Uganda, khat is grown in the central region, especially in Kasenge, Butambala District, Mabira Forest, and parts of the western region. In Kenya, it is grown in Meru County and Embu County.

chunks.title: Khat
chunks.text: Following a ban on khat in the British-governed Aden Protectorate, the Qāt Commission of Inquiry in Aden concluded that khat does not create an addiction like opium or hashish, noting that those who are suddenly deprived of it do not suffer physical consequences.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Kratom is a tropical plant (Mitragyna speciosa) native to Thailand and Southeast Asia, where its leaves have been used as a traditional medicine for centuries. Botanically related to coffee, it contains the indole alkaloids mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine. Kratom produces dose-dependent effects, acting as a stimulant at lower doses and producing opioid-like depressant effects at higher doses. It is considered habit-forming. Multiple strains exist, typically distinguished by vein color and region of origin.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, producing withdrawal symptoms including irritability, diarrhea, muscle and bone pain, insomnia, decreased appetite, restlessness, fever, and low motivation. While often reported as less severe than traditional opioid withdrawal, kratom withdrawal can still be significant, and severe cases may warrant treatment approaches similar to opioid addiction.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Kratom has a known addiction liability with approximately 25.5% of regular users meeting criteria for substance use disorder. Dependence may develop relatively quickly in vulnerable individuals, with tolerance often noted within weeks to months. Relapse risk is high, reported at 78-89% at three months post-cessation.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Psychosis and hallucinations have been reported with frequent high-dose use, with hallucinations noted in approximately 4.8% of poison control cases. Kratom use has a small but statistically significant association with externalizing mental health disorders and may worsen existing conditions. It remains unclear whether kratom directly causes psychosis or unmasks pre-existing vulnerability.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Seizures were reported in approximately 6.1% of poison control center exposures. Risk appears primarily associated with frequent use of high doses or overdose situations. At typical recreational doses, seizure risk appears low.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Kratom use is associated with acute liver injury in some users, presenting with abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pruritus, and jaundice; however, many users do not develop liver injury, and risk factors remain unclear.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mechanism unknown and poorly studied; proposed models exist but are not well established. Liver biopsies typically show cholestasis, though biomarkers may indicate cholestatic, mixed, or hepatocellular injury patterns.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Median latency from first use to symptom onset is approximately 20 days. Cases are likely underreported. It remains unclear which users are at heightened risk.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis has been reported as a rare but serious complication, primarily associated with high-dose use.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Elevated heart rate and blood pressure may occur during use; tachycardia was reported in approximately 17% of poison control exposures, though serious cardiac events are uncommon.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiac or respiratory arrest reported in 0.6% of poison control cases, typically involving other factors.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Kratom's pharmacological activity is primarily driven by two indole alkaloids, mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, both of which act as partial agonists at μ-opioid receptors, with 7-hydroxymitragynine showing the higher affinity. While most data indicates agonist activity across all three classical opioid receptor subtypes, some findings suggest antagonism at the δ-opioid receptor and only low affinity for the κ-opioid receptor. Both compounds display functional selectivity, notably lacking β-arrestin pathway recruitment. Mitragynine additionally stimulates α2-adrenergic receptors (reducing norepinephrine release), interacts with several serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine receptor subtypes, inhibits COX-2, and blocks voltage-gated calcium channels. Kratom contains at least 54 alkaloids in total, including rhynchophylline (a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist), which may contribute synergistically to the plant's overall pharmacological profile.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Both mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine readily cross the blood-brain barrier. Mitragynine undergoes hepatic metabolism via both phase I and phase II pathways, with resulting metabolites excreted in urine. In vitro studies indicate that kratom extracts inhibit CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP1A2, suggesting significant potential for drug interactions.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Functionally selective; lacks β-arrestin recruitment. 7-hydroxymitragynine shows higher affinity than mitragynine

chunks.text: Disputed; most data suggests agonism, some data suggests antagonism

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text:
Kratom is indigenous to Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, and Papua New Guinea, where its leaves have been used in traditional herbal medicine since at least the nineteenth century. The plant has historically been consumed through chewing, smoking, and preparation as a tea.

In Thailand, kratom served important social and ceremonial functions, being used as a snack to receive guests and as part of ritual worship of ancestors and gods. The substance was also valued for its practical applications; by 1836, it was reported to be used as an opium substitute in Malaysia, and similar use was documented in Thailand throughout the nineteenth century. Historically, its effects at low doses have been compared to those of coca, while higher doses have been likened to opium.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text: Mitragyna speciosa was first formally described by the Dutch colonial botanist Pieter Korthals in 1839, who initially named it Stephegyne speciosa. The plant underwent several reclassifications before George Darby Haviland established its current taxonomic name and classification in 1859.

chunks.title: Kratom
chunks.text:
Beginning in the 2010s, a tea-based preparation known as "4×100" emerged as a popular recreational drink among young people across Southeast Asia, particularly in Thailand. This cocktail combines kratom leaves with cough syrup, Coca-Cola, and ice. By around 2011, individuals who consumed this preparation were generally viewed more negatively than traditional kratom users, though not as stigmatized as users of substances like heroin.

In Western contexts, kratom has gained attention as a self-treatment option for opioid withdrawal, with many individuals using it to ease the transition away from opioid dependence. It has also been occasionally cited as an aid for addressing acute alcohol dependency.

The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)

chunks.title: LAE-32
chunks.text: LAE-32 is a semisynthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class, structurally related to LSD. First described by Albert Hofmann and colleagues by 1955, it was later studied by the CIA as part of Project MKULTRA. Unlike most classical psychedelics, its effects are reportedly characterized by sedation, depersonalization, and emotional indifference rather than typical psychedelic stimulation. It remains one of the least researched psychedelic substances.

chunks.title: LAE-32
chunks.text: LAE-32 has been reported to induce a schizophrenia-like condition characterized by depersonalization and indifference in mentally healthy individuals. The substance's primary psychological effects appear to involve significant dissociative and depersonalizing states that resemble psychotic symptomatology.

chunks.title: Lagochilus-Inebrians
chunks.text: Lagochilus inebrians is a shrub of the mint (Lamiaceae) family native to Central Asia, where it has been consumed as a tea for centuries by Tajik, Tatar, Turkmen, and Uzbek peoples. Its primary identified compound is lagochilin, a diterpene. The plant is reported to produce mild sedation, relaxation, and euphoria, though its overall psychoactive effects are considered subtle. Due to limited research, its safety profile remains largely unknown.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Lean is a polysubstance recreational drink combining prescription cough syrup containing codeine (an opioid) and promethazine (an antihistamine) with soft drinks and hard candy. Originating in Houston in the 1960s, it became culturally prominent through association with hip hop music, particularly in the Southern United States. Lean carries significant risks including addiction, respiratory depression, and overdose. It is especially dangerous when combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use due to the opioid component. Withdrawal has been described as feeling like 'death in your stomach' and discontinuing regular usage brings about significant withdrawal symptoms that make cessation difficult.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Lean carries significant psychological addiction potential due to the euphoric effects of codeine combined with the sedating properties of promethazine. Users frequently develop compulsive use patterns, with the drink's cultural normalization potentially masking the severity of dependence.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Lean does not appear to directly cause seizures but increases their likelihood in susceptible individuals. At least one documented fatality involved a seizure in a chronic user who had developed organ complications from prolonged use.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is the primary mechanism of acute toxicity and can occur at high doses or when combined with other depressants; this effect is dose-related and represents the main pathway to fatal overdose.

chunks.title: Lean

chunks.text: Codeine causes respiratory depression through opioid receptor activation in the brainstem respiratory centers, while promethazine potentiates this effect through CNS depression

chunks.title: Lean

chunks.title: Lean

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Lean produces its effects through the combined action of its two primary active ingredients. Codeine, a morphinan opioid, acts as a prodrug that is metabolized to morphine, which then activates μ-opioid receptors to produce analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression. Promethazine, a phenothiazine antihistamine, acts as a central nervous system depressant through histamine H1 receptor antagonism and contributes additional sedative effects. The combination appears to produce synergistic CNS depression, with promethazine potentially enhancing the euphoric effects of codeine while simultaneously increasing respiratory depression risk through its own depressant properties.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Codeine undergoes hepatic metabolism, with a portion converted to morphine via CYP2D6 O-demethylation, which is responsible for its opioid effects. The rate of this conversion varies significantly between individuals due to CYP2D6 genetic polymorphisms. Promethazine is also hepatically metabolized. When consumed orally as lean, both compounds are absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract when consumed as a beverage

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text:
Lean is thought to have originated in Houston during the 1960s, when blues musicians in the city's Fifth Ward, Third Ward, and South Park neighborhoods began mixing Robitussin cough syrup with beer. When wine coolers entered the market, they replaced beer as the preferred mixer. This practice was subsequently adopted by the generation of rappers who grew up in these same Houston neighborhoods.

The formula evolved significantly during the 1980s and 1990s, shifting to codeine-promethazine cough syrup as the primary ingredient. This transition paralleled changes in the broader drug landscape, as lean emerged partly as an alternative to other drug combinations that had become less accessible. The glutethimide and codeine combination popular from the 1970s through the early 1990s fell out of favor, and after pharmaceutical companies added naloxone to pentazocine products to prevent abuse of "T's and blues" (pentazocine/tripelennamine), codeine-based cough syrups became an attractive substitute.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text:
Lean remained largely a local Houston phenomenon until the 1990s, when DJ Screw began releasing mixtapes that referenced the drink. His music proved particularly suited to Houston's environment, where residents spent long hours driving through the sprawling, hot city. DJ Screw would record sessions in his apartment featuring rappers freestyling over beats, then slow the recordings down further on his cassette recorder. This distinctive chopped-and-screwed style has been characterized as sounding "as if the song itself has taken too much codeine promethazine."

The drink gained national attention in June 2000 when Three 6 Mafia released "Sippin' on Some Syrup" featuring UGK, introducing the term "purple drank" to audiences across the United States. The concoction's popularity subsequently spread throughout the Southern states. By 2004, a University of Texas at Austin study found that 8.3% of secondary school students in Texas had used codeine syrup recreationally. The Drug Enforcement Administration reported increasing busts involving the syrup across the Southern United States, particularly in Texas and Florida.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text:
Lean's cultural prominence led to commercial products loosely based on the concept. In June 2008, Houston-based Innovative Beverage Group released "Drank," a legal beverage marketed to "Slow Your Roll" using herbal ingredients like valerian root and rose hips along with melatonin, but containing no codeine or promethazine. Similar "anti-energy" or relaxation drinks emerged under names including "Purple Stuff," "Sippin Syrup," and "Lean." These products have drawn criticism for potentially serving as gateways to the dangerous illegal mixture, with the marketing compared to that of candy cigarettes.

The drink's influence on subsequent generations of artists became apparent in later years. In a 2019 interview, rapper Future discussed quitting lean and expressed regret upon learning that Juice Wrld had been influenced by his music to try the drug as a young person, asking "How many other sixth-graders did I influence to drink lean?" References to lean have appeared in mainstream hits, including Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road," though the artist has stated he does not endorse the drug.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Robert Earl Davis Jr., known as DJ Screw, was the Houston producer most responsible for popularizing lean and is widely credited as a source of inspiration for the chopped-and-screwed style of hip hop. His invocation of lean in lyrics combined with characteristically slow tempos defined a sound that rappers far beyond Houston would eventually adopt. DJ Screw died on November 16, 2000, from an overdose involving codeine-promethazine, Valium, and PCP.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: A protégé of DJ Screw, Big Moe released albums titled "City of Syrup" and "Purple World" that centered on the drink, and has been described as having "rapped obsessively about the drug." He died at age 33 on October 14, 2007, after suffering a heart attack one week earlier that left him in a coma. There was speculation that lean may have contributed to his death.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: Chad Lamont Butler, known as Pimp C, was a widely influential rapper from Port Arthur, Texas and member of the duo UGK, who appeared on the landmark track "Sippin' on Some Syrup." He was found dead on December 4, 2007, at the Mondrian Hotel in West Hollywood. The Los Angeles County Coroner's Office determined his death was "due to promethazine-codeine effects and other unestablished factors." While medication levels were elevated, they were not sufficient to classify the death as an overdose. However, Pimp C had a history of sleep apnea, and the coroner's office indicated that the combination of this condition with cough medication probably suppressed his breathing long enough to cause death.

chunks.title: Lean
chunks.text: American rapper Fredo Santana frequently referenced lean in his music. He died of a seizure on January 19, 2018. According to reports, he had been suffering from liver and kidney problems believed to be the result of his addiction to the substance.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.text: Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting benzodiazepine and the first compound of its class ever synthesized, discovered serendipitously in 1957 and marketed under the brand name Librium in 1960. It produces anxiolytic, sedative, hypnotic, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant effects, and is primarily prescribed for the management of anxiety disorders and acute alcohol withdrawal. Like all benzodiazepines, chlordiazepoxide carries significant risks of physical dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.text: Chlordiazepoxide can produce physical dependence and benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome. Its withdrawal profile resembles withdrawal from alcohol or barbiturates. Risk of unpleasant withdrawal increases with higher doses and longer use, but symptoms can still occur at standard doses and after short-term treatment.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.text: Chlordiazepoxide has significant abuse potential and is classified as habit-forming. Its presence is often found in urine testing from drug users without a prescription, suggesting misuse liability. The FDA requires boxed warnings for all benzodiazepines describing risks of abuse, misuse, and addiction.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.text: Possible carcinogenesis and mutagenesis have been listed among adverse effects from benzodiazepine use during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Liver problems including yellow eyes and skin (jaundice) are listed among side effects; individuals with severe liver deficiencies such as hepatitis or cirrhosis show decreased elimination by a factor of two.

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: Librium

chunks.title: Librium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Use during pregnancy may cause miscarriage, malformation, intrauterine growth retardation, functional deficits, and postnatal benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome. Crosses placenta and is excreted in breast milk.

chunks.text: Chronic use leads to development of tolerance with a decrease in benzodiazepine binding sites in the forebrain; studies in mice showed impairment of latent learning, and chlordiazepoxide caused the most profound reduction in serotonin turnover among benzodiazepines tested.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Lisdexamfetamine is a central nervous system stimulant of the amphetamine class, designed as a prodrug of dextroamphetamine. First approved by the FDA in 2007, it was specifically formulated to deter non-oral abuse by requiring metabolic conversion to release its active component. Prescribed for ADHD and binge eating disorder, it produces typical amphetamine effects including stimulation, focus enhancement, and euphoria, but with slower onset and longer duration than conventional amphetamines. Despite its anti-abuse design, it retains significant dependence potential.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Tolerance develops rapidly with recreational amphetamine abuse, requiring increasingly larger doses to achieve the same effect. Patients prescribed this drug often must increase their dosage over time to maintain efficacy. Physical dependence can develop with chronic use.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Lisdexamfetamine has a high potential for substance abuse and can produce dependence and addiction like other euphoric stimulants, particularly when taken above recommended dosages. While its prodrug design may reduce abuse potential compared to immediate-release amphetamines at therapeutic doses, addiction is a serious risk with heavy recreational use.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Using amphetamines in very high doses can result in stimulant psychosis which may include paranoia, delusions, and hallucinations. Approximately 5-15% of users who develop stimulant psychosis fail to recover completely. Psychosis very rarely arises from therapeutic use; the combination of prolonged high-dose use with sleep deprivation significantly increases risk.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Convulsions are reported as a manifestation of severe overdose and typically precede fatal poisoning.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects including arrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, increased heart rate, and circulatory collapse can occur, particularly in overdose situations. Rare cases of sudden cardiac death have been reported in individuals with underlying heart problems.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Contraindicated in patients with heart disease, arteriosclerosis, or severe hypertension.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: In rodents and primates, sufficiently high doses of amphetamine cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity characterized by reduced transporter and receptor function. There is no evidence that amphetamine is directly neurotoxic in humans at typical doses, though large doses may cause indirect neurotoxicity through increased oxidative stress.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Potential indirect neurotoxicity results from increased oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species and autoxidation of dopamine.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Direct neurotoxicity has not been demonstrated in humans.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Lisdexamfetamine is an inactive prodrug that is converted in the body to dextroamphetamine, which is responsible for the drug's pharmacological activity. Following ingestion, lisdexamfetamine is hydrolyzed by enzymes in red blood cells to release dextroamphetamine and L-lysine, with a conversion half-life of approximately one hour. Dextroamphetamine acts as a full agonist at trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), a key regulator of monoamine neurotransmission. It also inhibits the dopamine transporter, norepinephrine transporter, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2, with weaker affinity for the serotonin transporter. Through these mechanisms, dextroamphetamine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine into presynaptic neurons while promoting the release of monoamine neurotransmitters into the extracellular space. The parent compound lisdexamfetamine itself does not bind to monoamine reuptake sites.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Lisdexamfetamine is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract after oral administration. Unlike amphetamine, its absorption is not significantly affected by gastrointestinal pH. The prodrug is hydrolyzed by red blood cells to dextroamphetamine and L-lysine, with substantial conversion occurring even at low hematocrit levels. This enzymatic conversion is the rate-limiting step in bioactivation and is not mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes. Dextroamphetamine readily distributes into most tissues including the brain, with approximately 20% bound to plasma proteins. Dextroamphetamine is subsequently metabolized by CYP2D6, dopamine β-hydroxylase, flavin-containing monooxygenase 3, and glycine N-acyltransferase through pathways including aromatic para-hydroxylation, aliphatic hydroxylation, N-oxidation, N-dealkylation, and deamination. Approximately 96% of an oral dose is recovered in urine, with 42% as amphetamine, 25% as hippuric acid, and 2% as intact lisdexamfetamine.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
Absorption is not significantly affected by stomach acidity, unlike regular amphetamine
Food delays peak levels by about one hour and may slightly reduce overall absorption
The prodrug design means alternate routes like snorting or injection do not speed up effects, as conversion still depends on red blood cells

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Half-life refers to dextroamphetamine, the active metabolite
Lisdexamfetamine itself has a half-life of less than one hour
Urine pH significantly affects elimination: acidic urine shortens half-life to around 7 hours, while alkaline urine can extend it up to 34 hours
Peak dextroamphetamine concentrations occur approximately 3.5 hours after dosing

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text: Tolerance develops rapidly with recreational amphetamine use, often requiring increasingly larger doses to achieve the same effect during periods of extended use. Patients prescribed lisdexamfetamine therapeutically may also need dosage increases over time to maintain efficacy, though this occurs more gradually than with recreational abuse patterns.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
Lisdexamfetamine was developed by Robert Oberlender at New River Pharmaceuticals under the developmental name NRP104. The compound represents the first chemically formulated prodrug stimulant, created by covalently attaching dextroamphetamine to the naturally occurring amino acid L-lysine. This design was intended to produce a longer-lasting and less easily abused version of dextroamphetamine, as the requirement for conversion into the active compound via enzymes in red blood cells delays its onset of action regardless of the route of administration.

New River Pharmaceuticals was subsequently acquired by Shire Pharmaceuticals, which was later acquired by Takeda Pharmaceuticals, prior to the drug's market release.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
The United States Food and Drug Administration approved lisdexamfetamine for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in February 2007, with approval for use in adults following in April 2008. Health Canada approved the marketing of lisdexamfetamine for prescription use in August 2009, while the European Union granted approval in 2012.

In January 2015, the FDA expanded the approved indications to include the treatment of binge eating disorder in adults. The FDA also gave tentative approval to generic formulations of lisdexamfetamine in 2015, with the US patent protection expiring on 24 February 2023. The Canadian patent expired 20 years from its filing date of 1 June 2004.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
The International Nonproprietary Name "lisdexamfetamine" is a contraction of L-lysine-dextroamphetamine. As of November 2020, the compound is marketed under several brand names internationally, including Aduvanz, Elvanse, Juneve, Samexid, Tyvense, Venvanse, and Vyvanse.

Production quotas established for the United States in 2016 were set at 29,750 kilograms. By 2023, lisdexamfetamine had become the 76th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 9 million prescriptions written annually.

Lisdexamfetamine — unsafe combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds (Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences. In extreme cases, they can result in severe vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, and heart failure.)
- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines (The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops. The combination is generally unnecessary because of the stimulating effects of psychedelics. )
- DOx compounds (The combined stimulating effects of the two can lead to an uncomfortable body-load, while the focusing effects of amphetamine can easily lead to thought loops. Coming down from amphetamines while the DOx is still active can be quite anxiogenic. )

- NBOMe compounds (Amphetamines and NBOMes both provide considerable stimulation. When combined they can result in tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction and in extreme cases heart failure.

The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants are also not good in combination with psychedelics as they can lead to unpleasant thought loops. NBOMes are known to cause seizures and stimulants can increase this risk.)
- PCP (This combination can easily lead to hypermanic states)

If amphetamines wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages cause strain of the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications.)

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
Lisdexamfetamine — caution combinations:
- 2C-x compounds (The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops. The combination is generally unnecessary because of the stimulating effects of psychedelics. Combination of the stimulating effects may be uncomfortable.)
- Alcohol (Drinking on stimulants is risky because the sedative effects of the alcohol are reduced, and these are what the body uses to gauge drunkenness. This typically leads to excessive drinking with greatly reduced inhibitions, high risk of liver damage and increased dehydration. They will also allow you to drink past a point where you might normally pass out, increasing the risk. If you do decide to do this then you should set a limit of how much you will drink each hour and stick to it, bearing in mind that you will feel the alcohol and the stimulant less.

chunks.title: Lisdexamfetamine
chunks.text:
Extended release formulations may severely impede sleep, further worsening the hangover.)
- Caffeine (This combination of stimulants is not generally necessary and may increase strain on the heart, as well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort.)
- Cannabis (Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences)
- Cocaine (This combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart. It is not generally worth it as cocaine has a mild blocking effect on dopamine releasers like amphetamine)
- Diphenhydramine (Amphetamines as a stimulant may mask some of the negative side effects of DPH, leading to delusions of sobriety which has additional concern in states of delirium. The combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart and may cause some physical discomfort, and has the chance to cause life-threatening cardiovascular issues. The combination may also increase each other's neurotoxicity at higher dosages. chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: Lithium is an alkali-metal monovalent cation typically administered as carbonate or citrate salts. Classified as both a mood stabilizer and antidepressant, it is primarily used in the management of mood disorders. Unlike most psychiatric medications, which are complex organic compounds, lithium is a simple elemental ion, making it pharmacologically unique within its therapeutic class.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Lithium use during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of Ebstein's cardiac anomaly, a congenital heart defect, in exposed infants.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: This is a teratogenic effect specific to first trimester exposure during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: Lithium's biological effects are thought to stem primarily from the ability of the monovalent lithium ion (Li⁺) to compete with endogenous ions, particularly sodium (Na⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺), whose ionic radius (86 pm) closely approximates that of lithium (90 pm). Lithium enters cells through sodium transport mechanisms, including both voltage-gated and epithelial sodium channels as well as ligand-gated ion channels, and can cross nuclear and mitochondrial membranes. It can also enter and partially block potassium and calcium channels without permeating them. The full mechanisms underlying lithium's mood-stabilizing and antidepressant effects remain only partially understood.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: The mineral petalite (LiAlSi₄O₁₀) was first discovered in 1800 by Brazilian chemist and statesman José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva at a mine on the island of Utö, Sweden. It was not until 1817 that Swedish chemist Johan August Arfwedson, working in the laboratory of Jöns Jakob Berzelius, detected the presence of a novel element while analyzing petalite ore. This new element formed compounds resembling those of sodium and potassium, though its carbonate and hydroxide proved less soluble in water and less alkaline. Berzelius named the alkaline material "lithion" from the Greek word λιθoς (lithos, meaning "stone"), reflecting its discovery in a solid mineral rather than in plant ashes like potassium or animal blood like sodium.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: Arfwedson subsequently demonstrated the element's presence in the minerals spodumene and lepidolite. In 1818, Christian Gmelin became the first to observe that lithium salts produce a characteristic bright red flame coloration. Despite these advances, both Arfwedson and Gmelin failed in their attempts to isolate the pure element from its salts. Isolation was finally achieved in 1821 when William Thomas Brande obtained metallic lithium through electrolysis of lithium oxide, employing a technique previously used by Sir Humphry Davy to isolate potassium and sodium.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: In 1855, Robert Bunsen and Augustus Matthiessen developed a method to produce larger quantities of lithium through electrolysis of lithium chloride. This advancement eventually led to commercial production beginning in 1923 when the German company Metallgesellschaft AG implemented electrolysis of a liquid mixture of lithium chloride and potassium chloride. The element's industrial applications expanded significantly during World War II, when high-temperature lithium greases became essential for aircraft engines and similar applications. Demand increased dramatically during the Cold War due to lithium's role in nuclear fusion weapons production, as both lithium-6 and lithium-7 isotopes produce tritium when irradiated by neutrons. This made lithium valuable for tritium production and as a solid fusion fuel component in hydrogen bombs in the form of lithium deuteride. The United States became the primary lithium producer from the late 1950s through the mid-1980s.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: Applications in glass manufacturing and aluminum oxide processing dominated the lithium market until the mid-1990s. The development of lithium-ion batteries subsequently transformed demand, becoming the dominant use by 2007 and driving expansion of brine isolation operations to meet rising consumption.

chunks.title: Lithium
chunks.text: Australian psychiatrist John Cade is credited with reintroducing and popularizing lithium as a treatment for mania in 1949. Following Cade's work, lithium's mood-stabilizing properties for both manic and depressive episodes gained recognition throughout the mid-twentieth century, leading to widespread adoption in psychiatric practice across Europe and the United States.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.text: Loprazolam is an imidazobenzodiazepine with hypnotic, sedative, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties. Patented in 1975 and introduced into medical use in 1983, it is primarily prescribed for the short-term management of moderately-severe insomnia. As with other benzodiazepines, loprazolam carries significant risks of tolerance, physical dependence, and withdrawal with prolonged use. Elderly individuals are particularly susceptible to its effects, including impaired balance and increased fall risk.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, though risk is low if used for less than 4 weeks or very occasionally. Between 30% and 90% of long-term users experience withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation. Withdrawal symptoms tend to last between 3 weeks to 3 months, with 10-15% experiencing protracted withdrawal persisting for many months or occasionally several years.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming with risk of psychological dependence developing with regular use. Abnormal, often severe drug-seeking behavior has been reported following abrupt withdrawal from long-term use.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.text: Psychosis, confusion, and visual and auditory hallucinations with delusions can occur as major complications following abrupt or rapid withdrawal, especially from high doses. Paradoxical increase in aggression may also occur during use.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.text: Epileptic seizures, which may be fatal, can occur as a major complication after abrupt or rapid withdrawal, especially from high doses. Gradual dose reduction greatly minimizes this risk.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Regular use can cause cognitive and psychomotor impairments including drowsiness, confusion, amnesia, ataxia, and impaired balance that may persist into the next day; higher doses may impair long-term memory functions.

chunks.title: Loprazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Effects are more pronounced in the elderly, with significant impairment of standing reported up to 11 hours after a 1mg dose. Partial but incomplete tolerance develops to these impairments.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam is a short-acting depressant of the benzodiazepine class. First marketed by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals in the United States in 1977, it is prescribed for the short-term treatment of anxiety, insomnia, acute seizures, and sedation of hospitalized patients. It is characterized by its relatively rapid clearance compared to many other benzodiazepines. Like all benzodiazepines, lorazepam carries a significant risk of physical dependence and habit formation with repeated use.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops rapidly, with withdrawal symptoms possible after as little as one week of therapeutic use. Discontinuation can be life-threatening without proper medical tapering, with serious risk of seizures, hypertension, and death. As a potent short-acting benzodiazepine, lorazepam carries the highest risk of dependence within its class.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam is described as extremely psychologically addictive with a very high dependence potential. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, and the risk of abuse is increased in individuals with pre-existing substance dependence or psychiatric disorders.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Psychosis is rare during therapeutic or recreational use but can occur as a withdrawal symptom following abrupt discontinuation after chronic use. Paradoxical reactions including hallucinations and delirium occur in less than 1% of the general population but are more common in recreational abusers, individuals with psychiatric disorders, children, and those on high-dose regimens.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam has anticonvulsant properties and suppresses seizures during active use. However, abrupt withdrawal after regular use poses a significant seizure risk that can be life-threatening. Paradoxical worsening of seizures may rarely occur, particularly in individuals with epilepsy. Gradual tapering under medical supervision is essential to prevent withdrawal seizures.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: No evidence of carcinogenicity or mutagenicity has been found in available studies.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use may cause cognitive deficits, particularly affecting memory and new memory formation; these effects may persist for at least six months after discontinuation and may only be partially reversible, especially in elderly users.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Lorazepam appears to have more profound adverse effects on memory than other benzodiazepines, impairing both explicit and implicit memory. Cognitive impairments are more pronounced in the elderly. Partial tolerance to memory effects develops with regular use.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam is a high-potency benzodiazepine that acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. By binding to post-synaptic GABA-A ligand-gated chloride channels throughout the central nervous system, it increases the frequency of chloride ion channel opening in the presence of GABA, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission through cellular hyperpolarization. Lorazepam is reported to have a relatively high affinity for the GABA-A benzodiazepine site compared to other benzodiazepines. Its anticonvulsant properties may additionally involve binding to voltage-dependent sodium channels.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam is readily absorbed orally with an absolute bioavailability of approximately 90%, and is completely and rapidly absorbed when administered intramuscularly. It is hepatically metabolized primarily through direct glucuronidation to the inactive metabolite lorazepam-glucuronide, with CYP450 isoenzymes also reported to be involved. The glucuronide metabolite is eliminated by the kidneys, and lorazepam has no active metabolites. The elimination half-life is approximately 8 hours following oral administration, 11 hours for sublingual dosing, and 14 hours when given parenterally.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Lorazepam was initially patented in 1963 and is considered one of the "classical" benzodiazepines alongside diazepam, clonazepam, oxazepam, nitrazepam, flurazepam, bromazepam, and clorazepate. The compound was developed by D.J. Richards, who served as president of research at Wyeth Pharmaceuticals. The drug was introduced to the United States market in 1977 under the brand names Ativan and Temesta, with subsequent marketing under additional trade names in other regions. Wyeth's original patent on the compound has since expired. Lorazepam has achieved significant standing in modern pharmacology, being included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. The compound is now available as a generic medication in many countries. As of 2023, it ranked as the 100th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over six million prescriptions written annually.

chunks.title: Lorazepam
chunks.text: Non-medical use of lorazepam has been documented as a notable public health concern. A 2006 nationwide study by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration examining pharmaceutical-related emergency department visits found that sedative-hypnotics represent the pharmaceutical category most frequently used outside of prescribed medical purposes in the United States, accounting for 35% of drug-related emergency department visits. Within this category, benzodiazepines constitute the most commonly encountered class, with lorazepam specifically ranking as the third-most-common benzodiazepine involved in non-prescription emergency department presentations.

chunks.title: Lormetazepam
chunks.text: Lormetazepam is a short to intermediate-acting benzodiazepine of the 1,4-benzodiazepine class, structurally related to temazepam. Patented in 1961 and introduced for medical use in 1980, it is primarily prescribed for short-term treatment of insomnia in parts of Europe but is not approved in the United States or Canada. It produces sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic, and muscle relaxant effects. As with all benzodiazepines, it carries significant risks of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal.

chunks.title: Lormetazepam
chunks.text: Lormetazepam can cause physical dependence, with benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms emerging after dose reduction or discontinuation. This dependence is associated with altered GABA-BZD receptor-complex sensitivity. Withdrawal often resolves within 4-8 weeks, but about 10-15% of people may have symptoms for months, and rarely for years.

chunks.title: Lormetazepam
chunks.text: Psychological dependence may appear as craving or as feeling unable to manage daily life without the medication. People with prior sedative-hypnotic addiction may face greater risk.

chunks.title: Lormetazepam

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text: LSA is a naturally occurring psychedelic alkaloid of the lysergamide family, found primarily in morning glory and Hawaiian baby woodrose seeds. Structurally related to LSD, it was first assayed for human activity by Albert Hofmann in 1947. Its traditional use by indigenous Mexican peoples dates back to Aztec times, as documented by Richard Schultes in 1941. LSA is reported to produce mental effects resembling LSD, though with notably diminished visual activity.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text: LSA is non-habit-forming and the desire to use it typically decreases with use. It is most often self-regulating.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Vasoconstriction can cause reduced blood flow to muscles, particularly noticeable as soreness in the legs; these effects may build up with repeated use over short periods.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Sore legs indicate vasoconstriction effects are accumulating. Effects may take up to 3 days of abstinence to return to baseline. Seeds from commercial sources are sometimes coated with pesticides or methylmercury, which can cause additional nausea and toxicity unrelated to LSA itself.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text: With repeated use over short periods, it can take up to 3 days of abstinence for the body to return to baseline. The psychoactive effects weaken with frequent use while vasoconstriction effects accumulate.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text: Tolerance develops almost immediately after ingestion, preventing the full effects from being experienced more frequently than every 4-7 days without significantly increasing the dose.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text:
The use of LSA-containing morning glory seeds by indigenous peoples of Mexico and Latin America dates back to pre-Columbian times. Seeds from Ipomoea corymbosa (known as ololiuhqui) and Ipomoea tricolor (tlitliltzin) were employed in shamanic rituals across the region for centuries.

The first formal ethnobotanical documentation of this practice came from Richard Schultes in 1941, who described the traditional use of morning glory seeds by Mexican Native Americans going back to the Aztec period. In 1960, Don Thomes MacDougall expanded on this research, reporting that certain Zapotec communities consumed the seeds as sacraments, sometimes alongside Rivea corymbosa, another morning glory species containing similar lysergamide alkaloids.

Notably, Argyreia nervosa (Hawaiian baby woodrose), despite being a potent source of LSA, was not traditionally employed for entheogenic purposes in its native India. The psychoactive properties of this plant were first brought to wider attention in the 1960s.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text:
LSA was first tested for psychoactive effects in humans by Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann in 1947—notably before the compound was known to occur naturally in plants. In self-experiments using intramuscular administration of a 500 microgram dose, Hofmann reported experiencing a drowsy, dream-like condition with difficulty maintaining focused thought. After a brief period of sleep, the effects resolved completely within approximately five hours.

These early observations have contributed to ongoing questions about whether LSA alone accounts for the full psychoactive profile of morning glory seeds and Hawaiian baby woodrose. Anecdotal reports suggest that the effects of pure synthetic LSA differ somewhat from experiences produced by consuming these plant materials, which contain multiple lysergamide alkaloids rather than a single active compound.

chunks.title: LSA
chunks.text:
While Argyreia nervosa was not traditionally used as a psychoactive substance, the root of the plant has an established place in Ayurvedic medicine. It is regarded as a tonic for the nervous system and brain, traditionally taken as a rejuvenating preparation and aphrodisiac believed to enhance cognitive function.

Other documented traditional applications include treatments for conditions such as chronic ulcers, diabetes, anemia, urinary difficulties, and various cerebral disorders. The plant has also been used as an appetizer, cardiotonic, and general restorative, with traditional attributions of anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and antimicrobial properties.
