chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD is a semisynthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class, first synthesized by Albert Hofmann in 1938 from ergot alkaloids, with its psychoactive properties discovered in 1943. It is perhaps the most widely researched and culturally influential psychedelic substance, having played a central role in the 1960s counterculture movement. LSD is among the most potent psychoactive compounds known, producing effects at microgram doses. It is non-addictive with extremely low toxicity relative to dose.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD does not produce physical dependence. No withdrawal syndrome has been reported following discontinuation of use, even after repeated administration. A DSM-IV review noted that almost no hallucinogens produced dependence unlike other psychoactive drug classes.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD is widely considered non-addictive and the desire to use it can actually decrease with continued use, making it largely self-regulating. Attempts to train laboratory animals to self-administer LSD have been largely unsuccessful. While a small number of individuals have reported developing a problematic relationship with LSD or taking it daily for extended periods, psychological dependence is rare.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD can precipitate psychotic symptoms in individuals predisposed to psychosis or with pre-existing psychiatric conditions, though this appears to be quite rare. A Medline search in 2003 found only three case reports of LSD-induced psychosis in the previous 20 years. LSD does not appear to produce psychiatric illness de novo in otherwise emotionally healthy individuals. People whose relatives have schizophrenia or early-onset mental illness face heightened risk.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Seizures are very rare but can occur in individuals who are predisposed to them, particularly under physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, inadequate nutrition, overheating, or fatigue.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: No evidence of carcinogenicity or mutagenicity. Earlier rumors about chromosome damage from LSD use during pregnancy have been disproven by further research.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: A theoretical risk of cardiac fibrosis and valvulopathy from 5-HT2B receptor agonism has been proposed for long-term or chronic use, but preliminary animal studies found no heart structure changes or valvulopathy from chronic microdosing, and research is mixed on whether LSD is a potent 5-HT2B agonist at all.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Proposed mechanism involves serotonin 5-HT2B receptor agonism causing fibroblast proliferation in cardiac valve tissue

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risks are considered theoretical and require more research. Acute effects include transient increases in blood pressure and heart rate due to vasoconstriction. Expert review states hallucinogens do not cause life-threatening changes in cardiovascular function because they have little affinity for receptors mediating vital vegetative functions.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare cases of dangerous hyperthermia have been reported in the medical literature, typically at higher doses; one documented non-fatal case involved body temperature exceeding 106°F (41°C).

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Temperature dysregulation may relate to serotonergic effects on thermoregulatory centers

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Users should exercise caution in conditions of extreme heat or cold. This adverse effect appears to be uncommon.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Expert review indicates no evidence that LSD causes damage to any human organ at reasonable doses in careful contexts, with no negative cognitive, psychiatric, or toxic physical consequences documented from acute exposure.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Hallucinogens have little or no affinity for biological receptors and targets that mediate vital vegetative functions

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Senior LSD researcher Dr. David Nichols states that hallucinogens do not produce life-threatening effects on cardiovascular, kidney, or liver function. Earlier claims about chromosome damage have been disproven by subsequent research.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD primarily acts as a partial agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, which is understood to be the principal mechanism responsible for its psychedelic effects, though the precise nature of this relationship remains incompletely characterized. It displays high affinity at the 5-HT2A site relative to other psychedelics and is broadly non-selective across serotonin receptor subtypes, with agonist activity spanning the 5-HT1, 5-HT2, 5-HT5, 5-HT6, and 5-HT7 receptor families. LSD also acts as an agonist at all five dopamine receptor subtypes (D1 through D5) and has been found to bind to adrenoreceptor subtypes.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD is rapidly absorbed and undergoes hepatic metabolism via CYP450 isoenzymes. Its elimination half-life is approximately 3 hours, and the primary metabolite produced is 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-LSD.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Under typical use patterns, tolerance fully reverses after about 5 days without additional use. Anecdotal accounts describe possible weeks- to months-long tolerance after exceptionally large doses, although this has not been well documented in clinical literature.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: All psychedelics (via 5-HT2A receptor downregulation)

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Tolerance develops almost immediately after ingestion, forming in as little as three hours. Near-maximum tolerance levels are reached after 3-4 days of daily administration.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: LSD was first synthesized on November 16, 1938, by Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann while working at Sandoz Laboratories in Basel, Switzerland. The compound emerged from a research program investigating potentially useful derivatives of ergot, a fungus that grows on rye and other grains. LSD was the twenty-fifth lysergamide derivative Hofmann synthesized from lysergic acid, which explains the designation LSD-25 (from the German "Lysergsäure-diethylamid").

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: The psychoactive properties of LSD remained unknown for five years until April 16, 1943, when Hofmann unintentionally ingested an unknown quantity of the substance, possibly through skin absorption. Three days later, on April 19, 1943, Hofmann conducted the first intentional self-experiment, ingesting 250 micrograms in the belief that this would produce only a threshold effect based on the typical potency of other ergot alkaloids. The effects proved far more potent than anticipated. After experiencing the onset of powerful alterations in consciousness, Hofmann rode his bicycle home—an event now commemorated annually as "Bicycle Day" among psychedelic enthusiasts. He later described experiencing unprecedented colors and kaleidoscopic, fantastic images that surged behind his closed eyes, alternating and rearranging themselves in constant flux.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: In 1947, Sandoz introduced LSD to the medical community under the trade name Delysid, marketing it as an experimental tool for psychiatric applications. Two primary therapeutic models emerged: the "model-psychosis" approach, which used LSD to induce temporary psychotic-like states in healthy individuals for research purposes, and psycholytic or psychedelic therapy, which employed the substance to enhance psychotherapeutic treatments. The compound generated extraordinary interest within psychiatry during the 1950s and early 1960s. Within fifteen years of its introduction, research on LSD and related hallucinogens produced over 1,000 scientific papers, and the substance was prescribed to more than 40,000 patients. Psychiatrist Humphry Osmond pioneered applications for treating alcoholism with promising results, and the substance was reportedly tried in every type of mental disorder by 1960. Osmond also coined the term "psychedelic" (meaning "mind manifesting") to describe LSD and similar compounds, replacing the earlier "psychotomimetic" model which theorized the substance mimicked schizophrenia.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: The Sandoz patents on LSD expired in 1963, at which point the Czech company Spofa began production. Sandoz ceased production and distribution in 1965.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text:
During the 1950s, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency initiated a research program code-named Project MKUltra to investigate LSD's potential applications in mind control and chemical warfare. The CIA reportedly bought the entire global supply of LSD for $240,000 and distributed it through front organizations to American hospitals, clinics, prisons, and research centers.

As part of these experiments, LSD was given to groups that included CIA staff, members of the military, physicians, sex workers, psychiatric patients, and ordinary members of the public, often without their knowledge or consent. The most well-known example, Operation Midnight Climax, covertly dosed unwitting individuals so their reactions could be observed. These experiments resulted in at least one death. The U.S. Army Chemical Corps also evaluated LSD as a potential non-lethal incapacitant in the Edgewood Arsenal human experiments.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: By the mid-1960s, LSD occupied a central place in youth counterculture, especially in San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury neighborhood and in London. Several well-known intellectuals, including Aldous Huxley, Timothy Leary, Al Hubbard, and Alan Watts, promoted broad LSD use and strongly shaped the outlook of a new generation. In 1966, Timothy Leary founded the League for Spiritual Discovery, naming LSD as its sacrament. Owsley Stanley established the first major underground LSD production operation. During the same period, the Merry Pranksters, a group linked with novelist Ken Kesey, staged the Acid Tests, where LSD use was paired with light shows and improvised music. Their cross-country travels aboard a psychedelic-painted bus, as well as their meetings with leading figures from the Beat movement, were later chronicled in Tom Wolfe's "The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test" (1968). In January 1966, brothers Ron and Jay Thelin opened the Psychedelic Shop in Haight-Ashbury to encourage safer LSD use, helping make the neighborhood a center of hippie culture. In October 1966, they organized the Love Pageant Rally in Golden Gate Park to oppose California's approaching ban on the substance.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: A parallel movement emerged in London under British academic Michael Hollingshead, who first took LSD in America in 1961. After contact with Huxley, Leary, and Richard Alpert, Hollingshead returned to the United Kingdom in 1965 and created the World Psychedelic Center in Chelsea, London.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text:
On October 24, 1968, LSD possession became illegal in the United States. The counterculture's adoption of the substance had triggered broad controversy and backlash in American society, prompting aggressive measures under the Nixon administration's war on drugs. Research was abruptly halted, and psychedelic study moved underground.

The last FDA-approved study of LSD in patients ended in 1980, though healthy-volunteer research took place during the late 1980s. In Switzerland, legally approved and regulated psychiatric use of LSD remained available until 1993. The substance was placed under Schedule I of the 1971 United Nations Convention on Psychotropic Substances, establishing international prohibition.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Following decades of institutional suppression, scientific research involving LSD has undergone a significant revival as part of the broader "psychedelic renaissance." The substance is currently being investigated for treatment applications including alcoholism, substance addiction, cluster headache, autism, and anxiety associated with terminal illness. In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration designated a form of LSD (MM120) as a breakthrough therapy for generalized anxiety disorder, marking a significant shift in regulatory attitudes toward the substance.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: The influence of LSD on art and music became pronounced during the 1960s. San Francisco-based visual artists such as Rick Griffin, Victor Moscoso, and Wes Wilson contributed psychedelic poster and album art to the movement. A distinct visual art style emerged, inspired by the perceptual effects and hallucinatory experiences associated with the substance. Blotter art developed as a unique art form following LSD's prohibition, with decorative graphics printed on perforated sheets of absorbent paper infused with liquid LSD. This practice originated in the early 1970s, sometimes serving to identify the dose, maker, or batch. More than 350 blotter paper designs have been documented since 1975, and entire collections have been exhibited in galleries and museums.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Musically, LSD profoundly shaped the development of psychedelic rock through the Acid Tests and performances by bands like the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, and Big Brother and the Holding Company. The Grateful Dead became central to a culture of devoted followers known as "Deadheads," with their music heavily influenced by the substance. Psychedelic music of the era sought to replicate the LSD experience through exotic instrumentation, electric guitars with effects pedals, and elaborate studio techniques including sitars, tablas, backward tapes, panning, and phasing. In the United Kingdom, Michael Hollingshead introduced LSD to various artists and musicians including Storm Thorgerson, Donovan, Keith Richards, and members of the Beatles. Despite the substance's illegal status from 1966, it was widely used by groups including the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and the Moody Blues, influencing works such as "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" and Cream's "Disraeli Gears."

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Swiss chemist who first synthesized LSD in 1938 and discovered its psychoactive properties in 1943. His memoir "LSD, My Problem Child" documents both the scientific history and his personal experiences with the substance. He maintained connections with other notable psychedelic figures throughout his life, taking LSD on multiple occasions with German writer Ernst Jünger.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: British author of "Brave New World" who became a prominent advocate for psychedelic use after moving to Hollywood. His 1954 work "The Doors of Perception" documented his experiences with mescaline and placed him at the forefront of the counterculture's embrace of psychedelics. Dying from cancer on November 22, 1963, Huxley asked his wife to inject him with 100 micrograms of LSD, passing away later that day.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Harvard psychologist who became perhaps the most prominent and controversial advocate for LSD consumption. Along with Aldous Huxley, Al Hubbard, and Alan Watts, he advocated for mass consumption of psychedelics and profoundly influenced the counterculture generation. In 1966, he established the League for Spiritual Discovery with LSD as its sacrament.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: German writer and philosopher who experimented with various substances throughout his life, including ether, cocaine, hashish, mescaline, and LSD. He documented these experiences comprehensively in "Annäherungen" (1970, Approaches), and his novel "Besuch auf Godenholm" (1952) shows clear influence from early psychedelic experiments. Jünger met with Albert Hofmann and took LSD with him on several occasions. He is credited with coining the term "psychonaut."

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: Co-founder and former CEO of Apple Inc., who publicly discussed his experiences with psychedelics. He stated that "taking LSD was a profound experience, one of the most important things in my life."

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: American biochemist who reportedly credited LSD with helping him develop DNA amplification technology (the polymerase chain reaction), for which he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993.

chunks.title: LSD
chunks.text: French philosopher who experienced LSD with Simeon Wade in Death Valley. He later described it as "the greatest experience of his life" and one that "profoundly changed his life and his work." According to Wade, upon returning to Paris, Foucault discarded his manuscript for the second volume of "The History of Sexuality" and completely reconceived the entire project.

chunks.title: LSM-775
chunks.text: LSM-775 is a synthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class, first described by Albert Hofmann and colleagues in 1955. Structurally related to LSD, it features a morpholine group in place of LSD's diethylamine. It possesses roughly one-tenth the potency of LSD and is distinguished by its notably sedating, dream-like quality, often drawing comparisons to LSA. Nausea is a common and sometimes pronounced adverse effect. Very little data exists regarding its toxicity or long-term health effects.

chunks.title: LSM-775
chunks.text: LSM-775 is not expected to be habit-forming, and repeated administration may reduce the urge to take it again. Like many psychedelics, it likely has an inherent self-limiting pattern of use.

chunks.title: LSM-775
chunks.text: As with other psychedelics, there is potential for adverse psychological reactions including anxiety, paranoia, and panic attacks, though anxiety may be less common than with other psychedelics. Psychosis risk may be elevated in susceptible individuals or when combined with other substances.

chunks.title: LSM-775
chunks.text: Seizure risk is inferred from LSD-associated reports. The main concern appears to be for people with genetic susceptibility, especially when stressors such as dehydration, fatigue, or undernourishment are present.

chunks.title: LSM-775

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: LSZ is a semi-synthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class developed in the 2000s by a team led by David E. Nichols at Purdue University as a rigid analog of LSD, with its diethylamide group constrained into an azetidine ring. Like LSD, it is extremely potent and active in the microgram range. It appeared on research chemical markets around 2012 and is commonly described as producing LSD-like effects with a somewhat more introspective character.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: LSZ is not considered physiologically addictive. No physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms have been documented.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: LSZ is not considered habit-forming and the desire to use it may actually decrease with repeated use. It is typically self-regulating in nature.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: Adverse psychological reactions including severe anxiety, paranoia, and psychosis are possible, particularly in individuals predisposed to mental illness. As a psychological amplifier, LSZ can intensify existing mental states and may produce paranoia or distressing experiences such as feelings of dying.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: Not studied for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: LSZ acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist with particularly high affinity for the 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, and 5-HT2C receptors. Its psychedelic effects are believed to stem primarily from partial agonist activity at the 5-HT2A receptor, where its potency and efficacy are reported to be comparable to LSD. It also demonstrates potent 5-HT2C agonism and may exceed LSD's potency at the 5-HT1A receptor. LSZ additionally binds to dopamine receptors, though specific subtypes have not been characterized. The typically employed form is the (S,S)-diastereomer (LA-SS-Az), which is the most potent of its three possible diastereomers. Anti-inflammatory effects have also been identified in preclinical research.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: Tolerance to the effects of LSZ develops almost immediately after ingestion.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: The development of LSZ traces back to efforts by David E. Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University to create conformationally restricted analogues of LSD for use as pharmacological research tools. The goal was to better understand how LSD orients itself when binding to the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor and to map the receptor's topography more precisely. Initial attempts in the 1980s by Nichols and Robert Oberlender utilized LA-Aziridine, a closely related compound, but this proved to be highly chemically unstable, precluding in-vivo studies. The team eventually succeeded with LSZ, a rigid analogue in which LSD's N,N-diethylamide group has been constrained into a 2,4-dimethylazetidine ring structure. This modification introduces two additional chiral centers, resulting in three possible diastereomers.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text: The compound was first described in the scientific literature in 2002. Research determined that the (S,S)- isomer, designated LA-SS-Az, demonstrated the greatest potency for 5-HT2A receptor activation and psychedelic-like effects in animal models. Later crystallographic studies revealed that LSD's conformation within the closely related 5-HT2B receptor is essentially superimposable with the structure of LA-SS-Az. LSZ remains one of the only known LSD analogues with modifications at the amide position that retains similar or greater psychedelic potency.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text:
According to accounts from Krystle Cole in an interview with journalist Hamilton Morris, the clandestine LSD manufacturers William Leonard Pickard and Gordon Todd Skinner reportedly synthesized and experimented with a psychedelic they referred to as "diazedine" around the year 2000. Cole described the compound as "crazy, but nothing earth-shattering." The pair reportedly had ambitions to produce and distribute the substance as an alternative to LSD but encountered difficulties scaling the synthesis due to high production costs and low yields.

Notably, Pickard had been a student of Nichols at Purdue University and was aware of the LSZ research prior to its publication. Morris has speculated that "diazedine"—a name that appears to be a contraction of "dimethylazetidine"—is very likely the same compound as LSZ, though this has never been officially confirmed. Persistent rumors also suggest that LSZ may have been distributed on blotter paper under the name "λ" (lambda) during this period, though this similarly remains unverified.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text:
LSZ had little documented history of human use prior to 2012, when it began appearing on research chemical markets in the United Kingdom. The compound gained wider international availability through a cluster of mail-order vendors specializing in novel psychedelics that emerged during this period.

The substance was first definitively identified as a novel designer drug in Europe in December 2013. It is known to have been manufactured and distributed by Lizard Labs, a now-defunct company that specialized in lysergamide production through the 2010s and into the 2020s. Following its initial emergence, LSZ developed a reputation as a popular alternative to LSD and other lysergamides within the psychedelic research chemical community.

chunks.title: LSZ

- Amphetamines (Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences)
- Cannabis (Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.)
- Cocaine (Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences)
- Diphenhydramine (At 25-50mg, DPH may assist with side effects of the LSD such as nausea and anxiety. At higher dosages, the combination of a deliriant (DPH) and LSD is cautioned against. LSD is likely to increase the deliriant and negative effects of DPH, in addition to increasing the risk of severe injury and mental trauma. LSD and DPH at recreational dosages have additional cardiac concerns such as vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, which in combination may be exacerbated.)
- Mephedrone (The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops, in addition to the possible negative side effects of coming down from said stimulant while on a psychedelic.

chunks.title: LSZ
chunks.text:
In extreme cases, stimulants, especially in combination can result in severe vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, and heart failure.)
- Pregabalin (Caution should be given due to LSD’s stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of LSD. Additionally, Pregabalin may increase LSD’s inhibition and risk of injury.)

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop during chronic therapy. A withdrawal syndrome was reported after abrupt discontinuation in subjects receiving 210 mg per day for 12 to 16 consecutive days. Withdrawal symptoms include irritability, insomnia, restlessness, hot flashes, sweating, rhinorrhea, loose stools, hiccoughs, and anorexia, typically resolving over 48-96 hours. Disturbed sleep may persist for several weeks after discontinuing high-dose therapy.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.text: Classified as having low potential for abuse, with no indication of script-chasing or doctor-shopping detected among prescribed patients. However, patients with a history of substance abuse or dependence may be more likely to abuse dronabinol.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.text: Psychiatric adverse reactions may include psychosis, hallucinations, depersonalization, mood changes, and paranoia. High doses, abuse, or misuse increase risk. Panic reactions may be more likely in patients with a history of anxiety or nervousness.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.text: Patients who already have seizure disorders may experience seizures, especially during overdose.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Administration during pregnancy may cause fetal harm, including decreased maternal weight gain, reduced viable pups, increased fetal mortality, and early resorptions at doses inducing maternal toxicity in animal studies.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Adverse developmental and neurodevelopmental effects observed in pups at 2 to 20 times the maximum recommended human dose for AIDS patients. Breastfeeding is contraindicated due to potential for serious adverse reactions in infants.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Reversible effects on cognition, memory, and perception occur during use; pediatric patients may be more sensitive to neurological and psychoactive effects.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: These effects seem dose dependent, occur more often at higher doses, and vary substantially between patients. Older adults may also be more sensitive to neuropsychiatric effects.

chunks.title: Marinol

chunks.text: Sympathomimetic activity may result in tachycardia and conjunctival injection during use; orthostatic hypotension and syncope upon abrupt standing have been reported.

chunks.title: Marinol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Effects on blood pressure are inconsistent. Elderly patients may be more sensitive to postural hypotensive effects and are at increased risk for falls.

chunks.title: MBDB
chunks.text: MBDB is a synthetic entactogen of the substituted amphetamine and phenethylamine classes, structurally related to MDMA. First described in 1986 by a team including David E. Nichols and Alexander Shulgin, it was developed as a non-psychedelic entactogen. MBDB produces prosocial and empathogenic effects similar to MDMA but with notably reduced euphoria, stimulation, and psychedelia. It is sometimes characterized as a 'watered down' version of MDMA due to its comparatively subtle effect profile.

chunks.title: MBDB
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, though the abuse liability has been assessed as not constituting a significant risk to public health. The stimulant and euphoriant effects are less pronounced than MDMA, which may reduce compulsive redosing potential.

chunks.title: MBDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MBDB is a serotonergic neurotoxin, but at behaviorally comparable doses it seems less serotonergically neurotoxic than MDMA; in mice, unlike MDMA, it does not cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity.

chunks.title: MBDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxicity, though the specific pathway is not fully characterized in available data

chunks.title: MBDB
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Human reports have not documented adverse or toxic effects from MBDB.

chunks.title: Mbzp
chunks.text: MBZP is a stimulant of the piperazine class, specifically a derivative of benzylpiperazine (BZP). It has been sold as an ingredient in legal recreational products marketed as "party pills," initially in New Zealand and subsequently in other countries. Its effects are reported to be similar to those of BZP, though with a somewhat milder stimulant profile and a reduced tendency to produce side effects such as headaches and nausea.

chunks.title: Mbzp
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting some potential for psychological dependence with repeated use.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.text: mCPP is a stimulant substance of the phenylpiperazine class. It was first synthesized by Thomas H. Wicker Jr. in 1951 during doctoral research into potential antihistamines at the University of Florida. Unlike many other stimulants, mCPP is widely regarded as unpleasant, being notably associated with anxiety, migraines, and dysphoria. It is also an active metabolite of the antidepressant trazodone and is occasionally encountered as an adulterant in street MDMA.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.text: mCPP is not known to be addictive, though its addiction potential has not been formally studied. At common and high doses, it is generally regarded as aversive and dysphoria-producing, which likely limits compulsive redosing behavior.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular strain may occur during use, particularly at higher doses or when combined with other stimulants; the forced stimulation profile can increase heart rate and blood pressure.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk increases significantly with concurrent use of other stimulants.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: mCPP is notable for inducing anxiety, migraines, and severe headaches, likely mediated through 5-HT2C receptor activity; these effects appear to be intrinsic to the substance rather than limited to excessive doses.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Negative effects such as anxiety, headaches, and appetite loss are likely mediated by actions on the 5-HT2C receptor.

chunks.title: mCPP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Unlike many stimulants, mCPP is generally considered unpleasant even at typical doses.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA is a synthetic entactogen of the amphetamine class that produces stimulant and mild psychedelic effects alongside its empathogenic properties. First synthesized in 1910, its psychoactive effects were not recognized until 1930, and it emerged as a recreational substance in the late 1960s — predating the popularization of its close relative MDMA. Compared to MDMA, MDA is generally considered more stimulating with a stronger psychedelic edge. It is sometimes found in pills sold as MDMA, and vice versa.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA is generally not considered physically addictive, though cravings and withdrawal effects may occur if chronic users suddenly stop usage.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA can be considered moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence among certain users. Compulsive redosing may occur due to its euphoria-inducing effects, with a strong desire to repeat the experience commonly reported when coming down.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Psychological crisis requiring hospitalization, including psychotic episodes and severe panic attacks, is possible but rare. Regular use may lead to schizophrenia-like symptoms. Derealization can occur temporarily after a strong experience and may persist in cases of misuse.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Seizures are a rare effect but can occur in people predisposed to them, especially when taking heavier-than-recommended doses or while in physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, fatigue, or undernourishment. Convulsions are listed among symptoms of acute toxicity and overdose.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MDA is known to be more neurotoxic than MDMA, with estimates suggesting it may be approximately five times as neurotoxic; this is a primary safety concern with frequent use, high doses, or elevated body temperature during use.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxic effects occur in rodents, possibly related to MDA metabolism. Higher dopaminergic activity compared to MDMA is believed to contribute to the greater degree of neurotoxicity. MDA depletes serotonin and activates a neuroglia response.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Risk can be minimized by limiting use frequency, taking common doses, keeping body temperature low, and appropriate supplementation. The neuroglia response subsides after use.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MDA is reported to be hepatotoxic, though liver toxicity from use is considered rare.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute toxicity and overdose can cause dangerous cardiovascular strain including dramatically increased blood pressure and heart rate; death in overdose cases is usually caused by cardiac effects and subsequent hemorrhaging in the brain.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: MDA produces sympathomimetic effects and increases cortisol and prolactin levels. Typical dose ranges produce moderate increases in heart rate and blood pressure.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA acts primarily as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent (SNDRA), functioning as a substrate of the serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, and vesicular monoamine transporters. It is also an agonist of the serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, and 5-HT2C receptors, with direct 5-HT2A agonism underlying its psychedelic properties. MDA shows affinity for the α2A-, α2B-, and α2C-adrenergic receptors and the 5-HT1A and 5-HT7 serotonin receptors. At TAAR1, MDA is a potent agonist in rodent models but only a very weak partial agonist or antagonist at the human receptor. The enantiomers differ pharmacologically: (S)-MDA shows greater potency at the monoamine transporters, while (R)-MDA fully substitutes for serotonergic psychedelics in drug discrimination assays.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA has an elimination half-life of approximately 10.9 hours.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Partial agonist; higher efficacy than MDMA

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Potent high-efficacy agonist in rodent models; very weak partial agonist or antagonist at human receptor

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Tolerance to the psychedelic effects develops almost immediately after ingestion. Tolerance to the stimulant and entactogenic effects builds more gradually with repeated and heavy use, varying between individuals.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text:
MDA was first synthesized by German chemists Carl Mannich and W. Jacobsohn in 1910, though its psychoactive properties remained unknown for two decades. The compound's mind-altering effects were discovered through self-experimentation by American chemist Gordon Alles in July 1930, who administered a total of 126 milligrams to himself and experienced hallucinogenic effects, euphoria, and a sense of well-being alongside peripheral stimulant effects. Notably, Alles did not formally describe these findings in the scientific literature until 1959.

Following his experiments, Alles licensed MDA to the pharmaceutical company Smith, Kline & French. The first systematic animal studies commenced in 1939, with human clinical trials beginning in 1941 to evaluate the compound's potential therapeutic applications for Parkinson's disease. However, these early investigations found that MDA was actually detrimental to individuals with Parkinson's, leading researchers to abandon this avenue of exploration.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text:
Between 1949 and 1957, Smith, Kline & French conducted extensive human trials involving over five hundred subjects to assess MDA's potential as an antidepressant and appetite suppressant. The compound showed some promise in treating psychoneurotic depression and was described as having analeptic (stimulant) properties in humans by 1953.

This research eventually led to several patents: H.D. Brown patented MDA as a cough suppressant in 1958, Smith, Kline & French secured a patent for its use as an ataractic (tranquilizing agent) in 1960, and it was subsequently patented as an appetite suppressant under the trade name "Amphedoxamine" in 1961. In 1986, the World Health Organization recommended "tenamfetamine" as the compound's International Nonproprietary Name, suggesting that pharmaceutical development interest persisted into that decade.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text:
During the early Cold War period, the United States Army conducted experiments with MDA under the code designation EA-1298 as part of broader efforts to develop chemical agents that could function as truth serums or incapacitating weapons. These military and intelligence programs administered relatively unexplored psychoactive compounds to both knowing and unknowing subjects with minimal ethical oversight.

One such experiment proved fatal. In January 1953, a psychiatric patient named Harold Blauer died at the New York State Psychiatric Institute after being intravenously injected with 450 milligrams of MDA without his knowledge or consent. The Army had contracted with physicians at the institute to test new chemicals from Edgewood Arsenal, and Blauer's death occurred during what was reportedly his fifth injection as part of these experiments, which have since been associated with the larger Project MKUltra program.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: Several researchers investigated MDA's potential applications in psychotherapy during the 1960s and 1970s. Chilean psychiatrist Claudio Naranjo extensively documented the compound's therapeutic value, publishing his findings in the book "The Healing Journey." Psychologist Richard Yensen also explored the drug's utility in clinical settings. These researchers found that MDA facilitated emotional openness and introspection in patients, foreshadowing the later interest in MDMA for similar therapeutic purposes.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA began appearing in recreational contexts around 1963 to 1964, making it the first entactogen to achieve widespread non-medical use and predating its more famous derivative MDMA by more than a decade. The compound earned nicknames including the "hug drug" and was sometimes said to stand for "Mellow Drug of America," reflecting its reputation for enhancing empathy and emotional warmth. During this period, MDA was inexpensive and readily obtainable as a research chemical from scientific supply houses, alongside other compounds like mescaline and LSD that were sold under their chemical names. This accessibility contributed to its popularity as the psychedelic movement expanded in the late 1960s. By early 1968, clandestine production had grown significantly enough that the Bureau of Drug Abuse Control reported seizing over 1.4 kilograms of MDA along with 11 kilograms of precursor chemicals from an illegal laboratory in New York.

chunks.title: MDA
chunks.text: MDA experienced a notable resurgence in 1992 when a large batch of pills marketed as "Snowballs" circulated throughout the United Kingdom and Europe. These tablets unexpectedly contained MDA rather than MDMA, and were dosed at approximately 200 milligrams per pill—well into the strong to heavy dose range. This miscalculation resulted in widespread reports of intense and unexpected hallucinogenic experiences among users who had anticipated MDMA's effects, demonstrating MDA's more pronounced psychedelic character at higher doses.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.text: MDAI may be mildly habit-forming, but its abuse potential is generally low and most users are not expected to develop psychological dependence. If dependence does occur, stopping use may be accompanied by cravings and withdrawal effects.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: In the United Kingdom, three deaths in 2011-2012 were associated with MDAI exposure and involved symptoms compatible with serotonin syndrome. Two cases included additional substances, while one appeared to involve only MDAI.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Animal data indicate that MDAI produces far less serotonergic neurotoxicity than MDMA, and it has been characterized as an analogue with minimal neurotoxic effects. Even so, chronic use or combination with amphetamine may still confer a weak neurotoxicity risk.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Weak serotonergic neurotoxicity, potentially enhanced when combined with amphetamines

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: MDAI should not be treated as a completely non-neurotoxic substitute for MDMA. Risk appears higher with repeated long-term use or combinations with other drugs.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MDAI increases blood pressure similarly to MDMA during acute use; notably, it does not appear to increase heart rate or body temperature.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: No formal tests have been performed on cardiovascular toxicity. Blood pressure elevation documented in human studies.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Very high doses can interfere with thermoregulation, which contributed to fatalities in animal studies.

chunks.title: MDAI
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism

chunks.title: MDAI

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.text: MDEA is a substituted amphetamine and entactogen chemically related to MDMA, differing by an ethyl group on its nitrogen. First explored in humans by Alexander Shulgin in 1976, it was briefly introduced as a legal alternative following MDMA's scheduling in 1985. Its effects are comparable to MDMA but generally described as more sedating and "stoning," with a shorter duration. MDEA occasionally appears as an adulterant in ecstasy tablets, and very little data exists regarding its toxicity.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.text: Physical dependence is not prominently characterized, though withdrawal effects including cravings may occur with chronic use.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.text: With ongoing use, MDEA may produce moderate addiction risk, substantial abuse potential, and psychological dependence in some users. After dependence has formed, abrupt cessation can be followed by cravings and withdrawal effects.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.text: Regular use may lead to schizophrenia-like symptoms according to available sources.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.text: Convulsions are listed among overdose symptoms. Risk may be increased when combined with substances that lower seizure threshold.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated or high doses of MDEA are likely to carry neurotoxic risk. As a potent serotonin releaser, it is believed to reduce serotonin reuptake transporter availability in the brain, and the timeline for recovery remains uncertain.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Serotonergic neurotoxicity through down-regulation of serotonin reuptake transporters; animal studies with MDMA demonstrated lasting serotonergic changes which likely apply to MDEA as well.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: How quickly serotonergic alterations resolve in the brain is not well established. Some sources associate regular use with schizophrenia-like symptoms.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy MDEA use over extended periods is likely to harm the cardiovascular system and may contribute to valvulopathy; overdose-level exposure can produce acute tachycardia and hypotension.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Valvulopathy develops through agonist actions on the 5-HT2B receptor.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A study of long-term MDMA users found clinically evident valvular heart disease in 28% of participants who averaged 2-3 doses per week for 6 years; similar pharmacology suggests this concern may extend to MDEA.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MDEA and related compounds are hepatotoxic; regular use may cause liver damage.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hyperthermia is a significant acute risk, particularly with continuous activity without sufficient rest or rehydration; body temperature may rise to dangerous levels.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Because MDEA can be stimulating and euphoric, users may underestimate how much physical effort they are exerting. Alcohol and other diuretics may worsen these risks.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose may cause muscle rigidity and rhabdomyolysis.

chunks.title: MDEA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation are associated with severe overdose.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: MDMA is a classical entactogen of the substituted amphetamine class, first developed in 1912 by the pharmaceutical company Merck. It remained largely obscure until the 1970s, when it gained recognition in underground psychotherapy circles before spreading into nightlife and rave culture. Now one of the most popular recreational drugs worldwide, it is known for producing strong feelings of empathy, emotional closeness, and stimulation. Tablets sold as "ecstasy" frequently contain adulterants or other substances entirely.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Physical dependence potential is low, with MDMA often described as not physically addictive. However, approximately 60% of users experience withdrawal symptoms upon cessation, including fatigue, loss of appetite, depression, and difficulty concentrating. These symptoms are generally mild compared to substances with higher physical dependence potential.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: MDMA has moderate to high abuse potential but a low potential for genuine psychological dependence, estimated at lower than 10% and rated three-fourths to four-fifths that of cannabis by expert panels. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported during experiences, and context-dependent psychological dependence may develop when use is linked to specific activities such as parties or raves.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Psychotic episodes are rare but have been reported, typically at high doses or with heavy use. Possible psychological crises requiring hospitalization, including severe panic attacks and psychotic episodes, occur in a small minority of users. At higher doses, delirious external hallucinations may occur, which is not considered a typical or healthy response.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Seizures are rare but may occur in susceptible individuals, particularly at higher doses, with redosing, or in physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, fatigue, undernourishment, or overheating. More common in smaller individuals and those with pre-existing epilepsy. A small number of users have reportedly experienced seizures after taking moderate amounts of pure MDMA.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy or frequent use, particularly at higher doses, has been associated with neurotoxic damage to serotonergic axon terminals in striatal, hippocampal, prefrontal, and occipital regions; damage may persist for more than two years but appears partially reversible with abstinence. Typical recreational use at moderate doses and infrequent intervals presents less clear neurotoxicity risk.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Formation of toxic MDMA metabolites and induction of simultaneous serotonin and dopamine release, with consequent uptake of dopamine into serotonergic neurons and breakdown into toxic species. Elevated brain temperature positively correlates with neurotoxic effects.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Impairments in attention, learning, memory, visual processing, and sleep have been found in regular users, with magnitude correlated to lifetime usage. Effects are generally small overall and partially reversible. The extent to which typical recreational use causes lasting neurotoxicity remains controversial.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy or long-term use may increase the risk of valvular heart disease and primary pulmonary hypertension due to chronic activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors; acute cardiovascular stress including elevated heart rate and blood pressure occurs during intoxication.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Long-term repeated activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors induces cardiac fibrosis. MDMA also induces cardiac epigenetic changes including DNA hypermethylation.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects are expected during experiences. Risk of valvulopathy is associated with heavy or long-term use patterns rather than occasional use.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Liver toxicity has been reported rarely with MDMA use; the liver is stressed during acute intoxication due to extensive hepatic metabolism.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: MDMA undergoes extensive CYP-mediated hepatic metabolism, primarily via CYP2D6, with CYP3A4 and COMT also contributing. Autoinhibition of CYP2D6 creates nonlinear pharmacokinetics at higher doses.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Hepatotoxicity is considered rare. Individuals with pre-existing hepatic disorders may be at higher risk.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Kidneys are stressed during MDMA use; individuals with pre-existing kidney disorders may be at higher risk of complications.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Renal complications are generally associated with dehydration, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis rather than direct nephrotoxicity.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: 3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine (MDA, active)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: 4-hydroxy-3-methoxymethamphetamine (HMMA)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: 3,4-dihydroxyamphetamine (DHA/α-methyldopamine)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-hydroxyamphetamine (MDOH)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: MDMA functions primarily as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent. The substance enters monoaminergic neurons via the serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine transporters, then reverses their direction to produce efflux of these neurotransmitters into the synapse. This releasing action is facilitated by inhibition of vesicular monoamine transporter 2, which increases cytosolic monoamine concentrations available for release, and by agonist activity at trace amine-associated receptor 1, which triggers phosphorylation of the transporters. MDMA displays approximately tenfold greater affinity for serotonin transporters compared to dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, resulting in predominantly serotonergic effects. Beyond its releasing action, MDMA also exhibits weak partial agonist activity at serotonin 5-HT1 and 5-HT2 receptors, with 5-HT2B receptor signaling appearing necessary for the substance's serotonin-releasing effects. The characteristic entactogenic properties are thought to arise largely from serotonin release and may involve indirect oxytocin secretion mediated by 5-HT1A receptor activation.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: MDMA undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily mediated by CYP2D6, with additional contributions from CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19. The principal metabolic pathway involves O-demethylenation to HHMA followed by COMT-catalyzed methylation to HMMA. A secondary pathway proceeds through N-dealkylation to MDA, which then undergoes further metabolism to HHA and HMA. MDMA acts as both a substrate and inhibitor of CYP2D6, with autoinhibition believed to result from interaction between the enzyme and an MDMA metabolite. This autoinhibition produces nonlinear pharmacokinetics at higher doses, potentially resulting in disproportionately elevated plasma concentrations with repeated or escalating doses.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Autoinhibition of CYP2D6 can prolong elimination at higher doses
The MDA metabolite has a longer half-life of 16-38 hours
Genetic differences in CYP2D6 activity affect individual elimination rates

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Approximately 2.5 months after a single use in the absence of further consumption. A complete drug-free period of 6 days has been shown to reverse tolerance established through consecutive daily dosing. Most harm reduction guidance recommends waiting 1-3 months between uses, with 4-6 weeks considered an absolute minimum to allow adequate serotonin restoration.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Tolerance to MDMA's effects develops unusually quickly compared to many other substances. In controlled observations, daily administration of 120-160 mg resulted in complete loss of subjective effects by the fifth or sixth day, with only mild pupil dilation remaining. A notable phenomenon described as 'losing the magic' occurs with repeated use, where the characteristic empathogenic and prosocial effects diminish substantially while stimulant and euphoric properties may persist. Some users report this degradation after as few as 10 experiences, while others maintain full effects through dozens or even hundreds of uses. The empathogenic qualities appear particularly susceptible to tolerance, often fading before other effects.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Approximately 1 month after a single administration

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: MDMA was first synthesized in 1912 by German chemist Anton Köllisch while working at the pharmaceutical company Merck. Contrary to persistent myths about the compound being developed as an appetite suppressant or psychotherapy aid, it was actually created as an intermediate in the synthesis of methylhydrastinine, a potential hemostatic agent intended to control abnormal bleeding. Merck's interest in this project stemmed from a desire to circumvent an existing patent held by competitor Bayer for a similar compound called hydrastinine. The synthesis was described in German patent 274350, filed on December 24, 1912, though Merck showed no interest in MDMA as an active agent itself. The compound remained largely forgotten until 1927, when Merck chemist Max Oberlin conducted the first pharmacological tests while searching for substances with effects similar to adrenaline or ephedrine. Oberlin noted structural similarities to ephedrine and found that MDMA had comparable effects on blood glucose levels, similar actions on vascular smooth muscle, and stronger effects on uterine tissue. However, research was discontinued due to rising costs of the starting materials needed for synthesis.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: In 1952, Albert van Schoor performed simple toxicological tests at Merck, likely while investigating potential stimulants or circulatory medications. In 1959, Wolfgang Fruhstorfer synthesized MDMA for further pharmacological testing, though it remains unclear whether human effects were investigated. Outside of Merck, the United States Army commissioned toxicological studies between 1953 and 1954 at the University of Michigan, examining behavioral effects in animals injected with mescaline and several analogues including MDMA. This research remained classified until 1969 and was not published until 1973, and may have been conducted with the possibility of developing MDMA as a chemical incapacitant or interrogation aid.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Although MDMA may have been in non-medical use in the western United States as early as 1968, its psychoactive properties did not receive sustained attention until the work of American chemist Alexander Shulgin. According to Shulgin, he synthesized MDMA in 1965 while researching methylenedioxy compounds at Dow Chemical Company, though he did not investigate its psychoactive potential at that time. Around 1970, Shulgin provided synthesis instructions to a Los Angeles chemical company founder, who subsequently passed them to a contact in the Midwest. By August 1970, reports at meetings of crime laboratory chemists indicated MDMA was being used recreationally in the Chicago area. The drug likely emerged as a substitute for MDA, a structurally related compound that had become popular among psychedelic users and was subsequently placed in Schedule I in 1970.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Shulgin first learned of MDMA's psychoactive effects around 1975 from a student who described its "amphetamine-like content." The following year, a graduate student he advised at San Francisco State University described positive emotional experiences after she and two friends had consumed 100 mg of the compound. Following self-experimentation by a colleague, Shulgin synthesized MDMA and tried it himself in September and October 1976. He first reported on the drug at a conference in Bethesda, Maryland in December 1976. In 1978, Shulgin and pharmacologist David E. Nichols published the first scientific report on MDMA's psychoactive effects in humans, describing a controllable change in consciousness with emotional and sensual qualities and comparing it to marijuana, psilocybin without the hallucinatory component, or low levels of MDA.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: While Shulgin did not find his own experiences with MDMA particularly powerful, he was impressed by its capacity to reduce inhibitions and believed it could have therapeutic utility. He conceptualized the drug as allowing users to strip away habitual patterns and perceive the world more clearly, leading him to call it "window." Shulgin occasionally used MDMA for personal relaxation, referring to it as "my low-calorie martini," and introduced the compound to friends, researchers, and others he thought might benefit from it. In 1977, Shulgin introduced MDMA to Leo Zeff, a semi-retired psychotherapist who had previously used psychedelic substances in his practice. Zeff was profoundly impressed and came out of retirement to promote its therapeutic applications. Over the following years, he traveled throughout the United States and occasionally to Europe, eventually training an estimated four thousand psychotherapists in its use. Zeff named the drug "Adam," believing it allowed users to access a state of primordial innocence.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Psychotherapists who employed MDMA reported that it eliminated typical fear responses and enhanced communication. Sessions were typically conducted in the patient's or therapist's home, with the therapist's role minimized in favor of patient self-discovery facilitated by MDMA-induced feelings of empathy and openness. The drug was reportedly used to treat depression, substance use disorders, relationship difficulties, premenstrual syndrome, and autism. Practitioners claimed it dramatically accelerated the therapeutic process. In the western United States, it was used in couples counseling and became known as "empathy" in some therapeutic circles. Therapists and experimenters attempted to limit the spread of information about the drug while conducting informal research, hoping to avoid the criminalization that had befallen LSD and mescaline.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: While therapeutic interest grew among psychotherapists and experimenters, recreational use also began forming in parallel. By the late 1970s, a small scene had emerged and may have consumed about 10,000 doses in 1976. MDMA circulated through personal networks that included therapists, psychiatrists, psychedelic users, and affluent young professionals. Concern that legal restrictions might follow kept early distributors from pursuing large-scale operations. Between the 1970s and the mid-1980s, this relatively contained network is estimated to have consumed 500,000 doses. Into the early 1980s, production was largely controlled by a small Boston-based group of therapeutically minded chemists that had started manufacturing MDMA in 1976. This "Boston Group" often struggled to meet demand, leading to frequent shortages. MDMA also moved into nightlife settings, spreading to Boston and New York City nightclubs such as Studio 54 and Paradise Garage.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Michael Clegg, the Boston Group's Southwest distributor, saw a commercial opportunity and, with financial backing from Texas associates, formed his own "Texas Group." In 1981, Clegg introduced "Ecstasy" as a marketing-friendly street name. Starting in 1983, the Texas Group produced MDMA at scale in a Texas laboratory or brought it in from California, distributing tablets through pyramid-style sales networks and toll-free telephone numbers. The operation accepted credit card payments and paid taxes on sales. The tablets were branded as "Sassyfras" and packaged in brown bottles. The Texas Group promoted "Ecstasy parties" at bars and discotheques, presenting MDMA as a "fun drug" that was "good to dance to." It was distributed openly throughout Austin and the Dallas-Fort Worth area, becoming popular among young professionals, college students, and gay communities.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: After a year of planning and data collection, the Drug Enforcement Administration proposed scheduling MDMA on July 27, 1984. The agency was surprised when numerous psychiatrists, psychotherapists, and researchers filed objections and requested hearings. A DEA pharmacologist later acknowledged the agency had been unaware of MDMA's use in psychiatric practice. Administrative hearings were convened in February, June, July, and October of 1985 in Washington D.C., Los Angeles, and Kansas City. The sensationalist media coverage surrounding the proposed criminalization effectively advertised the drug to a broader public. In response to impending prohibition, the Texas Group dramatically escalated production from an estimated 30,000 tablets monthly to as many as 8,000 per day, potentially manufacturing two million tablets before the ban took effect. By some accounts, the organization was distributing 500,000 tablets per month in Dallas alone. By May 1985, MDMA use had become widespread in California, Texas, southern Florida, and the northeastern United States, with evidence of distribution in twenty-eight states and Canada.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Urged by Senator Lloyd Bentsen, the DEA announced an emergency Schedule I classification on May 31, 1985, citing increased distribution, escalating street use, and new evidence of neurotoxicity from the structurally related compound MDA. The ban took effect one month later on July 1, 1985, coinciding with Nancy Reagan's "Just Say No" campaign.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Based on expert testimony that MDMA possessed accepted medical applications, the presiding administrative law judge recommended classification as Schedule III, which would have permitted continued medical use. However, DEA Administrator John C. Lawn overruled this recommendation. Harvard psychiatrist Lester Grinspoon subsequently sued the DEA, arguing the agency had improperly disregarded evidence of medical utility. A federal court agreed, characterizing Lawn's reasoning as "strained" and "unpersuasive," and vacated the Schedule I classification. Less than a month later, however, Lawn reimposed Schedule I status, dismissing testimony from psychiatrists describing over 200 beneficial therapeutic cases on the grounds that these had not been published in peer-reviewed journals. The classification effectively terminated clinical research and therapeutic use in the United States.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Following prohibition, MDMA continued to spread through underground rave and dance music cultures, eventually becoming one of the most popular recreational drugs worldwide. By 2014, it was estimated to be among the most widely used recreational substances globally, alongside cocaine and cannabis. Efforts to restore medical access began almost immediately after scheduling. In 1986, Rick Doblin founded the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) to work within regulatory frameworks toward making MDMA and other psychedelic substances available for therapeutic applications. Building on earlier anecdotal reports from therapists, MAPS pursued rigorous clinical research on MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. In 2017, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted breakthrough therapy designation, recognizing the treatment's potential.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: The terminology surrounding MDMA continued to evolve after prohibition. While "Ecstasy" (often shortened to "E," "X," or "XTC") became the dominant street term for pressed pills and tablets, the term "Molly" (short for "molecule") emerged in the 2000s as slang for crystalline or powder MDMA purported to be of high purity. The British equivalent "Mandy" serves a similar function. However, both terms have evolved into generic terminology for various euphoric stimulants sold in powder or crystal form, regardless of actual MDMA content.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: German chemist who first synthesized MDMA in 1912 while employed at Merck. Köllisch was developing synthetic pathways to methylhydrastinine, a potential hemostatic agent, when he prepared MDMA as an intermediate compound. He had no interest in MDMA's pharmacological properties and likely never investigated its effects.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: American chemist and psychopharmacologist often called the "Godfather of Ecstasy." Shulgin synthesized MDMA in 1965 while working at Dow Chemical Company and later investigated its psychoactive properties following reports from students in the mid-1970s. After personally experimenting with the compound in 1976, he co-authored the first scientific publication on MDMA's psychological effects with David Nichols in 1978. Though he did not find his own experiences particularly remarkable, Shulgin recognized its therapeutic potential and systematically introduced it to therapists, researchers, and friends. He called the drug "window" for its perceived ability to strip away habitual patterns of perception.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: American psychotherapist sometimes called the "Johnny Appleseed of MDMA." Zeff had used psychedelic substances in his practice before semi-retiring. When Shulgin introduced him to MDMA in 1977, Zeff was so impressed that he came out of retirement to promote its therapeutic applications. Over the following years, he traveled extensively throughout the United States and occasionally Europe, training an estimated four thousand psychotherapists in therapeutic MDMA use. Zeff named the drug "Adam," believing it enabled users to access a primordial state of innocence and openness.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: American pharmacologist and medicinal chemist who co-authored the first scientific publication on MDMA's psychoactive effects in humans with Alexander Shulgin in 1978. Their report described the drug as inducing "an easily controlled altered state of consciousness with emotional and sensual overtones."

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: American entrepreneur who transformed MDMA from a therapeutic tool into a mass-market recreational drug. After working as the Southwest distributor for a Boston-based production group, Clegg established his own "Texas Group." In 1981, he coined the street name "Ecstasy" to enhance marketability. His organization mass-produced and openly distributed MDMA through pyramid sales structures, toll-free numbers, and credit card transactions. By some accounts, the Texas Group produced more MDMA in eighteen months than all other distribution networks combined.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: American psychedelic drug researcher and activist who founded the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) in 1986, shortly after MDMA was scheduled. MAPS has worked within regulatory frameworks to restore medical access to MDMA and other psychedelic substances. Under Doblin's leadership, MAPS sponsored clinical trials that led to the FDA granting breakthrough therapy designation to MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD in 2017.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text: Harvard psychiatrist who sued the DEA after Administrator John C. Lawn overruled an administrative law judge's recommendation to classify MDMA as Schedule III. Grinspoon argued the agency had improperly disregarded evidence of medical utility. A federal court agreed, calling Lawn's reasoning "strained" and "unpersuasive," and vacated the Schedule I classification. However, Lawn subsequently reimposed Schedule I status, effectively ending the legal challenge.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text:
MDMA — dangerous combinations:
- AMT
- DXM
- Lithium (High risk of serotonin syndrome)
- MAOIs (MAO-B inhibitors can increase the potency and duration of phenethylamines unpredictably. MAO-A inhibitors with MDMA will lead to hypertensive crises.)
- Mephedrone (Risk of serotonin syndrome as both drugs raise serotonin levels. Stimulants also increase the neurotoxic effects of MDMA, in addition to concerns of high blood pressure and unnecessary strain on the heart. As well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort due to the combination.)
- Tramadol (Tramadol and stimulants both increase the risk of seizures.)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text:
MDMA — unsafe combinations:
- PCP (This combination can easily lead to hypermanic states)
- Pregabalin (There is a significant risk of seizures from this combination. Amphetamines increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal. If amphetamines wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages cause strain of the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications. Medical dosages are not reported to be a concern)

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text:
MDMA — caution combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds
- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines (Some of the 5-MeO tryptamines are a bit unpredictable and should be mixed with MDMA with care)
- Alcohol (The combination of MDMA and alcohol may increase strain on the cardiovascular system and lead to increased alcohol consumption. MDMA may also impair one's ability to recognize their level of drunkenness, leading to increased alcohol consumption and poor decision-making. Alcohol may also increase the risk of dehydration and hyperthermia (increased body temperature) when combined with MDMA.)
- Amphetamines (This combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart, may cause some physical discomfort, and has the chance to cause cardiovascular issues. The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants can increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops and make the experience more uncomfortable, this combination raises these chances. Amphetamines will increase the neurotoxic effects of MDMA, in addition to causing further concerns of hyperthermia due to the inherent nature of the combination.

chunks.title: MDMA
chunks.text:
It will also raise one's body temperature, also likely making the combination more neurotoxic.)
- Caffeine (Caffeine is not really necessary with MDMA and increases any neurotoxic effects from MDMA)
- Cocaine (Cocaine blocks some of the desirable effects of MDMA while increasing the risk of heart attack.)
- DOx compounds (The combined stimulating effects of the two can be uncomfortable. Coming down on the MDMA while the DOx is still active can be quite anxiogenic. )
- GHB/GBL (Large amounts of GHB/GBL may overwhelm the effects of MDMA on the comedown.)
- MXE (There have been reports of risky serotonergic interactions when the two are taken at the same time, but MXE taken to the end of an MDMA experience does not appear to cause the same issues.)
- NBOMe compounds

chunks.text:
Legal status of MDMA by country:
- Australia: Schedule 8 (Controlled Drug) — Reclassified to Schedule 8 as of July 1, 2023, allowing for limited authorized medical use. Personal quantities under 1.5 grams or 5 single doses have been decriminalized in the Australian Capital…
- Austria: Illegal — Prohibited under the Suchtmittelgesetz (SMG). Possession, production, and sale are criminal offenses.
