chunks.title: Mdoh
chunks.text: MDOH is an entactogen, psychedelic, and stimulant of the phenethylamine and amphetamine classes. It is the N-hydroxy homologue of MDA, documented by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL. Described as intensely psychedelic, it produces enhanced appreciation of beauty and nature with effects closely resembling those of MDA. Shulgin speculated the two compounds may interconvert metabolically. Notable side effects include urinary retention, internal dryness, and a reportedly heavy comedown. The substance has not seen widespread use.

chunks.title: Mdoh
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Urinary retention and difficulty urinating have been reported as side effects, similar to those observed with MDMA.

chunks.title: Mdoh
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Described as less intense than with MDMA in at least one report.

chunks.title: Mdpa
chunks.text: MDPA is an obscure substituted methylenedioxyphenethylamine with very little history of human use. Its pharmacological profile remains largely unknown, though it is suspected to share properties with other MDxx compounds and may function as a monoamine releaser or reuptake inhibitor. Due to its extremely limited documentation and tentative classification as an empathogen, MDPA should be approached with significant caution.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.text: MDPHP is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and pyrovalerone classes, structurally related to α-PVP, α-PHP, and MDPV. Although first synthesized around 1960, recreational use did not emerge until the mid-2010s, primarily in Europe. Batch purity and composition have been highly variable, with other cathinones sometimes sold in its place, making its effects difficult to characterize reliably. Sensationalist media coverage has greatly exaggerated its dangers relative to available evidence.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.text: While seemingly less compulsive than related cathinones like α-PHP and MDPV, users can still become trapped in cycles of chasing progressively shorter-lasting euphoria and avoiding the comedown. Some users report compulsive redosing patterns despite the drug not being particularly euphoric, with the short-lasting positive effects and undesirable comedown driving continued use.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.text: Stimulant psychosis is possible with high doses, prolonged use, and sleep deprivation, but is not the typical effect at reasonable doses with adequate sleep. Case reports have documented psychosis and aggressiveness requiring police assistance. Nearly all severe experiences reported involve prolonged use over 1-2 days with little to no sleep. The psychological and cognitive negatives are significantly increased with multiple doses and sleep deprivation.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.text: Overdose carries an increased risk of seizure, though no specific case reports describing MDPHP-induced seizures have been published.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: No fatalities have been reported, although fatal toxicity is believed possible with overdose. One case of fetal death was temporally linked to MDPHP and α-PHP use in a pregnant female, though the exact cause of the intrauterine asphyxia was not determined.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure occur commonly during use; overdose could cause excessively elevated cardiovascular parameters, with complications such as myocardial infarction and stroke considered possible though not yet documented in medical case reports.

chunks.title: Mdphp
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Case reports have documented hypertension, thorax pain, and cold extremities in confirmed users. Cardiovascular changes at typical doses normally do not cause distress.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and pyrrolidine classes, first developed in the 1960s by Boehringer Ingelheim as a potential amphetamine alternative. It acts primarily as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor and is considered one of the most potent stimulants available. MDPV gained notoriety after 2004 when it appeared in products marketed as 'bath salts' sold in convenience stores. It is known for producing strong euphoria with mild empathogenic qualities, though it carries significant risk of compulsive redosing.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: When addiction develops, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur if usage is suddenly stopped. The drug causes highly unpleasant comedown symptoms including residual depressed mood, cramping, muscle soreness, and prolonged stimulation making sleep difficult.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV is considered highly addictive with a high potential for abuse and readily causes psychological dependence. It is strongly associated with compulsive redosing ('fiending') and irresistible cravings to re-administer, with robust reinforcing effects demonstrated in both human case reports and animal self-administration studies.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV may cause psychosis and mania at a significantly higher rate than other stimulants. Chronic abuse or single exposure overdose can lead to psychosis more readily than the vast majority of stimulants. Symptoms include hearing voices, visual hallucinations, urges to harm oneself, severe anxiety, mania, grandiosity, paranoid delusions, confusion, increased aggression, and irritability. High doses cause intense prolonged panic attacks, and sleep deprivation from extended use compounds psychotic risk. Electroconvulsive therapy has been used to treat persistent psychotic symptoms from repeated use.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: Seizures can occur in overdose situations and are treated with large doses of lorazepam in emergency settings.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular strain including very elevated heart rate and tachycardia occurs during intoxication and may persist into the comedown period; overdose cases may present with hypertensive emergency requiring emergency treatment.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Over-excitation of noradrenaline pathways causing sympathomimetic cardiovascular effects

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Treatment of hypertension with beta blockers is contraindicated as it may cause unopposed peripheral alpha-adrenergic effects with paradoxical blood pressure rise. Overdose treatment involves large doses of benzodiazepines for tachycardia and hypertensive emergency.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV acts as a potent norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI), blocking the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine to increase their concentrations in the synaptic cleft. Its activity at the dopamine transporter is approximately six to eight times stronger than at the norepinephrine transporter, while it is virtually inactive at the serotonin transporter. The (S)-enantiomer is the pharmacologically active form, with (R)-MDPV being far less potent. MDPV demonstrates substantially greater potency than amphetamine, cocaine, and mephedrone as an NDRI, and is among the most potent dopamine reuptake inhibitors characterized in vitro and in vivo. In addition to reuptake inhibition, MDPV acts as a weakly efficacious partial norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent in rat brain synaptosomes, though this releasing activity was not observed in human cell line assays. Serotonin plays a role in its pharmacology to a much lesser degree.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV demonstrates greater blood-brain barrier permeability than amphetamine, methamphetamine, methcathinone, and mephedrone in vitro. Hepatic metabolism occurs via CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and CYP1A2, beginning with demethylenation followed by methylation of the aromatic ring via catechol-O-methyltransferase. Further metabolism involves hydroxylation of the aromatic ring and side chain, oxidation of the pyrrolidine ring to a lactam, and subsequent ring opening to a carboxylic acid. Phase II glucuronidation allows renal excretion of metabolites, with only a small fraction excreted in feces.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: MDPV was first developed in the 1960s by a research team at Boehringer Ingelheim, a German pharmaceutical company. The compound was investigated as a potential alternative to racemic amphetamine and reportedly demonstrated some desirable qualities, including reduced toxicity compared to amphetamine. Despite these promising characteristics, the company chose not to pursue its development as a medicinal drug, and MDPV remained an obscure stimulant for several decades.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text:
MDPV resurfaced around 2004 when it was reportedly first made available to the public as a designer drug. In the United States, products containing MDPV were marketed and sold as "bath salts" in gas stations and convenience stores, employing a strategy similar to that used for synthetic cannabinoids sold as "Spice" and "K2" incense products. This deceptive labeling allowed the substance to be sold legally for a period while circumventing drug regulations.

Along with methylone and mephedrone, MDPV became one of the first substances identified in products sold under various guises including "bath salts," "plant food," and "fertilizer." The compound was also detected in some tablets sold as ecstasy. This period of legal availability ended in the United States when MDPV was banned in 2011.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: The widespread availability of MDPV was accompanied by numerous reports of psychological and physical harm, including an unusually large number of fatalities. Between September 2009 and August 2013, nine European countries reported a total of 107 non-fatal intoxications and 99 analytically confirmed deaths related to MDPV. Several notable incidents occurred in the United States during 2011. In April, two men in northwestern Pennsylvania were found dead in a remote location on government land, two weeks after being reported missing. While the official cause of death for both Troy Johnson, 29, and Terry Sumrow, 28, was hypothermia, toxicology reports confirmed both had ingested MDPV shortly before their deaths. The county coroner noted the amount was not sufficient to kill them directly but was "enough to get them messed up." MDPV containers, spoons, hypodermic syringes, and marijuana paraphernalia were found in their vehicle. That same month, a woman in Alton, Illinois, apparently died from an MDPV overdose.

chunks.title: MDPV
chunks.text: In May 2011, the CDC reported a hospital emergency department visit in Michigan following bath salts use, with one person dead on arrival. Associates reported the deceased had used bath salts, and toxicology revealed high levels of MDPV along with marijuana and prescription drugs. The autopsy cited MDPV toxicity as the primary factor contributing to death. An incident of hemiplegia has also been reported in association with MDPV use.

chunks.title: Meai
chunks.text: MEAI is a selective serotonin releasing agent of the substituted 2-aminoindane class. First synthesized in 1956 and pharmacologically characterized in 2017 by David Nutt and Ezekiel Golan, it was developed as a potential alcohol substitute intended to mimic mild aspects of alcohol intoxication without its more harmful effects. MEAI reportedly produces subtle psychoactive effects described as gentle inebriation with maintained mental clarity. It is currently under preclinical development for the treatment of alcoholism, cocaine use disorder, and obesity.

chunks.title: Mebroqualone
chunks.text: Mebroqualone is a quinazolinone-class GABAergic depressant and an analogue of mecloqualone, differing by the substitution of a bromine atom for chlorine on its 3-phenyl ring. Originally synthesized in the 1960s, it produces sedative, hypnotic, and muscle relaxant effects. It is characterized by its short duration of action and relatively high potency compared to methaqualone. Mebroqualone has appeared on the research chemical market as a designer drug analogue.

chunks.title: Meclofenoxate
chunks.text: Meclofenoxate is a cholinergic nootropic of the choline derivative class. Developed in 1959 at the French National Scientific Research Center, it is an ester of dimethylethanolamine (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It has been shown to improve memory performance in elderly patients and is prescribed in several European countries and Japan. It is contraindicated in individuals with depression, mania, epilepsy, or convulsions, and may interact dangerously with MAOIs.

chunks.title: Meclofenoxate
chunks.text: No physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms have been reported.

chunks.title: Meclofenoxate

chunks.title: Meclonazepam
chunks.text: Meclonazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative structurally related to clonazepam, first developed by Hoffmann-La Roche during the 1960s. It was initially investigated for potential antiparasitic applications, particularly in the treatment of schistosomiasis. Although it has appeared on the grey market as a recreational depressant, it has not achieved widespread use. As with other benzodiazepines, meclonazepam is considered habit-forming and carries the risk of physical dependence with repeated administration.

chunks.text: Categorized as habit-forming with recognized potential for recreational use due to its sedative and anxiolytic effects.

chunks.title: Meclonazepam
chunks.text: Meclonazepam produces its sedative and anxiolytic effects through modulation of the GABA-A receptor, consistent with the mechanism shared by other benzodiazepine compounds. It acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor.

Meclonazepam was first synthesized by a research team at Hoffmann-La Roche during the 1970s as a benzodiazepine derivative structurally related to clonazepam. Early investigations identified potential anti-parasitic applications against Schistosoma mansoni, the parasitic flatworm responsible for schistosomiasis, though this therapeutic avenue was never developed to the point of clinical approval.

The compound was never marketed as a pharmaceutical product. It later emerged on the grey market as a designer drug, though it has not achieved widespread popularity within recreational drug communities.

chunks.title: Medazepam
chunks.text: Medazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine derivative that functions as a prodrug to nordazepam. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties, with a notably extended half-life of 36 to 200 hours due to its major active metabolites. Medazepam is rarely prescribed and is reported to produce effects similar to diazepam. As with all benzodiazepines, it should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Mefloquine
chunks.text: Mefloquine is an antimalarial of the 4-quinolinemethanol class, developed by the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research in the 1970s and marketed under the brand name Lariam. Used for the prevention and treatment of malaria, it has generated significant controversy due to neuropsychiatric adverse effects — including hallucinations, vivid nightmares, anxiety, and depression — which may persist long after discontinuation. Its off-target partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors likely contributes to these effects.

chunks.title: Mefloquine
chunks.text: Psychiatric effects include nightmares, visual and auditory hallucinations, anxiety, depression, unusual behavior, and suicidal ideations. The FDA added a boxed warning in 2013 regarding neuropsychiatric side effects that may persist for months to years after discontinuation or may be permanent. Central nervous system events requiring hospitalization occur in approximately 1 in 10,000 people taking mefloquine for prophylaxis, while milder events such as vivid dreams and insomnia affect up to 25% of users. Mefloquine is contraindicated in those with a history of psychiatric disorders.

chunks.title: Mefloquine
chunks.text: Mefloquine reduces seizure threshold and neurological side effects include seizures. The drug is contraindicated in those with a previous history of seizures. Neurologic effects can occur at any time during use and may persist for months to years after discontinuation or become permanent.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text: Melatonin is an endogenous hormone and indoleamine compound naturally produced by the pineal gland in response to darkness, regulating sleep-wake cycles and circadian rhythms. First isolated and characterized by Aaron B. Lerner in 1958, it is widely available as an over-the-counter supplement for treating insomnia and promoting healthier sleep patterns. Beyond sleep regulation, melatonin functions as an antioxidant and influences mood, seasonal rhythms, and immune activity.

chunks.text: No physical dependence or withdrawal syndrome has been reported with melatonin use.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text: No evidence of psychological addiction or abuse potential has been documented. Melatonin is not associated with compulsive use patterns or reinforcing effects.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text:
Melatonin acts as a potent full agonist at melatonin receptor 1 (MT1) and melatonin receptor 2 (MT2), both G protein-coupled receptors of the Gi/o subtype, with MT1 also exhibiting Gq coupling. MT1 receptor activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cyclic AMP formation and downstream protein kinase A activity, while also activating phospholipase C and modulating ion channel flux. MT2 receptor activation similarly inhibits adenylyl cyclase and guanylyl cyclase while increasing protein kinase C activity. These receptors are expressed throughout the central nervous system, including the suprachiasmatic nucleus responsible for circadian rhythm regulation, as well as in peripheral tissues including the retina, cardiovascular system, and immune cells.

Beyond receptor-mediated effects, melatonin functions as a high-capacity free radical scavenger within mitochondria, directly neutralizing reactive oxygen and nitrogen species while promoting expression of antioxidant enzymes including superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase, and catalase through receptor-triggered signal transduction pathways.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text: Melatonin absorption and bioavailability vary widely between individuals. It is hepatically metabolized primarily by CYP1A2, with lesser contributions from CYP1A1, CYP2C19, and CYP1B1. The primary metabolic pathway transforms melatonin into 6-hydroxymelatonin, which is then conjugated with sulfate or glucuronide and excreted in urine. Immediate-release formulations cause blood levels to peak in approximately one hour.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text:
The discovery of melatonin traces back to early twentieth-century research on skin pigmentation in amphibians. In 1917, Carey Pratt McCord and Floyd P. Allen observed that feeding extracts from bovine pineal glands to tadpoles caused their skin to lighten through contraction of dark epidermal melanophores. This observation laid the groundwork for subsequent investigations into pineal gland secretions.

Four decades later, in 1958, dermatology professor Aaron B. Lerner and his research team at Yale University successfully isolated and identified the compound responsible for this skin-lightening effect. Working with bovine pineal gland extracts, Lerner was motivated by the possibility that pineal substances might prove beneficial for treating skin diseases. The compound they isolated was named melatonin, derived from the Greek words "melas" (meaning black or dark) and "tonos" (meaning labour, colour, or suppress), reflecting its role in preventing skin darkening. This naming convention followed the precedent set by serotonin, another agent affecting skin color that had been discovered in 1948.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text:
Research in the mid-1970s by Lynch and colleagues demonstrated that melatonin production in human pineal glands follows a circadian rhythm, with secretion increasing during darkness and decreasing during light exposure. This finding established melatonin's fundamental role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle in vertebrates.

The first patent for melatonin's therapeutic use as a low-dose sleep aid was awarded to Richard Wurtman at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1995, marking the transition from basic research to clinical application.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text:
Melatonin's reputation as a sedative and potential life-extending compound grew rapidly within health food store circuits during the early 1990s. By 1995, the supplement had achieved remarkable commercial success, with manufacturer Genzyme estimating that 20 million people in the United States purchased melatonin for the first time that year alone. Retail sales were estimated between $200 million and $350 million annually.

Media coverage during this period reflected both enthusiasm and caution. A 1994 article in Esquire magazine voiced typical warnings about insufficient knowledge regarding appropriate dosages and potential side effects. However, a 1995 Newsweek feature expanded on melatonin's potential virtues, including claims about immune system enhancement, cancer prevention, and lifespan extension.

chunks.title: Melatonin
chunks.text:
For decades following its discovery, melatonin was believed to be primarily an animal neurohormone. Although the compound was detected in coffee extracts during the 1970s, this was initially dismissed as a byproduct of the extraction process. The formal identification of melatonin in plants occurred in 1987, fundamentally changing understanding of the compound's biological distribution.

Subsequent research has found melatonin present in all plant species investigated, occurring in leaves, stems, roots, fruits, and seeds in varying concentrations. Notably high melatonin levels have been measured in common beverages including coffee, tea, wine, and beer, as well as in cereal crops such as corn, rice, wheat, barley, and oats.

chunks.title: MEM
chunks.text: MEM is a rare psychedelic amphetamine related to the DOx class, first synthesized and documented by Alexander Shulgin in his book PiHKAL. Little is known about its pharmacology, though it is noted for its relatively high potency and extended duration of action. Shulgin's research documented its frequent use in combination with MDMA, observing that this approach appeared to ease the onset and reduce the dosage needed for full psychedelic effects.

chunks.title: MEM

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text: Memantine is an adamantane derivative and NMDA receptor antagonist primarily prescribed for the management of moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. It works by blocking glutamate-mediated neuronal excitotoxicity, distinguishing it mechanistically from the cholinesterase inhibitors typically used in Alzheimer's treatment. At supratherapeutic doses, memantine can produce prolonged dissociative effects reportedly lasting 16 or more hours, placing it among the longest-duration dissociatives available.

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text: Recreational use is rare due to the drug's very long duration of action (>40 hours) and apparent lack of euphoric effects. Misuse potential is considered limited compared to other NMDA receptor antagonists.

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text: Psychosis is listed as a severe but rare side effect. Hallucinations and confusion are more common adverse effects (≥1% of patients) in clinical populations. At supratherapeutic recreational doses, dissociative effects may produce psychotomimetic symptoms.

chunks.title: Memantine

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text: Memantine acts as an uncompetitive antagonist of the NMDA receptor, binding within the open ion channel to block pathological calcium influx driven by excessive glutamate signaling. It displays preferential inhibition of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors, while its low affinity and rapid off-rate kinetics allow normal synaptic NMDA function to be preserved during physiological glutamate release. Beyond its primary mechanism, memantine acts as a non-competitive antagonist at 5-HT3 receptors with potency similar to its NMDA activity and as an antagonist at α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It has additionally been reported to act as an agonist at dopamine D2High receptors and as a weak agonist at sigma-1 receptors.

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text: Memantine has an oral bioavailability of approximately 100% and reaches peak plasma levels within 3 to 7 hours. It undergoes negligible metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes, producing three minor metabolites that retain minimal NMDA receptor antagonist activity. The drug is eliminated primarily through renal excretion, with 57 to 82% appearing unchanged in urine. Its elimination half-life ranges from 60 to 80 hours, and renal clearance is dependent on urinary pH, with more alkaline urine slowing elimination.

chunks.text: IC50 = ~500–1,000 nM; extrasynaptic IC50 = ~22 nM

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text:
Memantine was first synthesized and patented by Eli Lilly and Company in 1963, originally developed as a potential anti-diabetic agent. However, the compound proved ineffective at lowering blood sugar and the project stalled. Nearly a decade later, in 1972, researchers discovered that memantine possessed central nervous system activity, prompting Merz to acquire and develop the compound for neurological conditions, initially focusing on Parkinson's disease.

The drug's mechanism of action remained unclear during early development. Researchers initially theorized that memantine worked through direct or indirect modulation of dopaminergic, noradrenergic, and serotonergic systems. It was not until 1989—after clinical trials had already begun—that memantine was identified as an NMDA receptor antagonist. The earlier proposed mechanisms were subsequently recognized to occur only at concentrations approximately 100-fold higher than those achieved at therapeutic doses.

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text:
Memantine was first studied for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease in 1986. Three years later, in 1989, the drug received approval and was first marketed for dementia in Germany under the brand name Axura, making it one of the earliest NMDA receptor antagonists used clinically for neurodegenerative disease.

International expansion accelerated in 2000, when Merz established partnerships with several pharmaceutical companies: Forest Laboratories for development in the United States under the brand name Namenda, Suntory for the Japanese market, and Lundbeck for Europe and other markets under the name Ebixa. These collaborations facilitated regulatory approval in the European Union in 2002 and in the United States in 2003. By 2023, memantine had become the 145th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over three million prescriptions dispensed annually.

chunks.title: Memantine
chunks.text:
Recreational use of memantine at supratherapeutic doses has been documented. As a weak NMDA receptor antagonist, the drug produces dissociative effects reminiscent of phencyclidine at sufficiently high doses, and even therapeutic doses have been observed to produce mild dissociative-like effects in clinical studies.

Research examining self-reported use on Reddit revealed that memantine is used both recreationally for its dissociative properties and as a nootropic for perceived cognitive enhancement. The same analysis identified patterns of self-medication for various conditions without strong scientific basis supporting such uses. The drug's very long duration of action, exceeding 40 hours, has likely limited its appeal for recreational misuse compared to shorter-acting dissociatives. Similar patterns of non-medical use have been observed with the structurally related compound amantadine.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Mephedrone is a synthetic entactogen-stimulant of the substituted cathinone class. Originally synthesized in 1929, it was rediscovered in 2003 and rapidly gained popularity as an online research chemical between 2007 and 2009, particularly in the United Kingdom. Its effects are frequently compared to a combination of MDMA and cocaine. Mephedrone's short duration and intense rush are associated with compulsive redosing, and it is sometimes misrepresented as MDMA.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Physical dependence is unlikely to develop significantly. Withdrawal symptoms are minimal and not life-threatening, though dependence may manifest as restlessness, tremors, insomnia, and hyperactivity following cessation of regular use.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Chronic use is considered highly addictive with an extreme potential for abuse and psychological dependence. The urge to redose is notoriously strong, particularly with insufflation, with many users reporting difficulty controlling their intake within a single session. Compulsive redosing patterns similar to or exceeding those of other euphoric stimulants are commonly described, leading to consumption of far more than intended.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: High doses may lead to psychotic reactions including hallucinations, delusions, and erratic behaviour. Anxiety and paranoia are more commonly reported adverse effects. The most severe psychiatric effects appear to be associated with high doses or prolonged use, and risk may be elevated in individuals with predisposition to schizophrenia.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Seizures have been documented in clinical case series, with one hospital report finding 20% of treated patients experienced seizures. A fatal case in Sweden involved convulsions. Individuals with pre-existing seizure disorders may be at elevated risk when using stimulants.

Treatment with lorazepam may help prevent severe vasoconstriction in toxicity cases.

More experimental research is needed to fully characterise mephedrone's neurotoxicity in humans. Some studies showed no significant damage to dopamine nerve endings in striatum, while others suggested persistent changes.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Mephedrone acts primarily as a substrate-type releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor at the serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine transporters. It preferentially releases serotonin over dopamine, functioning as a full releaser of serotonin but only a partial releaser of dopamine. Beyond its transporter-mediated effects, mephedrone is a potent near-full agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor and shows significant affinity for the 5-HT2B, 5-HT2C, and α2-adrenergic receptors, though it is inactive as an agonist at 5-HT2B. It also activates rodent TAAR1 at micromolar potencies but does not appear to act as an agonist at the human TAAR1.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Mephedrone is rapidly absorbed following oral or intranasal administration, with peak plasma concentrations typically reached within 0.5 to 1 hour. It readily crosses the blood-brain barrier (brain-to-plasma ratio of approximately 1.85 in rats) and has a plasma elimination half-life of approximately 2 hours. The drug undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism primarily via CYP2D6, with major phase I pathways including N-demethylation, ketone reduction, and tolyl group oxidation. Absolute bioavailability in rats is approximately 10%, consistent with substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism, and plasma protein binding is approximately 22%. Mephedrone exhibits enantioselective pharmacokinetics in which the R-(+) enantiomer reaches higher peak concentrations and persists longer than the S-(-) enantiomer.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Repeated mephedrone use over time can blunt many effects, often requiring higher doses for similar results. Users often report that overuse degrades the initial 'magic,' a pattern similar to what is described with MDMA.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Mephedrone was first synthesized in 1929 by Saem de Burnaga Sanchez, who published his work in the Bulletin de la Société Chimique de France under the chemical name "toluyl-alpha-monomethylaminoethylcetone." Following this initial synthesis, the compound remained an obscure product of academic chemistry for over seven decades, attracting no significant attention from researchers or the broader public.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text:
The compound was rediscovered in 2003 when an underground chemist operating under the pseudonym "Kinetic" posted a synthesis report on The Hive, a now-defunct online forum for amateur chemistry discussion. Kinetic described synthesizing the substance out of curiosity and reported experiencing effects comparable to MDMA, noting a sense of well-being that he had not encountered from other substances. This post brought mephedrone to the attention of clandestine drug manufacturers.

Following this rediscovery, the drug was commercially introduced in Israel by Ezekiel Golan, a mathematician known as "Dr. Z" or "Dr. Zee." A related cathinone product called "hagigat" had been sold legally in Israel since approximately 2004. After Israeli authorities banned hagigat, modified formulations were developed and marketed by the company Neorganics under names such as "Neodoves pills," though this product line was discontinued in January 2008 following regulatory action. By 2007, mephedrone had become available for purchase through international online vendors.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: Between 2007 and 2010, mephedrone underwent rapid proliferation across Europe, Australia, and New Zealand. Law enforcement agencies first became aware of the compound in 2008, and by 2010 it had been reported in most European countries. The United Kingdom experienced particularly significant uptake, with usage growing substantially between the summer of 2009 and March 2010. During this period, mephedrone became readily available at music festivals, head shops, and through online retailers. A 2009 survey of Mixmag readers found it had become the fourth most popular recreational drug in the UK, trailing only cannabis, cocaine, and MDMA.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text: The drug attracted users from diverse social backgrounds. Researchers, charity workers, teachers, and users themselves all reported observing widespread and increasing use during 2009. Criminologist Fiona Measham of Lancaster University suggested that mephedrone's rapid adoption was partly attributable to the concurrent decline in quality of traditional stimulants. Data indicated that average cocaine purity in the UK had fallen from approximately 60% in 1999 to 22% by 2009, while roughly half of ecstasy tablets seized in 2009 contained no MDMA whatsoever. This decline has been partially attributed to the seizure of 33 tonnes of sassafras oil, a key MDMA precursor, in Cambodia in June 2008. Similar patterns emerged in the Netherlands, where testing found mephedrone present in approximately 20% of ecstasy tablets by mid-2009.

chunks.title: Mephedrone
chunks.text:
Media coverage around mephedrone's emergence was intense and often inaccurate or overstated. Major news outlets wrongly described the substance as commonly used as plant fertilizer. Vendors were instead using the "plant food" label to avoid laws against selling compounds meant to be consumed by people.

By late 2009, UK newspapers had started calling the drug "meow," "miaow," or "meow meow," even though those names were reportedly not widely used by actual users at that point. In November 2009, The Sun ran a sensational account alleging that a user had seriously injured himself while using mephedrone. The story was later linked to an obvious joke from an internet forum that had been copied into a police report and then treated as fact by journalists. The broader period involved substantial media hysteria, including deaths incorrectly blamed on the substance.

chunks.title: Mephenaqualone
chunks.text: Mephenaqualone is a central nervous system depressant of the quinazolinone class that produces sedative and hypnotic effects. It is a structural analogue of methaqualone, sharing similar pharmacological activity as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA receptor sites. Its toxicity profile remains poorly documented, and it is considered highly addictive with rapid tolerance development. Combining mephenaqualone with other depressants such as alcohol, opiates, or benzodiazepines significantly increases the risk of fatal respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Mephenaqualone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with prolonged use. Abrupt discontinuation can lead to withdrawal symptoms including increased anxiety, insomnia, and potential seizures, consistent with GABAergic substance withdrawal.

chunks.title: Mephenaqualone
chunks.text: Mephenaqualone is described as highly addictive and associated with significant abuse potential. Repeated exposure can quickly produce tolerance, prompting users to take larger amounts to obtain comparable effects.

chunks.title: Mephenaqualone
chunks.text: Seizures may occur during withdrawal following abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use, consistent with the withdrawal profile of other GABAergic substances.

chunks.title: Mephenaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose can cause respiratory depression, which may become life-threatening particularly when combined with other CNS depressants such as alcohol, opiates, or benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Mescaline is a naturally occurring psychedelic of the phenethylamine class. It is found in several cacti species, most notably peyote and San Pedro, and has a history of spiritual and medicinal use spanning over 3,000 years in South America. This tradition persisted even through post-Spanish Conquest suppression efforts. Mescaline can be obtained from natural plant sources or produced synthetically and is known for producing classical psychedelic effects.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: No physical dependence has been documented with mescaline use. The substance does not produce withdrawal symptoms upon cessation.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: There is no evidence of mescaline showing addiction or dependence. The substance does not appear to produce reinforcing effects that lead to compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Rarely, in susceptible individuals such as those with a family history of schizophrenia, mescaline may cause psychosis. The substance can potentially trigger latent mental disorders even with single use in predisposed individuals.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Mescaline has some potential to cause seizures, particularly when combined with substances that lower seizure threshold. Seizure risk is notably elevated in combination with lithium or tramadol.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Liver damage has been reported at toxic doses of approximately 2 grams or more; occasional use at typical recreational doses is not associated with hepatotoxicity.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mescaline accumulates in the liver at concentrations many times higher than blood or brain levels and combines extensively with hepatic proteins.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The liver is a primary site of mescaline distribution and metabolism.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory paralysis may occur at toxic doses of approximately 2 grams or more; this represents an overdose scenario rather than a risk at typical recreational doses.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, and palpitations occur during intoxication as part of sympathetic arousal; serious cardiovascular events are uncommon at typical doses and primarily concern individuals with pre-existing conditions.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mescaline elicits sympathetic nervous system arousal, with the peripheral nervous system being a major target for the substance.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Additional effects may include chest and neck pains and shortness of breath. Individuals with pre-existing circulatory or heart conditions should avoid mescaline.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: 3,4,5-Trimethoxyphenylacetic acid (TMPAA)

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Mescaline acts primarily as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, which appears to be the principal mechanism underlying its psychoactive effects; the 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin has been shown to block these effects in humans. It also binds the 5-HT2C receptor, where it displays pronounced biased agonism, and shows low efficacy at the 5-HT2B receptor. Mescaline lacks meaningful affinity for the monoamine transporters (SERT, NET, and DAT), though high doses in rodent models have been found to elevate serotonin metabolite levels, suggesting possible serotonin release or reuptake inhibition at elevated concentrations. It may also weakly promote dopamine release, though this is considered to be of modest significance.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Mescaline's oral bioavailability is not precisely established but appears to be at least 53%, based on the proportion excreted unchanged in urine. Oral doses undergo approximately 50% first-pass metabolism, after which further metabolism is relatively limited. The primary metabolic pathway is oxidative deamination, though the specific enzymes responsible remain uncertain; monoamine oxidase (MAO), diamine oxidase (DAO), and possibly other enzymes have been implicated. Mescaline does not appear to be metabolized by CYP2D6. The compound also exhibits relatively poor blood-brain barrier permeability due to its low lipophilicity, which is thought to contribute to its low potency.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text:
Exact bioavailability has not been precisely determined
Estimated at 53% or more based on the amount recovered unchanged in urine
Approximately half of each oral dose is processed by the liver before reaching general circulation

Average elimination half-life is approximately 3.6 hours
About 87% is eliminated in urine within 24 hours and 92% within 48 hours
Poor ability to cross from blood into the brain due to low fat-solubility may contribute to delayed onset of effects

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: At minimum one month between experiences is recommended for harm reduction purposes, though specific tolerance reset timelines have not been precisely characterized in clinical literature.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text:
Archaeological evidence from sites across the United States, Mexico, and Peru demonstrates that mescaline-containing cacti have been used in ceremonial and spiritual contexts for over 6,000 years. The San Pedro cactus has been in continuous spiritual and medicinal use in Peru for more than 3,000 years, a tradition that persisted even through post-Spanish Conquest attempts at suppression.

Upon early contact with the Huichol people in Mexico, Europeans documented the use of peyote in Native American religious ceremonies. At the time of the Spanish conquest, religious and ceremonial peyote use was widespread throughout the Aztec Empire and northern Mexico. However, religious persecution by colonial authorities confined its use primarily to areas near the Pacific coast and into southwest Texas.

By 1880, peyote practices began spreading northward, with the Kiowa and Comanche peoples inaugurating a new form of peyote ceremony. These religious traditions were legally incorporated in the United States in 1920 as the Native American Church and have since spread across North America as far as Saskatchewan, Canada.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text:
Botanical investigations of peyote commenced in the 1840s, and the drug was subsequently listed in the Mexican pharmacopeia. The first publication documenting the use of mescal buttons appeared in 1887, authored by John Raleigh Briggs. That same year, German pharmacologist Louis Lewin obtained his first sample of the peyote cactus, identified numerous previously unknown alkaloids within it, and later published the first methodical pharmacological analysis of the plant.

In 1897, German chemist Arthur Heffter achieved the isolation and identification of mescaline, demonstrating that this compound was exclusively responsible for the psychoactive and hallucinogenic effects of peyote. Subsequent research would reveal that other peyote constituents such as hordenine, pellotine, and anhalinine also possess pharmacological activity. The complete synthesis of mescaline was first accomplished by Ernst Späth in 1919.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text:
Investigations into the potential therapeutic applications of mescaline commenced during the 1950s. In 1955, English politician Christopher Mayhew participated in an experimental session for the BBC's Panorama program, ingesting 400 mg of mescaline under the supervision of psychiatrist Humphry Osmond. Although the footage was ultimately deemed too controversial for broadcast, Mayhew described the experience as "the most interesting thing I ever did."

Mescaline has influenced numerous artists and writers throughout the 20th and 21st centuries. Salvador Dalí experimented with the substance believing it would enable access to his subconscious for artistic purposes. Allen Ginsberg's peyote vision in San Francisco inspired Part II of his seminal poem "Howl," while Ken Kesey consumed peyote prior to writing One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. Hunter S. Thompson documented his first mescaline experience in "First Visit with Mescalito," published in Songs of the Doomed, and the substance features prominently in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. Philip K. Dick was inspired to write Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said after his own mescaline experience.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: English physician and writer Havelock Ellis authored one of the first written reports to the general public describing the subjective effects of a mescaline experience, published in 1898.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: English writer and philosopher Aldous Huxley documented his experiences with mescaline in The Doors of Perception, published in 1954. This essay became one of the most influential texts on psychedelic experience and helped bring mescaline to wider public attention.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre consumed mescaline shortly before the publication of his first book, L'Imaginaire. The experience developed into a notably difficult session during which he felt menaced by sea creatures. For many years afterward, Sartre persistently believed he was being followed by lobsters, leading him to become a patient of psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan in an attempt to dispel these visions. Imagery of lobsters and crabs subsequently appeared in his novel Nausea.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: American chemist and pharmacologist Alexander Shulgin credited a mescaline experience as the initial inspiration that led him to explore psychedelic compounds throughout his career. In 1974, he synthesized 2C-B, a psychedelic phenethylamine structurally related to mescaline. Shulgin would later rate mescaline among his most important phenethylamine compounds alongside 2C-E, 2C-T-7, and 2C-T-2.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Quanah Parker, appointed by the federal government as principal chief of the entire Comanche Nation, advocated for the syncretic Native American Church and fought for the legal recognition of peyote use within the movement's religious practices.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Serotonergic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT), Other 5-HT2A agonists

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2C; 5-HT2B receptor agonist; SERT; NET; DAT; Adrenergic receptors; Dopamine receptors; Histamine receptors; Muscarinic receptors; Trace amine receptors

At higher dosages, the combination of a deliriant (DPH) and mescaline is cautioned against. Mescaline is likely to increase the deliriant and negative effects of DPH, in addition to increasing the risk of severe injury and mental trauma.)
- DOx compounds
- MAOIs
- NBOMe compounds
- Pregabalin (Caution should be given due to mescaline’s stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of mescaline.

chunks.title: Mescaline
chunks.text: Additionally, Pregabalin may increase mescaline’s inhibition and risk of injury.)

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: MET is a lesser-known synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, structurally related to DMT. It produces powerful, short-lived psychedelic effects characterized by rapid onset and progressive stages. When smoked or vaporized, its effects have been compared to those of DMT but with a more grounded headspace and reduced subjective intensity. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, or toxicity, and it has only been available through online research chemical vendors since mid-2016.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: Early reports characterize MET as non-habit-forming, with interest in taking it potentially declining after regular use. Like most psychedelics, it is generally viewed as self-limiting.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available. Long-term health effects have not been studied.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: MET acts primarily as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors, with the 5-HT2A interaction considered the principal driver of its psychedelic activity. It shows very weak agonist activity at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2B receptors. In addition to its action at serotonin receptors, MET functions as a serotonin releasing agent, though with lower potency than its direct receptor activity.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: Reports indicate minimal, if any, cross-tolerance with other psychedelics, so other psychedelics would be expected to retain their full effects after MET use

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: In contrast to most psychedelics, MET is not reported to produce tolerance easily. However, its extended residual effects suggest mild tolerance may occur when doses are taken close together.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text:
MET was first documented in scientific literature in 1981, appearing in Michael Valentine Smith's book "Psychedelic Chemistry." The compound subsequently received a brief entry in Alexander Shulgin's 1997 publication "TiHKAL" (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved), though it did not receive extensive characterization in that work.

The substance emerged on the European drug market as a novel designer drug in 2014, marking its first appearance in recreational contexts. By mid-2016, MET had become available through online research chemical vendors, where it continues to be distributed for recreational and entheogenic purposes.

chunks.title: MET
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Reports indicate minimal, if any, cross-tolerance with other psychedelics, so other psychedelics would be expected to retain their full effects after MET use

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2C receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT1A receptor agonist (full); 5-HT2B receptor agonist; Serotonin releasing agent

chunks.title: Metaclazepam
chunks.text: Metaclazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative marketed under the brand name Talis. It is characterized as a relatively selective anxiolytic, producing less sedation and muscle relaxation compared to other benzodiazepines such as diazepam or bromazepam, while being slightly more effective in reducing anxiety. Its primary active metabolite is N-desmethylmetaclazepam. As with all benzodiazepines, metaclazepam carries a risk of dependence and should not be combined with other CNS depressants, including alcohol.

chunks.title: Metaclazepam
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, consistent with the psychological dependence potential typical of benzodiazepine-class compounds.

chunks.title: Metaxalone
chunks.text: Metaxalone is a centrally acting muscle relaxant marketed under the brand name Skelaxin. It is prescribed for the symptomatic relief of pain associated with acute musculoskeletal conditions such as strains and sprains. Its precise mechanism of action has not been established but is believed to involve general central nervous system depression rather than direct skeletal muscle relaxation. It is noted for a relatively low incidence of side effects, though it is considered high-risk in elderly populations.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Methadone is a synthetic opioid analgesic of the diphenylheptane class. First developed in Germany in 1937 by Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockmühl, it is primarily used for the management of severe pain and as a maintenance therapy for opioid dependence. It is distinguished from other opioids by its comparatively long duration of action, good oral bioavailability, and additional activity as an NMDA receptor antagonist. It shares the typical risks associated with other opioids such as morphine and fentanyl.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with repeated administration through neuroadaptation of opioid receptors. Withdrawal symptoms are reported as significantly more protracted than other opioids due to methadone's long half-life, and include body aches, diarrhea, nausea, anxiety, tremors, tachycardia, sweating, insomnia, fever, and elevated pain sensitivity.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Chronic use of methadone is considered extremely addictive with a high potential for abuse, comparable to morphine. It is capable of causing psychological dependence, with cravings developing when regular use is established.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Compared to other opioids, methadone has fewer active metabolites and therefore a lower risk of neuropsychiatric toxicity such as delirium at higher doses. However, withdrawal from methadone can cause cognitive symptoms including delirium, auditory and visual hallucinations, paranoia, and delusions.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Methadone is known to lower the seizure threshold. However, due to fewer active metabolites, higher doses are less likely to result in seizures compared to other opioids. Particular caution is warranted during benzodiazepine withdrawal as the combination may potentiate seizure risk.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: QT interval prolongation can occur even at therapeutic doses, with risk of potentially fatal torsades de pointes arrhythmia; higher doses (>200 mg/day) and pre-existing cardiac conditions increase this risk significantly.

Infants exposed in-utero or through breast milk are at risk of life-threatening respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Methadone acts primarily as a full agonist at the μ-opioid receptor, mimicking the activity of endogenous endorphins. In the racemic mixture, the (R)-enantiomer carries the bulk of opioid activity, with roughly 10-fold higher μ-opioid affinity than the (S)-enantiomer. Methadone also activates κ-opioid, δ-opioid, and σ receptors. Beyond opioid targets, it antagonizes the NMDA glutamate receptor, dampening a major excitatory pathway in the central nervous system. It further acts as a weak serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, antagonizes 5-HT3A receptors and several nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes (notably α3β4 and α4β2), and functions as an agonist at the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Methadone undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, with oral bioavailability ranging widely from 36% to 100% due to marked interindividual variation. The primary metabolic pathway involves sequential N-demethylation, catalyzed mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, with additional contributions from CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2C8, and CYP2D6. Methadone is also a substrate of P-glycoprotein, an efflux transporter expressed in the intestines and brain. Its high lipid solubility contributes to a prolonged and highly variable elimination half-life, typically 15 to 60 hours (mean approximately 22 hours), though individual values can span from as few as 4 hours to as many as 190 hours due to genetic variability in cytochrome P450 enzyme activity.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text:
Extensive processing by the liver before reaching the bloodstream significantly reduces the amount absorbed
Wide individual variation (36-100%) due to genetic differences in liver enzymes
P-glycoprotein in the intestines acts as a pump that pushes some of the drug back out before absorption

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Mean elimination half-life is approximately 22 hours
Individual variation is extreme, ranging from 4 to 190 hours in some cases
Genetic differences in liver enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2D6) are the primary source of this variability
Opioid-tolerant individuals may metabolize methadone more quickly (~24 hours) compared to opioid-naive individuals (~55 hours)
High fat solubility contributes to the drug's prolonged presence in the body
Peak plasma concentrations are reached between 1 and 7.5 hours after oral dosing

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: Opioids (incomplete cross-tolerance; patients tolerant to other μ-opioid agonists may be incompletely tolerant to methadone, complicating dose conversion and creating overdose risk)

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text: With sustained repeated methadone use, tolerance may develop to many effects. The timeline depends on the effect, and constipation-related tolerance tends to build especially slowly compared with other opioid effects. Methadone's NMDA receptor antagonist activity may also help limit tolerance development relative to other opioids.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text:
Methadone was developed in 1937 in Germany by chemists Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockmühl, working for I.G. Farbenindustrie AG at the Farbwerke Hoechst facility. The research was motivated by Germany's shortage of opium and morphine, creating demand for a synthetic opioid that could be manufactured from readily available precursors. On September 11, 1941, Bockmühl and Ehrhart filed a patent application for the compound under the designation Hoechst 10820, with the trade name Polamidon—a name that remains in regular use in Germany today.

Unlike morphine and other opium-derived alkaloids, the structure of methadone bore little resemblance to traditional opiates. The compound was brought to market in 1943 and saw widespread use by the German military during World War II as a substitute for morphine.

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text:
Following World War II, all German patents, trade names, and research records were requisitioned and expropriated by the Allied forces. Documentation from I.G. Farbenkonzern's research at Farbwerke Hoechst was confiscated by the U.S. Department of Commerce Intelligence and subsequently investigated by a Technical Industrial Committee of the U.S. Department of State before being transferred to the United States.

In 1947, the Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry of the American Medical Association assigned the compound the generic name "methadone." With the I.G. Farbenkonzern patent rights no longer protected, pharmaceutical companies could acquire commercial production rights for just one dollar. That same year, Eli Lilly and Company introduced methadone to the American market as an analgesic under the trade name Dolophine. An urban legend would later emerge claiming the name derived from Adolf Hitler, but Dolophine was actually a contraction combining the Latin words "dolor" (pain) and "finis" (end), literally meaning "pain end."

chunks.title: Methadone
chunks.text:
Research into methadone's potential for treating opioid addiction began in the 1950s at the Addiction Research Center of the Narcotics Farm in Lexington, Kentucky. In the 1960s, physicians Robert Dole and Marie Nyswander at Rockefeller University in New York City conducted further studies that proved influential in establishing methadone maintenance as a treatment modality.

By 1976, methadone clinics had opened across major American cities including Chicago, New York, and New Haven. New York City alone was treating approximately 38,000 patients through its methadone programs by this time. Methadone treatment for opioid dependence has since gained global recognition, with the substance included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

chunks.title: Methallylescaline
chunks.text: Methallylescaline (MAL) is a synthetic psychedelic of the substituted phenethylamine class and a structural analog of mescaline. Its effects were first described by Alexander Shulgin in PiHKAL, with anecdotal reports suggesting it most closely resembles mescaline among the various mescaline analogs, producing both hallucinogenic and stimulant properties. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, or toxicity, and it has minimal history of human use.

chunks.title: Methallylescaline
chunks.text: Methallylescaline was first synthesized and explored by American chemist Alexander Shulgin, who initially experimented with the compound in 1981. The following year, in 1982, Shulgin discovered its hallucinogenic properties. He subsequently documented his findings in his 1991 book PiHKAL: A Chemical Love Story, though the compound was notably absent from his later work, The Shulgin Index, Volume One: Psychedelic Phenethylamines and Related Compounds, published in 2011. The substance remained relatively obscure until it emerged as a novel designer drug in Europe around 2013. By mid-2016, methallylescaline began appearing through online research chemical vendors, where it has since been distributed for recreational and entheogenic use. The compound has accumulated only a brief history of human consumption, with limited data available regarding its pharmacological characteristics.

chunks.title: Methallylescaline
chunks.text: Shulgin himself described the common name "methallylescaline" as "completely unsound" from a chemical nomenclature standpoint. He noted that the name suggests a union of a methallyl group with escaline, which does not accurately reflect the compound's structure. In reality, the substance consists of mescaline with a 2-propene group attached to the methyl of the methoxy group at the 4-position. The technically correct name would be 4-methylallyldesmethylmescaline, yielding the acronym MAD. However, Shulgin found this abbreviation disagreeable and ultimately preferred the designation MAL despite its chemical inaccuracy.

chunks.title: Methamnetamine
chunks.text: Methamnetamine is a triple monoamine releasing agent of the amphetamine and naphthylaminopropane families, structurally related to both methamphetamine and the experimental compound naphthylaminopropane. It appeared as a designer drug in early 2015 and remained available until approximately 2016. The substance acts primarily as a serotonin releaser with mild psychedelic activity, producing subtle empathogenic and sedating effects. It is almost always combined with a stimulant to achieve more pronounced euphoria, as its effects alone tend to be relatively mild.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Methamphetamine is a potent synthetic stimulant of the substituted amphetamine class. First synthesized in 1893 by Japanese chemist Nagayoshi Nagai, it saw widespread use during World War II to combat fatigue and was later prescribed for obesity and attention deficit disorder under the brand name Desoxyn. Because it is more lipid-soluble than amphetamine, it enters the brain faster. Methamphetamine carries a significant risk of addiction and remains widely used as a street drug.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use. Withdrawal symptoms occur in up to 87.6% of chronic high-dose users and persist for three to four weeks with a marked crash phase in the first week. Symptoms include anxiety, drug craving, dysphoric mood, fatigue, increased appetite, lack of motivation, and vivid dreams. Depression from methamphetamine withdrawal lasts longer and is more severe than that of cocaine withdrawal.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Methamphetamine is widely considered one of the most addictive substances due to the intense euphoria it produces. It has extremely high abuse liability with strong compulsive redosing patterns, particularly when vaporized or injected. The drug produces powerful cravings and psychological dependence develops readily with repeated use.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Chronic high-dose use can induce stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, delusions, and delirium. This is similar to paranoid schizophrenia and may include bizarre and violent behavior. About 5-15% of users who develop amphetamine psychosis fail to recover completely. Symptoms are magnified by sleep deprivation which commonly accompanies heavy use. Psychosis very rarely arises from therapeutic use.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Seizures are an uncommon effect but can occur in those predisposed to them, especially during physical stress such as dehydration, fatigue, or malnourishment, or with extended misuse. Death from methamphetamine poisoning is typically preceded by convulsions and coma.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: At moderate to heavy recreational doses, methamphetamine is directly neurotoxic to dopaminergic and serotonergic neurons, causing adverse changes in brain structure and function including reductions in grey matter volume. Chronic abuse is associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Methamphetamine acts primarily as a potent releasing agent of dopamine, norepinephrine, and to a lesser extent serotonin through several converging mechanisms. As a potent full agonist at trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), it induces phosphorylation and functional reversal of monoamine transporters on the cell membrane, driving neurotransmitter efflux into the synaptic cleft. It also inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), preventing monoamine storage in synaptic vesicles and promoting their release into the cytosol. Additional contributing mechanisms include increased intracellular calcium driving dopamine transporter phosphorylation, enhanced expression of the dopamine-synthesizing enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, and reduced surface expression of dopamine transporters. Methamphetamine also acts as an agonist at alpha-2 adrenergic and sigma receptors (with greater affinity for σ1 than σ2) and inhibits both monoamine oxidase A and B.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Methamphetamine is metabolized primarily by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with amphetamine and 4-hydroxymethamphetamine as its principal metabolites. Several additional minor metabolites are produced, a number of which retain sympathomimetic activity. Methamphetamine is itself a CYP2D6 inhibitor, and co-administration of other CYP2D6 inhibitors prolongs its elimination half-life. The elimination half-life averages 9 to 12 hours but ranges broadly from 5 to 30 hours. Oral bioavailability is approximately 67%, rising to 79% via the intranasal route and 67 to 90% when smoked, with complete bioavailability when administered intravenously.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Repeated methamphetamine use over time can produce rapid tolerance, causing users to need larger doses for similar effects. Euphoria fades especially quickly, often becoming much weaker after the first few uses or after several doses in succession. Subjective effects such as empathy enhancement and openness also tend to vanish early, once initial exposures or broader tolerance have occurred. Chronically tolerant users may require dosages 2-3 times higher than amounts effective for naive users.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text:
The development of methamphetamine followed shortly after the creation of its parent compound. Romanian chemist Lazăr Edeleanu first synthesized amphetamine in Germany in 1887, naming it phenylisopropylamine. Six years later, Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi achieved the first synthesis of methamphetamine from ephedrine in 1893. Despite these discoveries, neither substance found pharmacological application for several decades.

A significant advancement came in 1919 when Japanese pharmacologist Akira Ogata developed a method to produce methamphetamine hydrochloride through the reduction of ephedrine using red phosphorus and iodine. This crystalline salt form would eventually become the basis for both pharmaceutical manufacturing and illicit production.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Beginning in 1938, methamphetamine became available as a nonprescription drug in Germany under the brand name Pervitin, manufactured by the Berlin-based Temmler pharmaceutical company. The German military subsequently incorporated the drug across all branches of the armed forces, valuing its stimulant properties and capacity to sustain wakefulness during extended operations. Soldiers gave the tablets colloquial nicknames including "Stuka-Tablets" and "Hermann-Göring-Pills," the latter a sardonic allusion to the Reichsmarschall's well-known drug dependencies.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: The severe consequences of use, particularly debilitating withdrawal symptoms, prompted military authorities to sharply reduce distribution by 1940. By 1941, access required a prescription, and supply was tightly controlled. Soldiers subsequently received only a few tablets at a time and were discouraged from combat use. As historian Łukasz Kamieński documented, soldiers who took Pervitin before battle typically found themselves unable to function effectively for one to two days afterward, experiencing severe drug hangovers that rendered them ineffective. In some cases, soldiers under the influence committed violent acts against civilians or turned on their own officers. Near the war's conclusion, methamphetamine became a component in an experimental combination drug designated D-IX. Beyond Germany, both Allied and Axis forces employed amphetamines and methamphetamine throughout the conflict for their performance-enhancing and fatigue-reducing properties.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text:
Following World War II, pharmaceutical methamphetamine transitioned into civilian medical use. Obetrol Pharmaceuticals patented Obetrol in the 1950s, establishing one of the first branded pharmaceutical methamphetamine products indicated for obesity treatment. The drug's psychological and stimulant properties made it an extremely popular weight-loss medication in the United States throughout the 1950s and 1960s.

As evidence of the drug's addictive properties accumulated, governments began implementing increasingly strict controls on its production and distribution. Pharmaceutical methamphetamine continues to be marketed under the trade name Desoxyn, with the trademark passing from Lundbeck to Italian pharmaceutical company Recordati in January 2013.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Illicit methamphetamine production has become concentrated in the Golden Triangle of Southeast Asia, with Shan State in Myanmar emerging as the world's leading manufacturing center. Operations in this region produce both ya ba (the tablet form popular in East Asia) and crystalline methamphetamine for distribution across East and Southeast Asia, the Pacific, and the United States. The Cantonese Chinese syndicate known as Sam Gor, or "The Company," is understood to be the primary international criminal organization driving this production expansion. Comprised of members from five different triads, the organization allegedly controls approximately 40 percent of the Asia-Pacific methamphetamine market while also trafficking heroin and ketamine. Sam Gor generates an estimated minimum of eight billion dollars annually and maintains operations spanning Myanmar, Thailand, New Zealand, Australia, Japan, China, and Taiwan. Previously operating manufacturing facilities in Southern China, the organization relocated production primarily to Shan State, contributing to a massive surge in regional crystal methamphetamine supply around 2019.

chunks.title: Methamphetamine
chunks.text: Despite well-documented risks of dependence and substantial media attention devoted to its dangers, methamphetamine remains widely used as a recreational substance globally.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic depressant of the quinazolinone class. Its sedative properties were first identified by researchers in the 1950s, and it was patented in the United States in 1962. During the 1970s, it saw widespread medical use for insomnia and muscle relaxation, as well as significant recreational popularity within the counterculture and disco scenes. Though largely discontinued as a pharmaceutical, it continues to be produced clandestinely, particularly in South Africa. Illicit methaqualone products are often adulterated, sometimes with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops rapidly, with daily use of even moderate doses producing addiction within a couple of weeks. Withdrawal symptoms include restlessness, irritability, insomnia, tremors, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and muscle twitches. Severe withdrawal can involve mental confusion, delirium, hallucinations, high fever, and epileptic-like seizures that can be fatal.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Methaqualone is described as extremely addictive with high abuse potential. Psychological dependence is very common with regular use, particularly at doses over 600 mg per day. Users report severe cravings for the drug persisting for extended periods after cessation.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Paranoia, panic, and anxiety can occur during use, particularly at certain doses. More severe psychiatric effects including mental confusion, delirium, nightmares, and hallucinations are primarily associated with withdrawal rather than acute intoxication.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Seizures represent a significant risk with methaqualone both in overdose and during withdrawal from chronic use. Convulsions have been documented in both circumstances, with withdrawal seizures being potentially fatal. The drug has anticonvulsant properties at normal doses, but tolerance develops to this effect with repeated administration.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is a significant effect at higher doses and can progress to respiratory arrest in overdose; the combination with other depressants substantially increases this risk.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Methaqualone overdose shows a lower incidence of respiratory depression compared to barbiturate poisoning, though it remains a primary cause of death in fatal overdoses.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiac effects including reduced heart rate and blood pressure occur during use; cardiac arrest is possible in severe overdose.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: Methaqualone

chunks.title: Methaqualone

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Methaqualone acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, enhancing the inhibitory chloride currents generated by GABA. Some minor direct agonist activity has also been observed, though it is not comparatively significant. Its binding site is located at the transmembrane β(+)/α(-) subunit interface, distinct from those of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and neurosteroids, though it may partially overlap with the etomidate binding site. Methaqualone may also function as a negative allosteric modulator at certain GABA-A receptor subtypes, and is therefore considered a mixed GABA-A receptor modulator. It shows negligible affinity for a wide array of other potential targets, including other receptors and neurotransmitter transporters.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Methaqualone is readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and distributes into body fat, liver, and brain tissue via plasma. Peak plasma concentrations are reached approximately 2 hours after oral administration. Its elimination half-life has been variably reported, with estimates ranging from approximately 4 hours to as long as 60 hours.

Physical dependence can develop within about two weeks when moderate doses are used every day. Tolerance to euphoric effects appears to develop faster than tolerance to respiratory depression, substantially increasing overdose risk when users raise doses to regain earlier subjective effects.
