chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text: Methaqualone was first synthesized in India in 1951 by M.I. Gujral as part of a research program seeking antimalarial compounds. Although the substance proved ineffective against malaria, researchers identified its hypnotic properties by 1955. A subsequent pharmacological study in 1957 confirmed methaqualone was the most active compound among the group synthesized during this research effort. The substance was patented in the United States by Wallace and Tiernan in 1962, setting the stage for its pharmaceutical development.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text:
Methaqualone entered pharmaceutical markets across multiple countries throughout the early 1960s, marketed as a safer alternative to barbiturate sedatives. In West Germany, Merck launched the drug under the brand name Revonal in 1960, offering 200 mg and 300 mg tablets. Reports of misuse led to prescription requirements being implemented in 1963, after which overdose incidents reportedly declined significantly.

Eisai Company introduced methaqualone to Japan in October 1960 as Hyminal, initially available without prescription. Widespread nonmedical use prompted authorities to designate it a "powerful drug" by June 1964, restricting sales to pharmacies with mandatory record-keeping requirements.

In the United Kingdom, Roussel Laboratories launched Mandrax in 1965, a preparation combining methaqualone with diphenhydramine. The product addressed significant demand for a nonbarbiturate sleeping medication following the thalidomide disaster. By 1968, methaqualone had become the most widely prescribed sedative in Britain. Its recreational popularity increased further when heroin became more restricted in April 1968 and injectable methamphetamine was withdrawn later that year.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text:
The FDA approved methaqualone in 1965 with minimal regulatory controls. William H. Rorer marketed the drug as Quaalude, advertising it as a safe and non-addictive medication primarily indicated for insomnia and anxiety. Despite early reports of nonmedical use emerging from other countries, the FDA approved a new 300 mg formulation in 1967, doubling the available per-tablet dosage.

By 1972, methaqualone had become one of the most popular recreational drugs in the country. Regulatory response came in 1973 when the substance was placed in Schedule II. Rorer subsequently sold its rights to Quaalude to Lemmon Pharmaceuticals in 1978. After experiencing declining popularity in the mid-1970s, recreational use resurged around 1978 before the substance was ultimately moved to Schedule I in June 1984.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text:
Methaqualone developed a substantial recreational following throughout the 1960s and 1970s, becoming particularly associated with the hippie movement and disco club scene. Users gave the drug numerous nicknames including "ludes," "disco biscuits," "mandies," and "randy mandies." The term "wall bangers" emerged in reference to the motor impairment the substance commonly produced.

The drug was widely characterized as an aphrodisiac beginning in this era, with some users referring to it as a "love drug" and claiming it could substantially enhance sexual desire. This reputation persisted in cultural memory and has been depicted in films such as The Wolf of Wall Street.

chunks.title: Methaqualone
chunks.text:
During the 1980s and 1990s, the South African apartheid regime operated Project Coast, a chemical and biological weapons program that at one point focused on nonlethal riot control agents, including methaqualone. This period contributed to the substance becoming established in the country.

Mandrax became particularly entrenched within coloured and Indian communities in South Africa. A distinctive consumption method known as "white pipe" developed, in which users combine crushed tablets with cannabis or tobacco and smoke the mixture through a broken-off bottle neck. Since at least 2001, the drug has remained widely used throughout South Africa, commonly referred to by local names including "smarties" and "geluk-tablette," the latter translating to "happy tablets." Clandestinely produced methaqualone continues to be seized by authorities in the country and elsewhere around the world.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: Methcathinone is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and phenethylamine classes. First synthesized in 1928 in the United States, it was later used as an antidepressant in the Soviet Union. Structurally, it can be considered the cathinone analogue of methamphetamine. It produces amphetamine-like stimulant effects and is prevalent in central and eastern Europe, where it is sometimes sold as mephedrone or manufactured from over-the-counter ephedrine-containing medications.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop with prolonged or high-dosage use, producing methamphetamine-like withdrawal symptoms. Discontinuation after chronic use is associated with depression, anxiety, anhedonia, and cognitive fatigue, though psychological withdrawal symptoms appear more prominent than classical physical dependence.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: Methcathinone is considered highly psychologically addictive with abuse potential similar to amphetamines. Extreme compulsive redosing is commonly reported, partly because initial effects may seem subtle, leading users to take additional doses. Animal studies have demonstrated pronounced drug-seeking behavior and craving.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: Chronic high-dose use may result in acute mental confusion ranging from mild paranoia to psychosis. These symptoms typically disappear quickly if use is stopped. Paranoia is also listed among acute cognitive effects at higher doses.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Methcathinone places considerable strain on the cardiovascular system, causing hypertension and tachycardia during use; risk of stroke or heart attack is elevated, particularly at high doses or with repeated administration.

chunks.text: Catecholamine release and reuptake inhibition causing sympathetic activation

chunks.title: Methcathinone

chunks.text: Illicitly manufactured methcathinone synthesized using potassium permanganate oxidation may contain manganese contamination, causing neurotoxicity with Parkinson-like symptoms (manganism); this risk is specific to contaminated batches rather than the pure compound.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: Methcathinone acts primarily as a norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent with strong affinity for both the dopamine transporter (DAT) and the norepinephrine transporter (NET). It has also been described as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Its affinity for the serotonin transporter (SERT) is comparatively lower.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text: The carbonyl group at the beta position of the cathinone backbone introduces polarity that somewhat reduces the compound's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier compared to amphetamine. No detailed metabolic pathway, enzyme, or elimination data are available in current sources.

chunks.title: Methcathinone
chunks.text:
Methcathinone was first synthesized in the United States in 1928. The compound was subsequently patented by the pharmaceutical company Parke-Davis in 1957. During the 1930s and 1940s, the Soviet Union employed the substance therapeutically as an antidepressant, where it was known as ephedrone (Эфедрон in Russian). Over time, methcathinone became established as a recreational substance in the Soviet Union and later in Russia, where it developed a long history of non-medical use.

International efforts to control methcathinone began in the mid-1990s when the United States government recommended to the United Nations Secretary-General that the substance be added to Schedule I of the Convention on Psychotropic Substances around 1994. Following this recommendation, China added methcathinone to its list of prohibited substances in 1995 and ceased any remaining pharmaceutical applications.

The substance remains prevalent in central and eastern European regions, where it is sometimes misrepresented as the more widely recognized cathinone derivative mephedrone. It is also frequently synthesized clandestinely from over-the-counter medications containing ephedrine or pseudoephedrine.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Methiopropamine is a synthetic stimulant of the thiophene class and a structural analogue of methamphetamine, first synthesized in 1942. Despite this structural similarity, it is neither an amphetamine nor a phenethylamine, as it features a thiophene ring in place of a benzene ring. It entered recreational drug markets around 2010 as a research chemical and legal high. Methiopropamine is generally characterized as a functional stimulant with limited euphoric properties.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Cravings and withdrawal effects may occur following cessation of chronic use, though physical dependence appears less prominent than psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Moderately addictive with high potential for abuse and capable of causing psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, particularly with insufflation or vaporization routes, though generally considered less severe than substances like MDPV or mephedrone.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Capable of producing stimulant psychosis with symptoms including paranoia, visual and auditory hallucinations, delusions, and incoherent speech. Risk is significantly elevated by high doses, repeated dosing, and accompanying sleep deprivation. Case reports document paranoid delusions, dysmorphophobia, and self-harming behavior in affected users.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular stimulation including chest tightness, chest pains, racing heart, vasoconstriction, and palpitations are somewhat common at higher doses and with repeated dosing; serious cardiovascular events appear to be associated with overdose or extreme use patterns rather than typical recreational use.

The rate of tolerance development has not been precisely characterized, though locomotor sensitization studies in rodents suggest neuroadaptive changes occur with repeated exposure.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Methiopropamine was first synthesized and reported in 1942. The work was primarily conducted at the University of Michigan, with limited pharmacological evaluation carried out at Parke Davis pharmaceutical company. This early research demonstrated that the compound possessed substantial pressor (blood pressure-increasing) activity. Following its initial characterization, the substance remained largely obscure for several decades with no significant research attention or recreational interest.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: Methiopropamine appeared for public sale in the United Kingdom in December 2010, marketed as a "research chemical" or "legal high" and sold in both powder and pill form. One of its earliest brand names was "Blow." The compound's structural resemblance to methamphetamine initially led vendors and users to anticipate stronger recreational properties than the substance could actually deliver. Throughout the 2010s, MPA was marketed under numerous brand names including Ivory Dove Ultra, China White, Walter White, Quick Silver Ultra, Bullet, Mind Melt, Pink Panthers, Poke, Rush, and Snow White. Products labeled as "Synthacaine" contributed to some users expecting cocaine-like effects, though these products were often found to contain additional substances beyond MPA alone.

chunks.title: Methiopropamine
chunks.text: MPA was frequently combined with other novel psychoactive substances and sold as branded blends. Notable products included Sparkle-E (combining MPA with MDAI, later reformulated with 5-MeO-DALT), Pink Panther (MPA with MDAI and other compounds), Green Beans and M&M (both containing MPA with NM2AI), and GoGaine (MPA with MDAI, later reformulated with ephedrine). These formulations evolved over time as manufacturers adjusted their compositions in response to market conditions and regulatory changes. In Scotland, MPA gained particular traction among people who inject drugs, reportedly replacing ethylphenidate as a preferred substance within certain user communities following controls placed on methylphenidate-based novel psychoactive substances.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text: Methoxetamine is a dissociative substance of the arylcyclohexylamine class, structurally related to ketamine and PCP. It was intentionally designed as a possible therapy for phantom limb syndrome and first appeared on grey markets in late 2010. MXE was noted for its ketamine-like dissociative effects with a pronounced psychedelic character. Once widely available as a research chemical, it is now considered largely extinct due to global bans on its production.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text: MXE does not appear to be physically addictive. However, when psychological dependence has developed, some withdrawal effects may occur upon sudden cessation of use.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text: MXE is considered moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and is capable of producing psychological dependence among certain users. Multiple reports describe it as 'more-ish' with tendencies toward compulsive redosing, and cases of daily habitual use have been documented across online communities.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated heavy use over extended periods may cause bladder and urinary tract problems similar to those seen with ketamine, including urinary frequency, urgency, pelvic pain, and hematuria; MXE's higher potency means smaller doses are required, potentially reducing but not eliminating this risk with chronic abuse patterns.

chunks.text: Many MXE effects can become less responsive after sustained repeated use. The pace varies considerably by person; some users report tolerance building over weeks, while others notice substantial tolerance after a single night of heavy consumption.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
Methoxetamine represents a deliberate exercise in rational drug design rather than accidental discovery. The compound was conceived by an anonymous chemist who sought to create a ketamine analogue with improved therapeutic properties. Structurally, MXE incorporates features from both ketamine and phencyclidine, sharing particular resemblance to 3-MeO-PCP while maintaining ketamine's core arylcyclohexylamine scaffold.

The design philosophy behind MXE centered on two primary objectives: enhancing the antidepressant potential observed with ketamine while minimizing the urological toxicity associated with chronic ketamine use. The reasoning held that a more potent compound would require lower doses, thereby reducing the accumulation of bladder-toxic metabolites linked to ketamine-associated cystitis. The compound was also reportedly developed with potential applications for phantom limb syndrome in mind.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
The qualitative effects of MXE were first documented on online drug forums in May 2010, with small-scale commercial availability following by September of that year. The compound's rapid proliferation drew the attention of European drug monitoring agencies; by November 2010, the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction had formally identified the substance as an emerging novel psychoactive compound.

Growth in the MXE market proved substantial over the following months. By July 2011, the EMCDDA had catalogued 58 separate websites offering the compound, typically at prices ranging from 145 to 195 euros for ten grams. The substance was distributed almost exclusively through online research chemical vendors rather than traditional street-level markets, positioning it firmly within the then-emerging novel psychoactive substances economy.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text: MXE developed a substantial following within psychonaut and electronic music communities during its period of availability. The dance music press documented the compound's penetration into club culture, with Mixmag reporting in January 2012 that users had coined the slang term "roflcoptr" for the substance. UK Home Office press releases subsequently referred to the drug as "mexxy," terminology that mainstream media would adopt. The compound acquired what many users describe as a cult status, valued for a distinctive quality frequently characterized as "magic"—combining pronounced euphoria, depth of introspection, and remarkable versatility across dosage ranges. Users praised its psychedelic character relative to other dissociatives and its suitability for both social settings and solitary exploration at higher doses.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text: However, regulatory action—particularly production bans in China, which had served as the primary manufacturing source—severely disrupted global supply. The compound became progressively more difficult to obtain, and by the mid-2010s was largely considered extinct from the research chemical marketplace. Contemporary discussions of MXE among former users often carry a tone of nostalgia, with one commentator noting that people speak of the substance in terms typically reserved for a departed lover or a prize catch that somehow escaped.

- Alcohol (There is a high risk of memory loss, vomiting and severe ataxia from this combination.)
- AMT
- Diphenhydramine (There is a high risk of serotonin syndrome from this combination. Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. MXE has a high likelihood of increasing DPH's deliriant effects at higher dosages and can greatly increase the risk of injury, mania, and psychosis. Medical dosages are unlikely to be of concern.)
- GHB/GBL (Both substances cause ataxia and bring a risk of vomiting and unconsciousness.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
If the individual falls unconscious while under the influence there is a severe risk of vomit aspiration if they are not placed in the recovery position.)
- Lithium (There is a risk of serotonin syndrome when combining Lithium with MXE, as Lithium can induce serotonin syndrome in conjunction with other serotonergic drugs, and MXE has shown a notable affinity for the serotonin transporter.)
- Opioids (This combination can potentiate the effects of the opioid)
- Tramadol

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
Methoxetamine — unsafe combinations:
- DXM (There is a risk of serotonin syndrome when combining DXM with MXE, due to DXM and MXE both being SRI’s. MXE and DXM having notable affinities for the serotonin transporter.)
- MAOIs (MAO-B inhibitors appear to increase the potency of MXE. MAO-A inhbitors have some negative reports associated with the combination but there isn't much information available)

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
Methoxetamine — caution combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds
- Amphetamines (Risk of tachycardia, hypertension, and manic states)
- Benzodiazepines (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess.)
- Cocaine (Stimulants taken with MXE can lead to hypermanic states much more easily, especially if sleep is avoided.)
- DOx compounds (As an NMDA antagonist MXE potentiates DOx which can be unpleasantly intense)
- MDMA (There have been reports of risky serotonergic interactions when the two are taken at the same time, but MXE taken to the end of an MDMA experience does not appear to cause the same issues.)
- NBOMe compounds (As an NMDA antagonist MXE potentiates NBOMes which can be unpleasantly intense)
- PCP (There are no reports available about this combination)
- Pregabalin (Pregabalin and MXE may synergize and increase each other’s negative side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and loss of consciousness.

chunks.title: Methoxetamine
chunks.text:
Caution is advised for anything above low dosages due to seizure concerns, and all dosages for individuals with higher risk seizure profiles and or behavior.)
- SSRIs (Depending on the SSRI this combination can be unpredictable)

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.text: Methoxphenidine is a dissociative substance of the diarylethylamine class and a more potent analogue of diphenidine. First described in a 1989 patent investigating treatments for neurotoxic injury, it emerged on the gray market shortly after the 2013 UK ban on arylcyclohexylamines. It has not been formally studied in humans. Methoxphenidine has been associated with multiple fatalities, reports of unpredictable effects and blackouts, and cases of acute psychosis. Careful dose moderation is strongly advised.

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.text: Addictive potential has not been established, though the substance is categorized as habit-forming. Strong tolerance development may contribute to compulsive redosing patterns.

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.text: Psychotic episodes have been reported, including at least one case associated with violent behavior resulting in a murder in June 2014. Acute intoxication has been reported to produce confusion.

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.text: Seizures have been reported at high doses according to user reports, warranting additional caution with dosing.

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute intoxication can produce hypertension and tachycardia; elevated blood pressure has been observed during use, along with peripheral vasoconstriction.

chunks.title: Methoxphenidine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects have been responsive to treatment with intravenous lorazepam in clinical settings.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.text: Methoxyacetyl-fentanyl is a highly potent synthetic opioid and fentanyl analogue classified as a depressant research chemical. Like other fentanyl analogues, it carries significant habit-forming potential. Its high potency presents serious overdose risks, as even minor dosing errors can prove fatal. Very limited information is available regarding its pharmacology and safety profile, making it an especially dangerous substance to use without proper harm reduction precautions.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.text: As an opioid classified as habit-forming, physical dependence with regular use is expected.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As an opioid, it carries significant potential for psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Potentially serious respiratory depression occurs during intoxication, which can be life-threatening; this risk is elevated at higher doses or when combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is the primary cause of death in fentanyl analog overdoses. Fentanyl analogs have killed hundreds of people throughout Europe and the former Soviet republics since the early 2000s.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.text: Methoxyacetylfentanyl is an opioid analgesic and a structural analog of fentanyl. While detailed receptor binding data for this compound has not been well characterized in the available literature, its classification as an opioid analgesic indicates activity at opioid receptors.

chunks.title: Methoxyacetyl-Fentanyl
chunks.text:
Methoxyacetylfentanyl, commonly abbreviated as MAF, emerged as part of a broader wave of synthetic opioid designer drugs that appeared on online markets during the 2010s. The substance belongs to a class of fentanyl analogs that have been associated with significant public health concerns across multiple regions.

The proliferation of novel fentanyl derivatives has occurred in distinct waves across different geographic regions. The first major resurgence began in Estonia and spread through Europe and former Soviet republics in the early 2000s, resulting in hundreds of fatalities. A second wave emerged around 2014 in the United States, with the prevalence and associated mortality escalating substantially from 2016 onward. In response to mounting concerns about novel synthetic opioids, methoxyacetylfentanyl was placed into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act in the United States in October 2017, a measure taken to address what regulators described as an imminent hazard to public safety.

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Methoxyketamine is a dissociative research chemical of the arylcyclohexylamine class and a structural analogue of ketamine. It is reported to produce dissociative and anesthetic effects comparable to those of ketamine, though at a slightly lower potency. The substance is considered extremely rare, with very limited availability and documentation. As with other dissociatives in its class, it may carry habit-forming potential.

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting some potential for psychological dependence, though specific details on addiction liability are not documented.

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Methoxyketamine is an arylcyclohexylamine and a structural analog of ketamine in which the chlorine atom has been replaced with a methoxy group. Based on its arylcyclohexylamine structure, methoxyketamine most likely acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, though its precise receptor pharmacology has not been well characterized. It is reported to be less potent than ketamine.

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Lower potency than ketamine; precise affinity not established

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text:
Methoxyketamine was first documented in the scientific literature in 1963, making it one of the earlier arylcyclohexylamine compounds to be described. The substance represents a structural analog of ketamine in which the chlorine atom has been substituted with a methoxy group. Chemical literature has documented its synthesis through the rearrangement of an amino ketone precursor.

Despite its relatively early documentation compared to many other dissociative research chemicals, methoxyketamine has remained exceedingly rare in both research and recreational contexts. The compound has not achieved significant prevalence in designer drug markets, and limited information exists regarding its pharmacological properties or subjective effects in humans.

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives, NMDA receptor antagonists

chunks.title: Methoxyketamine
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (uncompetitive)

chunks.title: Methoxypiperamide
chunks.text: Methoxypiperamide is a designer drug of the piperazine class, structurally the 4-methoxy-α-keto analog of methylbenzylpiperazine. It has been sold online as a research chemical, typically in combination with mephtetramine, as it is reported to be inactive on its own. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology or toxicity. Some jurisdictions have classified it as a hallucinogen, though its psychoactive profile remains poorly characterized.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Methylmethaqualone is a depressant research chemical and a more potent structural analogue of methaqualone. It is characterized by a comparatively short duration of action relative to its parent compound. The substance carries significant safety concerns, as it is suspected to be neurotoxic and has been reported to produce proconvulsive effects. Due to its limited research history and potential for harm, it should be approached with considerable caution.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting some potential for psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Animal studies demonstrate that convulsions occur at doses only slightly above the effective sedative dose, indicating a very narrow safety margin. Human users have reported pro-convulsive effects, and a high number of seizures have been associated with this substance, making it particularly hazardous at elevated doses.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: The drug is suspected to be neurotoxic, though the specific conditions, mechanisms, and extent of potential neurotoxic effects have not been fully characterized.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Methylmethaqualone produces its sedative and hypnotic effects through agonist activity at the β subunit of the GABA-A receptor. In animal models, it has been found to be approximately three times more potent than its parent compound methaqualone.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Methylmethaqualone is a designer drug analogue of methaqualone that appears to have emerged on the German black market during the late 1990s. The compound was made illegal in Germany in 1999, and around the same time, the United States Drug Enforcement Administration listed it as a "drug of forensic interest." Beyond these regulatory actions, very little documented information about this substance's history or cultural context is available.

chunks.title: Methylmethaqualone
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor agonist

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.text: Methylnaphthidate is a synthetic stimulant of the phenidate class and a structural analog of methylphenidate in which the core benzene ring is replaced by a naphthalene group. First investigated pharmacologically in the early 2000s, it appeared on the research chemical market around 2014. Unlike typical methylphenidate analogs, it is reported to function as a triple reuptake inhibitor with appreciable serotonergic activity. Very little is known about its toxicity or long-term health effects.

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.text: Methylnaphthidate has abuse potential comparable to amphetamine, cocaine, or methylphenidate because it acts at dopamine transporters, produces euphoria, and may not produce marked tolerance. Its euphoric rush is brief and compulsive, similar to cocaine, which can encourage repeated dosing.

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Toxic and fatal dose thresholds have not been established. Methylnaphthidate is a research chemical with minimal documented human-use history.

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure occur during use; the risk of cardiovascular strain increases with higher doses or when combined with other stimulants.

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Higher doses make adverse effects more probable and, in extreme cases, may result in severe injury or death.

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.text: Monoamine triple reuptake inhibitor (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin)

chunks.title: Methylnaphthidate
chunks.text: Binding profile: Monoamine triple reuptake inhibitor (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin)

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Methylone is a synthetic stimulant and entactogen of the cathinone class. First synthesized by Peyton Jacob III and Alexander Shulgin in 1996 as a potential antidepressant, it later gained popularity as a recreational substance. Methylone is frequently used as a substitute for MDMA due to overlapping effects, though Shulgin himself described it as lacking MDMA's "unique magic," noting it is more stimulating and less empathogenic. It has been commonly mis-sold as MDMA.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: When addiction has developed, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur if a person suddenly stops their usage. The nature and severity of withdrawal symptoms have not been well characterized.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Chronic use of methylone can be considered moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence among certain users. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, likely promoted by the substance's time compression effects which speed up the subjective experience.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Abuse at high dosages for prolonged periods can potentially result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Based on research into similar stimulants, approximately 5-15% of those who develop stimulant psychosis may not recover completely, though antipsychotic medications effectively resolve symptoms of acute psychosis. Psychosis very rarely arises from occasional or moderate use.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Limited data on seizure risk from methylone use alone.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Not studied for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available for methylone.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Higher doses and repeated use have been associated with chest pains, heart palpitations, and elevated blood pressure and heart rate; worrying cardiovascular increases have been reported at doses exceeding 180-200 mg.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular strain appears dose-dependent. Users with pre-existing heart or circulatory problems, high blood pressure, or diabetes should avoid use.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Animal studies have found methylone to be a monoaminergic neurotoxin producing serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotoxicity in rodents; however, one study suggests methylone may be less neurotoxic than MDMA at moderate doses.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Produces serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotoxicity via monoaminergic mechanisms

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Human neurotoxicity data is lacking. The significance of animal findings for human recreational use patterns remains unclear.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Temperature regulation suppression and increased body temperature occur during use, with hyperthermia risk elevated during physical activity in hot environments such as dance venues.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Proper hydration is important but over-drinking water can lead to water intoxication. Users should sip water rather than drinking large amounts.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: 3-Hydroxy-4-methoxymethcathinone (3-OH-4-MeO-MC)

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Methylone acts as a mixed releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Its serotonin transporter affinity (Ki of 242.1 nM) is roughly 3-fold lower than that of MDMA, while its norepinephrine and dopamine transporter affinities are comparable; its VMAT2 affinity is approximately 13-fold lower, contributing to a profile that balances reuptake inhibition with monoamine release rather than acting as a predominant releaser. Methylone is also a variable-potency partial agonist at 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, and 5-HT1D receptors and shows no significant activity at 5-HT2A or 5-HT2B receptors. Its activity at 5-HT2C is uncertain, with one study reporting no significant affinity and another finding potent near-full agonism via the Gαq signaling pathway.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: In humans, the mean elimination half-life of methylone following oral doses of 50 to 200 mg ranges from 5.8 to 6.9 hours. The two major metabolic pathways are N-demethylation to methylenedioxycathinone (MDC) and demethylation followed by O-methylation, producing 4-hydroxy-3-methoxymethcathinone (HMMC) and 3-hydroxy-4-methoxymethcathinone (3-OH-4-MeO-MC). An additional metabolite, 3,4-dihydroxymethcathinone (HHMC), has also been identified. In rats administered 5 mg/kg, approximately 26% was excreted as HMMC within 48 hours, with less than 3% excreted unchanged.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: One study found no significant affinity; another reported potent near-full agonism via Gαq pathway only

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Many effects can become tolerant rapidly with sustained repeated use, so comparable results may require higher doses.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Methylone was first synthesized by chemists Peyton Jacob III and Alexander Shulgin in the mid-1990s, with the compound first described in scientific literature by 1996. The synthesis occurred after the publication of Shulgin's PiHKAL in 1991, and consequently methylone was not included in that work; it was later documented in The Shulgin Index (2011). Jacob and Shulgin patented methylone as a potential antidepressant and antiparkinsonian agent, though these therapeutic applications were never developed or brought to market. Shulgin himself noted that the compound has "almost the same potency of MDMA, but it does not produce the same effects," describing it as having "an almost antidepressant action, pleasant and positive, but not the unique magic of MDMA."

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: The name "methylone" later created some confusion, as it is also a trademarked brand name for an injectable form of methylprednisolone, a corticosteroid hormone used to treat arthritis and severe allergic reactions. While an alternate chemical nomenclature of bk-MDMA (beta-keto-MDMA) was proposed, "methylone" had already become widely established before the trademark conflict was noticed. The analogous naming convention was however adopted for related compounds such as bk-MDEA and bk-MBDB.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text:
Methylone was encountered as a designer and recreational drug by 2004, approximately a decade after its initial synthesis. The compound was marketed under various product names, most notably "Explosion," which was confirmed through chemical analysis to contain methylone as its active ingredient. It was also sold as pure powder and in formulations marketed as household chemicals.

In the Netherlands, methylone was available in smartshops until early April 2005. In New Zealand, the substance was sold from November 2005 to April 2006 as an MDMA substitute under the brand name "Ease," before being withdrawn following legal disputes with the government.

During its period of legal availability, methylone was frequently mis-sold as MDMA. However, users have characterized it as less empathogenic and more stimulating than MDMA, with a notably shorter duration of effects.

chunks.title: Methylone
chunks.text: Despite never being developed following its original 1996 patent for antidepressant and antiparkinsonian use, methylone has re-emerged as a subject of clinical investigation. Under the developmental code TSND-201, Transcend Therapeutics is investigating the compound for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). As of July 2024, the substance is in phase 2 clinical trials for this indication.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate is a central nervous system stimulant of the phenidate class. First synthesized in 1944, it became one of the most widely prescribed medications for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy, marketed under brands such as Ritalin and Concerta. Outside clinical settings, it is used recreationally and as a cognitive enhancer, though its stimulant and euphoric effects are generally considered less pronounced than those of amphetamines.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Physical dependence and withdrawal are mainly reported with high-dose or non-medical use and are uncommon at therapeutic doses. Withdrawal symptoms following abrupt discontinuation may include lethargy, apathy, depression, and paranoia, but these are not life-threatening.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate has moderate liability among addictive drugs, with addiction and psychological dependence occurring primarily when used at high doses or in non-medical contexts. At therapeutic doses, it does not sufficiently activate the reward system to cause addiction; however, its dopamine reuptake inhibition can induce euphoria at higher doses, contributing to abuse potential.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate can worsen psychosis in people who are already psychotic; in very rare cases, it has been associated with the emergence of new psychotic symptoms. Visual hallucinations are very rarely reported. Overdose may trigger hallucinations and delirium. Should be used with extreme caution in people with bipolar disorder due to potential induction of mania or hypomania.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Seizures and convulsions are associated with abusive use, higher doses, and severe overdose rather than typical therapeutic use. Convulsions in overdose may be followed by coma.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute cardiovascular effects including elevated heart rate, blood pressure changes, and palpitations occur during use; these are typically mild at therapeutic doses. chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate acts primarily as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI), blocking both the dopamine transporter (DAT) and the norepinephrine transporter (NET) to increase extraneuronal concentrations of these neurotransmitters. Its activity is most pronounced at the dopamine transporter, with a lesser degree of norepinephrine reuptake inhibition. Both enantiomers of the racemic mixture display affinity for the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, though no direct binding to the serotonin transporter has been observed. Initial findings also suggested affinity at the 5-HT2B receptor, but a subsequent study found no significant activity at this site.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, resulting in oral bioavailability of approximately 11 to 52% with considerable individual variation. It is rapidly metabolized by the carboxylesterase enzyme CES1A1 via de-esterification to ritalinic acid, which possesses little to no pharmacological activity. The d-isomer is substantially more bioavailable than the l-isomer when taken orally and is primarily responsible for the pharmacological effects of the racemic mixture. Approximately 97% of the metabolized drug is excreted in urine, with less than 1% appearing unchanged. The elimination half-life of immediate-release formulations is approximately 2 to 3 hours.

chunks.text: Tolerance develops relatively quickly with repeated use, particularly to the euphoric and reinforcing effects. With continued high-dose or abusive use, progressively higher doses may be required to achieve the same effects.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate was first synthesized in 1944 by Swiss chemist Leandro Panizzon while working for the pharmaceutical company CIBA (now Novartis). Panizzon named the compound after his wife Marguerite, nicknamed "Rita," who became the first person to take the substance. Rita used methylphenidate to compensate for low blood pressure and described its effects to her husband, leading to the brand name "Ritalin." The drug was not identified as a central nervous system stimulant until 1954.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: Methylphenidate received approval for medical use in the United States in 1955 and was introduced to the market in 1957. It was originally marketed as a mixture of two racemates—80% erythro and 20% threo isomers—under the brand name Centedrin. Subsequent research demonstrated that the central stimulant activity was primarily associated with the threo racemate, leading to modern formulations that contain only the threo isomer in a 50:50 mixture of d- and l-isomers. When first released in the United States, methylphenidate was also available in a parenteral (injectable) form intended for use by medical professionals. This formulation was indicated to produce a focused, talkative state that could help patients overcome resistance to therapy. The parenteral form was later discontinued due to concerns about limited therapeutic benefit and the potential for inducing psychic dependence.

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text: The drug's initial medical applications included treatment of barbiturate-induced coma, narcolepsy, and depression. It was also prescribed for memory deficits in elderly patients. During its history, methylphenidate has been prescribed for various other conditions including chronic fatigue, and at one point was marketed as a general "pep pill."

chunks.title: Methylphenidate
chunks.text:
Beginning in the 1960s, methylphenidate came to be used for treating children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, building on foundational work by American psychiatrist Charles Bradley. Bradley had conducted earlier studies on the use of psychostimulant drugs such as Benzedrine with children then described as "maladjusted."

Production and prescription of methylphenidate rose substantially during the 1990s, particularly in the United States, as the ADHD diagnosis became better understood and more generally accepted within medical and mental health communities. In 2000, Alza Corporation received FDA approval to market Concerta, a modified-release formulation utilizing an osmotic-controlled release oral delivery system.

Long-acting formulations of methylphenidate are now considered among the most effective treatments for ADHD and are recommended as first-line options for children, adolescents, and adults. Studies spanning over twenty years have demonstrated the drug's safety and efficacy for long-term use. By 2023, methylphenidate had become the 50th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 13 million prescriptions written annually.

chunks.title: Methyprylon
chunks.text: Methyprylon is a sedative-hypnotic of the piperidinedione class, first developed in the 1940s by Hoffmann-La Roche. Structurally close to barbituric acid, it functions as a central nervous system depressant and was formerly prescribed for the treatment of insomnia. It was withdrawn from both the US and Canadian markets due to adverse effects, having been largely supplanted by benzodiazepines. Like other GABAergic sedatives, it carries risks of respiratory depression and dangerous interactions with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Metizolam is a synthetic depressant of the thienotriazolodiazepine class and the demethylated analogue of etizolam. A Japanese company patented it in 1995 as a possible anxiolytic, but it saw little to no human use before appearing as a grey-area research chemical in September 2015. Compared to etizolam, it is reportedly half as potent with a 60% longer half-life, producing similar anxiolytic, sedative, and muscle relaxant effects.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use. Abrupt discontinuation can be potentially dangerous or life-threatening, sometimes resulting in seizures or death. Withdrawal symptoms include rebound anxiety and insomnia. Gradual tapering over weeks is strongly recommended for regular users.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Thienodiazepines are described as extremely addictive with significant abuse potential. Compulsive redosing is a commonly reported effect, and tolerance to sedative-hypnotic effects develops within a couple days of repeated administration.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Paradoxical reactions including violent behavior, loss of impulse control, and irritability occur rarely, with an incidence rate below 1% in the general population. These occur with greater frequency in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, children, and patients on high-dose regimes. Delusions may occur during overdose.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Seizure risk is primarily associated with abrupt discontinuation following regular use, which can be life-threatening. Paradoxical seizures during use are rare, occurring with greater frequency in epileptics. Drugs that lower the seizure threshold should be avoided during withdrawal.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available. The long-term health effects have not been studied in any scientific context.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Metizolam acts as a full agonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor, enhancing the efficiency and effects of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). It is the demethylated analogue of etizolam, reported to be approximately half as potent.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text: Metizolam is absorbed fairly rapidly, with peak plasma levels reached between 30 minutes and 2 hours, and has a mean elimination half-life of approximately 3.4 hours. As a thienotriazolodiazepine, it is easily oxidized and rapidly metabolized, which contributes to a lower risk of accumulation even after prolonged use.

chunks.title: Metizolam
chunks.text:
Metizolam was first patented in 1995 by a Japanese pharmaceutical company as a potential medication for treating anxiety disorders. Despite this early patent, the compound was never developed for clinical use and has no documented history of medical application.

The substance emerged on the designer drug market in September 2015, when it began to be sold as a grey area research chemical through online vendors. Prior to this commercial availability, metizolam had little to no documented history of human use, making it one of many novel thienodiazepines to appear on the research chemical market with minimal pharmacological characterization in humans.

chunks.title: Mexazolam
chunks.text: Mexazolam is a long-acting benzodiazepine derivative marketed for the treatment of anxiety. It demonstrates preferential activity at α2/α3 GABAA receptor subunits, resulting in a lower sedative profile compared to classical benzodiazepines. Its active metabolites, including delorazepam and lorazepam, have notably long elimination half-lives. Clinical trials found it effective for short-term anxiety relief, though its therapeutic benefit has been reported to diminish after several weeks of continued use.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam is a short-acting depressant of the benzodiazepine class, specifically an imidazobenzodiazepine. Patented in 1974 and adopted for medical use in 1982, it is distinguished from other benzodiazepines by its rapid onset and brief duration of action. It is widely used clinically for procedural sedation, anesthesia, seizure management, and acute agitation, and is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. Like all benzodiazepines, it carries a risk of dependence with repeated use.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence occurs in approximately one-third of individuals treated with benzodiazepines for longer than 4 weeks. Midazolam infusions may induce tolerance and withdrawal syndrome in a matter of days. Sudden discontinuation can be dangerous or life-threatening, with withdrawal symptoms ranging from insomnia and anxiety to seizures and psychosis. Gradual tapering is essential to minimize withdrawal and rebound effects.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: High psychological dependence potential with risk increasing with dose and duration of treatment. Risk factors include dependent personality, use of short-acting and high-potency benzodiazepines, and history of substance abuse.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Psychosis may occur as a withdrawal symptom, particularly with abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use. Paradoxical reactions including anxiety, aggressive or violent behavior, and uncontrollable emotional responses can occur in rare susceptible individuals, particularly in children, elderly, those with history of alcohol use or aggressive behavior, and with intravenous administration.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: While midazolam itself has anticonvulsant properties, withdrawal from benzodiazepines can cause seizures that may be life-threatening. Paradoxical worsening of seizures occasionally occurs, and some benzodiazepines may trigger seizures in individuals with epilepsy. Gradual dose reduction is essential to prevent withdrawal seizures in dependent individuals.

chunks.title: Midazolam

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site. Rather than activating these receptors directly, it enhances the inhibitory effect of endogenous GABA by increasing the frequency of chloride ion channel opening, resulting in enhanced neural inhibition.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam undergoes biotransformation primarily via CYP3A4, which is present in both the liver and gastrointestinal tract mucosa. This dual-site metabolism results in substantial first-pass metabolism and relatively low oral bioavailability. The major metabolic product is alpha-hydroxymidazolam, accounting for 60 to 70% of biotransformation products. This metabolite is at least as potent as the parent compound at benzodiazepine receptors, though it contributes only approximately 10% of overall biological activity. A minor metabolite, 4-hydroxymidazolam, accounts for 5% or less of metabolic output. Midazolam also undergoes glucuronide conjugation. Elimination half-life in adults is generally short, though it is prolonged in the elderly, young children, and adolescents. Renal and hepatic function also affect pharmacokinetic parameters.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam was synthesized in 1975 by Walser and Fryer at Hoffmann-LaRoche, Inc. in the United States. The compound was patented in 1974 and came into medical use in 1982. Its water solubility distinguished it from earlier benzodiazepines, as this property made it significantly less likely to cause thrombophlebitis than similar drugs. The anticonvulsant properties of midazolam were studied in the late 1970s, though it did not emerge as an effective treatment for convulsive status epilepticus until the 1990s.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: The United States Food and Drug Administration first approved midazolam in 1985, and subsequent approvals for various indications have followed. As of 2010, midazolam had become the most commonly used benzodiazepine in anesthetic medicine, favored over alternatives like lorazepam and diazepam because it is shorter lasting, more potent, and causes less pain at injection sites. The drug has also gained increasing popularity in veterinary medicine due to its water solubility. In 2011, the European Medicines Agency granted marketing authorization for a buccal application form under the brand name Buccolam, initially approved for treating prolonged, acute, convulsive seizures in patients from three months to less than 18 years of age. This represented the first application of a paediatric-use marketing authorization by the EMA. In late 2018, the FDA approved an intramuscular preparation for treating status epilepticus in adults, followed by approval of a nasal spray in May 2019 for acute treatment of distinctive intermittent, stereotypic seizure episodes in patients 12 years of age and older.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines and is available as a generic medication worldwide, though it remains a controlled substance in many countries.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: Midazolam entered lethal-injection practice in some United States jurisdictions after pentobarbital's manufacturer barred its use in executions. In these protocols, the drug is used as a sedative intended to produce deep anesthesia before other agents are given to stop the prisoner's heart. Florida and Oklahoma have used it in three-drug protocols that also included vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride, while Ohio and Arizona have used it in two-drug protocols with hydromorphone. Florida used midazolam to execute William Frederick Happ in October 2013. Ohio used it in the January 2014 execution of Dennis McGuire, who was heavily anesthetized within 4 minutes but was not declared medically dead for another 20 minutes. Reporters observed gasping and apparent choking during that interval, leading to controversy over the dose, timing, and drug choice. Midazolam's use drew further controversy when condemned inmate Clayton Lockett apparently regained consciousness and spoke during his 2014 Oklahoma execution, which used an untested three-drug combination containing 100 mg of midazolam.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: In Glossip v. Gross, attorneys for three Oklahoma inmates argued that midazolam could not produce the unconsciousness needed for surgery and therefore violated the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment. In June 2015, the U.S. Supreme Court held that they had not shown midazolam to be cruel and unusual compared with known, available alternatives.

chunks.title: Midazolam
chunks.text: In 2018, it was revealed that the CIA had considered using midazolam as a "truth serum" on terrorist suspects in a project codenamed "Medication."

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: MiPLA is a lesser-known psychedelic of the lysergamide class and a structural isomer of LSD. First discovered by Albert Hofmann during the original structure-activity research for LSD, it was later studied in greater detail by David E. Nichols at Purdue University. MiPLA is reported to produce effects similar to LSD but with a shorter duration, subtler visuals, a less introspective headspace, and a generally less anxiety-provoking profile. It is approximately two- to threefold less potent than LSD.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: MiPLA is believed to have a low potential for dependence based on its structural and pharmacological similarities with LSD and other serotonergic psychedelics. No physical dependence has been documented.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: Like other serotonergic psychedelics, MiPLA is believed to have a low potential for abuse and psychological dependence, owing to its structural and pharmacological similarities with LSD. These claims are preliminary and based on anecdotal rather than clinical evidence.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: MiPLA may trigger psychiatric difficulties in people with pre-existing psychiatric conditions. People with their own history of mental illness, or a family history of it, are generally advised to avoid this substance. Delusions and other adverse psychological reactions are more likely at higher doses.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: The possibility of seizures is extrapolated from rarely reported cases with LSD. Seizures are thought to mainly be a risk in those who are genetically predisposed, particularly when accompanied by physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, fatigue, or undernourishment.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: Not studied for antimicrobial properties.

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text: MiPLA principally acts as a partial agonist at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, through which it is understood to exert its psychedelic effects. It also interacts with dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, and owing to its structural similarity to LSD, it shares a highly similar binding profile at monoamine receptors including serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine targets. MiPLA fully substitutes for LSD in rodent drug discrimination assays and produces the head-twitch response (a behavioral proxy for psychedelic activity), both at roughly one-third to one-half the potency of LSD.

chunks.title: MiPLA

chunks.title: MiPLA
chunks.text:
MiPLA was originally synthesized by Albert Hofmann at Sandoz Laboratories as part of the foundational structure-activity relationship research into LSD. Eli Lilly and Company subsequently filed a patent for the compound in 1956, with formal publication following in 1961.

The compound underwent more detailed investigation during the 1990s by David E. Nichols and his research team at Purdue University. MiPLA has primarily served as a pharmacological research tool for elucidating the serotonergic mechanisms through which LSD produces its hallucinogenic effects, with particular focus on its binding characteristics at the 5-HT2A receptor. Alexander Shulgin also documented early human trials with the substance in his "Pharmacology Notes #9" and "Pharmacology Notes C," reporting that subjects experienced LSD-like psychedelic effects at doses suggesting a potency approximately two to three times lower than LSD.

MiPLA first emerged on the recreational drug market as a novel designer drug around 2018.

chunks.title: MiPT
chunks.text: MiPT is a synthetic psychedelic of the tryptamine class, structurally related to DMT and DiPT. First synthesized by David Repke and colleagues in 1981, it was later documented by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. MiPT is notable for producing primarily cognitive and auditory psychedelic effects with a near-total absence of visual phenomena, distinguishing it from most other N,N-disubstituted tryptamines. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, or toxicity in humans.

chunks.title: MiPT
chunks.text: MiPT is not generally considered habit-forming, and repeated use may reduce rather than increase interest in taking it. Like many psychedelics, it is regarded as self-limiting.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.text: MK-801 is a dissociative research chemical and potent non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist discovered by a team at Merck in 1982. Primarily used in animal research to model psychosis and study neuroprotection, it is active in the microgram range with an exceptionally long duration of action. It carries significant risks including cognitive disruption, severe amnesia, psychotic-spectrum reactions, and high overdose potential due to its extreme potency. A multiple drug fatality involving MK-801 has been reported.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.text: Animal studies demonstrate addictive potential, with rats learning to lever-press for injections into the nucleus accumbens and frontal cortex. Dizocilpine produces conditioned place preference and enhances self-stimulation responding, indicating reinforcing properties independent of dopamine pathways.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.text: Frequently used in animal models to mimic psychosis due to its pronounced psychotomimetic effects. A single injection successfully models both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, while repeated administration produces neurochemical alterations similar to those found in first-episode schizophrenic patients. Chronic administration in laboratory animals resulted in neuropathological changes resembling those seen in schizophrenia.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: A fatal polydrug case has involved dizocilpine together with benzodiazepines and alcohol. Its high potency makes accurate dosing difficult, increasing overdose risk.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Administration induces the formation of brain lesions known as Olney's lesions in the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex; vacuoles begin forming within 30 minutes of a 1 mg/kg subcutaneous dose in rats, with subsequent neuronal necrosis and glial response.

chunks.title: MK-801
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: NMDA receptor antagonism leads to neuronal vacuolization, abnormal heat shock protein expression, increased glucose metabolism, and eventual necrosis accompanied by astrocyte and microglial activation.

chunks.title: MK-801

chunks.text: These neurotoxic effects prevented clinical development despite promising neuroprotective properties. Also associated with cognitive disruption, impaired acquisition of difficult learning tasks, and far worse amnesia and residual thinking deficits compared to similar dissociatives like ketamine and PCP.

chunks.title: Moclobemide
chunks.text: Moclobemide is a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A (RIMA) of the benzamide class, first introduced for medical use in 1989. It is prescribed primarily for major depressive disorder and social anxiety. Unlike older irreversible MAOIs, its reversible binding means dietary tyramine restrictions are generally unnecessary, and it carries a notably safer side effect and overdose profile. It is also used in pharmahuasca preparations as a substitute for naturally sourced harmala alkaloids.

chunks.title: Moclobemide
chunks.text: Withdrawal symptoms appear very uncommon relative to other antidepressants. One report described mild flu-like symptoms lasting 7 days after a high-dose regimen was rapidly reduced.

chunks.title: Moclobemide

chunks.title: Moclobemide

chunks.title: Moclobemide

chunks.title: Moclobemide

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Modafinil is a benzhydryl-class eugeroic stimulant first developed in France in the late 1970s by neurophysiologist Michel Jouvet and Lafon Laboratories. It is the main metabolite of adrafinil, with U.S. medical approval granted in 1998. It is prescribed for narcolepsy, sleep apnea, and shift work disorder, and is also commonly used off-label as a cognitive enhancer because its stimulant profile is relatively subtle compared with traditional stimulants.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: The dependence liability of modafinil is considered low. However, due to its effects on dopamine balance, there is some potential for physical dependence with regular use, particularly when consumed for performance enhancement purposes with the intention of functioning on reduced sleep.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Modafinil exhibits a low propensity for abuse compared to classical stimulants, as it lacks significantly expressed pleasurable or euphoric effects. However, emerging evidence suggests it works at similar neurobiological mechanisms as other addictive stimulants, warranting some caution.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Psychiatric symptoms including psychosis, mania, hallucinations, and delusions may occur, primarily in overdose situations. These reactions have been reported in individuals both with and without preexisting psychiatric history and may persist after discontinuation of the drug.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Seizures are a rare neurological complication that may arise primarily in overdose situations. The risk may be elevated when modafinil is combined with substances that lower the seizure threshold.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Modafinil can cause notable increases in heart rate and blood pressure through effects on autonomic cardiovascular regulation; these effects are primarily concerning for individuals with pre-existing cardiac conditions such as hypertension, arrhythmia, or structural heart abnormalities.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Stimulates release of norepinephrine and epinephrine, activating the sympathetic nervous system and causing vasoconstriction, increasing cardiac workload.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Contraindicated in uncontrolled moderate to severe hypertension, arrhythmia, cor pulmonale, and cases with signs of stimulant-induced mitral valve prolapse or left ventricular hypertrophy.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Modafinil can cause slight elevations in aminotransferase enzymes; there is no evidence of serious liver damage when enzyme levels remain within reference ranges.

chunks.title: Modafinil

chunks.text: Clinically insignificant in most users. Routine liver monitoring not typically required.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare but serious cutaneous adverse reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and DRESS syndrome have been reported; these are uncommon immune-mediated reactions rather than dose-dependent toxicity.

chunks.text: Immunological hypersensitivity response to modafinil or its metabolites.

chunks.title: Modafinil

chunks.text: Six cases of severe cutaneous reactions were reported to the FDA between December 1998 and January 2007. The FDA does not endorse modafinil for children due to increased risk of serious dermatological toxicity.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: The precise mechanism of action of modafinil is not fully understood. Its most clearly established pharmacological action is inhibition of the dopamine transporter (DAT), which increases extracellular dopamine concentrations. Modafinil also acts as a partial agonist at alpha-1B adrenergic receptors and appears to promote orexin (hypocretin) signaling, activate glutamatergic circuits, and inhibit GABAergic activity. Elevated concentrations of norepinephrine, serotonin, and histamine have been observed following administration, with some evidence suggesting these increases are secondary to modafinil's dopaminergic and orexinergic actions rather than direct transporter interactions.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Modafinil has an oral bioavailability of approximately 100% and reaches peak plasma concentrations within 2 to 3 hours of administration. It is metabolized primarily in the liver, with inactive metabolites excreted renally. Modafinil is a weak to moderate inducer of CYP3A4 and a weak inhibitor of CYP2C19, and may also induce CYP1A2 and CYP2B6 as well as inhibit CYP2C9. It may additionally induce P-glycoprotein. Elimination half-life is generally reported as 10 to 12 hours, though one source cites a broader range of 15 to 60 hours. Individual variation is influenced by sex, cytochrome P450 genotype, and liver and kidney function.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Modafinil was developed in France by neurophysiology professor Michel Jouvet and Lafon Laboratories. The compound emerged from research into a series of benzhydryl sulfinyl compounds initiated in the late 1970s. The first of these compounds to reach clinical use was adrafinil, which was offered as an experimental treatment for narcolepsy in France in 1986. Researchers subsequently identified modafinil as the primary active metabolite of adrafinil, differing from its parent compound only by lacking a polar hydroxyl group on its terminal amide. This metabolite demonstrated similar wakefulness-promoting activity but would eventually become far more widely used than the original compound.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text:
Modafinil received its first regulatory approval in France in 1994, where it was marketed under the brand name Modiodal. The United States Food and Drug Administration approved the drug in 1998 for the treatment of narcolepsy, followed by additional approvals in 2003 for shift work sleep disorder and obstructive sleep apnea. The United Kingdom approved modafinil in December 2002.

The pharmaceutical company Cephalon acquired the rights to modafinil from Lafon Laboratories, subsequently purchasing the French company outright in 2001. Cephalon marketed the drug in the United States under the brand name Provigil. In 2007, Cephalon introduced armodafinil, the isolated R-enantiomer of modafinil, as a second-generation product. The parent compound adrafinil, which never received FDA approval, was eventually withdrawn from the French market in 2011. Generic versions of modafinil became available in the United States in 2012 following extensive patent litigation.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Regulatory Approval and Commercialization

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Modafinil has seen significant adoption within military contexts as a fatigue countermeasure. During the Gulf War, the compound was used by the French Foreign Legion, the United States Air Force, and US Marines to enhance what military planners term "operational tempo"—the speed and intensity at which military operations are executed. Armed forces in the United States, United Kingdom, India, and France have evaluated modafinil as an alternative to traditional amphetamines for managing sleep deprivation during combat operations or extended missions. The US military ultimately approved modafinil for specific Air Force missions, replacing amphetamines as the standard fatigue management agent. The compound is also available to astronauts aboard the International Space Station to address fatigue resulting from circadian rhythm disruption in orbit.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: The regulation of modafinil as a doping agent has generated considerable controversy in competitive athletics, with several high-profile cases drawing significant media attention. The World Anti-Doping Agency officially added modafinil to its list of prohibited substances on August 3, 2004—just ten days before the opening of the 2004 Summer Olympics. Some athletes who tested positive argued that the substance was not explicitly banned at the time of their violations, though WADA maintained that modafinil was sufficiently related to already-prohibited substances to warrant enforcement.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: American sprinter Kelli White tested positive for modafinil following her 100-meter victory at the 2003 World Championships in Paris. Despite claiming she used the medication to treat narcolepsy, the International Association of Athletics Federations ruled that modafinil constituted a performance-enhancing drug, and White was stripped of her gold medals. Subsequent doping cases involving modafinil included cyclist David Clinger and basketball player Diana Taurasi in 2010, as well as rower Timothy Grant in 2015. The BALCO scandal also brought attention to unsubstantiated but widely circulated reports that baseball player Barry Bonds had included modafinil in his supplemental regimen alongside anabolic steroids and human growth hormone.

chunks.title: Modafinil
chunks.text: Beyond its approved medical indications, modafinil has gained substantial mainstream popularity as a cognitive enhancement agent or "smart drug," valued for its purported ability to improve memory, reduce the desire for sleep, and increase general productivity. By 2017, modafinil had become the 328th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States. Ongoing research has also investigated potential applications in addiction medicine, with some studies exploring whether modafinil may assist individuals recovering from cocaine dependence in maintaining abstinence.

chunks.title: Morpheridine
chunks.text: Morpheridine is a 4-phenylpiperidine opioid analgesic structurally related to pethidine (meperidine). It is approximately four times more potent than its parent compound and is notably reported to lack the convulsant properties associated with pethidine, though it retains standard opioid side effects including sedation and respiratory depression. Morpheridine is not currently used in clinical medicine and is controlled as a Schedule I substance under United Nations drug conventions.

chunks.title: Morpheridine

chunks.title: Morpheridine

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Morphine is the principal alkaloid of the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) and the prototypical opioid analgesic. First isolated by Friedrich Sertürner in 1805, it has served as the foundation from which numerous semi-synthetic opioids have been derived. Morphine produces potent analgesia, euphoria, and sedation, and is used clinically for the management of moderate to severe pain. Its use carries significant risks of tolerance, physical dependence, and abuse.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops readily with repeated administration, sometimes after only a short period of use. Withdrawal produces the prototypical opioid withdrawal syndrome with symptoms including anxiety, perspiration, muscle aches, severe cramping, diarrhea, vomiting, and intense drug craving progressing through distinct stages over 7-12 days. While withdrawal is not typically fatal in otherwise healthy individuals, it is intensely uncomfortable.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Morphine is ranked among the most addictive substances known, with studies placing it alongside heroin as the most addictive drug. Psychological dependence is complex and protracted, persisting long after physical withdrawal resolves. Relapse rates are estimated as high as 98%, and users commonly experience severe depression, anxiety, and overwhelming drug craving during recovery.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Confusion, nightmares, and hallucinations may occur as side effects, though these are not prominently reported at typical doses.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Constipation is one of the most common side effects, occurring consistently even at typical therapeutic doses due to reduced gut motility.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: μ-opioid receptor activation in the myenteric plexus inhibits gastric emptying and propulsive peristalsis, reduces gut secretion, and increases intestinal fluid absorption. May also involve inhibition of nitric oxide generation causing tonic gut spasms.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: Morphine

chunks.text: Chronic use causes hypogonadism and hormone imbalances in the majority of long-term users of both sexes; studies suggest up to 90% of chronic opioid users experience opioid-induced hypogonadism.

chunks.title: Morphine

chunks.title: Morphine

chunks.title: Morphine

chunks.title: Morphine

chunks.text: Excess consumption over time can cause changes in synaptic neuroplasticity; these effects are associated with chronic heavy use rather than occasional administration.
