chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Morphine acts primarily as an agonist at the μ-opioid receptor (MOR), which mediates its principal pharmacological effects. Its intrinsic activity at the MOR is context-dependent; it functions as a full agonist under some assay and tissue conditions while behaving as a partial agonist or antagonist in others. Morphine also activates κ-opioid and δ-opioid receptors, and interacts predominantly with the μ–δ-opioid receptor heteromer. Peripherally, it acts on μ-opioid receptors expressed in the myenteric plexus of the gastrointestinal tract, reducing gut motility.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Morphine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, resulting in an oral bioavailability of approximately 40 to 50%. It is approximately 35% protein bound with a volume of distribution of 5.31 L/kg. Metabolism occurs primarily via glucuronidation by UGT2B7 at the 3 and 6 positions, predominantly in the liver with minor contributions from the brain and kidneys. The major metabolite, morphine-3-glucuronide (approximately 60% of a dose), is pharmacologically inactive, while morphine-6-glucuronide (6 to 10% of a dose) is an active metabolite that retains μ-opioid receptor affinity and is estimated to account for approximately 85% of the observed pharmacological response. The elimination half-life is approximately 2 to 3 hours, and roughly 87% of a dose is excreted renally within 72 hours, with 2 to 10% recovered as unchanged morphine.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: The history of morphine is deeply intertwined with humanity's long relationship with the opium poppy. The earliest documented references to opium-based preparations can be traced to the 3rd century BC, when the Greek philosopher Theophrastus recorded their existence. Some scholars suggest that Sumerian clay tablets containing medical prescriptions may reference opium-derived remedies as far back as 2100 BC. Throughout antiquity and the medieval period, opium preparations remained valued in medical practice. Byzantine alchemists reportedly developed an opium-based elixir, though its specific formulation was lost following the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople. Around 1522, the Swiss physician Paracelsus described an opium preparation he named laudanum—derived from the Latin "laudāre," meaning "to praise"—which he extolled as a powerful painkiller while cautioning that it should be used sparingly.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text:
Morphine was first isolated from opium in December 1804 by German pharmacist Friedrich Sertürner in Paderborn, representing the first successful isolation of a medicinal alkaloid from any plant. Sertürner initially named the substance "morphium" after Morpheus, the Greek god of dreams, in reference to its pronounced sleep-inducing properties.

In 1817, Sertürner published accounts of experiments in which he administered morphine to himself, three young boys, three dogs, and a mouse—with all four human subjects nearly dying from the experience. The isolated compound proved approximately six times more potent than crude opium. Although Sertürner initially theorized that the lower doses required might reduce its addictive potential, he himself developed dependence on the substance. He later issued a stark warning about its dangers, writing that he felt obligated to draw attention to the "terrible effects of this new substance" so that "calamity may be averted."

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text:
Sertürner and Company first marketed morphine to the general public in 1817, promoting it both as a pain treatment and, paradoxically, as a remedy for opium and alcohol addiction. Large-scale commercial manufacturing began in Darmstadt, Germany, in 1827 when the pharmacy that would eventually become the pharmaceutical company Merck commenced production—with morphine sales becoming a substantial driver of the firm's early growth.

The substance's first documented use as a poison occurred in 1822, when French physician Edme Castaing was convicted of murdering a patient with morphine. The development of the hypodermic syringe between 1853 and 1855 significantly expanded morphine's clinical applications and accelerated its adoption in medical practice. A popular but likely apocryphal story from this period claims that Scottish physician Alexander Wood killed his wife Rebecca through an experimental morphine injection, though historical records indicate she actually survived her husband by a decade.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Commercial Development and Medical Adoption

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Morphine's extensive deployment as a battlefield analgesic during the American Civil War allegedly resulted in over 400,000 veterans developing what became known as "soldier's disease"—chronic morphine addiction. This claim remains historically contested, with some scholars suggesting the epidemic was exaggerated or fabricated; notably, the phrase "soldier's disease" does not appear in documented sources until 1915, decades after the war's conclusion. Morphine remained the most commonly misused narcotic analgesic worldwide until the development of heroin. Diacetylmorphine was first synthesized from morphine in 1874 and was subsequently introduced commercially by Bayer in 1898. The new derivative proved approximately 1.5 to 2 times more potent than morphine by weight. Prior to the synthesis of heroin and related compounds—including dihydromorphine around 1900, the dihydromorphinone class in the 1920s, and oxycodone in 1916—no synthetic alternatives existed that could match the analgesic efficacy of these opium-derived substances.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Recognition of morphine's addiction liability eventually prompted regulatory action. In 1914, the United States passed the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act, making morphine a controlled substance and establishing criminal penalties for possession without a prescription.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: Widespread Use and the Emergence of Heroin

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: The structural formula of morphine was determined by British chemist Robert Robinson by 1925, laying the groundwork for subsequent synthetic chemistry. In 1925, Hungarian pharmacologist János Kabay developed a method for extracting morphine from poppy straw—the dried pods and stems of the plant—rather than relying solely on the traditional labor-intensive process of collecting latex from scored unripe seed pods. This innovation, publicly announced in 1930, eventually became the predominant industrial extraction method. The first total synthesis of morphine from basic chemical feedstocks was achieved in 1952 by Marshall D. Gates, Jr. at the University of Rochester. Since then, at least three distinct synthetic routes using starting materials derived from coal tar and petroleum distillates have been patented, though the overwhelming majority of commercial morphine continues to be extracted from the opium poppy.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text: A significant discovery occurred in 2003 when researchers confirmed that morphine is produced endogenously within the human body. This finding resolved three decades of speculation prompted by the identification of the μ3-opioid receptor in human tissue, which appeared to respond specifically to morphine.

chunks.title: Morphine
chunks.text:
Modern morphine production relies primarily on poppy straw extraction rather than traditional latex collection. As of 2013, global production reached approximately 523 tons annually, with roughly 45 tons used directly for pain management—representing a 400% increase in direct medical use over the preceding two decades. The majority of this therapeutic use occurs in developed nations. Approximately 70% of manufactured morphine serves as a precursor for synthesizing other opioid medications, including hydromorphone, oxymorphone, and heroin.

The global distribution of morphine reflects stark international disparities. According to 2005 estimates from the International Narcotics Control Board, six countries—Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States—consumed 79% of the world's medical morphine supply. Meanwhile, less affluent nations representing 80% of the global population consumed only approximately 6% of available morphine stocks.

The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)

DPH may reduce the nausea caused by opioids. DPH inhibits CYP2D6 activity which can lead to a reduction of effects in some opioids and potentiation of effects in others.)

chunks.title: MT-45
chunks.text: MT-45 is a synthetic opioid of the piperazine class, structurally unrelated to most other opioid drugs. Developed in the 1970s by the Japanese pharmaceutical company Dainippon, it emerged on the research chemical market around 2013. MT-45 produces a mix of mild opioid and dissociative-like effects, and is associated with unusual side effects including persistent hearing loss, hair depigmentation, alopecia, and cataracts. Deaths have been attributed to its use both alone and in combination with other depressants.

chunks.title: MT-45
chunks.text: Although users often report disliking MT-45 and few describe sustained use, addiction can still occur. Some users may feel pushed to take additional doses before onset or during the comedown.

chunks.title: MT-45
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: MT-45 produces auditory issues in what appears to be a far more reliable manner than other opioids, with reports of tinnitus and hearing loss; in documented overdose cases, some individuals experienced transient hearing loss while at least one case involved persistent bilateral hearing loss that remained problematic at two-week follow-up, suggesting potential for very long-lasting or permanent damage.

chunks.title: MT-45

chunks.text: MXM is a dissociative anesthetic of the arylcyclohexylamine class, closely related to methoxetamine, ketamine, and PCP. It has been sold online as a designer drug and gained popularity as a replacement for methoxetamine following its prohibition in many jurisdictions. Anecdotal reports suggest it produces a more stimulating dissociative experience compared to methoxetamine, with effects closer to those associated with PCP and its analogues.

chunks.title: N-Acetylcysteine
chunks.text: N-Acetylcysteine is an N-acetyl derivative of the amino acid L-cysteine, classified as a nootropic. Initially patented in 1960, it is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent and an antidote for acetaminophen overdose. NAC functions as a prodrug to L-cysteine, replenishing stores of the antioxidant glutathione. It is increasingly explored for psychiatric applications including addiction suppression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and mood disorders through its modulation of glutamatergic pathways.

chunks.title: N-Acetylcysteine

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.text: N-Ethylhexedrone is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone class that functions as a norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Originally patented by Boehringer Ingelheim in 1964 as a potential appetite suppressant, it emerged on the research chemical market in late 2015 and rapidly became one of the most frequently seized cathinones in Europe and the United States. It is particularly notorious for its strong compulsive redosing potential and has been reported as caustic to nasal tissue when insufflated.

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.text: N-Ethylhexedrone is regarded as having moderate to high addiction liability and substantial abuse potential, and some users develop psychological dependence. It is known for compulsive redosing, with reports of strong urges to take more despite reduced positive effects. Because euphoria is brief, typically 30-60 minutes, repeated administration is encouraged, and some people have reported staying awake for days during compulsive use.

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.text: Abuse at high dosages for prolonged periods can result in stimulant psychosis presenting with anxiety, paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Psychosis typically appears after skipping at least one night of sleep, though heavy use on a single day can trigger psychotic symptoms. A review of related stimulants indicates approximately 5-15% of users who develop stimulant psychosis fail to recover completely.

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.text: N-Ethylhexedrone may lower the seizure threshold, so people with epilepsy should avoid it completely.

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: N-Ethylhexedrone increases cardiovascular stress during use, with effects including notably elevated heart rate, abnormal heartbeat, increased blood pressure, and vasoconstriction typically manifesting as cold extremities.

chunks.title: N-Ethylhexedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects are described as more pronounced and longer-lasting than with other stimulants. Those with cardiovascular disorders are advised to avoid the substance entirely.

chunks.title: N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil
chunks.text: N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil is an obscure nootropic substance of the benzhydryl class. It is the bis-fluoro-N-methyl analogue of modafinil, featuring fluorine substitutions on both of its benzene rings and a methyl group on the amide nitrogen. Despite its structural relationship to modafinil and adrafinil, it has no established research history, and neither pharmacological nor safety-profile similarities to these related compounds should be assumed.

chunks.text: If dependence develops, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur upon sudden cessation, though the nature and severity of withdrawal has not been systematically studied.

chunks.title: N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil
chunks.text: N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil has not been subject to pharmacological research beyond a single paper addressing its chemical properties. It is a benzhydryl compound structurally derived from flmodafinil (bisfluoromodafinil) through the addition of an N-methyl group on the amide nitrogen. Flmodafinil, the closest characterized structural relative, acts as a selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Whether N-methylbisfluoromodafinil shares this mechanism or a comparable binding profile has not been established.

chunks.title: N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil
chunks.text:
N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil is an obscure nootropic substance of the benzhydryl class with no documented history of formal research. It is structurally related to the established wakefulness-promoting agents modafinil and adrafinil, being the N-methylated derivative of bisfluoromodafinil (also known as flmodafinil or lauflumide). The substance is also known by the street name "Modafiendz," reflecting its marketing toward the online nootropic enthusiast community.

The parent compound, bisfluoromodafinil, has a more established developmental history. It was developed by NLS Pharma and patented in 2013, with preclinical research commencing in December 2015. Bisfluoromodafinil has been investigated for potential treatment of conditions including chronic fatigue syndrome, idiopathic hypersomnia, narcolepsy, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and Alzheimer's disease. However, N-Methylbisfluoromodafinil itself has not undergone any known pharmaceutical development or clinical investigation and exists primarily as a gray market nootropic.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.text: Naloxone is a synthetic opioid antagonist of the morphinan class, derived from oxymorphone. Patented in 1961 and approved in the United States in 1971, it is used primarily to rapidly reverse the respiratory depression and central nervous system effects of opioid overdoses. Naloxone has high affinity for mu-opioid receptors and produces no significant pharmacological effects in the absence of opioids. It is a key component of harm reduction strategies worldwide, widely distributed to emergency responders and community members. Administration to opioid-dependent individuals may precipitate acute withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.text: Naloxone does not produce physical dependence. However, administration to opioid-dependent individuals will precipitate acute opioid withdrawal.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.text: Naloxone is considered not habit-forming and has no reinforcing properties.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.text: Psychosis may occur as a symptom of precipitated opioid withdrawal when naloxone is administered to opioid-dependent individuals.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.text: Seizures have been associated with naloxone administration in rare cases.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Abrupt opioid reversal has been associated with rare but serious cardiovascular events including pulmonary edema and ventricular fibrillation, particularly in individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular disease.

chunks.title: Naloxone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Caution advised in patients with cardiovascular disease or those taking medications affecting cardiovascular function. Risk appears related to sudden catecholamine surge during precipitated withdrawal rather than direct naloxone toxicity.

chunks.title: Naloxone

chunks.title: Naphyrone
chunks.text: Naphyrone is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and naphthylaminopropane classes, derived from pyrovalerone. It functions as a serotonin–norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor (SNDRI). The substance gained attention as a designer drug marketed under the name "NRG-1," though laboratory analysis has revealed that the majority of products sold under this label contained other substances such as MDPV, mephedrone, or caffeine instead. No safety or toxicity data is currently available.

chunks.title: Naphyrone
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming. As a stimulant and triple reuptake inhibitor, psychological addiction potential is expected, though no specific data on naphyrone's addiction profile exists.

chunks.title: Naproxen
chunks.text: Naproxen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) belonging to the 2-arylpropionic acid (profen) family. Patented in 1967 and approved for medical use in 1976, it became available over-the-counter in 1994. Naproxen functions as a non-selective COX inhibitor and is widely used to manage pain, fever, and inflammatory conditions such as arthritis and gout. Notable risks include gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration, particularly with concurrent alcohol use.

chunks.title: Naproxen

chunks.text: Naproxen can cause heartburn, constipation, diarrhea, stomach ulcers, and stomach bleeding; boxed warnings address gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding.

chunks.title: NEB
chunks.text: NEB is a synthetic stimulant of the substituted cathinone class that has been sold as a designer drug. It is the β-ketone analogue of N,alpha-diethylphenylethylamine. First reported around 2011, it never achieved significant popularity. Anecdotal reports suggest its effects partially resemble those of other cathinones, producing short-acting stimulation with a predominantly dopaminergic rather than serotonergic profile. It is considered habit-forming.

chunks.title: NEB
chunks.text: NEB is considered a habit-forming stimulant research chemical.

chunks.title: Nefiracetam
chunks.text: Nefiracetam is a fat-soluble nootropic of the racetam family. It enhances GABAergic, cholinergic, and monoaminergic neuronal signaling, and is distinguished from other racetams by its notably high affinity for the GABAA receptor. Preliminary research suggests potential antidementia and neuroprotective properties. Long-term studies in humans and primates have found no evidence of toxicity, though certain animal species that metabolize it differently may be susceptible to adverse effects.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: NEP is a substituted cathinone that produces stimulating, euphoric, and mildly entactogenic effects. It first appeared on the research chemical market in 2016 as a contemporary designer drug. Structurally related to pentedrone, it differs by an additional ethyl group on the terminal nitrogen, reportedly making it roughly three times as potent. NEP is also closely related to N-ethylhexedrone and is noted for its relatively short duration of action.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: When addiction has developed, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur upon cessation. Physical dependence appears less prominent than psychological dependence, with sources primarily emphasizing compulsive use patterns rather than severe physical withdrawal.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: Moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and capable of causing psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing is a common pattern, with users entering an almost automatic state of redosing regardless of whether the effects remain pleasant. The short duration contributes to repeated administration, and once use deviates from planned limits, escalation is common.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: Extended use at high dosages can result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, and delusions. Compared to classic stimulants, paranoia, visual distortions, and unusual thinking appear to have faster onset, potentially becoming apparent within one day of heavy use. Sleep deprivation significantly increases risk. The most concerning effects can almost always be prevented by avoiding sleep deprivation and limiting use duration.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: No case reports of NEP-induced seizures exist, but like other stimulants it likely has seizure-inducing capacity. Best avoided in those with preexisting seizure disorders.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Increases heart rate significantly compared to other stimulants, even at low doses, along with elevated blood pressure and occasional abnormal heartbeat; acute myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, and stroke are presumed possible with large overdoses, though no formal data exists.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The magnitude of cardiovascular increase with common doses is unknown. Should be treated as if risk is greater than average until more data exists. Heart racing and palpitations are frequently reported with heavier use.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Intranasal use causes nasal discomfort and irritation; heavy use can produce significant nasal inflammation and occasionally bleeding, though severity varies substantially between batches.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Reports are inconsistent regarding irritation severity, possibly due to batch quality differences. Some batches cause minimal discomfort while others are described as almost unbearable.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: NEP is believed to act primarily as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, increasing the accumulation of these monoamines in the brain. One study has characterized it as a serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor with very poor affinity for the serotonin transporter, suggesting that its activity is heavily biased toward dopamine and norepinephrine. The structurally similar cathinone pentedrone has been shown to function as a reuptake inhibitor rather than a monoamine releaser, which may also apply to NEP, though interactions with additional receptor sites have not been ruled out.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text: With sustained repeated NEP use, tolerance may develop across many effects. Euphoria can begin declining within 2-3 doses, and continued use may mainly extend wakefulness and intoxication while positive effects become shorter and weaker.

chunks.title: NEP
chunks.text:
N-Ethylpentedrone emerged on the online research chemical market during the mid-2010s, with documented user experience reports beginning to appear around 2016. The compound represents a generation of synthetic cathinone derivatives developed as functional and structural alternatives to earlier stimulants in this chemical class. These substances, including NEP, are sometimes colloquially grouped under the imprecise umbrella term "bath salts," a label that emerged from early marketing strategies used to circumvent drug scheduling laws.

By 2020, NEP had established itself as a relatively popular option within research chemical communities, likely due to its availability and effects profile. Its development and distribution follow the pattern typical of novel psychoactive substances: synthesized to provide effects similar to controlled predecessors while initially existing in legal grey areas before eventually being scheduled in various jurisdictions.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Nicomorphine is a semi-synthetic opioid agonist of the morphine family, classified as both an opioid and a depressant. It is estimated to be two to three times more potent than morphine and is characterized by a notably rapid onset of effects, attributed to its increased lipid solubility. Nicomorphine sees limited medical use in a small number of countries. As with other opioids, it carries significant habit-forming potential.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming in drug factsheets.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Nicomorphine is a 3,6-dinicotinate ester of morphine that acts as a strong opioid agonist with analgesic potency approximately two to three times that of morphine. Its diester structure provides increased lipid solubility, enabling rapid and complete central nervous system penetration.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Nicomorphine is rapidly metabolized into morphine and the intermediate active metabolite 6-nicotinoylmorphine, with metabolic pathways varying by route of administration. Following intravenous administration, the parent compound has a half-life of approximately 3 minutes, with 6-nicotinoylmorphine persisting for 3 to 15 minutes before further conversion to morphine (half-life 135 to 190 minutes). Via the rectal route, the metabolic pathway differs: nicomorphine converts directly to morphine without detectable 6-nicotinoylmorphine, with morphine appearing within 8 minutes and subsequently undergoing glucuronidation to morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glucuronide. Rectal bioavailability of morphine and its active metabolites reaches 88%. Epidural administration results in substantially slower release, with nicomorphine remaining detectable for approximately 1.5 hours.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Nicomorphine was first synthesized in 1904. Over fifty years later, the compound was patented under the trade name Vilan by the Austrian pharmaceutical company Lannacher Heilmittel G.m.b.H. in 1957. That same year, Pongratz and Zirm published the synthesis methodology in the journal Monatshefte für Chemie, describing the treatment of anhydrous morphine base with nicotinic anhydride at elevated temperatures. Their article also detailed the preparation of the related analogues nicocodeine and nicodicodeine as part of a broader examination of amides and esters of various organic acids. Nicomorphine has found medical application primarily in German-speaking countries and other regions of Central Europe, as well as in some countries of the former Soviet Union. It is used clinically for the management of post-operative pain, cancer-related pain, and chronic non-malignant and neuropathic pain conditions. The compound was never introduced to the United States medical market.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Outside of pharmaceutical channels, nicomorphine occasionally appears on the European black market. It can be produced through improvised methods analogous to heroin homebake processes, involving the treatment of morphine with nicotinic anhydride or related chemicals.

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Opioids

chunks.title: Nicomorphine
chunks.text: Binding profile: μ-opioid receptor agonist (full)

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine is a naturally occurring alkaloid found primarily in tobacco and in trace amounts in plants such as tomatoes and aubergines. It acts as a stimulant at low doses, promoting the release of dopamine, serotonin, and adrenaline, while higher doses produce calming and muscle-relaxing effects. Widely regarded as one of the most addictive substances known, it is used both recreationally through tobacco products and therapeutically as a smoking cessation aid.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine produces significant physical dependence with chronic use. Withdrawal symptoms include somatic effects such as mild motor dysfunction and tremor, alongside depression, restlessness, insomnia, and in the long-term with abstinence, weight gain. Withdrawal symptoms peak within one to three days and can persist for several weeks, though withdrawal is not life-threatening.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine is consistently described as one of the most addictive drugs in existence. It activates the mesolimbic reward pathway and induces long-term ΔFosB expression in the nucleus accumbens, resulting in strong psychological dependence. Discontinuation produces affective withdrawal symptoms including anxiety, irritability, intense craving, and anhedonia.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Seizures are documented only at toxic or overdose-level doses and do not occur at typical recreational or therapeutic doses. Lethal nicotine poisoning rapidly produces seizures, and death from respiratory paralysis may occur within minutes of a severe overdose.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine is not classified as a carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer or the U.S. Surgeon General. However, while not carcinogenic itself, nicotine causes DNA damage in human cells as demonstrated by genotoxicity assays and may theoretically act as a tumor promoter by enhancing proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastasis via nicotinic receptor signaling. A 2018 National Academies report concluded that while tumor promotion is biologically plausible, existing evidence indicates this is unlikely to translate into increased human cancer risk. Notably, nicotine in the mouth and stomach can form N-nitrosonornicotine, a known Group 1 carcinogen.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Acute use causes transient increases in heart rate, blood pressure, and systemic vasoconstriction including coronary arteries; long-term exposure may impair endothelial function and potentially contribute to atherosclerosis, with cardiac arrhythmias primarily a concern in individuals with underlying heart disease. Short-term nicotine use in healthy individuals poses little cardiovascular risk.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A 2016 review concluded cardiovascular risks from nicotine via e-cigarettes are quite low in people without cardiovascular disease. A 2018 Cochrane review found nicotine replacement therapy can cause non-ischemic chest pain and palpitations in rare cases but does not increase serious cardiac adverse events compared to controls.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy chronic use is associated with less efficient brain network architecture and disruptions in topological organization of brain networks; adolescent exposure may impair neurodevelopment up to age twenty-five, and some research suggests potential damage to medial habenula neurons regulating nicotine avoidance behaviors in chronic users.

chunks.text: Nicotine is considered a possible teratogen in humans; it crosses the placenta and negatively affects fetal brain development, with prenatal exposure associated with lower birth weight, increased risk of miscarriage and stillbirth, and potential long-term metabolic and neurobehavioral consequences in offspring.

chunks.title: Nicotine

chunks.text: Nicotinic receptor activation disrupts fetal brain metabolism and neurotransmitter system function during development

chunks.text: Found in breast milk of mothers who smoke or inhale passive smoke. Rat studies showed in utero exposure led to offspring developing type 2 diabetes, obesity, hypertension, neurobehavioral defects, and infertility later in life.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic exposure suppresses both innate and adaptive immune responses, downregulating cell-mediated immunity against infections and potentially reducing immune surveillance against neoplastic diseases.

chunks.title: Nicotine

chunks.text: Activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (particularly α7 subtype) on immune cells reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-21, IL-22), suppresses T-cell proliferation and activation, and reduces antibody production

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: May aggravate tumor growth and metastases in cancer patients. Paradoxically, immunosuppressive effects show therapeutic potential for autoimmune diseases including inflammatory bowel disease and arthritis.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: May promote and aggravate periodontal diseases including periodontitis and gingivitis, particularly in the presence of harmful oral microorganisms.

chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Data remain insufficient, especially in vivo studies.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine acts as an agonist at most subtypes of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), with particularly high affinity at the α4β2 subtype (Ki = 1 nM), while functioning as an antagonist at the α9 and α10 subtypes. Activation of central nAChRs stimulates the release of multiple neurotransmitters including dopamine, norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and serotonin. Binding at α4β2 receptors on dopaminergic neurons within the mesolimbic pathway drives dopamine release, which underlies the substance's reinforcing properties. Nicotine also acts on nicotinic receptors in the adrenal medulla, triggering the release of epinephrine and norepinephrine into the bloodstream through calcium-dependent exocytosis. The naturally occurring (S)-enantiomer is 4 to 28 times more potent than (R)-nicotine in standard binding and functional assays.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Nicotine distributes rapidly through the bloodstream and crosses the blood-brain barrier within 10 to 20 seconds of inhalation. It is primarily metabolized in the liver by CYP2A6, with additional contributions from CYP2B6 and FMO3 (the latter selectively metabolizing the (S)-enantiomer). The major metabolite is cotinine, which is pharmacologically active and persists in the blood with a half-life of 15 to 20 hours. Nicotine itself has an elimination half-life of approximately 1 to 3 hours. Absorption is modulated by the molecule's ionization state, which is governed by pH relative to its pKa values.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Absorption through the buccal mucosa is relatively slow compared to inhalation routes

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Free-base nicotine was traditionally associated with higher bioavailability, but e-cigarette research has found that protonated nicotine salts can yield higher peak blood levels than equivalent free-base doses

chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Smoked
chunks.text: Reaches the brain within 10-20 seconds after inhalation

chunks.text: Other nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonists

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Tolerance to nicotine's effects develops rapidly with repeated use, often within days of regular administration. Chronic exposure leads to upregulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which paradoxically increases receptor density while reducing functional sensitivity. Tolerance develops differentially to various effects, with cardiovascular and subjective effects showing more rapid tolerance development than other pharmacological actions.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text:
Tobacco first arrived in Europe during the early 1530s, brought back by Spanish explorers from the Americas. The plant quickly gained a reputation as a medicinal wonder, with smoking believed to offer protection against various illnesses, including the plague. This perception of tobacco as a "holy herb" with curative properties contributed to its rapid adoption across the continent.

The substance takes its name from the tobacco plant Nicotiana tabacum, which was itself named after Jean Nicot de Villemain, a French ambassador stationed in Portugal. In 1560, Nicot sent tobacco plants and seeds to Paris, presenting them to the French King and actively promoting their medicinal applications. His enthusiastic advocacy helped establish tobacco's reputation among European aristocracy and medical practitioners.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: The active compound responsible for tobacco's effects was first isolated in 1828 by German chemists Wilhelm Heinrich Posselt and Karl Ludwig Reimann, who identified the substance as a poison. The chemical empirical formula was subsequently described by Melsens in 1843, while the complete molecular structure was elucidated by Adolf Pinner and Richard Wolffenstein in 1893. The first total synthesis of nicotine was achieved by Amé Pictet and A. Rotschy in 1904, confirming the structural work of the previous decade.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Following its introduction to Europe, tobacco's stimulating effects and the addictive properties of nicotine drove enormous demand that transformed colonial economics. By the early 17th century, tobacco cultivation had become central to the Virginia colonies in North America. John Rolfe's introduction of commercially viable tobacco farming in 1612 rescued the Jamestown settlement from economic collapse and famine. Within seven years, the colony was exporting over 20,000 pounds of tobacco annually, establishing the foundation for transatlantic trade networks. From the 17th century onward, tobacco smoking became deeply embedded in European social, economic, and cultural life, shaping daily rituals, trade relationships, and even international conflicts.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text: Beyond its use as a recreational substance, nicotine found extensive application as an agricultural pesticide. By the late 17th century, tobacco preparations were already being employed as insecticides. This application expanded dramatically following World War II, when global nicotine insecticide usage exceeded 2,500 tons annually. However, by the 1980s, consumption had declined to below 200 tons as cheaper synthetic alternatives with lower mammalian toxicity became available. The molecular structure of nicotine nevertheless provided the template for developing the neonicotinoid class of synthetic pesticides, which remain widely used in modern agriculture.

chunks.title: Nicotine
chunks.text:
Public health campaigns in the United Kingdom created the character Nick O'Teen, a villain developed for the Health Education Council to personify the harms of tobacco smoking and nicotine addiction. The character, depicted as a humanoid figure with cigarette-like features incorporated into his appearance, appeared in three animated public service announcements where he attempted to lure children into smoking before being thwarted by the superhero Superman.

The tobacco industry responded to growing health concerns by comparing nicotine to caffeine in 1980s advertising campaigns, attempting to normalize its use and reduce public perception of risk. This marketing strategy was later adopted by the electronic cigarette industry in the 2010s as a means of reducing stigmatization associated with nicotine consumption.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Nifoxipam is a synthetic depressant of the nitrobenzodiazepine class and an active metabolite of flunitrazepam. It has potential applications in the short-term management of anxiety, insomnia, and acute seizures, but is currently available exclusively through research chemical vendors as a novel psychoactive substance. As with other benzodiazepines, it carries a risk of dependence and habit formation with repeated use.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use over weeks, and withdrawal can be life-threatening. Abrupt discontinuation following extended use may result in hypertension, seizures, and potentially death. Gradual tapering over weeks is essential for safe discontinuation.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Described as extremely psychologically addictive with significant abuse potential. Compulsive redosing is a noted effect, and regular use leads to habituation. Rebound anxiety following cessation can drive cycles of continued use and dependence.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Paradoxical psychiatric reactions including aggression, violent behavior, irritability, loss of impulse control, and suicidal behavior occur rarely, with an incidence below 1% in the general population. Risk increases in recreational abusers, individuals with mental disorders, children, and those on high-dose regimens. Delusions may manifest during overdose.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Nifoxipam possesses anticonvulsant properties and does not induce seizures during typical use. Paradoxical seizure increase in epileptic individuals is rare. However, abrupt discontinuation after regular extended use carries significant seizure risk and may be fatal; gradual dose tapering is essential.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression occurs at high doses and can be life-threatening in overdose or when combined with other CNS depressants; this effect is dose-dependent and uncommon at typical doses when used alone.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: GABA-A receptor potentiation suppresses medullary respiratory drive in a dose-dependent manner

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Primary mechanism of death in benzodiazepine overdose, particularly in polydrug scenarios. Overdose may be treated with flumazenil, though care is primarily supportive.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Severe overdose may result in coma and permanent brain injury, primarily as a consequence of prolonged respiratory depression; this is mainly a concern in polydrug combinations or extreme dosing.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Hypoxic injury secondary to respiratory depression

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Generally favorable outcomes when treated promptly in a hospital environment.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Tolerance generally returns to baseline within 7-14 days after cessation of use. However, following prolonged or intensive use patterns, this recovery period may extend significantly longer in proportion to the duration and intensity of prior consumption.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text: Tolerance to sedative-hypnotic effects can emerge quickly, often after only a few days of uninterrupted use.

chunks.title: Nifoxipam
chunks.text:
Nifoxipam is a nitrobenzodiazepine that was originally identified as a minor metabolite of flunitrazepam (marketed as Rohypnol). While it exists primarily as an analytical reference material in pharmacological research, the compound has since emerged on the online designer drug market. It is currently sold by research chemical vendors as a recreational psychoactive substance.

Despite having potential applications for the short-term treatment of anxiety, insomnia, acute seizures, and sedation of hospitalized patients, nifoxipam has never been approved for medicinal use and remains unscheduled in most jurisdictions. The compound represents part of the broader trend of benzodiazepine metabolites and analogues appearing in the grey-market research chemical trade.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.text: Nimetazepam is an intermediate-acting hypnotic benzodiazepine first synthesized at Hoffmann-La Roche in 1964. It is the N-methylated analogue of nitrazepam and produces potent hypnotic, anxiolytic, sedative, and muscle relaxant effects. Originally prescribed for severe insomnia across East and Southeast Asia, it has become a significant drug of abuse in the region, particularly in Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines. Black market tablets are frequently counterfeit, often containing other benzodiazepines such as diazepam or nitrazepam.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.text: Nimetazepam physical dependence and withdrawal syndrome add to its addictive nature.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.text: Misuse and dependence are described in both patients and non-medical users, with a strong abuse reputation, declining prescriptions due to rampant misuse and addiction, and significant regional abuse.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Nimetazepam should not be combined with other CNS depressants. No lethal dose or LD50 value is identified.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam

chunks.text: Rat studies reported greater fetal damage than some other benzodiazepines at 100 mg/kg and testicular degenerative changes at high doses.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The testicular atrophic changes returned to normal after drug withdrawal for 12 weeks.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rat studies reported slight enlargement of the liver and adrenals in high-dose groups.

chunks.title: Nimetazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Histopathological examination found no change in the liver, adrenals, or ovaries in the quoted study.

While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.)
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)

The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. chunks.title: Nitemazepam
chunks.text: Nitemazepam is a novel research chemical of the benzodiazepine class, structurally derived from nimetazepam. Very limited information is available regarding its pharmacology, safety profile, or effects. Anecdotal reports suggest it may produce effects comparable to temazepam. As with other benzodiazepines, it is considered habit-forming. Due to the scarcity of data surrounding this substance, users should exercise extreme caution, as its risks and safe dosage range remain poorly understood.

chunks.title: Nitemazepam
chunks.text: Nitemazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative and the 7-nitro analogue of temazepam, as well as the 3-hydroxy derivative of nimetazepam. It is also an active metabolite of nimetazepam. Detailed receptor binding data and functional pharmacodynamic characterization are not available in the current literature.

chunks.title: Nitemazepam
chunks.text: Nitemazepam is metabolized to several products including 7-aminonitemazepam, nimetazepam, 3-hydroxynitemazepam, temazepam, and nimetazepam glucuronide. No specific metabolic enzymes or pharmacokinetic parameters have been characterized in the available literature.

chunks.title: Nitemazepam
chunks.text:
Nitemazepam, also known as 3-hydroxynimetazepam, is a benzodiazepine derivative that was originally synthesized during the 1970s. Despite its early development, the compound was never brought to market as a pharmaceutical product.

Decades after its initial synthesis, nitemazepam resurfaced as a designer drug within the research chemical market. The substance was first definitively identified in Europe in 2017, representing part of a broader trend of novel benzodiazepines entering grey market circulation.

chunks.title: Nitemazepam
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzodiazepines

chunks.title: Nitracaine
chunks.text: Nitracaine is a synthetic local anesthetic with stimulant properties, chemically related to both cocaine and dimethocaine. Structurally a benzoic acid ester, it features a nitro group that contributes to its anesthetic activity. Often marketed within the research chemical scene as a cocaine replacement, nitracaine has seen very limited reported human use, meaning its safety profile and long-term risks remain poorly characterized.

chunks.title: Nitracaine
chunks.text: Nitracaine is considered habit-forming, supporting a psychological habit risk, but dependence syndrome or withdrawal is not described.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Nitrazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic first synthesized in the late 1950s by Hoffmann-La Roche and introduced medically in 1965 under the brand name Mogadon. It possesses potent sedative, anxiolytic, amnestic, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant properties. Nitrazepam is primarily prescribed for short-term treatment of severe insomnia and disabling anxiety, reducing sleep onset time and increasing sleep duration. It is also used in managing myoclonic seizures.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops readily with continued use, producing a withdrawal syndrome similar to alcohol and barbiturate withdrawal. Common withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, insomnia, concentration problems, and fatigue. Neonatal withdrawal syndrome can occur in infants born to mothers using nitrazepam during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Recreational use is common and the drug is classified as habit-forming. Dependence can develop in as little as four weeks of regular use, with prescriptions recommended to not exceed seven to ten consecutive days.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Very infrequently, paradoxical reactions may occur including excitement, stimulation, hallucinations, hyperactivity, and insomnia.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Benzodiazepine use is associated with an increased risk of developing cancer.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Severe liver toxicity has been reported; nitrobenzodiazepines including nitrazepam are more hepatotoxic than other benzodiazepines due to metabolic activation by CYP3A4.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Metabolic activation by CYP3A4 leads to generation of free radicals, oxidation of thiol groups, and covalent binding with endogenous macromolecules, resulting in oxidation of cellular components and inhibition of normal cellular function.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use may lead to development of cognitive deficits; elderly patients are particularly susceptible and may develop a disability characterized by general mental deterioration, inability to walk, incontinence, dysarthria, confusion, and disorientation from doses as low as 5 mg.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Cognitive deficits in elderly patients can be misdiagnosed as dementia or brain disease. Effects of a single dose may persist up to 60 hours in elderly subjects.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Can cause severe respiratory distress in children, including swallowing incoordination, bronchospasm, delayed cricopharyngeal relaxation, and respiratory depression potentially requiring ventilatory support; may promote parasympathetic overactivity leading to potentially fatal respiratory distress.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Particularly dangerous in children and patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. May cause sudden death in children.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Nitrazepam is a benzodiazepine that acts as a full agonist at central benzodiazepine receptors, which are associated with inhibitory GABA-A receptors. This binding enhances GABA activity at GABA-A receptors, producing sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, amnestic, and skeletal muscle relaxant effects. The anticonvulsant properties may be partly or entirely attributable to binding to voltage-gated sodium channels rather than benzodiazepine receptors, with benzodiazepines slowing recovery of sodium channels from inactivation. Nitrazepam also binds to peripheral-type benzodiazepine receptors. The muscle relaxant effects are produced via inhibition of polysynaptic pathways in the spinal cord. At high doses, nitrazepam decreases histamine turnover as a result of its action at the benzodiazepine-GABA receptor complex, and it has demonstrated cortisol-suppressing properties in humans.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Nitrazepam is lipophilic and largely bound to plasma proteins, with high cerebral uptake. Oral bioavailability ranges from 53 to 94 percent, and food intake does not influence absorption rate or bioavailability. Peak plasma concentrations are reached approximately 2 hours after oral administration, with a range of 0.5 to 5 hours. The drug is metabolized hepatically by oxidative pathways. As a nitrobenzodiazepine, nitrazepam is metabolically activated by CYP3A4, which can generate reactive metabolites including free radicals. The elimination half-life ranges from 15 to 48 hours, with a mean of approximately 26 hours. Half-life is age-dependent, averaging around 29 hours in young people and extending to approximately 40 hours in the elderly. Nitrazepam is eliminated extremely slowly from the cerebrospinal fluid, with a half-life of 68 hours in that compartment.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text: Tolerance to nitrazepam's effects develops with regular use, typically appearing after approximately seven days of continuous administration. Tolerance to sleep-inducing and anticonvulsant effects develops readily, though some evidence suggests tolerance development is not uniform across all patients. In children treated for epilepsy, tolerance may develop within months of continued use, often necessitating dose escalation.

chunks.title: Nitrazepam
chunks.text:
Nitrazepam was first synthesized in the late 1950s by a team of researchers at Hoffmann-La Roche in Switzerland. The compound was patented in 1961 and subsequently entered medical use in 1965, marketed under the brand name Mogadon among others.

The drug was developed as a hypnotic agent of the benzodiazepine class, intended for short-term relief from severe, disabling anxiety and insomnia. Beyond its primary hypnotic applications, nitrazepam was found to possess sedative, amnestic, anticonvulsant, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties.

In clinical practice, nitrazepam has been employed not only for sleep disorders but also in the treatment of certain forms of epilepsy when other medications prove ineffective. It has demonstrated particular utility in the treatment of West syndrome, an age-dependent epilepsy affecting very young children, where it has shown greater effectiveness than clonazepam. A light-activated derivative known as fulgazepam has been developed for research purposes.

chunks.title: Nitrazolam
chunks.text: Nitrazolam is a hypnotic triazolobenzodiazepine that has been sold online as a designer drug. It is the triazolo analogue of nitrazepam and is estimated to be roughly four times more potent than its parent compound. Structurally, it is closely related to both clonazolam and flunitrazolam. As with other benzodiazepines, nitrazolam carries a risk of habit formation and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Nitrazolam
chunks.text: Nitrazolam is considered a habit-forming benzodiazepine depressant, supporting a psychological habit risk.

chunks.title: Nitrazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Combination with other CNS depressants should be avoided.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide is an atypical dissociative inhalant with the chemical formula N₂O. First identified by Joseph Priestly in 1772, its anesthetic properties were later discovered in the 19th century, earning it the name 'laughing gas' due to its euphoria and laughter-inducing effects. When inhaled, it produces rapid analgesia, mild sedation, and brief psychedelic dissociation. Widely used medically in surgery and dentistry, it is also commonly encountered recreationally through whipped cream chargers. Chronic abuse may cause neurological damage through vitamin B12 inactivation.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Physical dependence with psychological symptoms is possible with continuous use. The substance does not produce a classical physical withdrawal syndrome, though psychological dependence can develop in heavy users.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide has gained the nickname 'hippy-crack' due to its tendency toward compulsive redosing in some users. While uncommon, individuals with easy access to large quantities may use it many times daily. The substance is considered to have low to moderate abuse potential overall.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Psychological issues including personality changes, mood disorders, psychosis, and hallucinations can occur, primarily in the context of chronic heavy use and associated B12 deficiency rather than acute intoxication.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: A short period of slight hypoxia from nitrous oxide use could potentially raise the chance of seizure in some users. Persons suffering from epilepsy are advised not to consume nitrous oxide.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Occupational exposure to ambient nitrous oxide has been associated with DNA damage due to interruptions in DNA synthesis. This correlation is dose-dependent and does not appear to extend to casual recreational use, though further research is needed to confirm the exposure level required to cause damage.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Heavy and frequent long-term use can cause serious neurological damage including subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord; occasional recreational use at typical doses carries minimal risk, while chronic daily or weekly use significantly increases the likelihood of peripheral neuropathy.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide oxidizes the cobalt core of cobalamin (vitamin B12) from the monovalent to trivalent form, inactivating it for methionine synthase function. This enzyme inhibition disrupts DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance. NMDA receptor antagonism may also contribute to neurotoxicity, with evidence of Olney's lesions in rodents upon prolonged exposure.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Symptoms include limb weakness, numbness, ataxia, clumsiness, tingling, and imbalance. Heavy users (≥400g or ≥200L per session) or frequent users (daily/weekly) have developed peripheral neuropathy. Treatment is generally effective but symptoms may persist 6-12 months or longer. B12 supplementation may reduce risk but will not prevent issues if use is significant enough.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic heavy use can cause megaloblastic changes and, in severe cases, agranulocytosis; these effects are associated with prolonged B12 inactivation rather than occasional use.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Inactivation of vitamin B12 disrupts DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells including bone marrow precursors.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Mild megaloblastic changes can appear after 12 hours of continuous administration, increasing by 24 hours. Agranulocytosis raises infection risk in severe cases. Temporary infertility has been reported with continuous use.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hypoxia from improper use can cause low blood pressure, fainting, and cardiac arrhythmia; serious cardiac events are rare and typically associated with pre-existing conditions or continuous inhalation without oxygen.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Oxygen deprivation from pure nitrous oxide inhalation reduces tissue oxygenation, stressing cardiac function.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A short period of slight hypoxia generally won't be an issue for most people. Risk increases with continuous inhalation methods such as masks connected to gas canisters. Pre-existing coronary artery disease has been noted as a contributing factor in fatal cases.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High-pressure administration directly from tanks can rupture blood vessels in the lungs and cause pneumothorax; this risk is eliminated by releasing gas into a balloon first.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Excessive pressure forces air into the chest cavity, potentially collapsing the lungs.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Diffusion hypoxia can occur as rapid outward diffusion of N2O from pulmonary blood dilutes oxygen concentration in the lungs, affecting oxygen transfer across the alveolus.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Direct inhalation from tanks or whippits can cause frostbite to the lips, throat, larynx, and bronchi due to extremely cold gas temperatures.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Gas near the outlet of pressurized containers can reach temperatures as low as -55°C (-131°F), causing tissue freezing on contact.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Releasing gas into a balloon first allows it to warm to safe temperatures before inhalation. Severe tissue damage has been reported from direct inhalation.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide directly modulates a broad range of ligand-gated ion channels, though its complete mechanism of action remains incompletely understood. Its anaesthetic, hallucinogenic, and euphoriant effects are thought to arise predominantly from NMDA receptor antagonism, with an approximate EC50 of 30-40% concentration in cultured hippocampal neurons where it acts as a partial inhibitor even at 80%. The substance moderately blocks β2-subunit-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors with preference for α4β2 over α4β4 subtypes, weakly inhibits AMPA, kainate, GABAC, and 5-HT3 receptors, and slightly potentiates GABAA and glycine receptors. It also activates two-pore-domain potassium channels including TREK-1, which plays a role in neuronal excitability.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: The analgesic effects appear linked to the endogenous opioid system and descending noradrenergic pathways. Nitrous oxide may induce release of opioid peptides in the brainstem, causing disinhibition of noradrenergic neurons that then release norepinephrine into the spinal cord to modulate pain signalling at α2-adrenoceptors. The anxiolytic effects are associated with enhanced GABAA receptor activity, as they are partially reversed by benzodiazepine receptor antagonists. Additionally, nitrous oxide may influence nitric oxide signalling, possibly through effects on nitric oxide synthase.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide has low solubility in blood, which gives it rapid onset and rapid clearance with effects ending shortly after administration ceases. It is 30 to 40 times more soluble than nitrogen. The substance does not appear to be a significant substrate or inhibitor of major CYP450 enzymes. With prolonged or frequent use, nitrous oxide causes rapid oxidation of cobalamin's cobalt from the monovalent to the trivalent form, inactivating vitamin B12 as a coenzyme for methionine synthase.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide was first synthesized in 1772 by English natural philosopher and chemist Joseph Priestley, who initially called it "dephlogisticated nitrous air." He produced the gas by heating iron filings dampened with nitric acid and passing the resulting vapor through water to remove impurities. Priestley published his findings in his 1775 book "Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air." Early experimenters, including Priestley himself, initially believed the gas to be highly dangerous to animals based on observations of mice placed in jars of the substance.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: The therapeutic potential of nitrous oxide began to be explored following the work of Thomas Beddoes and James Watt, who published "Considerations on the Medical Use and on the Production of Factitious Airs" in 1794. Watt invented a novel machine to produce various gases along with a breathing apparatus for inhalation. In 1798, Beddoes established the Pneumatic Institution in Bristol, England, hiring twenty-year-old Humphry Davy as superintendent. Davy conducted extensive self-experimentation with the gas beginning in April 1799, discovering its euphoric and intoxicating properties. He coined the term "laughing gas" due to its tendency to induce laughter and feelings of giddiness.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: In 1800, Davy published "Researches, Chemical and Philosophical; chiefly concerning nitrous oxide," in which he documented the gas's analgesic effects and suggested its potential for surgical use, writing: "As nitrous oxide in its extensive operation appears capable of destroying physical pain, it may probably be used with advantage during surgical operations in which no great effusion of blood takes place." Despite this prescient observation, medical application would not be pursued for another four decades.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text:
Rather than being adopted for medical purposes, nitrous oxide first gained popularity as a recreational substance. Beginning in 1799, "laughing gas parties" became fashionable entertainment among the British upper class, where participants would inhale the gas to experience its euphoric and disinhibiting effects. These gatherings were an immediate success, with users appearing dreamy and sedated while frequently erupting in laughter.

From approximately 1800 to 1840, nitrous oxide was primarily used for recreation at travelling public shows rather than in medical settings. Showmen would demonstrate the gas's effects on stage, with volunteers inhaling and acting out their intoxication for audience entertainment. This practice spread to America, where travelling exhibitions introduced the substance to the public as early as the 1830s. The discovery of ether in 1830 eventually led nitrous oxide to fall somewhat out of favor as a recreational drug, though its use continued in various settings.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: The transition of nitrous oxide from recreational curiosity to medical tool occurred on December 10, 1844, when American dentist Horace Wells attended a public exhibition organized by Gardner Quincy Colton in Hartford, Connecticut. During the demonstration, Wells observed a man named Samuel Cooley inhale the gas and subsequently injure his leg while staggering about, yet remain unaware of any pain until the effects wore off. Recognizing the anesthetic potential, Wells arranged to have his own wisdom tooth extracted the following day while under the influence of nitrous oxide, with Colton administering the gas and dentist John Riggs performing the extraction. Wells reported experiencing no pain and proclaimed it "a new era in tooth pulling."

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Despite successful treatments of twelve to fifteen patients in Hartford with only two failures, Wells' first public demonstration to the medical faculty in Boston in January 1845 was partly unsuccessful, leaving his colleagues skeptical of the method's efficacy and safety. The practice did not achieve widespread adoption until 1863, when Gardner Quincy Colton began administering the gas at his newly established "Colton Dental Association" clinics in New Haven and New York City. Over the following three years, Colton and his associates successfully administered nitrous oxide to more than 25,000 patients, bringing the practice into general use.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Nitrous oxide proved insufficient as a sole anesthetic for major surgical procedures, leading to the adoption of stronger agents such as diethyl ether in 1846 and chloroform in 1847. However, the gas found an important role as an initiator for these more potent anesthetics. In 1876, Joseph Thomas Clover invented the "gas-ether inhaler," which allowed practitioners to begin anesthesia with a mild flow of nitrous oxide before gradually increasing the concentration of stronger agents. This technique of initiating anesthesia with nitrous oxide remained standard practice in many hospitals until the 1930s and continues in modified form today.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: Throughout the twentieth century, nitrous oxide maintained dual roles as both a medical tool and recreational substance. In the late 1800s, philosopher William James published accounts of his experiments with the gas, describing its effects as having "some metaphysical significance." The substance became increasingly accessible as it found commercial applications, particularly as a whipped cream propellant sold in small cartridges commonly known as "whippets." Recreational use saw apparent increases during the 1960s and 1970s, particularly among dental and medical personnel with professional access to the gas. A 1979 paper indicated that up to 20% of dental and medical students had experimented with it. By 2000, surveys found nitrous oxide to be the most common inhalant among 16 and 17-year-olds in the United States. In England and Wales, surveys from 2013-2014 found the substance more popular than cocaine, MDMA, or ketamine among 16 to 24-year-olds, with an estimated half million young people using it at nightspots, festivals, and parties.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: The gas has earned various street names reflecting its effects and cultural associations, including "laughing gas," "hippy crack," "nitro," and "NOS." In 2024, under the street name "Galaxy Gas," nitrous oxide experienced a surge in popularity among young people, partially driven by social media trends. Today, nitrous oxide remains on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines while simultaneously being one of the most commonly used inhalants worldwide.

Davy coined the term "laughing gas," documented the substance's euphoric and analgesic properties through self-experimentation, and suggested its potential for surgical use in his 1800 publication. His recommendation went unheeded for over four decades.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: American dentist who first recognized and demonstrated the anesthetic properties of nitrous oxide for dental procedures. After observing a man remain unaware of an injury while under the gas's influence at a public exhibition, Wells arranged his own tooth extraction under nitrous oxide anesthesia on December 11, 1844, marking the first use of the substance as an anesthetic drug in patient treatment.

chunks.title: Nitrous
chunks.text: American showman and entrepreneur who organized the nitrous oxide exhibition that inspired Horace Wells and later played a crucial role in popularizing the gas for dental use. Beginning in 1863, Colton established the "Colton Dental Association" clinics and administered nitrous oxide to over 25,000 patients within three years, bringing the practice into widespread acceptance.

chunks.title: Nitrous

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: NM-2-AI is a relatively obscure synthetic stimulant in the aminoindane class. Chemically, it is 2-aminoindane with N-methyl substitution and is structurally related to 2-AI and MDAI. Compared with 2-AI, reports describe it as less potent, longer lasting, and broadly similar in stimulant character. It has been sold online by research-chemical vendors as a designer drug.

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: Withdrawal effects are mentioned in the context of addiction, but specific physical dependence characteristics have not been documented for this substance.

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: Chronic use is considered moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing has been reported. When addiction develops, cravings and withdrawal effects may occur upon cessation.

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: As with other stimulants, abuse at high dosages for prolonged periods can potentially result in stimulant psychosis presenting with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions. Based on data from related amphetamine-type stimulants, approximately 5-15% of individuals who develop stimulant psychosis may fail to recover completely, though antipsychotic medications effectively resolve symptoms of acute episodes.

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: Seizure risk from NM-2-AI alone has not been documented, though combination with certain substances may increase seizure risk.

chunks.title: NM-2-AI
chunks.text: NM-2-AI is a novel stimulant belonging to the aminoindane chemical class. Structurally, it represents a rigid analogue of methamphetamine and shares close chemical relationships with other aminoindane compounds such as 2-AI and MDAI. The substance emerged on the online research chemical market as a designer drug, where it has been sold through various vendors. It remains a lesser-known compound compared to its aminoindane relatives, with limited documentation of its history or cultural significance beyond its presence in the contemporary designer drug landscape.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text: Noopept (omberacetam, GVS-111) is a peptide-derived nootropic first synthesized in 1996 and developed as a prescription medication in Russia. It has become one of the most widely used cognitive enhancers, often taken in combination 'stacks' with other nootropics. Noopept is commonly attributed with temporarily enhancing concentration, focus, and memory recall. Daily use may lead to dependence, with withdrawal reportedly causing negative cognitive effects.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text: Withdrawal from daily use reportedly causes negative cognitive effects and impaired ability, indicating some degree of physical adaptation with chronic use.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text: Daily use is reported to create dependency, suggesting some potential for psychological habituation with regular administration.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text: Noopept (omberacetam) functions as a prodrug of the endogenous dipeptide cycloprolylglycine. The active metabolite modulates AMPA receptors and exerts neuroprotective effects that appear dependent upon both AMPA receptor and TrkB receptor activation. In cell culture studies, cycloprolylglycine has been shown to increase brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Additional research suggests that noopept may act as an activator of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1), which could contribute to its pharmacological profile. Rat studies have attributed its effects to antioxidant activity, anti-inflammatory action, and the ability to inhibit neurotoxicity from excess calcium and glutamate, as well as improvements in blood rheology.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text: Noopept is orally bioavailable and acts as a prodrug, being metabolized to the active dipeptide cycloprolylglycine. As of 2017, its metabolism and elimination half-life in humans were not well characterized.

chunks.title: Noopept
chunks.text:
Noopept was developed by a Russian pharmaceutical company during the 1970s and remains a prescription medication in Russia. Its synthesis was first formally reported in scientific literature in 1996. The compound has been evaluated for potential neuroprotective applications, particularly in the context of brain injuries and stroke treatment.

In recent years, noopept has emerged as one of the most widely used substances within the nootropic class. Its growing profile and popularity have attracted attention from mainstream media on multiple occasions, contributing to its recognition beyond specialized research and enthusiast communities.

chunks.title: Nordazepam
chunks.text: Nordazepam is a 1,4-benzodiazepine derivative used primarily in the treatment of anxiety disorders. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant, sedative, and amnesic properties. Notably, it serves as an active metabolite of several other benzodiazepines, including diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, and clorazepate. As a partial agonist at the GABAA receptor, it is considered less potent than many other benzodiazepines. It has one of the longest elimination half-lives in its class and should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Nordazepam
chunks.text: Nordazepam is considered habit-forming, and benzodiazepines warrant caution in alcohol- or drug-dependent individuals.

chunks.title: Norflurazepam
chunks.text: Norflurazepam is a benzodiazepine analog that occurs naturally as an active metabolite of several established benzodiazepines, including flurazepam, flutoprazepam, and midazolam. It has been sold as a designer drug since 2016. Norflurazepam is notably long-acting and prone to accumulation in the body, binding non-selectively across benzodiazepine receptor subtypes. Its extended duration presents significant risks of compounding effects with repeated dosing, and it should not be combined with other CNS depressants.
