chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: Nutmeg is a common culinary spice derived from the seeds of Myristica fragrans, a plant indigenous to Indonesia and New Guinea. Its primary psychoactive constituent is myristicin, a phenylpropene aromatic ether. When consumed orally in quantities far exceeding culinary use, nutmeg produces deliriant, hallucinogenic, and oneirogenic effects. Its widespread availability as an ordinary household spice makes it one of the most accessible psychoactive substances.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: The intensely dysphoric and physically unpleasant nature of nutmeg intoxication provides minimal reinforcing effects, though recreational use does occur among those seeking a low-cost high, particularly adolescents and prisoners with limited access to other substances.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: High doses can cause serious toxic effects including acute psychosis. Delirium, anxiety, and confusion are common features of intoxication, with risks heightened in individuals with pre-existing psychiatric conditions.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: Myristicin, a major psychoactive component of nutmeg, can cause convulsions when consumed in large amounts.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Large doses can cause convulsions, delirium, confusion, severe headaches, amnesia, and generalized body pain; these effects may persist for several days following intoxication.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes

chunks.title: Nutmeg

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Large amounts consumed during pregnancy may cause premature labor and miscarriage; nutmeg was historically considered an abortifacient.

chunks.title: Nutmeg

chunks.text: May also interact with pain relievers such as pethidine during pregnancy. Safe only in small flavoring amounts during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Allergic reactions and contact dermatitis have been reported with nutmeg exposure.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: The psychoactive effects of nutmeg appear to derive from anticholinergic-like hallucinogenic mechanisms attributed primarily to myristicin and elemicin, two phenylpropanoid compounds present in the essential oil. Myristicin has additionally been identified as a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. The essential oil is a complex mixture containing dozens of terpenes and phenylpropanoids, and the overall psychoactive profile likely reflects contributions from multiple constituents rather than a single compound.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text:
Nutmeg is native to the Banda Islands, a cluster of eleven small volcanic islands within the Maluku archipelago of eastern Indonesia. These remote islands remained the world's sole source of both nutmeg and mace until the mid-nineteenth century. Archaeological excavations on Pulau Ai have yielded potsherd residues dating back approximately 3,500 years, representing the earliest known evidence of nutmeg use.

The spice circulated through Austronesian maritime trading networks from at least 1500 BCE. By the sixth century CE, nutmeg had spread westward to India and subsequently reached Constantinople. Arab merchants eventually traced the spice to its source in the Banda Islands by the thirteenth century, though they carefully concealed this information from European traders to maintain their commercial advantage.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: European pursuit of nutmeg commenced following the Portuguese conquest of Malacca in August 1511. Shortly after securing this strategic trading hub, Afonso de Albuquerque dispatched a three-ship expedition under António de Abreu to locate the legendary spice islands. Malay pilots guided the fleet through Java and the Lesser Sundas, reaching Banda in early 1512. This marked the first European contact with the islands, where the expedition spent approximately one month acquiring nutmeg, mace, and cloves. The Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires, stationed in Malacca from 1512 to 1515, documented these islands in his work Suma Oriental. However, Portugal never established permanent control over the trade. The Dutch East India Company waged a brutal campaign for monopoly over nutmeg production in 1621. The violence was catastrophic for the indigenous Bandanese population—historians estimate that of approximately 15,000 inhabitants, only around 1,000 survived, with the remainder killed, starved during flight, exiled, or sold into slavery. The Company subsequently constructed extensive plantation systems throughout the islands.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: During the Napoleonic Wars, British forces temporarily occupied the Banda Islands and transplanted nutmeg trees, along with their native soil, to Ceylon, Penang, Bencoolen, and Singapore. From these locations, cultivation spread to additional colonial territories including Zanzibar and Grenada. Dutch control of the Spice Islands persisted until the Second World War.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text:
Nutmeg has acquired symbolic importance in several regions shaped by its trade history. Grenada, which developed into a major producer following British colonial transplantation efforts, incorporated a stylized split-open nutmeg fruit into its national flag upon adoption in 1974. In the United States, Connecticut carries the nickname "the Nutmeg State," purportedly stemming from folklore about dishonest traders who carved wooden imitations to deceive buyers. The expression "wooden nutmeg" subsequently entered American vernacular as a general term for fraudulent merchandise.

Beyond culinary applications, nutmeg has traditionally been consumed for its psychoactive and reputed aphrodisiac properties, though clinical evidence supporting these uses remains limited. Its widespread availability and low cost have led to recreational experimentation, particularly among adolescents, college students, and incarcerated individuals seeking inexpensive intoxication.

chunks.title: Nutmeg
chunks.text: Binding profile: Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (non-selective)

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: O-Desmethyltramadol is an opioid analgesic and the primary active metabolite of tramadol. Since the 2010s, it has been available through the research chemical market as a standalone substance. It acts as a full agonist at the mu-opioid receptor with additional affinity for delta and kappa receptors, producing more typical opioid-like effects than its parent compound. It also exhibits some influence on monoaminergic systems.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops within a week of heavy daily use. Withdrawal effects match those of other opioids, including sweating, vomiting, flu-like symptoms, runny nose, chills, lethargy, and headache, though reportedly milder in intensity compared to stronger opioids like diamorphine. At least 3-5 days of moderate to strong flu-like illness should be expected upon cessation.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Moderate psychological addiction potential with risk of compulsive redosing. Tolerance develops rapidly with daily use, particularly with multiple daily doses, leading users to chase progressively harder to obtain positive effects, which is identified as a major driver of dependence.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Seizure risk may be lower than with tramadol, though this has not been definitively confirmed. The (S) enantiomer demonstrated seizure-inducing capability in rats at doses that also caused significant respiratory depression. Studies of tramadol intoxication found O-DSMT plasma levels correlated with seizure onset, though co-ingestion of benzodiazepines or other opioids appeared to reduce seizure risk.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term chronic use may be associated with elevated hepatic damage markers including α-GST, ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT, particularly in individuals who are CYP2D6 extensive or ultrarapid metabolizers; however, decades of tramadol use in humans has not produced clear evidence of severe hepatotoxicity when used moderately.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: O-DSMT generation is associated with increased serum lipid peroxidation and decreased total antioxidants, suggesting oxidative stress as a potential mechanism.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: One study of 60 patients on chronic tramadol therapy (200-400 mg/day for mean 3.9 years) showed significant increases in hepatic markers versus controls. Hepatotoxicity has been reported as a rare side effect affecting under 0.1% of patients. More research is needed for definitive conclusions.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is the primary life-threatening effect in overdose; a sensation of labored breathing may occur at strong doses and represents a danger sign in overdose situations.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mu-opioid receptor agonism causing central respiratory depression.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Fatality cases showed lung congestion with elevated lung weight, supporting respiratory depression as mechanism of death. At common doses, changes in respiratory sensation are typically not physically dangerous.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: O-Desmethyltramadol acts primarily as a μ-opioid receptor full agonist with substantial affinity (Ki of 19 nM for the racemic mixture), with the (+)-enantiomer exhibiting G-protein biased signaling and considerably higher affinity (Ki of 3 nM). The substance also binds δ- and κ-opioid receptors, though with comparatively much lower affinity. O-DSMT acts as a competitive antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors at pharmacologically relevant concentrations. The (−)-enantiomer retains some norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor activity, though the potency gap between opioid and monoaminergic activity is substantial enough that this property is functionally minimal for the racemic mixture. Additional in vitro findings include inhibition of muscarinic M1 receptor activity and inhibition of Substance P.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: O-Desmethyltramadol is pharmacologically active without requiring metabolic activation. It is metabolized in the liver into the active metabolite N,O-didesmethyltramadol via CYP3A4 and CYP2B6. The organic cation transporter OCT1, expressed on hepatocyte membranes, mediates uptake of the substance into the liver; individuals with reduced OCT1 activity metabolize it more slowly. Reported elimination half-life values range from approximately 6.7 to 9 hours, with oral peak plasma concentrations reached around 3 hours.

chunks.text: Ki = 19 nM (racemic); 3 nM ((+)-enantiomer); 674 nM ((−)-enantiomer)

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Competitive inhibition at pharmacologically relevant concentrations

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: (−)-enantiomer only; functionally minimal for racemic mixture

Peak plasma concentrations reached in approximately 3 hours

Reduced OCT1 activity leads to slower metabolism and stronger opioid effects

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Tolerance develops very rapidly with daily use, particularly when dosing multiple times per day. The most desirable effects may become difficult to obtain after just a few days of heavy use. This rapid tolerance development is identified as a major driver of dependence, as users continue attempting to achieve progressively harder to obtain positive effects.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text:
O-Desmethyltramadol has a limited independent history because it has never been marketed by pharmaceutical companies as a standalone medication, instead being encountered primarily as the principal active metabolite of the analgesic tramadol. Comparatively little research has been conducted on the compound relative to its parent drug.

The substance first appeared as a standalone product in the 2000s and gained modest popularity during the 2010s when grey market and research chemical vendors began selling it online. Analysis of commercial "incense" products purchased between 2008 and 2009 revealed O-desmethyltramadol was present in three of 140 samples tested, appearing either alone or in combination with caffeine. Outside of its role as a metabolite and research chemical, the compound has seen very limited legitimate human usage and remains unapproved for medicinal use in any country as of 2025.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text:
A series of fatal overdoses involving O-desmethyltramadol occurred in the late 2000s and early 2010s in connection with a commercial herbal preparation marketed as "Krypton." This product was found to contain kratom leaf powder adulterated with O-desmethyltramadol, representing one of the earliest documented instances of the compound being added to commercial products without consumer knowledge.

Beginning in November 2009, Swedish authorities identified nine cases of fatal overdose in which postmortem blood samples tested positive for both mitragynine (a kratom alkaloid) and O-desmethyltramadol in the absence of tramadol, indicating direct consumption of O-desmethyltramadol rather than metabolic conversion from tramadol. These cases were interpreted as involving the Krypton product, though all fatalities also involved additional drugs. A similar case was documented in Germany, where a user of an alleged kratom product tested positive for O-desmethyltramadol and kratom alkaloids without tramadol being detected.

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Opioids

chunks.title: O-Desmethyltramadol
chunks.text: Binding profile: μ-opioid receptor agonist (full); δ-opioid receptor agonist; 5-HT2C receptor antagonist; Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist; Substance P

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: O-PCE is a lesser-known novel dissociative of the arylcyclohexylamine class that produces dissociative, anesthetic, stimulating, and hallucinogenic effects, speculated to act primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist. Structurally related to MXE and deschloroketamine, it emerged as a contemporary designer drug marketed through online research chemical vendors as a replacement for MXE and other dissociatives. It is reportedly habit-forming, and its pharmacological profile remains poorly characterized.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: Cravings and withdrawal effects may occur when a person suddenly stops usage after addiction has developed, though the severity of physical dependence appears less pronounced than the psychological component.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: O-PCE is regarded as moderately addictive and as having high abuse potential, and it can cause psychological dependence in some users. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, particularly due to its potency and stimulating nature.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: Mania is listed among potential cognitive effects at higher doses. As with other dissociatives, O-PCE may carry some risk of adverse psychological reactions including delusions and psychosis, particularly at higher doses or in predisposed individuals.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: O-PCE's structural similarity to ketamine and deschloroketamine, which have been speculated to have antibacterial and immunomodulative properties, has raised concern about whether O-PCE shares these properties. This remains entirely unknown due to lack of scientific research, though prolonged use could potentially pose a threat to immune function if this proves to be the case.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity data available due to lack of scientific research.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Repeated and excessive use over extended periods may cause bladder and urinary tract problems similar to those seen with ketamine, including urinary frequency, urgency, pressure, pelvic and bladder pain, hematuria, and incontinence; occasional use appears to carry minimal risk.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The extent of bladder toxicity compared to ketamine is unclear. O-PCE's higher potency means less substance needs to be consumed to achieve similar effects. Anecdotal evidence suggests symptoms can be largely avoided by refraining from regular use (e.g., weekly at minimum) and carefully limiting intake.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: No formal pharmacological studies of O-PCE have been published. Based on structure-activity relationship analysis and its structural similarity to other arylcyclohexylamine dissociatives such as ketamine and methoxetamine, O-PCE is thought to produce its effects principally through NMDA receptor antagonism. Other neurotransmitter systems may also be involved, though this remains uncharacterized.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: Repeated O-PCE use over time can produce tolerance to many effects, so users may need larger amounts to obtain comparable results.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text:
O-PCE emerged as part of the wave of novel arylcyclohexylamine designer drugs that appeared on the online research chemical market following the decline in MXE availability. The compound was specifically developed and marketed as a functional replacement for MXE and other dissociatives that had become increasingly difficult to obtain due to international scheduling efforts.

The substance became available primarily through online research chemical vendors, where it continues to be sold for recreational purposes. Unlike many established dissociatives, O-PCE has received minimal attention in the scientific literature, with almost no formal research examining its pharmacological profile, toxicity, or potential for abuse and dependence in humans. This lack of scientific documentation is characteristic of many contemporary designer drugs that enter the market faster than researchers can study them.

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (uncompetitive)

chunks.title: O-PCE
chunks.text:
O-PCE — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol
- Depressants
- Stimulants

chunks.text:

- Germany: Controlled (NpSG) — Regulated under the Neue-psychoaktive-Stoffe-Gesetz (New Psychoactive Substances Act) since July 18, 2019. Manufacturing and importing for market distribution, administering to others, and commercial…

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.text: Opium is a naturally occurring opioid preparation obtained from the dried latex of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum. Its use dates back over 5,000 years to ancient Mesopotamia, making it one of the oldest known psychoactive substances. The latex contains dozens of alkaloids, most notably morphine and codeine, which produce analgesic, sedative, and euphoric effects. Opium carries a high potential for addiction, physical dependence, tolerance, and fatal overdose.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.text: Regular or long-term opium and morphine use can lead to tolerance and physical dependence.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.text: Opium's addictive character is tied to mu-opioid receptor activity that increases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, and long-term use is repeatedly described as causing addiction.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.text: Opium is described as having sufficient evidence for carcinogenicity in humans.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Reported harms include hypoventilation, prolonged apnea, respiratory obstruction, respiratory difficulties, lung edema, coma, and cardiac or respiratory collapse.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mu-opioid receptor effects produce respiratory depression and can progress to cardiorespiratory collapse in severe poisoning.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Alcohol and other depressants are described as additive or contributing factors in fatal opioid outcomes.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term opioid effects are linked to lower testosterone, loss of libido, impotence, amenorrhea, and infertility.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Opioid-driven impairment of hypothalamic function is identified as the mechanism.

chunks.title: Opium
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The effect is described for opium/opioid exposure during long-term use.

- United States: Medical product listings — US belladonna-and-opium suppository products are categorized under unapproved or other products.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam is an intermediate-acting benzodiazepine prescribed for the treatment of anxiety disorders, panic disorders, alcohol withdrawal, and insomnia. It is characterized by relatively low potency compared to other benzodiazepines, a slow onset of action, and a simple metabolic profile that makes it less susceptible to variability based on age or liver function. It is notably an active metabolite of both diazepam and temazepam. Higher doses may produce amnesia and lowered inhibitions.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, even at standard dosages and after relatively short-term use. Withdrawal symptoms are similar to those seen with alcohol and barbiturate withdrawal, including abdominal and muscle cramps, seizures, depression, insomnia, sweating, tremors, nausea, vomiting, and potentially hallucinations. Withdrawal should be medically supervised with gradual dose reduction.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam has documented abuse potential as a benzodiazepine, though its slow absorption and onset of action result in relatively lower abuse potential compared to faster-acting benzodiazepines such as temazepam, flunitrazepam, or triazolam. Misuse, defined as taking the drug to achieve a high or continuing use against medical advice, has been documented.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Paradoxical reactions including excitement, confusion, aggression, outbursts of anger, and restlessness may occur as side effects. Hallucinations have been reported primarily as a withdrawal symptom rather than during active use.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam itself has anticonvulsant properties as a benzodiazepine. However, seizures are a significant risk during withdrawal, particularly after prolonged use or abrupt discontinuation. Some benzodiazepines may trigger seizures in individuals with epilepsy. Flumazenil administration in long-term users may also precipitate seizures.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression may occur in overdose or when combined with other CNS depressants; at typical doses, significant respiratory effects are uncommon except in patients with pre-existing pulmonary conditions such as COPD or limited pulmonary reserve.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Enhanced GABAergic inhibition reduces respiratory drive in brainstem respiratory centers.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Contraindicated in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and limited pulmonary reserve. Risk of respiratory paralysis when mixed with other depressants including alcohol, GHB/GBL, or opioids.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hypotension may rarely occur during use; cardiovascular toxicity is occasionally observed in overdose situations.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Caution advised in patients for whom a drop in blood pressure may lead to cardiac complications.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam glucuronide (inactive)

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site located at the interface between the alpha and gamma subunits of the receptor. This binding potentiates the inhibitory effects of endogenous GABA in the central nervous system. Oxazepam also acts as an agonist at the translocator protein and has been shown to suppress cortisol levels.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam is metabolized through a relatively simple pathway involving direct glucuronidation, without requiring hepatic oxidation. The S-enantiomer is glucuronidated by UGT2B15, while the R-enantiomer is processed by UGT2B7 and UGT1A9, yielding a single major inactive glucuronide conjugate. Oxazepam itself is an active metabolite formed during the breakdown of diazepam, nordazepam, and temazepam, and it undergoes very little additional biotransformation following absorption. The mean elimination half-life is approximately 8.2 hours, with a reported range of 6 to 9 hours.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text:
Metabolized by direct glucuronidation rather than hepatic oxidation, reducing the amount lost during first-pass metabolism
Less susceptible to variability from liver impairment or age compared to many other benzodiazepines

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: 6-9 hours

chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Peak plasma levels occur approximately 3 hours after dosing
Among the most slowly absorbed of the common benzodiazepines

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Following prolonged use, gradual dose tapering under medical supervision is required rather than abrupt discontinuation. Complete tolerance reset timelines are not well-documented but extended abstinence periods are typically necessary.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Tolerance develops with regular use, typically within 4-6 weeks of continuous administration. As with other benzodiazepines, habituation can lead to significantly elevated dose requirements compared to initial effective doses.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Oxazepam was patented in 1962 and received approval for medical use in 1964. The compound became one of the most commonly prescribed benzodiazepines in multiple countries during the late 20th century. In Australia during 1990-1991, oxazepam along with diazepam, nitrazepam, and temazepam accounted for approximately 82% of benzodiazepine prescriptions listed on the pharmaceutical benefits scheme. The drug has been noted as a preferred benzodiazepine among novice users in several countries, attributed to its relatively slow absorption rate and low potential for accumulation in the body. However, this widespread availability also contributed to diversion and misuse; in Sweden between 1982 and 1986, benzodiazepines including oxazepam, diazepam, nitrazepam, and flunitrazepam represented 52% of all forged drug prescriptions, indicating their status as a major drug class subject to prescription fraud.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Research beginning in 2013 has examined the ecological effects of pharmaceutical contamination in aquatic environments. Laboratory studies exposing European perch to oxazepam concentrations equivalent to those present in European waterways (1.8 μg/L) documented increased activity, reduced sociality, and elevated feeding rates in exposed fish. Subsequent research in 2016 found that salmon smolt exposed to the compound for seven days prior to migration displayed intensified migratory behavior compared to controls. A 2019 study associated these behavioral changes with adverse survival outcomes, demonstrating that bolder, faster behavior in exposed smolt corresponded with increased mortality due to heightened vulnerability to predation. As a linguistic curiosity, the word "oxazepam" is reportedly the third-highest scoring word in Scrabble, valued at 392 points when played in the optimal position.

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzodiazepines, Other GABAergic depressants

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (benzodiazepine site); TSPO

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text:
Oxazepam — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol (Ethanol ingestion may potentiate the CNS effects of many benzodiazepines. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.)
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Opioids (Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)
- Tramadol (Central nervous system- and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. Vomit aspiration is a risk when passed out, lay down in recovery position if ingested.)

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text:
Oxazepam — unsafe combinations:
- Diphenhydramine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely. Low medical doses are unlikely to be of concern.)
- PCP (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely)

chunks.title: Oxazepam
chunks.text:
Oxazepam — caution combinations:
- DXM (Small doses of benzos can end a bad trip, but both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and this can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Ketamine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- MXE (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess.)

chunks.title: Oxazolam
chunks.text: Oxazolam is a benzodiazepine derivative classified as a depressant. It functions as a prodrug for desmethyldiazepam, meaning it is metabolically converted into its active form following administration. Oxazolam possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties. As with other benzodiazepines, it carries a risk of physical dependence and is considered habit-forming with repeated use.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam
chunks.text: Oxiracetam is a synthetic nootropic and mild central nervous system stimulant of the racetam family. It is among the earliest known derivatives of piracetam, distinguished by an additional hydroxy group on its pyrrolidone ring. Research into its efficacy in humans remains limited, though it has been investigated for potential benefits in dementia and cognitive impairment. It is not approved by the FDA for any medical use. Several studies suggest it is safe even at high doses over extended periods.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam
chunks.text: Chronic oxiracetam use is described as non-addictive with low abuse potential and no apparent psychological dependence, though this has not been clinically corroborated.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Half-life is reported as about 8 hours in healthy individuals and 10 to 68 hours in patients with renal impairment.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Renal impairment may prolong oxiracetam exposure.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Available evidence supports altered pharmacokinetics, not direct kidney injury.

chunks.title: Oxiracetam

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone is a semisynthetic opioid of the morphinan class, synthesized from poppy-derived thebaine. Developed in Germany in 1916 as part of efforts to improve upon existing opioids such as morphine and codeine, it entered clinical use the following year. It is widely prescribed for moderate to severe pain in both immediate and extended release formulations. Compared to other opioids, it is reportedly more stimulating and mood-elevating, contributing to its significant potential for recreational misuse.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops rapidly with regular use, reportedly faster than with morphine. Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, insomnia, muscle pain and weakness, restlessness, irritability, depression, sweating, cold shivers, vomiting, diarrhea, and painful cramps. Severe withdrawal is expected after abrupt cessation in dependent individuals.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone is highly addictive with significant potential for abuse and psychological dependence. Compulsive redosing is commonly reported, and many users find themselves consuming more than intended. The drug induces feelings of euphoria and relaxation that strongly reinforce continued use.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Hallucinations, confusion, and delirium are documented but uncommon side effects. These psychiatric manifestations are less frequent with oxycodone compared to some other opioids.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Seizures and convulsions are uncommon but have been reported.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: No carcinogenicity studies have been performed. Genotoxicity testing shows mixed results, with positive findings at high concentrations in some assays but negative results in others.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — carcinogenicity — evidence — in vitro — assay type
chunks.text: mixed results - genotoxic at 50 mcg/mL with metabolic activation and 400 mcg/mL without; clastogenic at ≥1250 mcg/mL with metabolic activation; negative in other assays

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Dose-dependent respiratory depression occurs at all doses, becoming clinically significant at higher doses or in opioid-naive individuals; overdose can result in respiratory arrest and death.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Direct depression of the respiratory center in the brainstem via mu-opioid receptor activation

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is the primary cause of opioid-related deaths. Risk is substantially increased when combined with other CNS depressants. Naloxone can reverse respiratory depression if administered promptly.

chunks.title: Oxycodone

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone is a semisynthetic opioid that acts as a highly selective full agonist of the μ-opioid receptor. Binding at this receptor activates G protein-coupled signaling that inhibits neurotransmitter release through reduced cAMP production, closure of calcium channels, and opening of potassium channels. Oxycodone also acts as an agonist at the κ-opioid and δ-opioid receptors, though with low affinity at both sites.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism (~95%) primarily through the cytochrome P450 system. CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 catalyze N-demethylation to the major metabolite noroxycodone (approximately 45-70% of the administered dose), while CYP2D6 catalyzes O-demethylation to oxymorphone (approximately 5-19%). Additional pathways include 6-keto-reduction and conjugation. Despite producing several metabolites with μ-opioid receptor activity, oxycodone itself accounts for approximately 83% of its analgesic effect after oral administration and approximately 95% after intravenous administration. Oral bioavailability averages 60-87% and is not affected by food. Oxycodone has a volume of distribution of 2.6 L/kg, with unbound brain concentrations approximately threefold higher than blood concentrations at equilibrium. The elimination half-life is approximately 3.2 hours for immediate-release formulations and 4.5 hours for extended-release formulations, with a clearance of 0.8 L/min. Oxycodone and its metabolites are primarily excreted in urine.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone tolerance can develop for many effects after sustained repeated use, sometimes within days of daily administration. The pace differs by effect: constipation-related tolerance develops especially slowly compared with analgesic and euphoric tolerance. People taking oxycodone daily may need to raise their dose substantially to obtain similar effects, with some chronic users reporting daily doses of 200 mg or more compared with initial effective doses of 5-10 mg.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text:
Oxycodone was first synthesized from the opium poppy alkaloid thebaine by Martin Freund and Edmund Speyer at the University of Frankfurt in Germany, with their synthesis published in 1916. Clinical application of the drug followed the next year, when it was initially employed for postoperative pain management among Central Powers soldiers during World War I, administered both intravenously and intramuscularly.

Edmund Speyer, born to a Jewish family in Frankfurt am Main in 1878, would later become a victim of the Holocaust. He perished on May 5, 1942, during the second day of deportations from the Łódź Ghetto—a fate documented in the ghetto's chronicle. When Freund died in 1920, Speyer had authored his obituary for the German Chemical Society.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: In early 1928, Merck introduced a combination product containing scopolamine, oxycodone, and ephedrine under the German initials SEE, later renamed Scophedal in 1942. This formulation was expressly designed to produce what its patent application and package insert described as "very deep analgesia and profound and intense euphoria," along with tranquilization and anterograde amnesia useful for surgical and battlefield injury cases. The ephedrine component was added to counteract circulatory and respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: The preparation became known as the "Miracle Drug of the 1930s" across Continental Europe and was selected by the Wehrmacht as a battlefield analgesic. Oxycodone was reportedly chosen over other opiates because it produced less sedation at equivalent analgesic doses compared to morphine, hydromorphone, and hydrocodone. Personal notes from Adolf Hitler's physician, Theodor Morell, reveal that Hitler received repeated injections of "Eukodal" (Merck's oxycodone product) and Scophedal, along with other opioids including pethidine, codeine, and morphine. Records indicate that oxycodone supplies became unobtainable after late January 1945 as the war concluded. Scophedal remained in production until 1987, though the formulation can still be extemporaneously compounded.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text: Oxycodone entered the American pharmaceutical market in May 1939. The first oxycodone-containing product to receive FDA approval was Percodan, granted on April 12, 1950. These initial formulations established oxycodone as a recognized option within American pain management practice.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text:
During the early 1990s, Purdue Pharma, a privately held company headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut, developed a controlled-release oxycodone formulation marketed as OxyContin (the suffix referencing its continuous, extended-duration pain relief). The FDA granted approval in 1995 without requiring long-term efficacy studies or formal assessment of the drug's addiction potential.

Upon release, OxyContin was promoted as a breakthrough for patients experiencing moderate to severe pain, and it rapidly became a commercial success, reportedly generating approximately $35 billion in revenue for Purdue Pharma. However, the controlled-release mechanism proved vulnerable to circumvention—crushing the tablets released the full oxycodone dose immediately rather than gradually. David Kessler, who served as FDA commissioner during the approval, later characterized the decision as "certainly one of the worst medical mistakes." By 2011, oxycodone had become the leading cause of drug-related deaths in the United States, though heroin and fentanyl overtook it in this regard from 2012 onward.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text:
The role of Purdue Pharma and its owners in the emerging opioid crisis became subject to intense public examination. In October 2017, The New Yorker published an investigation examining Mortimer Sackler and Purdue Pharma's connection to marketing practices that may have contributed to widespread oxycodone dependence. The article traced how business approaches pioneered by Raymond and Arthur Sackler in direct pharmaceutical marketing were subsequently applied to OxyContin promotion.

In 2019, The New York Times published reporting based on verified documents from a Massachusetts lawsuit filed by Attorney General Maura Healey. These materials revealed that Richard Sackler, son of Raymond Sackler, had instructed company officials in 2008 to "measure our performance by Rx's by strength, giving higher measures to higher strengths." The lawsuit alleged that both Purdue Pharma and members of the Sackler family were aware that prescribing high doses of OxyContin over extended periods would increase the risk of serious adverse effects, including the development of addiction.

chunks.title: Oxycodone
chunks.text:
In August 2010, Purdue Pharma introduced a reformulated OxyContin line incorporating a polymer called Intac, engineered to resist crushing or dissolution in water and thereby reduce non-medical use. The FDA approved relabeling this reformulated version as abuse-resistant in April 2013. The agency had revoked approval for the original sustained-release formulation due to documented widespread misuse.

Despite its complex and often controversial history, oxycodone maintains its place as a therapeutic alternative on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines and is available in generic form. As of 2023, it ranked as the 49th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 13 million prescriptions dispensed annually.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: Oxymorphone is a semi-synthetic opioid analgesic of the morphinan class, structurally related to morphine and heroin. First developed in Germany in 1914 and introduced to the American market in 1959, it was designed to produce fewer side effects than its predecessors. Oxymorphone is approximately seven times more potent than morphine and is used in the management of moderate to severe pain. Notably, it is almost entirely devoid of antitussive properties.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: Oxymorphone exerts its primary effects through agonism of the μ-opioid receptor. It also interacts with the δ-opioid receptor and, to a much lesser extent, the κ-opioid receptor. The nature of its δ-opioid interaction is not fully agreed upon: it has been characterized as antagonism, but has also been described as an activating interaction that may augment its μ-opioid effects. Through μ-opioid receptors on GABAergic interneurons, oxymorphone disinhibits descending pain modulation pathways. It is approximately 10 times more potent than morphine, with 1 mg of oxymorphone hydrochloride considered equivalent to approximately 9.85 mg of morphine sulfate.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: Oxymorphone undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism. Oral bioavailability is notably low at approximately 10%, attributable to substantial first-pass metabolism, though co-administration with a large fatty meal can increase it to approximately 40%. The primary metabolic pathway involves conjugation, with the oxymorphone conjugate accounting for the majority of urinary metabolites. Additional metabolism occurs via 6-keto reduction, yielding 6β-carbinol and 6α-carbinol derivatives that are subsequently conjugated. The elimination half-life is approximately 1.3 hours.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text:
Oxymorphone was first developed in Germany in 1914 as part of efforts to create opioid analgesics with improved side effect profiles compared to morphine and heroin. The compound exhibits actions and uses similar to morphine, though notably lacks cough suppressant activity.

During the 1930s, researchers developed mono-, di-, tri-, and tetra-ester derivatives of oxymorphone, similar to acetylation processes used with morphine and hydromorphone, though none of these variants were adopted for medical use. The drug was patented in the United States by Endo Pharmaceuticals in 1955 and received approval for medical use in 1959, when it was introduced to the American market under the brand name Numorphan. This name was derived by analogy to other opioid product names including Nucodan for oxycodone, Paramorphan for dihydromorphine, and Paracodin for dihydrocodeine.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: Prior to 2012, oxymorphone was commonly administered via insufflation among recreational users. In 2012, Endo Pharmaceuticals introduced a reformulated extended-release version of Opana designed to be crush-resistant, intended to reduce abuse through nasal administration. However, this reformulation had unintended consequences as users adapted by dissolving the tablets and injecting them intravenously. In January 2013, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported an illness cluster associated with intravenous abuse of Opana ER in Tennessee, presenting with symptoms resembling thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Subsequently, in January 2015, the Indiana State Department of Health identified the first HIV outbreak directly linked to prescription opioid abuse in Scott County, a small rural community in southeastern Indiana. By late March 2015, Austin, Indiana had become the epicenter of an HIV outbreak traced to injectable use of the reformulated Opana ER.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: Research into these events determined that the crush-resistant reformulation paradoxically increased the risk of blood-borne infection transmission by driving users from nasal to intravenous administration, ultimately creating greater public health risks than those associated with injectable heroin or cocaine.

chunks.title: Oxymorphone
chunks.text: In June 2017, amid the escalating opioid epidemic and evidence that the 2012 reformulation had failed to prevent illicit injection, the FDA took the unprecedented step of requesting that Endo Pharmaceuticals voluntarily remove reformulated Opana ER from the United States market. By July 6, 2017, Endo International complied with this request, marking a significant regulatory action in response to the opioid crisis. Generic versions of extended-release oxymorphone remain available in the United States.

chunks.title: Pagoclone
chunks.text: Pagoclone is an anxiolytic agent of the cyclopyrrolone class, a nonbenzodiazepine structurally related to zopiclone. Synthesized by Rhone-Poulenc & Rorer, it acts as a partial agonist at the benzodiazepine site of GABAA receptors, producing anxiolytic effects with comparatively little sedation at therapeutic doses. It was investigated for panic disorder and stuttering but never commercialized due to insufficient clinical efficacy. It has occasionally appeared on the research chemical market, though recreational use remains minimal.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.text: Paracetamol is a widely used non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic agent first synthesized in 1878. It is the most commonly taken pain and fever medication worldwide and is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. Available over the counter in numerous formulations, it is frequently combined with opioids and other drugs. Paracetamol is not considered to have recreational value. Overdose poses a serious risk of fatal liver failure and is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the Western world.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.text: Carcinogenic activity in female rats and an association with kidney cancer are noted, but confirmed human carcinogenicity is not established.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose can cause hepatic necrosis, liver failure, and acute liver failure, and prolonged daily use may damage the liver.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: CYP2E1 metabolism produces NAPQI; high doses deplete glutathione and allow reactive metabolite binding in liver cells.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Alcohol and some enzyme-inducing drugs may increase hepatotoxic risk.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Overdose may cause renal tubular necrosis and kidney failure; meta-analyses are described as suggesting increased kidney impairment and kidney cancer risk.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed renal mechanism.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Prolonged daily use is also described as possibly causing kidney damage.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Higher regular doses are linked to gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer risk, and bleeding events; overdose may include thrombocytopenia.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed mechanism.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: One knee-pain trial is described as showing hemoglobin drops consistent with gastrointestinal bleeding.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Dose-related adverse-effect summaries include increased mortality and cardiovascular outcomes such as stroke and myocardial infarction; paracetamol may slightly increase blood pressure and heart rate.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed cardiovascular mechanism.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Rare severe outcomes are reported in observational or meta-analytic summaries.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Reports note rare skin reactions that may be fatal, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

chunks.title: Paracetamol
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed mechanism.

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text: Parafluorofentanyl is an extremely potent synthetic opioid and analogue of fentanyl, originally developed by Janssen Pharmaceutica during the 1960s. It is classified as a depressant with significant habit-forming potential. The substance remains rare, and relatively little is known about its pharmacological profile or safety margins. Due to its exceptional potency, it should be handled with extreme caution, and combining it with other depressants is strongly discouraged due to the heightened risk of fatal respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text: Parafluorofentanyl is an opioid analgesic and a structural analogue of fentanyl. Beyond its classification as an opioid analgesic, detailed pharmacodynamic characterization is not available in the current literature.

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text:
Parafluorofentanyl was originally developed by Janssen Pharmaceutica during the 1960s as part of their extensive research into fentanyl analogs. The compound appeared briefly on the illicit United States market in the early 1980s, notably predating the introduction of the Federal Analog Act, which represented the first legislative attempt to control entire families of drugs based on structural similarity rather than scheduling each compound individually as it emerged.

Fentanyl analogs as a class have been responsible for thousands of fatalities across Europe and former Soviet republics since a resurgence in use that originated in Estonia during the early 2000s, with novel derivatives continuing to appear on illicit markets. In 2020, the United States Drug Enforcement Administration issued warnings regarding the increasing prevalence of parafluorofentanyl specifically in Arizona. Despite these developments, the substance remains relatively rare and poorly characterized in the scientific literature.

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Opioids

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text: Binding profile: μ-opioid receptor agonist (full)

chunks.title: Parafluorofentanyl
chunks.text:
Legal status of Parafluorofentanyl by country:
- United States: Controlled substance analog if intended for human consumption — Parafluorofentanyl may be subject to Federal Analog Act treatment as a fentanyl-like analog, with DEA attention in Arizona.

chunks.title: Pargy-LAD
chunks.text: PARGY-LAD is a synthetic psychedelic of the lysergamide class and a structural analog of LSD. It was developed by David E. Nichols and colleagues at Purdue University during the 1980s and later documented by Alexander Shulgin in TiHKAL. PARGY-LAD is considerably less potent than LSD and is largely characterized by its obscurity and lack of distinguishing features. Very little data exists regarding its pharmacology, metabolism, or toxicity, and it has minimal history of human use.

chunks.title: Pargy-LAD
chunks.text: Formal studies are lacking, but PARGY-LAD appears to have low habit-forming potential, with desire to use tending to decline after repeated administration.

chunks.title: Pargy-LAD
chunks.text: Lithium and psychedelic combinations may significantly increase psychosis risk, while cannabis and stimulants may increase adverse psychological reactions including anxiety, paranoia, panic attacks, and psychosis.

chunks.title: Pargy-LAD
chunks.text: Lithium with psychedelics may significantly increase seizure risk, and tramadol may lower seizure threshold in susceptible individuals.

chunks.title: Pargy-LAD
chunks.text:
Legal status of Pargy-LAD by country:
- Germany: Controlled under NpSG — Since July 18, 2019, Germany's New Psychoactive Substances Act has controlled Pargy-LAD; commercial supply and administration are punishable, while possession is illegal but not penalized.
- Latvia: Illegal — Controlled as an LSD structural analog after a June 1, 2015 amendment, despite not being individually scheduled.
- Switzerland: Not controlled — PARGY-LAD is not named in the relevant Swiss schedules or covered by the lysergic-acid derivative definition.
- United Kingdom: Class A — PARGY-LAD was specifically named in the Misuse of Drugs Act as of January 7, 2015.

chunks.title: PBP
chunks.text: PBP is a synthetic stimulant and research chemical originally developed in the 1960s. Structurally, it is the intermediate homologue between the better-known compounds α-PPP and α-PVP. It has surfaced in recent years as a novel designer drug and is considered habit-forming. Very limited information is available regarding its pharmacology, toxicity, and long-term safety profile, warranting particular caution with its use.

chunks.title: PCE
chunks.text: PCE (eticyclidine) is a dissociative anesthetic of the arylcyclohexylamine class that produces hallucinogenic effects. It is reported to be slightly more potent than its structural relative PCP (phencyclidine). Like other arylcyclohexylamines, it carries habit-forming potential. Limited documentation exists regarding its safety profile, and users should exercise considerable caution given the scarcity of available research on its effects and risks.

chunks.title: PCE
chunks.text: Classified as habit-forming, suggesting some potential for psychological dependence.

chunks.title: PCE
chunks.text: PCE (eticyclidine) is a dissociative anesthetic of the arylcyclohexylamine class. It is structurally related to phencyclidine (PCP) and is reported to be slightly more potent. Detailed receptor binding data for PCE remains limited in the available literature.

chunks.title: PCE
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Dissociatives, NMDA receptor antagonists

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: PCP is a dissociative anesthetic of the arylcyclohexylamine class, originally introduced as a medical anesthetic roughly sixty years ago, though most of its use has since occurred outside clinical settings. It functions primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist. PCP is commonly associated with erratic and sometimes violent behavior, though such incidents likely reflect overdose cases rather than typical use. Caution is warranted due to reports of mania, psychosis, and habit-forming potential.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: PCP is classified as habit-forming and is known to cause addiction with excessive use. It induces ΔFosB expression in the nucleus accumbens and has rewarding and reinforcing effects mediated in part by NMDA receptor blockade in dopaminergic pathways.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: PCP is more likely to produce psychosis compared to other dissociatives. Studies found agitation or hallucinations in up to 50% of patients at anesthetic doses, with greater psychiatric issues in approximately 17%. Recreational doses occasionally induce psychotic states with emotional and cognitive impairment resembling schizophrenic episodes. A 2019 review found that 26% of those diagnosed with hallucinogen-induced psychosis (including PCP) later transitioned to a schizophrenia diagnosis. High doses have been associated with dangerous psychotic states, including paranoia, delusions, and suicidal impulses. Flashbacks may occur despite stopping usage.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: High doses and overdoses may lead to convulsions and seizures. Benzodiazepines are the drugs of choice for controlling seizures when present during PCP intoxication. Certain antipsychotics such as phenothiazines may lower the seizure threshold and are not preferred for managing PCP-induced psychosis.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Neurotoxicity is a concern with PCP, particularly at high doses and with frequent use, though the clinical significance in humans remains controversial. Animal studies have shown that high doses of NMDA receptor antagonists can cause reversible vacuoles in brain tissue (Olney's lesions), but these findings are from non-human animals and may not directly apply to humans.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: NMDA receptor antagonism; causes schizophrenia-like changes in N-acetylaspartate and N-acetylaspartylglutamate levels in rat brain tissue

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Infrequent use and avoiding high doses is recommended to minimize potential neurotoxic effects. All Olney's lesion studies have been performed only on non-human animals.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) is described as a not-unusual manifestation of PCP toxicity and may occur during intoxication.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Urinary acidification during intoxication management can worsen rhabdomyolysis and induce acidosis.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: PCP acts primarily as a noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist, binding to a site within the ion channel that is accessible only when the channel has been opened by a coagonist such as glycine. It also functions as a potent partial agonist at dopamine D2 receptors (specifically the high-affinity state) and inhibits dopamine reuptake, leading to increased extracellular dopamine levels. PCP additionally shows high affinity for the σ2 receptor and inhibits nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Binding data indicate high selectivity for the NMDA receptor (Ki = 59 nM at the dizocilpine site) and σ2 receptor (Ki = 136 nM), with affinity exceeding 10,000 nM at most other assayed targets aside from the serotonin transporter (Ki = 2,234 nM).

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: PCP is both water- and lipid-soluble, allowing rapid distribution throughout the body. It undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, with approximately 90% metabolized via oxidative hydroxylation during the initial pass through the liver. The resulting metabolites are glucuronidated and excreted renally, while roughly 9% of an ingested dose is excreted unchanged in urine.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: Not-well-characterized site associated with monoamine reuptake inhibition

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: Approximately 90% of the drug is metabolized during its first pass through the liver, substantially reducing the amount that reaches systemic circulation

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
Phencyclidine was first synthesized in 1926 by German chemist Arthur Kötz and his student Paul Merkel during research involving Grignard reactions with piperidinocyclohexancarbonitrile compounds. The compound remained largely unexplored until 1956, when chemist H. Victor Maddox independently synthesized it and the pharmaceutical company Parke-Davis (now part of Pfizer) developed it as an anesthetic medication.

The drug's clinical career proved brief. By 1965, medical use in humans was prohibited in the United States due to an unacceptably high rate of adverse effects in patients. Veterinary applications continued for over a decade longer, but these too were discontinued in 1978. The development of ketamine, which produced similar anesthetic effects with better tolerability, rendered PCP obsolete in legitimate medicine.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
While still technically available as a medical anesthetic, PCP began appearing as a street drug in major American cities during the 1960s. Its recreational use grew substantially over the following decade, reaching a peak in the late 1970s. By 1978, prominent media outlets including People magazine and the CBS program 60 Minutes had declared it the nation's most pressing drug concern.

The trajectory reversed sharply in the following decade. Surveys of American high school students showed that 13% reported having tried PCP at least once in 1979; by 1990, this figure had dropped below 3%. Despite this overall decline, the substance has remained in circulation, particularly in certain American urban areas. Emergency department visits related to PCP increased between 2005 and 2011, and as of 2022, approximately 0.7% of American twelfth-grade students reported use within the prior year.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
PCP developed a fearsome popular reputation centered on claims that users became extraordinarily violent, impervious to pain, and capable of superhuman physical feats. Stories of users pulling out their own teeth, destroying property, and attacking others with unusual aggression became fixtures of drug scare coverage.

Research conducted by the Drug Abuse Warning Network during the 1970s found these media accounts to be substantially exaggerated. Studies indicated that violent incidents were uncommon and typically involved individuals with pre-existing patterns of aggressive behavior regardless of substance use. Notably, the dramatic violent reactions described in news coverage were not observed during the drug's legitimate clinical use as an anesthetic in the 1950s and 1960s, and subsequent investigations have frequently found reports of PCP-induced violence to lack evidentiary foundation.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: Media Portrayal and the Violence Narrative

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: The drug's notoriety during its peak usage period generated various cultural representations. American artist Jean-Michel Basquiat referenced the substance in his 1982 painting "Dustheads," which depicted two individuals using angel dust. The Japanese manga series City Hunter, created by Tsukasa Hojo in 1985, featured a drug called "Angel Dust," though a 2023 animated film adaptation reimagined this as a fictional nanomachine serum rather than the actual substance. The animated series Hazbin Hotel features a character who adopted "Angel Dust" as his chosen name.

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Other dissociatives

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text: Binding profile: NMDA receptor antagonist (uncompetitive); σ2; Dopamine D2 receptor agonist (partial); Dopamine reuptake inhibitor; SERT; PCP site 2; Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
PCP — dangerous combinations:
- 2C-T-x compounds
- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines
- AMT
- DXM
- GHB/GBL (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)
- MAOIs (This combination is very poorly explored)
- Tramadol

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
PCP — unsafe combinations:
- Alcohol (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)
- Amphetamines (This combination can easily lead to hypermanic states)
- Benzodiazepines (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely)
- Cocaine (This combination can easily lead to hypermanic states)
- DOx compounds (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)
- MDMA (This combination can easily lead to hypermanic states)
- SSRIs (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
PCP — caution combinations:
- Caffeine (Details of this combination are not well understood but PCP generally interacts in an unpredictable manner.)
- MXE (There are no reports available about this combination)
- Opioids (PCP can reduce opioid tolerance, increasing the risk of overdose)

chunks.title: PCP
chunks.text:
Legal status of PCP by country:
- Canada: Schedule I — PCP is in Schedule I under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act.
- Netherlands: List I — PCP is in List I under the Dutch Opium Law.
- United Kingdom: Class A — PCP is a Class A substance in the UK.
- United States: Schedule II — PCP is Schedule II, has ACSCN 7471, and human and veterinary uses were discontinued in 1965 and 1978.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.text: Pemoline is a stimulant of the 4-oxazolidinone class, structurally related to aminorex. First synthesized in 1913, its stimulant properties were not recognized until the 1930s. It acts primarily as a selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor with minimal noradrenergic activity, resulting in fewer cardiovascular side effects and lower misuse potential than most stimulants. Previously used for ADHD and narcolepsy, pemoline was withdrawn from most markets between 1997 and 2005 due to rare but serious liver toxicity, including fatalities.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Serious liver toxicity has caused liver transplantation or death, and many countries withdrew pemoline because of liver toxicity.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Pemoline is linked to rare but serious hepatotoxicity, elevated transaminases in about 1-2% of patients, at least 21 liver failure cases, and 13 liver replacement or death outcomes.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: The severe reactions are described as idiosyncratic, unpredictable, without a clear exposure-toxicity relationship, and sometimes sudden after months or years.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The FDA recommended regular liver testing, and the drug was withdrawn in many countries.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Reported adverse effects include insomnia, irritability, mild depression, drowsiness, hallucinations, and choreoathetosis symptoms in overdose.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed CNS mechanism.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Other stimulants and monoamine oxidase inhibitors are listed as contraindicated.

chunks.title: Pemoline
chunks.text: Binding profile: Stimulant (uncertain mechanism)

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.text: Pentazocine is a synthetic opioid analgesic of the benzomorphan class, first developed in 1958 and approved for medical use in 1967. It was the first mixed agonist-antagonist opioid to be marketed, acting primarily at kappa-opioid receptors. Unlike most opioids, pentazocine is subject to a ceiling effect and is notably more likely to produce psychotomimetic effects such as hallucinations, nightmares, and delusions. Oral formulations are often combined with naloxone to deter injection misuse.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.text: Pentazocine is considered a habit-forming opioid depressant.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.text: Pentazocine is described as fairly frequently causing hallucinations, nightmares, delusions, and psychotomimetic effects.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.text: Pentazocine is among agents that reduce seizure threshold, but seizure frequency is not quantified.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Pentazocine shares opioid adverse effects including drowsiness and respiratory depression; CNS depression can increase with other depressants.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Opioid receptor activity causes respiratory depression, with a ceiling effect described for dose-related respiratory depression.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Alcohol and other CNS depressants are specifically advised against.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Hallucinations, nightmares, delusions, and psychotomimetic effects are described as relatively frequent compared with many opioids.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: The source links the greater psychotomimetic risk to kappa-opioid receptor action.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Pentazocine is among agents that reduce seizure threshold.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: At high doses, pentazocine can raise blood pressure or heart rate, and intravenous administration after myocardial infarction may add cardiac workload.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed cardiovascular mechanism.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Use after myocardial infarction is advised against where possible.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Multiple injections have caused severe injection-site necrosis and sepsis, sometimes requiring amputation; rare agranulocytosis, erythema multiforme, and toxic epidermal necrolysis are also reported.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available evidence does not describe a detailed mechanism for tissue necrosis or immune/skin events.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Animal data suggest poorer subcutaneous tolerance than intramuscular tolerance.

chunks.title: Pentazocine
chunks.text:
Legal status of Pentazocine by country:
- Canada: Prescription product listed — A Canadian Talwin product exists for pentazocine.
- United States: Schedule IV — Pentazocine is Schedule IV in the United States; U.S. products also include Talwin and pentazocine/naloxone products.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.text: Chronic pentedrone use is described as moderately addictive with high abuse potential and liable to cause psychological dependence, cravings, and withdrawal effects.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.text: High-dose prolonged stimulant abuse is described as potentially causing stimulant psychosis with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.text: Combinations with highly stimulating 25x compounds or tramadol can increase seizure risk.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: Human toxicity data are limited. Pentedrone has been linked to at least one death in combination with alpha-PVP causing heart failure, and high-risk stimulant combinations may produce severe cardiovascular strain.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Dangerous combinations can raise heart rate and blood pressure to dangerous levels and may cause heart strain or heart failure in extreme cases.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Stimulant effects can produce excessive cardiovascular stimulation, vasoconstriction, and hypertension.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: One death is reported with combined pentedrone and alpha-PVP causing heart failure.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: High-dose prolonged stimulant abuse can result in stimulant psychosis with paranoia, hallucinations, or delusions.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Available reports describe this as a stimulant-class risk rather than a pentedrone-specific mechanism.

chunks.title: Pentedrone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Combinations with some substances may multiply risks of delusions, mania, and psychosis.
