chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate that produces potent sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic, muscle relaxant, and amnesic effects. It is used medically for the short-term treatment of insomnia, as an emergency anticonvulsant, and to induce medical comas. Pentobarbital acts on GABA-A receptors at a distinct allosteric site from benzodiazepines and is characterized by a relatively prompt onset of action. It is classified as habit-forming and is internationally scheduled as a controlled substance.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital produces severe physical dependence with chronic use. Barbiturate withdrawal is medically serious and can cause a life-threatening syndrome including seizures, psychosis, and death with abrupt discontinuation.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital is deemed extremely psychologically addictive, with compulsive redosing commonly reported. Short-acting barbiturates carry particularly high abuse potential, and the substance was widely abused beginning in the late 1930s.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Psychosis may occur as part of the life-threatening barbiturate withdrawal syndrome in dependent individuals. During intoxication, delusions of sobriety are reported at heavy doses, representing impaired reality testing rather than true psychosis.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital has anticonvulsant properties and suppresses seizures during use. However, abrupt discontinuation in dependent individuals may cause potentially fatal seizures as part of the withdrawal syndrome. Drugs that lower seizure threshold should be avoided during withdrawal.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Studies have linked barbiturate use with the development of cancer, though phenobarbital has been particularly implicated; evidence specific to pentobarbital is limited.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression is the primary acute toxicity and can progress to respiratory arrest and death, particularly at higher doses or when combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: GABAergic potentiation causes central depression of respiratory drive in the brainstem

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Respiratory arrest is the mechanism of death in pentobarbital overdose and its use in euthanasia and executions.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor, binding at the barbiturate site to prolong the duration of chloride ion channel opening. At higher concentrations, it is capable of directly activating the channel in the absence of GABA. This potentiation of GABAergic inhibitory tone is associated with marked decreases in GABA-sensitive neuronal calcium conductance. Pentobarbital also directly inhibits excitatory AMPA-type glutamate receptors, suppressing glutamatergic neurotransmission, and acts as an antagonist at NMDA receptors, kainate receptors, and neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α4 and α7 subunits).

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital undergoes first-pass metabolism in the liver and possibly the intestines via the hepatic microsomal enzyme system, with subsequent renal excretion. Oral bioavailability is approximately 70–90%, with 45–60% protein binding. The elimination half-life is dose-dependent, ranging from 5 to 50 hours.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Potentiator at α1–α6 subunits; direct agonist at high concentrations

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital was developed by chemists Ernest H. Volwiler and Donalee L. Tabern at Abbott Laboratories in 1930. That same year, physician John S. Lundy began clinical use of the compound and coined the brand name Nembutal, an amalgamation derived from the structural formula of its sodium salt—Na (sodium) combined with ethyl, methyl, butyl, and the common barbiturate suffix -al. The drug rapidly established itself in clinical practice as a sedative, short-term hypnotic, preanesthetic agent, and emergency anticonvulsant.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital became a widely abused pharmaceutical beginning in the late 1930s. Abbott's Nembutal capsules acquired the street name "yellow jackets" owing to the distinctive yellow color of the branded capsules. The formulation was available in 30, 50, and 100 mg capsules in yellow, white-orange, and yellow colors respectively, and the drug remained a commonly misused sedative throughout the mid-twentieth century.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Abbott Pharmaceutical ceased production of their Nembutal-branded pentobarbital capsules in 1999, reflecting a broader transition in clinical practice as the benzodiazepine family of drugs supplanted barbiturates for most sedative and anxiolytic applications. Pentobarbital retained utility in veterinary medicine as an anesthetic and euthanasia agent. The injectable formulation continues to be manufactured, with Danish pharmaceutical company Lundbeck (now produced through Akorn Pharmaceuticals) remaining the sole supplier of injectable pentobarbital approved for sale in the United States.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital has become a primary agent in physician-assisted death protocols across several jurisdictions. In the Netherlands, it constitutes part of the standard protocol for voluntary euthanasia, administered as a 9-gram oral solution in sugar syrup and alcohol following an antiemetic to prevent vomiting. Swiss protocols utilize intravenous sodium pentobarbital administration, which induces unconsciousness within approximately 30 seconds and cardiac arrest within 3 minutes. In the United States, oral pentobarbital is employed for physician-assisted death in states including Oregon, Washington, Vermont, and California.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Pentobarbital entered use in capital punishment following the 2011 cessation of sodium thiopental production by its sole U.S. manufacturer, which rendered importation of that traditional execution drug impractical. Pentobarbital was first employed in a U.S. execution in December 2010 in Oklahoma as part of a three-drug protocol. In March 2011, Ohio became the first jurisdiction to utilize pentobarbital as the sole lethal injection agent. This application generated significant international controversy. When Lundbeck discovered its product was being used for executions—a practice illegal under Danish law—public outcry in Danish media prompted the company to cease sales to U.S. states practicing capital punishment and to prohibit distributors from supplying any entities participating in human executions.

chunks.title: Pentobarbital
chunks.text: Despite these supply complications, multiple U.S. jurisdictions adopted pentobarbital protocols. Texas implemented a single-drug pentobarbital protocol in July 2012 following shortages of pancuronium bromide. Missouri modified its protocol in October 2013 to permit pentobarbital obtained from compounding pharmacies. In July 2019, U.S. Attorney General William Barr authorized the federal government to resume capital punishment after a 16-year suspension, with the federal protocol specifying intravenous administration of two syringes each containing 2.5 grams of pentobarbital sodium.

chunks.title: Pentylone
chunks.text: Pentylone is a stimulant of the substituted cathinone class, first synthesized in the 1960s. It reappeared on the research chemical market around 2010, sometimes found as a component of branded products such as NRG-1 and NRG-3, and has occasionally been misrepresented as MDMA. User reports vary considerably, ranging from mild stimulation to entactogen-like qualities at higher doses. Very little is known about its safety profile, particularly with long-term use.

chunks.title: Pethidine
chunks.text: Pethidine is a fully synthetic opioid analgesic of the phenylpiperidine class. First synthesized in 1938 by Otto Eisleb as a potential anticholinergic agent, its pain-relieving properties were subsequently identified by Otto Schaumann. Once widely prescribed for moderate to severe pain, pethidine has largely fallen out of clinical favor due to the neurotoxicity of its metabolite norpethidine, which can cause seizures and carries a notably elevated risk of serotonin syndrome compared to other opioids.

chunks.title: Pethidine
chunks.text: Prolonged pethidine use may lead to morphine-type dependence with withdrawal symptoms, and pethidine can cause physical dependence.

chunks.title: Pethidine

chunks.title: Pethidine

chunks.title: Pethidine

chunks.title: Pfbt
chunks.text: pFBT is a tropane derivative stimulant and local anaesthetic, structurally related to cocaine but estimated at roughly 30% of its stimulant potency while retaining comparable anaesthetic strength. First detected by the EMCDDA in 2008 as a designer drug analogue of cocaine, it has primarily appeared as an ingredient in "bath salt" powder products, frequently adulterated with other stimulants such as caffeine, dimethocaine, desoxypipradrol, or substituted cathinone derivatives.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Phenazepam is a benzodiazepine first developed in the Soviet Union in 1975. It is prescribed in Russia and other countries for psychiatric conditions including anxiety and schizophrenia, as well as for epilepsy, alcohol withdrawal, and surgical premedication. Phenazepam is notable for its exceptionally long duration of action and high potency. The substance has gained notoriety for problematic recreational use, with numerous reports of compulsive redosing and reckless behavior due to its subtle onset and extended effects.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, and treatment courses are typically limited to two weeks due to dependence risk. Abrupt discontinuation following prolonged use can cause severe withdrawal symptoms including restlessness, anxiety, insomnia, seizures, convulsions, and potentially death. Due to its intermediate half-life and active metabolites, withdrawal symptoms may take two or more days to manifest.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: High abuse potential with significant risk of psychological dependence. Anecdotal reports indicate a notable suggestibility for compulsive redosing and reckless usage patterns, particularly due to the drug's subtle onset and amnestic effects.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Seizures and convulsions are documented withdrawal symptoms following abrupt discontinuation of prolonged use. Gradual dose reduction is necessary to prevent withdrawal-induced seizures.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Phenazepam is a benzodiazepine that acts as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, enhancing the inhibitory effects of gamma-aminobutyric acid in the central nervous system. This mechanism produces anxiolytic, sedative, hypnotic, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant effects characteristic of the benzodiazepine class. The drug is notable for its high potency and prolonged duration of action compared to many other benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Phenazepam has an intermediate elimination half-life and produces active metabolites that contribute to its prolonged duration of action. The presence of these active metabolites means that effects and potential withdrawal symptoms may persist or emerge over an extended period following discontinuation. Blood concentrations during therapeutic use are typically less than 30 μg/L, though substantially higher concentrations have been observed in cases of impairment.

chunks.title: Phenazepam
chunks.text: Phenazepam is a benzodiazepine that was first developed in the Soviet Union in 1975. The synthesis method was developed at the Physico-Chemical Institute of the Academy of Sciences of the Ukrainian SSR during the 1970s. The substance is now produced in Russia and several other countries, where it is used in the treatment of various mental disorders including psychiatric schizophrenia and anxiety, as well as serving as a premedication before surgery due to its ability to augment the effects of anesthetics. In 2009, phenazepam gained popularity as a recreational drug, with misuse being reported in the United Kingdom, Finland, Sweden, and the United States. The substance was also found to be a component in some "herbal incense" mixtures in Australia and New Zealand in 2011, notably in a product called "Kronic." This particular product variety was withdrawn from the market shortly after discovery and replaced with a new formulation.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine is the simplest compound of its namesake chemical class, a naturally occurring stimulant found throughout nature in both plants and animals, including as a notable component of chocolate. It is closely related structurally to amphetamine and several neurotransmitters. Despite its intrinsic stimulant properties, phenethylamine is rapidly and completely metabolized in the human body, which largely prevents it from expressing meaningful pharmacological activity when consumed on its own.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine is pharmacologically inactive when taken alone due to rapid metabolism by monoamine oxidase. Misuse in combination with MAO inhibitors has been reported, though abuse potential is not well characterized.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Acts as a potent antimicrobial against certain pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli, including the O157:H7 strain, at sufficient concentrations.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenylacetic acid (primary urinary metabolite)

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine acts as a releasing agent of norepinephrine and dopamine, with in vitro potency at these targets roughly comparable to amphetamine. It is a potent agonist at trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) and inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) in monoamine neurons. In addition to its catecholamine-releasing activity, phenethylamine functions as a monoaminergic activity enhancer, increasing the action potential-mediated release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine at concentrations lower than those required for direct catecholamine release.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine is extremely rapidly metabolized, with an oral half-life of only 5 to 10 minutes. A significant portion of orally ingested phenethylamine is degraded in the small intestine by monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), producing phenylacetic acid as the primary urinary metabolite. Additional metabolizing enzymes in humans include MAO-A, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), the semicarbazide-sensitive amine oxidases AOC2 and AOC3, flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3), and aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT). This extensive and rapid enzymatic breakdown accounts for phenethylamine's negligible oral psychoactivity under normal conditions, though activity can emerge in the presence of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine has long held a special place in psychopharmacological research due to its status as the simplest member of the phenethylamine chemical class. Its clean molecular structure, natural presence in human tissues and bodily fluids, and close chemical relationship to both amphetamine and endogenous neurotransmitters have made it a subject of sustained scientific interest. The compound occurs widely throughout nature in both plants and animals, produced as a metabolic byproduct during the bacterial decomposition of phenylalanine in tissue. Multiple synthetic routes for phenethylamine were established in the mid-twentieth century. In 1948, R. F. Nystrom and W. G. Brown first reported a convenient synthesis involving the reduction of ω-nitrostyrene using lithium aluminium hydride in ether. An alternative method was later published in 1955 by J. C. Robinson and H. R. Snyder in Organic Syntheses, which employed the reduction of benzyl cyanide with hydrogen in liquid ammonia using a Raney-Nickel catalyst under high temperature and pressure conditions.

chunks.title: Phenethylamine
chunks.text: Phenethylamine gained popular attention through its association with chocolate, where it occurs as a significant component, particularly following microbial fermentation. This led to its characterization in mainstream media as "the love-sickness chemical," spawning a popular myth that individuals experiencing heartbreak compulsively consume chocolate to replenish depleted phenethylamine levels. While some researchers have speculated that phenethylamine may play a role in romantic affection, these claims have not been substantiated by direct experimental evidence. The compound has also been implicated in the euphoric effects of vigorous physical activity; research has demonstrated that thirty minutes of moderate- to high-intensity exercise significantly elevates urinary levels of phenylacetic acid, the primary metabolite of phenethylamine. Similar increases have been observed following skydiving, suggesting phenethylamine may contribute to the subjective pleasure associated with intense physical exertion.

chunks.text: Binding profile: TAAR1 agonist (trace amine-associated receptor); Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitor; Norepinephrine releasing agent; Dopamine releasing agent

chunks.title: Phenetrazine
chunks.text: Phenetrazine is a rare phenethylamine stimulant structurally related to 3-fluorophenmetrazine (3-FPM). Very little is known about its pharmacology or effects profile, and it is suspected to share properties with structurally similar compounds. Due to the scarcity of available research and user reports, particular caution is advised. It should not be confused with phenmetrazine, a distinct but related substance. Its habit-forming potential is considered likely given its stimulant classification.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Phenibut is a depressant and anxiolytic of the gabapentinoid class, structurally derived from the neurotransmitter GABA. Developed in the Soviet Union during the 1960s under Professor V. V. Perekalin, it remains a prescribed pharmaceutical in Russia for conditions including anxiety, insomnia, depression, and PTSD. Outside Russia, it is unapproved for clinical use and typically sold as a nutritional supplement. At common doses, it is noted for producing less drowsiness than other GABAergic substances such as benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with daily or near-daily use, sometimes within weeks of regular dosing. Withdrawal symptoms can be severe and include anxiety, insomnia, tremors, agitation, rapid heartbeat, nausea, vomiting, irritability, and fatigue. Baclofen has been used successfully to treat phenibut dependence.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Phenibut is moderately psychologically addictive, particularly with heavy or frequent use. The extended onset period can lead to compulsive redosing when users mistakenly believe the substance is not working, and rebound anxiety commonly drives continued use.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Acute psychosis and visual/auditory hallucinations have been reported primarily as withdrawal symptoms in recreational users discontinuing heavy use, rather than during intoxication. Withdrawal-associated psychosis appears to occur in cases of abrupt cessation following prolonged high-dose use.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Tonic-clonic seizures have been reported in recreational users who have overdosed. Seizures are not a typical occurrence at standard doses and appear to be associated with significant overdose.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Phenibut acts as a full agonist of the GABA-B receptor and as a blocker of α2δ subunit-containing voltage-dependent calcium channels (VDCCs), the latter mechanism being shared with gabapentinoids such as gabapentin and pregabalin. Phenibut's affinity for α2δ-containing VDCCs is higher than for the GABA-B receptor, and in rodent models, analgesic effects appear mediated by VDCC blockade rather than GABA-B agonism. Only (R)-phenibut has meaningful activity at GABA-B, while both enantiomers block VDCCs with similar potency. At higher doses, phenibut loses its GABA-B selectivity and gains additional activity as a GABA-A receptor agonist. Phenibut has also been reported to increase calcium-dependent spontaneous release of GABA in vitro, and its effects on dopamine remain unclear, with conflicting reports regarding whether it meaningfully raises dopamine levels.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Phenibut is not significantly metabolized and is largely excreted unchanged in the urine, with approximately 63-65% of the dose recovered renally. Following a single 250 mg oral dose in healthy volunteers, the elimination half-life was approximately 5.3 hours.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text:
Phenibut was synthesized during the 1960s at the Department of Organic Chemistry at the Al Gertsen Leningrad Pedagogical Institute under the supervision of Professor V. V. Perekalin. Following its development, the compound was researched for potential applications in treating various conditions including anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, insomnia, and general weakness or asthenia.

Early research indicated that while phenibut shared certain properties with traditional sedatives, it produced less impairment and fewer "narcotic-like" effects in animal studies. The compound was initially introduced under the brand name Citrocard during the late 1960s to early 1970s. On December 18, 1974, phenibut was officially added to the State Drug Register under Order No. 1126 by the USSR's Ministry of Public Health, establishing it as an approved neuropsychotropic medication.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: Phenibut gained notable recognition for its inclusion in Soviet space program protocols. According to Neumyvakin (1978), the substance was available to Russian cosmonauts during the Soyuz-19 mission in 1975. The compound has since been cited as a mandated component of cosmonaut medical kits, though the precise extent of its utilization throughout the broader Soviet and Russian space programs remains unclear.

chunks.title: Phenibut
chunks.text: While phenibut has maintained continuous pharmaceutical availability in Russia since its initial release, the substance has seen minimal expansion into medical settings beyond Russian borders and remains unapproved for clinical use in most other countries. However, beginning in the 2000s and accelerating through the 2010s, phenibut became widely accessible internationally through the nutritional supplement industry, marketed and sold without prescription in many regions where it lacks pharmaceutical approval.

chunks.title: Phenmetrazine
chunks.text: Phenmetrazine is a sympathomimetic stimulant of the phenylmorpholine class, first patented in 1952 by Boehringer-Ingelheim. Originally marketed as Preludin for use as an appetite suppressant, it was withdrawn from most markets by the 1980s due to widespread misuse and addiction concerns. It functions as a norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent, producing subjective effects comparable to amphetamine, though at roughly one-fifth to one-third the potency by weight.

chunks.title: Phenmetrazine

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Phenobarbital is a long-acting barbiturate that functions as a nonselective central nervous system depressant, producing potent anxiolytic, hypnotic, muscle relaxant, and amnesic effects. It is used medically as an anticonvulsant for the management of most seizure disorders except absence seizures. Compared to other barbiturates, it is distinguished by its extremely slow elimination rate and prolonged duration of action. It is classified as habit-forming.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Extremely physically addictive with life-threatening withdrawal potential. Abrupt discontinuation in dependent individuals may cause seizures, psychosis, and death. Medical supervision is essential for discontinuation.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: High psychological addiction potential with compulsive redosing commonly reported. Long-acting barbiturates have moderate to high abuse potential.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Psychosis is not typical during intoxication but may occur during withdrawal in physically dependent individuals. Withdrawal-induced psychosis can be severe and life-threatening.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Phenobarbital is an anticonvulsant that suppresses seizures during use. However, abrupt discontinuation in dependent individuals may paradoxically trigger severe, potentially life-threatening seizures. Drugs which lower the seizure threshold should be avoided during withdrawal.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Studies have linked the use of barbiturates, particularly phenobarbital, with the development of cancer.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Phenobarbital acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, binding at the barbiturate site to extend the duration of chloride ion channel opening and thereby enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission. It also directly blocks glutamatergic AMPA and kainate receptors, which is believed to contribute to its anticonvulsant properties. Additional targets include NMDA receptors, neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α4 and α7 subunits), and possibly voltage-gated calcium channels.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Phenobarbital has an oral bioavailability of approximately 90%, with peak plasma concentrations reached 8 to 12 hours after oral administration. It is metabolized hepatically, primarily through hydroxylation and glucuronidation, with CYP2C19 as a major metabolic enzyme. Phenobarbital is a potent inducer of multiple cytochrome P450 isozymes; CYP2B6 is specifically induced via the CAR/RXR nuclear receptor heterodimer. It exhibits low protein binding (20 to 45%) and is excreted primarily by the kidneys, with an elimination half-life ranging from approximately 53 to 118 hours.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: The barbiturate class emerged in 1902 when German chemists Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering synthesized barbital, the first compound of its kind, subsequently marketed as Veronal by Bayer. By 1904, Fischer had synthesized several related compounds including phenobarbital. The drug was introduced to market in 1912 by Bayer under the brand name Luminal, initially recognized for its sedative, hypnotic, and soporific properties.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text:
While phenobarbital's sedative effects were well-established by its 1912 market introduction, its potential as an anticonvulsant remained unknown. The young physician Alfred Hauptmann made this discovery serendipitously when he administered the drug to his epilepsy patients as a tranquilizer and observed a marked reduction in their seizures. Hauptmann conducted a careful extended study of his patients, most of whom had previously relied on bromide—the only available treatment at the time, which offered limited efficacy and caused severe side effects.

On phenobarbital, patients showed substantial improvement: the most severely affected experienced fewer and milder seizures, while some became entirely seizure-free. The drug was rapidly adopted as the first widely effective anticonvulsant, though World War I delayed its introduction to the United States.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text:
Phenobarbital became implicated in one of history's darkest chapters when it was employed in Nazi Germany's involuntary euthanasia programs. In 1939, a German family petitioned Adolf Hitler to have their disabled five-month-old son killed; the infant was administered a lethal dose of Luminal after Hitler dispatched his personal physician to examine the child. This event precipitated a broader clandestine program—within days, fifteen psychiatrists were summoned to Hitler's Chancellery and directed to commence systematic involuntary euthanasia.

By 1940, approximately fifty intellectually disabled children were killed by Luminal injection at a clinic in Ansbach, Germany. The drug continued to be used as an instrument of the Nazi children's euthanasia program until at least 1943.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text: Phenobarbital remained a commonly prescribed sedative and hypnotic for nearly five decades following its introduction. However, the emergence of benzodiazepines in the 1960s gradually displaced barbiturates for most sedative and anxiolytic applications due to their improved safety profile. Despite this shift, phenobarbital persists as the oldest continuously used anticonvulsant medication and is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

chunks.title: Phenobarbital
chunks.text:
Phenobarbital has been involved in several notable deaths throughout its history. In November 1970, an unidentified woman was discovered deceased in Bergen, Norway, in a case that remains unsolved. Known as the Isdal Woman, she died from a combination of burns, phenobarbital, and carbon monoxide poisoning; numerous theories have emerged about her death, with some investigators believing she may have been a spy.

British veterinarian Donald Sinclair, who served as the inspiration for the character Siegfried Farnon in James Herriot's "All Creatures Great and Small" book series, ended his life at age 84 by self-administering an overdose of phenobarbital. American activist Abbie Hoffman died on April 12, 1989, after consuming phenobarbital combined with alcohol; residue from approximately 150 pills was detected in his body during autopsy.

In March 1997, thirty-nine members of the Heaven's Gate religious group died in a mass suicide in Rancho Santa Fe, California. The members consumed lethal doses of phenobarbital mixed with vodka before lying down to die, believing they would be transported to an alien spacecraft.

chunks.title: Phentermine
chunks.text: Phentermine is a substituted amphetamine and sympathomimetic stimulant first approved for medical use in the United States in 1959. It functions primarily as a norepinephrine–dopamine releasing agent and is prescribed as a short-term appetite suppressant for the treatment of obesity. The drug gained notoriety as a component of the "fen-phen" combination, which was withdrawn in 1997 due to heart valve damage caused by its fenfluramine counterpart. It is classified as a Schedule IV controlled substance.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: Phenylpiracetam is a central nervous system stimulant and nootropic of the racetam class, structurally related to piracetam with an added phenyl group. First described in 1983 and approved for medical use in Russia in 2003, it is prescribed there for cognitive deficits, depression, and attention problems. Its stimulant effects are notably more pronounced than other racetams, attributed to its activity as a dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: The chronic use of phenylpiracetam can be considered non-addictive with a low potential for abuse. It does not appear to be capable of causing psychological dependence among users, although this has not been corroborated by clinical studies.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: Phenylpiracetam acts primarily as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor, with the (R)-enantiomer showing substantially greater potency for this action than the (S)-enantiomer. The racemic mixture also inhibits norepinephrine reuptake, though (R)-phenylpiracetam has approximately 11-fold lower affinity for the norepinephrine transporter than for the dopamine transporter, while the (S)-enantiomer appears selective for dopamine reuptake inhibition. The compound binds to α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors with an IC50 of 5.86 μM and may increase acetylcholine release within hippocampal cells. Like other racetams, phenylpiracetam has been described as an AMPA receptor potentiator.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: Phenylpiracetam is reported to have an oral bioavailability of approximately 100%. The compound is described as not being metabolized, with excretion occurring unchanged via urine (approximately 40%) and bile and sweat (approximately 60%). The elimination half-life is 3 to 5 hours in humans. In rodents, absorption occurs within 1 hour following oral administration or intramuscular injection, with an elimination half-life of 2.5 to 3 hours.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text:
Phenylpiracetam was first described in the scientific literature in 1983, developed at the Russian Academy of Sciences Institute of Biomedical Problems specifically as a medication for Soviet cosmonauts to address the prolonged stresses of working in space. The development effort was led by psychopharmacologist Valentina Ivanovna Akhapkina. The compound represents one of the earliest derivatives of piracetam to be synthesized and documented.

Pilot-cosmonaut Aleksandr Serebrov reported being issued phenylpiracetam during his 197-day mission aboard the Mir space station, noting that the drug was also included in the Soyuz spacecraft's standard emergency medical kit. He described its effects as acting "as the equalizer of the whole organism, 'tidying it up', completely excluding impulsiveness and irritability inevitable in the stressful conditions of space flight."

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text:
Following its development for the space program, phenylpiracetam became available as a prescription medication in Russia and was formally approved in 2003 for treatment of various conditions including cerebrovascular deficiency, depression, apathy, attention deficits, and memory decline. Clinical trials were conducted at institutions including the Serbsky State Scientific Center for Social and Forensic Psychiatry, the Moscow Institute of Psychiatry, and the Russian Center of Vegetative Pathology.

The drug is manufactured by Russian pharmaceutical companies Valenta Pharm and Pharmstandard and is sold under brand names including Phenotropil, Actitropil, and Nanotropil in Russia and certain other Eastern European countries. While not prescribed as a pharmaceutical in Western countries, it is readily available through online vendors as a dietary supplement in the United States.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: Development of the more active enantiomer, (R)-phenylpiracetam (code name MRZ-9547), began in the West by 2014 as a potential treatment for fatigue related to Parkinson's disease. Research during this period also identified (R)-phenylpiracetam as a selective atypical dopamine reuptake inhibitor. There was additional interest in the compound for fatigue related to depression and other conditions, though this line of research was not pursued and no recent development has been reported.

chunks.title: Phenylpiracetam
chunks.text: Due to its stimulant properties, phenylpiracetam has been placed on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of substances banned for in-competition use, applicable across all Olympic sports. Notably, phenylpiracetam is the only racetam compound on the WADA prohibited list, reflecting its unique stimulant characteristics within this drug class.

chunks.title: Picamilon
chunks.text: Picamilon is a synthetic compound formed by combining niacin and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), developed in the Soviet Union in 1969. It functions as a prodrug of GABA, crossing the blood-brain barrier before being hydrolyzed into its constituent components. Sold as a prescription anxiolytic in Russia, it is also used for its purported nootropic properties. In the United States, the FDA has deemed it an adulterating agent in dietary supplements, though it continues to appear in over-the-counter nootropic products.

chunks.title: Pinazepam
chunks.text: Pinazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative marketed under brand names such as Domar. It is distinguished from other benzodiazepines by a propargyl group at the N-1 position of its core structure. Pinazepam functions primarily as a pure anxiolytic, largely lacking the hypnotic, motor-impairing, and intellectual-dulling effects characteristic of most benzodiazepines, making it more suitable for daytime use. Its principal active metabolites are nordazepam and oxazepam. It is considered less toxic than diazepam in animal studies.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Pipradrol is a central nervous system stimulant of the diphenylmethane class. Originally developed in the 1940s, it saw clinical use in the treatment of depression, fatigue, dementia, and ADHD, among other conditions. Despite demonstrating therapeutic efficacy across a range of psychiatric applications, its significant abuse potential and associated adverse effects led to its withdrawal from medical use and subsequent international scheduling beginning in the 1970s.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Recognized abuse potential led to international regulation in the late 1970s, though it is generally considered to have lower abuse potential and milder stimulant effects compared to other stimulants in its class.

chunks.text: Psychosis and hallucinations are reported very rarely. The drug is contraindicated in individuals with pre-existing psychotic states or schizophrenia as it may worsen these symptoms.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Pipradrol acts primarily as a norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor, blocking the reuptake of these neurotransmitters at their respective transporters. Its rewarding effects appear to be mediated in part through activation of dopamine D1 receptors. Pipradrol exhibits a preferential action on higher brain centers with relatively minimal effects on blood pressure or respiration.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Pipradrol is rapidly absorbed following administration, with distribution to the liver, kidneys, and brain tissue. The drug is quickly metabolized and is no longer detectable in plasma approximately 4 hours after administration. Elimination occurs through both urinary (approximately 3.5%) and fecal (approximately 5%) excretion.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Pipradrol was developed in the United States during the 1940s and received its patent in 1953. By the mid-1950s, it had entered the pharmaceutical market under the brand name Meratran, primarily positioned as an antidepressant. Its clinical utility expanded to include adjunct treatment for a range of conditions such as obesity, senile dementia symptoms, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, narcolepsy, and even schizophrenia. The compound's relatively mild stimulant profile compared to more potent alternatives contributed to a favorable safety record, making it suitable for these varied therapeutic applications. Commercial preparations included Meratran tablets and Alertonic liquid, with the latter being marketed in Australia.

chunks.title: Pipradrol
chunks.text: Despite its therapeutic promise, growing concerns regarding abuse potential led to pipradrol's withdrawal from widespread medical use and subsequent international regulation during the late 1970s. This occurred alongside the scheduling of numerous other substances with documented histories of misuse. The compound was placed into controlled substance categories across multiple jurisdictions, though its comparatively moderate stimulant effects resulted in less restrictive classifications than those applied to stronger stimulants. Today, pipradrol has become an obscure pharmaceutical largely forgotten as a recreational substance. Its primary contemporary relevance lies in scientific research, where it occasionally serves as a reference compound for evaluating the pharmacological properties of other stimulant drugs.

chunks.title: Pipt
chunks.text: PiPT is a rare psychedelic of the tryptamine class, structurally related to DPT and other dialkyl tryptamine derivatives. It was notably left unevaluated by Alexander Shulgin in his 1997 book TiHKAL and was first identified as a designer drug in 2021 in British Columbia, Canada. Compared to its analogues, PiPT is reported to be relatively weak and short-lasting. Very little is known about its effects or safety profile.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: Piracetam is a nootropic substance of the racetam class and a cyclic derivative of the neurotransmitter GABA. First synthesized in 1964 by Corneliu E. Giurgea at the Belgian pharmaceutical company UCB, it became the first nootropic drug to modulate cognitive function without causing sedation or stimulation. Piracetam is the earliest and least potent racetam, requiring doses approximately 100 times higher than newer derivatives like noopept. It is prescribed in some countries for myoclonus and used off-label for cognitive enhancement.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: Piracetam's mechanism of action is not fully understood, though it influences both neuronal and vascular functions without acting as a sedative or stimulant. The drug is a positive allosteric modulator of the AMPA receptor, although this action is weak and may not fully account for its clinical effects. Piracetam is also an inhibitor of N-type calcium channels, with an IC50 of approximately 3 μM in rat neurons, well below the central nervous system concentrations achieved at typical doses. Rather than binding with high affinity to specific receptors, piracetam appears to modulate neurotransmission by interacting with polar heads in phospholipid membranes, stabilizing membrane fluidity and potentially increasing the density and function of postsynaptic receptors including NMDA receptors. Through this membrane-stabilizing action, piracetam enhances cholinergic neurotransmission via muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and may influence glutamatergic, serotonergic, and noradrenergic systems. GABA brain metabolism and GABA receptors are not affected by piracetam despite its structural similarity to GABA.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: At the vascular level, piracetam increases erythrocyte deformability, reduces platelet aggregation, diminishes erythrocyte adhesion to vascular endothelium, and reduces capillary vasospasm, collectively improving microcirculation including cerebral blood flow.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: Piracetam is rapidly and extensively absorbed following oral administration, with absolute bioavailability close to 100%. Peak plasma concentration is reached within 1 hour in fasted subjects, though food intake may delay this to 1.5 hours and reduce peak concentration by approximately 17%. The drug distributes to all tissues except adipose tissue with a volume of distribution of approximately 0.6 L/kg, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and is not bound to plasma proteins. Piracetam undergoes negligible metabolism, with approximately 90% of the dose excreted unchanged in the urine. Steady state plasma concentrations are achieved within 3 days of dosing.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text:
Piracetam was first synthesized sometime between the 1950s and 1964 by Corneliu E. Giurgea and his team at the Belgian pharmaceutical company UCB. There are reports of the compound being investigated for epilepsy treatment during the 1950s. Giurgea was struck by the substance's apparent ability to enhance mental functioning in healthy individuals while demonstrating a favorable safety profile. This unique combination of properties led him to coin the term "nootropic" to describe piracetam and similar cognitive-enhancing compounds.

The drug was launched clinically by UCB under the trade name "Nootropil" in the early 1970s, with formal marketing beginning in 1971. This made piracetam the first nootropic drug to modulate cognitive function without causing sedation or stimulation, establishing it as the prototype for an entirely new class of pharmaceuticals.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text:
Piracetam gained widespread medical acceptance in Europe, where it is now used in many countries as a prescription medication. In the United Kingdom, it is prescribed primarily for myoclonus, a condition involving spasmodic jerky contractions of muscle groups, though it sees considerable off-label use for other conditions including learning difficulties in children, memory loss and cognitive defects in the elderly, and sickle-cell vaso-occlusive crises.

The regulatory situation differs markedly in the United States, where piracetam has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for any medical use and is not permitted to be sold as a dietary supplement. Despite this lack of official approval, the substance remains readily available through online vendors.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: As the earliest racetam compound, piracetam established the foundation for subsequent, more potent racetam derivatives. While it requires significantly higher doses compared to later nootropics such as noopept, piracetam became regarded as a staple within the nootropic community. By 2009, piracetam had gained popularity as a cognitive enhancement drug among students seeking to improve academic performance.

chunks.title: Piracetam
chunks.text: Romanian psychologist and chemist who led the team at UCB that first synthesized piracetam. Giurgea's observations of the compound's cognitive-enhancing properties in healthy individuals, combined with its apparent safety, led him to develop the concept of nootropics as a distinct pharmacological category. His coining of the term 'nootropic' established the theoretical framework for an entire field of cognitive enhancement research.

chunks.title: PMA
chunks.text: PMA (para-methoxyamphetamine) is a substituted amphetamine with serotonergic properties that first appeared in the early 1970s. Unlike related compounds, it does not produce meaningful stimulant, entactogenic, or euphoric effects. PMA is notorious primarily as a dangerous adulterant in MDMA tablets and has been linked to hundreds of deaths worldwide. It can cause life-threatening hyperthermia and serotonin syndrome even at moderate doses, making it one of the most hazardous substances found in recreational drug markets.

PMMA is notorious for being sold in misrepresented MDMA tablets and capsules, and has been linked to numerous deaths internationally since the early 2010s.

In the United States, it is available as a dietary supplement. Sublingual administration of the powder form has been reported to cause painful chemical burns.

chunks.title: Prazepam
chunks.text: Prazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative developed by Warner-Lambert in the 1960s. It functions primarily as a prodrug for desmethyldiazepam (nordazepam), which is responsible for the majority of its therapeutic activity. Prescribed for short-term management of anxiety, it produces anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant effects. Its slow onset of action and very long-acting active metabolite distinguish it from many other benzodiazepines. As with all benzodiazepines, prolonged use carries significant risks of physical dependence and withdrawal.

chunks.title: PRE-084
chunks.text: PRE-084 is a selective sigma-1 receptor agonist and morpholine derivative that is structurally derived from PCP. It has demonstrated nootropic and antidepressant properties in animal studies, along with antitussive effects and increased expression of GDNF. PRE-084 is currently being investigated for its potential therapeutic applications in neurodegenerative conditions such as ALS and Parkinson's disease. Human research remains limited, and its safety profile is not well established.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Pregabalin is a depressant and anxiolytic substance of the gabapentinoid class, structurally related to GABA. First synthesized in 1990 and marketed under the trade name Lyrica in 2005, it is commonly prescribed for neuropathic pain, anxiety, epilepsy, and fibromyalgia. Compared to the related compound gabapentin, pregabalin offers greater bioavailability and potency. It is also used recreationally for its reported euphoric, anxiolytic, and pro-social properties.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop with chronic use, though the FDA determined the dependence profile is quantitatively less severe than benzodiazepines. Withdrawal symptoms after abrupt discontinuation include anxiety, insomnia, sweating, muscle spasms, gastrointestinal disturbances, palpitations, and flu-like symptoms. Even short-term users have reported withdrawal effects. Gradual tapering over at least one week is recommended.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Initially assessed as having low abuse potential, recreational use has prompted re-evaluation. Euphoric effects can lead to escalating doses above therapeutic ranges, particularly in individuals with current or past substance use disorders. At standard therapeutic doses the risk of addiction is low, but increases with higher doses and prolonged use.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Psychotic side effects including hallucinations and confusion occur in a minority of users even at therapeutic doses. Sleep deprivation strongly potentiates this risk, and individuals genetically predisposed to schizophrenia may be more susceptible. Hallucinations are reported in 0.1-1% of users.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Paradoxically, despite being an anticonvulsant, pregabalin may induce or increase seizure risk at recreational doses exceeding 600mg. There is little evidence of concern at medical doses. The drug may aggravate myoclonus and myoclonic seizures in susceptible populations. Risk factors include low sodium, sleep deprivation, and intensive physical activity.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Pregabalin acts by binding to the α2δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels in the central nervous system, with similar affinity for both the α2δ-1 and α2δ-2 subtypes. It is selective for this target; despite being a structural analogue of GABA, it has no activity at GABA-A, GABA-B, or benzodiazepine receptors and does not appear to alter brain GABA levels. Through its α2δ binding, pregabalin reduces the release of several excitatory neurotransmitters including glutamate, substance P, norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and calcitonin gene-related peptide. It also reduces the normal trafficking of calcium channels to the cell membrane and blocks thrombospondin-mediated formation of new excitatory synapses in animal models.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Pregabalin has high oral bioavailability (≥90%) with linear pharmacokinetics, reaching peak plasma concentrations within 1.5 hours. It undergoes negligible metabolism, with approximately 98% excreted unchanged in the urine via renal elimination. Its elimination half-life is approximately 6.3 hours, and steady state is achieved within 24 to 48 hours of repeated dosing.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Tolerance to the euphoric and depressant effects develops relatively quickly with repeated recreational use, often within several uses. At medical doses for conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder, long-term trials have demonstrated continued effectiveness without significant tolerance development. However, in recreational settings where higher doses are used, tolerance builds rapidly, sometimes leading users to escalate to doses exceeding 1 gram daily.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Pregabalin emerged from research conducted at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois. In 1988, medicinal chemist Richard Silverman enlisted the help of Dr. Ryszard Andruszkiewicz, a visiting scholar from the Technical University of Gdańsk, to synthesize a series of 3-alkyl-GABA and 3-alkyl-glutamate analogs. The research aimed to investigate these compounds' inhibition of GABA aminotransferase and glutamate decarboxylase.

Among the compounds synthesized, the S-isomer of 3-isobutyl-GABA demonstrated exceptional anticonvulsant properties, proving to be one of the most effective compounds that Parke-Davis had ever evaluated. This compound would eventually become known as pregabalin. In 1990, a license agreement was signed between Warner-Lambert (Parke-Davis's parent company) and Northwestern University, and a patent application was filed.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Following Pfizer's acquisition of Warner-Lambert in 2000, the pharmaceutical company gained exclusive rights to continue developing pregabalin. Under the trade name Lyrica, pregabalin entered the European market in September 2004. The United States Food and Drug Administration granted approval in December 2004, with the drug reaching the US market in September 2005. At the time of its introduction, pregabalin became the first medication approved for treating both diabetic peripheral neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia.

Subsequent regulatory approvals expanded the drug's therapeutic applications. European regulators approved pregabalin for generalized anxiety disorder in 2006, while the FDA approved it for fibromyalgia treatment in 2007, making it the first drug granted FDA approval specifically for this condition.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: Pregabalin achieved remarkable commercial success following its market introduction. During its first full year of sales, the drug attained "blockbuster" status with $1.2 billion in global revenue. Northwestern University initially received a 6% royalty on net sales, with portions shared between Silverman and Andruszkiewicz. Through investment and continued revenue, the university's earnings from pregabalin grew to approximately $1.4 billion, making it a substantial contributor to Northwestern's endowment.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text: As pregabalin use expanded globally, concerns about its safety profile emerged. Data from England and Wales documented a steep upward trajectory in death certificates mentioning pregabalin through 2017, despite the drug having been on the market for only a relatively short period. These safety concerns contributed to increased regulatory scrutiny in multiple countries during the late 2010s, with several nations implementing stricter prescribing controls and controlled substance classifications.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Pregabalin — dangerous combinations:
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, and may rapidly lead to unconsciousness. They both increase each other's side effects such as ataxia, sedation, and CNS depression. Blackout and memory loss risk is significantly increased. If the user falls unconscious while under the influence there is a severe risk of vomit aspiration if they are not placed in the recovery position. There is an increased risk of seizures from this combination.)
- NBOMe compounds (NBOMes and pregabalin are reported to have significant seizure concerns that are likely to increase in combination. Therapeutic dosages of pregabalin are unlikely to be of concern and may decrease NBOMes side effects such as vasoconstriction and anxiety.)
- Opioids

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Pregabalin — unsafe combinations:
- Amphetamines (There is a significant risk of seizures from this combination. Amphetamines increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal. If amphetamines wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages cause strain of the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications.)
- Caffeine (There is a risk of seizures from this combination, especially at higher dosages. Caffeine additionally reduces pregabalin’s anticonvulsant effects found in lower dosages. Caffeine increases respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal. If amphetamines wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages cause strain of the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications. Medical dosages are unlikely to be of concern.)
- Cocaine (There is a significant risk of seizures from this combination. Stimulants increase respiration rate, allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
If cocaine wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Both substances at recreational dosages strain the heart and may lead to further dangerous heart complications. The combination has a greater risk of methemoglobinemia when higher dosages are combined.)
- Diphenhydramine (There is a significant risk of seizures from this combination. The combination is likely to increase each other’s negative side effects, such as nausea, dizziness, and loss of consciousness. At higher dosages, pregabalin is likely to increase diphenhydramine’s deliriant effects, inhibition, and risk of injury. Medical dosages are not reported to be a concern.)
- DXM (Pregabalin and DXM may increase each other’s effects such as inhibition, dizziness, sedation. At higher doses this can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness. Both drugs have seizure concerns which is greatly increased in combination.)
- MDMA (There is a significant risk of seizures from this combination. Amphetamines increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal.

If mephedrone wears off first, recreational dosages of pregabalin may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. - Tramadol (There is a significant risk of seizures. Both substances are CNS depressants, potentiating each other strongly and unpredictably, raising the chances of memory loss, severe ataxia, and unconsciousness. The interaction will cause greater inhibition and risk of injury. If the user falls unconscious it is strongly recommended to put them into the recovery position and monitor breathing. Medical dosages are not reported to be a concern.)

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Pregabalin — caution combinations:
- 5-MeO-xxT tryptamines (Caution should be given due to 5-MeO-xxT drugs stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of 5-MeO-xxT drugs. Additionally, Pregabalin may increase 5-MeO-xxT drugs inhibition and risk of injury.)
- DOx compounds (Caution should be given due to DOx drugs stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of DOx drugs. Additionally, Pregabalin may increase DOx drugs inhibition and risk of injury.)
- Ketamine (Pregabalin and ketamine may synergize and increase each other's negative side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and loss of consciousness. Caution is advised for beyond medical dosages due to seizure concerns, and medical dosages for individuals with higher risk seizure profiles and or behavior.)
- LSD (Caution should be given due to LSD’s stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of LSD.

chunks.title: Pregabalin
chunks.text:
Additionally, Pregabalin may increase LSD’s inhibition and risk of injury.)
- Mescaline (Caution should be given due to mescaline’s stimulating effects and pregabalin’s seizure concerns at higher dosages. Pregabalin may reduce the vasoconstriction, anxiety, and other side effects of mescaline. Additionally, Pregabalin may increase mescaline’s inhibition and risk of injury.)
- MXE (Pregabalin and MXE may synergize and increase each other’s negative side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and loss of consciousness. Caution is advised for anything above low dosages due to seizure concerns, and all dosages for individuals with higher risk seizure profiles and or behavior.)
- Nitrous oxide (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other, and may increase the risk of loss of consciousness at higher dosages. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. The combination may increase inhibition and risk of injury. Additionally, abuse of nitrous while under the influence of pregabalin may increase the risk of seizures. Medical dosages are unlikely to be a concern.)

chunks.title: PRL-8-53
chunks.text: PRL-8-53 is a nootropic substituted phenethylamine first synthesized in the 1970s by medical chemistry professor Nikolaus Hansl at Creighton University. It is reported to act as a hypermnesic (memory-enhancing) drug, though evidence for its efficacy rests on a single human clinical study from 1978. The substance is not considered to have recreational value. Its development was discontinued not due to safety concerns, but following the retirement of its creator and a legal dispute with the university.

- Austria: PRO-LAD is technically not illegal but it may fall in the NPSG (Neue-Psychoaktive-Substanzen-Gesetz Österreich) as an analogue of LSD.
- Germany: PRO-LAD is controlled under the NpSG ( New Psychoactive Substances Act ) as of July 18, 2019. — Production and import with the aim to place it on the market, administration to another person and trading is punishable. Possession is illegal but not penalized.

chunks.title: Prochlorperazine
chunks.text: Prochlorperazine is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, first approved for medical use in 1956. It functions primarily as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist and is prescribed for the treatment of severe nausea and vomiting, schizophrenia, anxiety, and migraines. It is reported to be 10–20 times more potent than chlorpromazine. Notable risks include extrapyramidal symptoms such as tardive dyskinesia and the potentially fatal neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

chunks.title: Progesterone
chunks.text: Progesterone is an endogenous steroid sex hormone of the progestogen class, first isolated in crystalline form in 1934. It is the body's major progestogen, playing essential roles in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryogenesis. Its psychoactive properties stem primarily from its neurosteroid metabolites, particularly allopregnanolone and pregnanolone, which act as positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors. It is used clinically in contraception, hormone replacement therapy, and feminizing hormone therapy. Combining it with other depressants may be dangerous.

chunks.title: Prolintane
chunks.text: Prolintane is a synthetic central nervous system stimulant of the phenylalkylpyrrolidine class, developed in the 1950s as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Structurally related to compounds such as MDPV and α-PVP, it produces notably attenuated effects and was marketed in Europe for the treatment of fatigue, narcolepsy, and concentration difficulties. At common doses, its profile is described as subtle and functional. Chronic use or overdose can potentially induce psychosis, and it carries a moderate potential for abuse.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: Promethazine is a first-generation antihistamine of the phenothiazine class, developed by French chemists in the mid-1940s. It functions as a depressant with strong sedative, antiemetic, and anticholinergic properties. Commonly prescribed for allergies, nausea, and motion sickness, it is also known as one of the two active ingredients in 'lean' when combined with codeine. At high or toxic doses, its anticholinergic activity can produce deliriant effects.

chunks.text: Promethazine is not considered addictive and does not produce significant psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: At high doses, promethazine's anticholinergic properties may cause delirium with symptoms including confusion, hallucinations, and disorientation. This risk is elevated in elderly patients.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: Promethazine is a phenothiazine derivative that acts primarily as a potent histamine H1 receptor antagonist, producing antihistamine effects. It also exhibits moderate muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonism, which contributes to its sedative properties and anticholinergic effects. Additionally, promethazine acts as a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist, which may contribute to both sedation and mild analgesic effects. The compound shows weaker antagonist activity at dopamine D2 receptors, serotonin 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Promethazine also blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, providing local anesthetic properties.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: Promethazine has low oral bioavailability of approximately 25% due to extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver. The compound is predominantly metabolized to promethazine sulfoxide, with minor pathways producing desmethylpromethazine and a hydroxy metabolite. Hydroxylation is primarily mediated by CYP2D6. Promethazine is highly protein bound at 93%, mostly to albumin, and has a large volume of distribution of approximately 970L. Elimination occurs primarily through urinary excretion, with about 10% excreted as promethazine sulfoxide and less than 1% as unchanged parent drug.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text:
Promethazine was first synthesized in the 1940s by a team of scientists at Rhône-Poulenc laboratories in France, led by Paul Charpentier. The compound was developed by combining phenothiazine with a diamine side chain derived from diphenhydramine, as researchers sought to improve upon existing antihistamine medications. This same line of pharmaceutical research would later lead to the creation of chlorpromazine, a foundational antipsychotic medication.

Originally designated as compound 3,277 R.P., promethazine was initially used as an antipsychotic agent, though it possessed only approximately one-tenth the antipsychotic potency of chlorpromazine. The drug was granted FDA approval in the United States in 1951, making it one of the earlier phenothiazine derivatives to reach the American market.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: Promethazine gained cultural prominence through its recreational use, particularly within the Houston rap and hip-hop scene beginning around 1990. The drug became a key ingredient in a preparation known as "lean" or "purple drank," which typically combines promethazine-codeine cough syrup with ice, Sprite or another citrus soda, and occasionally Jolly Rancher candies for enhanced flavor. This trend experienced a resurgence in popularity during 2015 and 2016.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text:
A significant legal case involving promethazine reached the United States Supreme Court in 2009. Diana Levine, a patient who had been administered Wyeth's Phenergan via intravenous push for migraine treatment, developed gangrene due to improper injection technique, resulting in amputation of her right forearm below the elbow. A state jury awarded her $6 million in punitive damages.

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court on grounds of federal preemption and substantive due process. The Court upheld the lower courts' rulings, determining that Wyeth could have independently strengthened its warnings about IV-push administration without conflicting with federal law. This decision established that pharmaceutical manufacturers can be held liable for injuries when FDA-approved warnings are deemed insufficient by state courts. Following this ruling, the FDA mandated a boxed warning on injectable promethazine in September 2009, contraindicating subcutaneous administration and recommending intramuscular injection as the preferred route to reduce tissue damage risk.

chunks.title: Promethazine
chunks.text: Promethazine is available globally as a generic medication under numerous brand names including Phenergan, Avomine, Atosil, Promethegan, and many others. The drug is marketed both as a standalone medication and in various combination formulations with other active ingredients such as codeine, dextromethorphan, paracetamol, and pholcodine for different therapeutic applications. In 2023, promethazine ranked as the 230th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States with over one million prescriptions, while its combination with dextromethorphan ranked 252nd with similarly high prescription volumes.

chunks.title: Propofol
chunks.text: Propofol is an intravenous sedative-hypnotic of the alkylphenol class, first synthesized in 1973 by John B. Glen at Imperial Chemical Industries. Primarily used for the induction and maintenance of general anesthesia, it acts as a GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator with extremely rapid onset and short duration of action. Propofol is exceptionally dangerous outside medical settings due to its steep dose-response curve, respiratory depressant properties, and numerous reported fatalities from self-administration.

chunks.title: Propoxyphene

It possesses roughly one-third to one-half the analgesic potency of codeine and also exhibits antitussive and local anesthetic properties. Propoxyphene has been withdrawn from markets across the US, Europe, and elsewhere due to its narrow therapeutic index, risk of fatal overdose, and cardiotoxicity — particularly dangerous heart arrhythmias — especially when combined with alcohol.

chunks.title: Propranolol
chunks.text: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist and naphthalene derivative first approved by the FDA in 1967. It is prescribed for a broad range of conditions including hypertension, essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, and anxiety. As a racemic mixture, its S(-)-enantiomer demonstrates roughly 100 times greater binding affinity for beta-adrenergic receptors than its counterpart, accounting for most of its pharmacological activity.

chunks.title: Propranolol
chunks.text: Propranolol is a competitive, nonselective β-adrenergic receptor antagonist that blocks β1, β2, and β3 receptors with little intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, inhibiting the actions of epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is administered as a racemic mixture in which the S(−)-enantiomer has approximately 100 times the binding affinity for beta-adrenergic receptors. Propranolol also blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, a property underlying its membrane-stabilizing effects, although this occurs primarily at high blood concentrations. Additionally, it acts as a weak antagonist at serotonin 5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, and 5-HT2B receptors and shows very weak inhibitory effects on the norepinephrine transporter.

chunks.title: Propranolol
chunks.text: Propranolol is rapidly and completely absorbed following oral administration, with peak plasma levels reached in approximately 1 to 4 hours. Despite complete absorption, oral bioavailability is only approximately 25%. Food increases bioavailability without affecting time to peak levels. Propranolol is highly lipophilic and achieves high concentrations in the brain. It is metabolized through aromatic hydroxylation (mainly 4-hydroxylation), N-dealkylation, side-chain oxidation, and glucuronidation, with approximately 42% of a dose undergoing ring oxidation and 17% undergoing glucuronidation. The plasma half-life is approximately 3 to 6 hours, with an elimination half-life reported at approximately 8 hours.

chunks.title: Propranolol
chunks.text:
Propranolol was developed by Scottish scientist James W. Black during the 1960s, representing a landmark achievement as the first beta-blocker to be effectively used in the treatment of coronary artery disease and hypertension. The compound was patented in 1962 and received approval for medical use in 1964, with the United States Food and Drug Administration granting formal approval on November 13, 1967.

The drug was first brought to market in 1965 under the brand name Inderal by ICI Pharmaceuticals, now known as AstraZeneca. The trade name was created as a quasi-anagram of "Alderlin," the brand name of pronethalol, an earlier beta-blocker that propranolol replaced. Both names serve as a tribute to Alderley Park, the ICI research headquarters where the compounds were originally developed. Propranolol has since been recognized as a foundational cardiovascular medication, earning a place on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines and becoming widely available as a generic formulation.

chunks.title: Propranolol
chunks.text:
Beyond its medical applications, propranolol has gained recognition for its use in managing performance-related anxiety. A 1987 survey conducted by the International Conference of Symphony and Opera Musicians found that 27% of interviewed members reported using beta blockers such as propranolol for musical performances. The drug's ability to suppress sympathetic nervous system–mediated anxiety symptoms has made it popular among musicians, actors, and public speakers.

Propranolol has also been employed as a performance-enhancing substance in precision sports requiring high accuracy, including archery, shooting, golf, and snooker. This use attracted significant attention during the 2008 Summer Olympics when North Korean shooter Kim Jong-su, who had won silver in the 50-metre pistol event and bronze in the 10-metre air pistol competition, tested positive for propranolol and was subsequently stripped of both medals.

chunks.title: Propylhexedrine
chunks.text: Propylhexedrine is a stimulant of the cycloalkylamine class and a structural analog of methamphetamine, differing by a cyclohexane ring in place of a phenyl ring. First introduced in 1949 as the active ingredient in Benzedrex nasal decongestant inhalers, it was developed after amphetamine inhalers were restricted. It acts as a monoamine releasing agent but produces more pronounced peripheral effects—particularly vasoconstriction and cardiovascular strain—than amphetamine. The FDA has warned that recreational misuse of inhaler products can result in hospitalization or death.

chunks.title: Proscaline
chunks.text: Proscaline is a lesser-known psychedelic of the substituted phenethylamine class, structurally related to mescaline as its 4-propyloxy analog. Its synthesis was first published by David E. Nichols in 1977, and it was later evaluated by Alexander Shulgin, who estimated its potency at roughly five times that of mescaline. Shulgin documented his findings in the 1991 book PiHKAL. It belongs to a series of mescaline analogs including escaline and allylescaline, and appeared on the research chemical market in the 2010s.

chunks.title: Proscaline

It has been described as a partial agonist at the 5-HT2A receptor, activation of which is thought to be responsible for its psychedelic effects. Notably, proscaline displays considerably greater potency at the 5-HT2C receptor compared to the 5-HT2A or 5-HT2B receptors.

chunks.title: Proscaline
chunks.text:
Proscaline was first synthesized and investigated by Czech chemist Otakar Leminger in 1972. The compound was subsequently synthesized by David E. Nichols, who published his work in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry in 1977. Around this period, Alexander Shulgin independently explored the substance, evaluating its effects at doses up to 60 milligrams and estimating its potency to be approximately five times greater than that of mescaline.

Shulgin later documented his findings on proscaline in his 1991 book PiHKAL (Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved), which served as the primary reference for the compound's subjective effects for many years. Despite this early documentation, proscaline remained largely obscure until it appeared for sale on the online research chemical market during the 2010s. The substance was first identified as a novel designer drug in Europe in 2013.

chunks.title: Pseudoephrine
chunks.text: Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant of the substituted amphetamine class, widely used as an over-the-counter nasal decongestant. It occurs naturally in ephedra, a plant used for thousands of years in traditional Chinese medicine, and was first isolated in 1889. Though it produces mild stimulant effects at higher doses, it is reported to lack significant recreational value. Pseudoephedrine is contraindicated in individuals with cardiovascular disease, and its availability has been restricted in many regions due to its use as a precursor in methamphetamine synthesis.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Psilocin is a naturally occurring tryptamine psychedelic found in approximately 190 species of mushrooms across every continent. While psilocybin is the more commonly referenced compound, psilocin is the pharmacologically active substance responsible for the hallucinogenic effects—psilocybin serves as its prodrug, converting to psilocin in the liver. Psychedelic mushrooms containing psilocin have been used since prehistoric times, with evidence in cave art and documented ceremonial use by Mesoamerican peoples.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Psilocin acts as a non-selective serotonin receptor agonist, producing its hallucinogenic effects primarily through activation of the 5-HT2A receptor in the prefrontal cortex. The drug's psychedelic effects correlate directly with its occupancy at these receptor sites. Psilocin also demonstrates agonist or partial agonist activity at 5-HT2C and 5-HT1A receptors, which may contribute to its overall effects. Notably, psilocin exhibits functional selectivity at serotonin receptors, activating phospholipase A2 rather than phospholipase C as the endogenous ligand serotonin does. The compound shows pronounced biased agonism at the 5-HT2C receptor. Psilocin has no significant effect on dopamine receptors and only affects the noradrenergic system at very high doses. Early reports suggested psilocin acts as a potent positive allosteric modulator of tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), though subsequent studies failed to reproduce these findings.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Psilocin is the pharmacologically active compound produced following ingestion of psilocybin, which undergoes rapid dephosphorylation in the body. Psilocybin and synthetic acyl esters such as 4-AcO-DMT and 4-PrO-DMT serve as prodrugs that are converted to psilocin. The elimination half-life of psilocin ranges from 1 to 3 hours depending on the route of administration.
