chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Psilocin is a naturally occurring tryptamine psychedelic found within approximately 190 separate species of mushroom, growing on every continent across the planet. Psychedelic mushrooms containing psilocin and its prodrug psilocybin have been in use since before recorded human history, with their depiction found on prehistoric cave art. These mushrooms were famously used by the native peoples of Mesoamerica for religious and shamanic purposes.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text:
The Western rediscovery of psilocybin-containing mushrooms occurred in 1955 when Robert Gordon Wasson and Valentina Pavlovna Wasson encountered them during their research in Mexico. This rediscovery sparked scientific interest in the active compounds responsible for the mushrooms' psychoactive effects.

In 1958, Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann successfully isolated and named both psilocin and its phosphorylated cousin psilocybin from laboratory-grown specimens of the hallucinogenic mushroom Psilocybe mexicana. Hofmann also developed synthetic routes to produce these chemicals, enabling further scientific study independent of natural sources.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Psilocin and psilocybin became controlled substances in the United States and internationally under the United Nations in 1971. In the original writing of the United States Controlled Substances Act of 1970, only four plants were explicitly listed as scheduled drugs: marijuana and peyote in Schedule I, and opium poppy with coca leaves in Schedule II. The scheduling of psilocin and psilocybin represented an expansion of controlled substance regulations to include these tryptamine compounds.

chunks.title: Psilocin
chunks.text: Since its scheduling, psilocin has become of interest for potential medical applications in treating psychiatric disorders such as depression. Psilocybin, which converts to psilocin in the body, was approved for therapeutic use in Australia in 2023 and is currently in late-stage clinical trials in the United States and other countries. Psilocin is also being evaluated under the developmental code name PLZ-1015 for the treatment of pervasive developmental disorders like autism in children.

chunks.text: Swiss chemist who first isolated and named psilocin and psilocybin in 1958. Working with laboratory-grown specimens of Psilocybe mexicana, Hofmann not only identified these compounds but also developed synthetic routes for their production, enabling controlled scientific research into their properties.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Psilocybin mushrooms are a family of psychoactive fungi containing the tryptamine prodrug psilocybin, which is converted into its active metabolite psilocin after ingestion. Over 200 species have been identified across every continent, with evidence of human use predating recorded history. Their effects are often characterized as "earthy" and "dream-like" compared to other psychedelics. Wild specimens are easily mistaken for poisonous look-alikes, making proper identification essential for safety.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Physical addiction to psilocybin mushrooms has never been documented. They are not physiologically addictive and produce no physical withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Psilocybin mushrooms have virtually no psychological addiction potential. The desire to use them often decreases after use, and they are considered self-regulating. There is strong evidence of little to no potential for psychological dependence.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Adverse psychological reactions including anxiety, paranoia, delusions, and psychosis are possible, particularly among individuals predisposed to mental disorders. Psilocybin can precipitate or exacerbate latent mental illness, and risk is higher for people whose family history includes schizophrenia or early-onset mental illness. Lasting psychological problems are rare when experiences are properly managed.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Seizures are a rare effect, primarily occurring in individuals predisposed to them, particularly when in physically taxing conditions such as dehydration, malnourishment, overheating, or fatigue.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: The primary psychoactive compound in psilocybin mushrooms is psilocin, a tryptamine produced in the body from the prodrug psilocybin; other alkaloids such as baeocystin are also present. Psilocin acts as a partial agonist at several serotonin receptors, with high affinity for 5-HT2A. Activity at 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT1A receptors is believed central to its psychoactive effects, with 5-HT2A agonism considered necessary for hallucinogenic activity. Psilocin has no significant effect on dopamine receptors and only engages the noradrenergic system at very high dosages. Functional neuroimaging has shown psilocybin to dampen activity in certain brain regions, most notably the default mode network.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Psilocybin is pharmacologically inactive and serves as a prodrug for psilocin. Upon ingestion, psilocybin undergoes dephosphorylation to psilocin in the intestinal mucosa by alkaline phosphatase and nonspecific esterases, with additional conversion occurring in the liver.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Approximately 7 days to return to baseline tolerance levels. Some sources suggest spacing use 5-7 or more days apart to avoid diminished effects.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Psilocybin tolerance begins building very soon after ingestion. Because of this rapid tolerance, full effects are generally not repeatable more often than every 4-7 days unless the dose is increased substantially.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text:
Archaeological and artistic evidence suggests that psychoactive mushrooms have been used by humans in ceremonial contexts for thousands of years. Murals discovered in the Sahara desert of southeastern Algeria, dated to approximately 9000-7000 BCE, depict horned figures in dancer's garb holding objects resembling mushrooms. In Spain, pictographs estimated to be 6,000 years old were found near the town of Villar del Humo, illustrating what researchers have tentatively identified as Psilocybe hispanica, a hallucinogenic species native to the Iberian Peninsula.

The depth of mushroom use in Mesoamerican cultures is particularly well-documented through archaeological artifacts and colonial-era records. Various scholars have interpreted Mexican artifacts as evidence of ceremonial and ritual use by Mayan and Aztec civilizations spanning approximately 3,000 years. The Aztecs referred to psilocybin mushrooms as "teonanácatl" in Nahuatl, meaning "flesh of the gods" or "divine mushroom."

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: When Spanish explorers arrived in the New World during the sixteenth century, chroniclers documented the ceremonial use of mushrooms by indigenous populations. These accounts describe mushrooms being consumed during festivals celebrating the accession of emperors and marking successful trading expeditions by merchants. The Florentine Codex, compiled by Franciscan missionary Bernardino de Sahagún, provides detailed Aztec-language descriptions of the mushrooms and their ritual use, noting their intoxicating effects and capacity to produce visions. Dominican friar Diego Durán similarly recorded that mushrooms were ingested at festivals, often prepared with chocolate. Following their conquest of the Aztec Empire, Spanish colonial authorities moved to suppress indigenous religious practices they deemed pagan idolatry, including ceremonial mushroom use. The Spanish Inquisition brutally enforced prohibitions against traditional mushroom rituals. Despite this suppression, the mushroom cult survived underground for four centuries, with indigenous communities in remote regions continuing their practices in secret.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Contemporary ethnographic research has documented surviving traditions among the Mazatec, Mixe, Zapotec, and Cuitlatec peoples. Among the Mixe of Oaxaca, mushrooms hold particular significance in relation to Naaxwin, the Earth Mother deity regarded as omniscient and the source of all wisdom. Because mushrooms emerge from the earth, they are considered repositories of profound knowledge. Traditional preparation involves placing collected mushrooms on household altars or storing them in village churches for three days while offering incense, with practitioners observing dietary and sexual abstinence before consumption.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Mesoamerican Traditions and Colonial Suppression

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: The ritual use of psilocybin mushrooms in indigenous shamanic practice was rediscovered by Western researchers at the end of the 1930s. American banker and amateur ethnomycologist R. Gordon Wasson conducted fieldwork studying the ceremonial mushroom practices of Mazatec communities in Mexico. In 1957, Wasson published "Seeking the Magic Mushroom" in Life magazine, becoming the first person in modern times to document and publish a first-person account of the psychedelic experience. Wasson's Life article generated significant scientific interest. French mycologist Roger Heim accompanied Wasson on subsequent expeditions, identifying several of the ceremonially used species as belonging to the Psilocybe genus. Heim successfully cultivated the mushrooms in France and sent specimens to Albert Hofmann at Sandoz Pharmaceuticals in Switzerland for chemical analysis.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Hofmann, who had synthesized LSD in 1938, led the research team that isolated and identified psilocybin and psilocin as the psychoactive compounds in Psilocybe mexicana. His laboratory subsequently synthesized numerous structural analogs to study how molecular modifications affected psychoactivity, including 4-HO-DET and 4-AcO-DMT. Sandoz marketed pure psilocybin commercially under the trade name "Indocybin," distributing it to clinicians and researchers worldwide without reports of serious complications.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: In the early 1960s, Harvard University became a significant center for psilocybin research through the Harvard Psilocybin Project, led by Timothy Leary alongside associates Ralph Metzner and Richard Alpert. Leary obtained synthesized psilocybin directly from Hofmann through Sandoz. Studies conducted under this project, including the Concord Prison Experiment, produced promising results regarding psilocybin's potential applications in clinical psychiatry. However, Leary and Alpert's increasingly fervent public advocacy for widespread hallucinogen use attracted controversy and culminated in their well-publicized termination from Harvard. Growing concerns about unauthorized recreational use of psychedelics among the general public generated negative media coverage and prompted legislative responses.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: In 1966, the United States enacted laws prohibiting the production, trade, and consumption of hallucinogenic substances. Sandoz ceased manufacturing LSD and psilocybin that same year. The backlash against LSD swept psilocybin along with it into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act in 1970. These restrictions severely hampered human research with psychedelic substances, as funding became difficult to secure and scientists working in the field faced professional marginalization. Despite prohibition, interest in psilocybin mushrooms persisted in countercultural circles. Terence McKenna's "Psilocybin Magic Mushroom Grower's Guide" appeared in 1976, followed by Paul Stamets' "Psilocybe Mushrooms & Their Allies" in 1978, providing practical cultivation information to the general public.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: Academic Research and the Prohibition Era

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text:
Psychedelic research gradually regained momentum beginning in the 1990s, particularly in European academic institutions. Advances in neuroscience methodology and the development of brain imaging technologies provided new scientific rationales for investigating substances like psilocybin. Researchers recognized these compounds as valuable tools for probing the neural mechanisms underlying psychotic symptoms, ego disturbances, and hallucinations.

A notable cultural adaptation occurred in the Netherlands following the October 2007 announcement prohibiting psilocybin mushrooms, which took effect in December 2008. The ban did not extend to psilocybin-containing sclerotia, as authorities considered them weaker than fruiting bodies. These "magic truffles," which had previously generated minimal commercial interest, became the only legal option and subsequently emerged as a significant alternative in Dutch smart shops.

chunks.title: Psilocybin Mushrooms
chunks.text: American banker and self-taught ethnomycologist whose fascination with mushrooms began in 1927 during his honeymoon with Russian physician Valentina Pavlovna. Wasson conducted extensive fieldwork in Mexico studying the ceremonial mushroom practices of Mazatec communities. His 1957 Life magazine article "Seeking the Magic Mushroom" introduced the Western public to psilocybin mushrooms and became one of the most influential pieces of psychedelic journalism, catalyzing scientific interest and subsequent research.

chunks.text: French mycologist who accompanied Wasson on expeditions to Mexico following the Life magazine publication. Heim provided crucial scientific expertise in identifying the ceremonially used mushrooms as Psilocybe species and successfully cultivated them in laboratory conditions in France, enabling the subsequent chemical analysis that would identify psilocybin.

chunks.text: Swiss chemist at Sandoz Pharmaceuticals who had previously synthesized LSD in 1938. Upon receiving mushroom specimens from Heim, Hofmann led the research team that isolated and identified psilocybin and psilocin as the active compounds in Psilocybe mexicana. His laboratory synthesized numerous structural analogs to investigate structure-activity relationships, and he oversaw the commercial production of psilocybin under the trade name Indocybin.

Leary obtained research-grade psilocybin from Hofmann through Sandoz and conducted studies including the Concord Prison Experiment. His increasingly public advocacy for widespread psychedelic use led to his dismissal from Harvard and contributed to the political backlash that culminated in prohibition. Leary became both a countercultural icon and lightning rod for criticism of the psychedelic movement.

chunks.text: Poppy seed tea is an opioid preparation brewed from the straw, pods, or seeds of Papaver somniferum. It contains a mixture of opiate alkaloids—primarily morphine and codeine—and has been used traditionally across Central and Eastern Europe, the Near East, and parts of Central and South Asia for millennia. PST poses serious overdose risks due to highly inconsistent alkaloid concentrations between batches, and multiple fatalities have been reported.

chunks.title: PV-8
chunks.text: PV-8 is a synthetic stimulant of the pyrrolidinophenone class, structurally related to α-PHP as a higher homologue. It is classified as a research chemical with limited documentation regarding its effects and safety profile. Compared to α-PHP, PV-8 is reportedly less potent and produces diminished effects. As with other pyrrolidinophenone stimulants, it is considered habit-forming, and users should exercise particular caution given the scarcity of available research.

chunks.title: PVT
chunks.text: α-PVT is a synthetic stimulant of the cathinone and thiopropamine classes, first identified in Japan in 2013 as a designer drug. It is a structural analogue of α-PVP in which the phenyl ring is replaced by a thiophene group. α-PVT is considered rare and reportedly less potent than its parent compound. Very limited human data exists, and it has demonstrated high cytotoxicity against human cell lines, warranting particular caution.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: Pyrazolam is a research chemical depressant of the triazolobenzodiazepine class. Originally developed at Hoffmann-La Roche in the 1970s, it emerged on the research chemical market around 2012. Pyrazolam is distinguished from other benzodiazepines by its predominantly anxiolytic profile, producing comparatively less sedation and euphoria at common doses. It is structurally related to alprazolam and bromazepam and is notably reported to pass through the body unmetabolized.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use. Withdrawal following a few weeks or longer of steady dosing can be potentially life-threatening, with symptoms including hypertension and seizures; abrupt discontinuation after extended use may result in death. Gradual tapering over weeks is strongly recommended.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: Pyrazolam is described as extremely psychologically addictive, with compulsive redosing commonly reported as a cognitive effect. However, its comparatively limited sedative and euphoric effects relative to other benzodiazepines may somewhat reduce recreational appeal and abuse potential.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: While benzodiazepines have anticonvulsant properties during use, abrupt discontinuation after regular use can cause potentially fatal seizures. Paradoxical seizure reactions during use are rare in the general population, with an incidence rate below 1%, occurring more frequently in epileptics and high-dosage regimes.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: Tolerance typically returns to baseline within 7-14 days after cessation, though this period may be significantly longer for individuals with extended or intensive use histories.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text: Sedative-hypnotic tolerance can appear after only a few days of uninterrupted use.

chunks.title: Pyrazolam
chunks.text:
Pyrazolam was originally developed during the 1970s by a research team led by Leo Sternbach at Hoffman-La Roche, the pharmaceutical company responsible for discovering many clinically significant benzodiazepines. Despite its initial synthesis during this prolific period of benzodiazepine research, pyrazolam was never pursued for clinical development or pharmaceutical marketing.

The compound remained obscure for several decades until it was "rediscovered" and began appearing on the online research chemical market around 2012. The first official analytical report identifying pyrazolam as a novel substance originated from Finland in 2011, with subsequent reports emerging from the United Kingdom in 2012. Since its emergence, pyrazolam has become established as one of several designer benzodiazepines circulating within the research chemical community, valued particularly for its reported anxiolytic selectivity relative to other effects typical of the benzodiazepine class.

Pyrazolam — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol (Ethanol ingestion may potentiate the CNS effects of many benzodiazepines. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.)
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Opioids (Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)
- Tramadol (Central nervous system- and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. Vomit aspiration is a risk when passed out, lay down in recovery position if ingested.)

While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely. Low medical doses are unlikely to be of concern.)

chunks.title: Pyrophenidone
chunks.text: Pyrophenidone is a synthetic stimulant and pyrovalerone derivative that acts as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI). It is a research chemical reported to produce subjective effects similar to those of pyrovalerone. There is extremely limited information available regarding its pharmacology, toxicity, and safety profile, and it is considered to carry habit-forming potential. Thorough independent research is strongly recommended before considering any interaction with this substance.

chunks.title: Quazepam
chunks.text: Quazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine derivative developed by the Schering Corporation in the 1970s and first approved for medical use in 1985. It is prescribed for the treatment of insomnia. Quazepam is notable among benzodiazepines for its selective affinity for α1 subunit-containing GABAA receptors, giving it a pharmacological profile similar to zolpidem and zaleplon, with relatively fewer muscle-relaxant properties and less overdose potential than other benzodiazepines.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Quetiapine is a second-generation atypical antipsychotic of the dibenzothiazepine class, structurally related to clozapine. Developed by AstraZeneca and first approved by the FDA in 1997, it is prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and as an adjunct in major depressive disorder. It is also widely used off-label for insomnia, anxiety, and other conditions. While recreational use is uncommon, reports of misuse have emerged, primarily driven by its sedative and anxiolytic properties.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with continued use, and withdrawal symptoms may occur after abrupt cessation following several weeks of steady dosing. Gradual tapering is recommended to avoid acute withdrawal syndrome. Withdrawal symptoms include nausea, vomiting, sweating, lightheadedness, insomnia, nervousness, anxiety, tachycardia, and dyskinesia.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Limited abuse potential exists, primarily in individuals with a history of polysubstance abuse or mental illness, and especially in incarcerated settings where access to other intoxicants is restricted. Abuse is driven by sedative and anxiolytic effects rather than antipsychotic properties. Drug-seeking behaviors have been documented, including prisoners threatening legal action or self-harm when faced with discontinuation.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: As an antipsychotic, quetiapine treats rather than induces psychosis. However, occasional reports of drug-induced mania or hypomania exist. Discontinuation may result in rebound psychosis or recurrence of the underlying condition being treated.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: May lower the seizure threshold, though a clinical trial with 3,700 patients did not demonstrate an increased rate of seizures. Seizures are more commonly associated with overdose situations and may occur when combined with other drugs that lower seizure threshold.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Chronic use is associated with QT interval prolongation and an increased risk of sudden cardiac death, with risk being dose-dependent; low doses under 75 mg daily show minimal increase while higher doses approach risk levels of first-generation antipsychotics.

chunks.title: Quetiapine

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Quetiapine is a multi-receptor antagonist with its strongest binding affinities at histamine H1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, followed by serotonin 5-HT2A and dopamine D2 receptors. It additionally acts as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors while antagonizing several other serotonin subtypes (5-HT2B, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3, 5-HT6, 5-HT7), all five dopamine receptor subtypes (D1 through D5), alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Its pharmacological profile is dose-dependent: at low doses it functions primarily as an antihistamine and alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, moderate doses incorporate serotonin receptor antagonism, and higher doses recruit dopamine D2 antagonism. Relative to its other principal targets, quetiapine has comparatively low D2 affinity, dissociates rapidly from the D2 receptor, and achieves only approximately 30% D2 occupancy at therapeutic doses.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Quetiapine is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with peak plasma concentrations reached within 1 to 2 hours. Its absolute oral bioavailability is reported as low, and plasma protein binding is approximately 83%. Hepatic metabolism proceeds primarily via CYP3A4, with CYP2D6 playing a secondary role, through sulfoxidation and oxidation pathways. The principal active metabolite, norquetiapine (N-desalkylquetiapine), reaches roughly one-third the peak concentration of the parent compound and exhibits potent norepinephrine transporter inhibition that may contribute to antidepressant effects. The elimination half-life of quetiapine is approximately 6 to 7 hours, while norquetiapine has a longer half-life of 9 to 12 hours. Excretion occurs primarily via the kidneys (73%) and feces (20%), with less than 1% appearing as unchanged drug.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: Quetiapine was developed by the pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca during the mid-1980s through the 1990s as part of efforts to improve upon first-generation antipsychotic medications. The compound received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in September 1997 and was subsequently marketed under the brand name Seroquel. Within a decade of its initial approval, quetiapine had received regulatory authorization in over 80 countries worldwide.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text:
Quetiapine quickly became one of the most commercially successful psychiatric medications globally. By 2007, it was among the ten top-selling drugs worldwide alongside other second-generation antipsychotics. Annual sales reached approximately $5.7 billion globally, with roughly half of that revenue coming from the United States market alone.

The original U.S. patent was set to expire in 2011 but received a pediatric exclusivity extension that pushed expiration to March 2012. Following patent expiration, generic formulations became widely available. Despite increased competition from generics, quetiapine remained the most frequently prescribed second-generation antipsychotic in the United States by 2013, with over 14 million prescriptions dispensed that year. As of 2023, it ranked as the 65th most commonly prescribed medication in the country with more than 10 million annual prescriptions.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text: In 2010, AstraZeneca agreed to pay a $520 million settlement to resolve allegations of improper marketing practices and mishandling of clinical trial data. Internal company communications revealed that the manufacturer had suppressed and misrepresented research findings showing quetiapine lacked superior efficacy compared to older first-generation antipsychotic medications. Similar concealment occurred with studies demonstrating significant risks of obesity and weight gain. The company also reportedly resisted requests from the FDA to inform prescribing physicians about diabetes risks that were greater than previously acknowledged.

chunks.title: Quetiapine
chunks.text:
While recreational use remains relatively uncommon compared to other psychoactive substances, reports of quetiapine misuse have emerged in medical literature. This pattern appears driven primarily by the drug's sedative and anxiolytic properties rather than its antipsychotic effects, with individuals seeking it for sleep induction or general calming.

Non-medical use has been particularly noted within correctional settings. Some estimates suggest that a substantial proportion of inmates presenting with psychiatric complaints in certain facilities may be attempting to obtain quetiapine through feigned symptoms. The prevalence of misuse in prisons compared to community settings is attributed to quetiapine's availability as a regularly prescribed sedative within these institutions, combined with the general unavailability of more commonly sought substances behind bars.

chunks.title: Rilmazafone
chunks.text: Rilmazafone is a water-soluble prodrug developed by the pharmaceutical company Shionogi. Though not itself a benzodiazepine—lacking the characteristic fused benzene-diazepine ring structure—it is metabolized in the body by aminopeptidase enzymes into active benzodiazepine metabolites, principally rilmazolam, which produce sedative and hypnotic effects. It is prescribed in Japan for the treatment of insomnia. Rilmazafone has been identified as a new psychoactive substance in the U.S. and Europe.

chunks.title: Risperidone
chunks.text: Risperidone is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic of the benzisoxazole class. Developed in the late 1980s and approved for medical use in 1993, it is prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and irritability associated with autism. It functions primarily as a dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptor antagonist. Risperidone is sometimes used to attenuate the effects of serotonergic psychedelics. Serious adverse effects include tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and significant weight gain.

chunks.title: Rolicyclidine
chunks.text: Rolicyclidine is a dissociative anesthetic closely related to phencyclidine (PCP). It produces similar dissociative, anesthetic, and hallucinogenic effects but is slightly less potent and notably less stimulating. Its character has been described as more sedative, with qualities sometimes compared to barbiturates or other central nervous system depressants. Rolicyclidine has never been widely used and remains largely obscure. Combination with other CNS depressants should be avoided.

chunks.title: Ronlax
chunks.text: Ronlax is a brand name for ethyl loflazepate, a benzodiazepine derivative designed as a prodrug for its active metabolite descarboxyloflazepate. It possesses anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties, with a notably long elimination half-life. The substance is commercially available in several countries including Mexico, France, Belgium, and Portugal. Deaths from therapeutic doses have been reported in elderly patients due to benzodiazepine-related asphyxia.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvia divinorum is a plant species in the sage genus native to the cloud forests of Oaxaca, Mexico, containing the potent compound salvinorin A. Used traditionally by Mazatec shamans for spiritual healing and divination, it produces short but intense dissociative and hallucinogenic effects when smoked or chewed. Salvinorin A is the most potent naturally occurring hallucinogen and is structurally unique among psychoactive compounds, being a diterpenoid rather than an alkaloid. High doses can produce bizarre, potentially terrifying experiences.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: No evidence of physical dependence or withdrawal symptoms has been documented with salvia use.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvia divinorum does not appear to produce psychological dependence or compulsive redosing patterns. The often challenging and dysphoric nature of the experience may actually discourage repeated use.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvia can produce intense, bizarre, and otherworldly experiences that may be extremely confusing or terrifying, particularly at higher doses. Users commonly report panic, fear, paranoia, and a sense of encountering hostile or sinister presences. These acute psychological effects typically resolve as the short-acting substance wears off. One controversial case has been cited linking salvia use to depression and subsequent suicide, though no other cases have been reported alleging salvia as a serious factor in suicide or death.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvinorin A, the principal psychoactive constituent of Salvia divinorum, is a structurally unique trans-neoclerodane diterpenoid that acts as a potent and selective κ-opioid receptor agonist. Unlike classical hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, and mescaline, salvinorin A has no action at the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor. Research indicates it is also a potent D2 receptor partial agonist, which may contribute significantly to its effects. The compound additionally shows activity at CB1 cannabinoid receptors, particularly in inflamed gut tissue where it exhibits antispasmodic properties through a prejunctional mechanism. Salvinorin A is notable for being the most potent naturally occurring hallucinogen by mass, with activity at doses as low as 200 μg, and is the first documented diterpene hallucinogen. It contains no nitrogen atoms, distinguishing it structurally from alkaloid-based opioid receptor ligands and other naturally occurring hallucinogens.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvinorin A is present in dried Salvia divinorum plant material at approximately 0.18% concentration. The compound is synthesized and excreted by the plant via peltate-glandular trichomes located in the subcuticular layer. When consumed orally through chewing fresh leaves, effects develop over 10 to 20 minutes, suggesting slower absorption compared to other routes. The duration of effects varies with the method of ingestion and the amount of salvinorin A absorbed.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text:
Salvia divinorum is native to the Sierra Mazateca in Oaxaca, Mexico, where it has been used by the Mazatec people primarily to facilitate shamanic visions in the context of curing and divination. The Mazatec see the plant as an incarnation of the Virgin Mary and begin their rituals with invocations to Mary, Saint Peter, the Holy Trinity, and other saints. Traditional ritual use involves being in a quiet place after ingestion of freshly harvested leaves—the Mazatec shamans say that "La Maria speaks with a quiet voice."

Beyond its visionary applications, the plant is also used in smaller amounts as a diuretic and to treat various ailments including diarrhea, anemia, headaches, rheumatism, and a semi-magical disease known as panzón de borrego (swollen belly). The history of the plant remains unclear, with speculation ranging from it being a wild plant native to the area, a cultigen developed by the Mazatecs, or a cultigen introduced by another Indigenous group. Botanists have been unable to determine whether it is a hybrid or a cultigen.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Salvia divinorum was first recorded in print by Jean Basset Johnson in 1939 while studying Mazatec shamanism. He later documented its use and reported its effects through personal testimonials. However, botanical identification proved difficult for many years due to Mazatec secrecy about growing sites, as flowers were needed for definitive species identification. In 1962, Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann and ethnomycologist R. Gordon Wasson traveled throughout the Sierra Mazateca researching Mazatec rituals while searching for specimens. They were initially unable to locate live plants, but eventually the Mazatec provided them with flowering specimens. These were sent to botanists Carl Epling and Carlos D. Játiva, who described and named the plant as Salvia divinorum in reference to its use in divination and healing. Hofmann later objected to this naming, noting that "Salvia divinorum means 'Salvia of the ghosts,' whereas Salvia divinatorum, the correct name, means 'Salvia of the priests.'" Nevertheless, the name Salvia divinorum remains in botanical literature due to priority rules. By 1985, up to fifteen populations of the plant had been located.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Gordon Wasson tentatively postulated that the plant could be the mythological pipiltzintzintli, the "Noble Prince" of the Aztec codices. This speculation has been debated among ethnobotanists, with some skepticism from Leander J. Valdés and counterpoints more supportive of Wasson's theory from Jonathan Ott. The identity of another mysterious Aztec entheogen, poyomatli, has also been suggested as possibly being Salvia divinorum.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text:
The psychoactive mechanism of salvinorin A was not identified until 2002, when Bryan Roth and his team elucidated how the compound produces its effects. Following this, Salvia divinorum became increasingly known in modern Western culture. According to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, approximately 1.8 million persons aged 12 or older in the United States had used Salvia divinorum in their lifetime by 2006, with roughly 750,000 having done so that year. By 2007, the annual figure had risen to approximately 1 million US users.

A survey of salvia users found that 38% described the effects as unique compared to other methods of altering consciousness, while 23% compared the effects to yoga, meditation, or trance states.

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: Interest in Salvia divinorum escalated dramatically in Western news media during the late 2000s, particularly in the United States. Media coverage frequently raised alarms over salvia's legal status, comparing it to LSD or describing it as "the new pot," with particular focus on use by younger teenagers. Headlines often included danger-oriented language such as "Dangerous Herb is Legal" or "Deadly Dangers Of A Street Legal High." A particular focus of US media coverage was the case of Brett Chidester, a 17-year-old Delaware student who died by suicide in January 2006. His parents argued that salvia-induced depression was largely responsible for his death, pointing to earlier writings about his salvia experiences that suggested he thought "existence in general is pointless." Some media stories presented these earlier experience reports as if they were part of his suicide note, though the actual role of the drug in the incident remained unclear. Delaware subsequently passed legislation classifying salvia as a Schedule I controlled substance, nicknamed "Brett's law."

chunks.title: Salvia
chunks.text: In 2007, videos appeared on YouTube showing alleged salvia users laughing uncontrollably and apparently unable to perform simple tasks or communicate. Salvia researcher Daniel Siebert criticized these videos in an interview with the San Francisco Chronicle, stating they "make salvia look like some horrible drug that makes people nuts and dangerous" and prevent people from realizing "there are sensible ways to use something like this."

chunks.text: Swiss chemist best known for synthesizing LSD, Hofmann traveled with Gordon Wasson to the Sierra Mazateca in 1962 to research Mazatec rituals and collect plant specimens. He later expressed dissatisfaction with the botanical naming of the species, preferring the grammatically correct 'Salvia divinatorum' over the accepted 'Salvia divinorum.'

chunks.title: Salvinorin-B-Methoxymethyl-Ether
chunks.text: Salvinorin B methoxymethyl ether is a semi-synthetic κ-opioid receptor agonist derived from salvinorin B, itself obtained from the naturally occurring salvinorin A found in Salvia divinorum. It is approximately five times more potent than salvinorin A in animal studies and exhibits a notably longer duration of action. Developed primarily as a scientific research tool, it has an extremely limited history of human use and its safety profile remains largely uncharacterized.

chunks.title: SAM-e
chunks.text: SAM-e is a naturally occurring cosubstrate involved in methyl group transfers throughout the body, first discovered by Giulio Cantoni in 1952. Sold as a dietary supplement or prescription drug depending on jurisdiction, it is primarily used as a nootropic for mood support, with reviews suggesting antidepressant efficacy comparable to tricyclic antidepressants. Notable safety concerns include the potential to trigger manic episodes and the risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic medications.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Scopolamine is a naturally occurring tropane alkaloid found in plants of the Solanaceae family, including Datura species, where it serves as the primary psychoactive compound. Structurally related to atropine and hyoscyamine, it acts as a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist. While medically approved for the prevention of motion sickness and postoperative nausea, recreational doses produce intense deliriant hallucinations. Medium to high doses carry significant adverse effects, and extreme caution is strongly advised.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop with chronic therapeutic use. Withdrawal symptoms include nausea, dizziness, vomiting, gastrointestinal disturbances, sweating, headaches, bradycardia, hypotension, and various neuropsychiatric manifestations. Severe symptoms may require medical attention.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Psychological addiction potential is minimal due to the typically unpleasant nature of the experience. Recreational use is rare as effects are often described as mentally and physically distressing rather than rewarding.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Scopolamine is formally classified as a deliriant and can exacerbate psychosis and cause psychiatric reactions including hallucinations, confusion, agitation, and restlessness. Mass hospitalizations for psychosis have occurred following ingestion of scopolamine-containing substances; more than 20 people were hospitalized with psychosis in Norway in 2008 after ingesting counterfeit tablets containing scopolamine.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Seizures and seizure-like activity are documented neuropsychiatric effects but are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients at therapeutic doses. Convulsions have been reported in overdose cases.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Plants naturally containing scopolamine, including Atropa belladonna (deadly nightshade), Brugmansia (angel's trumpet), Datura (jimsonweed), Hyoscyamus niger, Mandragora officinarum, Scopolia carniolica, Latua, and Duboisia myoporoides, have been recognized and utilized for various purposes in both the New and Old Worlds since ancient times, and possibly since prehistory. Throughout history, these scopolamine-containing plants have been employed psychoactively for spiritual and magical purposes. In western culture, they were particularly associated with witchcraft, where preparations were made into topical ointments—most notably the legendary "flying ointment." In these entheogenic preparations, scopolamine was considered the primary psychoactive compound responsible for hallucinogenic effects. Indigenous groups throughout the Americas, including Native American tribes such as the Chumash, similarly employed these plants in their spiritual practices.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Biblical texts contain multiple references to mandrake, a psychoactive and hallucinogenic plant root containing scopolamine. The plant was associated with fertility and sexual desire, featuring prominently in the story of Rachel, who sought the root while struggling with infertility.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text:
Scopolamine was officially isolated in 1880 by the German scientist Albert Ladenburg, making it one of the earlier alkaloids to be purified from plant sources. The compound was first described in scientific literature in 1881. Following its isolation, scopolamine became available in various purified salt forms, including hydrochloride, hydrobromide, hydroiodide, and sulfate preparations.

Medical applications developed rapidly. In 1899, Dr. Schneiderlin recommended the combination of scopolamine and morphine for surgical anesthesia, and the practice began seeing sporadic use. The application to obstetric anesthesiology was first proposed by Richard von Steinbuchel in 1902. Carl Gauss at Freiburg, Germany took up this work beginning in 1903, developing and refining the technique. The method, which exploited the drug synergy between scopolamine and morphine, became known as "Dämmerschlaf" (twilight sleep) or the "Freiburg method." This approach remained widely used in the United States until the 1960s, when growing chemophobia and a cultural shift toward more natural childbirth led to its abandonment.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Scientific Discovery and Early Medical Applications

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Aboriginal peoples of the eastern Australian states had developed a traditional bush medicine from the soft corkwood tree (Duboisia myoporoides). This preparation was employed by the Allied forces during World War II to prevent seasickness among soldiers crossing the English Channel during the Invasion of Normandy. The substance was subsequently found to be useful in the production of both scopolamine and hyoscyamine, which found applications in eye surgery. This discovery led to the establishment of a multimillion-dollar pharmaceutical industry in Queensland based on the cultivation and processing of Duboisia.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text: Military Applications and Australian Industry

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text:
Scopolamine was first synthesized in 1959, though extraction from plant sources has remained more efficient than synthesis to the present day. The compound received its first FDA approval on December 31, 1979, and is currently available in both oral tablet and transdermal formulations.

Due to its dose-dependent adverse effects, scopolamine became the first drug to be commercially offered as a transdermal delivery system when Scopoderm TTS was introduced in 1981. This innovation in drug delivery helped manage the compound's side effect profile while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. The medication appears on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, and as of 2023, it ranked as the 69th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States with more than 9 million prescriptions annually.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text:
The effects of scopolamine were investigated for potential use as a truth serum in interrogation settings during the early 20th century. However, these investigations were ultimately abandoned due to the compound's significant side effects, which compromised the reliability of any information obtained.

Despite the formal discontinuation of such research, documented cases of governmental use have emerged. In 2009, evidence confirmed that the Czechoslovak state security secret police had employed scopolamine on at least three occasions to extract confessions from individuals accused of antistate dissent.

chunks.title: Scopolamine
chunks.text:
Powdered scopolamine has acquired the street name "devil's breath" and has become associated with criminal activity, particularly robbery and assault. The highest documented prevalence of misuse occurs in Colombia, where unofficial estimates suggest approximately 50,000 scopolamine-related incidents occur annually.

A 2012 travel advisory issued by the U.S. Overseas Security Advisory Council warned travelers about the criminal use of scopolamine in Colombia, noting that the substance is most commonly administered to victims in liquid or powder form through contaminated foods and beverages. In popular media and television, scopolamine has been portrayed as a method to brainwash or control individuals, facilitating fraud and other crimes against incapacitated victims.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate that produces potent anxiolytic, hypnotic, muscle relaxant, and amnesic effects. Marketed under the brand name Seconal by Eli Lilly, it is used medically for the short-term treatment of insomnia and as an emergency anticonvulsant. Compared to longer-acting barbiturates, it is distinguished by its rapid onset, typically taking effect within fifteen minutes. It is classified as habit-forming and is internationally scheduled as a controlled substance.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with extended use. Barbiturate withdrawal is medically serious and can cause a life-threatening syndrome with symptoms including anxiety, insomnia, decreased appetite, tremors, seizures, and potentially death.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital is considered extremely psychologically addictive, with a particularly high risk of abuse and addiction even among barbiturates. It was widely abused recreationally in the 1960s-1980s before being largely replaced by benzodiazepines due to its high abuse potential.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Delusions and confusion may occur during overdose. Psychosis is a documented risk during barbiturate withdrawal syndrome and may accompany life-threatening withdrawal symptoms.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: While barbiturates have anticonvulsant properties during use, abrupt discontinuation in dependent individuals can cause life-threatening seizures. Drugs that lower seizure threshold should be avoided during withdrawal. Switching to a longer-acting barbiturate such as phenobarbital may be beneficial for managing withdrawal.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Studies have linked the use of barbiturates, particularly phenobarbital, with the development of cancer, though evidence specific to secobarbital is limited.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABA-A receptor, binding at the barbiturate site associated with the chloride ionophore. This interaction increases the duration for which the chloride channel remains open, prolonging the inhibitory effect of GABA. Secobarbital also displays antagonist activity at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α4 and α7 subtypes) and at several ionotropic glutamate receptors, including AMPA, kainate, and NMDA subtypes.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital is metabolized primarily by hepatic microsomal enzymes, with metabolic products excreted in the urine and less commonly in the feces. Approximately 45-60% of the drug binds to plasma proteins. The elimination half-life ranges from 15 to 40 hours.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Potentiates α1, α2, α3, α4, α5, and α6 subunit-containing receptors

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: The exact timeframe for tolerance to return to baseline is unknown.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Tolerance to the sedative-hypnotic effects develops after prolonged use. The rate of tolerance development varies between individuals and depends on frequency and dosage of use.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital was first developed in Germany in 1914 as part of ongoing barbiturate research. Eli Lilly and Company subsequently patented the compound in the United States in 1934 and later introduced it to the American pharmaceutical market in 1959 under the brand name Seconal. The drug was initially indicated for the treatment of insomnia. Eli Lilly also marketed a combination product called Tuinal, which contained both secobarbital and amobarbital.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Secobarbital became widely abused for recreational purposes throughout the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. The drug's distinctive bright orange-red bullet-shaped capsule, marketed by Eli Lilly under the proprietary name Pulvule, gave rise to numerous street nicknames including "reds," "red devils," "red dillies," "seccies," "Cardinals," "ruby slippers," and "red hearts." A less common nickname, "dolls," was partly responsible for the title of Jacqueline Susann's novel Valley of the Dolls, whose main characters use secobarbital and similar drugs. Among barbiturates, secobarbital carries a particularly high risk of abuse and addiction, and accidental overdoses were commonly associated with the drug during this period. Several notable figures allegedly died by suicide or accidental overdose involving secobarbital, including actresses Carole Landis, Judy Garland, and Lupe Vélez, playwright Tennessee Williams, table tennis champion Ruth Aarons, and journalist Dorothy Kilgallen.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: The drug was also associated with several significant historical events. In 1969, secobarbital was allegedly used to sedate Black Panther leader Fred Hampton before he was killed during a police raid on December 4th. Following the 1978 mass deaths at Jonestown, approximately 1,000 pills of Seconal were recovered at the Peoples Temple settlement along with substantial quantities of other sedatives and analgesics. Prescription use began declining in the early 1980s as benzodiazepines emerged as safer alternatives for sedation and sleep, and secobarbital's high abuse potential became a primary factor in its diminishing medical role.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text:
Secobarbital has found contemporary application as an agent in medical-assisted dying and palliative sedation. In the Netherlands, individuals seeking euthanasia may orally consume 100 mL of concentrated syrup containing either 15 grams of pentobarbital or 15 grams of secobarbital.

In the United States, secobarbital and pentobarbital became the most commonly prescribed drugs under physician aid-in-dying laws, beginning with Oregon in 1998, followed by Washington in 2008 and Vermont in 2013. Canada authorized secobarbital for physician-assisted dying in 2017.

chunks.title: Secobarbital
chunks.text: Ranbaxy Pharmaceuticals obtained the rights to market Seconal from Eli Lilly in 1998 and maintained the brand until September 2008. During Marathon Pharmaceuticals' subsequent ownership of the brand, the company substantially increased the drug's price. By February 2015, when Marathon sold the rights to Valeant Pharmaceuticals, the average retail price per 100 mg capsule had risen from approximately one dollar to over thirty dollars. Bausch Health, the company formerly known as Valeant, ceased manufacturing Seconal in January 2022.

- Germany: Anlage III BtMG — Listed in Anlage III of the Betäubungsmittelgesetz (Narcotics Act). Requires a special narcotic prescription form (Betäubungsmittelrezept) for medical dispensing.

- Switzerland: Verzeichnis B — Specifically named controlled substance under Verzeichnis B of Swiss narcotics legislation. Medicinal use is permitted with appropriate authorization.

- United States: Schedule II — Controlled under the Controlled Substances Act. Schedule II classification indicates high abuse potential with accepted medical use under severe restrictions. Marketed as Seconal Sodium for treatment…

chunks.title: Sentia
chunks.text: Sentia is a commercial non-alcoholic botanical spirit launched in 2021, developed by Professor David Nutt and GABA Labs. Marketed as an alternative to alcohol, it contains a proprietary blend of botanical and spice extracts — including damiana, hawthorn, tulsi, gentian, and 5-HTP — selected for their purported activity on the GABA system. Its effects are reported as subtle and mild, producing gentle relaxation without notable impairment, roughly comparable to a small amount of alcohol.

chunks.title: Sentia
chunks.text:
Legal status of Sentia by country:
- United Kingdom: Apparently lawful under cited legislation — The cited text says UK restrictions do not appear to apply because the ingredients are already permitted as foods or supplements.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Sertraline is an antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class, sold under brand names including Zoloft and Lustral. Developed by Pfizer and approved for medical use in 1991, it is prescribed for major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Sertraline became one of the most commonly prescribed psychotropic medications worldwide and is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with regular use, and discontinuation syndrome is common in medical settings. Withdrawal symptoms typically appear within a few days of stopping or reducing dose and include flu-like symptoms, dizziness, electric shock sensations, anxiety, insomnia, irritability, and headache. Symptoms usually resolve within 1-3 weeks, though a minority experience prolonged or severe symptoms lasting more than 6 weeks. Restarting the medication can usually eliminate withdrawal symptoms within 24 hours.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Sertraline is not considered to have significant abuse potential or psychological addiction liability. It does not produce euphoria or reinforcing effects that typically drive compulsive use patterns.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Rare reports of psychotic symptoms including auditory hallucinations and paranoid ideation have been documented. Mania and hypomania have been reported relatively rarely, including in children and adolescents, sometimes triggered by doses as low as 25-50 mg daily. Hallucinations and delirium have been observed in overdose cases and as part of serotonin syndrome.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Seizures are listed among manifestations of acute overdose but appear to be uncommon. In documented overdose cases involving very high doses, seizures were not a prominent feature, with most symptomatic patients experiencing only mild effects.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — lethal dosage — notes
chunks.text: The drug is largely safe in fairly large overdose. No cases of fatal overdose with sertraline alone have been reported; most fatal cases involve co-ingestion with other drugs. Analysis of 52 sertraline-only overdoses with a mean dose of 727 mg showed no significant symptoms in 34 cases, with symptomatic patients experiencing only mild CNS, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal effects. Another analysis of 40 overdoses with doses up to 8000 mg found that among 17 sertraline-only ingestions, 10 were asymptomatic. The manufacturer reported ingestions up to 2600 mg in four patients with suicidal intent, all requiring minimal treatment.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare cases of hepatotoxicity have been reported, typically presenting as elevated transaminases, jaundice, and fatigue; this appears to be an idiosyncratic reaction occurring in a very small proportion of users regardless of dose, though doses over 100 mg may carry slightly higher risk.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Hypothesized to be immunologic in nature. In vitro studies suggest mitochondrial permeability transition pore induction via adenine nucleotide translocase as a potential mechanism, leading to ATP depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: A premarketing study showed 0.8% of participants had elevations in serum transaminase by the first week, gradually returning to normal upon drug withdrawal. Typically the drug has no effect on liver function or such a minimal effect that discontinuation is not warranted. Fatal hepatotoxicity has been reported in at least one case involving a patient with history of alcohol abuse. Non-fatal cases generally resolve upon discontinuation.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Cardiovascular effects are generally less problematic than with tricyclic antidepressants; tachycardia is the primary effect seen during overdose, and ECG changes have occasionally been recorded. Hypotension may occur transiently when treatment first begins but appears quite rare.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: In vitro studies show inhibition of cardiac ion channels including hERG with an IC50 of 0.7 μM, which is close to mean peak plasma concentrations at 200 mg daily dosing.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Sertraline use during the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with a 2.7-fold increase in septal heart defects in offspring, with an overall 29-42% increase in congenital heart defects among children whose mothers were prescribed sertraline during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Gastrointestinal effects including nausea and diarrhea are common adverse effects; the incidence of diarrhea is higher with sertraline compared to other SSRIs, especially at higher doses.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Sertraline appears to be associated with microscopic colitis, a rare condition of unknown etiology. Rare cases of pancreatitis have been reported but not definitively connected to sertraline.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare reports of abnormal bleeding have been documented; SSRIs inhibit serotonin uptake into platelets, significantly reducing platelet serotonin concentrations and impairing aggregation.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Inhibition of serotonin reuptake transporters on platelets reduces serotonin concentrations, which plays an important role in platelet aggregation.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The risk of problematic bleeding responses is still low but should be considered, particularly when combined with antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulants.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that acts primarily by binding to the serotonin transporter (SERT), inhibiting neuronal reuptake of serotonin and potentiating serotonergic activity in the central nervous system. The therapeutic benefits typically emerge after 4-6 weeks of administration, believed to result from neuroadaptations including downregulation of presynaptic 5-HT1A autoreceptors and downstream increases in brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression. Sertraline also displays affinity for sigma-1 receptor binding sites and exhibits relatively high activity as a dopamine transporter inhibitor, occupying approximately 20% of DAT receptors at doses of 200mg and above, though the clinical relevance of these secondary actions remains uncertain. The drug shows weak inhibitory effects on norepinephrine reuptake and has been observed to increase extracellular dopamine in the nucleus accumbens and striatum at clinically relevant doses in animal studies.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Sertraline exhibits little to no affinity for GABA, histamine, acetylcholine, benzodiazepine, or serotonergic receptors (5-HT1A, 5-HT1B, 5-HT2), and does not exert significant anticholinergic, antihistamine, or adrenergic blocking activity.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Sertraline undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, with bioavailability estimated above 44%. The primary metabolic pathway is N-demethylation to desmethylsertraline (N-desmethylsertraline), which is substantially weaker (5-50 fold less potent) as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor. CYP2C19 appears to play the most important role in metabolism, followed by CYP2B6, with additional contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Secondary metabolic pathways include N-hydroxylation, oxidative deamination, and glucuronide conjugation. Sertraline is highly plasma protein bound (98-99%) and widely distributed with a volume of distribution exceeding 20 L/kg. Excretion occurs to similar degrees in urine and feces, with unchanged sertraline representing only 12-14% of fecal elimination and being undetectable in urine. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers show 2.7-fold higher sertraline levels compared to normal metabolizers.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text:
Extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver reduces the amount reaching the bloodstream
Taking with food slightly increases peak levels and total exposure
Peak blood levels occur between 4.5 and 8.4 hours after dosing

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Average elimination half-life is 26 hours with a wide range of 13 to 45 hours
Desmethylsertraline metabolite has a longer half-life of 62 to 104 hours
Steady-state concentrations reached after approximately 1 week of daily dosing
Genetic differences in CYP2C19 and CYP2B6 enzymes affect how quickly the body processes sertraline

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Therapeutic efficacy may decline over extended periods of treatment, though a useful degree of effectiveness is maintained in many patients. The risk of relapse appears to increase notably over a period of months to years of continuous use.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: The history of sertraline traces back to the early 1970s when Pfizer chemist Reinhard Sarges developed a series of psychoactive compounds, including lometraline, based on the structures of the neuroleptics thiothixene and pinoxepin. This work led to tametraline, a norepinephrine and weaker dopamine reuptake inhibitor, though its development was halted due to undesired stimulant effects observed in animal studies. In 1977, Pfizer pharmacologist Kenneth Koe became interested in the tametraline series after comparing structural features of various reuptake inhibitors. He collaborated with chemist Willard Welch to synthesize previously unexplored tametraline derivatives. While Welch produced several potent norepinephrine and triple reuptake inhibitors, one compound from the generally inactive cis-analogs unexpectedly demonstrated serotonin reuptake inhibition. Welch prepared stereoisomers of this compound, which were tested in vivo by behavioral scientist Albert Weissman. The most potent and selective (+)-isomer was selected for further development and eventually named sertraline.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: The discovery was largely serendipitous. Weissman and Koe later recalled that the group had not set out to produce an SSRI-type antidepressant, describing their inquiry as not "very goal driven." According to Welch, the team worked outside the mainstream at Pfizer and "did not have a formal project team." They faced initial bureaucratic resistance to pursuing sertraline development, as Pfizer was considering licensing an antidepressant candidate from another company. The compound was patented by Pfizer in 1979.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Throughout the 1980s, in vitro and in vivo research demonstrated that sertraline was an effective serotonin uptake blocker with good oral bioavailability. Studies confirmed the compound was largely devoid of non-serotonin actions and did not inhibit monoamine oxidase. Human tolerance studies showed that doses up to 400 mg per day could be tolerated, and the substance produced fewer side effects than tricyclic antidepressants.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text:
Sertraline was approved in the United Kingdom in 1990. The following year, the US Food and Drug Administration approved it based on the recommendation of the Psychopharmacological Drugs Advisory Committee, which reached consensus that sertraline was safe and effective for treating major depression. However, the approval was not without controversy. Paul Leber, director of the FDA Division of Neuropharmacological Drug Products, noted that granting approval was a "tough decision" since the treatment effect on outpatients with depression had been "modest to minimal." Other experts criticized the poor design of Pfizer's clinical trials, noting that the drug's effect on inpatients had not differed from placebo and that approximately 40% of participants had dropped out of the trials.

Sertraline entered the US market in February 1992 under the brand name Zoloft. During the early part of its commercial history, it was one of only a few SSRIs available, alongside fluoxetine, paroxetine, and fluvoxamine.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text:
Until 2002, sertraline was approved only for adults aged 18 and over. That year, the FDA approved its use for treating children aged 6 or older with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder. In 2003, the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency issued guidance that, apart from fluoxetine, SSRIs were not suitable for treating depression in patients under 18, though sertraline could still be used in the UK for OCD in children and adolescents.

In 2005, the FDA added a boxed warning concerning pediatric suicidal behavior to all antidepressants, including sertraline. In 2007, labeling was changed again to include a warning regarding suicidal behavior in young adults ages 18 to 24. During this period, many health professionals remained unaware of some problematic aspects of the drug, particularly its withdrawal symptoms, which contributed to a lack of knowledge among patients as well.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text:
By approximately 2005, sertraline was generating annual revenue of $2 to $3 billion. The US patent for Zoloft expired in 2006, after which sertraline became available as a generic medication and has since been marketed under numerous brand names worldwide.

Sertraline became the most commonly prescribed psychotropic medication in the United States by 2016. In 2013, it was the most popular antidepressant in the US with over 40 million prescriptions, making it the second most popular psychiatric medication overall. By 2023, it was the eleventh most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 42 million prescriptions. The drug also ranks among the top 10 most prescribed medications in Australia between 2017 and 2023. Sertraline is included on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: Commercial Success and Generic Availability

chunks.title: Sertraline
chunks.text: According to Google Trends data, sertraline has been the most sought-after antidepressant worldwide before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic led to increased searches for antidepressants generally, with sertraline, fluoxetine, duloxetine, and venlafaxine showing the highest search volumes.

chunks.title: Sildenafil
chunks.text: Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor originally researched as a treatment for angina before its erectile function-enhancing properties were serendipitously discovered in the late 1980s. Approved for medical use in 1998 and widely known by the brand name Viagra, it is primarily prescribed for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Co-administration with nitrates or alkyl nitrites (poppers) is contraindicated due to the risk of potentially fatal hypotension.

chunks.title: Sildenafil
chunks.text:
Legal status of Sildenafil by country:
- Canada: Prescription medicine — Canadian sildenafil products include prescription tablets, and Canadian product-monograph indications are documented.
- United States: FDA-approved medicine — In the United States, sildenafil has an FDA indication for pulmonary arterial hypertension in adults.

chunks.title: Sinicuichi
chunks.text: Sinicuichi (Heimia salicifolia) is a flowering plant of the Lythraceae family, native to the Americas from the southwestern United States through Central America to Argentina. It has a history of shamanic use among indigenous peoples of Central America and Mexico, traditionally prepared by fermenting wilted leaves in sun-exposed water. Its primary alkaloid is vertine (cryogenine). Reported effects are mainly auditory in nature, though its psychoactivity remains disputed.

chunks.title: Sonata
chunks.text: Zaleplon is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic of the pyrazolopyrimidine class, sold under the brand name Sonata. It is primarily prescribed for the short-term treatment of insomnia in adults. Although chemically unrelated to benzodiazepines, it shares similar pharmacological properties through its interaction with the GABA receptor complex. Zaleplon is notable for its exceptionally short half-life of approximately one hour. It should not be combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Sonata
chunks.text:
Legal status of Sonata by country:
- United States: Schedule IV — Zaleplon is a U.S. Schedule IV drug and has a DEA number.

chunks.title: Sufentanil
chunks.text: Sufentanil is a synthetic opioid analgesic of the anilidopiperidine class, first synthesized at Janssen Pharmaceutica in 1974. It is considered the most potent opioid painkiller approved for human use, estimated at 500 to 1,000 times the potency of morphine and approximately 5 to 10 times that of fentanyl. Primarily employed in surgical anesthesia and post-operative pain management, sufentanil carries a significant risk of life-threatening respiratory depression.

chunks.text: µ-opioid receptor agonist (full, highly selective)
