chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone is an antidepressant of the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) class, chemically classified as a triazolopyridine derivative. First approved by the FDA in 1981, it is primarily indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder. Trazodone is notable for its pronounced sedative and anxiolytic properties, which have led to widespread off-label use for insomnia and anxiety disorders. Its antidepressant efficacy is considered comparable to that of TCAs, SSRIs, and SNRIs.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone shares properties with SSRIs including the possibility of discontinuation syndrome if stopped too quickly. Gradual tapering is recommended when discontinuing treatment.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone is not associated with abuse potential or recreational use. No reports of compulsive use patterns or psychological dependence have been documented.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: The unmasking of bipolar disorder and mania may occur with trazodone and other antidepressants. No specific psychotic symptoms documented beyond manic episodes.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone is classified as an agent that reduces seizure threshold. Patients with seizure disorders or risk factors should be monitored.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias have been reported with trazodone therapy, including in patients without pre-existing cardiac disease; identified arrhythmias include isolated PVCs, ventricular couplets, and short episodes of ventricular tachycardia.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Not recommended during initial recovery phase of myocardial infarction. Patients with pre-existing cardiac disease should be closely monitored. Concomitant administration of drugs that prolong QT interval or inhibit CYP3A4 may increase arrhythmia risk. In a fatal overdose case, torsades de pointes and complete atrioventricular block developed.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Rare cases of liver toxicity have been observed, possibly due to the formation of reactive metabolites.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Priapism is a relatively rare but serious side effect that can cause permanent neurological damage if left untreated; the risk appears greatest during the first month of treatment at low dosages.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: More than 200 cases have been reported. Manufacturer estimates incidence of any abnormal erectile function at approximately 1 in 6,000 male patients. Patients must seek immediate medical attention if priapism is suspected. Clitoral priapism and spontaneous orgasms have also been reported in women.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Memory, alertness, and cognition may be decreased, especially in elderly patients due to CNS depressant effects; sedation commonly occurs and may impair ability to operate machinery or drive.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Studies on cognitive function are mixed, with some finding improvement, others finding no change, and some finding impairment. Compared to moclobemide, more impairment of vigilance occurs with trazodone.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Trazodone is associated with an increased risk of falls and hip fractures in older adults, likely related to sedation and orthostatic hypotension.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Orthostatic hypotension may cause dizziness and increase falling risk, with potentially devastating consequences for elderly patients.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Elevated prolactin concentrations have been observed in people taking trazodone, appearing to increase by approximately 1.5- to 2-fold.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone functions primarily as a serotonin receptor antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI). Its most prominent action is potent antagonism of the 5-HT2A receptor, with roughly half of brain 5-HT2A receptors occupied at doses as low as 1 mg and near-complete saturation at 10 mg. It also antagonizes 5-HT2B receptors and acts as a partial agonist at the 5-HT1A receptor, while binding to the 5-HT2C receptor with lower affinity. Trazodone inhibits the serotonin transporter, with SERT occupancy estimated at approximately 86% at 100 mg/day. It additionally blocks α1- and α2-adrenergic receptors and weakly antagonizes histamine H1 receptors, while lacking affinity for muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Trazodone is well-absorbed after oral administration, with a bioavailability of approximately 65 to 80%. Absorption is somewhat delayed and enhanced by food, though food may sometimes decrease peak blood levels. The drug is 89 to 95% protein-bound with a volume of distribution of 0.8 to 1.5 L/kg. It undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism through hydroxylation, N-oxidation, and N-dealkylation. CYP3A4 mediates N-dealkylation to produce the active metabolite m-chlorophenylpiperazine (mCPP), while CYP2D6 contributes to hydroxylation of the meta-chlorophenyl ring. Elimination is biphasic, with an initial distribution phase half-life of 3 to 6 hours and a terminal elimination half-life of approximately 5 to 9 hours. Roughly 70 to 75% of trazodone is excreted renally, about 21% via feces, and less than 1% as unchanged drug in urine.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Near-complete receptor saturation at 10 mg

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Estimated occupancy of 86% at 100 mg/day and 90% at 150 mg/day

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Reported as both agonist and antagonist across sources

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text:
Food may enhance overall absorption but can decrease peak blood levels
Bioavailability has been reported as 65 to 80% in some reviews and 63 to 91% in others

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text:
Peak blood levels occur 1 to 2 hours after ingestion
Elimination follows a two-phase pattern with an initial distribution phase of 3 to 6 hours
Terminal elimination half-life has been reported as approximately 7.3 hours
Extended-release formulations have a longer elimination half-life of 9.1 to 13.2 hours
Peak levels of the active metabolite mCPP occur 2 to 4 hours after ingestion

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text:
Trazodone was developed in Italy during the 1960s by Angelini Research Laboratories as a second-generation antidepressant. Its development was guided by the mental pain hypothesis, a theory derived from clinical observations proposing that major depression is associated with a decreased pain threshold. In contrast to most antidepressants available at the time, trazodone demonstrated minimal effects on muscarinic cholinergic receptors, distinguishing it pharmacologically from its predecessors.

The drug was patented and marketed internationally, beginning with Italy in 1972 and West Germany in 1977. In 1981, trazodone received approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration, becoming the first antidepressant approved in the country that was neither a tricyclic nor a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. The medication has since become widely prescribed, ranking as the 21st most commonly prescribed medication in the United States by 2023 and the fifth most common antidepressant, with over 24 million prescriptions annually.

chunks.title: Trazodone
chunks.text: Within recreational psychedelic communities, trazodone has gained recognition as a "trip killer"—a medication employed to attenuate or terminate unwanted psychedelic experiences. By 2024, it had been recommended for this purpose 77 times on the social media platform Reddit, with suggested doses ranging from 50 to 150 mg. Among substances discussed for trip termination, trazodone ranked among the most frequently recommended, exceeded only by alprazolam, benzodiazepines as a class, and quetiapine.

chunks.text: Binding profile: 5-HT2A receptor antagonist; Serotonin reuptake inhibitor; 5-HT1A receptor agonist (partial); 5-HT2B receptor antagonist; 5-HT2C; Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist; Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist; Histamine H1 receptor antagonist

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine of the triazolobenzodiazepine subclass, primarily used as a hypnotic agent for the short-term management of insomnia. It is distinguished by its notably brief half-life compared to many other benzodiazepines and does not produce active metabolites. At higher doses, it may induce significant amnesia and lowered inhibitions. Like all benzodiazepines, triazolam carries a risk of habit formation and dependence.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: With long-term use, triazolam is associated with tolerance and physical dependence. Discontinuation may lead to withdrawal, ranging from uncomfortable symptoms to a severe syndrome with stomach cramps, vomiting, muscle cramps, sweating, tremor, and, rarely, convulsions. Rebound insomnia may occur even after short-term, single-dose therapy.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam is classified as habit-forming and susceptible to misuse and abuse. Its rapid onset of action and short half-life contribute to its abuse potential, though its relative obscurity compared to other fast-acting benzodiazepines limits diversion for recreational use.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam was withdrawn in the United Kingdom due to risk of psychiatric adverse drug reactions, particularly at higher dose ranges. Delirium, confusion, and amnesia have been reported. Abnormal dreams or nightmares occur rarely.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Seizures are listed as a potential symptom of overdose. Withdrawal from triazolam may cause convulsions in rare cases, particularly following abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use of triazolam may cause cognitive impairment, anterograde amnesia, daytime sedation, and motor incoordination; residual hangover effects including psychomotor impairment may persist into the next day even after single doses.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: The elderly are particularly susceptible to these effects. Falls and hip fractures are frequently reported, especially in elderly persons. Partial but incomplete tolerance develops to balance and steadiness impairments.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Triazolam is FDA Pregnancy Category X and has the potential to cause birth defects when used during pregnancy.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Alpha-hydroxytriazolam (active, minor clinical significance)

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam acts as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine binding site, enhancing the inhibitory effects of GABA by increasing its affinity for the receptor. This promotes chloride ion conductance and neuronal hyperpolarization, reducing cellular excitability. Triazolam also interacts with the translocator protein (TSPO) as a modulator.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam is lipophilic and undergoes hepatic metabolism via oxidative pathways. Oral bioavailability is approximately 44%, while sublingual administration achieves approximately 53%. The drug and its metabolites are excreted primarily in the urine as conjugated glucuronides, with only small amounts of unmetabolized triazolam appearing in urine. The two primary metabolites account for roughly 80% of urinary excretion.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.section: Pharmacology — route half life notes — Oral
chunks.text: Half-life estimates include approximately 2 hours and a range of 1.5 to 5.5 hours

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Tolerance to the sedative and hypnotic effects of triazolam develops with repeated use, typically within days to weeks of continuous administration. As with other benzodiazepines, tolerance to different effects may develop at varying rates, with partial but incomplete tolerance reported for certain effects such as balance and coordination impairment.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Triazolam was patented in 1970 and subsequently entered the pharmaceutical market in the United States in 1982 under the brand name Halcion. The drug gained widespread clinical adoption, and by 2017 it ranked as the 289th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States with over one million prescriptions annually. Following its market introduction, triazolam became the subject of regulatory scrutiny in several countries due to concerns about adverse psychological reactions, particularly at higher dose ranges. Some nations temporarily withdrew the drug from their markets, though subsequent review by the FDA and regulatory bodies in most other countries reaffirmed its safety profile when used at lower doses with appropriate clinical guidance and labeling.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Beyond its primary indication for insomnia, triazolam has found particular utility in specific clinical and practical contexts. It is frequently prescribed to airline passengers as a sleep aid for short- to medium-duration flights. Additionally, the drug's pronounced amnestic properties have made it a common choice in sedation dentistry, where its ability to induce anterograde amnesia helps patients undergo dental procedures with minimal subsequent recall of the experience.

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Cross-tolerant with: Benzodiazepines, Other GABAergic depressants

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text: Binding profile: GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator (benzodiazepine site); TSPO

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text:
Triazolam — dangerous combinations:
- Alcohol (Ethanol ingestion may potentiate the CNS effects of many benzodiazepines. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.)
- GHB/GBL (The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Opioids (Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely)
- Tramadol (Central nervous system- and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. Vomit aspiration is a risk when passed out, lay down in recovery position if ingested.)

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text:
Triazolam — unsafe combinations:
- Diphenhydramine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely. Low medical doses are unlikely to be of concern.)
- PCP (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely)

chunks.title: Triazolam
chunks.text:
Triazolam — caution combinations:
- DXM (Small doses of benzos can end a bad trip, but both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and this can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- Ketamine (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.)
- MXE (Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess.)

chunks.title: Troparil
chunks.text: Troparil is a phenyltropane-based stimulant and dopamine reuptake inhibitor first synthesized by Clarke and colleagues in the 1970s. Developed as a research tool for studying dopamine transporters, it produces cocaine-like stimulant effects but with a longer duration and no local anesthetic action, making it a pure stimulant with slightly less cardiotoxicity. Recreational use remains extremely rare due to the difficulty of its synthesis. The substance is reported to be painful to insufflate.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 is a synthetic opioid of the benzamide chemical class that produces analgesic, sedating, and euphoric effects. Developed by Upjohn in the 1970s through extensive structure-activity research, it demonstrates approximately 7.5 times the potency of morphine. Despite its research origins, U-47700 has very little history of human use and limited toxicity data. Reports indicate unusual caustic properties that may cause significant tissue damage, particularly when injected.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: Physical dependence can develop in a short period with chronic use. Withdrawal symptoms emerge within 2-4 hours after the last dose and can be especially painful. Cravings and withdrawal effects occur if use is suddenly stopped.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 has a high potential for abuse and is capable of causing psychological dependence. The short duration of effects combined with the addictive properties of opioids creates a strong risk of compulsive redosing.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Respiratory depression with U-47700 is reported to be significantly stronger compared to other common opioids such as heroin and morphine at relative doses; severe overdoses can result in coma or death without immediate medical attention.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Mu-opioid receptor agonism causing central respiratory depression

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: At low to moderate doses, breathing is slowed mildly to moderately. At high doses and overdoses, shortness of breath, abnormal breathing patterns, semi-consciousness, or unconsciousness may occur.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: U-47700 crystals are particularly corrosive and caustic to mucous membranes; even with regular saline washing, multiday insufflation can create bleeding sores and scabs in the septum and nasal lining that may persist for days after cessation.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — mechanism
chunks.text: Direct chemical caustic action destroying living tissue

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Vaporization can damage the lungs. Sublingual administration is likely to damage skin in the mouth. Routine maintenance such as soaking the sinus cavity with water before and after insufflation is recommended.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 is a selective agonist of the μ-opioid receptor, with approximately 7.5 to 10 times the potency of morphine in animal models despite having 2 to 4 times weaker binding affinity at all three opioid receptors. The compound possesses significantly lower affinity for the κ-opioid and δ-opioid receptors. As with other opioids, U-47700 exerts its effects by binding to and activating the μ-opioid receptor, structurally mimicking endogenous endorphins to produce analgesia, sedation, and euphoria.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 undergoes hepatic metabolism involving mono- and didesmethylation followed by hydroxylation. The desmethyl metabolites have negligible affinity for opioid receptors and are not thought to contribute to the pharmacological activity of the parent compound.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: Tolerance to many of the effects of U-47700 develops with prolonged and repeated use. The rate at which this occurs varies for different effects, with tolerance to constipation-inducing effects developing particularly slowly compared to other effects. This results in users needing to administer increasingly large doses to achieve the same effects.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text:
U-47700 was developed by a research team at the Upjohn pharmaceutical company during the 1970s. The compound emerged from extensive work elucidating the quantitative structure-activity relationship of the benzamide scaffold. Upjohn researchers systematically identified the key functional groups that produced the greatest opioid activity, filing over a dozen patents on related compounds as they optimized each moiety. This iterative process ultimately determined that U-47700 was the most active compound in the series.

The substance is a structural isomer of the earlier opioid AH-7921. While U-47700 itself was never developed for medical use, its structure served as the foundation for subsequent research into selective kappa-opioid receptor ligands. Compounds derived from this work include U-50488, U-51754 (which contains a pyrrolidine rather than a dimethylamine substituent), and U-69,593. These selective kappa ligands continue to be used in pharmacological research.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 emerged on the gray-market research chemical scene and became available through online vendors. The substance acquired several street names including "pinky," "pink," "pink heroin," and "U4." Very little was known about its toxicity profile in humans at the time of its emergence, as it had minimal history of human use prior to its appearance in the research chemical market.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text:
The use of U-47700 became associated with numerous overdose deaths internationally. Combined consumption of U-47700 with fentanyl caused a fatality in Belgium, while another death in Germany involved the combination of U-47700 with fentanyl and flubromazepam. Additional fatalities were reported in Ireland and Italy.

In the United States, at least 17 opioid overdoses and several deaths had been connected with U-47700 by April 2016. The number of confirmed fatalities rose to at least 15 by September 2016, and by December 2017, at least 46 deaths had been associated with the substance. Notably, U-47700 was found in combination with fentanyl during the autopsy of American musician Prince in 2016.

chunks.title: U-47700
chunks.text: U-47700 is the title of a 2021 Dutch science fiction short film directed by Erasmo de la Parra. The film depicts characters addicted to a new drug containing the substance.

chunks.title: U-51754
chunks.text: U-51754 is a potent synthetic opioid and structural analogue of U-47700. It is reported to exhibit κ-opioid receptor activity, which is suspected to produce dysphoric effects and auditory hallucinations in addition to typical opioid action. As a research chemical with limited documentation, very little is known about its safety profile, pharmacology, or long-term risks. Extreme caution is warranted due to its high potency and poorly understood effects.

chunks.title: UR-144
chunks.text: UR-144 is a synthetic cannabinoid of the tetramethylcyclopropyl indole class, developed by Abbott Laboratories in 2006 as a potential CB2-targeted medication. It produces cannabis-like effects and has been described as somewhat more psychedelic than other synthetic cannabinoids, though information about its activity remains limited. It became one of the most commonly detected synthetic cannabinoids globally by 2012. UR-144 has been associated with seizures and unconsciousness, and its frequent sale in inconsistently dosed herbal blends poses significant additional risk.

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.text: Valerylfentanyl is a synthetic opioid and depressant of the fentanyl analogue family. It is a higher homologue of butyrfentanyl, though it exhibits greatly reduced potency compared to its parent compound. Classified as a research chemical, valerylfentanyl carries the risks common to synthetic opioids, including habit-forming potential and the danger of respiratory depression associated with this class of substances.

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Potentially serious respiratory depression can occur, which may be life-threatening and is the primary cause of overdose fatalities associated with fentanyl analogues.

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.text: Valerylfentanyl is an opioid analgesic and a structural analog of fentanyl, representing a higher homologue of butyrfentanyl. In mice, it fully substituted for oxycodone and produced antinociception with a potency comparable to morphine, consistent with activity at μ-opioid receptors. It notably failed to stimulate locomotor activity in mice at doses up to 100 mg/kg.

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.text: Fully substituted for oxycodone in discriminative stimulus assays in mice

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.text: Opioids (fentanyl, morphine, oxycodone, heroin, and other μ-opioid receptor agonists)

chunks.title: Valerylfentanyl
chunks.text:
Valerylfentanyl is an opioid analgesic belonging to the fentanyl analog class of designer drugs. It has appeared on online drug markets, though it remains one of the less commonly encountered fentanyl derivatives with limited documentation in the scientific and illicit drug monitoring literature.

The substance emerged within the broader context of novel fentanyl analogs that began proliferating in illicit drug markets during the early 2000s. This trend first gained significant attention in Estonia and subsequently spread through Europe and former Soviet republics. A second major wave of fentanyl analog proliferation began around 2014 in the United States, with a marked acceleration from 2016 onward. This period saw the continuous appearance of novel derivatives as manufacturers sought to circumvent existing drug scheduling while supplying opioid markets.

chunks.title: Viloxazine
chunks.text: Viloxazine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor of the morpholine class. First described in 1972 and marketed in Europe as an antidepressant from 1974, it was withdrawn in 2002 for commercial reasons before being repurposed and approved in the United States for ADHD treatment in 2021. It produces mild amphetamine-like stimulant effects without known abuse liability and is not a controlled substance. Rarely, it may cause suicidal thoughts or activate mania in individuals with bipolar disorder.

chunks.title: W-15
chunks.text: W-15 is a synthetic opioid research chemical with a structurally distinct profile unrelated to nearly all other known opioid compounds. It is reported to be approximately 5.4 times more potent than morphine. As with other opioids, it carries significant habit-forming potential. W-15 should not be combined with other central nervous system depressants, as this combination poses serious risks of respiratory depression and overdose.

chunks.title: Yerba-Mate
chunks.text: Yerba mate is a stimulant beverage derived from the leaves of Ilex paraguariensis, a plant of the holly genus native to South America. Its primary active compounds are the xanthine alkaloids caffeine, theobromine, and theophylline. First cultivated and consumed by the indigenous Guaraní people of present-day Paraguay, it has since become a widely consumed social beverage across South America and is now found globally in various energy drinks. Drinking very hot mate has been associated with an increased risk of certain cancers.

chunks.title: Yopo
chunks.text: Yopo is a psychedelic snuff derived from the seeds of Anadenanthera peregrina, a perennial tree native to the Caribbean and South America. Its primary active constituent is bufotenin, with trace quantities of DMT and 5-MeO-DMT. Traditionally used in indigenous healing ceremonies and rituals, the seeds are toasted, ground, and insufflated — a route of administration that is notably painful. Effects onset rapidly but are characteristically short-lived, typically fading within minutes.

chunks.title: Zolazepam
chunks.text: Zolazepam is a pyrazolodiazepinone derivative structurally related to benzodiazepines, used exclusively in veterinary medicine as an anaesthetic. Developed for Parke-Davis with a patent filed in 1969, it is typically administered in combination with the NMDA antagonist tiletamine or the α2 adrenergic receptor agonist xylazine. Zolazepam is reported to possess several times the potency of diazepam and is notably water-soluble. It should not be combined with other CNS depressants.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the imidazopyridine class, first approved by the FDA in 1992 for the treatment of insomnia. It acts at the GABA-BZ receptor complex, sharing pharmacological properties with benzodiazepines while producing comparatively less anxiolysis, muscle relaxation, and anticonvulsant activity. At higher doses, zolpidem can produce realistic hallucinations resembling those of deliriants, significant amnesia, and marked disinhibition.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with prolonged use, producing withdrawal symptoms resembling benzodiazepine withdrawal. Abrupt discontinuation may cause tremors, delirium, irritability, and in severe cases, seizures. Reported cases of high-dose dependence document daily doses up to 6,000 mg, with tapering or benzodiazepine substitution typically required for discontinuation.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem misuse has been associated with dependence and addiction, often driven by its euphoric effects. A 2014 review found evidence of drug-seeking behavior, with zolpidem prescriptions making up 20% of falsified or forged prescriptions. Recreational use is more prevalent in those with a history of drug dependence, though addiction can develop in individuals without such history.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Hallucinations through multiple senses and delusions are reported, particularly at higher doses. Complex sleep behaviors with amnesia are well-documented. Delirium may occur during withdrawal from chronic use. Visual hallucinations have been noted more frequently when zolpidem is combined with antidepressants.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Seizures are primarily a withdrawal risk rather than an acute effect. Abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use or high doses may cause seizures, particularly in chronic users who have developed physical dependence. Gradual dose reduction is recommended to minimize this risk.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Two-year animal studies showed no evidence of carcinogenicity in mice; renal tumors observed in rats were attributed to spontaneous occurrence. Zolpidem showed no mutagenic activity in multiple genotoxicity assays. However, a 2017 meta-analysis of epidemiological studies found zolpidem use associated with a 34% increased cancer risk, though results were tentative due to confounding factors including smoking and alcohol use.

chunks.title: Zolpidem

chunks.text: Anterograde amnesia may occur, particularly at doses above 10 mg; a marked reduction in next-morning recall of information relayed during peak drug effect has been observed in controlled studies.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Complex sleep behaviors including sleepwalking, sleep-driving, eating, and conversations while asleep have been documented, typically occurring after the first dose or within the first few days of treatment. FDA added a black box warning in 2019 regarding serious injuries and fatalities related to these behaviors.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem acts as a positive allosteric modulator at GABAA receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site to enhance GABAergic inhibition in the central nervous system. It exhibits pronounced selectivity for GABAA receptors containing the α1 subunit, with approximately 10-fold lower affinity for α2- and α3-containing receptors and no appreciable affinity for those containing the α5 subunit. This subunit selectivity confers strong hypnotic properties with comparatively weak anxiolytic, myorelaxant, and anticonvulsant activity.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract with an absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 70%, reaching peak plasma concentrations within roughly 1.6 to 2 hours. The elimination half-life in healthy adults is approximately 2 to 3 hours. Hepatic metabolism is the primary route of elimination, predominantly via CYP3A4 (approximately 61%), with contributions from CYP2C9 (22%), CYP1A2 (14%), and minor involvement of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 (each less than 3%). Less than 1% of the drug is excreted unchanged in urine, and all three principal metabolites are pharmacologically inactive.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem demonstrates a favorable tolerability profile with low risk of tolerance development when used according to prescribing guidelines. Clinical studies have shown maintained efficacy in decreasing sleep latency for up to 35 days of continuous use.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text: Zolpidem entered clinical use in Europe in 1988 through the pharmaceutical company Synthelabo. Following its European introduction, Synthelabo collaborated with Searle to pursue regulatory approval in the United States. The FDA granted approval in 1992, and the drug was marketed under the brand name Ambien. Generic formulations became available in 2007, significantly expanding accessibility. By 2023, zolpidem had become the 54th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over 11 million prescriptions dispensed annually.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text:
Beyond its established use as a hypnotic, research has identified potential therapeutic applications for zolpidem in treating disorders of consciousness. Studies have demonstrated that the drug can rapidly and effectively restore brain function in some patients who have entered vegetative states following brain injury, potentially reversing abnormal metabolism in damaged neural tissue.

The United States Air Force has approved zolpidem as one of its authorized "no-go pills" since at least 2012. These medications are provided to aviators and special operations personnel to assist with sleep during mission preparation, though a mandatory six-hour restriction on subsequent flight operations follows use of the drug.

chunks.title: Zolpidem
chunks.text:
Zolpidem has received substantial media coverage concerning complex sleep behaviors, wherein users engage in activities such as sleepwalking or driving automobiles while not fully conscious. High-profile incidents have included a motor vehicle accident involving U.S. Congressman Patrick Kennedy and a fatal fall from the Sydney Harbour Bridge in Australia attributed to an individual reportedly using the medication.

In May 2018, television actress Roseanne Barr attributed a racist tweet comparing former Obama advisor Valerie Jarrett to an ape to the effects of zolpidem. Manufacturer Sanofi responded publicly, stating that "racism is not a known side effect" of Ambien.

Z-drugs including zolpidem have been documented in connection with drug-facilitated sexual assault. This issue received significant attention during the prosecution of former NFL safety Darren Sharper, who was accused of using his prescription tablets to incapacitate victims. Separately, use of zolpidem by Australian swimmers during the 2012 London Olympics generated controversy regarding medication use in athletic competition.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Zopiclone is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class, commonly grouped among the 'Z-drugs' that emerged in the 1980s and 1990s as treatments for insomnia. First introduced by Rhône-Poulenc in 1986, it acts on the GABA-benzodiazepine receptor complex despite being structurally unrelated to benzodiazepines or barbiturates. Zopiclone is reported to produce hallucinogenic effects when taken without the intent to sleep and is considered habit-forming. A persistent metallic taste is a commonly noted side effect.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Physical dependence develops with prolonged use, even at therapeutic doses. Withdrawal symptoms similar to benzodiazepine withdrawal can occur even after gradual dose reduction, including significant agitation and anxiety that may require emergency medical attention. Convulsions are not typical at therapeutic doses and withdrawal is not considered life-threatening.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Zopiclone has significant potential for psychological dependence, with cases of addiction and habituation well-documented. Compulsive redosing and blackouts are reported, and animal self-administration studies suggest high reinforcing potential. Some evidence suggests it may be more addictive than benzodiazepines. Those with a history of substance misuse or mental health disorders are at increased risk.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Hallucinations, confusion, nightmares, and paradoxical effects are reported rarely. Hallucinogenic effects may occur if the drug is taken while attempting to stay awake rather than for sleep.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Withdrawal symptoms from therapeutic doses do not typically present with convulsions and are therefore not considered life-threatening in this regard.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — findings
chunks.text: Long-term use has been associated with cognitive impairment including anterograde amnesia; impairments in body balance, standing steadiness, and motor coordination occur during intoxication and may persist the following day, with only partial tolerance developing to these effects over time.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.section: Harm potential — toxicity — organ toxicity — notes
chunks.text: Falls and hip fractures are frequently reported and are a significant cause of death in elderly users. Motor vehicle accident risk increases by approximately 50% even at prescribed doses, with impaired driving persisting after one year of use. Alcohol significantly increases these impairments.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Zopiclone acts as a positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site on receptor subtypes containing α1, α2, α3, and α5 subunits. It functions as a full agonist at this site, enhancing the inhibitory actions of GABA at the chloride channel complex. Although one study found slight selectivity for the α1 and α5 subtypes, zopiclone is generally regarded as unselective across the four GABA-A subtypes it binds. It also shows agonist activity at the translocator protein.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Zopiclone is rapidly absorbed after oral administration with a bioavailability of approximately 75–80% and peak plasma concentrations within 1–2 hours. Plasma protein binding is weak, averaging 52–59%. It is extensively metabolized in the liver through decarboxylation (roughly 50% of a dose, with decarboxylated products excreted via the lungs), demethylation, and side chain oxidation. CYP3A4 and CYP2E1 have been identified as the principal hepatic enzymes involved, while hepatic microsomal enzymes have also been described as not significantly involved in clearance. The two major metabolites are N-desmethylzopiclone, which has been variably reported as pharmacologically active (with partial agonist and predominantly anxiolytic properties) or as inactive, and zopiclone-N-oxide, which has been described as both weakly active and inactive. The elimination half-life averages approximately 5 hours, ranging from 3.5 to 6.5 hours.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: Zopiclone was developed by the French pharmaceutical company Rhône-Poulenc S.A. and first introduced to the market in 1986. Rhône-Poulenc has since become part of Sanofi, which remains the primary global manufacturer. Upon its release, zopiclone was marketed as offering improvements over benzodiazepines for treating insomnia, though subsequent meta-analyses have found it comparable to benzodiazepines across all assessed parameters. The substance remained unscheduled in the United States until April 4, 2005, when the Drug Enforcement Administration placed it under Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act, citing evidence of addictive properties similar to those of benzodiazepines. Zopiclone as marketed globally is a racemic mixture containing two stereoisomers, of which only one possesses pharmacological activity. In 2005, the same year as federal scheduling, the Massachusetts-based pharmaceutical company Sepracor began marketing the active stereoisomer separately as eszopiclone under the brand name Lunesta in the United States. This development effectively placed what functions as a generic medication in most countries under new patent protection within the American market.

chunks.title: Zopiclone
chunks.text: In France, zopiclone ranks among the ten most commonly obtained medications through fraudulent prescriptions, indicating significant diversion from legitimate pharmaceutical channels.
